# Theory of Valid Three-by-Three Magic Squares of Squares

28 September 2026

## Abstract

A valid magic square of squares is a $3\times3$ magic matrix of nine distinct positive integer squares. This article gives exact rational and integral formulations, effective restrictions on specified arithmetic strata, and computer-assisted exclusions of rational families. **No valid square, global nonexistence theorem, or absolute denominator bound is obtained.** Every statement retains its arithmetic domain and quantifiers.

The five-square formulation defines a genus-forty-nine fibration covering the full nondegenerate problem. Its generic curve has exactly 128 boundary points over both $\mathbb Q(m)$ and $\mathbb C(m)$. Every allowed rational specialization has precisely these 128 degenerate points; any additional rational point would give a valid square. The test fibers $m=2$, $m=4$ and $m=5$ are completely determined and have no additional points, by exact elliptic descents, coupled height identities, whole-disk $13$-adic, $31$-adic and $7$-adic arguments and final coefficient sieves. The $m=4$ proof retains an actual specialized rank increase in one stable factor. The $m=3$ fiber follows from $m=2$ by parameter symmetries. Generic classification and a fixed-fiber theorem do not determine the remaining rational specializations.

The geometric rational curves are now completely classified. An explicit nonzero regular quartic symmetric differential on the smooth resolution has an integrable equation. Its first integral reduces every rational plane image to a short list of lines and conics; necessary genus-one double covers exclude every nonboundary full-root lift. Exact branch normalizations then show that the projective surface has precisely 128 geometrically rational curves, all rational conics over $\mathbb Q$ lying in the repeated-entry boundary. The resolution has these strict transforms and 256 exceptional rational curves, hence 384 in total. Thus no nondegenerate rational family exists in any degree, even geometrically. This curve classification does not exclude isolated rational points or classify genus-one curves. The same quartic is proved nonzero on every genus-one normalization, which must therefore be immersed in the resolution. The only geometric genus-one curves with plane-image degree at most six are the sixteen central boundary components, which have no real points. The quintic exclusion retains every projective coefficient boundary and has an independent replay of all3344 finite coefficient schemes. The rational-normalization sextic exclusion exhausts1434 inertia patterns by exact twisted-cubic reconstruction and closed coefficient schemes, including every deficient reduction and all80 final degenerate pencil points. Remaining rational-normalization images have degree at least seven. A plane image whose own normalization has genus one has even degree at least eight: all degree-six square-root line-bundle configurations are excluded by independently replayed homogeneous ideal certificates. At an admissible rational point its null directions and leaf constants lie in totally real fields of degree two or four whose completions at three equal $\mathbb Q_3(\sqrt3)$; the paired direction and leaf constant generate the same field, and neither is rational. These auxiliary-field restrictions do not exclude the point.

Independent arithmetic arguments separately exclude rational families of projection degrees one through four. Their final quartic cases use four exact chord eliminants: every candidate quadratic field is split, nonreduced, or has genus $6$ or $24$, contradicting the required rational quotient field. These finite certificates remain independent checks on the low-degree cases. A separate theorem proves full parameter-image birationality for rational families; the all-degree differential proof does not require that theorem.

The full-root curve has geometric and rational-function-field gonality sixteen, including every allowed rational fiber. Effective divisors of degree at most fifteen are unique in their classes. The genus-five center has gonality four, five elliptic components of tetragonal pencils, and exact arithmetic Jacobian $\mathbb Z^5\oplus\mathbb Z/4\oplus(\mathbb Z/2)^6$. Its degree-32 primitive isogeny, rational kernel, squareclass image and divisor representatives are explicit. The four cross-pair elliptic factors now have complete generic group $\mathbb Z^2\oplus\mathbb Z/2$, with a proved primitive basis and height matrix $\operatorname{diag}(4,2)$. The eight triple factors have complete generic group $\mathbb Z^2\oplus\mathbb Z/2$ and primitive height matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}3&-1\\-1&3\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. Consequently the genus-seventeen noncentral Jacobian has exact generic rank twenty-nine. The full genus-forty-nine Jacobian has zero constant trace; its complete integral lattice and effective height bounds remain uncomputed. On every rational base cover, the old offset elliptic group remains saturated and acquires no new torsion, so any additional family must contribute an independent section.

The varying-base arithmetic retains specialized rank jumps. A uniform dyadic and odd-prime descent restricts the indexed common Kummer covers; the remaining alternatives require specified rank gains or lift to two explicit genus-three quotient types. The latter have exact maps, compatible Kummer classes, point-independent height bands and effective divisibility bounds under their stated rank hypotheses. In one remaining orbit, every odd valuation of $1+m^2$ is even, and the normalized base lies on a Pythagorean conic. A necessary genus-five four-square cover has only its eight infinity points over that entire rational function field, through an exact rank-zero and torsion calculation. Further covers and isolated specialized fibers can still acquire points. At every normalized base in this remaining orbit, a rank-independent all-place descent now gives an explicit finite set of connected genus-129 twists. Odd-prime cluster constraints, real signs and a dyadic linear test restrict the constants; dyadic depth two for the other parameter requires a prime congruent to five modulo eight in the integer hypotenuse of the base. A further direct Kummer argument forces every prime of both integer hypotenuses to be congruent to one modulo eight, and both normalized dyadic depths to be at least three. The restored central radical gives an explicit genus-seventeen intermediate curve and a complete genus-193 single-factor lift. Two root-sign-invariant half classes now have exact formulas in the integer coordinates of both parameters; after dividing by the base hypotenuse, their positive squarefree representatives are coprime. A nonsquare first half class forces a specified elliptic rank increase, while rank one forces a square divisibility condition on the other parameter. A base-dependent Legendre-symbol matrix can now force that same divisibility without any rank hypothesis; full column rank is an explicit sufficient condition, not a uniform theorem for every base. Independently of these orbit restrictions, the original four edge radicals force the two quartic parameter integers to have identical prime-power parts at every prime congruent to seven modulo eight. Their common part squared divides the product of the four boundary factors. Every nonboundary point must introduce a prime congruent to one modulo eight into at least one quartic parameter integer. The retained pq branch has a further fourth-power residue restriction. The prime support and twist count still vary with the base. The complete noncentral node content is now the gcd of the two primitive edge-root products. After removing it, their residual norm has only prime factors congruent to one modulo eight. Bounded residual norm gives finitely many fixed genus-193 fibers; bounded aggregate squareclass of the twelve pair twists gives finitely many genus-three slope fibers and hence finitely many primitive squares. The unrestricted bounded-invariant finiteness statements are ineffective. At specified center-prime support, the residual-norm stratum is effectively enumerable and now has an explicit height cutoff at every orientation rank. Uniformly in the prime identities, the largest center prime times one plus the logarithm of the residual norm must grow at least on the scale of the center logarithm divided by its iterated logarithm, with constants depending on the number of center primes. Neither invariant nor the center-prime set is bounded absolutely.

The global arithmetic formulations include the two-circle completion criterion, fixed-minimum bounds, exact Gaussian denominator identities and synchronized mixed squareclasses. At fixed center-prime support, orientation rank at most three has an effective center cutoff; uniformly over prime identities it satisfies $\log c=O_s(Q^2\log^2Q)$, with $s$ the number of center primes and $Q$ their maximum. The rank-four region and the prime identities remain unbounded. Root-sign orbit norms and complementary products are uniformly nonintegral, but this does not bound their denominators. The admissible open surface has an exact infinite Brauer--Manin characterization whose intersection remains unevaluated. Intrinsic proper K3 quotients considered here have only constant rational Brauer classes.

Two complementary residual norms now give a global effective center bound. If $R$ is the reduced edge-product norm and $R_c$ the reduced corner-product norm, then $c^4<(2/15889)R^2R_c$, with no restriction on center-prime support. Fixed ordered ratios permit exact reconstruction by nested rational-square tests. Every one of the six product-ratio norms also satisfies the same explicit all-rank logarithmic height envelope; their minimum may be used. Bounded minimum gives global finiteness through the complete genus193,321 and257 signed fibers, while specified center-prime support makes that stratum effective. More generally, the second-smallest of the six norms exceeds $\sqrt6\,c$. Thus bounding any two norms gives an explicit finite center search, independently of prime support. Fixing two actual ratios leaves at most two positive product candidates, decidable by exact original-root tests. The exact product-content network also gives $c<(2985984Z_0/5)^{2/7}$ for the integer aggregate cofactor after removing central and noncentral contact squares, and $c^4<2R_{\min}^5H^4$ for the maximum exclusive product factor $H$. These retain the residual square part or exclusive factors; neither input has an absolute upper bound. These conditional bounds do not supply an absolute upper bound for any of the residual norms.

Several specified six-square constructions and common elliptic section orbits are completely excluded, with every residual root and primitive-content condition retained. Established external theorems are cited with exact coordinate correspondences. Finite computations specify complete domains, exact predicates, proper-chart coverage and independent certificates; none substitutes a height-limited search for a global conclusion.

**Keywords:** magic squares of squares; rational points; Pell equations; Gaussian integers; elliptic curves; arithmetic surfaces.

A fixed edge ratio also gives a finite list of explicit genus-three content curves. Their Jacobians have three identified elliptic factors, all of positive rank on an actual distinct point. If the two congruent-number factors have certified rank one, an explicit corrected height gives a finite p-adic locus containing the rational points regardless of the third factor’s rank. This criterion still requires certified local calculations and rational-point identification; it is not a uniform denominator bound.

## Notation and logical conventions

A square always means a square in the indicated ring or field. All integer and rational calculations are exact. The root of an entry is its nonnegative square root. The symbol $\mathbb Q^{\times2}$ denotes the nonzero rational squares. For a nonzero rational number $a$, $[a]$ denotes its squareclass in $\mathbb Q^\times/\mathbb Q^{\times2}$. For positive $a$, $\operatorname{sf}(a)$ is its positive squarefree integer representative. The valuation $v_p$ is normalized by $v_p(p)=1$. The rational height is $H(a/b)=\max(|a|,b)$ for coprime integers $a,b$ with $b>0$. Constants in $\ll_\varepsilon$ and $O_\varepsilon$ may depend on the displayed subscript; effectiveness is asserted only when an explicit construction or bound is given.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $\mathcal A(e;x,y)$ | Canonical linear magic matrix; see (1.1) |
| $c$ | Positive center root; the center entry is $c^2$ |
| $x,y$ | Canonical integral offsets, with $0<y<x$ |
| $\ell$ | Least positive root, with $\ell^2=c^2-x-y$ |
| $\alpha,\beta$ | Normalized offsets $x/c^2,y/c^2$ |
| $r,s$ | Slope and scale, $r=y/x$, $s=x/c^2$ |
| $D_i,L_i$ | Integral and normalized opposite offsets: $(x,y,x+y,x-y)$ and $D_i/c^2$ |
| $R(t)$ | Circle offset function $4t(1-t^2)/(1+t^2)^2$ |
| $H_i$ | Opposite-pair denominators; in a Pell subsection, local notation for high roots |
| $A_i$ | Opposite-pair content or deficit, as defined in (4) |
| $\mathcal O_c$ | The exact finite offset set at center root $c$ |
| $\mathscr M,\mathscr T,\mathscr S,\mathscr P$ | Exact normalized, circle, integral, and two-circle loci |
| $X$ | The projective full-root surface when used geometrically; elsewhere an elliptic abscissa |
| $\mathscr A$ | Canonical primitive arrays, identified with admissible rational points of $X$ |
| $S$ | The Gaussian orientation matrix when used with phases; elsewhere a stated finite set of primes or places |
| $P,B$ | The product of four deficits and the balanced factor in the phase theorems; defined locally |
| $\tau_m$ | Rational Cayley index of the phase character $m$ |

The letter $H$ also denotes the root hyperplane class in intersection-theoretic sections. Such local notation is specified at each use. Norms indicate their field or ring. Root-height bounds, entry-height bounds, and parameter heights are distinct.

An **exact characterization** is an equivalence with the defining magic-square conditions. A **necessary restriction** is an implication from that locus and need not be sufficient. A **family theorem** has only its specified parameter domain. A **conditional theorem** proves an implication under explicitly stated hypotheses; it does not assert that those hypotheses hold generally. **Effective finiteness** includes a computable height bound or finite determining set. A cardinality bound or an application of Faltings' theorem alone need not be effective. Computer-assisted statements are identified by finite domains, exact predicates, and recorded results; they are not replaced by conclusions drawn from a height-limited experiment.

External results are imported under the hypotheses and correspondences stated at their uses; their proofs are not reproduced. Proofs below establish the specialized deductions or exact formulations needed here. No priority claim is made. The article retains established characterizations, restrictions, and criteria with a specified implication for the admissible locus. Section 4.4 states their common formulation; each subsequent result retains its arithmetic domain and quantifiers.

## 1. Exact formulations and elementary arithmetic

The purpose of this section is to specify, without loss or duplication, the
objects under consideration.  The statements are equivalences or elementary
necessary conditions.  In particular, none of the necessary conditions is
asserted to imply the existence of a square.

### 1.1. Definitions and the linear normal form

#### Definition 1.1

A *magic square of squares* is a matrix $M=(M_{ij})\in \mathbb Z_{\geq 0}^{3\times3}$ such that:

1. every $M_{ij}$ is an integer square;
1. the nine entries are pairwise distinct;
1. the three row sums, the three column sums, and the two diagonal
   sums have one common value.

The nonnegative square roots of the entries are called its *roots*.
The square is *primitive* if the greatest common divisor of its nine
roots is $1$.  The root of the central entry is its *center root*.
Two squares are *geometrically equivalent* if they differ by an element
of the dihedral group $D_4$, acting by rotations and reflections of the array.
They are *similar* if, after such an action, the entries of one are a
positive rational square multiple of the entries of the other.

#### Lemma 1.2 (Opposite entries)

Let a $3\times3$ matrix over a field of characteristic $0$ have common row,
column, and diagonal sum $S$, and let its center be $e$.  Then $S=3e$,
and each pair of entries in positions opposite about the center has sum $2e$.

**External correspondence.** Auel–Singer [2], Section 1.1: their center root $M$ is $c$, their center entry is $e=c^2$, and their magic sum $N$ is $S=3e$.

#### Lemma 1.3 (Positivity)

Every entry of a magic square of squares is positive.

**External correspondence.** Auel–Singer [2], Lemma 1.2: distinct rational square entries give positive integer entries after clearing root denominators.

For quantities $e,x,y$ define

$$
\mathcal A(e;x,y)=
\begin{pmatrix}
e+x&e-x-y&e+y\\
e-x+y&e&e+x-y\\
e-y&e+x+y&e-x
\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{1.1}
$$

#### Proposition 1.4 (Linear normal form)

Every $3\times3$ magic matrix over a field of characteristic $0$ has the
form (1.1), uniquely in its given orientation.
Conversely, every matrix of the form (1.1) is magic,
with common sum $3e$.

**External correspondence.** This is Lucas's normal form, as recorded in [2], equation (1). In its variables $(x_L,y_L,z_L)$, take $(x_L,y_L,z_L)=(-y,-x,e)$. The resulting matrix is (1.1), in exactly the displayed orientation.

#### Proposition 1.5 (Canonical orientation and distinctness)

Every magic square of squares has a unique geometrically equivalent
orientation of the form $\mathcal A(c^2;x,y)$ satisfying

$$
c>0,\qquad 0<y<x,\qquad x+y<c^2,\qquad x\ne2y.
\tag{1.2}
$$

Conversely, under $0<y<x$, the entries of
$\mathcal A(c^2;x,y)$ are positive and distinct if and only if the last
two conditions in (1.2) hold.

**Proof.**
Under a clockwise quarter-turn, the ordered pair of upper-corner offsets
$(x,y)$ becomes $(-y,x)$; reflection in the vertical axis sends it to
$(y,x)$.  These transformations generate all signed permutations
of $(x,y)$.  Distinctness of the four corner entries implies
$x\ne0$, $y\ne0$, and $|x|\ne|y|$.  Exactly one signed permutation therefore
has $x>y>0$.

In this orientation the offsets from the center are

$$
0,\quad \pm x,\quad\pm y,\quad\pm(x+y),\quad\pm(x-y).
$$

Their largest absolute value is $x+y$, giving the positivity criterion.
The four positive offsets are distinct except possibly for
$y=x-y$, which is exactly $x=2y$.  This proves both assertions.
$\square$

#### Remark 1.6

The condition $x\ne2y$ is retained explicitly throughout.  Consequently,
the exact formulations below do not depend on a theorem excluding four
distinct rational squares in arithmetic progression.

#### Proposition 1.7 (Primitive scaling)

Every magic square of squares is uniquely a positive integer square
multiple of a primitive magic square of squares in its given orientation.
Every similarity class has exactly one primitive representative in the
canonical orientation (1.2).
Each primitive canonical representative determines exactly eight distinct
oriented matrices at each positive integer root scale.

**Proof.**
Let $d$ be the greatest common divisor of the nine positive roots.
Dividing the entries by $d^2$ produces a primitive square.  Any other such
factorization would contradict the definition of the greatest common
divisor.

Suppose two primitive squares in fixed matching orientations have root
vectors related by a positive rational factor $a/b$ with
$\gcd(a,b)=1$.  The integrality of the second root vector implies that
$b$ divides every root of the first, hence $b=1$.  Primitivity of the
second then implies $a=1$.  Proposition 1.5 gives the
claimed canonical uniqueness.  Finally, a nonidentity symmetry of the
array moves at least one cell; it cannot fix a matrix whose entries are
all distinct.  Thus every $D_4$ orbit has eight elements.
$\square$

### 1.2. An exact rational system

Write $\mathbb Q_{>0}^{\square}=\{q^2:q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\}$.
For $(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb Q^2$ set

$$
(L_1,L_2,L_3,L_4)=(\alpha,\beta,\alpha+\beta,\alpha-\beta).
$$

#### Definition 1.8

The *normalized solution set* is

$$
\mathscr M=\left\{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb Q^2:
\begin{array}{l}
0<\beta<\alpha,\quad\alpha+\beta<1,\quad\alpha\ne2\beta,\\[2pt]
1+L_i,\ 1-L_i\in\mathbb Q_{>0}^{\square}
\quad(1\le i\le4)
\end{array}\right\}.
\tag{1.3}
$$

#### Theorem 1.9 (Exact rational equivalence)

There is a bijection between $\mathscr M$ and the primitive canonical
magic squares of squares.  The normalized matrix associated with
$(\alpha,\beta)$ is $\mathcal A(1;\alpha,\beta)$.  If $c$ is the least
common multiple of the reduced positive denominators of its eight
noncentral positive roots, its primitive integral representative is

$$
c^2\mathcal A(1;\alpha,\beta)
=\mathcal A(c^2;c^2\alpha,c^2\beta).
\tag{1.4}
$$

In particular, existence of a magic square of squares is equivalent to
$\mathscr M\ne\varnothing$.

**Proof.**
Given a primitive canonical square with center root $c$, division by $c^2$
gives a pair in (1.3); its eight positive roots are
the corresponding integer roots divided by $c$.

Conversely, a pair in (1.3) gives a positive,
distinct, rational-square matrix by Proposition 1.5.
Multiplication by the square of the stated least common multiple makes
all roots integral, including the central root $c$.  Thus the offsets
$c^2\alpha,c^2\beta$ are integers as differences of integer squares.
If the resulting roots had a common divisor $d>1$, division by $d$
would give a smaller positive integral center root with all normalized
roots still integral after multiplication.  Every reduced denominator
would then divide $c/d$, contradicting the defining minimality of $c$.
This proves primitivity.  Uniqueness follows either from this same
denominator characterization or from Proposition 1.7.
$\square$

#### Remark 1.10 (Square-root coordinates)

An equivalent system retains eight root coordinates:

$$
z_{i,+}^2=1+L_i,\qquad z_{i,-}^2=1-L_i
\qquad(1\le i\le4),
\tag{1.5}
$$

over $\mathbb Q$, together with the inequalities and noncollision condition
in (1.3).  Requiring all $z_{i,\pm}>0$ makes the
projection to $\mathscr M$ bijective.  If arbitrary nonzero signs are
allowed instead, its fibers have size $2^8$.  The polynomial equations
alone, without the specified open conditions and rationality, are not
the solution set of the integer problem.

### 1.3. Four rational circles

Define

$$
R(t)=\frac{4t(1-t^2)}{(1+t^2)^2},\qquad
\zeta_\pm(t)=\frac{1-t^2\pm2t}{1+t^2}.
\tag{1.6}
$$

The identities

$$
1\pm R(t)=\zeta_\pm(t)^2
\tag{1.7}
$$

hold identically in $\mathbb Q(t)$.

#### Lemma 1.11 (One opposite pair)

For rational $L$ with $0<L<1$, the following are equivalent:

1. $1+L$ and $1-L$ are rational squares;
1. there are positive rational $u,v$ with
   $u^2+v^2=1$ and $2uv=L$;
1. there is $t\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1)$ with $R(t)=L$.

For each such $L$ there are exactly two parameters in (3).  They are
interchanged by the fixed-point-free involution

$$
\iota(t)=\frac{1-t}{1+t}.
\tag{1.8}
$$

**External correspondence.** Conrad [26], Theorem 1.2 and equation (5.1), parametrizes $U^2+V^2=1$ by $U=(1-t^2)/(1+t^2)$ and $V=2t/(1+t^2)$. Here the opposite roots are $U+V$ and $|U-V|$, and the offset is $L=2UV=R(t)$.

#### Definition 1.12

The *four-circle parameter set* is

$$
\mathscr T=\left\{(t_1,t_2,t_3,t_4)\in
(\mathbb Q\cap(0,1))^4:
\begin{aligned}
R(t_3)&=R(t_1)+R(t_2),\\
R(t_4)&=R(t_1)-R(t_2),\\
R(t_1)&\ne2R(t_2)
\end{aligned}\right\}.
\tag{1.10}
$$

#### Theorem 1.13 (Four-circle equivalence and multiplicity)

The map

$$
\mathscr T\longrightarrow\mathscr M,\qquad
(t_1,t_2,t_3,t_4)\longmapsto(R(t_1),R(t_2))
$$

is surjective and has fibers of size $16$.  Its fibers are exactly the
orbits of the four independent involutions $t_i\mapsto\iota(t_i)$.

**Proof.**
For rational $0<t<1$, one has $R(t)>0$.  Also
$1-R(t)=\zeta_-(t)^2>0$, since the only zero of $1-t^2-2t$ in this
interval is irrational.  Therefore the equations in
(1.10) imply $0<R(t_2)<R(t_1)$ and
$R(t_1)+R(t_2)<1$.  The remaining square conditions follow from
(1.7), and the explicit noncollision condition is
preserved.  Thus the map has image in $\mathscr M$.

Conversely, apply Lemma 1.11 independently to the four
positive offsets $L_1,L_2,L_3,L_4$ of a point of $\mathscr M$.
There are two choices for each parameter and no further restriction on
these choices, because the defining equations depend only on the offsets.
This gives precisely $2^4=16$ tuples and the stated involution action.
$\square$

#### Remark 1.14 (A polynomial presentation)

Put $q_i=4t_i(1-t_i^2)$ and $h_i=(1+t_i^2)^2$, and define

$$
\begin{split}
F_+&=q_3h_1h_2-q_1h_2h_3-q_2h_1h_3,\\
F_-&=q_4h_1h_2-q_1h_2h_4+q_2h_1h_4.
\end{split}
$$

The two rational equalities in (1.10) are equivalent
over the stated domain to $F_+=F_-=0$, or equivalently to
$F_+^2+F_-^2=0$.  The last equivalence uses the ordering of $\mathbb Q$;
it does not assert an equivalence over $\mathbb C$.  The rational domain
and the noncollision condition remain part of this presentation.

### 1.4. Primitive integral coordinates and local consequences

#### Theorem 1.15 (Exact integral formulation)

The primitive canonical squares are in bijection with the integer triples
$(c,x,y)$ satisfying

$$
\begin{gathered}
c>0,\quad0<y<x,\quad x+y<c^2,\quad x\ne2y,\\
c^2\pm x,\quad c^2\pm y,\quad
c^2\pm(x+y),\quad c^2\pm(x-y)
\text{ are integer squares},\\
\gcd(c,x,y)=1.
\end{gathered}
\tag{1.11}
$$

The corresponding matrix is $\mathcal A(c^2;x,y)$.

**Proof.**
The normal form, positivity, distinctness, and the square conditions have
already been established.  It remains to verify the stated primitivity
criterion.

If a prime $p$ divides all nine roots, it divides $c$, and $p^2$ divides
the difference between any entry and the center.  In particular,
$p\mid x,y$.  Conversely, if $p\mid c,x,y$, then every entry in
(1.1) is divisible by $p$.  An integer square divisible
by a prime has its root divisible by that prime.  Thus $p$ divides all
nine roots.  The existence of a prime divisor of one of these common
divisors is consequently equivalent to that for the other, proving

$$
\gcd(c,x,y)=1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\gcd(\text{the nine roots})=1.
$$

This establishes the theorem.  No equality of the two greatest common
divisors is needed or asserted.
$\square$

#### Proposition 1.16 (Parity and center-prime restrictions)

For every triple in (1.11), all nine roots are odd,
every prime divisor of $c$ is congruent to $1$ modulo $4$, and

$$
24\mid x,\qquad24\mid y.
\tag{1.12}
$$

In particular, $\gcd(c,6)=1$ and $c\equiv1\pmod4$.

**External correspondence.** The primitive parity and center-prime restrictions are recorded in Boyer's research resource [31]. Its linear coordinates $(x_B,y_B,z_B)$ correspond to $(c^2,x,y)$ here: $x_B$ is the center entry, not its root. Its primitive-entry congruence $1\pmod{24}$ is exactly (1.12) together with $c^2\equiv1\pmod{24}$.

For the remainder of this section write

$$
(D_1,D_2,D_3,D_4)=(x,y,x+y,x-y).
\tag{1.13}
$$

#### Lemma 1.17 (One exceptional opposite pair)

If $p\mid c$ for a triple in (1.11), then at most
one of $D_1,D_2,D_3,D_4$ is divisible by $p$.  Moreover,
$p$ divides a noncentral root if and only if its opposite-pair offset is
divisible by $p$.  Consequently, such a prime divides either just the
central root or the central root and the two roots of a single opposite
pair.

**Proof.**
By Proposition 1.16, $p$ is odd.  The coefficient
vectors of the four linear forms in (1.13) are
$(1,0),(0,1),(1,1),(1,-1)$.  The determinant of any two distinct such
vectors is $\pm1$ or $\pm2$, hence is nonzero modulo $p$.
If $p$ divided two offsets, it would therefore divide both $x$ and $y$,
contrary to $\gcd(c,x,y)=1$.  Finally,
$c^2\pm D_i\equiv\pm D_i\pmod p$, so either root in that pair is
divisible by $p$ precisely when $p\mid D_i$.
$\square$

### 1.5. Unique integral data for the circle parameters

#### Lemma 1.18 (Parity normalization)

For each involution pair $\{t,\iota(t)\}$ in
Lemma 1.11, exactly one member has reduced expression
$n/m$ with

$$
m>n>0,\qquad\gcd(m,n)=1,\qquad m\not\equiv n\pmod2.
\tag{1.14}
$$

**Proof.**
If $m,n$ have opposite parity, then $m-n,m+n$ are odd and coprime,
so the reduced numerator and denominator of
$\iota(n/m)=(m-n)/(m+n)$ are both odd.  If $m,n$ are both odd,
their sum and difference have greatest common divisor $2$; after
division by $2$, the resulting numerator and denominator are coprime
and have opposite parity, because their difference is the odd number
$n$.  These are the only possibilities for coprime $m,n$.
$\square$

For data satisfying (1.14), put

$$
H=m^2+n^2,\qquad F=m^2-n^2,\qquad T=2mn,\qquad Q=2FT.
\tag{1.15}
$$

#### Lemma 1.19 (Reduced denominators)

The integers in (1.15) satisfy

$$
H^2=F^2+T^2,\quad H,F\text{ odd},\quad T\text{ even},\quad
\gcd(F,T)=\gcd(H,F)=\gcd(H,T)=1.
$$

Furthermore,

$$
\gcd(Q,H)=\gcd(F+T,H)=\gcd(F-T,H)=1,
\tag{1.16}
$$

and

$$
R(n/m)=\frac Q{H^2},\qquad
\sqrt{1+R(n/m)}=\frac{F+T}{H},\qquad
\sqrt{1-R(n/m)}=\frac{|F-T|}{H}.
\tag{1.17}
$$

Both root fractions are reduced, and $F\ne T$.

**Proof.**
The displayed Pythagorean identity is immediate.  If an odd prime
divides any two of $H,F,T$, the identities
$H+F=2m^2$ and $H-F=2n^2$, together with $T=2mn$,
force it to divide both $m$ and $n$.  This is impossible.  The parity
conditions exclude a common factor $2$ in the relevant pairs.
The first equality in (1.16) follows because
$H$ is odd.  If a prime $p$ divided $H$ and $F\pm T$, then
$F^2+T^2\equiv2T^2\equiv0\pmod p$, again impossible because $p$ is odd
and $\gcd(H,T)=1$.  The formulas (1.17) follow from
(1.7).  Finally, $F=T$ would imply $H^2=2F^2$,
which is impossible for positive integers.
$\square$

Apply this normalization separately to the four parameters of
Theorem 1.13, adding subscripts $i$ to
$m,n,H,F,T,Q$.  Define

$$
c=\operatorname{lcm}(H_1,H_2,H_3,H_4),\qquad A_i=\frac c{H_i}.
\tag{1.18}
$$

#### Proposition 1.20 (Opposite-pair contents)

For the associated primitive square,

$$
D_i=A_i^2Q_i,\qquad
\sqrt{c^2+D_i}=A_i(F_i+T_i),\qquad
\sqrt{c^2-D_i}=A_i|F_i-T_i|.
\tag{1.19}
$$

The greatest common divisor of the two roots in the $i$th pair is
exactly $A_i$.  The four $A_i$ are pairwise coprime.  Consequently

$$
g=\frac c{A_1A_2A_3A_4}\in\mathbb Z_{>0},\qquad
H_i=g\prod_{j\ne i}A_j.
\tag{1.20}
$$

No assertion that $g$ is coprime to the $A_i$ is included.

**Proof.**
Lemma 1.19 and
Theorem 1.9 identify the primitive center
root with the least common multiple in (1.18), and give
(1.19).  Any common divisor of $F_i+T_i$ and
$F_i-T_i$ divides both $2F_i$ and $2T_i$.  Both of these sums and
differences are odd, and $\gcd(F_i,T_i)=1$, so their greatest common
divisor is $1$.  Thus the pair content is $A_i$.

If a prime divided both $A_i$ and $A_j$ for $i\ne j$, it would divide
$c$ and the roots in two different opposite pairs.  This contradicts
Lemma 1.17.  Therefore the $A_i$ are pairwise coprime.
Since each divides $c$, their product divides $c$, proving the
integrality of $g$ and the remaining identities.
$\square$

#### Theorem 1.21 (Exact integral circle system)

Primitive canonical magic squares of squares are in bijection with the
following data:

- four ordered pairs $(m_i,n_i)$ satisfying (1.14);
- pairwise coprime positive integers $A_1,A_2,A_3,A_4$ and a positive
   integer $g$;

subject, with (1.15) for each index, to

$$
\begin{aligned}
H_i&=g\prod_{j\ne i}A_j\qquad(1\le i\le4),\\
A_3^2Q_3&=A_1^2Q_1+A_2^2Q_2,\\
A_4^2Q_4&=A_1^2Q_1-A_2^2Q_2,\\
A_1^2Q_1&\ne2A_2^2Q_2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1.21}
$$

The bijection is given by

$$
c=gA_1A_2A_3A_4,\qquad x=A_1^2Q_1,\qquad y=A_2^2Q_2.
$$

**Proof.**
The forward direction follows from the unique parity normalization and
Proposition 1.20.

Conversely, the first group of identities gives $c=A_iH_i$ for every
$i$, and (1.19) provides integer roots for all four
pairs.  Each $D_i=A_i^2Q_i$ is strictly between $0$ and $c^2$ by
Lemma 1.11.  The second and third equalities in
(1.21) imply $x+y=D_3<c^2$ and $x-y=D_4>0$.
The last inequality supplies distinctness.  Thus the resulting matrix
is a magic square of squares in the canonical orientation.

Its two roots in pair $i$ have greatest common divisor $A_i$ by the
same argument as in Proposition 1.20.  A prime dividing
every root would therefore divide every $A_i$, which pairwise
coprimality excludes.  The square is primitive.  Finally, every opposite
pair has a unique parity-normalized parameter by
Lemmas 1.11 and 1.18;
$A_i=c/H_i$ and $g=c/\prod_iA_i$ are then forced.  Hence the correspondence
is a bijection, not merely a surjection.
$\square$

#### Proposition 1.22 (Valuations of pair offsets)

Let $p^e\Vert c$ in the preceding data and put $a_i=v_p(A_i)$.
At most one $a_i$ is positive, and

$$
v_p(D_i)=
\begin{cases}
2a_i,&a_i<e,\\
2e+v_p(Q_i),&a_i=e.
\end{cases}
\tag{1.22}
$$

Here $v_p$ denotes the usual exponent of $p$ in a nonzero integer.

**Proof.**
Pairwise coprimality gives the first assertion.  Since $H_i=c/A_i$,
if $a_i<e$ then $p\mid H_i$ and $p\nmid Q_i$ by
(1.16).  The first case follows from
$D_i=A_i^2Q_i$.  If $a_i=e$, the same identity gives the second case
without an additional coprimality assertion.
$\square$

### 1.6. The exact set of offsets at a fixed center

Let

$$
\mathscr C=\{c\in\mathbb Z_{>0}:p\mid c\Longrightarrow p\equiv1\pmod4\}.
\tag{1.23}
$$

The condition is vacuous for $c=1$.  Every primitive center root lies
in $\mathscr C$ by Proposition 1.16.

#### Definition 1.23

For $c\in\mathscr C$ define its *opposite-pair offset set* by

$$
\mathcal O_c=\{D\in\mathbb Z:0<D<c^2,\quad
c^2+D\text{ and }c^2-D\text{ are integer squares}\}.
\tag{1.24}
$$

We use the Gaussian integer ring $\mathbb Z[i]$ and its norm
$N(a+ib)=a^2+b^2$.  Its units are $\{1,-1,i,-i\}$.

#### Lemma 1.24 (Gaussian factorization facts)

The ring $\mathbb Z[i]$ is a unique factorization domain.  Every rational
prime $p\equiv1\pmod4$ has a factorization
$p=\pi_p\overline{\pi_p}$ with $N(\pi_p)=p$, where
$\pi_p$ and $\overline{\pi_p}$ are nonassociate Gaussian primes.

**External input.** Unique factorization and the splitting of rational primes in $\mathbb Z[i]$ are used in the form given in Conrad [27]. The Gaussian primes denoted $\pi_p$ below have norm $p$; their conjugates provide the other prime above $p$.

#### Theorem 1.25 (Gaussian description and exact cardinality)

Let $c\in\mathscr C$, with factorization $c=\prod_{p\mid c}p^{e_p}$,
and fix one Gaussian prime $\pi_p$ of norm $p$ for each $p\mid c$.
Then

$$
\mathcal O_c=
\left\{
\left|\operatorname{Im}\left[
\left(\prod_{p\mid c}\pi_p^{\,e_p+j_p}
\overline{\pi_p}^{\,e_p-j_p}\right)^2\right]\right|:
\begin{array}{l}
j_p\in\mathbb Z,\quad-e_p\le j_p\le e_p,\\
(j_p)_{p\mid c}\ne(0)_{p\mid c}
\end{array}
\right\}.
\tag{1.25}
$$

Its cardinality is

$$
|\mathcal O_c|=\frac{\displaystyle\prod_{p\mid c}(2e_p+1)-1}{2}.
\tag{1.26}
$$

The only duplication in (1.25) is the simultaneous
replacement of every $j_p$ by $-j_p$.

**Proof.**
First identify $\mathcal O_c$ with the positive integer pairs

$$
U>V>0,\qquad U^2+V^2=c^2,
\tag{1.27}
$$

by $D=2UV$.  If $D\in\mathcal O_c$ and
$a=\sqrt{c^2+D}>b=\sqrt{c^2-D}>0$, the identity
$a^2+b^2=2c^2\equiv2\pmod8$ implies that $a,b$ are odd.
Then $U=(a+b)/2$ and $V=(a-b)/2$ are positive integers satisfying
(1.27).  Conversely, since $c$ is odd, any pair in
(1.27) has opposite parity; its offset $D=2UV$ obeys
$0<D<c^2$ and $c^2\pm D=(U\pm V)^2$.
Both correspondences are inverse.

By unique factorization, all Gaussian integers of norm $c^2$ are
exactly

$$
Z=\varepsilon\prod_{p\mid c}\pi_p^{\,e_p+j_p}
\overline{\pi_p}^{\,e_p-j_p},\qquad
\varepsilon\in\{1,-1,i,-i\},\quad -e_p\le j_p\le e_p.
\tag{1.28}
$$

Indeed, the exponents of the two primes above $p$ must be nonnegative
and sum to $2e_p$, and no other Gaussian prime can occur.
The four axis points $Z\in\{c,-c,ic,-ic\}$ correspond exactly to
the all-zero vector $(j_p)$.

Every other point in (1.28) has nonzero real and
imaginary parts.  Their absolute values cannot be equal, since that
would make $c^2$ twice a nonzero integer square.  Multiplication by
units and complex conjugation therefore gives an orbit of eight
distinct points, with a unique representative $U+iV$ satisfying
(1.27).  Each such orbit has the common offset
$|\operatorname{Im}(Z^2)|=2|\operatorname{Re}(Z) \operatorname{Im}(Z)|$.

No two of these orbits have the same offset: $D$ and $c$ determine the
positive roots $a,b$, hence the ordered pair $(U,V)$ above.  Units
do not change exponent vectors in (1.28), and
conjugation negates all of them.  This proves the claimed duplication
rule and the set formula.  Finally, there are
$4\prod_p(2e_p+1)$ norm-$c^2$ points, of which four lie on the axes;
division by the orbit size $8$ gives (1.26).
The empty product convention also gives the correct value $0$ at $c=1$.
$\square$

#### Remark 1.26 (Choice of Gaussian prime)

Replacing $\pi_p$ by its conjugate negates the corresponding coordinate
$j_p$.  Replacing it by an associated Gaussian prime changes the product
in (1.25) by a unit.  The imaginary part of its square
therefore changes at most by a sign.  Thus $\mathcal O_c$ is independent
of all the choices used to describe it.

#### Proposition 1.27 (Link with integral circle coordinates)

For the data in Theorem 1.21, define

$$
Z_i=A_i(m_i+in_i)^2=A_i(F_i+iT_i).
\tag{1.29}
$$

Then $N(Z_i)=c^2$ and $\operatorname{Im}(Z_i^2)=D_i$.
If the exponents of the two Gaussian primes above $p^e\Vert c$ in
$Z_i$ are $e+j_{i,p}$ and $e-j_{i,p}$, then

$$
v_p(A_i)=e-|j_{i,p}|.
\tag{1.30}
$$

In particular, at any center prime at most one index $i$ has
$|j_{i,p}|<e$.

**Proof.**
The norm and imaginary-part identities follow from
$F_i^2+T_i^2=H_i^2$, $A_iH_i=c$, and $Q_i=2F_iT_i$.
The Gaussian integers $m_i+in_i$ and $m_i-in_i$ are coprime:
a common odd Gaussian prime would divide both $2m_i$ and $2in_i$,
contrary to $\gcd(m_i,n_i)=1$; the prime above $2$ divides neither
because $m_i,n_i$ have opposite parity.  Consequently, for a fixed
split rational prime, at most one of its conjugate Gaussian primes
occurs in $(m_i+in_i)^2$.  The smaller of its two exponents in $Z_i$
is therefore exactly $v_p(A_i)$.  This minimum is
$\min(e+j_{i,p},e-j_{i,p})=e-|j_{i,p}|$.
The last statement follows from pairwise coprimality of the $A_i$.
$\square$

### 1.7. Finite height sections and the complete global set

#### Definition 1.28

For $c\in\mathscr C$, let

$$
\mathscr S_c=\left\{(x,y)\in\mathbb Z^2:
\begin{array}{l}
x>y>0,\quad x\ne2y,\quad\gcd(c,x,y)=1,\\[2pt]
x,\ y,\ x+y,\ x-y\in\mathcal O_c
\end{array}\right\}.
\tag{1.31}
$$

For real $C\ge1$ define the *center-height section*

$$
\mathscr S_{\le C}=\coprod_{\substack{c\in\mathscr C\\c\le C}}
\bigl(\{c\}\times\mathscr S_c\bigr),
\qquad
\mathscr S=\coprod_{c\in\mathscr C}
\bigl(\{c\}\times\mathscr S_c\bigr).
\tag{1.32}
$$

The disjoint-union notation records the center as part of each object.

#### Theorem 1.29 (Exact fixed-center and global descriptions)

The set $\mathscr S$ is in bijection with the primitive canonical magic
squares of squares, under $(c,x,y)\mapsto\mathcal A(c^2;x,y)$.
Every height section $\mathscr S_{\le C}$ is finite, and

$$
\mathscr S=\bigcup_{N=1}^{\infty}\mathscr S_{\le N},
\qquad
\mathscr S_{\le1}\subseteq\mathscr S_{\le2}\subseteq\cdots.
\tag{1.33}
$$

Writing
$n(c)=(\prod_{p\mid c}(2v_p(c)+1)-1)/2$, one has the elementary bound

$$
|\mathscr S_c|\le\binom{n(c)}2,\qquad
|\mathscr S_{\le C}|
\le\sum_{\substack{c\in\mathscr C\\c\le C}}\binom{n(c)}2,
\tag{1.34}
$$

where $\binom n2=n(n-1)/2$ for $n\ge0$.

**Proof.**
Membership of $x+y$ in $\mathcal O_c$ already imposes $x+y<c^2$.
The four offset memberships in (1.31) are exactly the eight
square conditions of (1.11).  The remaining
inequalities and the primitivity condition agree as well.  Thus
Theorem 1.15 proves the bijection; the center
restriction follows from Proposition 1.16.

Theorem 1.25 makes $\mathcal O_c$ a finite set
of size $n(c)$.  Each element of $\mathscr S_c$ determines a distinct
two-element subset $\{x,y\}$ of $\mathcal O_c$, since the condition
$x>y$ recovers its order.  This proves the first cardinality bound.
There are only finitely many positive integers $c\le C$, so summation
gives the second and proves finiteness.  Finally, every positive
integer center lies below some positive integer $N$, proving
(1.33).
$\square$

#### Corollary 1.30 (Four offsets are required)

If $\mathscr S_c\ne\varnothing$, then

$$
\prod_{p\mid c}(2v_p(c)+1)\ge9.
$$

**Proof.**
The four positive offsets are distinct by $x>y>0$ and $x\ne2y$.
Hence $|\mathcal O_c|\ge4$, and (1.26) gives the result.
$\square$

#### Corollary 1.31 (All oriented integral squares)

Let $\mathscr W$ denote the set of all oriented magic squares of squares,
with no primitivity requirement.  There is a bijection

$$
\mathbb Z_{>0}\times D_4\times\mathscr S
\longrightarrow\mathscr W,\qquad
(d,\sigma,(c,x,y))\longmapsto
d^2\,\sigma\bigl(\mathcal A(c^2;x,y)\bigr).
\tag{1.35}
$$

Consequently, $\mathscr W$ is empty if and only if $\mathscr S$ is empty,
and also if and only if $\mathscr M$ or $\mathscr T$ is empty.

**Proof.**
Existence and uniqueness of the primitive scale and canonical orientation
are Proposition 1.7; the primitive triple is unique by
Theorem 1.29.  The action has no stabilizer because all
entries are distinct.  The final equivalences follow from the preceding
exact correspondences.
$\square$

#### Remark 1.32 (Logical scope)

The exact sets (1.3), (1.10),
(1.11), (1.21), and
(1.31) describe the same existence problem, with the stated
multiplicities.  Restrictions such as (1.12), the prime
condition (1.23), and
(1.22) are consequences of those exact systems.
They are not substitutes for the simultaneous eight square conditions.
Finiteness of every height section neither implies finiteness of
$\mathscr S$ nor supplies an upper bound on the height of all its
elements.  None of the statements of this section asserts that
$\mathscr S$ is empty or nonempty.

#### Corollary 1.33 (An effective heavy-block exclusion)

In the synchronized Gaussian-block families of Section 6, let $c=P^2QR$ with $P,Q,R>1$ pairwise coprime odd integers
supported on primes $1\pmod4$. For the CFF and two EFF profiles
`I0:0000/0011/0101`, `I2:0000/0011/0101`, and
`I2:0000/0101/0110`, every primitive full square satisfies

$$
P>10^6.
\tag{1.36}
$$

The norms $Q,R$ and the center height are unrestricted. In particular,
the repeated prime $p$ exceeds $10^6$ in these profiles when $c=p^2qr$.

Here the heavy Gaussian block has the form $A=a+ib$, $N(A)=P$,
and its phase is $U=A^4/P^2$. One-sided support permits the exhaustive
normalization $a>b>0$, $\gcd(a,b)=1$, and opposite parity. Consequently

$$
\operatorname{Re}U=\frac{P^2-8a^2b^2}{P^2}.
$$

The necessary fixed-curve conditions (P2Q-CE-2)–(P2Q-CE-3) and
(P2Q-EFF2-1) in the structural manuscript require, respectively,
one of $F_8(C),F_8(-C),F_6(C),F_6(-C)$, or $E(C)$ to be a rational
square at this real coordinate. Proposition 4.1e there gives the
polynomials, the complete finite enumeration, and its exact certificate.
The $159139$ primitive phase representatives with $P\le10^6$ give
no square in any branch. Homogenization has even degree, so each test
is exactly a nonnegative integer-square test. Two separate enumeration
and evaluation implementations agree.

This excludes a bounded heavy-block range at all center heights. It
neither determines the entire finite families nor excludes the other
ten synchronized profiles. All original signed magic relations and
square-root conditions remain required above the cutoff.

## 2. The minimum entry and quadratic norms

This chapter describes the set of primitive magic squares by the square
root of the least entry.  A quadratic norm argument gives an explicit
bound for the center at each fixed minimum.  The resulting fibers are
finite and satisfy uniform cardinality estimates.  A second use of
quadratic norms bounds the number of possible minima in a prescribed
center range.

### 2.1. The minimum in canonical coordinates

Use the primitive canonical matrix (1.1), with $e=c^2$ and the chamber (1.2). Its least and greatest entries are $c^2-x-y$ and $c^2+x+y$. Define the least positive root by

$$
\ell^2=c^2-x-y.
\tag{2.3}
$$

Thus $\ell$ is odd in a primitive array. The established minimum-entry input is stated in Section 13.

### 2.2. The exact Pell description

#### Definition 2.1

For a positive integer $\ell$, put

$$
\mathcal P_\ell=
\{(M,H)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^2:H^2+\ell^2=2M^2,\ H>\ell\}.
$$

List its elements as $(M_j,H_j)$, $j\ge1$, in increasing order of $H_j$,
and define

$$
d_j=\frac{H_j^2-\ell^2}{2}=M_j^2-\ell^2.
\tag{2.4}
$$

The inequalities $\ell<M_j<H_j$ follow from the defining equation.
The positive integer $d_j$ is the common difference of the progression
$\ell^2,M_j^2,H_j^2$.

The sequence is infinite: $(M,H)=(5\ell,7\ell)$ belongs to
$\mathcal P_\ell$, and the transformation below has unbounded iterates.
There is at most one positive $M$ for each $H$, so the ordering is
unambiguous.

#### Proposition 2.2 (Finite representatives of Pell orbits)

Let

$$
\mathcal G_\ell=\{(M,H)\in\mathcal P_\ell:H\le7\ell\},
\qquad g_\ell=\#\mathcal G_\ell.
$$

Then $1\le g_\ell<\infty$, and $\mathcal P_\ell$ is the disjoint union
of the forward orbits of $\mathcal G_\ell$ under

$$
F(M,H)=(3M+2H,4M+3H).
\tag{2.5}
$$

In the increasing ordering,

$$
(M_{j+g_\ell},H_{j+g_\ell})=F(M_j,H_j),\qquad H_{g_\ell}=7\ell.
\tag{2.6}
$$

**External correspondence.** Morgenstern [3], the fixed-smallest-entry progression construction: the least entry is $\ell^2$, the other progression roots are $(M,H)$, and multiplication of $H+M\sqrt2$ by $3+2\sqrt2$ gives (2.5). The seed interval is $\ell<H\le7\ell$.

#### Theorem 2.3 (Exact minimum-entry equivalence)

For a positive odd integer $\ell$, canonical primitive square magic
arrays with least entry $\ell^2$ are in bijection with triples of
indices $i<j<k$ satisfying

$$
\begin{aligned}
d_i+d_j&=d_k, & d_j&\ne2d_i,\\
U^2&=\ell^2+d_i+2d_j,
&V^2&=\ell^2+2d_i+d_j,\\
U,V&\in\mathbb Z_{>0},
&\gcd(\ell,M_i,M_j)&=1.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2.7}
$$

Here $U,V$ are the unique positive roots in
(2.7).  The array corresponding to the triple is

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
U^2&\ell^2&V^2\\
H_i^2&M_k^2&H_j^2\\
M_j^2&H_k^2&M_i^2
\end{pmatrix},
\tag{2.8}
$$

and its canonical parameters are

$$
(c,x,y)=(M_k,d_j,d_i).
\tag{2.9}
$$

Equivalently, the additive condition in (2.7) is

$$
H_i^2+H_j^2-H_k^2=\ell^2.
\tag{2.10}
$$

**Proof.**

In (1.1), substitute
$c^2=\ell^2+x+y$.  The three progressions beginning at $\ell^2$ have
common differences $y$, $x$ and $x+y$.  Their remaining entries are

$$
\ell^2+y,\ \ell^2+2y;\qquad
\ell^2+x,\ \ell^2+2x;\qquad
\ell^2+x+y,\ \ell^2+2x+2y.
$$

They determine unique Pell pairs with steps
$d_i=y<d_j=x<d_k=x+y$.  The two entries not in these progressions
are exactly those in (2.7).
The distinctness condition is $x\ne2y$ by
Proposition 1.5.

Conversely, the hypotheses give positive $x=d_j>y=d_i$ and
$c^2=M_k^2=\ell^2+x+y$.  Substitution in the canonical array yields
(2.8).  Its entries are squares, its line sums
are $3c^2$, and its entries are distinct by $d_j\ne2d_i$.

For primitivity, any prime common to the nine roots divides
$\ell,M_i,M_j$.  If a prime $p$ divides these three roots, then $p^2$
divides $\ell^2$, $d_i=M_i^2-\ell^2$ and
$d_j=M_j^2-\ell^2$.  The displayed formulas for all nine squared roots
then show that $p^2$ divides every entry, so $p$ divides every root.
Thus (2.7) is equivalent to primitivity.  The recovered
steps determine the triple uniquely, proving bijectivity.  The final
equivalence follows directly from (2.4).
$\square$

#### Corollary 2.4 (Prime divisors of the minimum)

If $\ell$ occurs as the least root of a primitive magic square of squares,
every prime divisor of $\ell$ is congruent to $1$ or $7$ modulo $8$.

**Proof.**

The root $\ell$ is odd.  If $p\mid\ell$ and
$p\equiv3$ or $5\pmod8$, then $2$ is a quadratic nonresidue modulo $p$.
The congruence $H^2\equiv2M^2\pmod p$ forces $p\mid H,M$ for every
$(M,H)\in\mathcal P_\ell$.  In particular
$p\mid\gcd(\ell,M_i,M_j)$, contrary to
Theorem 2.3.
$\square$

### 2.3. A gap between arbitrary Pell solutions

Write $K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$ and $\mathcal O=\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$, the
ring of integers of $K$.  Conjugation and norm are denoted by

$$
\overline{a+b\sqrt2}=a-b\sqrt2,\qquad
N(a+b\sqrt2)=a^2-2b^2.
$$

For $(M_j,H_j)\in\mathcal P_\ell$, set

$$
a_j=H_j+\sqrt2M_j.
\tag{2.11}
$$

Then

$$
N(a_j)=-\ell^2,\qquad
\bar a_j=-\frac{\ell^2}{a_j},\qquad
H_j=\frac{a_j-\ell^2/a_j}{2},\qquad
a_j>(1+\sqrt2)\ell.
\tag{2.12}
$$

#### Lemma 2.5 (Uniform Pell gap)

Let $\ell$ be positive and odd.  For any two distinct elements of
$\mathcal P_\ell$ with $H_j<H_k$,

$$
\frac{H_k}{H_j}>\frac{\ell+2}{\ell}.
\tag{2.13}
$$

Consequently, with

$$
\delta_\ell=\frac{4(\ell+1)}{(\ell+2)^2},
\tag{2.14}
$$

one has

$$
H_k^2-H_j^2>\delta_\ell H_k^2.
\tag{2.15}
$$

**Proof.**

The equation $H^2+\ell^2=2M^2$ implies that $H$ and $M$ are odd: first
reduce modulo $2$ and then modulo $4$.
Put $\rho=a_k/a_j>1$.  By (2.12),

$$
\rho+\rho^{-1}
=\frac{2T}{\ell^2},\qquad
T=2M_jM_k-H_jH_k.
$$

Since $\rho>1$, one has $T>\ell^2$.  Both $T$ and $\ell^2$ are odd
integers, so $T\ge\ell^2+2$.  It follows that

$$
\frac{(\rho-1)^2}{\rho}\ge\frac4{\ell^2},\qquad
\rho>1+\frac2\ell.
$$

Furthermore

$$
\frac{H_k}{H_j}
=\rho\frac{1-\ell^2/a_k^2}{1-\ell^2/a_j^2}>\rho.
$$

This proves (2.13); squaring and rearranging gives
(2.15).
$\square$

The assertion concerns arbitrary distinct Pell solutions.  No condition
that they belong to the same orbit is imposed.

### 2.4. A uniform norm bound

#### Theorem 2.6 (The quadratic-norm band bound)

Let $\ell$ be positive and odd, let $i<j<k$, and put

$$
D=H_i^2+H_j^2-H_k^2.
$$

If $|D|\le\ell^2$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
H_i^2&<3\ell^6,\\
4(\ell+1)H_k^2
&<(3\ell^6+\ell^2)(\ell+2)^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2.16}
$$

If $D=\ell^2$, the second inequality strengthens to

$$
4(\ell+1)H_k^2<(3\ell^6-\ell^2)(\ell+2)^2.
\tag{2.17}
$$

**Proof.**

Consider the algebraic integer

$$
\begin{aligned}
S&=a_i^2+a_j^2-a_k^2\\
 &=(2D+\ell^2)+2\sqrt2
 (H_iM_i+H_jM_j-H_kM_k).
\end{aligned}
$$

Its rational coefficient is odd, so $S\ne0$ and $N(S)$ is a nonzero
integer.  As $0<a_i<a_j<a_k$, its conjugate satisfies

$$
0<\bar S
=\ell^4(a_i^{-2}+a_j^{-2}-a_k^{-2})
<\frac{2\ell^4}{a_i^2}<\ell^2.
\tag{2.18}
$$

The last inequality follows from
$a_i>(1+\sqrt2)\ell$.

On the other hand,

$$
S+\bar S=4D+2\ell^2\in[-2\ell^2,6\ell^2].
$$

If $S\ge0$, then $S<6\ell^2$.  If $S<0$, then
$|S|=\bar S-(S+\bar S)<3\ell^2$.  Thus in both cases

$$
1\le|N(S)|=|S|\bar S
<\frac{12\ell^6}{a_i^2}.
$$

Since $H_i<a_i/2$, this proves (2.16).

Lemma 2.5 gives

$$
\delta_\ell H_k^2
<H_k^2-H_j^2=H_i^2-D.
$$

The right side is at most $H_i^2+\ell^2$ throughout the band, and is
$H_i^2-\ell^2$ when $D=\ell^2$.  Inserting
(2.16) and the value of $\delta_\ell$ gives
(2.16) and (2.17).
$\square$

#### Corollary 2.7 (Center bound)

Every primitive magic square of squares with least root $\ell$ and central
root $c$ satisfies

$$
8(\ell+1)c^2+\ell^4<3\ell^6(\ell+2)^2.
\tag{2.19}
$$

In particular $c=O(\ell^{7/2})$ with an absolute implied constant.

**Proof.**

Theorem 2.3 supplies an exact triple, and
$H_k^2=2c^2-\ell^2$.  Substitution into
(2.17) gives the asserted inequality.
Since $(\ell+2)^2/(\ell+1)=\ell+3+1/(\ell+1)$ is
$O(\ell)$ for $\ell\ge1$, it also gives the stated order bound.
$\square$

#### Corollary 2.8

The least root satisfies $\ell\ge10^7$, hence $\ell\ne1$, by the external minimum-entry bound in Section 13. The later norm inequalities use only $\ell\ge2$.

### 2.5. The minimum-dependent norm refinement

#### Definition 2.9

For a positive odd integer $\ell$, define

$$
w_\ell=\max\{w\in\mathbb Z_{>0}:w\text{ is odd},\ 8w^2<9\ell^4\},
\qquad \nu_\ell=9\ell^4-8w_\ell^2.
\tag{2.20}
$$

The set defining $w_\ell$ is nonempty and finite.  Thus
$\nu_\ell$ is a positive integer. Since $\ell^2$ is an admissible odd value of $w$, one also has $w_\ell\ge\ell^2$ and $1\le\nu_\ell\le\ell^4$.

#### Theorem 2.10 (Refined norm inequalities)

For every exact Pell triple $i<j<k$ with
$H_i^2+H_j^2-H_k^2=\ell^2$ and odd $\ell>0$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
H_i^2&<\frac{3\ell^6}{\nu_\ell},\\
4\nu_\ell(\ell+1)H_k^2
&<(3\ell^6-\nu_\ell\ell^2)(\ell+2)^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2.21}
$$

Every primitive magic square of squares therefore satisfies

$$
8\nu_\ell(\ell+1)c^2+\nu_\ell\ell^4
<3\ell^6(\ell+2)^2.
\tag{2.22}
$$

**Proof.**

For the algebraic integer $S$ in the proof of
Theorem 2.6, the exact-triple assumption gives

$$
S=3\ell^2+2\sqrt2W,\qquad
W=H_iM_i+H_jM_j-H_kM_k.
$$

The integer $W$ is odd.  By (2.18),

$$
0<3\ell^2-2\sqrt2W<\ell^2.
$$

Hence $W>0$, $8W^2<9\ell^4$, and $W\le w_\ell$.  In particular

$$
N(S)=9\ell^4-8W^2\ge\nu_\ell>0.
$$

The upper estimate for $|N(S)|$ in Theorem 2.6 is unchanged,
so

$$
\nu_\ell<\frac{12\ell^6}{a_i^2},\qquad
H_i^2<\frac{3\ell^6}{\nu_\ell}.
$$

This proves (2.21).  The uniform gap then gives

$$
\delta_\ell H_k^2
<H_i^2-\ell^2
<\frac{3\ell^6}{\nu_\ell}-\ell^2,
$$

which is (2.21).
Finally, substituting $H_k^2=2c^2-\ell^2$ and simplifying gives
(2.22).
$\square$

#### Remark 2.11

The definition of $\nu_\ell$ involves only integers.  Equivalently, if

$$
t_\ell=\left\lfloor\sqrt{\frac{9\ell^4-1}{8}}\right\rfloor,
$$

then $w_\ell=t_\ell$ when $t_\ell$ is odd, and
$w_\ell=t_\ell-1$ when $t_\ell$ is even.
Here $(9\ell^4-1)/8$ is an integer for odd $\ell$.
For example $w_7=51$ and $\nu_7=801$.
The refined inequalities apply to exact triples; the full band
$|D|\le\ell^2$ is covered separately by Theorem 2.6.

#### Corollary 2.12 (Strict relation between minimum and center)

Every primitive magic square of squares satisfies

$$
\nu_\ell c^2<\ell^7,
\qquad\text{and therefore}\qquad \ell>c^{2/7}.
\tag{2.23}
$$

**Proof.**

Corollary 2.8 gives $\ell\ge2$.  The identity

$$
8\ell(\ell+1)-3(\ell+2)^2=(\ell-2)(5\ell+6)\ge0
$$

and (2.22) imply

$$
8\nu_\ell(\ell+1)c^2
<3\ell^6(\ell+2)^2
\le8\ell^7(\ell+1).
$$

Cancellation proves the first inequality.  The second follows from
$\nu_\ell\ge1$.
$\square$

#### Proposition 2.13 (Minimum-prime-power norm sieve)

Let $\ell$ be positive and odd. For every prime $p\mid\ell$ with
$p\equiv1,7\pmod8$, put $e_p=v_p(\ell)$. For those primes with
$p\equiv1\pmod8$, also define

$$
\sigma_p=2^{(p-1)/4}\pmod p\in\{1,-1\}.
$$

For a positive integer $w$, define $P_p(w)$ by the following conditions:

* if $v_p(w)\ge2e_p$, it holds;
* otherwise $r=v_p(w)$ must be even, and, if $p\equiv1\pmod8$,
  additionally $\left(\frac{w/p^r}{p}\right)=\sigma_p$.

At $p\equiv7\pmod8$ no restriction on the unit part is imposed. Define

$$
\begin{split}
w_\ell^*&=\max\left\{w\in\mathbb Z_{>0}:\ w\text{ odd},\quad
8w^2<9\ell^4,\quad
P_p(w)\text{ for every }p\mid\ell,\ p\equiv1,7\pmod8\right\},\\
\nu_\ell^*&=9\ell^4-8(w_\ell^*)^2.
\end{split}
\tag{2.23a}
$$

The set is nonempty because it contains $w=\ell^2$. In particular,

$$
\ell^2\le w_\ell^*\le w_\ell,\qquad
1\le\nu_\ell\le\nu_\ell^*\le\ell^4.
$$

For every exact positive Pell triple $i<j<k$ with
$H_t^2+\ell^2=2M_t^2$ and
$H_i^2+H_j^2-H_k^2=\ell^2$, one has

$$
\begin{aligned}
H_i^2&<\frac{3\ell^6}{\nu_\ell^*},\\
4\nu_\ell^*(\ell+1)H_k^2
&<(3\ell^6-\nu_\ell^*\ell^2)(\ell+2)^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently every primitive magic square of squares satisfies

$$
8\nu_\ell^*(\ell+1)c^2+\nu_\ell^*\ell^4
<3\ell^6(\ell+2)^2,
\qquad
\nu_\ell^*c^2<\ell^7.
$$

The last inequality uses the already established exclusion $\ell=1$.

**Proof.** Put $W=H_iM_i+H_jM_j-H_kM_k$. The proof of Theorem 2.10
shows that $W$ is positive and odd and that $8W^2<9\ell^4$.
It remains to prove each congruence restriction.

Fix $p\mid\ell$, $p\equiv1,7\pmod8$, put $e=v_p(\ell)$,
and work in $R=\mathbb Z/p^{2e}\mathbb Z$. Choose a square root
$\kappa$ of $2$ in $R$; it exists by simple-root lifting from
$\mathbb F_p$. For each Pell pair $(M,H)$, one has

$$
HM\equiv\epsilon\kappa M^2\pmod{p^{2e}}
\quad\text{for some }\epsilon\in\{1,-1\}.
$$

To see this, if $r=v_p(M)<e$, the Pell equation forces
$v_p(H)=r$. The units $h=H/p^r,m=M/p^r$ obey
$h^2-2m^2\equiv0\pmod{p^{2e-2r}}$. Since at most one of
$h-\kappa m,h+\kappa m$ is divisible by the odd prime $p$, one
factor is divisible by $p^{2e-2r}$. Multiplication by $p^{2r}m$
gives the claim. If $v_p(M)\ge e$, the Pell equation also gives
$v_p(H)\ge e$, and both sides of the asserted congruence vanish.

Write $a=M_i^2,b=M_j^2,c_0=M_k^2$ in $R$.
The exact additive relation implies $c_0=a+b$, so

$$
\frac W\kappa=(\epsilon_i-\epsilon_k)a+
(\epsilon_j-\epsilon_k)b.
$$

If both coefficients vanish this is zero. If precisely one is nonzero,
it is $\pm2a$ or $\pm2b$. If both are nonzero, their signs agree,
and it is $\pm2(a+b)=\pm2c_0$.
Thus $W\equiv0$ or $\pm2\kappa M_t^2\pmod{p^{2e}}$ for one
$t\in\{i,j,k\}$. If $v_p(W)<2e$, it follows that
$v_p(W)=2v_p(M_t)$ is even. If $p\equiv1\pmod8$, both $-1$
and $2$ are quadratic residues modulo $p$, so the unit part obeys

$$
\left(\frac{W/p^{v_p(W)}}p\right)=\left(\frac\kappa p\right)
=\kappa^{(p-1)/2}=2^{(p-1)/4}=\sigma_p.
$$

This does not depend on the choice of square root $\kappa$. If
$p\equiv7\pmod8$, the two signs in $\pm2\kappa$ give both
unit squareclasses and yield no further restriction on the unit part.
The definition therefore gives $W\le w_\ell^*$, and the positive norm
in Theorem 2.10 satisfies

$$
N(3\ell^2+2\sqrt2W)=9\ell^4-8W^2\ge\nu_\ell^*.
$$

Replace the lower norm bound $\nu_\ell$ by $\nu_\ell^*$ in the
proofs of Theorem 2.10 and Corollary 2.12. All upper estimates and the
uniform Pell gap are unchanged, which proves the displayed formulas.
$\square$

### 2.6. Finite fibers and their disjoint union

Let $\mathscr A_\ell$ be the set of canonical primitive square magic
arrays whose least entry is $\ell^2$.  For positive odd $\ell$, define
the rational number

$$
R_\ell=
\frac{(3\ell^6-\nu_\ell\ell^2)(\ell+2)^2}
{4\nu_\ell(\ell+1)}.
\tag{2.24}
$$

#### Theorem 2.14 (Finite minimum fibers)

For every positive integer $\ell$, the set $\mathscr A_\ell$ is finite.
It is empty for even $\ell$.  For odd $\ell$ it is in bijection with
the finite set of triples $i<j<k$ in $\mathcal P_\ell$ satisfying

$$
\left\{
\begin{aligned}
&H_k^2<R_\ell,\qquad H_i^2+H_j^2-H_k^2=\ell^2,\\
&d_j\ne2d_i,\qquad\gcd(\ell,M_i,M_j)=1,\\
&\ell^2+d_i+2d_j\in\{n^2:n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\},\\
&\ell^2+2d_i+d_j\in\{n^2:n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\}.
\end{aligned}\right.
\tag{2.25}
$$

If $R_\ell\le0$, this set is empty.

**Proof.**

Even minima are excluded by Proposition 1.16.  For odd $\ell$,
Theorem 2.3 is an exact bijection without the first
inequality in (2.25).  Every triple in that bijection
already satisfies this inequality by
Theorem 2.10.  Conversely, the remaining equations
and conditions in (2.25) imply all the hypotheses of
Theorem 2.3.  Thus adding the inequality preserves
the bijection.  Only finitely many positive integer roots lie below
the fixed number $\sqrt{R_\ell}$, proving finiteness.
$\square$

#### Corollary 2.15 (Integral center cutoff and disjoint finite strata)

For every positive odd integer $\ell$, put

$$
\begin{aligned}
A_\ell&=3\ell^6(\ell+2)^2-\nu_\ell\ell^4,
&B_\ell&=8\nu_\ell(\ell+1),\\
C_\ell&=\left\lfloor\sqrt{\left\lfloor
\frac{A_\ell-1}{B_\ell}\right\rfloor}\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2.26}
$$

These are well-defined integers with $A_\ell,B_\ell>0$ and $C_\ell\ge0$.
Every array in $\mathscr A_\ell$ has $\ell<c\le C_\ell$.
Let $\mathscr A$ denote the set of all canonical primitive square magic
arrays and let

$$
\mathcal L_0=\{\ell\in\mathbb Z_{\ge3}:\ell\text{ is odd and every prime
 divisor of }\ell\text{ is }1\text{ or }7\pmod8\}.
$$

Then there is an exact disjoint union

$$
\mathscr A=\coprod_{\ell\in\mathcal L_0}\mathscr A_\ell,
\tag{2.27}
$$

in which each stratum is the finite set characterized in
Theorem 2.14.  Equivalently, the inequality
$H_k^2<R_\ell$ there can be replaced by the integer inequality
$M_k\le C_\ell$.

**Proof.**

The estimate $\nu_\ell\le\ell^4$ gives

$$
A_\ell\ge\ell^6\bigl(3(\ell+2)^2-\ell^2\bigr)>0.
$$

As $A_\ell$ is an integer, $A_\ell\ge1$; hence the inner floor defining
$C_\ell$ is nonnegative.  The strict bound
(2.22) is $B_\ell c^2<A_\ell$.
For positive integer $c$ it is exactly equivalent to

$$
c^2\le\left\lfloor\frac{A_\ell-1}{B_\ell}\right\rfloor,
\qquad\text{or equivalently}\qquad c\le C_\ell.
$$

The lower inequality $\ell<c$ follows from $c^2=\ell^2+x+y$ and
$x,y>0$.  Under the exact Pell relation, substitution of
$H_k^2=2M_k^2-\ell^2$ makes the inequalities
$H_k^2<R_\ell$ and $M_k\le C_\ell$ equivalent.
Each array has a unique least root, and its least root belongs to
$\mathcal L_0$ by Proposition 1.16 and
Corollaries 2.7 and 2.11.
This proves both the union and its disjointness.
$\square$

The same integral formula gives a sharper cutoff. Replace $\nu_\ell$ by $\nu_\ell^*$ in (2.24) and (2.26), obtaining $R_\ell^*$ and $C_\ell^*$. Proposition 2.13 and the same strict-integer conversion show

$$
\ell<c\le C_\ell^*\le C_\ell.
\tag{2.27a}
$$

Both quantities remain positive or nonnegative as appropriate, since $\nu_\ell^*\le\ell^4$. Replacing $R_\ell$ or $C_\ell$ by these smaller cutoffs in the exact finite-stratum characterization preserves its bijection: every genuine triple satisfies the stronger bound, and all the original equations remain imposed.

#### Remark 2.16

The additive Pell condition accounts for seven entries of the array.
A nonempty set of exact Pell triples need not give a square magic
array, because the two square conditions in (2.7),
distinctness, and primitivity must still hold.  Moreover, finiteness of
each $\mathscr A_\ell$ does not imply finiteness of
$\bigcup_{\ell\ge1}\mathscr A_\ell$.  The center bounds in this chapter
depend on $\ell$ and are not absolute upper bounds on all centers.

### 2.7. Uniform cardinality bounds for minimum fibers

For a positive integer $n$, write $\tau(n)$ for the number of its
positive divisors and $v_p(n)$ for the exponent of the prime $p$ in $n$.
The notation $A\ll_\eta B$ means that $A\le C_\eta B$ for a positive
constant depending only on $\eta$.

#### Lemma 2.17 (Units and ideal counts)

The units $u\in\mathcal O$ with $u>0$ in the embedding
$\sqrt2>0$ and $N(u)=1$ are exactly

$$
u=(3+2\sqrt2)^n,\qquad n\in\mathbb Z.
$$

For every positive integer $n$, the number of nonzero integral ideals
of $\mathcal O$ of norm $n$ is at most $\tau(n)$.  For odd $\ell$, the
number of such ideals of norm $\ell^2$ is exactly

$$
\prod_{p\equiv1,7\pmod8}(2v_p(\ell)+1).
\tag{2.28}
$$

**External input.** The quadratic ring-of-integers, prime-splitting, ideal-factorization and unit theorems are used with $K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$, $\mathcal O_K=\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$, discriminant $8$, and fundamental positive norm-one unit $3+2\sqrt2$; see [28]. Formula (2.28) distributes each split-prime exponent between its two prime ideals.

#### Proposition 2.18 (Number of Pell orbits)

For every positive odd $\ell$,

$$
g_\ell\le
\prod_{p\equiv1,7\pmod8}(2v_p(\ell)+1)
\le\tau(\ell^2).
\tag{2.29}
$$

**Proof.**

Multiplication of $a=H+\sqrt2M$ by $\epsilon=3+2\sqrt2$ gives the
transformation (2.5).  Every orbit has a fixed
principal ideal $(a)$ of absolute norm $\ell^2$.  Conversely, if two
positive generators $a,a'$ of norm $-\ell^2$ generate the same ideal,
then $a'/a$ is a positive norm-one unit.  By
Lemma 2.17, it is a power of $\epsilon$, so the two
generators belong to the same orbit.  The orbits therefore inject into
the integral ideals of norm $\ell^2$.  Apply
(2.28).  No assertion that every ideal is
principal is required.
$\square$

#### Lemma 2.19 (Divisor estimate)

For every $\eta>0$, there is a constant $C_\eta$ such that
$\tau(n)\le C_\eta n^\eta$ for all positive integers $n$.

**External input.** This is the standard divisor estimate; see [29], Theorem 315, with the exponent $\eta$ corresponding to its arbitrary positive exponent.

#### Theorem 2.20 (Uniform size of minimum fibers)

For every $\eta>0$, the number of exact triples
$i<j<k$ in $\mathcal P_\ell$ satisfying
$H_i^2+H_j^2-H_k^2=\ell^2$ is $O_\eta(\ell^\eta)$, uniformly over
positive odd $\ell$.  In particular

$$
\#\mathscr A_\ell\ll_\eta\ell^\eta.
\tag{2.30}
$$

If

$$
N_{\min}(B)=\#\{\text{canonical primitive magic squares of squares}:
\ell\le B\},\qquad B\ge1,
$$

then

$$
N_{\min}(B)\ll_\eta B^{1+\eta}.
\tag{2.31}
$$

No separate upper bound on the center is imposed in this definition.

**Proof.**

The exact-triple bound (2.17) implies
$H_k\le A\ell^{7/2}$ for an absolute constant $A$.
For example, $(\ell+2)^2/(\ell+1)\le(9/2)\ell$ for $\ell\ge1$
gives $H_k^2<(27/8)\ell^7$.
Along each forward orbit,

$$
\frac{H'}H=3+4\frac MH>3+2\sqrt2=\epsilon.
$$

As its first root exceeds $\ell$, an orbit contains
$O(1+\log\ell)$ roots below $A\ell^{7/2}$, with an absolute constant.
By Proposition 2.18, the total number of roots below
this bound is

$$
O\bigl(\tau(\ell^2)(1+\log\ell)\bigr).
$$

The number of triples is no greater than the cube of this number.
Lemma 2.19, with an arbitrarily small positive exponent,
and $(1+\log\ell)^3\ll_\eta\ell^\eta$ give the asserted bound after
adjusting the exponents.  The exact bijection of
Theorem 2.3 bounds $\#\mathscr A_\ell$ by the number
of these triples.  Summing the resulting estimate for $\ell\le B$
proves (2.31).
$\square$

### 2.8. Counting minima through positive norms

For real numbers $C,B\ge1$, define

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal N(C,B)&=
\#\{\text{canonical primitive magic squares of squares}:
C\le c\le2C,\ \ell\le B\},\\
\mathcal L(C,B)&=
\{\ell\le B:\mathscr A_\ell\text{ contains an array with }
C\le c\le2C\}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2.32}
$$

These sets are finite by Theorem 2.14.

#### Theorem 2.21 (Norm bound for the number of minima)

Put

$$
K(C,B)=\left\lceil\frac{B^7}{C^2}\right\rceil-1.
\tag{2.33}
$$

If $K(C,B)=0$, then $\mathcal L(C,B)$ and the set counted by
$\mathcal N(C,B)$ are empty.  If $K=K(C,B)\ge1$, then

$$
\#\mathcal L(C,B)\ll K\log(2K)\log(2B),
\tag{2.34}
$$

with an absolute implied constant.  Consequently, for every $\eta>0$,

$$
\mathcal N(C,B)\ll_\eta
\min\bigl\{B^{1+\eta},\
B^\eta K\log(2K)\log(2B)\bigr\}.
\tag{2.35}
$$

**Proof.**

For any $\ell\in\mathcal L(C,B)$, Corollary 2.12 gives

$$
1\le\nu_\ell<\frac{\ell^7}{c^2}\le\frac{B^7}{C^2}.
$$

Since $\nu_\ell$ is an integer, it follows that
$1\le\nu_\ell\le K(C,B)$.  This proves the claim when $K=0$.

For each positive odd $\ell$, associate the algebraic integer

$$
\alpha_\ell=3\ell^2+2w_\ell\sqrt2\in\mathcal O.
$$

Its norm is $\nu_\ell$, and the definition of $w_\ell$ gives

$$
3\le\alpha_\ell<6\ell^2\le6B^2.
\tag{2.36}
$$

The map $\ell\mapsto\alpha_\ell$ is injective because its rational
coefficient is $3\ell^2$.

For a fixed positive norm $n\le K$, there are at most $\tau(n)$
integral ideals of norm $n$, by Lemma 2.17.
Positive generators of any one principal ideal that have norm $n$
differ by positive norm-one units, hence by powers of
$\epsilon=3+2\sqrt2$.  The multiplicative sequence of such generators
has at most

$$
1+\frac{\log(6B^2)}{\log\epsilon}
$$

members in $[1,6B^2)$.  Both endpoints of this interval are used:
positivity without the lower bound would allow arbitrarily many
negative powers of $\epsilon$.
It follows that the number of possible $\alpha_\ell$ is

$$
\ll\log(2B)\sum_{n\le K}\tau(n).
$$

The elementary identity and estimate

$$
\sum_{n\le K}\tau(n)
=\sum_{a\le K}\left\lfloor\frac Ka\right\rfloor
\le K\sum_{a\le K}\frac1a
\le K(1+\log K)
$$

prove (2.34).  The argument counts all integral
ideals as an upper bound and does not require that each ideal be
principal.

For $\ell\le B$, Theorem 2.20 bounds
$\#\mathscr A_\ell$ by $O_\eta(B^\eta)$.  Multiplying this estimate
by (2.34) gives the second term of
(2.35); the first follows independently from
(2.31).
$\square$

If $B,C$ are positive integers, the integer in (2.33) also has
the exact expression

$$
K(C,B)=\left\lfloor\frac{B^7-1}{C^2}\right\rfloor.
\tag{2.37}
$$

The strict upper bound for $\nu_\ell$ explains the subtraction by one.

#### Corollary 2.22 (Minimum-height ranges)

For every fixed $\beta>2/7$ and every $\varepsilon>0$,

$$
\mathcal N(C,C^\beta)
\ll_{\varepsilon,\beta}
C^{\min\{\beta,7\beta-2\}+\varepsilon},\qquad C\ge1.
\tag{2.38}
$$

For $0\le\beta\le2/7$, the set counted by
$\mathcal N(C,C^\beta)$ is empty for every $C\ge1$.

**Proof.**

If $\beta\le2/7$, then $\ell\le C^\beta\le C^{2/7}$ and $c\ge C$
contradict $\ell>c^{2/7}$.
If $\beta>2/7$, then
$K(C,C^\beta)<C^{7\beta-2}$.  Theorem 2.21 gives,
for arbitrarily small $\eta>0$, the two bounds with powers
$\beta(1+\eta)$ and $7\beta-2+\beta\eta$, up to logarithmic factors.
Choose $\eta$ sufficiently small in terms of $\varepsilon$ and
$\beta$, and absorb the logarithms into a further positive power
smaller than $\varepsilon$.  This proves
(2.38).
$\square$

#### Corollary 2.23 (Relative minimum bound)

For $X\ge1$ and fixed $\beta\ge0$, put

$$
N_{\mathrm{rel},\beta}(X)=
\#\{\text{canonical primitive magic squares of squares}:
c\le X,\ \ell\le c^\beta\}.
$$

If $0\le\beta\le2/7$, then $N_{\mathrm{rel},\beta}(X)=0$.
If $\beta>2/7$, then for every $\varepsilon>0$,

$$
N_{\mathrm{rel},\beta}(X)
\ll_{\varepsilon,\beta}
X^{\min\{\beta,7\beta-2\}+\varepsilon}.
\tag{2.39}
$$

**Proof.**

The zero assertion follows immediately from
Corollary 2.12.  For the other assertion, partition the
positive center range into dyadic intervals
$2^j\le c<2^{j+1}$.  On such an interval, the relative condition
implies $\ell\le2^\beta(2^j)^\beta$.
The proof of Corollary 2.22 applies with any fixed
positive factor before $C^\beta$; that factor only changes the implied
constant.  Each interval therefore contributes

$$
O_{\varepsilon,\beta}
\bigl((2^j)^{\min\{\beta,7\beta-2\}+\varepsilon}\bigr).
$$

Since $\beta>2/7$, the exponent before $\varepsilon$ is positive.
Summing the resulting geometric progression through $2^j\le X$
proves (2.39).
$\square$

#### Remark 2.24 (Scope of the counting statements)

The estimates in this chapter are upper bounds; they do not assert
that any counted set is nonempty.  The exponent $7\beta-2$ is smaller
than $\beta$ precisely in the range $2/7<\beta<1/3$.
The relative condition $\ell\le c^\beta$ is distinct from the fixed
outer condition $\ell\le X^\beta$ on the entire range $c\le X$.
The dyadic argument above uses the corresponding condition.  Finally, these
minimum-sensitive estimates can be combined with any separately
proved bound for the full center range by taking the smaller of the
applicable upper bounds; no such additional estimate is assumed in
this chapter.

### 2.9. Effective fibers with bounded norm defect

#### Theorem 2.25 (Explicit bounded-defect heights)
 The norm defects
$\nu_\ell$ and $\nu_\ell^*$ provide another finite-fiber parameter, with
an explicit stopping height. Unlike fixed minimum-prime support, the
following result allows all prime supports to vary.

For an integer $N\ge1$, define the positive even integer

$$
 A_N=12^{7168}\max\{9,N\}^{1024}.
$$

Every pair $\ell,w\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$ satisfying
$1\le9\ell^4-8w^2\le N$ obeys

$$
 \boxed{\log\ell\le A_N,\qquad\log w\le A_N,\qquad
         \ell<3^{A_N}.}
 \tag{2.40}
$$

In particular, either of the strata $\nu_\ell\le N$ and
$\nu_\ell^*\le N$ contains only finitely many canonical primitive
full squares, and all their center roots satisfy the exact integer
cutoff

$$
 \boxed{c<3^{7A_N/2}.}
 \tag{2.41}
$$

There is no bound on the identities or number of minimum primes in
these assertions. The constants are explicit but are not asserted to
be practical search limits.

**Proof and external hypotheses.** Put $\nu=9\ell^4-8w^2$. Apply
Bérczes–Evertse–Győry, *Effective results for hyper- and superelliptic
equations over number fields*, Theorem 2.1, equation (2.4), to

$$
 f(X)=8X^2+\nu,\qquad b=9,\qquad f(w)=9\ell^4.
$$

The number field is $K=\mathbb Q$ and the set of places is
$S=\{\infty\}$, so the unknowns are rational integers. In the theorem's
notation $m=4,n=2,d=s=1$, $|D_K|=Q_S=1$, and
$\widehat h=\log\max\{9,\nu\}$. Its requirements $m\ge3,n\ge2$ hold;
$b$ is nonzero; and $f$ has no multiple roots, since its discriminant
is $-32\nu\ne0$. No Mordell--Weil basis, unproved rank assertion, or
additional conjecture is required by that theorem.

The theorem gives

$$
 h(w),h(\ell)
 \le(6ns)^{14m^3n^3s}|D_K|^{2m^2n^2}
      Q_S^{3m^2n^2}\exp(8m^2n^3d\widehat h)
 =12^{7168}\max\{9,\nu\}^{1024}\le A_N.
$$

For positive integers these absolute logarithmic heights equal their
natural logarithms. As $\exp(1)<3$, the first cutoff follows strictly.

For the original defect choose $w=w_\ell$; for the refined defect
choose $w=w_\ell^*$. Both are positive integers satisfying exactly
$\nu=9\ell^4-8w^2>0$. A primitive full square also obeys
$\nu_\ell c^2<\ell^7$ from Corollary 2.12, so $c<\ell^{7/2}$.
Combining the inequalities gives (2.41). The exponent
$7A_N/2$ is an integer because $A_N$ is even. This integer cutoff
avoids any reliance on uncertified floating-point exponential or
logarithmic comparisons.

#### Corollary 2.26 (Effective critical minimum bands)
 For every
specified rational $K>1$, put $N_K=\lceil K^7\rceil-1$. Then every
primitive full square satisfying

$$
 \ell\le Kc^{2/7}
$$

has $\nu_\ell<K^7$, because
$\nu_\ell c^2<\ell^7\le K^7c^2$. Consequently

$$
 \boxed{\ell\le Kc^{2/7}
       \quad\Longrightarrow\quad c<3^{7A_{N_K}/2}.}
 \tag{2.42}
$$

For $K=a/b>1$ with positive integers $a,b$, the constant is computed
without real rounding as $N_K=\lfloor(a^7-1)/b^7\rfloor$; for integer
$K\ge2$, it is simply $K^7-1$. The weaker condition
$\ell>c^{2/7}$ excluded only the unit-factor boundary. This corollary
gives a finite certified stopping height for every fixed rational
multiple above that boundary. It does not improve the unrestricted
center-counting power exponent or place every solution in such a band.

**Terminating decision procedure.** For a specified $N$, enumerate the
positive odd minima $\ell<3^{A_N}$, compute the selected defect exactly,
and retain only those at most $N$. The established prime restrictions
and minimum-entry exclusion can be applied before forming candidates.
For every retained minimum, the finite Pell lists and exact residual
square, distinctness, and gcd tests in Theorem 2.3 decide its full-square
fiber. Equivalently, the center cutoff above and the exact finite-center
offset inventory give a finite decision procedure. The assertion is
termination with a proved stopping bound; no bound on practical runtime
or successful construction is claimed.

The result does not follow by merely taking a finite union of the old
fixed-minimum bounds: they bound $\ell$ from a bound on $\nu_\ell$. Here the superelliptic theorem supplies that missing
reverse bound. It does not make the six-variable minimum-support
$S$-unit theorem effective: no bound on the defect is known from a
specified minimum support alone. Similarly, it supplies no effective
height for all fixed slopes or step classes. Letting $N$ vary again
leaves an unbounded union; global finiteness and an effective absolute
center bound remain unproved.

**External dependency.** A. Berczes, J.-H. Evertse and K. Gyory,
*Effective results for hyper- and superelliptic equations over number
fields*, Publicationes Mathematicae Debrecen **82/3-4** (2013), 727--756,
Theorem 2.1 and equation (2.4), printed page 730;
<https://doi.org/10.5486/PMD.2013.5748>. The same statement is on printed
page 4 of <https://arxiv.org/pdf/1301.7168>. The source defines $\widehat h$ using
the coefficients of $f$ and $b$ together, which accounts for the factor
$\max\{9,\nu\}$. This specialization is an application of an explicit
published height theorem, not a proof of that external theorem.

### 2.10. Quantitative escape and exact bounded-defect minimum generation

#### Corollary 2.27 (Explicit minimum escape)

Retain
$A_N=12^{7168}\max\{9,N\}^{1024}$ from Theorem 2.25, and set
$C_N=3^{7A_N/2}$ for integers $N\ge1$. Every primitive full square with
$c\ge C_N$ satisfies

$$
 \boxed{\nu_\ell>N,\qquad \nu_\ell^*>N,\qquad
              \ell^7>(N+1)c^2.}
 \tag{2.43}
$$

The first two assertions are contrapositives of the corresponding
bounded-defect height cutoffs. Since $\nu_\ell$ is an integer and
$\nu_\ell c^2<\ell^7$, the third follows. This is an exact integer
staircase of necessary height restrictions, requiring no approximate
logarithmic rejection test.

There is also a convenient asymptotic form with explicit constants.
For every primitive full square with $c\ge C_9$,

$$
 \boxed{\begin{aligned}
 \nu_\ell
 &>\frac{1}{12^7}\left(\frac27\log c\right)^{1/1024},\\
 \ell
 &>\frac1{12}\,c^{2/7}
                \left(\frac27\log c\right)^{1/7168}.
 \end{aligned}}
 \tag{2.44}
$$

Indeed $c\ge C_9$ gives $\nu_\ell>9$. The explicit superelliptic bound
and the original minimum cone then give

$$
 \frac27\log c<\log\ell
 \le12^{7168}\nu_\ell^{1024}.
$$

Taking positive roots proves the first assertion; insert it into
$\ell^7>\nu_\ell c^2$ to obtain the second. These inequalities improve
the power-law minimum-to-center boundary by a logarithmic factor, without
changing its power exponent. In particular, on any sequence of primitive
full squares whose center roots satisfy $c\to\infty$,
$\ell/c^{2/7}\longrightarrow\infty$. This statement is conditional on
such a sequence existing and does not assert existence.

#### Proposition 2.28 (All-height count and norm-orbit generation)
 For $N\ge1$, let
$M(N)$ count the positive odd integers $\ell$ with $\nu_\ell\le N$.
Then

$$
 \boxed{M(N)\le(2A_N+2)\operatorname{isqrt}(9N)
                  \bigl(\operatorname{isqrt}(4N)+1\bigr)
       \ll N^{1025}.}
 \tag{2.45}
$$

Here $\operatorname{isqrt}(m)=\lfloor\sqrt m\rfloor$. The implied constant is absolute and very large. The same upper bound
holds for minima with $\nu_\ell^*\le N$, since these form a subset.
These are counts of minima with no center cap, not counts of full
magic squares.

To prove the assertion, associate to each minimum
$\alpha_\ell=3\ell^2+2w_\ell\sqrt2$. It is an algebraic integer with
positive norm $\nu_\ell\le N$, and

$$
 1\le\alpha_\ell<6\ell^2
       <6\cdot3^{2A_N}<3^{2A_N+2}.
$$

The map is injective because its rational coefficient is $3\ell^2$.
Let $n=N(\alpha_\ell)$ and $\epsilon=3+2\sqrt2$. Since its irrational
coefficient is positive, $\alpha_\ell>\sqrt n$. There is a unique
integer $k\ge0$ for which
$\beta=\alpha_\ell\epsilon^{-k}$ lies in
$[\sqrt n,\epsilon\sqrt n)$. It is still an algebraic integer, say
$\beta=a+b\sqrt2$. Writing $t=\beta/\sqrt n$ gives

$$
 a=\frac{\sqrt n}{2}(t+t^{-1})<3\sqrt n,\qquad
 0\le b=\frac{\sqrt n}{2\sqrt2}(t-t^{-1})<2\sqrt n.
$$

Thus its integer coordinates lie in the box
$1\le a\le\operatorname{isqrt}(9N)$,
$0\le b\le\operatorname{isqrt}(4N)$. Since $\beta\ge\sqrt n\ge1$
and $\epsilon>3$, the displayed upper bound on $\alpha_\ell$ implies
$0\le k\le2A_N+1$. The seed box and this exponent range give the exact
count. Finally $A_N\ll N^{1024}$ and the box contains $O(N)$ pairs.

**Exact norm-orbit generation.** The same proof gives an enumeration of
all minima counted by $M(N)$ without scanning every integer below
$3^{A_N}$:

1. In the displayed integer box, retain $(a,b)$ exactly when
   $1\le n=a^2-2b^2\le N$ and $9b^2<4a^2$. These conditions are
