phase point is discarded by division there. All actual phases are
nonzero and finite, so none occurs at a zero or pole of $u,v,w$.

Faltings' theorem makes $H_k(K)$ finite for every fixed admissible
$k$. For bounded $P$ there are finitely many coefficient quadruples
and hence finitely many $k$ and phase tuples. The exact Cartesian
denominator $c_0^2$ of each $T_i$ then gives finitely many $c_0$;
also $B\le P$. This proves (U-ORIENT-RANK-FIN), including all
prime supports and slopes in its domain. The case $c_0=1$ already
has $c=B\le P$.

**4. The effective rank-at-most-two branch.**
The basis-column argument shows that at most two projective row
directions occur. Thus the four imaginary-part forms lie on one
or two unit circles. Clear their coefficient denominators by
$P^2$, using $E_i\mid P$. The two rows
$l_3-l_1-l_2=0$, $l_4-l_1+l_2=0$ have integer entries bounded
by $3P^2$. The elementary independence and nonzero binary
norm-difference argument of (U-ORIENT-HEIGHT) applies with arbitrary
rational unit coefficients; it does not use the locations of exceptions.
Its $2\times2$ minors are bounded by $K_0=18P^4$.
The same rational-root and unit-normalization estimate gives
$c_0^4\le512K_0^6$, hence $c_0<384P^6$.
Multiplication by $B$ proves the asserted height bound.
With only one circle, a nonzero cleared row gives the stronger
$c_0^2\le3\sqrt2P^2$, so this case is included too.

**Meaning of the restriction.** For fixed $D$, every sequence
of primitive full squares with $P\le D$ and $c\to\infty$ must
have orientation rank four eventually. In particular it must have
at least four projective orientation blocks. The statement permits
$P\to\infty$ as slowly as $c^{o(1)}$ and supplies no bound for
rank four. Its finiteness conclusion is restricted to bounded $P$ and
orientation rank at most three; it supplies no absolute center bound.

The proof is a structural extension of the repeated-row
finiteness theorem, not an additional equation on the exact locus.
It constrains a specified all-slope family that the repeated-row theorem
left open. The algebra and finite sign classification have two
independent implementations; the infinite arithmetic conclusion
also uses the written argument and Faltings' theorem. 

**Corollary 7.3 (Three genus-one quotients of the phase curve).**
Let $H_k$ be (U-ORIENT-GENUS3), with $k\in K^{\times2}$,
$N(k)=1$, $K=\mathbb Q(i)$. Choose $t\in K$ with $t^2=-k$,
and write

$$
 a=k^2-6k+1,\quad b=12k(1-k),\quad
 q=-6k(k^2-4k+1).
$$

In addition to the degree-two map $(v,h)\mapsto(v^2,h)$ to
$E_0:\ h^2=D_k(Y)$, there are degree-two maps to

$$
\begin{split}
 E_+:\ z^2&=a(u^2-2t)^2+b(u^2-2t)+q+2ka,\\
 E_-:\ z^2&=a(u^2+2t)^2+b(u^2+2t)+q+2ka,\\
 \phi_+(v,h)&=(v+t/v,h/v^2),\\
 \phi_-(v,h)&=(v-t/v,h/v^2).
\end{split}
\tag{U-ORIENT-THREE-QUOTIENTS}
$$

These affine maps extend to morphisms of smooth projective curves.
All three quotient curves are smooth of genus one. Their Jacobians
are elliptic curves over $K$, and

$$
 \operatorname{Jac}(H_k)\ \sim_K\
 \operatorname{Jac}(E_0)\times
 \operatorname{Jac}(E_+)\times\operatorname{Jac}(E_-).
 \tag{U-ORIENT-JACOBIAN-SPLIT}
$$

A $K$-point is not assumed on a quotient merely from its equation;
an actual phase point supplies one by the displayed maps.

**Proof.** The identity

$$
 D_k(v^2)/v^4
 =a(v^2-k/v^2)^2+b(v^2-k/v^2)+q+2ka
$$

gives the maps. Each $E_\pm$ has the form $z^2=au^4+B_\pm u^2+C_\pm$,
where

$$
 B_\pm=b\mp4at,\quad C_\pm=q-2ka\mp2bt
     =4kQ_\pm,\quad
 Q_\pm=-2k^2+9k-2\pm6t(k-1).
$$

The exact identities

$$
 B_\pm^2-4aC_\pm=16k(k^2+1)^2,\qquad
 Q_+Q_-=(k^2+4)(4k^2+1)
$$

show that their even quartics have discriminants
$16384k^3(k^2+1)^4aQ_\pm\ne0$.
Thus all three are smooth genus-one curves. The maps have degree
two, as $v$ satisfies respectively $v^2=Y$,
$v^2-uv+t=0$, or $v^2-uv-t=0$.

Their invariant differential pullbacks are

$$
 2v\,dv/h,\qquad (v^2-t)\,dv/h,\qquad(v^2+t)\,dv/h.
$$

Their determinant relative to $(dv/h,v\,dv/h,v^2\,dv/h)$ is
$4t\ne0$. The induced homomorphism from $\operatorname{Jac}(H_k)$
to the product of the three elliptic Jacobians therefore has full
differential rank and is an isogeny.

On $v\ne0$, the two latter quotient points must satisfy the exact
synchronization conditions

$$
 u_+^2-u_-^2=4t,\qquad z_+=z_-.
 \tag{U-ORIENT-QUOTIENT-SYNC}
$$

Conversely these equations recover
$v=(u_++u_-)/2\ne0$ and $h=z_+v^2$, hence a point of $H_k$.
This recovers the phase-curve point only; the preceding finite phase
reconstruction and all norm-one, positivity and original-square
conditions must still be checked. Existence or positive rank on
separate quotients is not a simultaneous-lifting certificate.
The splitting gives access to elliptic arithmetic, but no ranks,
height levels, or complete point determination are asserted
uniformly in $k$.

**Corollary 7.4 (Transfer to all final classes on the eight-square locus).**
Let $C,x,y$ be positive integers with $0<y<x$, $x+y<C$, $x\ne2y$,
such that the eight numbers $C\pm x,C\pm y,C\pm(x+y),C\pm(x-y)$
are distinct integer squares and their eight roots have gcd one.
The center $C$ need not be a square. Let $A_i$ be the four opposite-pair
root gcds and put $P=\prod_iA_i$. With

$$
 Z_i=(u_i+v_i)/2+i(u_i-v_i)/2,\qquad N(Z_i)=C,
$$

write $j_{i,p}=v_{\pi_p}(Z_i)-v_{\bar\pi_p}(Z_i)$ at
$p^E\Vert C$. For a balanced prime $j_{i,p}=0$, necessarily $E$
is even. Put

$$
 B_i=\prod_{j_{i,p}=0}p^{E/2},\quad B=\prod_iB_i,
 \quad C_0=C/B^2,
 \quad S=(\operatorname{sgn}j_{i,p})_{i,p\mid C_0}.
$$

As before use rank zero when $C_0=1$.
Then for each fixed $D$,

$$
 \boxed{\{\text{primitive eight-square arrays}:P\le D,
             \ \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Q}S\le3\}
             \text{ is finite}.}
 \tag{U-EIGHT-ORIENT-RANK-FIN}
$$

Moreover, without restricting the positions of pair gcds,

$$
 \boxed{\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Q}S\le2
   \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
   C<384^2B^2P^{12}\le384^2P^{14}.}
 \tag{U-EIGHT-ORIENT-RANK2-HEIGHT}
$$

If $C=d h^2$, $d$ squarefree, then $B\mid P\mid h$. Thus bounded
$h$ and rank at most three give finiteness across all slopes and all
final classes $d$; at rank at most two there is the effective bound
$d<384^2h^{12}$. For a fixed reduced slope $r=m/n$,

$$
 P^2\mid nm(n+m)(n-m),\qquad
 C<384^2\{nm(n^2-m^2)\}^{7}
 \quad(\operatorname{rank}S\le2).
 \tag{U-EIGHT-ORIENT-SLOPE-HEIGHT}
$$

The sharper estimates remain valid under their additional
no-edge-exception or unbalanced hypotheses.

**Proof.** The primitive eight-square normalization already used
in (U-EIGHT-TWO-COLUMN-HEIGHT) gives an odd center with all primes
$1\bmod4$, pairwise coprime $A_i$, and $A_i^2\mid C$.
It does not require $C$ to be square. Extremize on $C_0$:

$$
 T_i=\prod_{p^E\Vert C_0}(\pi_p/\bar\pi_p)^{E\sigma_{i,p}},
 \qquad Z_i^2/C=\gamma_iT_i.
$$

Both Cartesian coordinates of $T_i$ have exact denominator $C_0$.
The coefficients have denominators dividing
$E_i^2$, where $E_i=A_iB/B_i^2\mid P$, as in the full-square case.
Crucially each $\gamma_i$ is still a Gaussian square. At an
unbalanced prime the correction exponent is

$$
 j_{i,p}-E\operatorname{sgn}(j_{i,p})
 =-2\min\{v_{\pi_p}(Z_i),v_{\bar\pi_p}(Z_i)\}
                     \operatorname{sgn}(j_{i,p}),
$$

which is even. At a removed balanced prime, the exponent in every
other row is $\pm E$, again even. Squared Gaussian unit factors
also contribute Gaussian squares. Thus the argument excluding
$k=\pm i$ survives the nonsquare center; it is not an assumption
that the individual $Z_i^2/C$ are Gaussian squares.

All the repeated-row unit-circle arguments and the genus-three
argument apply with these same coefficients. Finitely many phases
bound the exact denominator $C_0$, and $B\le P$, proving finiteness.
For rank at most two, the common denominator and minor estimates
are $P^2$ and $18P^4$, so
$C_0^2\le512(18P^4)^6<384^4P^{24}$, proving the height bound.
If $C_0=1$, $C=B^2\le P^2$ already suffices.

Finally the primitive fixed-slope identities give
$A_i^2=\gcd(C,n_i)$ for $(n_i)=(n,m,n+m,n-m)$.
They give the displayed divisibility and height bound. On an actual
normalized intermediate $\mathcal K_r$ point, this $d$ is exactly
its final denominator class. Thus the theorem controls a specified
branch of the simultaneous-lifting problem across varying classes.
It does not force $d=1$, bound unbounded $h$ or $P$, or constrain the
remaining rank-four arrays. Nor is the full-square half-class
criterion for small orientation rank extended to nonsquare centers.

### 7.9. Explicit finite phase enclosures on the original surface
Write the projective full-root surface in coordinates
$[c:u_1:v_1:\cdots:u_4:v_4]$ as

$$
 u_i^2+v_i^2=2c^2\quad(1\le i\le4),\qquad
 u_3^2=u_1^2+u_2^2-c^2,\qquad
 u_4^2=u_1^2-u_2^2+c^2.
 \tag{U-PHASE-ROOT-SURFACE}
$$

On $c\ne0$, put $\alpha=(u_1^2-c^2)/c^2$ and
$\beta=(u_2^2-c^2)/c^2$. Thus $u_i^2/c^2=1+L_i$ and
$v_i^2/c^2=1-L_i$, where
$(L_1,L_2,L_3,L_4)=(\alpha,\beta,\alpha+\beta,\alpha-\beta)$.
The admissible canonical chamber has
$0<\beta<\alpha$, $\alpha+\beta<1$, and $\alpha\ne2\beta$.
All equations below use these original root coordinates; no new
independent variables are introduced.

Set

$$
 Z_i=\frac{u_i+v_i}{2}+i\frac{u_i-v_i}{2},\qquad z_i=Z_i/c.
$$

Then $Z_i\overline Z_i=c^2$, and the actual phases from
(U-ORIENT-CORRECTIONS) are $\rho_i=z_i^2$. Define the following
finite set of twenty integer characters:

$$
 \mathcal C=\{e_i+e_j,e_i-e_j:1\le i<j\le4\}
 \ \cup\ \{(1,\epsilon_2,\epsilon_3,\epsilon_4):\epsilon_j=\pm1\}.
 \tag{U-PHASE-CHARACTERS}
$$

For $m\in\mathcal C$, let $n=|\operatorname{supp}m|\in\{2,4\}$,
and define rational homogeneous polynomials of degree $n$ by

$$
 W_m=\prod_{m_i=1}Z_i\prod_{m_i=-1}\overline Z_i=A_m+iB_m.
$$

On the surface,

$$
 A_m^2+B_m^2=c^{2n},\qquad
 \lambda_m=W_m/c^n=\prod_i z_i^{m_i},\qquad N(\lambda_m)=1.
$$

At a rational point, its Cayley index $\tau_m\in\mathbb P^1(\mathbb Q)$
is the unique $[a:b]$ such that

$$
 \lambda_m=\frac{b^2-a^2+2iab}{a^2+b^2}.
 \tag{U-PHASE-CAYLEY}
$$

Equivalently $\tau_m=[B_m:A_m+c^n]$ off $\lambda_m=-1$;
at that point use the other chart $[c^n-A_m:B_m]=[1:0]$.
For primitive integers $a,b$, its height is
$H(\tau_m)=\max(|a|,|b|)$.

**Theorem 7.5 (Explicit proper fibers and bounded-index enclosure).**
For every $m\in\mathcal C$ and every rational index $[a:b]$, the equation

$$
 \boxed{F_{m,a,b}=(a^2+b^2)c^n-(b^2-a^2)A_m-2abB_m=0}
 \tag{U-PHASE-FIBER}
$$

defines a proper closed subset of the full-root surface. On $c\ne0$
its geometric zero set is exactly the fiber $\tau_m=[a:b]$; scheme
multiplicity is not asserted to be one.

For a positive integer $M$, let

$$
 \mathcal T_M=\{[a:b]\in\mathbb P^1(\mathbb Q):H([a:b])\le M\},
 \qquad
 G_M=\prod_{m\in\mathcal C}\prod_{[a:b]\in\mathcal T_M}F_{m,a,b}.
 \tag{U-PHASE-ENCLOSURE-POLYNOMIAL}
$$

Use the unique primitive representative with $b>0$, or $(a,b)=(1,0)$.
Then

$$
 \boxed{Z_M=X\cap V(G_M)\subsetneq X,\qquad
 \dim Z_M\le1,\qquad
 \deg G_M\le56(2M^2+M+1).}
 \tag{U-PHASE-ENCLOSURE-PROPER}
$$

On $c\ne0$, $Z_M$ is the union of precisely the twenty characters'
fibers with index height at most $M$. The displayed factored polynomial
is an explicit finite equation; expanding it is unnecessary.

**Proof of the fiber identity.** Write $C=c^n$,
$d=a^2+b^2$, $e=b^2-a^2$, and $f=2ab$. Direct expansion gives

$$
 (dA_m-eC)^2+(dB_m-fC)^2-2dC F_{m,a,b}
   =d^2(A_m^2+B_m^2-C^2).
$$

For a set-theoretic proof over an algebraic closure, put
$\kappa=(e+if)/d$ and $\lambda=W_m/C$. Both are nonzero and
have inverse given by the conjugate expression. Therefore

$$
 2\kappa\lambda\,\frac{F_{m,a,b}}{dC}
       =-(\lambda-\kappa)^2.
 \tag{U-PHASE-FIBER-IDENTITY}
$$

This proves the exact fiber assertion even over non-real fields.

**Proof of properness on the original surface.** On $c=1$, the
function field over $\mathbb Q(i)(\alpha,\beta)$ is obtained by
adjoining the eight roots $\sqrt{1+L_i},\sqrt{1-L_i}$. The eight
linear polynomials are distinct. Valuation at each of their lines
shows that no nonempty product is a square, even over
$\overline{\mathbb Q}(\alpha,\beta)$. Hence this is a degree-$256$
multiquadratic extension, with basis the monomials in the eight roots
having each exponent zero or one. This also verifies geometric
integrality on the chart under consideration.

Every monomial of $A_m$ or $B_m$ selects exactly one root from each
pair indexed by $\operatorname{supp}m$ and no root from another pair.
It therefore belongs to a nonconstant basis word. The constant basis
coefficient of $F_{m,a,b}$ is the nonzero integer $a^2+b^2$.
Consequently $F_{m,a,b}\notin I_X$. This proof tests the actual
surface ideal, not merely whether an ambient expression is nonzero.
Since $I_X$ is prime, their finite product is nonzero modulo $I_X$.
This proves properness and the dimension bound. There are twelve
characters of degree two and eight of degree four, for a total of
$56$. Enumerating $1\le b\le M$, $-M\le a\le M$, and the single
infinite index gives $|\mathcal T_M|\le2M^2+M+1$, proving the degree
bound. $\square$

For example, for $m=(1,-1,0,0)$, equation (U-PHASE-FIBER) is

$$
 2(a^2+b^2)c^2-(b^2-a^2)(u_1u_2+v_1v_2)
                -2ab(u_1v_2-v_1u_2)=0.
 \tag{U-PHASE-PAIR-EXAMPLE}
$$

The left side is $2F_{m,a,b}$.

**Theorem 7.6 (Arithmetic containment for bounded deficits and rank at most three).**
For the primitive full-square data of (U-ORIENT-CORRECTIONS),

$$
 \boxed{\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Q}S\le3
    \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    \min_{m\in\mathcal C}H(\tau_m)\le2PB^2\le2P^3.}
 \tag{U-PHASE-INDEX-BOUND}
$$

Consequently, for every fixed positive integer $D$,

$$
 \boxed{\{Q\in\mathscr A:P\le D,\ \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Q}S\le3\}
      \subset Z_{2D^3}\subsetneq X.}
 \tag{U-PHASE-STRATUM-CONFINEMENT}
$$

The containing polynomial has degree at most
$448D^6+112D^3+56$. This is a finite, explicitly indexed geometric
enclosure of that arithmetic stratum, uniform over slopes and center
prime supports. It does not establish an enclosure of every
admissible rational point.

**Proof.** The exhaustive sign-matrix dichotomy in
(U-ORIENT-RANK-FIN) gives a character $m\in\mathcal C$ with
$m^{\mathsf T}S=0$: repeated projective rows give a two-supported
character, and four distinct rows of rank three give a relation with
four coefficients of absolute value one. If $c_0=1$, use any pair
character. Thus $\prod_iT_i^{m_i}=1$ and

$$
 \lambda_m^2=\prod_i\rho_i^{m_i}=\prod_i\gamma_i^{m_i}.
$$

Choose $q_i\in\mathbb Q(i)$ with $q_i^2=\gamma_i$ and $N(q_i)=1$.
Because $E_i^2\gamma_i\in\mathbb Z[i]$, the element $E_iq_i$ is
integral over $\mathbb Z[i]$. Its integral closedness gives
$E_iq_i\in\mathbb Z[i]$. Inverting $q_i$ just conjugates it.
It follows that
$\lambda_m=\pm\prod_iq_i^{m_i}$ has Cartesian denominator dividing

$$
 N_m=\prod_{i\in\operatorname{supp}m}E_i
       \ \mid\ \prod_iE_i=PB^2\le P^3.
$$

Write $\lambda_m=(r+is)/N_m$ with integers $r,s$;
$r^2+s^2=N_m^2$. Unless $\lambda_m=-1$, its Cayley index is
$[s:N_m+r]$, whose primitive height is at most $2N_m$.
The omitted index is $[1:0]$ and has height one. This proves the
bound and hence containment by the explicit fiber theorem. $\square$

**Corollary 7.7 (Every fixed enclosure has finitely many admissible points).**
For every fixed $M$, the set $Z_M(\mathbb Q)\cap\mathscr A$ is finite,
without assumptions on $P$ or orientation rank.

$$
 |Z_M(\mathbb Q)\cap\mathscr A|<\infty.
 \tag{U-PHASE-FIXED-ENCLOSURE-FIN}
$$

This is ineffective and does not determine the points or assert emptiness.

**Proof.** It suffices to fix a character and its unit value
$\lambda_m=\kappa$. For a two-supported character, the actual phases
satisfy $\rho_i\rho_j^{\pm1}=\kappa^2$. Thus two imaginary parts
are fixed rational unit linear forms on a common unit circle, and
the other two lie on two further unit circles. The proof of
(U-ORIENT-PAIR-COVER) applies directly to these fixed coefficients;
its genus-three and genus-five alternatives do not require any
factorization or denominator hypothesis. Parallel coefficient
vectors repeat absolute offsets; the shared-corner orthogonal
exception has no positive admissible point. All remaining cases
give finitely many phase tuples by Faltings and the stated treatment
of singular points.

For a four-supported character, put $\ell=(1,-1,-1,1)$ and replace
$\rho_i$ by $\rho'_i=\rho_i$ when $m_i=\ell_i$ and by
$\rho'_i=-\overline\rho_i$ otherwise. These replacements preserve
imaginary parts and Gaussian-square status. They give

$$
 k=\rho'_1\rho'_4/(\rho'_2\rho'_3)=\pm\kappa^2,
 \qquad k\in\mathbb Q(i)^{\times2},\quad N(k)=1.
$$

Choose square roots $s_j^2=\rho'_j$ of norm one for $j=1,2,3$.
Then $u=s_2s_3$, $v=s_1/s_3$, $w=s_1/s_2$ give the exact
parametrization
$(\rho'_1,\rho'_2,\rho'_3,\rho'_4)=(uvw,uv/w,uw/v,ku/(vw))$.
Consequently the same finite-fiber map to the smooth genus-three
curve (U-ORIENT-GENUS3) applies, now with $k$ fixed directly by
$\kappa$. Faltings over $\mathbb Q(i)$ again gives finitely many
phase tuples. Each tuple has finitely many square-root choices
$z_i$ and therefore finitely many normalized original root points.
The finite union over $m$ and $\kappa$ proves the assertion. $\square$

**Equations on the offset plane as well.** If an equation in the two
original normalized offsets is preferred, form

$$
 \mathcal N_M(\alpha,\beta)=
 \prod_{\epsilon\in\{\pm1\}^8}
 G_M(1,\epsilon_1u_1,\epsilon_2v_1,\ldots,
                         \epsilon_7u_4,\epsilon_8v_4),
 \tag{U-PHASE-OFFSET-NORM}
$$

and replace all root squares by $1\pm L_i$ after multiplying.
The product is invariant under each independent root sign, so it
is a polynomial in $\mathbb Q[\alpha,\beta]$. It is the field norm
of a nonzero element of the multiquadratic extension and is therefore
nonzero. Its degree is at most $128\deg G_M$. Every point in the
stratum of (U-PHASE-STRATUM-CONFINEMENT) projects to its zero set.
This supplies an elimination certificate that actually cuts the
original offset plane. Homogenization gives a corresponding equation
on a projective offset chart. Taking the finite union under the
square's symmetries covers alternative choices of canonical chamber.

### 7.10. Exact phase-denominator conservation across every orientation rank
For a primitive full square retain $z_i=Z_i/c$ and the twenty characters
$\mathcal C=\mathcal C_2\cup\mathcal C_4$ of (U-PHASE-CHARACTERS).
Write $q_m$ for the least positive integer clearing both Cartesian
coordinates of $\lambda_m=\prod_i z_i^{m_i}$. This is an arithmetic
function of a rational point, not a homogeneous coordinate on $X$.
At $p^e\Vert c$, the Gaussian valuations of $z_i$ are $j_{i,p}$ and
$-j_{i,p}$, with at least three of the four $|j_{i,p}|$ equal to $e$.
Put $a_{i,p}=e-|j_{i,p}|$; at most one is positive.

**Theorem 7.8 (Exact denominators, index heights and conservation).**
For every admissible rational point, without a bound on $P$ or
orientation rank,

$$
 q_m=\prod_{p\mid c}p^{|m\cdot j_p|},\qquad
 a_m^2+b_m^2=\delta_m q_m,\qquad
 \frac{q_m}{2}\le H(\tau_m)^2\le2q_m.
 \tag{U-PHASE-EXACT-DENOM}
$$

Here $[a_m:b_m]$ is the primitive Cayley index and $\delta_m=1$ for
opposite parities and $2$ for two odd coordinates. In particular
$h(\lambda_m)=\tfrac12\log q_m$ for the absolute logarithmic Weil
height over $\mathbb Q(i)$.

For each $i<j$, the complementary denominators satisfy

$$
 q_{e_i+e_j}q_{e_i-e_j}=c^2,\qquad
 \gcd(q_{e_i+e_j},q_{e_i-e_j})=A_iA_j.
 \tag{U-PHASE-COMPLEMENT}
$$

Consequently there are coprime positive integers $r_{ij},s_{ij}$ with

$$
 q_{e_i+e_j}=A_iA_jr_{ij}^2,\quad
 q_{e_i-e_j}=A_iA_js_{ij}^2,\quad
 r_{ij}s_{ij}=c/(A_iA_j).
$$

The complete products are

$$
 \boxed{\prod_{m\in\mathcal C_2}q_m=c^{12},\qquad
        \prod_{m\in\mathcal C_4}q_m=c^{12},\qquad
        \prod_{m\in\mathcal C}q_m=c^{24}.}
 \tag{U-PHASE-DENOM-CONSERVATION}
$$

For every four-supported character, $q_m/P$ is a positive integer
square. More generally, every subset $T\subset\mathcal C_4$ of size
$r$ satisfies

$$
 c^{b_r}P^{d_r}\mid\prod_{m\in T}q_m,
 \qquad
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrr}
 r&1&2&3&4&5&6&7&8\\\hline
 b_r&0&0&0&2&4&6&8&12\\
 d_r&1&2&3&2&1&0&1&0
\end{array}
 \tag{U-PHASE-SUBSET-DIVISIBILITY}
$$

**Proof.** Clearing a norm-one Gaussian rational requires exactly
$p^{|m\cdot j_p|}$ at each conjugate prime pair. Gaussian units do not
alter this integer denominator. For coprime $a,b$, the common divisor
of $a^2+b^2$, $b^2-a^2$ and $2ab$ is exactly one or two according to
the stated parity. This proves the exact index formula, including
$[1:0]$, and its height comparison. The normalized Weil height has
one negative Gaussian valuation of absolute size $|m\cdot j_p|$ per
prime and field degree two, giving the factor one-half.

At least one of $|j_i|,|j_j|$ is $e$. Therefore

$$
 |j_i+j_j|+|j_i-j_j|=2e,\qquad
 \min(|j_i+j_j|,|j_i-j_j|)=a_i+a_j.
$$

Both exponents have parity $a_i+a_j$. This proves the product, gcd,
and square quotients in (U-PHASE-COMPLEMENT).

For the four-supported characters, signs and permutations reduce the
local allocation column to $(t,e,e,e)$ with $0\le t\le e$.
Writing $a=e-t$, the sorted multiset of eight absolute dot products is

$$
 a,a,a,\quad2e-a,2e-a,2e-a,\quad2e+a,4e-a.
 \tag{U-PHASE-LOCAL-MULTISET}
$$

Its sum is $12e$, every entry is at least $a$ and congruent to $a$
modulo two, and the sum of its first $r$ entries is $b_re+d_ra$.
These primewise statements give the asserted divisibilities and the
four-character product. Multiplying the six complementary identities
gives the pair-character product. $\square$

There is an exact parity refinement. Let $\epsilon_i\in\{0,1\}$
record whether the imaginary numerator of $z_i$, with odd denominator,
is even or odd, and put $r=\sum_i\epsilon_i$. Reduction modulo two
in $\mathbb Z[i]$ gives

$$
 \delta_m=2^{\sum_{i\in\operatorname{supp}m}\epsilon_i\bmod2},
 \qquad
 \prod_{m\in\mathcal C}(a_m^2+b_m^2)
       =2^{\kappa}c^{24},
 \quad\kappa=2r(4-r)+8(r\bmod2)\in\{0,8,14\}.
 \tag{U-PHASE-INDEX-NORM-PRODUCT}
$$

Indeed each reduced phase is $1$ or $i$ modulo two, and inversion
has the same reduction. There are $2r(4-r)$ pair characters and
$8(r\bmod2)$ four-characters with odd parity. No fixed value of
$\kappa$ independent of root-sign choices is asserted.

**Consequences for simultaneous heights.** There is always a pair
of phases with the same $\epsilon_i$, so both complementary indices
have $\delta=1$. One of their denominators is at most $c$, giving

$$
 \min_{m\in\mathcal C}H(\tau_m)\le\sqrt c.
 \tag{U-PHASE-SMALL-INDEX}
$$

This is a height-dependent bound, not absolute confinement. If both
complementary indices are at most $M$, then $c\le2M^2$ by
(U-PHASE-COMPLEMENT). Thus for $c>2M^2$ at most six pair indices can
have height at most $M$.

If the four-character heights are ordered as
$H_{(1)}\le\cdots\le H_{(8)}$, then

$$
 H_{(r)}\ge2^{-1/2}c^{b_r/(2r)}P^{d_r/(2r)}.
 \tag{U-PHASE-ORDERED-HEIGHTS}
$$

This follows by applying (U-PHASE-SUBSET-DIVISIBILITY) to the $r$
smallest indices and $q_m\le2H_{(r)}^2$. In particular every
four-character index is at least $\sqrt{P/2}$, the fourth is at
least $(cP)^{1/4}/\sqrt2$, the sixth at least $c^{1/2}/\sqrt2$,
and the eighth at least $c^{3/4}/\sqrt2$.

The existing rank-at-most-three denominator bound sharpens its
index and enclosure bounds to

$$
 \operatorname{rank}S\le3\Longrightarrow
 \min_mH(\tau_m)\le\sqrt{2PB^2}\le\sqrt2 P^{3/2},
 \qquad
 \{P\le D,\operatorname{rank}S\le3\}\subset Z_{M_D},
 \quad M_D=\lfloor\sqrt{2D^3}\rfloor.
 \tag{U-PHASE-SHARP-ENCLOSURE}
$$

Thus the explicit containing degree is at most
$56(2M_D^2+M_D+1)=O(D^3)$. The $O(D^6)$ enclosure remains
valid but is subsumed by this one.

### 7.11. A finite enclosure including bounded rank-four contributions
Remove the balanced center factor $B$ and let $c_0=c/B$. For a
projective sign column $\sigma\in\{\pm1\}^4/\{\pm1\}$, set

$$
 C_\sigma=\prod_{p\mid c_0,\ [\operatorname{sgn}j_p]=\sigma}p^{e_p},
 \quad
 W_m=\prod_\sigma C_\sigma^{|m\cdot\sigma|},
 \quad
 K_m=\prod_{m\cdot\sigma\ne0}C_\sigma,
 \quad A=P/B.
$$

Signs of the representatives do not affect these quantities. Then

$$
 \frac{W_m}{A}\le q_m\le W_mPB^2,\qquad
 K_m^2\le W_m\le K_m^4,
 \tag{U-PHASE-WEIGHTED-COMPARISON}
$$

and hence

$$
 K_m\le\sqrt{2P/B}\,H(\tau_m),\qquad
 H(\tau_m)\le\sqrt{2PB^2}\,K_m^2.
 \tag{U-PHASE-BLOCK-CONCENTRATION}
$$

For an unbalanced prime,
$\big||m\cdot j_p|-e_p|m\cdot\sigma_p|\big| \le\sum_i(e_p-|j_{i,p}|)$; multiplying these error factors gives
$A=P/B$. At a balanced prime exactly one row is zero, and its
contribution to $q_m$ lies between one and $p^{3e_p}$. Thus the
remaining error is at most $B^3$, proving the first comparison.
Every nonzero character/sign dot product has absolute value two
or four, proving the second. The height comparisons follow from
(U-PHASE-EXACT-DENOM).

Let $R=\min_{m\in\mathcal C}K_m$. Equivalently, $R$ is the least
whole-prime-power factor that can be removed from $c_0$ so that the
remaining orientation columns have rational rank at most three.
Indeed deleting the support of one character leaves its kernel;
conversely every rank-at-most-three sign matrix has one of the
specified twenty characters in its kernel. Consequently

$$
 \boxed{\{Q\in\mathscr A:P\le D,\ R\le T\}
   \subset Z_{\lfloor\sqrt{2D^3T^4}\rfloor}\subsetneq X.}
 \tag{U-PHASE-RANK4-ENCLOSURE}
$$

Every such stratum has finitely many admissible rational points by
(U-PHASE-FIXED-ENCLOSURE-FIN). This includes rank-four matrices with
bounded contribution from columns outside a rank-three kernel, and
recovers the repeated-row theorem when $T=1$. Prime identities, exponents
and slopes in the remaining part are unrestricted. Neither $P$ nor
$R$ is bounded globally.

The denominator and primitive-index identities are arithmetic
relations. Taking reduced denominators is not an algebraic function
on freely scaled root coordinates, so these identities must not be
presented as additional polynomial equations cutting $X$. Their
products and simultaneous lower bounds alone do not bound the
smallest phase index.

### 7.12. Two distinct phase indices determine an effectively finite admissible set
The characters in (U-PHASE-CHARACTERS) are chosen up to overall sign,
so any two distinct members are linearly independent. For such $m,n$
and fixed rational Cayley indices $s,t$, let

$$
 V_{m,n;s,t}=X\cap V(F_{m,s},F_{n,t}).
$$

Here the polynomials are the original-coordinate quadratic or quartic
forms (U-PHASE-FIBER). Their degrees are $n_m=|\operatorname{supp}m|$
and $n_n=|\operatorname{supp}n|$.

**Theorem 7.9 (Uniform two-character finite-fiber certificate).**
No positive-dimensional geometric component of $V_{m,n;s,t}$ contains
an admissible rational point. Consequently its admissible rational
points are effectively enumerable, and their number is at most

$$
 \boxed{64n_mn_n\le1024.}
 \tag{U-PHASE-TWO-INDEX-FIN}
$$

This holds for every pair of distinct characters and every pair of
rational indices, without bounds on orientation rank, gcds, slopes,
or prime support. The assertion about components includes singular
rational points and intersections of conjugate components.

**1. Valuations on a projective curve.** Let $C$ be a geometric
irreducible curve in $X$ not contained in $c=0$, let $\widetilde C$
be its smooth projective normalization, and put
$d=\deg\nu^*\mathcal O_X(1)>0$. At a zero of the pulled-back center
section of order $e>0$, choose a local trivialization. The projective
root sections have no common zero. At most one of the four pairs
$(u_i,v_i)$ can vanish: if two do, then at $c=0$ two distinct linear
forms among $x,y,x+y,x-y$ vanish, forcing all root sections to vanish.
For each of the other three pairs, one of $Z_i,\overline Z_i$ is a
unit and their product has order $2e$. Therefore

$$
 \operatorname{ord}(z_i)=j_i\in[-e,e],\qquad
 \#\{i:|j_i|=e\}\ge3.
 \tag{U-PHASE-CURVE-VALUATIONS}
$$

No $z_i$ has a zero or pole away from $c=0$. Thus every character
constant on $C$ annihilates every such valuation column.

There are useful degree identities as well, taking degree zero for
a constant function:

$$
 \deg(\lambda_{e_i+e_j}|_{\widetilde C})+
 \deg(\lambda_{e_i-e_j}|_{\widetilde C})=d,
 \qquad
 \sum_{m\in\mathcal C_2}\deg(\lambda_m)=
 \sum_{m\in\mathcal C_4}\deg(\lambda_m)=6d.
 \tag{U-PHASE-CURVE-DEGREES}
$$

The degree of a rational function is half the sum of the absolute
orders of its divisor. Apply the complementary absolute-value identity
and the four-character multiset at every zero of $c$, then use
$\sum e=d$. These are identities on arbitrary curves, not assertions
that rational points lie on any chosen curve.

**2. The two-circle lemma used below.** The proof of
(U-ORIENT-PAIR-FIN) for one and two circle directions only assumes
fixed rational unit coefficient vectors and the two magic equations
$l_3=l_1+l_2$, $l_4=l_1-l_2$. It does not require Gaussian allocation
or denominator bounds. Its conclusion is that no nonconstant geometric
curve satisfying this fixed-coefficient system can pass through a point
with the required distinct nonzero offset values.

For one circle, if both linear relations vanished identically, their
unit coefficient vectors would satisfy $a_3=a_1+a_2$ and
$a_4=a_1-a_2$, contradicting the parallelogram identity for four unit
vectors. A nonzero linear relation cuts the circle finitely.
For two circles, on an admissible component the linear equations have
rank two. A rank failure in a singleton edge would give three rational
unit vectors forming an equilateral triangle, impossible over
$\mathbb Q$; singleton corners or coincident coefficient vectors force
repeated absolute offsets. The two-versus-two partitions have rank two
by the same norm comparison given in that proof. Their common kernel
is a plane. If the difference of the two circle norms vanished on this
plane, it would be the graph of a rational orthogonal map: projection
to either coordinate plane is injective because a rational vector of
zero Euclidean norm is zero. This again contradicts the parallelogram
identity for the four coefficient vectors. Otherwise a nonzero binary
quadratic has only finitely many projective zeros, each with at most
two unit normalizations. These arguments are algebraic over the fixed
rational coefficients and therefore also rule out a positive-dimensional
complex component through an admissible rational point.

**3. All character pairs.** Suppose a positive-dimensional component
contains an admissible rational point $Q$, and choose a geometric curve
$C$ in it through $Q$. It is not contained in $c=0$, and the character
values are the specified constants in $K=\mathbb Q(i)$ of norm one.
The following cases exhaust the 190 unordered pairs.

- **Two pair characters, same support (six pairs).** They fix $z_i^2$
  and $z_j^2$. Their imaginary parts fix two independent offsets and
  hence both $\alpha,\beta$, leaving only finitely many root choices.
- **Two pair characters, different supports (sixty pairs).** Sharing
  one index puts three phases in one circle direction and the fourth
  in a second direction. Disjoint supports put two phases in each of
  two directions. All connecting constants are in $K$ and have norm
  one. Squaring the root phases gives the actual phases $\rho_i$;
  the two-circle lemma applies.
- **A pair character and a four-character whose restricted signs
  align on the pair (forty-eight pairs).** Dividing their constant
  relations produces a second constant relation on the complementary
  pair. Apply the disjoint-pair case.
- **A pair character and a four-character with opposite relative
  signs on the pair (forty-eight pairs).** For the valuation argument,
  signs and relabeling reduce their kernels to
  $j_1+j_2=0$ and $j_1-j_2+j_3+j_4=0$. The first forces
  $|j_1|=|j_2|=e$, since otherwise two entries would be interior.
  The second then forces $j_3=j_4=-j_1$. Thus all divisor columns
  lie on one fixed line generated by a sign vector $\epsilon$.
  Normalize $\epsilon_1=1$ and put $T=z_1$. On the normalization,
  $z_i/T^{\epsilon_i}$ has zero divisor and is therefore constant.
  Evaluate it at any lift of $Q$: all phases are finite and nonzero
  there, so the constant equals
  $z_i(Q)/z_1(Q)^{\epsilon_i}\in K$ and has norm one. The one-circle
  lemma contradicts nonconstancy. This evaluation does not require
  the lift or the geometric component to be rational.
- **Two four-characters differing in one or three signs (sixteen
  pairs).** Up to overall sign, their difference fixes $2j_i=0$.
  The other three valuations must have absolute value $e$, but the
  remaining character relation is then a signed sum of three copies
  of $e$, which cannot vanish. Thus no zero of $c$ can occur on the
  curve, contradicting $d>0$.
- **Two four-characters differing in two signs (twelve pairs).**
  Their sum and difference give constant squares of two disjoint
  pair characters. Each pair character is consequently constant on
  the geometric component. Evaluating at $Q$ shows that its constant
  is itself in $K$ and has norm one, even if taking square roots of
  the originally given constants did not manifest this. The disjoint
  two-circle argument again applies.

The displayed counts sum to 190 and the elementary cases cover every
pair. Exact enumeration of all character kernels against all cube-edge
valuation directions gives the same classification. This proves that
no positive-dimensional component contains any admissible rational
point, including a rational singular point on such a component.

The remaining points are isolated. The surface is a degree-64 complete
intersection of six quadrics, so the isolated-point form of Bezout
bounds their number by $64n_mn_n$. Primary decomposition, removal of
positive-dimensional components, and exact zero-dimensional solving
therefore give a terminating enumeration algorithm. Each surviving
rational point is finally checked for positivity and distinctness.
$\square$

**Theorem 7.10 (Effective joint index-to-height bound).**
Let $H_X(Q)$ be the maximum absolute value of the primitive integral
root coordinates of an admissible rational point. There is an explicitly
specified computable absolute integer $C_*$ such that, for every two
distinct characters $m,n$,

$$
 \boxed{H_X(Q)\le C_*\max\{H(\tau_m(Q)),H(\tau_n(Q))\}^{128(n_m+n_n)}
       \le C_*\max\{H(\tau_m(Q)),H(\tau_n(Q))\}^{1024}.}
 \tag{U-PHASE-TWO-INDEX-HEIGHT}
$$

The constant is defined below by fixed universal resultants; its huge
numerical value is not evaluated. This supplies a finite algorithm and
a polynomial bound, not a practical unrestricted search cutoff.

**Proof and definition of the constant.** Clear each fiber equation by
$2^{n_m}$ or $2^{n_n}$. In nine homogeneous root variables take the six
fixed quadrics and these two integer forms, with degrees
$(d_1,\ldots,d_8)=(2,2,2,2,2,2,n_m,n_n)$, and put
$E=\prod_i d_i=64n_mn_n$. For eight distinct coordinates $X_1,\ldots,X_8$
consider the one-parameter deformation

$$
 f_i+tX_i^{d_i}\quad(1\le i\le8)
$$

and its resultant with a generic linear form $L_U=\sum_{j=0}^8U_jX_j$.
At $t=\infty$ the eight monomials have one projective common point,
so for generic $t$ the system is a zero-dimensional complete intersection
of degree $E$; the resultant $R(t,U)$ is nonzero. Every isolated point
$Q$ of the original system occurs as a limit of its deformed solutions.
Indeed its eight local equations have height eight in the regular
local ring of $\mathbb P^8$, hence form a regular sequence. In the
one-dimensional local deformation, $t$ is a parameter and a
nonzerodivisor; its finite local branches specialize to $Q$. This
is the local complete-intersection flatness argument and retains
singular isolated points with their multiplicities.

The product formula for the resultant over the deformed points now
shows that the first nonzero coefficient $R_e(U)$ of $t$ is divisible
by $L_Q(U)=\sum_j Q_jU_j$. One may normalize the projective coordinates
of each Puiseux branch to have a nonzero finite limit; the lowest-order
coefficient is the product of their limit linear forms, times a nonzero
scalar. Every admissible rational point is isolated by
(U-PHASE-TWO-INDEX-FIN), so this applies to all such points.

Let $\mathcal R_{n,n'}$ be the primitive universal integer homogeneous
resultant for degrees $(2,2,2,2,2,2,n,n',1)$, normalized up to sign,
and let $\|\mathcal R_{n,n'}\|_1$ be the sum of absolute coefficients.
For $M=\max(H(\tau_m),H(\tau_n))\ge1$, the cleared fiber coefficient
norm is at most $224M^2$; this follows from
$2^{n+1}+3\cdot2^{3n/2}\le224$ for $n\le4$.
Adding its deformation monomial is bounded by $256M^2$.
Each fixed quadric with its deformation has coefficient norm at most
five. The universal resultant has degree $E/d_i$ in the coefficients
of its $i$th polynomial. Submultiplicativity of coefficient norms gives

$$
 \|R_e\|_1\le C_{n,n'}M^{128(n+n')},\qquad
 C_{n,n'}=\|\mathcal R_{n,n'}\|_1\,
                 5^{3E}256^{64(n+n')},\quad E=64nn'.
$$

Define $C_*=\max_{n,n'\in\{2,4\}}C_{n,n'}$. This is a fixed finite
integer given by an effective algebraic construction; no unknown
rational points occur in its definition.

Finally use primitive integral coordinates for $Q$. Gauss' lemma makes
$L_Q$ an integer polynomial factor of $R_e$. Multiplicative Mahler
measure satisfies $\mathcal M(AB)=\mathcal M(A)\mathcal M(B)$,
$\mathcal M(B)\ge1$ for a nonzero integer polynomial, and
$\mathcal M(R_e)\le\|R_e\|_1$. Jensen's formula in the variable with
the largest coefficient of a linear form gives
$\mathcal M(L_Q)\ge\max_j|Q_j|$. Hence
$H_X(Q)\le\|R_e\|_1$, proving the bound. The Mahler statements follow
by iterated one-variable Jensen integration; no arithmetic conjecture
or effective version of Faltings is used. $\square$

Ordering all twenty Cayley heights increasingly as $H_{[1]},H_{[2]},\ldots$
gives the unconditional all-rank restriction

$$
 H_{[2]}\ge(H_X(Q)/C_*)^{1/1024}.
 \tag{U-PHASE-SECOND-INDEX-ESCAPE}
$$

At a sufficiently high point, at most one index can fall below this
explicit polynomial threshold. The fixed-enclosure finiteness
already implies that the smallest index escapes along every unbounded-height
sequence, but without an effective rate. A bound for one index gives the ineffective finite
fiber; bounds for two give effective enumeration and the displayed
height bound. None supplies an absolute bound for the smallest index,
and none proves global geometric confinement.

**A higher-descent layer.** The matrix formulas below are imported from Xu, arXiv:2609.03238v2, Proposition 3.4 and Theorems 4.8–4.10. Their higher-reciprocity proof is an external dependency. For $a,b\equiv1\bmod8$, $(a/b)=1$, put $U=[a/b]_4$, $V_4=[b/a]_4$, $\mathcal R=[2,a,b]_{\rm R}$, $c_\ell=[(1+\sqrt2)/\ell]$, and $e_\ell=(\ell-1)/8\bmod2$. The pure Cassels matrices are

$$
C_{ab}=\begin{pmatrix}X&Y\\Y^t&Z\end{pmatrix},\quad
X=\begin{pmatrix}0&\mathcal R\\\mathcal R&0\end{pmatrix},\
Y=\begin{pmatrix}c_a+V_4&V_4\\U&c_b+U\end{pmatrix},\
Z=\begin{pmatrix}0&U+V_4\\U+V_4&0\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{22m}
$$

For $2ab$, replace $Y$ by
$\left(\begin{smallmatrix}e_a+V_4&V_4+\mathcal R\\U+\mathcal R&e_b+U\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.
Their Selmer dimensions are four. No analytic BSD or representation-defect assertion from that source is needed here.

The character identity
$((1+\sqrt2)/p)=((1+\sqrt{-1})/p)$ for $p\equiv1\bmod8$ identifies $c_p=0$ with $8\mid h(-4p)$. If a step in this layer is forced to have rank at least three, the alternating matrix must vanish: for $ab$ this requires
$c_a=c_b=U=V_4=\mathcal R=0$; for $2ab$ it requires
$e_a=e_b=U=V_4=\mathcal R=0$, hence $a,b\equiv1\bmod16$.
If both kernels $ab$ and $2ab$ occur on rank-three branches, all these bits vanish.

There is also a coordinate-level link to (22h). Write
$\mu=[a^{u_a}b^{u_b}]$, $\eta=[2a^{v_a}b^{v_b}]$.
In the source's basis $(\Lambda_a,\Lambda_b,\Lambda'_a,\Lambda'_b)$, the same pure midpoint class is

$$
\boxed{h_0=(1+u_a,1+u_b,1+v_a,1+v_b)^t,\qquad C_{ab}h_0=0.}
\tag{22n}
$$

The conversion permutes the Kummer coordinates and removes the two dyadic bits by the rational torsion class $(2,2ab,ab)$. If $c_a=c_b=0$, summing rows gives
$\mathcal R(u_a+u_b)=0$ and $(U+V_4)(v_a+v_b)=0$.
Thus $\mathcal R=1$ forces phase zero in (22j); both steps having this profile exclude every $5\bmod8$ center prime. If $U\ne V_4$, then $\eta\in\{[2],[2d]\}$, forcing every $\mathcal B_1$ prime to be balanced in this step's own corner. This profile is therefore impossible for an individual step in the small-$5$ family above. In a center consisting entirely of primes $5\bmod8$, at most one row that is a unit at every center prime can have this latter semiprime profile: two would have identical Gaussian orientations everywhere, hence associated Gaussian factorizations of the same norm and repeated positive offsets. These consequences use the cited matrix input; the coordinate conversion and ensuing linear algebra are exactly (22m)--(22n).

## 8. Rank-two configurations on a common elliptic curve

 If $\operatorname{rank}\Gamma_x=2$, write its primitive relation as

$$
A_xP_{x,-1}+B_xP_{x,0}+C_xP_{x,1}=O.
\tag{23}
$$

Exactly two coefficients are odd. With coherent 2-adic choices of the root signs in (16),

$$
2^{v_2(y)-1}\mid A_x+B_x+C_x.
\tag{24}
$$

For arbitrary initial signs, a correspondingly signed coefficient sum satisfies this divisibility. The $y$-direction has modulus $2^{v_2(x)-1}$. A group progression $P-Q,P,P+Q$ is impossible when $P$ also has the middle numerical abscissa; permutations that destroy this matching-order hypothesis have not been excluded.

The following denominator conditions hold for every step triple, whether its rank is two or three; only the subsequent restrictions on relation coefficients require a relation. Write the three square abscissas in lowest terms as $X_j=b_j^2/N_j^2$. Their denominator exponents satisfy

| Prime | Necessary condition on $e_j=v_p(N_j)$ |
|---|---|
| $2$ | $e_-=e_0=e_+\ge1$ |
| $p\equiv1\pmod8$ | The maximum occurs at least twice |
| $p\equiv3\pmod8$ | $e_-=e_0=e_+$ |
| $p\equiv5\pmod8$ | $e_-=e_+\ge e_0$ |
| $p\equiv7\pmod8$ | $e_0=\max(e_-,e_+)$ |

Thus, with $L=\operatorname{lcm}(N_-,N_0,N_+)$, the deficits $B_j'=L/N_j$ are pairwise coprime and $L=g'B_-'B_0'B_+'$. All deficits are odd; middle-deficit primes are $1\pmod4$, and endpoint-deficit primes are $1$ or $7\pmod8$. No coprimality between $g'$ and the deficits is implied.

At a good prime dividing exactly two of the three denominators, the reduction of the remaining point has nontrivial order dividing both its relation coefficient and $\#E_d(\mathbb F_p)$. In particular that coefficient cannot be $\pm1$. This reduction statement requires the remaining denominator to be a $p$-unit; a mere deficit in its exponent is insufficient. For good $p\equiv3\pmod4$, the group order is $p+1$. If instead $0<v_p(N_k)<v_p(N_i)=v_p(N_j)$, all three points reduce to the identity; at odd primes the formal-group filtration gives $p^{v_p(B_k')}\mid c_k$, where $c_k$ is the corresponding relation coefficient. Thus a good prime in either deficit case is incompatible with $c_k=\pm1$, but only the first case yields a divisor of the finite reduction group order.

The CM restriction already applies to a relation in **one** direction, independently of the other triple's rank. For a relation with coefficients $(A,B,C)$, at an all-unit center prime,

$$
1<\operatorname{ord}(2\overline P_+)
\mid\gcd(A^2+C^2,\#E_1(\mathbb F_p)).
$$

Here the reduced step curve is identified with $E_1$. If $p\equiv5\pmod8$, this order is odd, so $\gcd(A^2+C^2,\#E_1(\mathbb F_p)/8)>1$. Thus if this one endpoint norm is a power of two, every $5\pmod8$ center prime must have a corner exception. The coefficient parity already restricts such a norm to $1$ or $2$.

When both triples have rank two, put

$$
\mathcal N_x=A_x^2+C_x^2,\qquad \mathcal N_y=A_y^2+C_y^2.
$$

At each all-unit center prime, the two CM reductions share the same nontrivial divisor

$$
1<k_p\mid\gcd(\mathcal N_x,\mathcal N_y,\#E_1(\mathbb F_p)).
\tag{25}
$$

For $p\equiv5\pmod8$, $k_p$ is odd and the two middle coefficients cannot both be odd. Neither endpoint norm is divisible by four. Therefore either $\gcd(\mathcal N_x,\mathcal N_y)\in\{1,2\}$, or both norms being odd, forces every $5\pmod8$ center prime to have a corner exception. Combined with (12), either condition excludes a squarefree center having exactly three prime factors, all $5\pmod8$. The half-class refinement gives $\epsilon_p(1/r_p)=-\epsilon_p(r_p)$: in exactly one direction the endpoint half-classes differ from the middle class, forcing the middle relation coefficient to be even. Moreover, if both middle coefficients are odd, every all-unit center prime must satisfy the stronger class-number condition (22e), including primes $1\bmod8$. These restrictions apply on the rank-two branch; a rank-three triple has no relation (23).

## 9. Simultaneous lifting, descent, and rational-point determinations

 The universal parameters determine $r=R(t_2)/R(t_1)$ and $s=R(t_1)$. Fix such an admissible rational slope $r$ and put

$$
\mathcal A_r=\{1,r,1+r,1-r\},\qquad 0<s<1/(1+r).
$$

The exact slope fiber of (2) is $\mathcal H_r:z_{a,\pm}^2=1\pm as$. Its smooth projective model fits into the connected covering ladder

$$
\boxed{
\mathcal H_r\overset{2}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal K_r
\overset{4}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal Z_r\overset{2}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal D_r
\overset{16}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal G_r,
\qquad(g_H,g_K,g_Z,g_D,g_G)=(321,129,33,17,2).}
\tag{26}
$$

Here

$$
\mathcal D_r:\ u_a^2=1-a^2s^2,
\qquad
\mathcal G_r:\ Y^2=X\prod_{a\in\mathcal A_r}(X-a^2),
\tag{27}
$$

with $u_a=z_{a,+}z_{a,-}$, $X=s^{-2}$, $Y=(\prod_a u_a)/s^5$. Every map in (26) except the first is étale; $\mathcal H_r\to\mathcal K_r$ is branched. The intermediate $\mathcal Z_r$ is described below.

The first lifting condition has an intrinsic Jacobian form. A nonbranch rational point $P=(X,Y)$ of $\mathcal G_r$ lifts to $\mathcal D_r$ exactly when

$$
X,\ X-a^2\in\mathbb Q^{\times2}\quad(a\in\mathcal A_r),
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
[P-\infty]\in2J(\mathcal G_r)(\mathbb Q).
\tag{28}
$$

For a chosen lift, set $\lambda_a=[2(1+u_a)]$. It lifts to $\mathcal K_r$ exactly when the four $\lambda_a$ agree, and to the full $\mathcal H_r$ exactly when all are trivial. Sufficiency is explicit: with $h_a^2=2(1+u_a)$,

$$
z_{a,+}=\frac{h_a+2as/h_a}{2},\qquad
z_{a,-}=\frac{h_a-2as/h_a}{2}.
\tag{29}
$$

The identities $2(1+u_a)(1+as)=(1+as+u_a)^2$ and $(1+as)(1-as)=u_a^2$ give

$$
\boxed{\lambda_a=[1+as]=[1-as].}
\tag{29a}
$$

Changing any $u_a$ sign, or the sign of $s$, cannot repair a failed lift.

Let $Q=(U_Q,V_Q)$ be a genus-two half of $P-\infty$ in Mumford coordinates. Put $\rho_0=1/s$, $\rho_a=u_a/s$, $e_0=0$, $e_a=a^2$. Zarhin's formulas give $U_Q(e_i)=\prod_{j\ne i}(\rho_i+\rho_j)$, hence

$$
\boxed{[U_Q(0)]=\prod_a\lambda_a,\qquad
[X(R_{a,b})]=\lambda_a\lambda_b.}
\tag{29b}
$$

The genus-two and all six elliptic second descents evaluate the same four obstruction classes. The pairwise classes contain three independent conditions; their product around every triangle is one.

The intermediate quadratic cover is

$$
\mathcal Z_r=\mathcal D_r\!\left(\sqrt{\prod_a(1+u_a)}\right)
=\mathcal D_r\!\left(\sqrt{U_Q(0)}\right).
\tag{29c}
$$

It is the maximal abelian intermediate cover of $\mathcal K_r/\mathcal G_r$, with group $C_4\times C_2^3$, and is one coordinate of the genus-two multiplication-by-four pullback. The degree-128 cover $\mathcal K_r/\mathcal G_r$ itself has a nonabelian group of nilpotency class two, with commutator subgroup of order four. It cannot be replaced by ordinary four-divisibility. The four final tests separate into the product test, two further compatibility tests after that product is trivial, and one common squareclass that must be trivial for the final branched double cover.

Each $\lambda_a$ is a positive norm from $\mathbb Q(i)$, since $2(1+as)=(1+as)^2+u_a^2$. Its positive squarefree representative has no prime $3\bmod4$. This is automatic on $\mathcal D_r$, not an additional global obstruction.

**One elliptic doubling test retains the residual compatibility.** Put
$q_a(s)=1+as$, $Q_\pm(s)=\prod_a(1\pm as)$, and

$$
E_{+,r}:v^2=Q_+(s),\qquad P_0=(0,1),
$$

with a branch point, for example $s=-1$, chosen as elliptic origin. A $\mathcal Z_r$-point gives $P_+=(s,v)\in E_{+,r}(\mathbb Q)$. If $W_a$ are its four branch points, the functions $q_a/q_1$ have divisors $2W_a-2W_1$ and take value 1 at $P_0$. The full elliptic Kummer map therefore gives the exact equivalence

$$
\boxed{\mathcal Z_r\text{-point lifts to }\mathcal K_r
\iff P_+-P_0\in2E_{+,r}(\mathbb Q).}
\tag{29d}
$$

These are precisely the two compatibility bits left after $\prod_a\lambda_a=1$. The product and pair tests are respectively
$b_0=\prod_a\lambda_a$, $b_1=\lambda_1\lambda_r$, and $b_2=\lambda_1\lambda_{1+r}$.
On $\mathcal Z_r$ there is also $P_-=(-s,v_-)$, with
$v_-=(\prod_a u_a)/v$; already $P_+-P_-\in2E_{+,r}(\mathbb Q)$.

For an explicit small model, let $T_r\subset\mathbb P^3$ be

$$
w_3^2+w_4^2=2w_1^2,\qquad
r w_2^2+(1-r)w_3^2=w_1^2.
\tag{29e}
$$

Set $D=w_2^2-rw_1^2$, $N=w_1^2-w_2^2$. Then
$s=N/D$ and $q_i=((1-r)/D)w_i^2$.
This genus-one curve, based at $(1:1:1:1)$, maps to $E_{+,r}$ by translated multiplication by two. Adding
$D=(1-r)c_0^2$ gives a genus-five curve $T_r^{\rm full}\subset\mathbb P^4$ and a double cover of $T_r$ branched at its eight points above $s=\infty$. With connected normalizations,

$$
\boxed{\mathcal Z_r=\mathcal D_r\times_{\mathbb P^1_s}E_{+,r},\quad
\mathcal K_r=\mathcal D_r\times_{\mathbb P^1_s}T_r,\quad
\mathcal H_r=\mathcal D_r\times_{\mathbb P^1_s}T_r^{\rm full}.}
\tag{29f}
$$

Thus the residual ladder is a pullback of a genus-five/elliptic/elliptic tower. The gluing to $\mathcal D_r$ retains the nonabelian structure over $\mathcal G_r$; replacing that gluing by unrelated elliptic points would lose conditions.

**The last class is exactly denominator parity.** Write $s=A/B$ in lowest terms, $B>0$. On $\mathcal K_r$ the common positive class satisfies

$$
\boxed{\lambda_a=d=[B]\quad\text{for every }a,\qquad
\mathcal K_r\text{-point lifts to }\mathcal H_r
\iff B\text{ is a perfect square}.}
\tag{29g}
$$

For an odd prime $p$, if $v_p(s)\ge0$, the factors $1\pm s$ have unit sum and square product, so both have even valuation. If $v_p(s)<0$, then $v_p(1+s)=v_p(s)=-v_p(B)$. At 2, the common-class condition and the additive relations between the four offsets force $s,rs\in8\mathbb Z_2$ and $d\in\mathbb Q_2^{\times2}$, so $B$ is odd and no dyadic discrepancy remains. Positivity fixes the sign. This proves (29g); it identifies, rather than discards, the branched obstruction.

Consequently a second exact universal formulation is

$$
\boxed{\begin{gathered}
r,s\in\mathbb Q,\quad 0<r<1,\quad r\ne\tfrac12,\quad
0<s<\frac1{1+r},\\
u_a\in\mathbb Q,\quad u_a^2=1-a^2s^2\quad(a\in\mathcal A_r),\\
P_+=(s,v)\in E_{+,r}(\mathbb Q),\quad
P_+-P_0=2Q\quad\text{for some }Q\in E_{+,r}(\mathbb Q),\\
\operatorname{den}(s)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^{\,2}.
\end{gathered}}
\tag{U-E}
$$

All other forbidden slopes from (18) follow as necessary consequences and may still be imposed. The denominator condition can be written $s=A/B_0^2$, $A,B_0\in\mathbb Z$, $B_0>0$, $\gcd(A,B_0)=1$; necessarily $\gcd(B_0,6)=1$ and $24\mid A$. To verify equivalence, the first two lines give a $\mathcal Z_r$-point, the third gives a $\mathcal K_r$-lift by (29d), and the last gives the full lift by (29g). Conversely a magic square satisfies every line. This connects genus-two descent, elliptic doubling and primitive denominator arithmetic in one system.

**Slope--scale denominator synchronization.** The four square-denominator conditions in (U-E) interact arithmetically with the reduced slope, rather than acting independently. Write

$$
r=\frac mn,\qquad s=\frac A{H^2},\qquad
\gcd(m,n)=\gcd(A,H)=1,\qquad 0<m<n,\quad A,H>0,
$$

and set

$$
\gamma=\gcd(A,n),\quad
G_0=\gcd(m,H^2),\quad
G_+=\gcd(n+m,H^2),\quad
G_-=\gcd(n-m,H^2).
$$

Every solution necessarily satisfies

$$
\boxed{
\frac n\gamma,\ G_0,\ G_+,\ G_-\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^{\,2},
\qquad 24\mid\frac A\gamma .}
\tag{29l}
$$

The $n/\gamma$ and $24$-divisibility clauses can equivalently be written, for positive integers $a,b$,

$$
A=24\gamma a,\qquad n=\gamma b^2,\qquad
\gcd(24a,b)=1,\qquad \gcd(24\gamma a,H)=1.
\tag{29m}
$$

The three square-gcd clauses in (29l) remain required; (29m) alone is not equivalent to all of (29l).

Indeed, for $k\in\{m,n+m,n-m\}$ one has $\gcd(k,n)=1$ and

$$
\gcd(Ak,nH^2)=\gamma\gcd(k,H^2),\qquad
\operatorname{den}\!\left(\frac{Ak}{nH^2}\right)
=\frac{nH^2}{\gamma\gcd(k,H^2)}.
$$

The three reduced denominators are squares, so $n/\gamma,G_0,G_+,G_-$ have one squareclass. The three $G$'s are pairwise coprime: the corresponding $k$'s are pairwise coprime except possibly at $2$, while $H$ is odd. Their common squarefree part is therefore $1$. Finally their reduced numerators are
$ (A/\gamma)(k/G_k)$. At least one of the three quotients $k/G_k$ is odd and at least one is prime to $3$; divisibility of all four offsets' reduced numerators by $24$ gives $24\mid A/\gamma$. In valuation form,

$$
v_2(A)\ge v_2(n)+3,\qquad
v_3(A)\ge v_3(n)+1,\qquad
\min\{v_p(k),2v_p(H)\}\equiv0\pmod2
\tag{29n}
$$

for every $p\mid H$ and $k\in\{m,n+m,n-m\}$. This is a coordinate consequence of the primitive-deficit identities. Specifically, writing $h=\gcd(x,y)$ and retaining the deficits $A_i$ from (F), one has

$$
\boxed{n/\gamma=A_1^2,\quad G_0=A_2^2,\quad
G_+=A_3^2,\quad G_-=A_4^2,\quad A/\gamma=h.}
\tag{29o}
$$

To see this, $x=hn,y=hm$ and $\gcd(h,c)=1$, while $\gcd(x,c^2)=A_1^2$ and $H=c/A_1$. Thus $A=hn/A_1^2$ and $\gamma=n/A_1^2$; the other identities follow from (7) and pairwise coprimality of the deficits. In particular its factor $24$ is exactly the existing condition $24\mid h$.

**Finite residual supports have an exact scope.** If $r=m/n$ in lowest terms, put
$S_r=\{p:p\mid2mn(n^2-m^2)\}$.
On $\mathcal D_r$, the product and pair classes $b_0,b_1,b_2$ lie in

$$
\langle\,2,\ p\mid mn(n^2-m^2),\ p\equiv1\bmod4\,\rangle.
\tag{29h}
$$

Outside $S_r$, all four coefficients are units: nonnegative $v_p(s)$ gives even individual valuations, while negative $v_p(s)$ gives equal valuations, which cancel in the pair and product classes. Primes from other factors of the discriminant need not be added.

On $\mathcal K_r$, every odd prime factor of $d$ has negative odd valuation in all four $as$. Hence

$$
\boxed{p\mid d\Rightarrow p\equiv1\pmod4,\quad
r,1+r,1-r\in\mathbb Q_p^{\times2}.}
\tag{29i}
$$

Equivalently it splits completely in $\mathbb Q(i,\sqrt r,\sqrt{1+r},\sqrt{1-r})$. This concerns prime factors of the intermediate obstruction, not arbitrary center primes. If the denominator of $s$ is square away from $S_r$, then $d$ is supported on the finite subset $\mathcal P_r\subset S_r$ passing (29i). An odd exponent in $mn(n^2-m^2)$ excludes a prime from $\mathcal P_r$; even exponent alone is insufficient. In particular, a prime $5\bmod8$ dividing $n-m$ or $n+m$ cannot pass, because it would require 2 to be a local square.

Further, every $\mathcal K_r$-point has
$d\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times2}$ for
$\ell\in\{2,3,7,11,19,23,31,79\}$, and
$s,rs\in8\mathbb Z_2\cap3\mathbb Z_3$.
The odd-prime statements follow by exhaustive evaluation of the finitely many nonzero residue classes on the defining equations modulo each listed prime; this list is not asserted complete. Thus, under the stated denominator condition, the exponent vector of $d$ is in the kernel of the corresponding local-character matrix on $\mathcal P_r$. If that kernel is zero, the last lift is automatic. Requiring a square denominator everywhere, as in (U-E), is the exact unconditional criterion.

**Slope-dependent squareclass rows.** Let $r=m/n$, with
$0<m<n$, $\gcd(m,n)=1$, and let a rational point of
$\mathcal K_r$ have nonzero finite scale $s$ and common positive
squareclass $d=[\operatorname{den}(s)]$. Use the positive squarefree
integer representative for $d$. Define

$$
\mathcal Q_r=
\{q\text{ odd prime}:v_q(mn(n^2-m^2))\text{ is odd}\}.
$$

Then

$$
\boxed{
d\in\mathbb Q_q^{\times2}\quad(q\in\mathcal Q_r).
}
\tag{U-FINAL-SLOPE-CHAR}
$$

In particular $q\nmid d$ and $\left(\frac dq\right)=1$ for every
such $q$. These are conditions on the last common class of an actual
intermediate point; they do not by themselves exclude a slope or
require that any intermediate rational point exists.

**Direct proof.** At every odd prime $q$, the common-class conditions
give

$$
[1+as]=[1-as]=d
\quad(a\in\{1,r,1+r,1-r\}).
$$

If $v_q(d)$ is odd, (29i) says that all three nontrivial coefficients
are $q$-adic squares, so their valuations are even. Therefore
$q\in\mathcal Q_r$ implies $q\nmid d$.

Suppose nevertheless that $d$ is a nonsquare unit at $q$.
If $v_q(as)>0$, then $1+as$ is a square in $\mathbb Q_q$,
contradicting its class $d$. Thus $v_q(as)\le0$ for every $a$.
When $v_q(as)<0$,
$v_q(1+as)=v_q(as)$ must be even because $d$ is a unit.
When it is zero it is already even. Thus all four $v_q(as)$
are even; subtracting $v_q(s)$ makes every $v_q(a)$ even.
This is impossible at a prime in $\mathcal Q_r$: for odd primes
the four integer blocks $m,n,n-m,n+m$ are pairwise coprime,
so an odd valuation of their product occurs in one block and makes
one of $r,1+r,1-r$ have odd valuation. This proves the assertion.

**Norm interpretation.** Write $1\pm as=d z_{a,\pm}^2$.
Then

$$
as=1-dz_{a,-}^2,\qquad -as=1-dz_{a,+}^2
$$

are norms from $\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)$. Their ratios imply

$$
(d,-1)=(d,r)=(d,1+r)=(d,1-r)=0
\quad\text{in }\operatorname{Br}(\mathbb Q)[2].
$$

At a prime where a coefficient has odd valuation and $d$ is an
unramified nonsquare, norms have even valuation, giving the same
contradiction. The elementary proof above avoids needing the norm
interpretation as an external input.

**Finite-support linear algebra.** Under the existing
assumption that the denominator of $s$ is square outside $S_r$,
write $d=\prod_{p\in\mathcal P_r}p^{e_p}$. Every $q\in\mathcal Q_r$
is outside $\mathcal P_r$, by (29i). Append to the existing local
character matrix the binary row

$$
\sum_{p\in\mathcal P_r}
e_p\,\frac{1-(p/q)}2=0
\qquad(q\in\mathcal Q_r).
$$

The possible class space decreases strictly precisely when the
row span increases the rank on the specified column space. A zero resulting
kernel makes the final lift automatic under this finite-support
assumption. Positive remaining dimension does not prove realizability.
With unrestricted denominator support, the condition remains an exact
pointwise character condition, but does not turn the support into a
fixed finite set.

These rows need not be independent of existing rows or of reciprocity.
For $r=24/29$, these rows are $q=5,29,53$. They are already
implied by (29i) and the existing universal conditions at 2 and 3:
the coefficient squareclasses are $174,1537,145$, and reciprocity
first forces $(d/29)=1$, then $(d/53)=(d/5)=1$.
No gain at that particular slope is claimed.

### 9.1. Even-valuation boundary characters of the last class

Let $r=m/n$, $0<m<n$, $\gcd(m,n)=1$, and let a rational
$\mathcal K_r$-point have nonzero finite scale $s$ and common positive
squareclass $d$. Use its positive squarefree representative. In addition
to the odd-valuation rows (U-FINAL-SLOPE-CHAR), define

$$
\mathcal E_r=
\{p\mid mn(n^2-m^2):p\equiv3\pmod4\}
\ \cup\
\{p\mid n^2-m^2:p\equiv5\pmod8\}.
$$

Then

$$
\boxed{d\in\mathbb Q_p^{\times2}\qquad(p\in\mathcal E_r).}
\tag{U-FINAL-EVEN-CHAR}
$$

There is no parity restriction on the positive boundary valuation.
Thus these rows can add information when every relevant coefficient
valuation is even, a case in which the three coefficient norm symbols
are trivial on every unramified squareclass.

**Proof.** The eight nonzero factors satisfy

$$
[1+as]=[1-as]=d,\qquad a\in\{1,r,1+r,1-r\}.
$$

The support restriction (29i) excludes $p\mid d$ for every
$p\in\mathcal E_r$: a prime $3\bmod4$ cannot divide $d$, and a
prime $5\bmod8$ dividing $n-m$ or $n+m$ would require $2$ to
be a local square. Consequently it remains to rule out an unramified
nonsquare $d$.

If $v_p(as)>0$, both $1\pm as$ are squares at the odd prime $p$.
If $v_p(as)<0$, then

$$
\frac{1+as}{1-as}\in -1\cdot(1+p\mathbb Z_p),
$$

so equality of the two factor classes requires $-1$ to be a local
square.

Suppose first that $p\equiv3\bmod4$. Negative valuations are impossible;
under the nonsquare assumption positive valuations are also impossible.
Thus all four $as$ have valuation zero. Subtracting $v_p(s)$
shows that all three nontrivial coefficients have valuation zero,
contradicting $p\mid mn(n^2-m^2)$.

Now let $p\equiv5\bmod8$ divide $n^2-m^2$. Since $p$ is odd,
$m,n$ are units and exactly one of $1+r,1-r$, say $b$, has
positive valuation. The other one, say $a$, is a unit congruent to
$2\pmod p$. If $v_p(s)\ge0$, then $v_p(bs)>0$ and $d$ is
square. If $v_p(s)<0$, both $s$ and $as$ have negative valuation,
and

$$
[1+s]=[s],\qquad [1+as]=[as].
$$

Their common class would make $a$ a local square, contrary to
$(2/p)=-1$. This proves the result.

### 9.2. Small-prime conditions on the final class at a unit slope

Let $r=m/n$, with $0<m<n$, $\gcd(m,n)=1$, and let
$s\ne0$ be the scale of a rational $\mathcal K_r$-point.
Let $d=[\operatorname{den}(s)]$ be its positive common class.
Then

$$
\boxed{\begin{aligned}
p\in\{5,13\},\quad p\nmid mn
&\ \Longrightarrow\ d\in\mathbb Q_p^{\times2},\\
17\nmid mn(n^2-m^2)
&\ \Longrightarrow\ d\in\mathbb Q_{17}^{\times2}.
\end{aligned}}
\tag{U-FINAL-SMALL-CHAR}
$$

These implications include all valuation parities of $d$ and $s$.
In particular, at $r=24/29$,

$$
\boxed{d\in\mathbb Q_{13}^{\times2}\cap
\mathbb Q_{17}^{\times2}.}
\tag{U-FINAL-24-29-CHAR}
$$

These two rows concern the common class left undetected by
(U-KUMMER-KERNEL).

At this slope the same argument gives the scale restriction

$$
s\in5\mathbb Z_5\cap13\mathbb Z_{13}\cap17\mathbb Z_{17}.
\tag{U-FINAL-24-29-SCALE}
$$

Consequently, for $s=A/B$ in lowest terms, $B>0$, the existing
dyadic and ternary conditions together with these rows give
$26520\mid A$ and $\gcd(B,5\cdot13\cdot17)=1$.

**Finite residue lemma.** For $p\in\{5,13,17\}$, let $N_p$
consist of zero and all nonsquares in $\mathbb F_p^\times$, and put

$$
D_p=\{t\in\mathbb F_p:1+t,1-t\in N_p\}.
$$

The exact sets are

$$
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
p&D_p&
\{(x,y)\in D_p^2:x+y,x-y\in D_p\}\\ \hline
5&\{\pm1\}&\varnothing\\
13&\{\pm1,\pm6\}&\varnothing\\
17&\{\pm4,\pm6\}&\varnothing .
\end{array}
$$

For each of these primes there is also no residue $r_0$ for which
$r_0,1+r_0,1-r_0$ are all nonzero squares.
All statements follow by listing the nonzero squares and the at most
sixteen ordered pairs in each row. The accompanying certificate uses
the definitions of the sets, with no precomputed character tables.

**Proof of (U-FINAL-SMALL-CHAR).** The slope is a unit at each prime
under consideration. If $v_p(s)>0$, the factor $1+s$ is a local
square, so its common class $d$ is trivial.

If $v_p(s)=0$, at least one of $1+s,1-s$ is a unit. Hence $d$
has even valuation. If it were the unramified nonsquare class, every
one of the eight factors $1\pm as$ would reduce to a nonsquare or
zero. Taking $x=\bar s$ and $y=\overline{rs}$, this gives
$x,y,x+y,x-y\in D_p$, contrary to the finite residue lemma. Thus
$d$ is again trivial.

It remains to exclude $v_p(s)<0$. For any unit coefficient $a$,
$[1+as]=[as]$; comparison with $a=1$ forces $a$ to be a local
square. If $\bar r\ne\pm1$, all four coefficients are units and the
last clause of the residue lemma gives a contradiction.
If $\bar r=\pm1$ and $p=5$ or $13$, one unit coefficient
$1+r$ or $1-r$ is congruent to $2$. But $2$ is nonsquare
at both primes, giving the same contradiction. The hypothesis for
$p=17$ excludes $\bar r=\pm1$. This exhausts all scale valuations.

For (U-FINAL-24-29-SCALE), the proof has already excluded negative
valuations at $5,13,17$. The residues of $r$ are $1,8,2$,
respectively. Direct substitution into the eight linear factors,
now requiring square or zero residues, leaves only $s=0$ in each
of the three fields. This finite claim is also included in the
certificate. Finally $24\mid A$ is the existing condition on
$\mathcal K_r$; the product $24\cdot5\cdot13\cdot17=26520$.

### 9.3. Complete local test for the final common class

Fix coprime integers $0<m<n$, with $n\ne2m$, and put

$$
r=m/n,\qquad \mathcal A_r=\{1,r,1+r,1-r\},
\qquad
B_r=\left|2mn(n^2-m^2)(4n^2-m^2)(n^2-4m^2)\right|.
$$

Let $X_{r,d}$ be the smooth projective curve with affine equations

$$
d z_{a,\pm}^2=1\pm as\qquad(a\in\mathcal A_r).
\tag{U-LOCAL-CLASS-CURVE}
$$

Here $d$ is a nonzero squareclass, represented globally by a squarefree
integer. A local point will be called nonboundary when $s$ is finite,
nonzero, and none of the eight right sides vanishes.

**Proposition 9.1 (Complete local-class criterion).**

There is an effectively computable finite set of odd primes

$$
\mathcal R_r\subseteq
\{p:p\le 412164\}\ \cup\ \{p:p\mid B_r\}
\tag{U-LOCAL-CLASS-CUTOFF}
$$

with the following property. The curve $X_{r,d}$ has a nonboundary
point over every completion of $\mathbb Q$, with a positive real
scale in $0<s<1/(1+r)$, if and only if:

1. $d>0$ and $d\in\mathbb Q_2^{\times2}$;
2. $d\in\mathbb Q_p^{\times2}$ for every $p\in\mathcal R_r$;
3. for every odd $p\mid d$,

   $$
   -1,r,1+r,1-r\in\mathbb Q_p^{\times2}.
   \tag{U-LOCAL-CLASS-SPLIT}
   $$

The characterization at 2 also has a short direct proof. Multiply
the equations by $d$, then scale all eight roots by a common
power of 2 so that they are integral and at least one is odd. Write
the resulting center and offsets as $C,x,y$. One exterior row has
three squares summing to $3C$, so $C\in\mathbb Z_2$. If $C$
were even, each opposite pair would have sum divisible by 4 and
both roots even, a contradiction. Thus $C$ is odd and every root
is odd. The exterior row now gives $3C\equiv3\pmod8$, hence
$C\equiv1\pmod8$. Since $C$ and $d$ differ by a rational
square, $d\in\mathbb Q_2^{\times2}$. Sufficiency follows by taking
the scale sufficiently small 2-adically. The positive real condition
is immediate from (U-LOCAL-CLASS-CURVE).

The equivalence just stated is

$$
X_{r,d}(\mathbb A_{\mathbb Q})\ne\varnothing
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{conditions 1--3 hold, with the stated positive real branch}.
\tag{U-LOCAL-CLASS-CRITERION}
$$

The finite set is canonical:

$$
\mathcal R_r=
\{p\text{ odd}:X_{r,u_p}(\mathbb Q_p)=\varnothing\},
\tag{U-LOCAL-CLASS-ROWS}
$$

where $u_p$ is any nonsquare $p$-adic unit. Thus this proposition
gives a stopping rule for finding **all local-square character rows
for the fixed slope**, followed by the candidate-dependent splitting
test (U-LOCAL-CLASS-SPLIT).

### 9.4. Odd local squareclasses: only three possibilities

At an odd prime $p$, the local square class $1$ is always soluble:
choose $s\ne0$ sufficiently small that all $as\in p\mathbb Z_p$.

Suppose $v_p(d)$ is odd. From the two equations for $a=1$, neither
$v_p(s)>0$ nor $v_p(s)=0$ is possible: in the corresponding case both
right sides are units, and in the latter at least one is a unit.
Consequently $v_p(s)<0$ is odd. The same argument for each $a$
gives $v_p(as)<0$ odd. The quotients of the equations then show
that $-1$ and every $a\in\mathcal A_r$ are local squares, since
each factor $1\pm1/(as)$ is a square in $1+p\mathbb Z_p$.
This proves necessity of (U-LOCAL-CLASS-SPLIT), including at primes dividing $B_r$.

Conversely, suppose (U-LOCAL-CLASS-SPLIT) holds. **Every** local squareclass $d$
is then soluble. Choose $k$ large and set

$$
s=d p^{-2k}.
$$

For all four coefficients $a$, one has $v_p(as)<0$, and

$$
\frac{1+as}{d}=a p^{-2k}\left(1+\frac1{as}\right),
\qquad
\frac{1-as}{d}=-a p^{-2k}\left(1-\frac1{as}\right)
$$

are squares. This construction applies to unit and ramified $d$.

It follows that the possible local squareclass sets are exactly of
the following forms, where $u_p$ is a nonsquare unit:

$$
\{1\},\qquad \{1,u_p\},\qquad
\{1,u_p,p,u_pp\}.
\tag{U-LOCAL-CLASS-TYPES}
$$

The last case occurs exactly when (U-LOCAL-CLASS-SPLIT) holds. In particular, if the
nonsquare unit class fails, both ramified classes fail too; this is
why primes in $\mathcal R_r$ give unconditional local-square rows,
rather than implications restricted to $p\nmid d$.

### 9.5. An explicit smooth model and the cutoff

List

$$
b_1=1,\qquad
\{b_1,\ldots,b_8\}=\{\pm1,\pm r,\pm(1+r),\pm(1-r)\}.
$$

A smooth projective model in $\mathbb P^8$, with coordinates
$[c:z_1:\cdots:z_8]$, is the complete intersection

$$
d z_j^2-b_j d z_1^2-(1-b_j)c^2=0
\qquad(2\le j\le8).
\tag{U-LOCAL-CLASS-MODEL}
$$

On $c\ne0$, its scale is $s=d z_1^2/c^2-1$. The eight
linear radicands are independent modulo squares over an algebraic
closure: each has a distinct simple zero. Thus the curve is
geometrically integral. It is a complete intersection of seven
quadrics of degree $128$ and genus

$$
g=1+\tfrac12(14-9)128=321.
$$

Equivalently, the scale map has degree 256 and nine branch points, each with inertia order two; Riemann--Hurwitz gives $2g-2=-512+9\cdot128=640$.

If $p\nmid B_r d$, the $b_j$ are nonzero distinct units and
$p\ne2$. The Jacobian criterion proves that (U-LOCAL-CLASS-MODEL) is smooth over
$\mathbb Z_p$. At $c=0$, every $z_j\ne0$, and the columns
$z_2,\ldots,z_8$ give seven independent pivots. On $c\ne0$,
at most one $z_j$ vanishes. If it is $z_1$, all other $z_j$
are nonzero and give the same pivots. If it is $z_j$ with $j>1$,
its row has nonzero $c$-derivative, while the other six rows have
their separate nonzero $z_i$-pivots. If none vanishes, the seven
diagonal pivots again suffice. Listing all coefficient differences
shows their prime support is contained in $B_r$.

For a unit $d$ at such a prime, the Weil bound gives

$$
\#X_{r,d}(\mathbb F_p)\ge p+1-642\sqrt p>0
\qquad\text{if }p>642^2=412164.
\tag{U-LOCAL-CLASS-WEIL}
$$

Every residue point lifts by Hensel's lemma. Any resulting smooth
$\mathbb Q_p$-point has a $p$-adic open disk of local points,
so a point outside the finite boundary can be chosen. **No subtraction
of branch or infinity points from the Weil bound is needed.** This
proves the finite support assertion (U-LOCAL-CLASS-CUTOFF).

### 9.6. Effective decisions at the finitely many remaining primes

At a good odd prime $p\nmid B_r$, properness and smooth lifting
give an elementary finite-field decision. The nonsquare unit twist
is soluble if and only if either all $b_j$ are squares modulo $p$
(a point at infinity), or some $\bar s\in\mathbb F_p$ makes
all eight $1+b_j\bar s$ nonsquares or zero. Zero values must be
retained in this test.

At a bad prime, use the explicit projective model (U-LOCAL-CLASS-MODEL) after clearing
denominators. For example, if $B_j=n b_j\in\mathbb Z$, its equations
are

$$
d(nz_j^2-B_jz_1^2)-(n-B_j)c^2=0.
\tag{U-LOCAL-CLASS-INTEGRAL}
$$

There is a terminating exact local decision, without a conjectural
height bound:

- Search the nine projective charts in which a chosen coordinate is
  $1$, with all other coordinates in $\mathbb Z_p$. At precision
  $p^k$, keep exactly the residue solutions of (U-LOCAL-CLASS-INTEGRAL).
- If there is no local point, some finite precision has no surviving
  chart. Otherwise the finite branching residue tree would have an
  infinite path, giving a point by compactness.
- Simultaneously test residue approximations for a nonzero $7\times7$
  Jacobian minor. If the equations vanish to order greater than twice
  the valuation of that minor, multivariate Hensel lifting, with the
  remaining affine coordinate fixed, certifies a local point.
- If a local point exists, the characteristic-zero curve is smooth,
  so one such minor is nonzero there. Sufficiently accurate residue
  approximations eventually give this Hensel certificate.

One of these two searches therefore stops. This proves computability
of every entry in (U-LOCAL-CLASS-ROWS), including at bad reduction. This assertion
is a terminating algorithm, not a practical complexity bound.

**Scope.**

The theorem characterizes everywhere local **common classes**, with
potentially different scales $s_p$ at different primes. It does not
produce a rational $\mathcal K_r$-point, establish a rational scale
shared across places, or force $d=1$. It does not yield finite global
support for $d$. The class $d=1$ passes for every slope, in full
agreement with the finite-local nonobstruction near $s=0$.

Within a finite prescribed support, the rows indexed by
$\mathcal R_r$ can be appended to the existing character matrix;
strict matrix improvement still requires a rank computation. Beyond
that setting, the exact output is a finite local class filter plus
the splitting condition at each candidate-dependent prime divisor
of $d$. The complete local characterization consists of
the explicit cutoff and the complete characterization.

**External input and hypotheses.**

André Weil, *Sur les courbes algébriques et les variétés qui s'en
déduisent*, 1948, §IV, no. 21, Theorem 13, Corollary 3, proves
$|1+q^n-\nu_n|\le2gq^{n/2}$. The original proof was checked in
[the retyped full text](https://denisevellachemla.eu/Weil-courbes-varietes.pdf),
PDF page 61 (printed page 60). The formula and its application to
smooth geometrically integral projective curves were also checked
against J. S. Milne's [author exposition](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1509.00797),
page 2. Only the Weil bound is imported here; the local classification,
model, cutoff specialization, and termination argument are proved above.

**A smaller cyclic quotient adds rank information.** The genus-five curve
$\mathcal V_r:v_+^2=Q_+(s),\ v_-^2=Q_-(s)$ is an étale cyclic four-cover of $\mathcal G_r$. To exhibit the cyclic structure, let $e_j$ be the elementary symmetric functions of $\mathcal A_r$ and put
$A(X)=X^2+e_2X+e_4$, $B(X)=e_1X+e_3$. Then
$A^2-XB^2=Y^2/X$; adjoining $S^2=X$, $w^2=A+BS$ and $w'=Y/(Sw)$ gives the automorphism
$(S,w,w')\mapsto(-S,-w',w)$ of order four.
The same identity shows $X=(XB/A)^2+(Y/A)^2$ on the positive locus. With $\mathcal B_r=\mathcal G_r(\sqrt X)$,
$\mathcal Z_r=\mathcal D_r\times_{\mathcal B_r}\mathcal V_r$, and

$$
J(\mathcal V_r)\sim_{\mathbb Q}
J(\mathcal G_r)\times B^{(4)}\times E_{+,r}^{\,2}.
\tag{29j}
$$

The point $P_0$ on $E_{+,r}$ is nontorsion for every admissible slope: the possible torsion orders reduce to explicit rational-root tests, with only the forbidden slope $1/3$ at order four. The two $E_+$ copies enter the Prym, giving for a candidate

$$
\boxed{\operatorname{rank}J(\mathcal Z_r)(\mathbb Q)\ge
\operatorname{rank}J(\mathcal D_r)(\mathbb Q)+2\ge15.}
\tag{29k}
$$

The analogous rank of $J(\mathcal V_r)$ is
$\operatorname{rank}J(\mathcal G_r)+\operatorname{rank}B^{(4)} +2\operatorname{rank}E_{+,r}\ge\operatorname{rank}J(\mathcal G_r)+3$.
These are factor and rank restrictions, not point determinations.

The genus-five quotient $\mathcal C_r:u_a^2=1-a^2\tau$, $\tau=s^2$, is precisely $[2]^{-1}(\mathcal G_r)/\{\pm1\}$ in its Jacobian, the genus-five Kummer section in Hast’s descent. It has five elliptic factors: the four cubics $B_{a,b,c}:v^2=(1-a^2\tau)(1-b^2\tau)(1-c^2\tau)$ and the quartic $B^{(4)}:v^2=\prod_{a\in\mathcal A_r}(1-a^2\tau)$. Their origins are infinity for a cubic and the branch point $(\tau,v)=(1,0)$ for the quartic. All four cubic images lie in $2B_{a,b,c}(\mathbb Q)$; the quartic image lies in $P_0+2B^{(4)}(\mathbb Q)$, where $P_0=(0,1)$.

For the two additive cubic triples $\{1,r,1+r\}$ and $\{1,r,1-r\}$, the torsion group is $C_2\times C_6$ and $P_0$ has order $3$, supplying a rational $3$-isogeny. An affine $\mathcal C_r$-point with $\tau\ne0$ forces both factors to have positive rank. For every admissible slope, the other two cubics and the quartic already have nontorsion boundary points, independently of a candidate. Thus any such nonzero-$\tau$ point forces all five ranks to be positive. On the larger nonsingular domain $r\notin\{0,\pm1,\pm2,\pm1/2\}$, the extra exceptions for the two boundary cubic arguments are $r=\pm1/4,\pm4$; these normalize to the forbidden four-square progression slope.

### 9.7. A finite three-isogeny test covers every admissible slope

Write $r=m/n$ in lowest terms, $0<m<n$, $r\ne1/2$.
Apply the construction below to both

$$
(a,b)=(n,m),\qquad (a,b)=(n-m,m).
$$

In either case $a,b>0$, $a\ne b$. Put

$$
L=a^2+ab+b^2,\quad M=a^2b^2(a+b)^2,\quad
D=(a-b)(2a+b)(a+2b).
$$

The additive cubic factor has the integral model

$$
E_{a,b}:Y^2=(X+(ab)^2)(X+(a(a+b))^2)(X+(b(a+b))^2)
=X^3+(LX+M)^2,
\quad 4L^3-27M=D^2.
\tag{U-THREE-MODEL}
$$

It is nonsingular, and $T=(0,M)$ has order three. A three-isogenous
curve, after a rational square/cube scaling, is

$$
\widehat E_{a,b}:Y^2=X^3-3(-3LX+3D^2)^2.
\tag{U-THREE-DUAL}
$$

The unscaled isogeny has abscissa

$$
X\longmapsto
\frac{X^3+\frac43L^2X^2+4LMX+4M^2}{X^2},
$$

and ordinate multiplier $(X^3-4LMX-8M^2)/X^3$; its target is
$Y^2=X^3-3(LX-D^2/9)^2$. Scaling by $(9,27)$ gives
(U-THREE-DUAL). The identity of the two models and the isogeny equation
have exact polynomial certificates.

Here is a finite over-cover of both descent images; it deliberately
allows extraneous classes. For every pair of coprime squarefree positive
integers $u_1,u_2$ with $u_1u_2\mid\operatorname{rad}(2M)$, form

$$
C_{u_1,u_2}:\quad
u_1x^3+u_2y^3+\frac{2M}{u_1u_2}z^3-2Lxyz=0.
\tag{U-THREE-CUBIC}
$$

The associated class is $[u_1^2u_2]\in\mathbb Q^\times/\mathbb Q^{\times3}$.
There are exactly $3^{\omega(2M)}$ such classes.

For the other image use $K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$, with
$\zeta=(-1+\sqrt{-3})/2$. For each prime $p\mid D$, $p\equiv1\pmod3$,
choose an Eisenstein integer $\pi_p$ of norm $p$. Take

$$
v=\zeta^e\prod_{p\mid D,\ p\equiv1(3)}v_p,
\qquad e\in\{0,1,2\},\quad v_p\in\{1,\pi_p,\overline\pi_p\}.
$$

Write $v=(c+d\sqrt{-3})/2$, $N=v\overline v$. Form

$$
\widehat C_v:\quad
dx^3-3cy^3+\frac{6D^2}{N}z^3+3cx^2y-9dxy^2
-6Lx^2z-18Ly^2z=0.
\tag{U-THREE-DUAL-CUBIC}
$$

Its class is $[v^2\overline v]\in K^\times/K^{\times3}$.
These are exactly $3^{1+h}$ distinct supported classes, where
$h=\#\{p\mid D:p\equiv1\pmod3\}$. Every coefficient is integral.

Choose any finite collection of prime powers. Remove a class only when
its cubic, divided first by its coefficient gcd, has no primitive
solution modulo one of those prime powers. Let $U(a,b)$ and
$V(a,b)$ denote the retained sets from (U-THREE-CUBIC) and
(U-THREE-DUAL-CUBIC). Then, without a rank, BSD, or Tate--Shafarevich
finiteness assumption,

$$
\boxed{3^{\operatorname{rank}E_{a,b}(\mathbb Q)+1}
\le |U(a,b)|\,|V(a,b)|.}
\tag{U-THREE-BOUND}
$$

Every admissible simultaneous circle point, hence every intermediate
common-class point and every full square, has positive rank on both
additive factors. Consequently

$$
\boxed{|U(n,m)|\,|V(n,m)|\ge9,\qquad
|U(n-m,m)|\,|V(n-m,m)|\ge9.}
\tag{U-THREE-SLOPE}
$$

A product smaller than nine excludes the entire slope, at every center
height and for every final common squareclass. There is no restriction
on the numerator, denominator, or prime factorization of the slope in
the validity of this test.

**Proof of completeness and the bound.** The three-descent maps are
$\alpha(X,Y)=[Y-LX-M]$ on $E_{a,b}$, with
$\alpha(O)=1$, $\alpha(T)=[1/(2M)]$, and
$\widehat\alpha(X,Y)=[Y-(-3LX+3D^2)\sqrt{-3}]$ on the dual model.
The rational three-isogeny index formula is

$$
|\alpha(E_{a,b}(\mathbb Q))|
|\widehat\alpha(\widehat E_{a,b}(\mathbb Q))|
=3^{\operatorname{rank}E_{a,b}(\mathbb Q)+1}.
$$

This is Proposition 2.2 of
[Cohen--Pazuki, *Elementary 3-descent with a 3-isogeny*](https://www.impan.pl/shop/publication/transaction/download/product/82564).
Their Theorems 3.1 and 4.1 identify the covering cubics. No conjectural
