**One convergent series on an entire disk.** The exact birational map
(CE8), with origin $(z,w)=(1,7)$, satisfies
\[
\frac{dX}{2Y}=-\frac{dz}{2w}.
\tag{CE-DIFFERENTIAL}
\]
This identity follows by differentiating its rational expressions and
reducing by $w^2=f(z)$. In particular the factor is rational; no
field-valued scalar is omitted from the annihilator.

Write $z=1+4v$. The polynomial expansion is
\[
\frac{f(1+4v)}{49}=1+q(v),\qquad
q(v)=q_1v+q_2v^2+q_3v^3+q_4v^4,
\]
\[
q_1=\frac{8A(B+2)}{49},\quad
q_2=\frac{16A\theta}{49},\quad
q_3=q_4=\frac{256A}{49}.
\]
Their basis coordinates are $(24/7,-8,24/7)$,
$(-16/7,-48/7,48/7)$, and $(-256/7,256/7,0)$ twice.
Hence $q_j\in2^{j+2}\mathcal O_K$. The binomial branch
\[
w(v)=7\sqrt{1+q(v)}
\]
converges on $v\in\mathbb Z_2$ and has
$w-7\in4\mathcal O_K\langle v\rangle$. For any global quartic
point in this $z$-disk, exactly one of its two global $w$ signs
belongs to this branch, so using it loses no rational coordinate.

To verify a single formal-logarithm identity across the whole disk,
put $u=4v$, $d=2A(B+2)$, $\sigma=A(B+2)$, and
\[
N=14(w+7)+du,\quad N_1=N+\sigma u^2,
\quad N_2=N^2-dNu-392Au^3-196Au^4.
\]
The map (CE8) gives $T=-14uN_1/N_2$. The three restricted series
$N/4,N_1/4,N_2/16$ are units: the first two are 1 modulo 2,
and the last is $(N/4)^2$ modulo 2. Consequently
\[
T(v)=-14v\frac{N_1/4}{N_2/16}
\in2v\mathcal O_K\langle v\rangle.
\]
The entire disk therefore maps into the formal neighborhood. The
differential identity and value zero at $v=0$ give on this disk
\[
\log_E(P(v))=-\frac27\int_0^v(1+q(t))^{-1/2}\,dt.
\tag{CE-DISK-LOGARITHM}
\]
No undetermined locally constant term occurs.

**A complete bound for the infinite tail.** Write
\[
(1+q(v))^{-1/2}=1+\sum_{n\ge1}g_nv^n.
\]
For $k\ge1$, the degree-$n$ coefficient of $q(v)^k$ belongs to
$2^{n+2k}\mathcal O_K$, while
$v_2\binom{-1/2}{k}\ge1-2k$. Therefore
$g_n\in2^{n+1}\mathcal O_K$ for every $n\ge1$. Define
\[
F(v)=-2\lambda(\log_E(P(v)))
=\frac47\lambda\left(\int_0^v(1+q(t))^{-1/2}\,dt\right).
\]
Its linear coefficient is $4\lambda(1)/7$, of valuation exactly
two. The coefficient of $v^{n+1}$ for $n\ge1$ has valuation at
least $n+3-v_2(n+1)\ge3$, tending to infinity. Thus
\[
F(v)=4v\bigl(\lambda(1)/7+2vG(v)\bigr),
\qquad G\in\mathbb Z_2\langle v\rangle.
\]
The parenthesis is a unit for every $v\in\mathbb Z_2$. Global
points are annihilated by $\lambda$, so $v=0$ is the only possible
global rational coordinate in this disk. Hence $z=1$. The polynomial
$f$ is even; applying the same result to $-z$ leaves only $z=-1$
in the other odd disk. At either coordinate $w=\pm7$, proving
(CE-RATIONAL-COORDINATES).

**Coverage and all residual roots.** Every completion obeys
$z^2+r^2=2$ by (U-BEU-UNIQUE-CONICS). If $v_2(z)<0$, then
$v_2(r)=v_2(z)$ and $(r/z)^2=2/z^2-1\equiv-1\pmod4$,
impossible. If $z$ is even integral, including zero, $2-z^2$ has
odd valuation. Thus $z\in\mathbb Z_2^\times$, so the two disks
just treated cover every completion candidate.

At $z=\pm1$, $s=1$, and all remaining conditions have
\[
r^2=h^2=1,\quad V^2=49,\quad y_1^2=25,\quad y_2^2=1,
\quad\kappa^2=(\theta-1)^2.
\]
They all lift, and reconstruction gives independently signed roots
$(w_0,w_1,w_2)=(7,5,1)$. The original parameters are $t=0,\infty$,
both inadmissible because of repeated entries. The omitted chart
$t=1$ has the nonsquare value $8192$ and was already excluded.
This proves (U-BEU-COMPLETE-EXCLUSION). $\square$

The exact correspondence (CE1)–(CE2) now gives the asserted full
rational-point list on $C$: at $z=\pm1$, $\kappa=\pm(\theta-1)$
and $V=\pm7$. Its two points at infinity are not rational because
the leading coefficient $-7$ is nonsquare. The theorem exhausts
this family and this genus-two curve, not the full magic-square surface.


### 9.55. Complete rational exclusion of the January Wesołowski recipe

For the January 2020 construction recorded on
[Boyer's research page](http://multimagie.com/English/SquaresOfSquaresSearch.htm),
use its displayed positions and the local parameter data
\[
w=6n^2+6n+2,\quad u=2n+1,\quad
v=3n^2+2n,\quad z=3n^2+4n+1.
\]
The three missing entries are
\[
\begin{aligned}
C&=(2v^2-z^2)u^2+(2z^2-v^2)w^2,\\
D&=2(u^2v^2+w^2z^2)-(wv+uz)^2,\\
H&=2(u^2v^2+w^2z^2)-(wv-uz)^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{U-JANUARY-DATA}
\]
These letters are local to this family.

**Theorem.** For finite rational $n\ne-1/2$, the entry $C$ is
not a rational square. At $n=-1/2$ and at the homogenized parameter
$n=\infty$, the three missing entries coincide. Hence this recipe
has no admissible rational completion, including every even-denominator
parameter.
\[
\boxed{\text{The January recipe has no nine-distinct-square completion.}}
\tag{U-JANUARY-COMPLETE-EXCLUSION}
\]

**Exact quotient.** Put $t=2n+1$. Expansion gives
\[
64C=81t^8+324t^7+72t^6-36t^5-2t^4
       +12t^3+8t^2-12t+1.
\]
For $t\ne0$, a square $C$ gives the rational point
\[
x=3t-t^{-1}+3,\qquad y=8\sqrt C/t^2
\]
on
\[
\mathcal F:\quad y^2=x^4-34x^2+192x-287.
\tag{U-JANUARY-QUARTIC}
\]
The polynomial map
\[
X=(y+x^2-1)/2,\qquad Y=x(X-8)+24
\]
lands on the elliptic curve
\[
E:\quad Y^2=X(X^2-7X+64).
\tag{U-JANUARY-ELLIPTIC}
\]
For $X\ne8$ its inverse is
$x=(Y-24)/(X-8)$, $y=2X-x^2+1$. These identities are exact
polynomial substitutions. The original parameter is retained:
a converse lift must have $L^2=x^2-6x+21$ and
$t=(x-3+L)/6$.

**Complete two-isogeny descent.** For
$Y^2=X^3+aX^2+bX$, use the standard descent map
$\alpha(P)=[X(P)]$, with $\alpha(O)=1$ and
$\alpha((0,0))=[b]$. Its supported squareclasses are the signed
squarefree divisors $d$ of $b$, with covering equation
\[
N^2=dU^4+aU^2V^2+(b/d)V^4.
\]
The rank formula is
$2^{\operatorname{rank}E(\mathbb Q)}=|\alpha(E)|\,|\alpha'(E')|/4$.
The external descent construction and support restriction are
[Cremona, *Higher Descents on Elliptic Curves*](https://johncremona.github.io/papers/d2.pdf),
Section 2.2, equations (3)–(5); the following arithmetic evaluates
them on this specific model.

Here $a=-7,b=64$. The quadratic $X^2-7X+64$ is positive on
$\mathbb R$, so all nonzero rational abscissas are positive. Thus
$\alpha(E)\subset\{1,2\}$, and equality holds because $(8,24)$
has class 2. The dual model is
\[
E':Y^2=X(X^2+14X-207).
\]
Its possible classes are $\{1,-1,3,-3,23,-23,69,-69\}$.
The classes 1 and $-23$ occur at $O$ and $(0,0)$. For the
other six, the covering quartics have the following exhaustive
primitive projective residue values:

| Classes $d$ | Modulus | Quartic value residues |
|---|---:|---|
| $-1,23$ | 16 | $7,12,15$ |
| $3,-69$ | 16 | $3,11,12$ |
| $-3,69$ | 9 | $2,5,6,8$ |

None is a square residue. Coverage follows by normalizing one unit
coordinate to one: there are 24 projective primitive representatives
modulo 16 and 12 modulo 9. Thus
$\alpha'(E')=\{1,-23\}$, proving
\[
\operatorname{rank}E(\mathbb Q)=0.
\]

The point $(8,24)$ doubles to $(0,0)$ and has order four.
The discriminant is $-2^{16}3^2\cdot23$. Exact counts at the
good primes 5 and 7 are respectively 4 and 8. Torsion reduction
at both places therefore proves the complete point list
\[
E(\mathbb Q)=\{O,(0,0),(8,24),(8,-24)\}.
\]
For a finite point of $\mathcal F$, the polynomial map has finite
image. The image $(0,0)$ forces $(x,y)=(3,-8)$. An image with
$X=8$ must have $Y=24$; substituting $y=17-x^2$ into the
quartic forces $x=3,y=8$. Consequently
\[
\boxed{\mathcal F(\mathbb Q)_{\rm affine}=\{(3,8),(3,-8)\}.}
\tag{U-JANUARY-QUARTIC-POINTS}
\]
The two rational points at infinity on its smooth projective model
map to $O$ and $(8,-24)$, so no finite point was omitted.

**Parameter coverage and residual entries.** For finite nonzero
$t$, the required coordinate $x=3$ would give $3t^2=1$, with
no rational solution. Thus $C$ is nonsquare for every finite
$n\ne-1/2$. At $n=-1/2$, direct substitution in the original
three entries gives $C=D=H=1/64$. At $n=\infty$, homogenizing
their degree-eight polynomials gives $C=D=H=324$. Each parameter
therefore repeats entries in three different positions. These are
the only omitted charts, completing the proof. $\square$

This is an exclusion of the displayed rational recipe. No assertion
that arbitrary magic squares admit its parameterization is made.


### 9.56. Complete rational exclusion of the fixed Hurban progression

**Theorem.** If all six rational numbers
\[
 25+\xi,\quad25-\xi,\quad1+\xi,\quad49-\xi,\quad
 1+2\xi,\quad49-2\xi
\tag{HU-1}
\]
are squares, then $\xi=0$ or $24$. This concerns the full
simultaneous lift; it does not determine every rational point on a
single auxiliary genus-two curve.

**The two elliptic height functions.**

Use the rank-one curves
\[
 E_1:y^2=x(x+49)(x+100),\qquad E_2:y^2=x(x+1)(x+49).
\]
Both ranks are exactly one. Full two-descent uses six global parity
columns for $E_1$ and four for $E_2$. At 2 the certified local image
has dimension three; at the odd bad primes it has dimension two.
The bad sets are $\{2,3,5,7,17\}$ and $\{2,3,7\}$, respectively.
Complete intersection leaves eight classes in each case. Independent
lower classes are represented by $(-49,0),(70,1190),(-50,50)$ for
$E_1$, and $(-1,0),(7,56),(1,10)$ for $E_2$. Each set has Kummer
dimension three. The middle point in each list is a rational half
of $(0,0)$; retaining it avoids losing a torsion direction in the
Kummer image. The dimension-certified local descent procedure and
its exact witnesses give the upper bound, so no analytic rank or
saturation assumption enters.

Write $r_i$ for (HU-1), in its displayed
order, and choose
\[
 v^2=r_2/r_1,\quad b^2=r_0r_1r_4,\quad
 W=b(1+v^2)^2/2.
\]
The rational point lies on
\[
C:\quad W^2=13(1+v^2)(25v^2+12)(51v^2-1).
\]
Its two elliptic images are
\[
f_1=\left(-\frac{4(25v^2+12)}{1+v^2},-\frac{4W}{(1+v^2)^2}\right),
\qquad
f_2=\left(\frac{51v^2-1}{1+v^2},\frac{4vW}{(1+v^2)^2}\right).
\]
Their differential pullbacks are $13v\,dv/W$ and $13\,dv/W$.
Substitution verifies both maps, and the independent differentials
show $J(C)\sim_{\mathbb Q}E_1\times E_2$. No square requirement is
lost: a rational point of $C$ lifts to all six radicals exactly when
\[
\frac{2(25v^2+12)}{1+v^2},\quad\frac{26}{1+v^2},\quad
\frac{2(12v^2+25)}{1+v^2},\quad\frac{51-v^2}{1+v^2}
\]
are nonzero squares. These are $r_0,r_1,r_3,r_5$; the conic identity
supplies $r_2$ and the curve equation supplies $r_4$.
Translate the two elliptic images by
$(-100,0)$ and $(-1,0)$, respectively, obtaining
\[
 x(Q_1)=50r_4/r_1,\qquad x(Q_2)=-r_0/r_2.
\tag{HU-2}
\]
None of the denominators or roots used here vanish on a rational full
lift. At each possible zero $\xi=-25,25,-1,49,-1/2,49/2$, a
different member of (HU-1) is negative or has odd 2-adic valuation and is
therefore not a rational square. The full cover
also has no rational point over $\xi=\infty$, since its opposite
leading radicands would require $-1$ to be a rational square.

Use the height normalization of Section 9.28:
\[
 h_{i,\ell}(Q)=\bigl(\max(0,-v_\ell x(Q))-\mu_{i,\ell}(Q)\bigr)
                 \log_{11}\ell\quad(\ell\ne11),
\]
and at 11 use $\omega_i=dx/(2y)$, the complement
$X_{\rm short}\omega_i$, and
\[
 h_{i,11}=-2\log_{11}\sigma_i,\quad
 \sigma_i(z)=z+O(z^5),\quad
 \zeta_i=(\log\sigma_i)',\quad d\zeta_i=-X_{\rm short}\omega_i.
\tag{HU-3}
\]
The finite and 11-adic normalizations obey the same division-polynomial
functional equation, and their sum is a quadratic global height.
Both elliptic ranks equal one; set
$\alpha_i=h_i(P_i)/\log_i(P_i)^2$ using any certified nontorsion
point. Consequently $h_i(Q)=\alpha_i\log_i(Q)^2$ for every rational
$Q$, without a saturation hypothesis.

The natural two quotient models of the even sextic are related to
the translated models (HU-2) by $X=169x+325$, $Y=\pm2197y$.
Thus both absolute model-scaling factors are 13. Their local constants
cancel in the bielliptic height difference. The required function is
\[
 \rho=h_{1,11}(Q_1)-h_{2,11}(Q_2)-2\log_{11}v
       -\alpha_1\log_1(Q_1)^2+\alpha_2\log_2(Q_2)^2.
\tag{HU-4}
\]
The level identity below follows directly from the rank-one global
height identities and the product formula. In particular it does not
require extending a theorem stated for monic sextics to this nonmonic
sextic. The natural-model calculation is a consistency check on the
bielliptic interpretation; all arithmetic uses the displayed small
elliptic models.

For every prime $\ell\ne11$ put
\[
 W_\ell=\max(0,-v_\ell x(Q_1))-\mu_{1,\ell}
        -\max(0,-v_\ell x(Q_2))+\mu_{2,\ell}
        +v_\ell(r_2)-v_\ell(r_1).
\tag{HU-5}
\]
The required complete local certificate, using all six conditions (HU-1),
is

| Prime | Permitted $W_\ell$ |
|---|---|
| 2 | $3/4$ |
| 3, 7, 13 | 0 |
| 5 | $-2,-1$ |
| 17 | $-1/2$ |
| Every other prime except 11 | 0 |

The table holds throughout every local domain of the simultaneous six-square locus. The independent polynomial-ball certificate
covers the following necessary local domains: $\xi\in8\mathbb Z_2$,
$3\mathbb Z_3$, $125\mathbb Z_5\cup(24+125\mathbb Z_5)$,
$7\mathbb Z_7\cup(24+49\mathbb Z_7)$, and
$17\mathbb Z_{17}\cup(7+17\mathbb Z_{17})$, together with the
reciprocal chart $1/\xi\in17\mathbb Z_{17}$. Each is an entire
polynomial ball; exact homogeneous duplication gives the correction
prefix, and a complete finite projective orbit check proves its tail
zero. The pairs of corrections on these nine balls are respectively
\[
 (5/4,2),\ (1/2,1/2),\ (0,0),\ (1,0),\ (0,0),\ (1,1),\
 (1/2,0),\ (1/2,0),\ (1/2,0).
\]
At 13 both elliptic models have good reduction, and the two quotient abscissae have no poles on the full-lift locus. At any other good
prime the possible denominator contributions cancel exactly against
$v_\ell(r_2)-v_\ell(r_1)$. For completeness, negative valuations at 3, 7 and 11 are excluded
by the nonsquare ratio $r_0/r_1\equiv-1$, and at 5 by
$r_4/r_0\equiv2$. At 2, writing $r_0=u^2,r_1=w^2$ gives
$u^2+w^2=50$; equal negative root valuations yield valuation
$2v_2(u)+1<0$, and unequal ones give a negative even valuation,
both impossible. The complete integral residue tests modulo
$8,3,125,7,11,17$ give the balls above; in the nonzero 7-adic
class, positive even valuation of $r_0$ refines the class to
$\xi\equiv24\pmod{49}$. The entire reciprocal chart covers all
negative 17-adic valuations.

At any other good prime, nonintegral $\xi$ makes the valuations of
$r_1,r_2$ equal and both elliptic abscissae units. For integral $\xi$,
at most one of $r_1,r_2$ is a nonunit, except possibly at 13. A pole
of $Q_1$ then cancels $-v_\ell(r_1)$, or a pole of $Q_2$ cancels
$+v_\ell(r_2)$. At 13, simultaneous positive square valuations of
$r_1,r_2$ would contradict $r_1+r_2=26$; nonintegral $\xi$ is handled
as before. This accounts for every finite prime and every denominator. The product
formula and global height identity give
\[
 \rho\in\{c_0,c_{24}\},\qquad
 c_0=-\tfrac34\log_{11}2+2\log_{11}5+\tfrac12\log_{11}17,
 \quad c_{24}=c_0-\log_{11}5.
\tag{HU-6}
\]
Indeed $\rho=-\sum_{\ell\ne11}W_\ell\log_{11}\ell$, since
$\log_{11}v=\sum_{\ell\ne11}v_\ell(v)\log_{11}\ell$.
The boundary points at $\xi=0,24$ attain the indicated levels.

The reflection $\xi\mapsto24-\xi$ permutes the six radicals by
$(0\ 3)(1\ 2)(4\ 5)$. Therefore an actual full lift satisfies
both (HU-6) for its own genus-two image and the same condition for its
reflected genus-two image.

**All possible 11-adic disks.**

A negative valuation of $\xi$ is impossible: the quotient
$(25+\xi)/(25-\xi)$ would have nonsquare residue $-1$ in
$\mathbb F_{11}$. For integral $\xi$, testing every residue
against all six square conditions gives exactly $\xi\equiv0,2\pmod{11}$.
These are the boundary classes $0,24$. At each boundary all six
radicands are units, so their square roots extend throughout the entire
disk. On the genus-two curve these give the eight disks of
$(v,W)=(\pm1/5,\pm338/25),(\pm5,\pm16562)$.
The height function is unchanged by either sign change, because local
heights and squared logarithms are even and $\log_{11}(-1)=0$.
It suffices, after reflection if necessary, to treat $\xi\in11\mathbb Z_{11}$.

**Exact leading constants.**

At the two positive-sign boundary points, the translated elliptic
images are
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
 \xi&Q_1&Q_2\\\hline
 0&(2,102)&(-25,120)\\
 24&(2450,124950)&(-49/25,1176/125).
\end{array}
\]
Exact rational doubling and Fermat quotients give

| Boundary | $\log_1 Q_1/11,\log_2 Q_2/11$ | $\zeta_1(Q_1),\zeta_2(Q_2)$ | $11\alpha_1,11\alpha_2$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\xi=0$ | $(8,2)$ | $(10,6)$ | $(7,1)$ |
| $\xi=24$ | $(3,9)$ | $(5,1)$ | $(7,1)$ |

Every entry is modulo 11. In particular the logarithms have valuation
one, both zeta constants are integral, and both alpha constants have
valuation minus one.

Here is the exact method, so these are not unproved numerical values.
For $N=16$, rational group laws give $NQ$ in the formal group
with $t=-x/y$ of valuation one. Its reductions at every bad prime
are nonsingular. If $D^2$ is the reduced denominator of $x(NQ)$,
then
\[
 \log(NQ)=t+O(11^3),\qquad
 h(NQ)=2\log_{11}(D/t)+O(11^2).
\]
The coefficient of $11$ in a unit logarithm is computed by its
Fermat quotient modulo 121. To compute zeta, let
$J_N=d\log\psi_N/dz$. Repeated doubling uses
\[
 J_{2n}=4J_n+n\frac{3x(nQ)^2+2(A+B)x(nQ)+AB}{y(nQ)}.
\]
The normalized sigma multiplication formula gives
\[
 \zeta(Q)=\frac1{Nt}-\frac{J_N}{N^2}+O(11).
\]
These identities determine the actual constants of (HU-3), including their
integration constants.

Differentiation of (HU-4) gives
\[
 d\rho=-2(\zeta_1+\alpha_1\log_1)\omega_1
       +2(\zeta_2+\alpha_2\log_2)\omega_2-2\,dv/v.
\]
With respect to $\xi$, the two differential coefficients at zero
are $1/50,1/10$, and at 24 are $1/98,1/490$.
Consequently
\[
 \rho'(0)\equiv1,\qquad\rho'(24)\equiv10\pmod{11}.
\tag{HU-7}
\]
For $s\in\mathbb Z_{11}$, the expansions are
\[
 \frac{\rho(11s)-c_0}{11}\equiv s+6s^2,\qquad
 \frac{\rho(24+11s)-c_{24}}{11}\equiv10s+8s^2\pmod{11}.
\tag{HU-8}
\]
The quadratic terms are exactly
$-11\alpha_1\omega_1^2+11\alpha_2\omega_2^2$ at the boundary.
All other higher contributions vanish modulo 11 after division by 11,
as proved next.

**Uniform coefficient bounds on the entire disks.**

Write $u=\xi-\xi_b$ at either boundary. On the entire disk, every
radical used in the two quotient maps, and every denominator, is a unit.
Thus $\omega_i=g_i(u)\,du$ and $X_{{\rm short},i}$ belong to
$\mathbb Z_{11}[[u]]$. The square-root branches are the unique
Hensel branches through the chosen boundary points. The actual Coleman
functions on this disk satisfy
\[
 L_i(u)=L_i(0)+\int_0^u g_i(t)\,dt,
\quad Z_i(u)=Z_i(0)-\int_0^u X_{{\rm short},i}(t)g_i(t)\,dt,
\]
\[
 h_{i,11}(u)-h_{i,11}(0)=-2\int_0^u Z_i(t)g_i(t)\,dt.
\]
Their constants are the actual boundary values certified above. Good
reduction and avoidance of the origin of each elliptic model ensure
that these primitives describe the height and zeta functions on the
whole residue disk; no extension across disconnected local subsets is
being presumed.

Each integration introduces at most one denominator of size at most
the coefficient degree. The height term therefore has degree-$n$
coefficient valuation at least $-2\lfloor\log_{11}n\rfloor$.
The rational logarithm has the stronger one-integration bound.
In the squared-log term write
$L_i(u)^2-L_i(0)^2=2L_i(0)\Delta L_i+(\Delta L_i)^2$.
Since $\alpha_iL_i(0)$ is integral and $v_{11}(\alpha_i)=-1$,
the coefficient $a_n$ of $\rho(\xi_b+u)-\rho(\xi_b)$ satisfies
\[
 v_{11}(a_n)\ge-1-2\lfloor\log_{11}n\rfloor\qquad(n\ge2).
\tag{HU-9}
\]
For $u=11s$, every degree $n\ge3$ therefore has valuation at
least two; these valuations tend to infinity. This proves (HU-8) on the
entire disk. For $u=121s$, division by 121 leaves every degree
$n\ge2$ divisible by 11. Hence, using the unit derivative (HU-7),
\[
 \rho(\xi_b+121s)-\rho(\xi_b)
 =121s\bigl(\rho'(\xi_b)+11sG(s)\bigr),
 \qquad G\in\mathbb Z_{11}\langle s\rangle.
\tag{HU-10}
\]
Its only zero is $s=0$.

**The two equations leave only the boundary.**

Take $\xi=11s$. The reflected equation is based at $24$, so
(HU-8) and (HU-6) require, modulo 11,
\[
 s+6s^2\in\{0,7\},\qquad s+8s^2\in\{0,4\}.
\tag{HU-11}
\]
Here $\log_{11}5/11\equiv4$. Testing all eleven residues gives only
$s=0$; the first condition allows $s=0,1,8,9$, and the second retains only $s=0$. Therefore $\xi\in121\mathbb Z_{11}$.
The first height difference is then divisible by 121, while
$c_{24}-c_0$ has valuation exactly one. Thus its exact level must be
$c_0$. Equation (HU-10) forces $\xi=0$. Reflection handles the
other residue class and forces $\xi=24$.

For the original Hurban recipe put
\[
Q=2z^2+2z+1,\qquad\xi=\frac{100z(z+1)(2z+1)}{Q^2}.
\]
The first two radicands are already squares, with roots
$5(2z^2+4z+1)/Q$ and $5(2z^2-1)/Q$; the four remaining
completion conditions are precisely $r_2,r_3,r_4,r_5$.
For this recipe, $\xi=0$ gives
$z=0,-1,-1/2,\infty$, and $\xi=24$ gives
$z=1,1/2,-2/3,-3/4$. Indeed
\[
 100z(z+1)(2z+1)-24(2z^2+2z+1)^2
 =-4(z-1)(2z-1)(3z+2)(4z+3).
\]
There are no other omitted recipe parameters: $Q=2z^2+2z+1$ has
negative discriminant and no rational zero, and the parameter at
infinity was included. At the two possible offset values, the six
squared entries in (HU-1) are respectively
$(25,25,1,49,1,49)$ and $(49,1,25,25,49,1)$.
They are repeated-entry boundary configurations. This excludes every
admissible rational completion of the Hurban recipe without a height
cutoff and without asserting the full point set of the auxiliary curve.


### 9.57. Excluding the central progression proportional to 1, 25, 49

Suppose the fixed central three-square progression is proportional to
$1,25,49$, with its opposite endpoints in corner positions. After
rational-square scaling, write the center as 25 and the fixed corner
offset as 24. The other corner offset $\xi$ then requires, among the
six unprescribed entries, the four numbers
$25+\xi,25-\xi,1+\xi,1-\xi$ to be rational squares.

Their product supplies a point on
\[
 C:w^2=(625-\xi^2)(1-\xi^2).
\]
For $\xi\ne0$, the exact birational map
\[
 x=50(w+25)/\xi^2,\qquad y=\xi(x^2-2500)/50
\]
lands on $y^2=(x-626)(x^2-2500)$. Put
$x=4X+626,y=8Y$ to obtain
\[
 E:Y^2=X(X+144)(X+169).
\]
Complete two-descent has Selmer dimension two: the certified local Kummer images have dimension three at 2 and dimension two at 3, 5 and 13, and their full intersection leaves four global classes. Full rational two-torsion therefore forces rank zero. Good reduction at 7 and 11 gives
$\#E(\mathbb F_7)=\#E(\mathbb F_{11})=8$, so the rational torsion
has at most eight points. The eight displayed points
\[
 O,(0,0),(-144,0),(-169,0),(156,\pm3900),(-156,\pm156)
\]
therefore form the entire rational point set.

The inverse coordinate is $\xi=50y/(x^2-2500)$. The four points
with $X=\pm156$ give $\xi=\pm1,\pm25$, all with $w=0$.
The point $X=0$ gives $(\xi,w)=(0,-25)$; the elliptic origin
gives $(0,25)$. The two remaining 2-torsion points, $x=\pm50$,
give the two rational infinities of the quartic. This covers every
omitted birational chart because the quartic is smooth and the map is
an isomorphism of its smooth projective model with the elliptic curve.

The original four square tests exclude $\xi=\pm1$, since then one
of $1\pm\xi$ equals 2; they exclude $\xi=\pm25$ by negativity.
A full lift at infinity would require $-1$ to be a rational square.
Thus only $\xi=0$ remains, a repeated-entry configuration.

Together with Section 9.56, this proves that an admissible
magic square cannot contain a central progression proportional to
$1,25,49$, whether its endpoints occupy edge or corner positions.
This is a restriction on that specified central progression, not an
exclusion of all fixed-progression fibers.

In canonical coordinates the resulting necessary restriction is
\[
\boxed{|D_i|/c^2\ne24/25\quad(i=1,2,3,4).}
\tag{U-CENTRAL-PROGRESSION-1-25-49}
\]
It retains its specified normalized progression; no uniform fixed-progression exclusion is inferred.

### 9.58. A reflected height criterion for fixed central edge progressions

This is a conditional arithmetic criterion with a uniform algebraic
construction. It does not assert its rank or local hypotheses for all
progressions. The Hurban fiber in Section 9.56 satisfies every hypothesis; the
$7:13:17$ test below fails the rank hypothesis in both orientations.

**Exact family and maps.**

After a common rational-square rescaling of the entries, choose
positive integers $a,b,c$, with
$a^2+b^2=2c^2$, $d=c^2-a^2\ne0$, and $K=a^2+c^2$.
An ordering of the two endpoints is not required. The six remaining
square conditions of the fixed central edge progression are
\[
 r=(c^2+\xi,c^2-\xi,a^2+\xi,b^2-\xi,a^2+2\xi,b^2-2\xi).
\tag{RT1}
\]
The reflection $\iota(\xi)=d-\xi$ permutes these six conditions by
$(0\ 3)(1\ 2)(4\ 5)$. The boundary values are $0,d$.
All constructions below retain every condition (RT1); only nonzero
radicands are needed in the displayed affine charts. In fact a rational
full lift cannot have a zero radicand: at $\xi=\pm c^2$ the opposite
radicand is $2c^2$; at $\xi=-a^2,b^2$ another radicand is a
negative nonzero square; and at $\xi=-a^2/2,b^2/2$ another radicand
is respectively $a^2/2,b^2/2$. None is a rational square. At infinity,
the opposite leading radicands would require $-1$ to be a rational
square. Thus no rational full-lift point is lost by these affine charts.

From $v^2=r_2/r_1$, $B^2=r_0r_1r_4$, put
\[
 \xi=\frac{c^2v^2-a^2}{1+v^2},\qquad w=B(1+v^2)^2.
\]
The genus-two subcover is
\[
 w^2=K(1+v^2)(2c^2v^2+d)((a^2+2c^2)v^2-a^2).
\tag{RT2}
\]
Its elliptic quotients are
\[
 E_1:y^2=x(x+b^2)(x+4c^2),\qquad
 E_2:y^2=x(x+a^2)(x+b^2),
\]
with $f_1=(-2\xi-2c^2,-2B)$ and
$f_2=(2\xi+a^2,2vB)$. Translate by $(-4c^2,0)$ and
$(-a^2,0)$ to obtain
\[
 x(Q_1)=2c^2r_4/r_1,\qquad x(Q_2)=-a^2r_0/r_2.
\tag{RT3}
\]
The natural models of (RT2) arise from these translated models by the
same absolute scale $K$: $X=K^2x+2a^2c^2K$, $Y=\pm K^3y$.
The differential pullbacks in the $\xi$ coordinate are
\[
 \omega_1=\frac{d\xi}{2\sqrt{r_0r_1r_4}},\qquad
 \omega_2=\frac{d\xi}{2\sqrt{r_0r_2r_4}}.
\]

Choose the positive rational square roots at the boundaries. The
translated images at zero are
\[
 P_1=(2a^2,2a(a^2+2c^2)),\qquad P_2=(-c^2,cd).
\tag{RT4}
\]
At $d$, the images are
\[
 P_{1,d}=\left(\frac{2c^2b^2}{a^2},
                   \frac{2c^2b^2(a^2+2c^2)}{a^3}\right),\qquad
 P_{2,d}=\left(-\frac{a^2b^2}{c^2},\frac{a^2b^2d}{c^3}\right).
\]
Exact group-law calculation gives the useful identity
\[
 \boxed{P_{i,d}=-P_i+(0,0).}
\tag{RT5}
\]
The maps, common scaling, and (RT5) are exact symbolic identities;
the certificate described in Section 14 replays them independently. In particular
the same rank-one height ratios govern both boundary disks.

**Arithmetic hypotheses.**

Fix a prime $p\ge5$ of good reduction for both elliptic curves,
away from the denominators and zero values of the displayed boundary
coordinates, $a,b,c,d,K$. Assume the following independently
certified data.

1. Both elliptic curves have rank one. Choose any certified nontorsion
   point $R_i$ and define
   $\alpha_i=h_i(R_i)/\log_i(R_i)^2$. Boundary points may be used
   only after their nontorsion is certified. Use $\omega=dx/(2y)$,
   short-coordinate complement, and the finite normalization
   $h_{i,\ell}=(\max(0,-v_\ell x)-\mu_{i,\ell})\log_p\ell$.
   At $p$, require the matching normalization
   $h_{i,p}=-2\log_p\sigma_i$,
   $\zeta_i=(\log\sigma_i)'$,
   $d\zeta_i=-X_{\rm short}\omega_i$,
   $\sigma_i(z)=z+O(z^5)$.
2. At both boundary points, the actual elliptic logarithms lie in
   $p\mathbb Z_p$, the zeta constants are integral, and
   $v_p(\alpha_i)\ge-1$. These are arithmetic inputs, not inferences
   from rank or from good reduction alone.
3. Every rational full lift of (RT1) lies in the union
   $\xi\in p\mathbb Z_p\cup(d+p\mathbb Z_p)$. The proof of this
   local restriction must include nonintegral parameters, zero-radicand
   charts, and every permitted sign branch.
4. For every actual full lift, the function
   \[
   \rho=h_{1,p}(Q_1)-h_{2,p}(Q_2)-2\log_p v
       -\alpha_1\log_1(Q_1)^2+\alpha_2\log_2(Q_2)^2
   \tag{RT6}
   \]
   lies in a certified finite set $\Omega\subset\mathbb Q_p$.
   One obtains this set from all non-$p$ local corrections using
   \[
   \rho=-\sum_{\ell\ne p}
   \left(\frac{h_{1,\ell}-h_{2,\ell}}{\log_p\ell}
         +v_\ell(r_2)-v_\ell(r_1)\right)\log_p\ell.
   \]
   This equality follows directly from global quadraticity, rank one,
   and the product formula. A separate full-domain finite-level
   certificate is required; samples of local points do not suffice.

Let $c_0=\rho(0)$, $c_d=\rho(d)$. Define finite residue sets
\[
 U_b=\left\{\overline{(\omega-c_b)/p}:
       \omega\in\Omega,\ v_p(\omega-c_b)\ge1\right\}
 \subset\mathbb F_p\qquad(b=0,d).
\]
The zero difference is included and has residue zero. Require also
that every nonzero $\omega-c_0$, $\omega\in\Omega$, has valuation
strictly less than two.

**The finite paired predicate.**

Let $A_b=\overline{\rho'(b)}$, and let $g_{i,b}$ be the
coefficient of $d\xi$ in $\omega_i$ at the boundary. Put
\[
 B_b=\overline{-p\alpha_1g_{1,b}^2+p\alpha_2g_{2,b}^2}.
\]
These coefficients are integral under the hypotheses. Explicitly,
\[
 (g_{1,0},g_{2,0})=(1/(2ac^2),1/(2a^2c)),\qquad
 (g_{1,d},g_{2,d})=(1/(2ab^2),1/(2b^2c)).
\]
The linear coefficient is evaluated from the actual constants by
\[
 \rho'=-2(\zeta_1+\alpha_1\log_1)g_1
       +2(\zeta_2+\alpha_2\log_2)g_2
       -\frac{K}{r_1r_2}.
\]

**Paired-height criterion.** If $A_0\ne0$ and the complete finite
set
\[
 \left\{s\in\mathbb F_p:
       A_0s+B_0s^2\in U_0,\quad
       -A_ds+B_ds^2\in U_d\right\}
\tag{RT7}
\]
is exactly $\{0\}$, then every rational full lift of (RT1) is one of
the boundary parameters $\xi=0,d$.

**Proof.** After reflection, every actual full lift lies in
$\xi=ps$. All radicands, denominators, and square-root branches are
units on this residue disk. Integration of the invariant differential
and the complementary differential, with their actual boundary
constants, gives the degree-$n$ estimate
\[
 v_p([u^n](\rho(b+u)-c_b))
 \ge-1-2\lfloor\log_p n\rfloor\qquad(n\ge2).
\]
The reason is that each primitive contributes at most one integration
denominator, $\alpha_i\log_i(P_{i,b})$ is integral, and only the
squared-log increment can lose one additional power of $p$.
For $p\ge5$, every $n\ge3$ term has valuation at least two
after substitution $u=ps$. Hence the two normalized expansions
reduce to the two polynomials in (RT7), including every sign branch.
The paired predicate forces $\xi\in p^2\mathbb Z_p$.

The level-separation hypothesis now forces the exact level $c_0$.
On this smaller disk the same coefficient bound gives
\[
 \rho(p^2s)-c_0=p^2s\bigl(\rho'(0)+psG(s)\bigr),
 \qquad G\in\mathbb Z_p\langle s\rangle.
\]
The bracket is a unit, so $s=0$. Reflection gives the second
boundary. No Mordell--Weil saturation or height cutoff is used.

**Two scope checks.**

For $(a,c,b)=(1,5,7)$, the certified prime is 11,
$(A_0,B_0,A_d,B_d)=(1,6,10,8)$,
$U_0=\{0,7\}$, $U_d=\{0,4\}$. The predicate has only zero,
and the independent local-height and logarithm certificates verify
every hypothesis. This is the completed Hurban exclusion.

For the genuinely different progression $(a,c,b)=(7,13,17)$, the
three relevant elliptic factors have exact ranks
\[
 \operatorname{rank}E(289,676)=2,\quad
 \operatorname{rank}E(49,676)=2,\quad
 \operatorname{rank}E(49,289)=1,
\]
where $E(A,B):y^2=x(x+A)(x+B)$. Both endpoint orientations therefore
fail the rank-one-pair hypothesis. Exact lower Kummer classes and complete independently replayed
two-descent upper certificates give these three ranks. No rational-point exclusion
or purported uniform rank theorem is inferred. The next missing
uniform implication is arithmetic control of the ranks, level sets,
and paired predicates on a specified progression class; the algebraic
reflection alone does not supply it.


## 10. Global loci, finite covers, and counting bounds

 Define

$$
\mathcal S_c=\{c\in\mathbb Z_{>0}:p\mid c\Longrightarrow p\equiv1\pmod4\},
\quad
\mathcal P_c=\{(x,y)\in\mathcal O_c^2:x>y,\ \gcd(c,x,y)=1\},
$$

$$
\boxed{\mathcal B=\bigcup_{c\in\mathcal S_c}\{c\}\times\mathcal P_c,\qquad
\mathscr M_{\rm int}
=\{(c,x,y)\in\mathcal B:x+y,x-y\in\mathcal O_c\}.}
\tag{U-G}
$$

This is a complete, unbounded, duplicate-free global specification modulo common square scaling and rotations/reflections. The two positive corner offsets are acted on by signed permutations; $x>y>0$ chooses one representative. Primitivity removes scaling. The last two membership tests impose the four remaining square conditions and positivity. Distinctness is automatic: $x=2y$ would give four squares in arithmetic progression. Root signs do not distinguish square-entry arrays.

The set $\mathcal B$ is an explicitly defined countable superset of the exact solution set $\mathscr M_{\rm int}$, which is equivalent to (U). Residue, prime-support, Gaussian and certified descent restrictions define intermediate supersets. Some restrictions depend on square roots absent from the coordinates of $\mathcal B$; those restrictions require the indicated additional root coordinates.

For $c=\prod_{i=1}^k p_i^{e_i}>1$, the exact ambient count is

$$
\boxed{P(c):=\#\mathcal P_c
=8^{k-1}\prod_{i=1}^k e_i-2^{k-1}.}
\tag{U-GC}
$$

Indeed, Gaussian factorization gives $4\prod_i(2e_i+1)$ signed ordered representations of $2c^2$ as a sum of two squares. Four are $(\pm c,\pm c)$; every remaining sign/order orbit has size eight, giving
$N(c)=\#\mathcal O_c=(\tau(c^2)-1)/2$,
where $\tau$ is the divisor-counting function. The number before removing scaling is
$T(c)=\binom{N(c)}2=(\tau(c^2)^2-4\tau(c^2)+3)/8$.
Every such pair has a unique common gcd of its five integer roots, so
$T(c)=\sum_{d\mid c}P(c/d)$.
Möbius inversion and
$(2e+1)^2-(2e-1)^2=8e$, $(2e+1)-(2e-1)=2$
give (U-GC). Set $P(1)=0$. For a squarefree center with three prime factors this is $60$, rather than $78$ before removing common scaling.

With $C$ bounding the primitive center root, not its squared entry, the full ambient locus satisfies

$$
\boxed{\#\{(c,x,y)\in\mathcal B:c\le C\}
\sim\kappa_{\rm gen}C(\log C)^3,}
\tag{U-GH}
$$

$$
\kappa_{\rm gen}=
\frac{(\pi/8)^4}{48}
\prod_{p\equiv1\ (4)}
(1+6/p+1/p^2)(1-1/p)^6
\prod_{p\equiv3\ (4)}(1-1/p^2)^4>0.
\tag{U-GK}
$$

Both products converge absolutely. For a self-contained reduction to the standard analytic input, define the multiplicative function $f$ by $f(1)=1$, $f(p^e)=8e$ for $p\equiv1\pmod4$, and $f(p^e)=0$ otherwise. Its local series is $(1+6z+z^2)/(1-z)^2$, so its Dirichlet series is

$$
\zeta(s)^4L(s,\chi_4)^4
(1-2^{-s})^4
\prod_{p\equiv1\ (4)}(1+6p^{-s}+p^{-2s})(1-p^{-s})^6
\prod_{p\equiv3\ (4)}(1-p^{-2s})^4.
$$

The factors after $\zeta^4L^4$ converge absolutely for $\Re(s)>1/2$.
The Selberg--Delange theorem therefore gives a leading term
$L(1,\chi_4)^4G(1)C(\log C)^3/\Gamma(4)$,
where $G$ is that convergent factor and $\chi_4$ is the nonprincipal character modulo four.
The theorem's hypotheses also follow directly from $f\ge0$,
$\sum_{p\le X}f(p)\log p=4X+O_A(X/\log^A X)$ for every fixed $A>0$,
and prime-power convergence for any $\sigma>1/2$.
On $\mathcal S_c$, (U-GC) equals
$(f(c)-4\cdot2^{\omega(c)})/8$; the subtracted function has total $O(C)$ by the same theorem with prime average one. Using $L(1,\chi_4)=\pi/4$ and $\Gamma(4)=6$ proves (U-GH)--(U-GK).

The elementary divisor estimate independently gives $O_\varepsilon(C^{1+\varepsilon})$ for every $\varepsilon>0$. Requiring $\omega(c)\ge3$ leaves the leading term (U-GH) unchanged: centers with fewer primes contribute only $O(C\log^2 C)$. Additional necessary conditions may define smaller subsets of this ambient locus. Formula (U-GH) is neither a count of actual solutions nor a lower bound for them.

**Definition 10.1 (A locus of necessary conditions).** Let $\mathfrak Q$ be a finite collection of moduli, and let $\mathcal B^\sharp_{\mathfrak Q}$ contain exactly those triples in $\mathcal B$ satisfying

$$
\boxed{\begin{gathered}
\omega(c)\ge3,\quad x+y<c^2,\quad24\mid x,\quad24\mid y,\quad x\ne6y,\\
p^e\Vert c,\ e\le2\Longrightarrow p^{2e}<c,\\
\omega(c)=3\Longrightarrow\gcd(\widehat g,c/\widehat g)>1,\\
r=y/x\notin\{1/4,1/3,1/2,2/3,3/4\},\\
\text{the finite slope conditions (U-SLOPE-ALL), (U-SLOPE-ADD), (U-SLOPE-F),}\\
\text{(U-J-GOOD)}\Longrightarrow\dim\mathcal S_J(r)\ge5,\quad r\notin\{21/106,35/83,714/1019\},\\
\text{the eight gcd-square conditions (U-EIGHT-SIEVE),}\\
K_{\rm cor}\mid xy,\quad K_{\rm diag}\mid xy(x^2-y^2),\\
\text{the common-step inequalities (13b), (13e), (13f),}\\
(c,x,y)\bmod M\in\mathcal R_M\quad(M\in\mathfrak Q).
\end{gathered}}
\tag{U-ENV}
$$

Here $\widehat A_i=\sqrt{\gcd(c^2,D_i)}$ and
$\widehat g=c/\prod_i\widehat A_i$, defined after (U-EIGHT-SIEVE).
The genus-two dimension conjunct is a finite Selmer condition; (U-J-EXCLUDE) and (U-J-EXCLUDE35) are its evaluated consequences. The separate exclusion $714/1019$ is the actual rank-one rational-point theorem (U-J-POINTS714), and is not a consequence of insufficient Selmer dimension. The prime-power inequality is (U-DOMINANT) for exponents at most two. These are positive integers: at an odd center prime at most one $D_i$
is divisible, by $\gcd(c,x,y)=1$, and $c$ is odd.
On a solution they equal $A_i,g$ in (F).
Thus (U-THREE-PRIME) is a necessary condition expressed entirely in $c,x,y$.

This is a global superset without an upper bound on its variables. It contains every primitive solution, and

$$
\mathscr M_{\rm int}
=\{(c,x,y)\in\mathcal B^\sharp_{\mathfrak Q}:
x+y,x-y\in\mathcal O_c\}.
\tag{U-EX}
$$

The minimum height bound and any finite set $A\subset\mathcal L_{\rm cert}$ define the smaller necessary-condition locus

$$
\mathcal B^{\sharp,\min}_{\mathfrak Q,A}
=\{(c,x,y)\in\mathcal B^\sharp_{\mathfrak Q}:
\exists\ell\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\setminus A,\quad
c^2-x-y=\ell^2,\quad
8\nu_\ell^*(\ell+1)c^2+\nu_\ell^*\ell^4<3\ell^6(\ell+2)^2\}.
\tag{U-MIN-ENV}
$$

Here $\nu_\ell^*$ is defined in (2.23a); it is at least $\nu_\ell$ from (2.22). The locus requires the smallest entry to be a square and satisfies the stronger prime-power-sieved norm bound. Its intersection with the two final offset-membership conditions is exactly $\mathscr M_{\rm int}$, by (U-EX). Every fixed odd minimum has a finite fiber with an explicit center bound, but no absolute bound on all minima follows.

Enlarging $\mathfrak Q$ gives nested envelopes. The table (15f), moduli $25,49$, and the center-zero cases give explicit residue conditions. The twelve-factor slope system uses prime factorizations and finite local squareclass linear algebra. The six pair factors have the dyadic modulus in (U-SLOPE-SEL); the remaining factors use the dimension-certified local images (U-SLOPE-C6). They include $x\ne6y$ and every exclusion (U-SLOPE-Z). The gcd-square conditions require only $c,x,y$, and apply to every prime and valuation. Further certified Selmer obstructions can define smaller supersets preserving (U-EX). These inclusions alone imply no improvement in the asymptotic counting exponent.

**Theorem 10.2 (The global height-counting bound).** Let
$N_{\rm magic}(C)=\#\{(c,x,y)\in\mathscr M_{\rm int}:c\le C\}$.
The surface geometry and the low-degree-curve exclusion (U-Q) give

$$
\boxed{N_{\rm magic}(C)\ll_\varepsilon C^{3/8+\varepsilon}
\qquad\text{for every }\varepsilon>0.}
\tag{U-COUNT}
$$

The deduction uses the rational-quartic exclusion in (U-Q) in addition to the external counting theorem. The weaker $O_\varepsilon(C^{1/2+\varepsilon})$ follows by the same argument using only the no-conic result (U-D). Neither exponent is asserted to be optimal.

Here is the complete bridge. Let $X\subset\mathbb P^8$ be the projective root surface, of degree $64$, and $Y\to X$ its resolution. As in (37), $H^2=64$ and $K_Y=3H$. The primitive coordinate height of a positive magic point lies between $c$ and $\sqrt2c$, so a bound in projective height $B$ transfers with $B=\sqrt2C$.

First, the exact rigidity threshold is

$$
\boxed{X\text{ has finitely many geometric integral curves of degree }
\delta\le31;\text{ degree }32\text{ has a moving family}.}
\tag{U-RIG}
$$

Degree here means degree in the root embedding. If $D$ spans a proper $\mathbb P^r$, the restricted surface quadrics have one-dimensional common zero locus: a surface component would force the integral nondegenerate $X$ into that proper space. General $r-1$ combinations cut a complete-intersection curve containing $D$, whence $\delta\le2^{r-1}$. Lines are immediate; for $r\ge2$, Castelnuovo's bound
$p_a(D)\le(r-1)\binom m2+me$, with
$\delta-1=(r-1)m+e$, $0\le e<r-1$,
gives $2p_a(D)-2-3\delta<0$ for every $\delta\le21$.

For $22\le\delta\le31$, only spans $r=6,7,8$ remain. In span six, a general hyperplane section $\Gamma\subset\mathbb P^5$ has finite quadratic base locus. Reduce its coordinate ring by a further general linear form. The resulting Artinian ideal contains a regular sequence of five quadrics. The **proved five-quadric case** of Eisenbud--Green--Harris identifies its Hilbert function with that of a monomial quotient containing all five squares. Standard monomials form a downward-closed family $\mathcal F$ of subsets of a five-element set, with $|\mathcal F|=\delta$. Deleting any specified element injects sets containing it into those not containing it, so

$$
p_a(D)\le1+\sum_{S\in\mathcal F}|S|-\delta
<1+\frac32\delta.
$$

Strictness follows because equality in all five injections would force the entire $32$-element Boolean lattice. This uses Güntürkün--Hochster's Theorem 1.13, not the general EGH conjecture.

In span seven, $\Gamma\subset\mathbb P^6$ is in symmetric position and has finite quadratic base locus. Castelnuovo, Eisenbud--Harris and Petrakiev's Theorem 2.17 exclude $h_\Gamma(2)=13,14,15,16$: each would put a curve in that base locus. Their degree thresholds hold for $\delta\ge22$. Hence $h_\Gamma(1)=7$, $h_\Gamma(2)\ge17$. Uniform-position subadditivity gives $h_\Gamma(3)\ge\min(\delta,23)$ and $h_\Gamma(4)\ge\min(\delta,33)$, so

$$
p_a(D)\le(\delta-7)+(\delta-17)+\max(0,\delta-23).
$$

This again gives $2p_a(D)-2-3\delta<0$.

In span eight, $D$ cannot lie on a surface of degree $s\le8$: since $\delta>2s$, every defining quadric would contain that surface, contradicting integrality and $\deg X=64$. Eisenbud--Harris therefore gives $p_a(D)\le\pi_1(\delta,8)-1$, where

$$
\pi_1(\delta,r)=r\binom m2+m(e+1)
+\max\!\left(0,\left\lfloor\frac{3-r+e}{2}\right\rfloor\right),
\quad\delta-1=rm+e,\quad0\le e<r.
$$

For $\delta=22,\ldots,31$ the genus bounds are
$19,21,24,26,29,32,35,38,41,44$, again sufficient.

The strict transform $\widetilde D$ maps finitely and birationally to $D$, so
$0\le p_a(\widetilde D)\le p_a(D)$. Adjunction gives, throughout $\delta\le31$,

$$
-2-3\delta\le\widetilde D^2
=2p_a(\widetilde D)-2-3\delta<0.
$$

These degree and self-intersection bounds permit only finitely many numerical classes. Indeed decompose
$[\widetilde D]=(\delta/64)H+v$ with $v\perp H$.
The Hodge index theorem makes $H^\perp$ negative definite, and the displayed bounds confine $v$ to a bounded region of the Néron--Severi lattice. Each negative numerical class contains at most one integral curve, since two distinct curves have nonnegative intersection. This proves the required finiteness.

Sharpness is explicit. Fix an opposite pair by $A=uM$, $H=vM$, $u^2+v^2=2$. The generic fiber is five quadrics in $\mathbb P^6$, of degree $32$. With $\alpha=u^2-1$ fixed, the remaining roots adjoin square roots of $1\pm\beta$ and $1\pm\alpha\pm\beta$. Their six finite zeros are distinct outside $\alpha\in\{0,\pm1,\pm2\}$ and their squareclasses are independent. The degree-$64$ cover of the $\beta$-line has seven branch points, including infinity; Riemann--Hurwitz gives genus $49$. This equals its complete-intersection arithmetic genus, proving generic smoothness. The moving family does not assert any admissible rational point on a fiber.

The finite list in (U-RIG) has a terminating algebraic construction. For $\delta\le31$ and $0\le q\le(\delta-1)(\delta-2)/2$, form
$\operatorname{Hilb}^{\delta t+1-q}(X)$.
Its Gotzmann cutoff is $s=\binom\delta2+1-q\le466$.
Grassmannian multiplication-rank equations in degrees $\max(2,s)$ and $\max(2,s)+1$, with containment of the six quadrics, define the scheme. Its geometrically integral fiber locus is open and finite by (U-RIG), hence lies on zero-dimensional components. Its geometrically integral fibers, together with their Galois orbits, therefore form a finite algebraic set. This is a statement about curves and does not determine their rational points.

Second, Salberger's Theorem 0.9(b) covers all but $O_\varepsilon(B^{3/8+\varepsilon})$ height-$B$ rational points of $X$ by
$O(B^{3/16}\log B+1)$ geometrically integral curves of uniformly bounded degree. His Theorem 1.17 gives
$O_{\delta,8}(B^{2/\delta}\log B+1)$
points on any integral degree-$\delta$ curve in $\mathbb P^8$.

The fixed finite set of curves of degrees at most $31$ contributes at most
$O(B^{1/3}\log B+1)$ admissible points. For degree at most five the normalization has genus at most one. In genus zero, (U-D), the even-degree boundary argument, and the **rational** quartic part of (U-Q) exclude admissible points lifting rationally to the normalization. In genus one, each fixed curve contributes $O((1+\log B)^{r/2})$ points, where $r$ is its Mordell--Weil rank, by the canonical-height lattice bound; if its normalization has no rational point it contributes none there. There are only finitely many such curves, so these polylogarithmic terms are absorbed by $O(B^{1/3})$. Singular points form a finite exception and contribute $O(1)$. The other fixed curves have degree at least six and the uniform curve estimate applies. Curves not defined over $\mathbb Q$ contribute only rational points in their intersections with distinct conjugates, again finitely many. Thus the elliptic-quartic exclusion is not a dependency of (U-COUNT).

All remaining covering curves have degree at least $32$, giving a total

$$
O\!\left(B^{1/4}(\log B)^2+B^{3/16}\log B+1\right).
$$

Since $1/4<3/8$ and $1/3<3/8$, the exceptional-point term dominates, proving (U-COUNT). No assertion that an isolated rational point belongs to a low-genus curve is used. The rigidity threshold improves the subsidiary curve term, not the overall exponent.

The bound applies to the full solution locus. The explicit cover below is distinct from Salberger's smaller cover and has no exceptional points. Neither (U-GH) nor (U-COUNT) gives an effective absolute height bound or proves existence.

**An explicit global cover by height-dependent curves.** A local determinant/lattice argument gives the following construction independently of (U-Q) and of the existence of admissible rational points.

Write the root array as
$[A\ B\ C;\ D\ M\ E;\ F\ G\ H]$.
Every projective root point modulo $3$ has $M\ne0$ and all nine squared coordinates equal to $M^2$. Indeed a zero center would force both members of every opposite pair to vanish, and when the center is a unit the table (15f) forces both offsets to vanish modulo $3$. There are exactly $256$ sign choices after normalizing $M=1$.
Independent root signs preserve the squared array and its height, so every rational square array has a unique representative with all eight normalized roots congruent to $1$ modulo $3$. Rotations and reflections can still be removed separately.

Put $a=A/M$ and $z=C/M$. The resulting residue disc has the exact analytic chart

$$
\begin{aligned}
h^2&=2-a^2,& f^2&=2-z^2,& b^2&=3-a^2-z^2,\\
d^2&=1+z^2-a^2,& e^2&=1+a^2-z^2,& g^2&=a^2+z^2-1,
\end{aligned}
\quad a,z\in1+3\mathbb Z_3,
\tag{U-3}
$$

where each of the six roots is the unique square root congruent to $1$ modulo $3$. The six root derivatives are units; their Jacobian minor is $2^6hfbdeg$. Thus the whole chart is smooth. Every such parameter pair lifts locally, so this chart alone is **not** another local obstruction.

Choose an integer degree $\nu\ge4$. A basis of the degree-$\nu$ coordinate ring consists of the monomials

$$
M^{r_0}A^{r_1}C^{r_2}
\prod_{R\in\{B,D,E,F,G,H\}}R^{\epsilon_R},
\quad
r_i\ge0,\quad\epsilon_R\in\{0,1\},\quad
r_0+r_1+r_2+\sum_R\epsilon_R=\nu.
$$

The six monic square relations give independence as well as spanning. Its size is

$$
N=[t^\nu]\frac{(1+t)^6}{(1-t)^3}
=32\nu^2-96\nu+112.
\tag{U-HILB}
$$

Denote these monomials by $m_1,\ldots,m_N$ and their normalized analytic functions by $f_j=m_j/M^\nu$.

Fix integers $k,\ell\ge1$ and one residue pair
$\mathbf r=(a_0,z_0)$ modulo $3^k$, with $a_0,z_0\equiv1\pmod3$.
At that pair expand

$$
f_j(a_0+u,z_0+v)=\sum_{p,q\ge0}c^{\mathbf r}_{j,pq}u^pv^q,
\qquad c^{\mathbf r}_{j,pq}\in\mathbb Z_3.
$$

These integral coefficients are computed to finite precision by the six simple-root square equations. Their constant square roots need not be rational.
Define the full-rank integer coefficient lattice

$$
\boxed{\Lambda_{\mathbf r,k,\ell}=
\left\{\mathbf b\in\mathbb Z^N:
\sum_j b_jc^{\mathbf r}_{j,pq}
\equiv0\pmod{3^{\,k(\ell-p-q)}}\
\text{ for }p+q<\ell\right\}.}
\tag{U-LAT}
$$

Its index is at most

$$
3^S,\qquad
S=k\sum_{t=0}^{\ell-1}(t+1)(\ell-t)
=k\binom{\ell+2}{3}.
$$

The pigeonhole principle in an integer box therefore supplies a nonzero
$\mathbf b\in\Lambda_{\mathbf r,k,\ell}$ with
$\|\mathbf b\|_\infty\le3^{\lceil S/N\rceil}$.
The nonzero form $F_{\mathbf r}=\sum_jb_jm_j$ does not vanish identically on $X$, by basis independence.

Let $B\ge1$ be an integer root-height bound. At any primitive root vector $P$ of height at most $B$ whose normalized parameters lie in this disc, $M$ is a $3$-adic unit. The congruences, including the integral Taylor tail, give $3^{k\ell}\mid F_{\mathbf r}(P)$, whereas
$|F_{\mathbf r}(P)|\le N3^{\lceil S/N\rceil}B^\nu$.
Consequently the explicit integer inequality

$$
\boxed{N\,3^{\left\lceil k\binom{\ell+2}{3}/N\right\rceil}B^\nu
<3^{k\ell}}
\tag{U-CERT}
$$

proves $F_{\mathbf r}(P)=0$ for **every** such point. The coefficient lattice is defined by finite congruences, and the stated short-vector bound proves the existence of the required form.

Ordinary exact LLL reduction gives a constructive alternative: its first vector has Euclidean norm at most $2^{(N-1)/4}\det(\Lambda)^{1/N}$. A convenient conservative integer certificate is therefore (U-CERT) with its left side multiplied by $2^N$. This changes only the constant in $k$, not the asymptotic exponent. For any produced form, the sharper directly checkable conditions are its exact Taylor congruences and $\|F\|_1B^\nu<3^{k\ell}$. No floating-point logarithm is needed to select $k$: increase it until the appropriate integer inequality holds.

There are $3^{2(k-1)}$ residue pairs. Their explicitly constructible divisors
$X\cap V(F_{\mathbf r})$, each of total degree $64\nu$, cover all sign-normalized height-$B$ root points, with **no exceptional set**. Repeated components may be deduplicated, but are not assumed absent.
Put

$$
\rho=\ell-\frac{\binom{\ell+2}{3}}N.
$$

Choose $\ell$ maximizing $\rho$, equivalently the largest integer with
$\ell(\ell+1)/2\le N$; ties do not matter.
Then $\rho>0$ and

$$
\rho=\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}\sqrt N+O(1),\qquad
\frac{2\nu}{\rho}\longrightarrow\frac38.
$$

Condition (U-CERT) permits
$k=(\nu/\rho)\log_3 B+O_\nu(1)$.
Thus for every $\varepsilon>0$ one can fix $\nu$ and construct

$$
\boxed{O_\varepsilon(B^{3/8+\varepsilon})
\text{ covering divisors of degree }O_\varepsilon(1).}
\tag{U-COV}
$$

Covering all root-sign choices instead multiplies the number by at most $256$.
This bounds the number of covering curves; it is not a bound on their rational points. It is distinct from Salberger's $O(B^{3/16}\log B)$ curves plus an exceptional point set used in (U-COUNT).

To make the cover global rather than a fixed cutoff, apply the construction for every $B=2^n$ and retain the shell $2^{n-1}<H(P)\le2^n$, together with the height-one case. This gives a completely specified countable union of bounded-degree curve problems containing every possible solution, each subject to (U-ENV) and the exact defining equations. The cover changes with the shell: it is not a fixed finite algebraic locus, a proof of non-density, or an existence theorem.

**Several equations per disc and exact component removal.** Fix an integer $1\le r<N$ and put

$$
\rho_r=\ell-\frac{\binom{\ell+2}{3}}{N-r+1}>0.
$$

Minkowski's second theorem for the sup-norm cube gives
$\prod_{j=1}^N\lambda_j\le\det\Lambda$.
Since $\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^N$, all successive minima are at least one, hence
$\lambda_r\le(\det\Lambda)^{1/(N-r+1)}$.
The LLL bound yields $r$ independent vectors of Euclidean norm at most
$2^{(N-1)/2}\sqrt N(\det\Lambda)^{1/(N-r+1)}$.
For $\rho_r=a/b$ in lowest terms, the integer condition

$$
\boxed{3^{2ka}>
N^{2b}\,2^{b(N-1)}B^{2b\nu}}
\tag{U-MULT}
$$

therefore constructs $r$ independent forms modulo $I_X$, all vanishing at every height-$B$ point in the disc. For each fixed $r$,
$2\nu/\max_\ell\rho_r\to3/8$,
so the number of discs remains $O_{\varepsilon,r}(B^{3/8+\varepsilon})$.
As before, each actual form can be certified by its Taylor congruences and $\|F\|_1B^\nu<3^{k\ell}$.

Retain all certified forms found. With root coordinates $Z_1,\ldots,Z_9$, set

$$
\Delta=\left(\prod_iZ_i\right)\prod_{i<j}(Z_i^2-Z_j^2),
\qquad
J_{\mathbf r}=(I_X+(F_1,\ldots,F_r)):\Delta^\infty.
\tag{U-BASE}
$$

Every admissible point in the disc belongs to
$V(J_{\mathbf r})(\mathbb Q)\cap\{\Delta\ne0\}$,
with its original height, residue, positivity and arithmetic conditions. If $J_{\mathbf r}=(1)$, the corresponding locus is empty. If its projective zero locus is zero-dimensional, it has finitely many geometric points. Otherwise its common curve components and isolated points both remain part of that locus. Linear independence of the forms does not imply proper intersection. When two degree-$\nu$ forms do intersect $X$ properly, Bézout bounds the resulting point scheme by $64\nu^2$.

There is also a useful rank certificate. If a degree-$\nu$ subspace of forms vanishing on the base locus has codimension $s$ in the coordinate ring, every curve component of degree $\delta$ forces

$$
s\ge H_D(\nu)\ge\sum_{j=0}^{\nu}\min(\delta,j+1).
$$

Indeed a general hyperplane section has $\delta$ distinct points; products of linear forms interpolate independently at any $j+1$ selected points. Summing the resulting hyperplane-section Hilbert-function bound gives the inequality. Consequently

$$
\boxed{s\le\nu\Longrightarrow\text{no curve component},\qquad
s\le6\nu-10,\ \nu\ge5
\Longrightarrow\text{all curve components have degree at most five}.}
\tag{U-RANK}
$$

The second alternative, combined with (U-Q), leaves only finitely many possible admissible exceptions: singular points, intersections of conjugate components, and isolated points. The rank conditions do not establish admissibility of those points. The generic lattice-index estimate may leave all short forms vanishing on a common curve. For $r/N\to\eta<1$ that estimate has exponent $3/(8\sqrt{1-\eta})$, so forcing almost $N$ independent forms does not preserve the original exponent.

**The denominator parameters give a second, sometimes smaller cover.** Let $S$ be the integral image closure of the four circle parameters in $(\mathbb P^1)^4$, birational to the full root surface. Use this component, not an unsaturated zero locus obtained by clearing the two rational equations. On a common resolution let $T_i$ be the pullback of the $i$th factor's degree-one divisor. Fixing any two generic parameters determines two independent offsets and leaves $4\cdot4=16$ choices for the other two. Hence

$$
T_i^2=0,\qquad T_iT_j=16\ (i\ne j),\qquad
L^2=192,\quad L=\sum_iT_i.
\tag{U-SEG}
$$

The ordinary Segre image is thus an integral degree-$192$ surface in $\mathbb P^{15}$.

The exact arithmetic identity
$\prod_iH_i=c^3g$
controls its height. For primitive opposite-parity circle parameters,
$m_i^2+n_i^2=H_i$ and

$$
\tfrac14\sqrt{c^3g}
\le\prod_i\max(|m_i|,|n_i|)
\le\sqrt{c^3g}.
$$

Choosing the all-one root-sign chart changes each parameter by a fixed rational Möbius map with numerator and denominator among $\pm m_i,\pm n_i,\pm m_i\pm n_i$. Thus the Segre height $\mathcal H$ there satisfies

$$
\boxed{\mathcal H\le4\sqrt{c^3g}.}
\tag{U-HEIGHT}
$$

In this chart all $t_i\in3\mathbb Z_3$ and $R'(0)=4$ is a unit. The two equations solve $t_3,t_4$ integrally and analytically in $t_1,t_2$. Applying the coefficient-lattice construction with Hilbert leading term $96\nu^2$ gives any fixed number of simultaneous auxiliary forms on
$O_\varepsilon(\mathcal H^{3/(8\sqrt3)+\varepsilon})$ discs.
This is an explicit cover, with all component-removal rules of (U-BASE).

**A point-count bound on the same arithmetic strata.** The improvement also counts actual solutions, using the rational-family exclusion (U-R8) below. To prove the needed degree comparison, normalize a root curve $D$ meeting the admissible locus and write $\delta=H\cdot D$. Let $E_i$ be the common-zero divisor of its center section and the two root sections in opposite pair $i$. The induced conic map has
$2\deg t_i=\delta-\deg E_i$.
At a center zero at most one entire opposite pair can vanish: vanishing of two pairs would force all root coordinates to be zero. Also its common vanishing order is at most the center's order. Hence $\sum_iE_i\le\operatorname{div}(M)$, proving

$$
\boxed{\tfrac32\delta\le L\cdot D\le2\delta.}
\tag{U-DEG}
$$

This argument uses sections on the normalization and remains valid over singular root points.

By (U-RIG), Segre curves of degree at most $47$ meeting the admissible locus form a finite fixed list; the fixed-opposite-pair fibers have Segre degree $48$. By (U-R8), rational members capable of contributing an admissible point that lifts rationally to their normalization have degree at least $12$, so their point contribution is $O(\mathcal H^{1/6}\log\mathcal H)$. Fixed genus-one members contribute polylogarithmically, and fixed higher-genus members contribute finitely many points by Faltings. Singular points and conjugate-component intersections add finite exceptions.

Salberger's degree-$192$ cover uses
$O(\mathcal H^{3/(16\sqrt3)}\log\mathcal H)$ curves plus
$O_\varepsilon(\mathcal H^{3/(8\sqrt3)+\varepsilon})$ exceptional points.
Its remaining curves have degree at least $48$, contributing at most
$O(\mathcal H^{3/(16\sqrt3)+1/24}(\log\mathcal H)^2)$.
Both this exponent and $1/6$ are below $3/(8\sqrt3)$.
These estimates give the circle-only bound with exponent $\sqrt3(3+\theta)/16$. Combining this embedding with the root height, as proved in (U-MIX) below, gives the stronger statement: for any fixed $0\le\theta\le1$,

$$
\boxed{\#\{(c,x,y)\in\mathscr M_{\rm int}:
c\le C,\ g\le C^\theta\}
\ll_{\varepsilon,\theta}
C^{\,3\sqrt{3+2\theta-\theta^2}/16+\varepsilon}.}
\tag{U-STRAT}
$$

This is a bound on genuine solutions, not just covering curves. It improves $3/8$ for every $\theta<1$; for $g=1$ its exponent is $3\sqrt3/16\approx0.324760$. Its proof explicitly uses (U-R8) and Faltings; the implied constants need not be effective. The unrestricted exponent remains $3/8$.

**Weighted covers use the individual deficits.** For fixed positive integer weights $\mathbf w$, the Segre--Veronese divisor
$L_{\mathbf w}=\sum_iw_iT_i$
has degree $32\sum_{i<j}w_iw_j$ and height
$O_{\mathbf w}(\prod_iH_i^{w_i/2})$.
On a fixed height box $H_i\ll C^{a_i}$ its constructive-cover exponent is

$$
\kappa(\mathbf w)=
\frac3{8\sqrt2}\,
\frac{\sum_iw_ia_i}{\sqrt{\sum_{i<j}w_iw_j}}.
$$

When $0\le a_i\le1$ and $A=\sum a_i\ge3$, put $B_2=\sum a_i^2$. Its infimum over positive rational weights is
$\sqrt{3(A^2-3B_2)}/8$, approached at $w_i\propto A-3a_i$.
For a proof, put $b_i=A-3a_i$, $D=A^2-3B_2>0$, and decompose $w=\lambda b+v$ with $a\cdot v=0$. The cross term in $q(w)=\sum_{i<j}w_iw_j$ vanishes, and
$(\mathbf1\cdot v)^2\le(4-A^2/B_2)\|v\|^2\le\|v\|^2$.
Thus $q(v)\le0$ and $q(w)\le3(a\cdot w)^2/(2D)$, with equality at the stated weights. The zero-$D$ boundary follows by positive perturbation.

In arithmetic notation this becomes

$$
\boxed{\kappa_{\rm opt}
=\frac38\sqrt{1+\frac{\gamma^2}{3}-\sum_i b_i^2},
\quad
\gamma=\frac{\log g}{\log c},\quad
b_i=\frac{\log A_i}{\log c},\quad
\sum_i b_i=1-\gamma,\quad
w_i\propto b_i+\gamma/3.}
\tag{U-WEIGHT}
$$

The weighted **cover** improves $3/8$ when $\sum_i b_i^2>\gamma^2/3$.
For uniform statements, fix rational exponent boxes or a finite mesh with a budgeted exponent error, and use fixed positive rational weights on each box. Zero weights may be approached but cannot be inserted into the birational-degree formula. A different real choice at every unknown point is not by itself a uniform theorem. Retain the better of this cover and the root cover on each box.

**Weighted actual point counts.** The same arithmetic and curve-degree restrictions give a point-count envelope. The individual projection degrees improve it further. On an admissible rational family put $d_i=\deg(t_i)$ and $\delta=H\cdot D$. Then

$$
d_i\ge2\ (i=1,2,3,4),\qquad
d_i\le\delta/2,\qquad \sum_i d_i\ge3\delta/2,\qquad\delta\ge8.
$$

All four lower bounds are (U-CANCEL); the last three statements follow from (U-DEG) and (U-R8). To justify the nonconstant side maps, fix $\alpha+\beta=\kappa$ or $\alpha-\beta=\kappa$ with $0<\kappa<1$. The remaining six radicands, as functions of $\alpha$, have distinct zeros
$\{-1,1,\kappa-1,\kappa+1,(\kappa-1)/2,(\kappa+1)/2\}$.
Their squareclasses are independent and infinity is a seventh branch point, so each fixed-parameter fiber is a degree-$64$ cover of a line of genus $49$. A rational or elliptic curve cannot map nonconstantly to it. The corner fibers have the same conclusion by the preceding six-radicand argument. Thus every $t_i$ is nonconstant on an admissible low-genus family. These are function-field restrictions, not extra pointwise inequalities on a single tuple.

For fixed positive integer weights set

$$
W_{\mathbf w}=\sum_iw_i,\quad M_{\mathbf w}=\max_iw_i,\quad
s_{\mathbf w}=W_{\mathbf w}-M_{\mathbf w},\quad
q_{\mathbf w}=\sum_{i<j}w_iw_j.
$$

Let $j$ index a largest weight, let $M'_{\mathbf w}$ be the second largest, and set $\ell_i=2$ for all four indices. The smallest rational-curve degree allowed by all the displayed degree inequalities is

$$
\lambda_{\mathbf w}=4s_{\mathbf w}+\ell_j(M_{\mathbf w}-M'_{\mathbf w}).
$$

Ties cause no ambiguity because the extra term is zero. For a proof, put $k=\delta/2\ge4$ and $e_i=k-d_i$. These nonnegative deficits satisfy
$\sum_i e_i\le k$ and $e_i\le k-\ell_i$.
To maximize $\sum_iw_ie_i$, fill a largest-weight coordinate to $k-\ell_j$ and place the remaining $\ell_j$ in a second-largest one. This is feasible since $k\ge\ell_j+\ell_{j'}$. Therefore
$\sum_iw_id_i\ge ks_{\mathbf w}+\ell_j(M_{\mathbf w}-M'_{\mathbf w})\ge\lambda_{\mathbf w}$.
It is an exact optimization of these degree inequalities; it does not assert existence of a curve attaining them.

For arbitrary curves the common-zero divisors in (U-DEG) give

$$
\Delta_{\mathbf w}=L_{\mathbf w}\cdot D
=\tfrac12\left(W_{\mathbf w}\delta-\sum_iw_i\deg E_i\right)
\ge\tfrac12s_{\mathbf w}\delta.
$$

Hence curves of weighted degree below $16s_{\mathbf w}$ meeting the admissible locus belong to the finite root-degree-at-most-$31$ list. Write
$e_{\mathbf w}=3/\sqrt{32q_{\mathbf w}}$.
In weighted height $T$, Salberger's exceptional-point term has exponent $e_{\mathbf w}$; the fixed rational-curve term has exponent $2/\lambda_{\mathbf w}$; and the moving-curve term has exponent $e_{\mathbf w}/2+1/(8s_{\mathbf w})$. Fixed genus-one and higher-genus contributions are respectively polylogarithmic and finite, as in (U-STRAT). Thus

$$
\boxed{N_{\mathbf w,\mathrm{adm}}(T)\ll_{\varepsilon,\mathbf w}
T^{\,\max\{e_{\mathbf w},\,
e_{\mathbf w}/2+1/(8s_{\mathbf w})\}+\varepsilon}.}
\tag{U-WPOINT}
$$

The rational-curve term is dominated for every weight vector, using the cancellation theorem rather than an unproved curve classification. Put $d_0=M_{\mathbf w}-M'_{\mathbf w}$, and let $a,b$ be the two smallest weights. Then
$q_{\mathbf w}\le s_{\mathbf w}(s_{\mathbf w}+d_0)$, since the difference is $a^2+ab+b^2$.
Thus $\lambda_{\mathbf w}=4s_{\mathbf w}+2d_0$ satisfies
$\lambda_{\mathbf w}^2\ge16q_{\mathbf w}$ and
$2/\lambda_{\mathbf w}\le2\sqrt2/\sqrt{32q_{\mathbf w}}<e_{\mathbf w}$.
This is why that term is absent from (U-WPOINT), not an assumption that the rational curves themselves are absent.

The moving-curve term must be retained. Fixed-parameter genus-$49$ fibers can have small weighted degree even when one weight is large; the improved rational-curve bound does not apply to them.

For a fixed box $H_i\ll C^{a_i}$, define

$$
\boxed{\begin{aligned}
\mathcal K(\mathbf a)=\min\Bigg\{\frac38,\
\inf_{\mathbf w\in\mathbb Q_{>0}^4}
\max\Bigg(&\frac{3\sum_iw_ia_i}{8\sqrt{2q_{\mathbf w}}},\\
&\frac{3\sum_iw_ia_i}{16\sqrt{2q_{\mathbf w}}}
+\frac{\sum_iw_ia_i}{16s_{\mathbf w}}\Bigg)\Bigg\},\\
\#\{(c,x,y)\in\mathscr M_{\rm int}:c\le C,\ H_i\ll C^{a_i}\}
&\ll_{\varepsilon,\mathbf a}C^{\mathcal K(\mathbf a)+\varepsilon}.
\end{aligned}}
\tag{U-WENV}
$$

The height-box constants are fixed. Clearing weight denominators preserves these exponents. For each $\varepsilon$, one fixed positive rational weight vector approximates the infimum sufficiently closely; no point-dependent choice of weights is required. The root bound supplies the $3/8$ alternative.

There is a single algebraic feasibility formulation for the weighted optimization. Choose one of the four possible largest-weight indices, so $s_{\mathbf w}$ is linear, and normalize $\sum_i a_iw_i=1$. A proposed exponent $K>0$ is attained by positive real weights precisely when there exists $z>0$ such that

$$
\boxed{\begin{gathered}
w_i>0,\quad \sum_i a_iw_i=1,\quad z^2\le2q_{\mathbf w},\\
3\le8Kz,\qquad
3s_{\mathbf w}+z\le16Kzs_{\mathbf w}.
\end{gathered}}
\tag{U-WOPT}
$$

Choosing $z=\sqrt{2q_{\mathbf w}}$ proves equivalence to the two terms in (U-WENV). For rational input $K,\mathbf a$, these are rational polynomial conditions. Strict improvements can be approximated by rational weights. This optimizes a proved upper bound, not the true counting function.

The cover-optimal weights in (U-WEIGHT) transfer directly to this point bound on many multi-deficit boxes. Put $D=1+\gamma^2/3-\sum_i b_i^2>0$ and $s_*=1-b_{\max}$. At $w_i=b_i+\gamma/3$ one has $q_{\mathbf w}=D/2$. The cover-optimal exponent is also the optimal weighted point exponent whenever its moving-curve comparison $D\le9s_*^2$ holds. The rational-curve term is already dominated for every weight. Zero weights are handled by positive approximation, with $D>0$ essential; uniform application uses fixed exponent boxes.

**Root and circle heights in one counting envelope.** The two embeddings can be used simultaneously. On a common resolution their additional intersection numbers are

$$
H T_i=32.
$$

Indeed fixing one circle parameter fixes the two opposite roots as multiples of the center. The resulting two linear equations leave five quadrics in $\mathbb P^6$; their generic integral genus-$49$ fiber has degree $32$. For fixed positive rational $u,w_1,\ldots,w_4$, clear denominators and embed the integral graph of the circle maps using
$D_{u,\mathbf w}=uH+\sum_iw_iT_i$. Its degree and height exponent on $c\le C,\ H_i\ll C^{a_i}$ are

$$
d_{u,\mathbf w}=64u^2+64uW_{\mathbf w}+32q_{\mathbf w},
\qquad \tau_{u,\mathbf w}(\mathbf a)=u+\tfrac12\sum_iw_ia_i.
$$

The height is $O_{u,\mathbf w}(C^\tau)$. The graph construction handles the circle maps' base points; no base-point-free assertion on the original singular surface is needed. With $u>0$, zero circle weights are also allowed by retaining only the corresponding positive-weight maps: the root factor still gives a birational embedding of that graph.

Write

$$
\lambda_{u,\mathbf w}=8u+\lambda_{\mathbf w},
\qquad m_{u,\mathbf w}=32u+16s_{\mathbf w}.
$$

Every admissible rational curve contributing points from its normalization has mixed degree at least $\lambda_{u,\mathbf w}$. This follows from the same simultaneous degree inequalities as before, giving
$\delta(u+s_{\mathbf w}/2)+\ell_j(M_{\mathbf w}-M'_{\mathbf w})$ with $\delta\ge8$.
An arbitrary curve of root degree $\delta$ has mixed degree at least
$\delta(u+s_{\mathbf w}/2)$. Thus curves of mixed degree less than $m_{u,\mathbf w}$ come from the fixed finite root-degree-at-most-$31$ locus.

Apply the surface cover and uniform curve estimate to this mixed image. The exceptional-point, fixed rational-curve, and moving-curve terms give the unified envelope

$$
\boxed{\begin{aligned}
\mathcal K_{\rm mix}(\mathbf a)
&=\inf_{\substack{u\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\\\mathbf w\in\mathbb Q_{>0}^4}}
\tau_{u,\mathbf w}(\mathbf a)
\max\left\{\frac3{\sqrt{d_{u,\mathbf w}}},
\frac3{2\sqrt{d_{u,\mathbf w}}}+\frac2{m_{u,\mathbf w}}\right\},\\
\#\{(c,x,y)\in\mathscr M_{\rm int}:c\le C,\ H_i\ll C^{a_i}\}
&\ll_{\varepsilon,\mathbf a}C^{\mathcal K_{\rm mix}(\mathbf a)+\varepsilon}.
\end{aligned}}
\tag{U-MIX}
$$

Fixed genus-one curves contribute polylogarithmically; fixed higher-genus curves contribute finitely by Faltings. Singular image points and intersections of conjugate curves retain the same finite exceptional contributions as before. The root-only and circle-only exponents occur as limits, so (U-MIX) supersedes their minimum. Its implied constants need not be effective.

The rational-curve contribution is dominated here as well. Besides $\lambda_{\mathbf w}^2\ge16q_{\mathbf w}$, the preceding calculation gives $\lambda_{\mathbf w}\ge2W_{\mathbf w}$. Hence

$$
(8u+\lambda_{\mathbf w})^2
\ge64u^2+32uW_{\mathbf w}+16q_{\mathbf w}
\ge\tfrac12d_{u,\mathbf w}.
$$

Therefore $2/\lambda_{u,\mathbf w}\le2\sqrt2/\sqrt{d_{u,\mathbf w}}<3/\sqrt{d_{u,\mathbf w}}$. The simultaneous cancellation restriction removes this term from the global envelope for all weights.

This remains a single algebraic optimization. Choose a largest circle-weight index and normalize $\tau=1$; only four index cases are needed. A positive exponent $K$ is feasible exactly when, for some $z>0$,

$$
z^2\le d_{u,\mathbf w},\qquad
3\le Kz,\qquad
3m_{u,\mathbf w}+4z\le2Kzm_{u,\mathbf w}.
\tag{U-MIX-OPT}
$$

Choose $z=\sqrt{d_{u,\mathbf w}}$ for the converse. Rational inputs give polynomial conditions; strict gains admit fixed rational weights. This optimizes a proved upper bound, not the unknown true count.

For the common-factor stratum take $w_i=1$. Then
$d=64(u+1)(u+3)$, $\lambda=8u+12$, and $m=32u+48$.
Both curve terms are below $3/\sqrt d$ for all $u\ge0$. Since
$\prod_iH_i=c^3g$, on $g\le C^\theta$ the height exponent is
$u+(3+\theta)/2$. Minimizing gives $u=2\theta/(1-\theta)$ for $0\le\theta<1$, and proves the strengthened (U-STRAT):

$$
\frac3{16}\sqrt{3+2\theta-\theta^2}<\frac38
\quad(0\le\theta<1).
$$

The endpoint $\theta=1$ uses the root bound. Irrational weights are handled by rational approximation with the $\varepsilon$ allowance.

The exceptional-point term has an exact optimum on an arithmetic exponent profile
$a_i=1-b_i$, $b_i\ge0$, $\sum_i b_i=1-\gamma\le1$:

$$
\boxed{\kappa_{\rm mix,opt}=\frac38\sqrt{1-\sum_i b_i^2}.}
\tag{U-MIX-PROFILE}
$$

To prove this, put $h=u+W_{\mathbf w}/2$ and $v_i=w_i/(2h)$. Then
$d=64h^2(1-\|\mathbf v\|^2)$ and
$\tau=h(1-\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf v)$.
The inequality
$(1-\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf v)^2 \ge(1-\|\mathbf b\|^2)(1-\|\mathbf v\|^2)$
follows by writing $\mathbf v=t\mathbf b+\mathbf z$ with
$\mathbf z\perp\mathbf b$; the difference is
$\|\mathbf b\|^2(1-t)^2+(1-\|\mathbf b\|^2)\|\mathbf z\|^2$.
The case $\mathbf b=0$ follows directly. Equality is attained at
$u=\gamma,\ w_i=2b_i$, up to common scaling and positive approximation.

The full actual-point envelope also has a four-variable expression, with no redundant scale parameter. In terms of $\mathbf b=\mathbf1-\mathbf a$ it is

$$
\boxed{\mathcal K_{\rm mix}(\mathbf1-\mathbf b)
=\inf_{\substack{v_i\ge0,\ \sum_i v_i\le1\\\|\mathbf v\|^2<1}}
(1-\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf v)
\max\left\{
\frac3{8\sqrt{1-\|\mathbf v\|^2}},
\frac3{16\sqrt{1-\|\mathbf v\|^2}}+
\frac1{16(1-v_{\max})}
\right\}.}
\tag{U-MIX-SIMPLEX}
$$

Set $u=1-\sum_i v_i$ and $w_i=2v_i$ to obtain this expression from (U-MIX). Boundary weights are interpreted by positive approximation; the excluded norm-one vertices have singular denominators. Thus the formula specifies the same infimum over fixed embeddings, not a point-dependent choice.
For every nonzero deficit profile, choosing $\mathbf v=\mathbf b/2$ gives the explicit bound

$$
\mathcal K_{\rm mix}(\mathbf1-\mathbf b)
\le\frac38\,\frac{1-B/2}{\sqrt{1-B/4}}<\frac38,
\qquad B=\sum_i b_i^2>0.
$$

The moving term is subordinate because $v_{\max}\le1/2$ and
$\sqrt{1-\|\mathbf v\|^2}\le1<3(1-v_{\max})$.
This specialization is a convenient consequence of the full envelope, not an additional independent restriction.

Let $D=1-\sum_i b_i^2>0$. At the cover-optimal weights $u=\gamma,w_i=2b_i$, that value is also an actual-point exponent in (U-MIX) whenever

$$
D\le9(1-b_{\max})^2.
$$

This is the moving-curve comparison; no rational-curve comparison remains. For uniform statements use fixed exponent boxes or a finite mesh with a budgeted exponent error. Point-dependent real weights are not a substitute for this step.

A direct global consequence needs no mesh. For $0\le\beta\le1$,

$$
\boxed{\begin{aligned}
\#\{(c,x,y)\in\mathscr M_{\rm int}:c\le C,\ \max_i A_i\ge c^\beta\}
&\ll_{\varepsilon,\beta}C^{\eta_{\rm mix}(\beta)+\varepsilon},\\
\eta_{\rm mix}(\beta)&=
\begin{cases}
\frac38\sqrt{1-\beta^2},&0\le\beta\le4/5,\\
(5-4\beta)/8,&4/5\le\beta\le1.
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}}
\tag{U-LARGE-A}
$$

Choose the heavy circle index with $A_i\ge c^\beta$, so $H_i\le c^{1-\beta}$, and take the union over four indices. In the first branch use $u=1-\beta,\ w_i=2\beta$, other circle weights zero. The surface degree is $64(1-\beta^2)$, and the moving term is dominated through $\beta=4/5$. The rational term is dominated at every index by (U-CANCEL). The second branch uses $u=1,w_i=8$, giving degree $24^2$; the exceptional and moving exponents in mixed height both equal $1/8$. Its arithmetic exponent is $(5-4\beta)/8$.

These bounds improve $3/8$ for every fixed $\beta>0$. For instance $\beta=1/2$ gives $3\sqrt3/16\approx0.324760$. The fixed-weight tail is a safe bound; the full envelope (U-MIX) can be smaller.

For the four-conic envelope, the only exponent profile at which the mixed exceptional-point optimum gives no strict gain is $b_1=\cdots=b_4=0$, equivalently $A_i=c^{o(1)}$ and $g=c^{1-o(1)}$. The eight-conic and uniform-fiber bounds below further partition this range and strengthen (U-LARGE-A). None supplies an effective absolute height bound.

**All eight progression conics and their arithmetic deficits.** Write the squared-entry grid as
$z_{ij}^2=c^2+ix+jy$, $i,j\in\{-1,0,1\}$. Let $\mathcal L$ consist of its three rows, three columns and two diagonals, and let $\mathcal L_0$ be the four lines through $(0,0)$. For each line $\ell$, denote its three integer roots by $a_\ell,b_\ell,d_\ell$, with $b_\ell$ the midpoint, and put

$$
\boxed{\begin{gathered}
G_\ell=\gcd(a_\ell,b_\ell,d_\ell),\qquad
a_\ell^2+d_\ell^2=2b_\ell^2,\\
\{G_\ell:\ell\in\mathcal L_0\}=\{A_1,A_2,A_3,A_4\},\\
B_{x,\pm}^2=\gcd(c^2\pm x,y),\qquad
B_{y,\pm}^2=\gcd(c^2\pm y,x).
\end{gathered}}
\tag{U-EIGHT-GCD}
$$

The last four quantities are the gcds on the four outer lines. Their defining integer gcds are squares, since they equal gcds of three squared roots. A reduced circle parameter $t_\ell=n_\ell/m_\ell$, with coprime opposite-parity integers, satisfies

$$
m_\ell^2+n_\ell^2=b_\ell/G_\ell,\qquad
H(t_\ell)^2\asymp b_\ell/G_\ell\ll c/G_\ell.
$$

The constants account only for fixed conic symmetries. Thus $G_\ell\ge c^{b}$ gives $H(t_\ell)^2\ll C^{1-b}$ when $c\le C$.

The same data have a necessary projection requiring none of the missing roots:

$$
\boxed{\begin{gathered}
\gcd(c^2,D)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^{\,2}
\quad(D\in\{x,y,x+y,x-y\}),\\
\gcd(c^2\pm x,y),\ \gcd(c^2\pm y,x)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^{\,2}.
\end{gathered}}
\tag{U-EIGHT-SIEVE}
$$

Here $\mathbb Z_{>0}^{\,2}=\{n^2:n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\}$. For a progression of squares with midpoint squared value $M$ and step $D$,
$\gcd(M,D)=\gcd(M-D,M,M+D)$ is the square of the gcd of its roots. On a genuine solution the eight square roots in (U-EIGHT-SIEVE) are exactly the $G_\ell$. The first two tests already follow from the ambient locus $\mathcal B$; the other six project missing square conditions. Primitivity alone does not imply them: the ambient triple $(c,x,y)=(145,6864,4896)$ has corner roots $167,119,161,127$, yet $\gcd(c^2,x+y)=5$ and $\gcd(c^2-x,y)=17$. This example proves nonredundancy relative to the ambient locus, not relative to every conjunct of (U-ENV).

All eight gcds are pairwise coprime. An odd prime dividing two of them makes the squared-entry linear form vanish on two distinct grid lines, forcing all nine roots to vanish modulo that prime; the prime two is absent because primitive roots are odd. Consequently

$$
\boxed{\begin{gathered}
\prod_{\ell\ni(i,j)}G_\ell\mid z_{ij},\qquad
\prod_{\ell\in\mathcal L}G_\ell\le(\sqrt2\,c)^3,\\
(B_{x,+}B_{x,-})^2\mid y,\qquad
(B_{y,+}B_{y,-})^2\mid x.
\end{gathered}}
\tag{U-EIGHT-INC}
$$

Each outer gcd is coprime to $c$ and to $h=\gcd(x,y)$, and has prime support only in $1,7\bmod8$. For example a prime dividing $B_{x,+}$ makes $y=0$ and $x=-c^2$ locally, while $c$ is a unit. The opposite midpoint is then a square congruent to $2c^2$, forcing $2$ to be a quadratic residue. The incidence inequalities are upper bounds on the gcds; they do not force any one gcd to have positive power growth.

On the common resolution let $T_\ell$ be the degree-one class of the $\ell$-th conic map. Then

$$
\boxed{H^2=64,\quad HT_\ell=32,\quad
T_\ell^2=0,\quad T_\ell T_k=16\quad(\ell\ne k).}
\tag{U-EIGHT-GRAM}
$$

Fixing one parameter imposes two linear root ratios and leaves five quadrics in $\mathbb P^6$, giving degree 32. Fixing two parameters generically determines the squared-entry plane point and imposes four independent sign relations: distinct grid lines share at most one root. Thus 16 of its 256 projective root-sign lifts remain, proving the last intersection number.

Every one of these eight maps has degree at least two on an admissible rational full-root curve. For the six parallel progressions, normalizing the step by the square of the relevant midpoint root gives $R(t_\ell)$. The quadratic extension obtained by adjoining its square root is still the original $x$- or $y$-step cover. A degree-one $t_\ell$ would make that cover genus one, since $R$ has four odd-order branch places. This contradicts the two independent $E_1$ factors in its Jacobian supplied by (U-P). The two diagonal cases follow from (U-CANCEL).

All eight fixed-parameter fibers have genus 49 on the admissible rational parameter set. For an outer line, normalize its midpoint root to one and write $\kappa=R(t_\ell)\in(0,1)$. The six remaining radicands are

$$
z-\kappa,\ z,\ z+\kappa,\quad
2z-1-\kappa,\ 2z-1,\ 2z-1+\kappa.
$$

Their zeros are $-\kappa,0,\kappa,(1-\kappa)/2,1/2,(1+\kappa)/2$. Collisions in the open interval occur only at $\kappa=1/3,1/2$, neither possible for a rational conic parameter because $1-\kappa$ is not a rational square. The degree-64 multiquadratic cover has these six branch places and infinity, giving genus 49 by Riemann–Hurwitz.

**Curve constraints from incidence and intersection theory.** For an integral root curve with normalization $\widetilde C$, let $\delta=H\cdot C$, and now write $d_\ell=\deg(t_\ell|_{\widetilde C})$. Let $E_\ell$ be the common-zero divisor of its three root sections. If $I$ is the nine-by-eight grid-point/line incidence matrix and $r_v=\sum_\ell I_{v\ell}$, then

$$
