2d_\ell=\delta-\deg E_\ell,\qquad
I(\deg E_\ell)_\ell\le\delta\mathbf1.
$$

Two distinct triples cannot vanish at the same parameter without all root coordinates vanishing, so their common-zero supports are disjoint. This proves the incidence inequality, including over singular root points.

Put $S_\ell=T_\ell-H/2$. Equation (U-EIGHT-GRAM) gives $HS_\ell=0$, $S_\ell^2=-16$, and $S_\ell S_k=0$ for distinct indices. Hodge index therefore gives

$$
C^2\le\frac{\delta^2-\sum_\ell(\delta-2d_\ell)^2}{64}.
$$

For every curve of nonnegative self-intersection, the normalized common-zero degrees consequently satisfy

$$
\boxed{\mathbf z\ge0,\qquad I\mathbf z\le\mathbf1,\qquad
\|\mathbf z\|^2\le1,\qquad
z_\ell=(\delta-2d_\ell)/\delta.}
\tag{U-EIGHT-HODGE}
$$

The quadratic condition strengthens incidence: six parallel coordinates equal to $1/2$, with diagonal coordinates zero, satisfy incidence but have squared norm $3/2$.

Negative-self-intersection curves of bounded root degree form a finite fixed list on this resolution. To see this despite any extra blowups, choose an ample $A=mH-E$ with $E$ effective and exceptional. For nonexceptional integral curves, $A\cdot C\le m\delta$. Choose $N$ with $NA\pm K$ ample; adjunction gives $C^2\ge-2-Nm\delta$. Hodge index with $A$ bounds the numerical classes, and a negative class contains at most one integral curve. Thus such curves can be treated as fixed components. Every remaining curve has nonnegative square and, by (U-RIG), root degree at least 32.

For fixed nonnegative weights $\mathbf w=(w_\ell)_{\ell\in\mathcal L}$, set

$$
W=\sum_\ell w_\ell,\qquad q=\sum_{\ell<k}w_\ell w_k,\qquad
\mu(\mathbf w)=
\max_{\substack{\mathbf z\ge0,\ I\mathbf z\le\mathbf1\\
\|\mathbf z\|^2\le1}}\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf z.
$$

The mixed divisor $D=uH+\sum_\ell w_\ell T_\ell$, with $u>0$, therefore has the moving-curve degree floor

$$
m_{\rm mov}=32u+16(W-\mu(\mathbf w)).
$$

For rational curves whose normalization has a rational point, the root degree is even and at least twelve by (U-R12), and all $d_\ell\ge2$. A genus-zero normalization without rational points contributes only singular rational image points; these finite exceptions retain the fixed-component treatment.

First, each parallel triple has at least one degree at least three. A row progression has full elliptic abscissa $X_j=(1+j\beta)/\alpha=1/R(t_j)$, so taking degrees on the step double cover gives $\deg f_j=\deg_Ct_j$. If all three were two, the middle parameter would give at most eight branch points, leaving genus two or three by (U-P). The Gram and polarization exclusions following (U-D) apply to precisely this triple, independently of the ambient root degree. Columns are identical.

For $\delta\ge10$, incidence and $d_\ell\le\delta/2$ give $d_\ell+d_k\ge5$ whenever the two grid lines meet. Together with the preceding directional conditions, these imply

$$
\left(\sum_\ell w_\ell d_\ell\right)^2\ge\frac{100}{7}q.
$$

Here is an elementary proof. Truncate the degrees at three and put $x_\ell=d_\ell-2$. Choose one row and one column with $x_\ell=1$; on the remaining coordinates the inequalities are $0\le x_\ell\le1$ and $x_\ell+x_k\ge1$ on the complete multipartite graph with part sizes $2,2,1,1$. Its vertices are half-integral: an unanchored bipartite component of active equations admits an alternating perturbation, whereas an odd cycle forces value $1/2$. A zero coordinate forces all other parts to one, so there are at most two zeros; without zeros there are at most six halves. Thus every vertex degree profile dominates, up to permutation, either $(2,2,3,3,3,3,3,3)$ or $(5/2,5/2,5/2,5/2,5/2,5/2,3,3)$.

For the first profile, let $S,T$ be the sums of the two low and six high weights. Then $q\le S^2/4+ST+5T^2/12$ and

$$
(2S+3T)^2-\tfrac{100}{7}(S^2/4+ST+5T^2/12)
=(3S-8T)^2/21.
$$

For the second, grouping the six low and two high weights gives
$(5S/2+3T)^2\ge15q$. Convexity proves the displayed bound for the full degree polytope. Writing $\lambda=\sum w_\ell d_\ell\ge2W$, it follows that

$$
9(10u+\lambda)^2-4(64u^2+64uW+32q)
\ge644u^2+104uW+\tfrac47q>0.
$$

Consequently every admissible rational family satisfies

$$
\boxed{\frac{2}{D\cdot C}
\le\frac{2}{10u+\sum_\ell w_\ell d_\ell}
<\frac{3}{\sqrt{64u^2+64uW+32q}}.}
\tag{U-EIGHT-RAT}
$$

Thus the determinant contribution dominates every rational-curve contribution. No separate rational term is needed.

**The joint eight-conic counting envelope.** For fixed rational $u>0,w_\ell\ge0$, clear denominators and use the root factor together with the positive-weight conic factors in the graph embedding. The root factor makes this embedding birational even when some conic weights are zero. Its degree is

$$
\mathfrak d=64u^2+64uW+32q.
$$

On a fixed height box $c\le C,\ H(t_\ell)^2\ll C^{a_\ell}$, its height is $O(C^\tau)$, where $\tau=u+\frac12\sum_\ell a_\ell w_\ell$. Salberger's covering theorem, the preceding curve floors, and the fixed-curve arguments give

$$
\boxed{\begin{aligned}
\mathcal K_8(\mathbf a)
&=\min\left\{\frac38,\
\inf_{\substack{u\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\\
\mathbf w\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}^8}}
\tau\max\left(
\frac3{\sqrt{\mathfrak d}},\
\frac3{2\sqrt{\mathfrak d}}+\frac2{m_{\rm mov}}
\right)\right\},\\
N_{\rm box}(C)&\ll_{\varepsilon,\mathbf a}
C^{\mathcal K_8(\mathbf a)+\varepsilon}.
\end{aligned}}
\tag{U-EIGHT-COUNT}
$$

The constants defining the box are fixed. The covering curves have bounded mixed degree and $u>0$, so the finite-list argument for their negative components applies. Fixed genus-one components contribute polylogarithmically and fixed higher-genus components finitely, as before. Singular and conjugate-component exceptions retain their previous treatment. Each infimum is approached by fixed rational weights; a different unbounded choice for every unknown point is not being assumed.

This envelope contains the four-center envelope: on its four-weight face the center incidence condition gives $\sum z_\ell\le1$, so $\mu=\max w_\ell$, and the rational term is already dominated as proved above. The four gcds can instead improve the count when all original $A_i$ are small.

For any of the eight individual gcds, the same argument giving (U-LARGE-A) applies with $A_i$ replaced by $G_\ell$. A joint improvement uses two disjoint parallel outer lines with both gcds at least $c^{49/100}$. Take $u=1$, weight 49 on those lines, and zero elsewhere. Then

$$
\mathfrak d=83168,\quad \tau=2599/100,\quad
m_{\rm mov}=1600-784\sqrt2.
$$

The moving-curve term is below the determinant term, and hence

$$
N(C;G_{\ell_1},G_{\ell_2}\ge c^{49/100})
\ll_\varepsilon C^{\,3\sqrt{5198}/800+\varepsilon},
\qquad 3\sqrt{5198}/800\approx0.270364.
\tag{U-EIGHT-PAIR}
$$

No center gcd is required to be large. This is a bound on the indicated stratum, not an asserted solution.

For a second explicit stratum, suppose all six parallel progression gcds are at least $c^{1/4}$. Give their conic maps equal weights, give the two diagonal maps zero weights, and approach $u=0$ through fixed positive rational weights. At the limit,

$$
\mathfrak d=480,\quad \tau=9/4,\quad
\mu=\sqrt6,\quad m_{\rm mov}=16(6-\sqrt6).
$$

The support value follows from Cauchy--Schwarz, with equality at $z_\ell=1/\sqrt6$ on the six parallel coordinates; these satisfy every incidence inequality. The moving term is below the determinant term. Thus

$$
\boxed{N(C;G_\ell\ge c^{1/4}\text{ on all six parallel lines})
\ll_\varepsilon C^{\,9\sqrt3/(16\sqrt{10})+\varepsilon}.}
\tag{U-EIGHT-SIX}
$$

The exponent is approximately $0.308094$. It is the exact optimum of (U-EIGHT-COUNT) for this height box. Indeed normalize $\tau=1$, let $P,Q$ be the sums of parallel and diagonal weights, and use

$$
\mathfrak d/64\le(1+P/8)^2-P^2/24-Q^2/8,\qquad
3P/8+Q/2\le1.
$$

The maximum is $40/27$, attained only at $P=8/3,Q=u=0$ with equal parallel weights. All boundary infima mean approximation by fixed $u>0$; no degenerate graph embedding is used.

More generally, for $0\le\beta\le1/2$ the six-parallel-gcd box has the exact geometric envelope

$$
\boxed{\eta_6(\beta)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac38\sqrt{1-6\beta^2},&0\le\beta\le1/6,\\[1mm]
\dfrac{3\sqrt{30}}{40}(1-\beta),&1/6\le\beta\le1/2.
\end{cases}}
\tag{U-EIGHT-PARALLEL}
$$

Thus $N(C;G_\ell\ge c^\beta\text{ on the six parallel lines}) \ll_{\varepsilon,\beta}C^{\eta_6(\beta)+\varepsilon}$.
To prove the optimum, normalize $\tau=1$ and let $P,Q$ be the total parallel and diagonal weights. Then

$$
\mathfrak d/64\le(1+\beta P/2)^2-P^2/24-Q^2/8,\qquad
(1-\beta)P/2+Q/2\le1.
$$

The maximum has $Q=0$, equal parallel weights, and
$P=12\beta/(1-6\beta^2)$ until $\beta=1/6$, then $P=2/(1-\beta)$.
Equivalently use $u=1-6\beta$, parallel weights $2\beta$, in the first branch, and a limit $u\to0$ in the second. With common parallel weight $w$,
$\mathfrak d=64u^2+384uw+480w^2$ and
$m_{\rm mov}=32u+16(6-\sqrt6)w$. Direct coefficient comparison gives
$m_{\rm mov}^2>(16/9)\mathfrak d$, so the moving contribution is below the determinant contribution. The unrestricted exponent remains $3/8$.

There is also a precise limitation. Without arithmetic height savings, the mixed height exponent is $\tau=H\cdot D/64$, and Hodge index gives $D^2\le64\tau^2$. Therefore its determinant exponent cannot fall below $3/8$. Adding conic coordinates alone does not improve that term when all eight $G_\ell=c^{o(1)}$; a further gain in this remaining range requires an additional restriction or a different counting argument.

**Finite arithmetic fibers.** Let $\mathcal D_2$ be the set of positive squarefree $d$ with $\operatorname{rank}E_d(\mathbb Q)\ge2$. Equations (16)–(17) define maps

$$
\mathscr M\longrightarrow\mathcal D_2\times\mathcal D_2,
\qquad(\alpha,\beta)\longmapsto(d_1,d_2).
\tag{33}
$$

Each coordinate map has finite fibers. More precisely, for an absolute constant $C$, the number of normalized candidates with either specified step class $d$ is at most

$$
C^{3\operatorname{rank}E_d(\mathbb Q)+1}.
\tag{34}
$$

This follows from the classification and bounds for elliptic triples with a linear abscissa relation; the positive, distinct locus avoids their exceptional elliptic translates. The set $\mathcal D_2$ has density zero among squarefree integers, and the corresponding possible integer step values have density zero among positive integers. Neither statement implies finiteness or emptiness.

Independently, for a specified finite set $S$ of allowed center primes, the number of primitive candidates is finite, bounded by

$$
\exp\bigl(30^{15}(3s_S+1)\bigr),\qquad
s_S=\#\{p\in S:p\equiv1\pmod4\}.
\tag{35}
$$

Here is the exact correspondence to [13, Theorem1.1]. For the first three opposite products and offsets, put
\[
w_i=(q_i-iD_i)/c^2,\qquad (D_1,D_2,D_3)=(x,y,x+y).
\]
These are norm-one elements of $\mathbb Q(i)$ with positive real part, in a multiplicative group of rank at most $s_S$. The offset identity gives
\[
w_1-w_1^{-1}+w_2-w_2^{-1}-w_3+w_3^{-1}=0.
\]
There is no vanishing two-term subsum: opposite signs would force zero or equal absolute offsets, and equal signs would contradict positive real parts. There is no three-term subsum because three complex numbers of modulus one summing to zero have a primitive cube root of unity as a quotient, impossible in $\mathbb Q(i)$. Complementation rules out four- and five-term subsums. Dividing by $w_3$ gives a nondegenerate five-variable equation, whose tuple lies in the image of three copies of the phase group, of rank at most $3s_S$. Theorem1.1 with $n=5$ gives $\exp((6n)^{3n}(3s_S+1))$, exactly(35).

The five quotients recover $w_1,w_2,w_3$ up to common sign; positive real parts remove that ambiguity. Their imaginary parts recover normalized offsets, and the positive original roots with primitive normalization recover at most one square. This proves the required injectivity. The independent proof and source check are `rank4_next/trace_center_norm/fixed_center_support_ess.md`, `next_pythagorean_cover/fixed_center_phase_finiteness_review.md`, and `simultaneous_units/fixed_center_support_ess_criteria_review.md`. This expands the existing proof of(35); it is not an additional finiteness theorem. It is a count bound, not a height bound; fixing the number of primes while allowing their identities to vary is insufficient.

**Uniform arithmetic fibers.** The fixed-fiber finiteness statements admit
uniform cardinality bounds. Let $C_\tau:Y^2=f_\tau(Z)$ be a smooth
genus-two curve whose squarefree polynomial $f_\tau$ has degree five or
six and splits over $\mathbb Q$. All six branch points are rational,
including infinity in the degree-five case. Suppose an integral model has
good reduction outside the prime divisors of $2D_\tau$, where
$D_\tau\ne0$ and $|D_\tau|\ll H(\tau)^K$ for a fixed $K$.
Then

$$
\boxed{\#C_\tau(\mathbb Q)\ll_\varepsilon H(\tau)^\varepsilon.}
\tag{U-SPLIT-FIBER}
$$

Here is a proof retaining the relevant arithmetic hypotheses. All
Weierstrass points are rational, so $J_\tau[2]\simeq(\mathbb Z/2)^4$
has trivial Galois action. Let $S_\tau$ be the primes dividing $2D_\tau$.
Kummer classes of rational points are unramified at every odd
good-reduction prime. The squareclasses unramified outside $S_\tau$
are generated by $-1$ and its primes, giving

$$
\operatorname{rank}J_\tau(\mathbb Q)+4
\le4(|S_\tau|+1),\qquad
\operatorname{rank}J_\tau(\mathbb Q)\le4|S_\tau|.
$$

The elementary bound
$\omega(N)\ll\log(2|N|)/\log\log(3|N|)$ therefore makes this rank
$o(\log H(\tau))$. Dimitrov–Gao–Habegger's uniform Mordell theorem,
Theorem 1.1, supplies a constant $B_2$, depending only on genus two
and $\mathbb Q$, such that

$$
\#C_\tau(\mathbb Q)
\le B_2^{1+\operatorname{rank}J_\tau(\mathbb Q)}.
$$

This theorem includes points of every height. It proves
(U-SPLIT-FIBER), without a rank conjecture or a small-height exception.
No numerical value or effective height cutoff is asserted for its
constant.

The four relevant integral models are listed below. In each row the
parameter is $k=n/d$ in lowest terms, $d>0$; for the slope row
$k=r$. The model is $W^2=f_k(Z)$. The last column contains every
bad prime, including primes from leading coefficients and twists.

| Fiber | $f_k(Z)$ | Bad-prime support integer |
|---|---|---|
| Corner opposite pair | $(d^2-Z^2)((d+n)^2-Z^2)((d-n)^2-Z^2)$ | $2nd(n^2-d^2)(n^2-4d^2)$ |
| Side opposite pair | $(d^2-Z^2)((2d+n)^2-Z^2)((2d-n)^2-Z^2)$ | $2nd(n^2-d^2)(n^2-4d^2)(n^2-9d^2)$ |
| Off-center progression | $2(Z+2n)Z(Z-2n)(Z-d+n)(Z-d)(Z-d-n)$ | $2nd(d^2-n^2)(d^2-4n^2)(d^2-9n^2)$ |
| Slope | $Z(Z-d^2)(Z-n^2)(Z-(d+n)^2)(Z-(d-n)^2)$ | $2nd(d^2-n^2)(4d^2-n^2)(d^2-4n^2)$ |

For the first two rows, fix $k=\alpha,\beta$ or
$k=\alpha+\beta,\alpha-\beta$, respectively, and multiply the six
remaining root radicands. Their branch points before scaling are
$\pm1,\pm(1+k),\pm(1-k)$, or
$\pm1,\pm(2+k),\pm(2-k)$. They are distinct on $0<k<1$.

For an off-center progression, divide by its midpoint square and write
its three entries as $1-k,1,1+k$, where $k=R(t_\ell)$.
The six remaining radicands are

$$
z-k,\ z,\ z+k,\quad
2z-1-k,\ 2z-1,\ 2z-1+k.
$$

Their branch points are
$-k,0,k,(1-k)/2,1/2,(1+k)/2$.
The only collisions in $0<k<1$ occur at $k=1/3,1/2$.
Neither is attained by a rational progression parameter because
$1-k$ would have to be a rational square. With $Z=2dz$, their
product is the product of the six displayed integral linear factors
divided by $8d^6$; multiplying its square root by $4d^3$ gives
the factor $2$ in the table.

The slope row is the integral rescaling of $\mathcal G_r$ in (27).
Its branch points are distinct for $0<r<1,\ r\ne1/2$.
Every support integer in the table is nonzero on the relevant
admissible parameters and polynomially bounded in their heights.
Its prime support follows directly from the pairwise branch differences
and leading coefficient.

A full fixed-conic fiber maps to its tabled genus-two quotient with
degree $32$, and the full slope fiber maps to $\mathcal G_r$
with degree $256$. Moreover $H(R(t))\ll H(t)^4$.
Thus, with $\mathcal L$ denoting all eight progression lines in
(U-EIGHT-GCD),

$$
\boxed{
\#\{\text{primitive candidates with specified }t_\ell=t\}
\ll_\varepsilon H(t)^\varepsilon\quad(\ell\in\mathcal L),\qquad
\#\{\text{primitive candidates with specified }r\}
\ll_\varepsilon H(r)^\varepsilon.}
\tag{U-FIBER-UNIFORM}
$$

Only the positive distinct-entry locus is counted. Root-sign choices
and the finite conic symmetries affect only absolute factors. These are
uniform bounds for all primitive candidates in each fiber, without
restricting their centers or the heights of their remaining coordinates.

For step squareclasses, (20) gives
$\operatorname{rank}E_d(\mathbb Q)\le2\omega(d)$.
Combining this with (34) yields

$$
\boxed{
\#\{\text{primitive candidates with }d_i=d\}
\ll_\varepsilon d^\varepsilon,\qquad
\#\{\text{primitive candidates with }\min(d_1,d_2)\le D\}
\ll_\varepsilon D^{1+\varepsilon}.}
\tag{U-STEP-COUNT}
$$

Here $d$ is positive and squarefree, $i=1,2$, and $D\ge1$.
This is a uniform counting consequence of the existing descent and
fixed-class bounds, not an additional equation on a candidate.

There are $O(T^2)$ rational numbers of height at most $T$.
Consequently, for $T,R\ge1$, (U-FIBER-UNIFORM) also gives

$$
\boxed{\begin{aligned}
\#\{\text{primitive candidates}:\min_{\ell\in\mathcal L}H(t_\ell)\le T\}
&\ll_\varepsilon T^{2+\varepsilon},\\
\#\{\text{primitive candidates}:H(r)\le R\}
&\ll_\varepsilon R^{2+\varepsilon}.
\end{aligned}}
\tag{U-PARAM-COUNT}
$$

No center bound is needed in either statement.

If $h=\gcd(x,y)$, then $H(r)=x/h<c^2/h$.
For $0\le\theta<2$, this proves the additional height-stratum bound

$$
\boxed{
\#\{(c,x,y)\in\mathscr M_{\rm int}:c\le C,\ h\ge c^\theta\}
\ll_{\varepsilon,\theta}C^{4-2\theta+\varepsilon}.}
\tag{U-FIBER-H}
$$

It improves $3/8$ when $\theta>29/16$.
The case $h\ge c^2$ is empty.

By (U-EIGHT-GCD), $G_\ell\ge c^\beta$ implies
$H(t_\ell)\ll C^{(1-\beta)/2}$ for $c\le C$.
Combining (U-PARAM-COUNT) with the geometric estimate
(U-EIGHT-COUNT) gives, for every fixed $0\le\beta\le1$,

$$
\boxed{\begin{aligned}
&\#\{(c,x,y)\in\mathscr M_{\rm int}:c\le C,\
             \max_{\ell\in\mathcal L}G_\ell\ge c^\beta\}
\ll_{\varepsilon,\beta}C^{\zeta(\beta)+\varepsilon},\\
&\zeta(\beta)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac38\sqrt{1-\beta^2},&0\le\beta\le55/73,\\[2mm]
1-\beta,&55/73\le\beta\le1.
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}}
\tag{U-FIBER-GCD}
$$

The breakpoint is the exact solution of
$1-\beta=(3/8)\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$ in $[0,1)$.
This supersedes the corresponding large-$A_i$ consequence
(U-LARGE-A), includes the four outer gcds, and improves the geometric
tail. It does not assert that any gcd is necessarily a fixed positive
power of the center.

Finally let $\mathcal K_8(\mathbf a)$ denote the proved eight-conic
exponent in (U-EIGHT-COUNT). On any fixed height box satisfying

$$
H(t_\ell)^2\ll C^{a_\ell}\quad(\ell\in\mathcal L),\qquad
H(r)\ll C^\sigma,\qquad
\min(d_1,d_2)\ll C^\eta,
$$

with $a_\ell,\sigma,\eta\ge0$, all geometric and arithmetic fiber
estimates combine as

$$
\boxed{
N_{\rm box}(C)\ll_\varepsilon
C^{\,\min\{\mathcal K_8(\mathbf a),\
                   \min_{\ell\in\mathcal L}a_\ell,\ 2\sigma,\ \eta\}
       +\varepsilon}.}
\tag{U-FIBER-ENV}
$$

All box constants and exponents are fixed before counting; any
unavailable coordinate bound is omitted from the minimum. Constants
need not be effective. Neither this envelope nor the fiber estimates
provide a finite global height cutoff.

The formulations can therefore be summarized without changing the solution set. In the last line below, an admissible point over $s$ is a finite point on the full cover $\mathcal H_r$ with $0<r<1$, the slope restrictions (18), (U-SLOPE-ALL), (U-SLOPE-ADD) and (U-SLOPE-F), and $0<s<1/(1+r)$:

$$
\boxed{\begin{aligned}
\mathscr M
&=\psi(\mathscr T)\\
&=\{\psi(\mathbf t):\mathbf t\in(\mathbb Q\cap(0,1))^4,\
                    \Phi(\mathbf t)=0\}\\
&=\{(s,rs):r,s\in\mathbb Q,\ \exists\,P\in\mathcal H_r(\mathbb Q)
       \text{ admissible over }s\}.
\end{aligned}}
\tag{36}
$$

Thus (U) is a four-circle defining system, (P) is its polynomial packaging, (F) records its primitive integer arithmetic, (U-2C) gives a bijective two-circle description with two norm-square conditions and one square-gcd condition, and (U-E) organizes the exact lifting conditions by slope as a genus-two first lift, one elliptic doubling test and square denominator. The Gaussian, squareclass, Selmer, relation and rank restrictions all apply to the same tuples through (5). Their conjunction **with the defining equations removed** is not known to be sufficient. No argument yet makes (U) inconsistent or supplies a solution.

**Logical relation of the restrictions.** If $\mathfrak R_{\rm pt}$ is the collection of proved pointwise implications $H_R\Rightarrow C_R$ in this article, with every hypothesis and common-lift choice retained, then

$$
\mathscr T_{\rm constrained}
=\{\mathbf t\in\mathscr T:\bigwedge_{R\in\mathfrak R_{\rm pt}}(H_R(\mathbf t)\Rightarrow C_R(\mathbf t))\}
=\mathscr T.
\tag{U-ALL}
$$

Every equality is an assertion about the exact locus. A selected collection of necessary conditions, with the defining equations omitted, is only a containing set.


The envelope (U-ENV) is defined by selected necessary conditions and retains the exact completion relation (U-EX). Curve restrictions do not imply that every isolated rational point lies on a classified curve. Counting estimates do not imply an absolute point-height bound.

## 11. Restrictions on algebraic families

 Let a plane curve $\Gamma\subset\mathbb P^2_{[w:\alpha:\beta]}$, not contained in a branch line, have degree $n$ and normalization $T$. The nine branch lines are $w=0$, $w\pm\alpha=0$, $w\pm\beta=0$, $w\pm\alpha\pm\beta=0$. Let $k$ be the rank of the eight restricted radicand classes over $\overline{\mathbb Q}(T)$, and $b$ the number of points with nonzero valuation-parity vector. Each component $C$ above $\Gamma$ satisfies

$$
2g(C)-2=2^k(2g(T)-2+b/2),\qquad
H\cdot C=2^{k-1}n.
\tag{40}
$$

A rational component forces $k\le2$. An elliptic component over a rational base has $b=4$ and $k\le3$; over an elliptic base it has $k\le2$ and the cover is unramified. Rational and elliptic families therefore require at least six and five independent multiplicative square identities, respectively, among the eight restricted radicands. Their root-sign orbits have at least $64$ and $32$ components, since the component count is $2^{8-k}$.

For a nonarrangement plane line, the exact formulas are

$$
k=b-1,\qquad g(C)=1+2^{b-3}(b-4).
$$

Only $\alpha=0$ and $\beta=0$ have $b\le4$; both give repeated entries. Every admissible nonbranch plane line consequently has lift genus at least five. A second restriction uses the same step classes as (33). Suppose a smooth projective geometrically integral curve $C/\mathbb Q$ carries a nonconstant family in $U$, and $P\in C(\mathbb Q)$ is admissible. Put $d=\operatorname{sf}(\alpha(P))$. If the cover

$$
\widetilde C_\alpha:\ v^2=\alpha/d
$$

is connected, its Prym has $E_d^2$ as a $\mathbb Q$-isogeny factor. If it splits, $J(C)$ has that factor instead. Writing $b_\alpha$ for its geometric branch count, the connected case gives

$$
\dim\operatorname{Prym}(\widetilde C_\alpha/C)
=g(C)-1+b_\alpha/2\ge2,
\qquad b_\alpha\ge6-2g(C).
\tag{42}
$$

The same holds for $\beta$. Thus rational and elliptic families require respectively at least six and four branch points for **each** step cover; neither step can have constant squareclass in their function fields. At the minimum counts, the two-dimensional Prym is isogenous to a square of one congruent-number curve. Geometrically this always requires two copies of the fixed $j=1728$ elliptic curve.

Independent step-cover characters supply the two squared elliptic factors in distinct character spaces. If the covers coincide but the positive specialized step classes are distinct, the corresponding elliptic curves are not $\mathbb Q$-isogenous, so the same Prym has dimension at least four and $b\ge10-2g(C)$.

The Prym restrictions do not exclude every low-genus curve or control rational points outside such curves. Branching is a function-field condition: at a single rational point all eight radicands are squares, so their pointwise squareclass rank cannot replace $k$ in (40).

**Rational CM factors and finite branch models.** The family restriction above sharpens over $\mathbb Q$. For a full-root curve $C/\mathbb Q$ with an admissible rational specialization, take the untwisted cover $D_\alpha:v^2=\alpha$, assumed geometrically connected. Its Prym contains $E_1^2$ as a **rational** isogeny factor. Indeed the three maps

$$
X_j=\frac{1+j\beta}{\alpha},\qquad
Y_j=\frac{\prod_{k=-1}^1a_{j,k}}{\alpha v},
\qquad a_{j,k}^2=1+j\beta+k\alpha,
\tag{U-P}
$$

land on $E_1$ and are anti-invariant. Twisting by the specialized step class and applying the rank-two progression theorem forces two independent homomorphisms. The same holds for $\beta$.

For $g(C)=0$ and $b_\alpha=6$, this gives $J(D_\alpha)\sim_{\mathbb Q}E_1^2$. Hence only finitely many rational genus-two branch models, up to $\mathrm{PGL}_2(\mathbb Q)$ and square factors, are possible, independent of the specialized step class. Their Jacobians have conductor 1024 and good reduction away from 2. However every such genus-two curve has **bad curve reduction at 3**: good reduction would give $\#D_\alpha(\mathbb F_9)=22$, while its hyperelliptic map gives at most 20. This distinction between curve and Jacobian reduction is essential.

This finite class is nonempty: $y^2=6t^6-9t^4-9t^2+6$ has two explicit degree-two elliptic quotients isomorphic over $\mathbb Q$ to $E_1$. Existing datasets are not a complete enumeration. For $g(C)=1$, $b_\alpha=4$, the two-dimensional Prym is likewise isogenous to $E_1^2$.

At any common good prime, the Frobenius quotient $P_{D_\alpha,p}(T)/P_{C,p}(T)$ must be divisible by

$$
(1-a_p(E_1)T+pT^2)^2.
\tag{U-F}
$$

This is a specialization-independent exclusion test for an entire family. Minimal Pryms also prohibit stable degenerations with a nonseparating node at odd primes. In the elliptic-base case, an isolated pair collision at a good odd prime is excluded under the precise local-reduction hypotheses of van Bommel–Maistret–Shi–Sutherland, Proposition 2.4; the full defining divisor, not just its four branch points, must be retained. Compact-type degenerations are not excluded.

**Degree and Gaussian boundary restrictions.** Every closed point of the root surface on $M=0$ has residue field containing $\mathbb Q(i)$: some nonzero opposite pair satisfies $a^2+b^2=0$. Thus every rationally defined curve not contained there has even root-projective degree $H\cdot C$. For a rational parametrization by primitive homogeneous root polynomials, every irreducible center factor splits over $\mathbb Q(i)$, and after common rational rescaling the center polynomial is a Gaussian norm $A(t)^2+B(t)^2$. This is the function-field counterpart of the center-prime norm restriction; integer block inequalities do not transfer automatically because polynomial units are arbitrary constants.

For a rational or elliptic full-root family meeting the admissible locus,

$$
\deg_C(t_1),\deg_C(t_2)\ge2,\qquad
\deg_C(\alpha),\deg_C(\beta)\in4\mathbb Z,\quad
\deg_C(\alpha),\deg_C(\beta)\ge8,\quad H\cdot C\ge4.
\tag{U-D}
$$

An explicit half of the middle map on $D_\alpha$ is
$(-t_1,(1+t_1^2)v/2)$ on $E_1$; the degree-four doubling map and genus at least two give the bound. In particular no root-projective curve of degree at most three in these genera can contribute an admissible rational point.

The rational degree-four case is completely excluded. Its three half-maps to $E_1$ would each have degree two. A genus-two step cover is impossible by the orthogonality argument: a nonzero cross-pairing would induce a rational degree-three isogeny, and three orthogonal vectors cannot fit in a two-dimensional space. In genus three, a rank-two Gram matrix would force a signed relation with three odd coefficients, contradicting the primitive-relation restriction after specialization. Hence the Jacobian would be isogenous to $E_1^3$. The positive Gram determinants are $8,6,4$; determinant $6$ would give a rational order-three subgroup of $E_1^3$, which is impossible.

The remaining orthogonal case gives three commuting elliptic involutions. Its hyperelliptic model is $w^2=(z^4+az^2+1)(z^4+bz^2+1)$, and exact binary-quartic invariants show that its three elliptic quotients cannot all have $j=1728$. The determinant-four case gives an $S_4$ action, forcing the octahedral model $w^2=z^8+14z^4+1$. One elliptic quotient has $j=35152/9$, which is not an algebraic integer and therefore cannot have CM or be isogenous to $E_1$. These exhaust the rational quartic cases.

For an elliptic base at root degree four, the three degree-two half-maps are again independent and lie in the Prym. The middle half has degree two, so the step cover has at most eight branch points; the three independent elliptic factors give Prym dimension at least three. Therefore its branch count is six or eight, and its genus is four or five.

At genus four, the Prym polarization has type $(1,1,2)$. The induced isogeny $E_1^3\to P$ has degree $\det(G)/2$, excluding determinant six by the same rational order-three-subgroup obstruction. Determinant eight produces an involution with a genus-three quotient, contradicting Riemann–Hurwitz. Determinant four gives a faithful $C_2\times S_4$ action of order 48; its inertia orders belong to $\{2,3,4,6\}$, whose Riemann–Hurwitz denominators cannot yield $(2g-2)/48=1/8$.

At genus five, a nonzero off-diagonal Gram entry would give an order-three automorphism with a genus-three quotient, again contradicting Riemann–Hurwitz. The three half-deck involutions therefore commute, and together with the step involution generate $(C_2)^4$. Its quotient has genus zero and five branch points. The three specified elliptic quotients force three of the five four-point branch subsets to have $j=1728$: their intervening degree-four quotients are by the full translation group $E_1[2]$, so preserve the elliptic isomorphism class. But a five-point set has at most two such harmonic four-subsets. After normalizing one to $\{\infty,0,1,-1\}$, the other subsets require the fifth point respectively in $\{2,1/2\}$, $\{-2,-1/2\}$, $\{3,-3\}$ or $\{1/3,-1/3\}$; these sets are disjoint. This closes the elliptic quartic case as well.

The Gram-rank, polarization and Riemann--Hurwitz arguments above give

$$
\boxed{g(C)\in\{0,1\},\quad C\text{ defined over }\mathbb Q
\text{ and containing an admissible rational point}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad H\cdot C\ge6.}
\tag{U-Q}
$$

This excludes entire rational and elliptic full-root families of root-projective degree at most five. It does not exclude isolated points or higher-degree families.

There is a stronger map-degree consequence independent of the ambient degree. In each corner-step triple at least one half-map must have degree at least three: if all three had degree two, the middle map would give $\deg(t_i)=2$ and branch count at most eight, reducing to the excluded cases above. At rational root degree six, the polarization and incidence arguments below force all six half-map degrees to be three. Degree-three maps need not have deck involutions.

**Degree-six arithmetic and incidence restrictions.** These statements retain the hypotheses in (U-Q): a $\mathbb Q$-defined full-root family with a rational admissible specialization, rather than an isolated point. Let $\Gamma$ be its squared-entry plane image of degree $n$, with normalization $T$, and let $C\to T$ have degree $2^k$. The nine branch lines are $w,w\pm a,w\pm b,w\pm a\pm b$. At a point of $T$, retain their nine vanishing parities $e(P)\in\mathbb F_2^9$ before quotienting by the all-ones vector. No more than three lines are concurrent, so these vectors have weight at most three; two have equal inertia if and only if they are equal. Moreover

$$
\boxed{\sum_P e(P)=(n\bmod2)(1,\ldots,1).}
\tag{U-BI}
$$

For an elliptic lift with $k\le2$, this forces $n$ even. A rational plane cubic cannot have just three branch points: their supports would partition the nine lines into three triple points; projection from any such smooth point would give a degree-two map with three ramified fibers. The node and cusp cases cannot realize those parity supports either. Since $H\cdot C=2^{k-1}n$, both rational and elliptic degree-six families therefore satisfy

$$
\boxed{(k,n)=(0,12)\quad\text{or}\quad(1,6).}
\tag{U-S6}
$$

The full inverse image of $\Gamma$ consequently splits geometrically into at least 128 components. For $k=0$, all nine line divisors on $T$ are even. For $k=1$ and rational $T$, all branch points have the same incidence support of at most three lines: two points for a rational lift, four for an elliptic lift. If the support has at least two lines, these points lie above one plane intersection and force a singular image.

For each step cover $D_i\to C$, all three half-map degrees lie in $\{2,3\}$ and their induced homomorphisms are independent over $\mathbb Q$. The finite Gram argument uses $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q}(E_1)=\mathbb Z$, the exactly-two-odd relation rule, and the impossibility of a degree-one difference map. Hence each Prym contains $E_1^3$.

For a rational $C$, the minimal possibility $g(D_i)=3$ is excluded. The proof combines the small Gram determinant list, irreducible odd-primary Galois modules, and integral polarizations; the last two determinant-16 forms are

$$
G_A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&0\\0&3&1\\0&1&3\end{pmatrix},\qquad
G_B=\begin{pmatrix}3&-1&-1\\-1&3&-1\\-1&-1&3\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Their relevant kernels are respectively $E_1[2]\times E_1[8]$ and $E_1[4]^2$. Exact enumeration leaves 15 and 43 stable maximal isotropic kernels of order 16. Every quotient lattice has a vector $u$ with $u,iu$ in the lattice and $\bar u^tG u=1$. Such a vector splits off a principally polarized elliptic factor, impossible for a smooth Jacobian. Independent Hermite-normal-form enumerations reproduce every kernel and verify every witness.

Consequently, in both directions,

$$
\boxed{C\simeq\mathbb P^1,\ H\cdot C=6
\ \Longrightarrow\
g(D_1),g(D_2)\in\{4,5\},\quad
b(D_i/C)\in\{10,12\},\quad
\deg f_{i,j}=3,\quad\deg t_i=3.}
\tag{U-C3}
$$

All pairings within a triple lie in $\{0,\pm1\}$; a pairing of absolute value two would yield a degree-two map, incompatible with a hyperelliptic genus-four/five curve. This is a classification of the specified finite torsion kernels.

For an elliptic $C$, the step Prym has dimension at least three, so its branch count is at least six. In the minimal case $b=6$, the induced polarization has type $(1,1,2)$ and the relevant kernel has order eight. The $G_A$ case is excluded. For $G_B$, 45 of the 51 stable isotropic kernels have the same norm-one obstruction. Six remain, all of type $(C_2)^3$, and the three half-maps have degree three. To specify this finite boundary, write
$\ker G_B=\{(U,V,-U-V):U,V\in E_1[4]\}$ in the basis
$P=(i,1-i)$, $Q=(1+\sqrt2,\sqrt2(1+\sqrt2))$.
In coordinates $U=pP+qQ$, $V=rP+sQ$ modulo four, the six kernels have these generating triples:

| Kernel | Generators $(p,q,r,s)$ |
|---|---|
| 17 | $(0,0,0,2),(0,2,2,0),(2,0,0,0)$ |
| 18 | $(0,0,0,2),(0,2,2,0),(2,0,2,0)$ |
| 20 | $(0,0,2,0),(0,2,0,0),(2,0,0,2)$ |
| 22 | $(0,0,2,0),(0,2,0,2),(2,0,0,2)$ |
| 24 | $(0,0,2,2),(0,2,0,0),(2,0,0,2)$ |
| 25 | $(0,0,2,2),(0,2,0,2),(2,0,0,0)$ |

These are presentations, not a claim of six distinct polarized isomorphism classes or of realizability. Testing elliptic factors with an index-two Gaussian sublattice did not remove them.

**Combining odd half-degrees with branch incidence.** In the rational $(k,n)=(1,6)$ branch, let $\sigma$ be the root-sign involution of $C\to T$, and lift it to each step cover by fixing the step square root. If a full progression map $\phi=2f$ is invariant under an involution with a fixed point, then $f$ itself is invariant: the possible two-torsion translation vanishes at that point. This would make its degree even. Every half here has degree three, so its corresponding lift must be free. Genus four is impossible, and the three row signs and the three column signs must each agree.

The common incidence support is consequently a permutation triple. Only two such triples are concurrent in the fixed arrangement: the center line and one opposite edge pair. Thus

$$
\boxed{\begin{gathered}
C\simeq\mathbb P^1,\ H\cdot C=6,\ k=1
\ \Longrightarrow\ g(D_1)=g(D_2)=5,\\
S=\{w,w+a+b,w-a-b\}\quad\text{or}\quad
\{w,w+a-b,w-a+b\}.
\end{gathered}}
\tag{U-SIGN}
$$

Both branch points of $T$ lie over the same one of $[0:1:-1]$ and $[0:1:1]$. Their residue field is exactly $\mathbb Q(i)$, by the nonzero opposite roots at the center-zero boundary. After rational parameter changes, the root double cover has the form
$z^2=t^2+1$, with branch values $\pm i$.
On each genus-five step cover the lift fixing its square root is free, with genus-three quotient; the other lift has four fixed points and genus-two quotient. These are necessary conditions on the sextic, not a parameterization or an exclusion of it.

**A polarization lemma excludes the sextic-image subcase.** Write the root double cover as $z^2=t^2+1$. For either step, its genus-five cover $D$ has quotients
$F=D/\sigma$ of genus three and $G=D/(\tau\sigma)$ of genus two. The branch divisors satisfy
$B_F=B_G\sqcup\{i,-i\}$, so, after a rational coordinate choice,

$$
\boxed{F:y^2=(t^2+1)g(t),\qquad G:\eta^2=g(t),\qquad
\deg g=6,\quad g\text{ squarefree},\quad g(\pm i)\ne0.}
\tag{U-NEST}
$$

Here $J(F)\sim_{\mathbb Q}E_1^3$. The three maps $2f_j$ descend to degree-six maps on $F$ with Gram matrix twice that of the cubic halves. Its possible determinants are $16,20,21,24,27$; odd-primary Galois-module parity excludes all but 16. Thus the cubic Gram form must be $G_B=4I-J$.

Write $f_j\sigma=f_j+T_j$, with $0\ne T_j\in E_1[2](\mathbb Q)$. Three distinct values would have sum zero and make an odd-degree map descend through a double cover. Three equal values would make the three pair sums descend to degree-two maps on $F$ with Gram $2I$, giving the already excluded three $j=1728$ bielliptic quotients. Hence exactly two distinct translation values occur, one repeated. Their repeated pair supplies a degree-two map $F\to E_1$; all three halves induce cubic maps $F\to E_1/\langle T_j\rangle$, whose pullbacks of the elliptic two-isogenies give the same nontrivial étale class defining $D\to F$.

If $A=q^*J(F)\subset J(D)$, its induced polarization has type $(1,2,2)$, and the half-map pullbacks give $E_1^3\to A$ of degree four, pulling that polarization back to $G_B$. Thus its kernel is an isotropic order-four subgroup $K\subset\ker G_B$ with $K^\perp/K$ killed by two. Let $\Lambda_0=\mathbb Z[i]^3$. A cyclic order-four $K$ would have $|2K^\perp|=8$, so it cannot give $K^\perp/K$ killed by two. Thus $K$ is killed by two, and
$\Lambda_0\subset\Lambda_A\subset\frac12\Lambda_0$.
The Riemann form of $A$ is represented by $G_B$. Since
$G_B(e_i-e_j)=4(e_i-e_j)$, both $e_i-e_j$ and $i(e_i-e_j)$ lie in its radical modulo two. Any index-two lattice $\Lambda_F\subset\Lambda_A$ on which that form is even must contain the radical and $2\Lambda_A$. Consequently it contains every $e_i+e_j$ and $i(e_i+e_j)$.

The three vectors $e_1+e_2,e_1+e_3,e_2+e_3$ therefore give elliptic homomorphisms into $J(F)$ with Gram matrix $2I$ for its principal form $G_B/2$. They force three commuting degree-two elliptic quotients of the hyperelliptic genus-three curve $F$, each with $j=1728$, exactly the excluded configuration. A nontrivial kernel in one of those homomorphisms would instead give a principally polarized elliptic factor and already contradict smooth-Jacobian indecomposability. Hence

$$
\boxed{C\simeq\mathbb P^1,\ H\cdot C=6,\ 
C\text{ defined over }\mathbb Q\text{ with an admissible rational point}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad k=0,\ n=12.}
\tag{U-SX}
$$

This excludes the rational sextic-image subcase. A hypothetical rational root curve of degree six must consequently have a plane image of degree twelve with even contact with every one of the nine branch lines; its full root preimage has 256 geometric components. This is the input to the complete exclusion (U-R8) below. The proof uses the displayed elliptic factors.

For an elliptic base $C$ in the remaining $k=1$ branch, every step triple still has an odd-degree half. The same involution lemma forces each step cover to have odd genus. Thus its branch count is $8$ or $12$, and its genus is $5$ or $7$. At genus seven all three halves have degree three: a degree-two half together with the double cover of the elliptic base would give genus at most five by Castelnuovo–Severi. The quotient subfields cannot coincide because one map is in the anti-invariant Prym direction. In particular the six minimal branch-count-six Prym presentations above are possible only when $k=0$.

**The two step covers cannot be chosen independently.** If their characters are independent over $\overline{\mathbb Q}(C)$, their geometrically connected compositum $W=C(\sqrt\alpha,\sqrt\beta)$ has

$$
J(W)\times J(C)^2\sim_{\mathbb Q}
J(D_\alpha)\times J(D_\beta)\times J(D_{\alpha\beta}),\qquad
g(W)=g(D_\alpha)+g(D_\beta)+g(D_{\alpha\beta})-2g(C).
\tag{U-V4}
$$

Its Jacobian contains $E_1^6$, and the third branch divisor is the symmetric difference of the first two. Rational-squareclass independence alone would not ensure geometric connectedness; constant twists must be separated.

For rational degree-six $C$, a nonsquare constant twist $\beta/\alpha=\delta f^2$ is excluded: positivity makes $\delta>0$, and the common genus-four/five Jacobian would contain both $E_1^3$ and $E_\delta^3$, which are not isogenous over $\mathbb Q$, forcing dimension at least six. If the two rational squareclasses actually coincide, all six cubic half-maps lie on one genus-four/five cover. No cross-pair can be proportional, since equality after doubling would impose the plane conic
$\beta(1+j\beta)=\alpha(1+k\alpha)$, contradicting the degree-six/twelve plane image. Thus their $6\times6$ Gram matrix has diagonal 3, off-diagonal entries $0,\pm1$, and rank at most five. The complete exclusion (U-R8) below subsumes this rational degree-six configuration without requiring its Gram classification. Constant-twist cases over an elliptic base are not eliminated by that argument.

**The rational degree-six coefficient locus is empty.** Write $[u:v]$ on $\mathbb P^1$ and let $W,A,B$ be binary forms of degree $12$ with common gcd $1$ and
$\mathbb Q(A/W,B/W)=\mathbb Q(u/v)$.
The field equality says that the plane map is birational onto its image; together with the gcd condition it fixes its degree at $12$. The $k=0,n=12$ conclusion in (U-SX) is equivalent to the existence of nine binary sextics $F_{ij}$ such that

$$
\boxed{F_{ij}(u,v)^2=W(u,v)+iA(u,v)+jB(u,v),
\qquad -1\le i,j\le1.}
\tag{U-D12}
$$

Require generic nonzero, pairwise distinct entries and an admissible real specialization. Such a real open set on $\mathbb P^1$ contains rational parameters. The following argument proves that (U-D12) has no such nonconstant solution.

Put $c=F_{00}$, so $W=c^2$, and work over $K=\mathbb Q(i)$. By (U-C3), all six half maps have degree three. The full progression abscissas $(W+jB)/A$ and $(W+jA)/B$ therefore have degree twelve on $\mathbb P^1$, giving

$$
\gcd(A,W+jB)=\gcd(B,W+jA)=1\quad(j=-1,0,1).
\tag{U-COP}
$$

In particular both corner offsets are coprime to $c$, and roots in any one grid row or column are pairwise coprime.

Every irreducible rational factor of $c$ splits over $K$, because its center-zero residue field contains $i$. Write
$c=\kappa\prod(p_\nu\bar p_\nu)^{e_\nu}$,
where the $K$-irreducibles are distinct and
$\sum e_\nu\deg p_\nu=3$.
For any normalized opposite-pair offset $\gamma\in\{\alpha,\beta,\alpha+\beta,\alpha-\beta\}$, take $f^2=c^2(1+\gamma)$ and $g^2=c^2(1-\gamma)$. Gaussian factorization of
$(f+ig)(f-ig)=2c^2$ gives

$$
\gamma=b_\gamma\prod u_\nu^{2a_{\gamma,\nu}}
+\bar b_\gamma\prod u_\nu^{-2a_{\gamma,\nu}},
\quad
u_\nu=p_\nu/\bar p_\nu,\quad
|a_{\gamma,\nu}|\le e_\nu,\quad
b_\gamma\bar b_\gamma=\tfrac14.
\tag{U-GAUSS}
$$

Arbitrary Gaussian constants are retained. Every nonzero pole order is even and equals $2|a_{\gamma,\nu}|$. Coprimality forces $|a_{\alpha,\nu}|=|a_{\beta,\nu}|=e_\nu$ for $\alpha=A/c^2$, $\beta=B/c^2$.

If these two full allocations agree up to reversal, $\alpha,\beta$ lie in the field generated by the degree-six function $\prod u_\nu^{2a_{\alpha,\nu}}$, contradicting $\mathbb Q(\alpha,\beta)=\mathbb Q(t)$. This excludes a single rational center factor.
For two distinct factors of degrees two and four, put $x=u_1^2$, $y=u_2^2$, of degrees two and four. The different full allocations have forms
$\alpha=axy+a'/(xy)$ and $\beta=bx/y+b'y/x$.
Multiplying the identity for $\alpha+\beta$ by $xy$ gives a nonzero polynomial of bidegree at most $(2,2)$, since a diagonal allocation has exponents in $\{-1,0,1\}$. But $K(x,y)=K(t)$ and $[K(t):K(y)]=4$, contradicting its degree at most two in $x$.

For a center $q_1^2q_2$ with distinct quadratics, the different corner allocations instead have forms
$\alpha=au^4v^2+a'u^{-4}v^{-2}$ and
$\beta=bu^4v^{-2}+b'u^{-4}v^2$,
where $u,v$ are Möbius functions with disjoint zero/pole pairs. Their four monomials are independent: otherwise $u^8$ would be a Möbius transform of $v^4$, contradicting degrees eight and four (a degenerate relation forces a constant). Neither diagonal can occupy a full allocation space, so each must cancel a center factor. They cannot both cancel the same rational factor, since their sum and difference recover the two full corner offsets. One must cancel the simple factor. At $v=0$ its leading coefficient is
$a'u^{-4}\pm bu^4$; its derivative at a zero is $\pm8bu^3\ne0$.
It therefore creates an odd pole, impossible in (U-GAUSS).

The only remaining center is
$c=\kappa q_1q_2q_3$,
three distinct irreducible norm quadratics. Normalize the corner allocations as

$$
\alpha=a(uv)^2w^2+a'(uv)^{-2}w^{-2},\qquad
\beta=b(uv)^2w^{-2}+b'(uv)^{-2}w^2,
$$

with three Möbius ratios having disjoint zero/pole pairs. A diagonal cannot cancel at $u$ or $v$: the derivative of its nonzero coefficient in $w$ again makes the resulting pole odd. Cancellation at $w=0$ and its conjugate $w=\infty$ requires the degree-two map $uv$ to ramify at both. It is then a Möbius transform of $w^2$, placing $\alpha,\beta$ in $K(w^2)$, again contrary to birationality. Thus all four opposite pairs are primitive relative to the center.

The general theorem below gives the contradiction and proves

$$
\boxed{\text{Every rational full-root family with an admissible rational
specialization has even root degree at least eight}.}
\tag{U-R8}
$$

Here a specialization is a rational point of the normalization; a rational singular image point need not lift rationally and is handled separately in the counting bounds. Elliptic degree-six curves and isolated rational points are not excluded by this theorem.

**A center-factor theorem for rational families of arbitrary degree.** Suppose a rational full-root curve is parametrized birationally by its root normalization. With center polynomial $c$ and offset numerators $A,B$, one has

$$
\boxed{\gcd\!\bigl(c,A B(A+B)(A-B)\bigr)=1
\Longrightarrow
c\text{ has at least four distinct irreducible factors over }\mathbb Q.}
\tag{U-FSUP}
$$

This concerns polynomial factors, not primes dividing an isolated integer center. All four coprimalities matter; birationality of the squared-entry plane image is unnecessary.

Here is a proof. For nonconstant rational functions $u,v$ with disjoint zero/pole supports, the four functions $u^4v^4,u^4,v^4,1$ are linearly independent. A nondegenerate relation would give $u^4=M(v^4)$. If the Möbius map $M$ preserves $\{0,\infty\}$, the supports coincide. Otherwise the irreducible Kummer curve $Y^4=M(X^4)$ has four or eight simple order-four branch points, hence genus three or nine by Riemann--Hurwitz. It cannot be dominated by $\mathbb P^1$. A degenerate relation already forces a constant.

The lemma shows that any two distinct full-allocation spaces in (U-GAUSS) have zero intersection, by grouping shared and differing factors. If both corner offsets occupy one space, both diagonals must occupy it too. Their coefficient norms would require
$aa'=bb'=(a+b)(a'+b')=(a-b)(a'-b')=1/4$,
but adding the last two gives $1/2=2(aa'+bb')=1$, a contradiction.
Thus the corners occupy distinct spaces. A diagonal sharing a corner space would put the other corner in their intersection; diagonals sharing one space would put both $\alpha$ and $\beta$ in that space by taking their half-sum and half-difference. Both are impossible. The four offsets therefore occupy four distinct opposite allocation pairs, excluding centers with one or two factors.

With exactly three factors, set
$u_i=(p_i/\bar p_i)^{e_i}$, $x_i=u_i^4$ and $U=\prod u_i^2$.
Multiplying the two offset relations by $U$ gives two independent trilinear equations $P=Q=0$ in $(\mathbb P^1)^3$. Independence follows from the distinct diagonal allocation pairs. Every normalized root is a constant linear combination of $\prod u_i^{\pm1}$ and its inverse. Root birationality implies $K(t)=K(u_1,u_2,u_3)$.
For $L=K(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ the extension $K(t)/L$ is Galois with group in $\mu_4^3$.
A nonidentity automorphism of $\mathbb P^1$ has fixed points. If it scaled two $u_i$ nontrivially, such a point would belong to both disjoint zero/pole supports. It therefore acts on only one coordinate. Group closure makes this the same coordinate for every element. At least two $u_i$ consequently lie in $L$, so their fourth powers have degree at least four on the normalization of the image curve.

Two coprime divisors of multidegree at most $(1,1,1)$ intersect in a curve whose degree in each coordinate is at most two. Shared factors cannot evade this: strip the multihomogeneous gcd of $P,Q$. Each common irreducible factor omits a coordinate unless $P,Q$ are proportional. An omitted-coordinate factor containing the image would give a bidegree-at-most-$(1,1)$ relation between two $x_i$, excluded by the four-function lemma. The image must therefore lie in the proper residual intersection, contradicting its coordinate degree at least four. This proves (U-FSUP) and completes (U-R8).

The degree restriction (U-R8) is a hypothesis of the deduction of the global stratum bound (U-STRAT); it does not exclude isolated rational points.

If the two geometric quadratic step characters coincide and their Prym dimension is two, then $\beta/\alpha$ must be a square in $\mathbb Q(C)$ at a positive admissible family. Otherwise the same Prym would contain two nonisogenous positive twists, each twice, and need dimension at least four. Thus the minimal coincident-cover case also forces equality of the two step squareclasses at every admissible specialization.

**Cancellation consumes ramification.** The center-factor restriction extends without assuming that the four opposite pairs are primitive. For any admissible rational full-root family, with primitive root polynomials on its normalization $\mathbb P^1$,

$$
\boxed{\begin{gathered}
c\text{ has at least three distinct irreducible factors over }\mathbb Q,\\
\deg(t_i)\ge2\qquad(i=1,2,3,4).
\end{gathered}}
\tag{U-CANCEL}
$$

These are function-field restrictions. They do not impose a new prime-factor bound on an isolated integer center. The stronger four-factor conclusion (U-FSUP) retains its four coprimality hypotheses.

Here is the cancellation argument, including repeated factors. Over $K=\mathbb Q(i)$ write
$c=\kappa\prod_{\nu=1}^r(p_\nu\bar p_\nu)^{e_\nu}$,
$u_\nu=p_\nu/\bar p_\nu$, and $d_\nu=\deg p_\nu$.
The conjugate factors are distinct and separable; their zero and pole supports are pairwise disjoint. The boundary argument above proves the splitting. A rational parameter coordinate makes infinity a nonzero center value. The Gaussian allocation of any offset $\zeta\in\{\alpha,\beta,\alpha+\beta,\alpha-\beta\}$ is

$$
\zeta=b\prod_\nu u_\nu^{2a_\nu}
       +\bar b\prod_\nu u_\nu^{-2a_\nu},
\qquad |a_\nu|\le e_\nu,\qquad b\bar b=\tfrac14.
$$

Call it full at $\nu$ when $|a_\nu|=e_\nu$; otherwise it cancels at that factor. At most one offset can cancel at any factor. Otherwise two entire opposite root pairs and the center vanish there, forcing both offset numerators and all root coordinates to vanish, contrary to primitivity. Nonzero pole orders are even.

Two full offsets cannot have the same allocation up to simultaneous reversal. If they did, all four offsets, being constant linear combinations of either two, would belong to the same two-dimensional allocation space. Rational conjugacy makes both coefficients of every nonzero member nonzero, preserving full pole order. The separation lemma in the proof of (U-FSUP) identifies its allocation, and all four coefficient norms would be $1/4$, giving the same contradiction
$1/2=2(1/4+1/4)=1$.

Suppose two offsets $P,Q$ are full. Conjugate individual $p_\nu$ as necessary and split the factors into nonempty sets $I,J$ according to whether their allocation signs agree or disagree. Put
$u=\prod_{\nu\in I}u_\nu^{e_\nu}$,
$v=\prod_{\nu\in J}u_\nu^{e_\nu}$. Then

$$
P=au^2v^2+a'u^{-2}v^{-2},\qquad
Q=bu^2v^{-2}+b'u^{-2}v^2,\qquad aa'=bb'=\tfrac14.
$$

Either other offset is $T=r_0P+s_0Q$, with $r_0s_0\ne0$.
Let $\mathcal C$ contain every factor at which either remaining offset is partial. At such a factor the partial offset is unique; define its cancellation depth by
$\ell_\nu=e_\nu-|a_{T,\nu}|\ge1$.
Put $S_L=\sum_{\nu\in L}d_\nu$.

At a zero of a factor in $I$, the leading pole coefficient is
$r_0a'/v^2+s_0b'v^2$. Lowering the pole by $2\ell_\nu$ forces this coefficient to vanish to order at least $2\ell_\nu$. Its derivative with respect to the finite nonzero value $v$ is nonzero at a zero. Hence $v$ has ramification index at least $2\ell_\nu$ at every one of that factor's $2d_\nu$ roots. The opposite Gaussian term has positive order and does not affect this necessary vanishing. The same argument applies to $J$, using $u$.

The degree of $v$ is $D_J=\sum_{\nu\in J}e_\nu d_\nu$. Its own zeros and poles consume $2(D_J-S_J)$ of its total ramification $2D_J-2$, leaving $2S_J-2$. Cancellations in the two remaining offsets occur on disjoint supports and consume this one shared budget. Therefore

$$
\boxed{\begin{aligned}
\sum_{\nu\in I\cap\mathcal C}d_\nu(2\ell_\nu-1)&\le S_J-1,\\
\sum_{\nu\in J\cap\mathcal C}d_\nu(2\ell_\nu-1)&\le S_I-1,\\
\sum_{\nu:\ \text{all four offsets full at }\nu}d_\nu
&\ge2+2\sum_{\nu\in\mathcal C}d_\nu(\ell_\nu-1).
\end{aligned}}
\tag{U-CANCEL-BUDGET}
$$

In particular, for either individual offset,
$S_{I,\mathrm{cancel}}\le S_J-1$,
$S_{J,\mathrm{cancel}}\le S_I-1$, and its full factors have total half-degree at least two. The stronger shared, depth-sensitive version requires no squarefreeness assumption.

If the center has at most two factors, at least two offsets are full. One factor gives only one full allocation space, already impossible. With two factors there are precisely two full allocation spaces and at most one full offset in each. The other two offsets must cancel different factors, forcing
$d_1\le d_2-1$ and $d_2\le d_1-1$. This proves the three-factor conclusion in (U-CANCEL).

Gaussian pole counting gives
$\deg(t_T)=\sum_\nu |a_{T,\nu}|d_\nu$.
If this equals one, only one quadratic factor has nonzero allocation, of absolute value one. All other factors cancel, leaving two other offsets full everywhere. Its full-factor half-degree is at most one, contradicting the budget. A constant nonzero offset would cancel every factor, leaving the other three full and giving the same contradiction. Thus all four circle degrees are at least two on rational families. On elliptic families the genus-$49$ fixed fibers imply nonconstancy, and a degree-one map to $\mathbb P^1$ is impossible.

**Arithmetic of the Gaussian center boundary.** Let $K=\mathbb Q(i)$, and use polynomial offset numerators $A,B$, so the squared root coordinates are $c^2+jA+kB$. Every projective full-root point over $K$ with $c=0$ satisfies $AB=0$.

For suppose $AB\ne0$. The boundary root coordinates make $A,B,A+B,A-B$ squares in $K$. Hence $X=A/B$, $X-1$, and $X+1$ are squares. The cases $X=\pm1$ would require $\sqrt2\in K$, which is impossible. Otherwise the full two-descent criterion gives a non-two-torsion point in $2E_1(K)$, where $E_1:Y^2=X^3-X$.

In fact $E_1(K)\simeq C_2\times C_4$ and $2E_1(K)=\{O,(0,0)\}$. The rank is zero: the ranks over $\mathbb Q$ of $E_1$ and its $-1$-twist are zero by Fermat's square-area theorem, and the twist has the same equation. Good reduction at primes above $3$ and $5$ has respectively $16$ and $8$ points, bounding the torsion order by $8$ using prime-to-residue-characteristic injectivity. The eight visible points are $O,(0,0),(\pm1,0),(i,\pm(1-i)),(-i,\pm(1+i))$; the last four double to $(0,0)$. This proves the boundary assertion.

If $q$ is an irreducible quadratic factor of a primitive rational family's center polynomial, it splits over $K$. Evaluation at either root is defined because the root forms have no common zero. The boundary assertion and rational conjugacy imply that $q$ divides exactly one of $A,B$. Divisibility of both would make every root form divisible by $q$, violating primitivity. Thus exactly one corner offset is partial there, while both edge offsets are full, including when $q$ has multiplicity greater than one in $c$.

If every center factor were quadratic, the two edge offsets would be globally full and no factor would be full for all four offsets. Their shared ramification budget (U-CANCEL-BUDGET) requires all-four-full factors of total half-degree at least two, a contradiction. Consequently

$$
\boxed{\begin{gathered}
q\mid c,\ \deg q=2\ \Longrightarrow\
q\text{ divides exactly one of }A,B;\\
c\text{ has an irreducible factor of degree at least }4;\\
\delta\ge10\quad\text{for a birational rational full-root family}.
\end{gathered}}
\tag{U-GAUSS-BOUNDARY}
$$

The final line uses (U-R8) and the degree-eight factor classification (U-OCTIC-STRUCT). It concerns families parameterized by $\mathbb P^1_{\mathbb Q}$; isolated rational singular image points are not excluded by this assertion. This is not a restriction on the prime factors of an isolated integer center.

**Residue fields constrain higher center factors.** Every center-zero closed point has a residue field containing $\mathbb Q(i)$: some opposite pair has nonzero squared values $D,-D$, and the ratio of its roots squares to $-1$. If an edge offset vanishes there, the other corner is nonzero and root ratios additionally give $\sqrt2$. Thus an edge-canceling factor has degree divisible by four.

For a quartic factor write $q=p\bar p$, $p=t^2+ut+v$ irreducible over $K=\mathbb Q(i)$, and $\Delta=u^2-4v$. Its residue field is $L=K(\sqrt\Delta)$. Then

$$
\boxed{\begin{aligned}
q\text{ cancels an edge}&\Longrightarrow \Delta/2\in K^{\times2},\\
q\text{ is full for all four offsets}
&\Longrightarrow\operatorname{rank}(Y^2=X^3-\Delta^2X)(K)>0.
\end{aligned}}
\tag{U-QUARTIC-FIELD}
$$

Here is the torsion input for the second assertion. For every quadratic extension $L/K$, $E_1(L)_{\rm tors}$ has exponent dividing four. Reduction above $3$ gives orders $16$ or $64$, and above $5$ gives orders $8$ or $32$; hence all torsion is a two-group. A point of order eight would halve a point $T$ of order four. If $2T=(0,0)$, then $X(T)=\pm i$, and halving forces $L=K(\sqrt2)$. It also requires $1+i$, or its sign/conjugate, to be a square in that field. For $z\in K$, this occurs precisely when $z$ or $z/2$ is a square in $K$; their norms $2,1/2$ exclude it. If $2T=(\pm1,0)$, then $X(T)=\pm1\pm\sqrt2$, again forcing $L=K(\sqrt2)$. Squaring $a+b\sqrt2$ to obtain any such value requires $a^2=(\pm1\pm i)/2$, whose norm $1/2$ is impossible for a $K$-square. This excludes order eight and every higher two-power order.

An all-four-full boundary point supplies a non-two-torsion point in $2E_1(L)$; the torsion bound makes it nontorsion. Quadratic rank decomposition and $\operatorname{rank}E_1(K)=0$ give (U-QUARTIC-FIELD). If $[\Delta]$ has a rational representative $D$, that rank is $2\operatorname{rank}E_D(\mathbb Q)$; hence the squarefree part of $|D|$ must be congruent. In particular $L=\mathbb Q(\zeta_8)$ cannot support an all-four-full factor, by the noncongruence of $1,2$.

The boundary lemma also applies to an elliptic normalization. If $r_2$ is the number of distinct quadratic closed points of its center divisor, their fields are $K$ and each lies in one corner common-zero divisor. These divisors are disjoint. For central conic degrees $d_x,d_y\ge2$,

$$
\boxed{2r_2\le( \delta-2d_x)+(\delta-2d_y)\le2\delta-8.}
\tag{U-ELLIPTIC-BOUNDARY}
$$

Thus an elliptic root-degree-six family cannot have three distinct quadratic center points. Higher-degree or nonreduced center divisors remain possible.

**Real topology strengthens cancellation.** Let $f:\mathbb P^1(\mathbb C)\to\mathbb P^1(\mathbb C)$ be a nonconstant rational map satisfying

$$
f(\bar z)=\frac1{\overline{f(z)}}.
$$

Suppose that all its critical values belong to $S^1\cup\{0,\infty\}$, and that it has no critical point on $\mathbb P^1(\mathbb R)$. Then

$$
f(z)=\lambda\left(\frac{z-a}{z-\bar a}\right)^d,
\qquad a\notin\mathbb R,\quad |\lambda|=1,\quad d=\deg f,
\tag{U-UNIT-TOPO}
$$

after allowing the conjugate choice of $a$. In particular it has only one distinct zero and one distinct pole, and no critical point over $S^1$. If all critical values lie on $S^1$ itself, then $d=1$.

**Proof.** Put $\Gamma=f^{-1}(S^1)$. Reality implies that the real projective line is contained in $\Gamma$. Since it contains no critical point, the inverse function theorem shows that $\Gamma$ agrees locally with that real projective line near each of its points. Compactness therefore makes the real projective line an isolated component of $\Gamma$.

Each component $U$ of the complement of $\Gamma$ maps properly onto one of the two complementary target disks, with ramification possible only over that disk's center, meaning zero or infinity. Properness follows from finiteness of a rational map; restriction to a connected component preserves it. The map is onto because its image is nonempty, open and relatively closed. Removing its finite fiber over the disk center leaves $U$ connected and gives a connected finite unramified cover of a punctured disk. Every such cover is a punctured disk, represented in coordinates by $z\mapsto z^n$. Filling the unique missing point yields a disk. Thus every complementary component of $\Gamma$ is simply connected.

There can be no further component of $\Gamma$. Indeed, if a point of $\Gamma$ lay in one source hemisphere, a sufficiently narrow collar of the real projective line in that hemisphere would contain a simple closed curve avoiding $\Gamma$ and enclosing that point. The curve lies in one complementary component, itself contained in that hemisphere, but cannot contract there: in disk coordinates it has nonzero winding number about the enclosed omitted point. This contradicts simple connectedness. Equivalently, a finite graph on the sphere whose complementary components are disks is connected, whereas the real projective line is already an isolated component.

Consequently $\Gamma=\mathbb P^1(\mathbb R)$, so there are no critical points over $S^1$. Its two complementary source hemispheres are the only two complementary components, and reality exchanges the target disks. The punctured-disk argument gives one zero of multiplicity $d$ in one hemisphere and one pole of multiplicity $d$ in the other. They are conjugate by the reality identity, giving the displayed formula and $|\lambda|=1$. If critical values zero and infinity are also forbidden, Riemann–Hurwitz forces $d=1$. ∎

The proof concerns complex critical values, not only the real restriction of the map. Properness and the one-interior-branch-value condition are essential; an arbitrary map of real circles would not imply this conclusion.

### 11.1. A strict cancellation budget at arbitrary multiplicity

Use the established Gaussian allocation presentation for an admissible rational full-root family:

$$
c=\kappa\prod_\nu(p_\nu\bar p_\nu)^{e_\nu},\qquad
u_\nu=p_\nu/\bar p_\nu,\qquad d_\nu=\deg p_\nu.
$$

All factors are separable, and their supports are pairwise disjoint. Their roots are nonreal: a real zero of $p_\nu$ would also be a zero of $\bar p_\nu$.

Suppose two globally full offsets $P,Q$ are of the same type: both corner offsets $\alpha,\beta$, or both edge offsets $\alpha+\beta,\alpha-\beta$. Each of the remaining offsets is then $T=rP+sQ$, where $|r|=|s|\ne0$. Orient the Gaussian factors and split them into the nonempty agreement and disagreement sets $I,J$, so that

$$
u=\prod_{\nu\in I}u_\nu^{e_\nu},\qquad
v=\prod_{\nu\in J}u_\nu^{e_\nu},
$$

$$
P=a u^2v^2+\bar a u^{-2}v^{-2},\qquad
Q=b u^2v^{-2}+\bar b u^{-2}v^2,
\qquad |a|=|b|=\tfrac12.
$$

Put $S_L=\sum_{\nu\in L}d_\nu$. Let $\mathcal C$ contain the factors at which one of the remaining offsets is partial, and let $\ell_\nu\ge1$ be its cancellation depth. At most one offset is partial at any factor.

At zeros and poles of $u$, cancellation of the appropriate $T$ forces respectively

$$
v^4=-\frac{r\bar a}{s\bar b},\qquad
v^4=-\frac{s b}{r a}.
$$

Both constants have modulus one. Lowering the pole order by $2\ell_\nu$ forces ramification index at least $2\ell_\nu$ at all $2d_\nu$ roots of that canceled factor. The analogous assertion holds for $u$ at factors in $J$.

The zeros and poles of $v$ consume $2(\deg v-S_J)$ of its total ramification $2\deg v-2$, leaving an external budget $2S_J-2$. If the ordinary cancellation inequality

$$
\sum_{\nu\in I\cap\mathcal C}d_\nu(2\ell_\nu-1)\le S_J-1
$$

is an equality, all external critical points lie at canceled center roots, have values on $S^1$, and are nonreal. Its other critical points are nonreal zeros and poles, with values zero or infinity. The lemma therefore applies and shows that $v$ has only one distinct zero and one distinct pole: $S_J=1$. Consequently equality is impossible when $S_J\ge2$. Integrality improves the inequality by one in that case; when $S_J=1$, the ordinary budget is already zero. Applying the same argument to $u$ proves

$$
\boxed{\begin{aligned}
\sum_{\nu\in I\cap\mathcal C}d_\nu(2\ell_\nu-1)
&\le S_J-1-\mathbf1_{S_J\ge2},\\
\sum_{\nu\in J\cap\mathcal C}d_\nu(2\ell_\nu-1)
&\le S_I-1-\mathbf1_{S_I\ge2},\\
\sum_{\nu\notin\mathcal C}d_\nu
&\ge2+2\sum_{\nu\in\mathcal C}d_\nu(\ell_\nu-1)
 +\mathbf1_{S_I\ge2}+\mathbf1_{S_J\ge2}.
\end{aligned}}
\tag{U-CANCEL-REAL}
$$

The final sum is exactly the all-four-full support. In particular its half-degree is at least four when both partition maps have at least two distinct zeros, and at least three when precisely one has a unique zero. The degree-one-support cases are handled by the indicator terms; replacing the right sides indiscriminately by $S_J-2,S_I-2$ would be incorrect.

This improved budget does **not** require squarefreeness. It does require a same-type full pair. A pair of unequal type can give cancellation values off the unit circle, and this proof does not apply to it.

**Three-factor cancellation configurations.** Suppose there are exactly three center factors. If only one offset $F$ is globally full, the other three offsets $G_i$ are partial at distinct factors $i=1,2,3$. Normalize $F$'s allocation to $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$; write $a_i$, $|a_i|<e_i$, for $G_i$'s own-factor allocation.
If $G_i$'s signs at the other two factors $j,k$ agree, orient them to agree with $F$. The quotient of their unsquared Gaussian monomials has support only at $i$. Cancellation of $G_j,G_k$ would force
$d_j+d_k\le d_i-1$.
If those signs differ, the two dominant-term quotients have supports $\{i,k\}$ and $\{i,j\}$, giving

$$
d_j\le d_i+d_k-1,\qquad d_k\le d_i+d_j-1.
$$

The same-sign alternative is incompatible with either alternative for row $j$. Hence every off-diagonal sign pair is opposite and

$$
\boxed{d_i<d_j+d_k\quad(i,j,k\text{ distinct})}
\tag{U-CANCEL-TRIANGLE}
$$

in this one-full-offset case.

When $d_1=d_2=d_3=1$, write

$$
u_i=\frac{t-r_i}{t-s_i},\qquad
P_i=\frac{(t-r_i)(t-s_i)}{r_i-s_i},\qquad
\frac{u_i'}{u_i}=\frac1{P_i}.
$$

Constant factors in $u_i$ can be absorbed into Gaussian coefficients. The quadratics $P_i$ have disjoint roots. Orient $G_i$'s other signs as $+e_j,-e_k$. Cancellation at the roots of $P_j,P_k$ forces respectively

$$
(a_i-e_i)P_k-2e_kP_i\in K^\times P_j,\qquad
(a_i+e_i)P_j+2e_jP_i\in K^\times P_k.
$$

Thus the unique relation $h_1P_1+h_2P_2+h_3P_3=0$, with every $h_i\ne0$, satisfies

$$
\frac{h_j}{h_i}=\frac{e_i+a_i}{2e_j},\qquad
\frac{h_k}{h_i}=\frac{e_i-a_i}{2e_k}.
$$

Putting $T_i=e_i h_i$ gives $T_i=T_j+T_k$ for all three indices, forcing all $T_i=0$, a contradiction.

If at least two offsets are full and all $d_i=1$, their sign partition is a singleton against two factors. The budget prohibits cancellation on the two-factor side. Two partial offsets are therefore impossible. With three full offsets, their three pairwise sign partitions have each factor as singleton once, so a remaining offset cannot cancel any factor. The all-full case is excluded by (U-FSUP).

The pattern $d=(2,1,1)$ is also impossible at any multiplicities. One full offset contradicts (U-CANCEL-TRIANGLE). With two full offsets, a singleton of degree one prohibits all cancellation on the other side. A singleton of degree two cannot itself cancel; the other two offsets would have to cancel both degree-one factors, exceeding their shared budget $2-1$. With three full offsets, a canceled factor would have to have degree strictly smaller than each of the other two; this pattern has none. Again the all-full case is excluded by (U-FSUP). Consequently

$$
\boxed{r=3\Longrightarrow
(d_1,d_2,d_3)\notin\{(1,1,1),(2,1,1)\}
\text{ up to permutation},\quad \sum_i d_i\ge5.}
\tag{U-THREE-CENTER}
$$

There is a further exclusion in the one-full-offset case: the three partial offsets cannot all cancel their own factor completely. Otherwise, with $v_i=u_i^{e_i}$, their Gaussian monomials can be oriented cyclically as $v_2/v_3,v_3/v_1,v_1/v_2$. Their nonzero linear relation becomes a homogeneous cubic in $X_i=v_i^2$, with all six coefficients of $X_i^2X_j$, $i\ne j$, nonzero. Its image contains the three coordinate vertices, from poles of the $v_i$, and one additional point on each coordinate axis, from their zeros. The axis restrictions have three distinct simple roots, so all six points are smooth. No line or conic can contain this image: each coordinate axis meets it in three distinct points. The cubic is therefore integral. On its normalization, adjoining $\sqrt{X_1/X_3}$ and $\sqrt{X_2/X_3}$ gives a rank-two Kummer cover with six distinct inertia-two branch points. Its genus is at least $4g+3\ge3$, but the original $\mathbb P^1$ supplies both square roots and dominates it, impossible. Consequently

$$
\boxed{r=3,\ \text{exactly one full offset}
\Longrightarrow \text{some partial own-factor allocation is nonzero}.}
\tag{U-THREE-ZERO}
$$

In particular, a three-factor squarefree center requires at least two globally full offsets.

**The degree-eight contradiction lemma.** Since
$\delta=2\sum_\nu e_\nu d_\nu$, the preceding exclusions imply

$$
\boxed{\delta=8\Longrightarrow
c=\kappa q_1q_2q_3q_4,\quad
q_i\text{ distinct irreducible norm quadratics},\quad
\deg(t_i)\in\{3,4\}\ (1\le i\le4).}
\tag{U-OCTIC-STRUCT}
$$

Here is the additional proof of the projection assertion. Each factor is simple, and an offset's circle degree is four minus its number of canceled factors. Suppose an offset $T$ cancels two factors.
If two other offsets are full, the shared budget permits at most two canceled factors altogether, so all three other offsets are full. Every full pair must have a $2|2$ sign partition separating the two canceled factors. In
$\mathbb F_2^4/\langle(1,1,1,1)\rangle$, the sum of the two canceled coordinates would therefore equal one on all three pairwise differences of three vectors. Two differences sum to the third, a contradiction.
If exactly one other offset $F$ is full, label the pattern
$T:\{1,2\}$, $G_1:\{3\}$, $G_2:\{4\}$.
Relative to $F$, each $G_i$ must have opposite signs at 1 and 2: otherwise a quotient supported on at most factors 3 and 4, with external ramification budget at most two, would ramify at all four roots of factors 1 and 2. Orient both $G_i$ as $+,-$ there. Their monomial quotient now has support only at 3 and 4, with exponents $\pm1$, so has degree two. Cancellation of $T$, a linear combination of $G_1,G_2$, again forces four critical points, impossible. These exhaust the possibilities.

**Degree-two central projections force squarefree centers.** At arbitrary rational root degree, suppose one of the four central circle projections satisfies $\deg(t_T)=2$.
If at least two other offsets are full, the shared budget requires all-four-full factors of total half-degree at least two. They exhaust
$\sum |a_{T,\nu}|d_\nu=2$, so $T$ is full precisely on this retained support, with multiplicity one, and has zero allocation elsewhere. The other three offsets are then full everywhere. Equality in the depth-sensitive budget forces every canceled depth to equal one, proving squarefreeness.

Otherwise $T$ is supported on two distinct quadratic factors $q_1,q_2$, each with multiplicity one. A single supported factor, or a partial allocation at a supported factor, would leave two other offsets full everywhere. There is exactly one full offset $F$; the other two $G_1,G_2$ cancel respectively at $q_1,q_2$, and are full at every factor canceled by $T$.
Orient $F$ positively everywhere and $G_1$ positively at $q_2$. Among the factors canceled by $T$, write $S_\pm=\sum d_\nu$ according to $G_1$'s signs and
$C_\pm=\sum d_\nu(2e_\nu-1)$.
The monomial quotient has support $q_1$ and the negative group, while the monomial product has support $q_1,q_2$ and the positive group. Their external ramification budgets give

$$
C_+\le S_-,\qquad C_-\le S_++1,\qquad
2\sum_{\nu\text{ canceled by }T}d_\nu(e_\nu-1)\le1.
$$

The sum is integral and nonnegative, so all remaining multiplicities are one. Therefore

$$
\boxed{\deg(t_T)=2\Longrightarrow c\text{ is squarefree}.}
\tag{U-DEG2-CENTER}
$$

In the one-full-offset case this also gives a discrete sign restriction. Normalize $F$ positively, $G_1$ positively at $q_2$, and $G_2$ positively at $q_1$. Let $a,b,c,d$ be the total half-degrees of the factors canceled by $T$ with sign pairs $++,+-,-+,--$ in $G_1,G_2$. The two individual budgets give

$$
a+b\le c+d\le a+b+1,\qquad
a+c\le b+d\le a+c+1.
$$

Applying the ramification argument to $G_1,G_2$, whose quotient and product each have the two retained quadratic factors in their support, gives $|a+d-b-c|\le1$. Thus $b=c$, $d-a\in\{0,1\}$, and

$$
\boxed{(a,b,c,d)\in
\{(n,n,n,n),(n,n,n,n+1),(n,n+1,n+1,n+1)\},
\quad n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}.}
\tag{U-DEG2-SIGNS}
$$

Since the canceled support has half-degree $\delta/2-2$, this case cannot have $\delta\equiv0\pmod8$.

**Conjugate critical fibers exclude root degree ten.** Suppose a nonconstant Gaussian unit function $w$ satisfies $w(\bar z)=1/\overline{w(z)}$. If $z\notin\mathbb R$, $w(z)\ne0,\infty$, $|w(z)|=1$, and the ramification index at $z$ is at least two, then

$$
w(\bar z)=w(z),\qquad \deg w\ge4.
\tag{U-CONJ-FIBER}
$$

Indeed the same fiber contains the distinct conjugate points, each with multiplicity at least two.

For cancellation $T=r_0P+s_0Q$ with $|r_0|=|s_0|$, the Gaussian coefficients have equal modulus $1/2$. The quotient $w$ of the two unsquared Gaussian monomials therefore satisfies $w(z)^2=C$, $|C|=1$, at a canceled factor where their polarities agree. Lowering the pole order by at least two forces ramification index at least two. If $P,Q$ are globally full, this quotient is the square of the opposite sign-partition map; that map itself satisfies (U-CONJ-FIBER), since squaring is unramified at a finite nonzero value. A corner offset has equal-absolute-value coefficients when expressed using any two of the other three offsets.

At root degree ten, $\sum e_\nu d_\nu=5$. The center-support restrictions and (U-GAUSS-BOUNDARY) leave only the squarefree half-degree patterns

$$
(3,1,1),\qquad(2,2,1),\qquad(2,1,1,1).
$$

Every pattern contains a quadratic factor $q$, hence a canceled corner $T$.

If at least two offsets are globally full, apply (U-CONJ-FIBER) to any full pair at $q$. The opposite partition map has degree at least four; the two degrees sum to five, so $q$'s side consists of that single simple quadratic. The shared budget prohibits every cancellation on the opposite side. Thus $T$ is the only partial offset and the other three are full. For each of their three pairs, the sign partition must again be $\{q\}\mid\{\text{all other factors}\}$. Three distinct sign vectors modulo simultaneous reversal cannot have all pairwise differences equal to one nonzero vector. This is impossible.

With exactly one full offset and three factors, squarefreeness forces all three partial own-factor allocations to zero, contrary to (U-THREE-ZERO). With four factors, the three quadratics cancel only corners, so the quartic cancels one edge $T$, and the other edge is full. The two corners divide the three quadratic cancellations in a two-to-one split. Orient their Gaussian monomials to agree at the quartic; their quotient has degree three, supported with exponent of absolute value one at the three quadratics. The cancellation $T=x+y$ or $x-y$ at the quartic has equal coefficients, contradicting (U-CONJ-FIBER). Zero full offsets are impossible: three factors cancel at most three offsets, and in the four-factor case the quadratics cancel only the two corners and the quartic at most one further offset. The cases are exhaustive. Hence

$$
\boxed{\delta\text{ is even and }\delta\ge12
\quad\text{for every admissible rational full-root family}.}
\tag{U-R12}
$$

The degree is that of the birational root image. The assertion does not bound the center of an isolated integer square or remove rational singular points lacking rational normalization lifts.

**Degree-two projections and residue fields.** If a degree-two central projection has at least two other full offsets, the preceding structural lemma gives three other full offsets, a squarefree center, and all-four-full support of half-degree two. Among three full offsets is a same-type full pair. Its two nonempty sign supports have $S_I+S_J\ge3$, so (U-CANCEL-REAL) requires all-four-full half-degree at least three. This contradiction excludes the entire three-full branch.

In the remaining one-full branch, the two retained factors $q_1,q_2$ are quadratic and the other partial offsets $G_1,G_2$ cancel them separately. Equation (U-GAUSS-BOUNDARY) forces $G_1,G_2$ to be the corners, so the degree-two offset $T$ and the globally full offset are the edges. Every factor canceled by $T$ has residue field containing $\mathbb Q(\zeta_8)$, and therefore has degree divisible by four. The four sign-class half-degree sums in (U-DEG2-SIGNS) are all even. Its three allowed patterns leave only

$$
\boxed{\begin{gathered}
\deg(t_T)=2\ \Longrightarrow\
(a,b,c,d)=(2k,2k,2k,2k),\\
\delta=16k+4,\qquad k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}.
\end{gathered}}
\tag{U-DEG2-EXACT}
$$

The center is squarefree. At the minimum degree twenty it has exactly two retained quadratics and four canceled quartics, one in each sign class; each quartic residue field is $\mathbb Q(\zeta_8)$.
