The final equality is an equality of positive squarefree integers: $\gcd(Q_i,H_i)=1$. In particular, bounding $M_i$ bounds each of its two displayed squarefree factors. This index introduces no cancellation between the step and phase classes.

**A single mixed character has a genus-two target.** Over $K_0=\mathbb Q(i)$ let $z$ be a phase with normalized offset $\alpha=(z^2-z^{-2})/(2i)$. For $\eta\in K_0^\times$, adjoining just
\[
w^2=\alpha z/\eta
\]
gives a double cover of $X$ with the nonconstant genus-two target
\[
2i\eta W^2=z^5-z,\qquad W=zw.
\tag{U-MIX-COVER}
\]
The identity follows by multiplication. The polynomial $z^5-z$ is squarefree, so the smooth projective target has genus two. The cover is geometrically connected because $\alpha$ has an odd-order zero at the generic $\alpha=0$ divisor while $z$ is a unit there. It is the mixed-product intermediate quotient of the cover extracting the step and phase roots separately. At actual points, (U-EVEN-PHASE-CLASS) gives $[\alpha z]=[i^\epsilon M_i]$, with the Gaussian unit determined by the phase convention.

There is also an explicit model over $\mathbb Q$. For any fixed positive squarefree $M$, put
\[
C_M:\quad Y^2=M t(1-t^4).
\tag{U-MIX-BOLZA}
\]
If $Q_iH_i=Mh^2$, then the actual pair gives
\[
t=\frac{n_i}{m_i},\qquad Y=\frac{Mh}{2m_i^3}.
\tag{U-MIX-AP-MAP}
\]
Indeed $t(1-t^4)=Q_iH_i/(4m_i^6)$. Conversely a rational point in the primitive opposite-parity conic chart, with $0<t<1$, gives a central three-term progression with mixed index $M$. This converse recovers that progression only; it does not supply the remaining six square entries.

A finite image of one chosen $M_i$ gives finitely many normalized progression directions by Faltings. Each fixed admissible offset $0<\alpha<1$ leaves the genus-two quotient
\[
V^2=(1-\beta^2)\bigl((1+\alpha)^2-\beta^2\bigr)
                 \bigl((1-\alpha)^2-\beta^2\bigr),
\tag{U-MIX-FIXED-OFFSET}
\]
whose six roots are distinct. For a fixed edge offset $\gamma=\alpha+\beta$ or $\gamma=\alpha-\beta$, use the other sum/difference coordinate $v$ instead; the corresponding quotient is
\[
V^2=(1-v^2)\bigl(4-(\gamma+v)^2\bigr)
                  \bigl(4-(\gamma-v)^2\bigr).
\]
Its six roots $\pm1,\pm(2+\gamma),\pm(2-\gamma)$ are distinct for $0<\gamma<1$. Hence that finite image implies finiteness of primitive full squares. This conclusion is ineffective and is also implied by the existing fixed-step-class theorem, since (U-MIX-INDEX) then confines the step class to a finite set. The smaller geometric cover supplies no new bound on $M_i$.

**Explicit elliptic quotient.** Let
\[
K=\mathbb Q(r),\quad r^2=2,\quad k=1+r,\quad
\delta=(4+2r)M=2rkM,
\]
and define
\[
E_\delta:\quad y^2=x^3+4\delta x^2+2\delta^2x.
\tag{U-MIX-ELLIPTIC}
\]
Its $j$-invariant is $8000$. A degree-two map $C_{M,K}\to E_\delta$ is
\[
u=\frac{t-k}{t-(1-r)},\qquad
X=-\frac{u^2+k^2}{2k^2},\qquad
x=\delta X,\qquad
y=\frac{\delta Y(u-1)^3}{4k}.
\tag{U-MIX-ELLIPTIC-MAP}
\]
These expressions extend to a morphism of smooth projective curves. For rational finite $t$, the denominator $t-(1-r)$ is nonzero and $u\ne1$. The map therefore retains the actual rational parameter without a chart exception in (U-MIX-AP-MAP).

To verify the equation, put $f(t)=t^5-t$. Direct factorization gives
\[
(u-1)^6f\!\left(\frac{(1-r)u-k}{u-1}\right)
=(40-28r)(u^2-1)(u^2-k^4)(u^2+k^2).
\]
Substituting $u^2=-k^2-2k^2X$ gives
\[
-M(u-1)^6f(t)=16k^2\delta X(X^2+4X+2),
\]
which proves the map. The quotient uses $u^2$ and $Y(u-1)^3$; its hyperelliptic-involution complement is the conjugate elliptic quotient. An arbitrary $K$-point of $E_\delta$ need not recover rational $t$ and need not satisfy the residual square conditions.

**Theorem (even rank and two forced independent points).** For every positive squarefree $M$, the Mordell–Weil rank of $E_\delta(K)$ is even. Every nonbranch rational point of $C_M$ maps to a nontorsion point of $E_\delta(K)$. Consequently each opposite pair of every admissible square satisfies
\[
\operatorname{rank}E_{(4+2\sqrt2)M_i}(\mathbb Q(\sqrt2))\ge2.
\tag{U-MIX-RANK-TWO}
\]
The conclusion is uniform in the orientation support, the deficit product, and the prime factors of the indices.

**Proof.** Write $\sigma$ for the nontrivial automorphism of $K/\mathbb Q$. The identities $\delta=k^2\sigma(\delta)$ and $k\sigma(k)=-1$ show that
\[
T(x,y)=\bigl(k^2\sigma(x),k^3\sigma(y)\bigr)
\quad\text{satisfies}\quad T^2=[-1]
\tag{U-MIX-SEMILINEAR}
\]
on $E_\delta(K)$. Thus its rational Mordell–Weil space is a vector space over $\mathbb Q(i)$ and its rank is even. If $P$ is nontorsion, $P,T(P)$ are independent modulo torsion: applying $T$ to $aP+bT(P)=0$ modulo torsion yields $(a^2+b^2)P=0$ modulo torsion.

It remains to prove that the curve map gives a nontorsion point. All two-torsion is $K$-rational, with nonidentity abscissas
\[
0,\qquad\delta(-2+r),\qquad\delta(-2-r).
\]
First suppose $M$ has an odd prime divisor $p$. At any place $v\mid p$ of $K$, the curve
\[
E_0:\quad y^2=x^3+4x^2+2x
\]
has good reduction because its discriminant is $512$. The coefficient $\delta$ has odd valuation, so $L=K_v(\sqrt\delta)$ is ramified quadratic with absolute ramification index two. A torsion point of $E_\delta(K_v)$ untwists to a point $R\in E_0(L)$ satisfying $\tau R=-R$ for the nontrivial inertia automorphism $\tau$. If $R$ has odd prime order $\ell$, its reduction is both unchanged by inertia and negated, hence is zero. Thus $R$ belongs to the formal group.

There is no prime-to-$p$ torsion in this formal group. For $p\ge5$ there is no $p$-torsion either. In the multiplication-by-$p$ series, coefficients of degrees $2,\ldots,p-1$ are divisible by $p$, since the reduction has initial degree at least $p$. For a formal parameter $a$ of positive integral valuation, $pa$ therefore has strictly smaller valuation than every other term: terms of degree at least $p$ have valuation at least $p\,v(a)>2+v(a)$. Hence $[p](a)\ne0$. When $p=3$, the base three-division polynomial factors as
\[
\psi_3(X)=(X^2+4X-2)(3X^2+4X+2).
\tag{U-MIX-THREE-DIVISION}
\]
Its factors have discriminants $24$ and $-8$, neither a square in $K$. Thus no twist in question has a $K$-rational three-torsion abscissa. This excludes all odd torsion, including the residue characteristic.

For four-torsion use the full-two-torsion halving criterion: $(e_j,0)$ is divisible by two over $K$ exactly when both differences $e_j-e_l$ are squares in $K$. Each negative nonzero abscissa has a negative difference from zero in the real embedding $r>0$, so neither corresponding point can be halved. At zero the two differences are
\[
\delta(2-r)=4M,\qquad\delta(2+r)=4k^2M.
\]
Both are squares in $K$ exactly when $M$ is a square in $K$, which for positive squarefree rational $M$ means $M\in\{1,2\}$. Therefore, whenever $M$ has an odd prime factor,
\[
E_\delta(K)_{\rm tors}=E_\delta[2](K).
\tag{U-MIX-TORSION}
\]

For $M=1,2$ the curves are $K$-isomorphic. For $M=1$, the good reductions at $r\equiv3\pmod7$ and $r\equiv6\pmod{17}$ have $8$ and $24$ points, respectively. Injection of prime-to-residue-characteristic torsion at these two places bounds total torsion order by eight. Full two-torsion then bounds its exponent by four.

A nonbranch rational point of $C_M$ has $Y\ne0$, so its elliptic image has $y\ne0$ and is not two-torsion. All possible four-torsion doubles to $(0,0)$. The duplication formula then gives $x^2=2\delta^2$, or $x/\delta=\pm r$. Equation (U-MIX-ELLIPTIC-MAP) would force
\[
u^2=-k^2(1\pm2r).
\]
The right side has norm $-7$, whereas a square in $K$ has nonnegative rational norm. Thus the image is not four-torsion either. It is nontorsion in every case, and (U-MIX-SEMILINEAR) supplies the second independent point. $\square$

**The Jacobian has the same forced rank.** The quotient and its conjugate induce a $\mathbb Q$-isogeny
\[
\operatorname{Jac}(C_M)\sim_{\mathbb Q}
\operatorname{Res}_{K/\mathbb Q}E_\delta.
\tag{U-MIX-JACOBIAN}
\]
Indeed their pulled-back regular differentials are
\[
\frac{t-k}{2k}\frac{dt}{Y},\qquad
\frac{t-(1-r)}{2(1-r)}\frac{dt}{Y}.
\]
Their coefficient determinant in the basis $t\,dt/Y,dt/Y$ equals $-r/2\ne0$. The map to the restriction of scalars therefore induces an isomorphism on regular one-forms, hence an isogeny of the two-dimensional abelian varieties. The point at infinity of the odd-degree model supplies a rational base point for the Jacobian map. It follows that
\[
\operatorname{rank}\operatorname{Jac}(C_M)(\mathbb Q)
=\operatorname{rank}E_\delta(K),
\tag{U-MIX-JACOBIAN-RANK}
\]
which is even and at least two whenever $C_M$ has a nonbranch rational point.

Since full two-torsion contributes dimension two, a certified two-Selmer dimension at most three for $E_{(4+2\sqrt2)M}/K$ excludes every nontrivial central progression with mixed index $M$. This is a necessary arithmetic test. A surviving Selmer group, elliptic rank, or quotient point does not establish a common rational lift. No finite image of the mixed indices has been proved.

### 12.9. Exact cancellation across all complementary products

Retain $H=c^4$, the twelve forms $G_m$ of Section 12.7, and the
opposite-pair content product $P=\prod_iA_i$. Set
\[
e_m=\operatorname{den}(G_m/H)=\frac{H}{\gcd(H,G_m)}.
\]
These are product denominators, distinct from the individual critical
denominators $d_S$. Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
Q_0&=x^2+y^2,\\
Q_1&=x^2+xy+2y^2,&Q_2&=x^2-xy+2y^2,\\
Q_3&=2x^2+xy+y^2,&Q_4&=2x^2-xy+y^2,\\
Q_5&=x^2+xy-y^2,&Q_6&=x^2-xy-y^2,
\end{aligned}
\qquad b_j=\gcd(H,Q_j)>0.
\]

**Theorem (joint center cancellation).** At every primitive admissible
full-root point, the seven $b_j$ are pairwise coprime and
\[
\boxed{\prod_m\gcd(H,G_m)=b_0^4b_1b_2b_3b_4b_5^2b_6^2.}
\tag{Q-JOINT-CANCEL}
\]
Moreover
\[
\boxed{\gcd\!\left(P,\prod_{j=0}^6b_j\right)=1,\qquad
\gcd\!\left(P,\prod_mG_m\right)=1,\qquad
\gcd_mG_m=1.}
\tag{Q-DEFICIT-COPRIME}
\]
In particular every reduced critical numerator $N_S$ is coprime to $P$.
No orientation-rank or prime-support hypothesis is imposed.

**Proof.** Fix $p^e\Vert c$. First suppose $p\mid P$. Exactly one
opposite pair has positive $p$-adic content. Its offset and product vanish
modulo $p$, whereas the other three offsets and products are units.
The four possibilities for the offset line are $x=0$, $y=0$, $x=y$,
and $x=-y$. Substitution into the table of $G_m$, with
$q_i^2=-D_i^2$ modulo $p$, makes every $G_m$ a nonzero power of two
times a unit square, up to sign. The seven $Q_j$ also take unit values:
after removing a unit square their possible nonzero factors are
$\pm1,2,4$. Since center primes are odd, this proves both coprimality
claims at positive-content primes.

Suppose now $p\nmid P$. Every $D_i$ is a unit. The split Gaussian
valuation formula gives a choice of $i\in\mathbb Q_p$ and signs
$\sigma_i\in\{\pm1\}$ such that
\[
q_i=-i\sigma_iD_i+O(p^{4e}).
\]
Changing these signs permutes the four values within each of the two
A-orbits and within the B-orbit in Section 12.7. For the all-positive
choice the reductions modulo $p^{4e}$ are

| $m$ | Boundary value of $G_m$ |
|---:|---|
| 27, 29 | $-8Q_0$ |
| 39 | $-4Q_1$ |
| 46 | $-4Q_3$ |
| 71 | $-4Q_2$ |
| 78 | $-4Q_4$ |
| 114, 116 | $-4Q_0$ |
| 53 | $4Q_5$ |
| 58 | $-4Q_6$ |
| 83 | $4Q_6$ |
| 92 | $-4Q_5$ |

All displayed constant factors are $p$-adic units. Taking valuations
truncated at $4e$ proves (Q-JOINT-CANCEL) prime by prime.

To show that at most one $Q_j$ vanishes at such a prime, note that $y$
is a unit and that the resultants of distinct $Q_j(r,1)$ are among
\[
\{2,5,8,9,11,18,-4\}.
\]
Their leading coefficients are one or two. A common zero therefore
requires $p\in\{2,3,5,11\}$. Center primes exclude $2,3,11$. The
prime 5 cannot occur with $p\nmid P$: otherwise all four nonzero
offsets $x,y,x+y,x-y$ would be squares modulo 5, whereas nonzero
squares $x,y\in\{1,4\}$ force either $x-y=0$ or $x+y=0$.
This proves pairwise coprimality of the $b_j$.

Finally every $G_m$ is odd. A common divisor of the twelve values
divides the sum of the four B-forms, namely $4H$, and hence divides
$H$. At a center prime at most one $q_i$ is a nonunit, so at least
one of $q_1q_2,q_3q_4$ is a unit. Differences of B-forms include
$8q_1q_2$ and $8q_3q_4$, excluding any common center prime. Thus
$\gcd_mG_m=1$. Since $N_mN_{255-m}=G_m$, the numerator assertion
follows as well. $\square$

**Corollary (product and least-common-multiple laws).** Put
\[
c_+=\prod_{p\mid P}p^{v_p(c)}.
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{\prod_m e_m=
\frac{c^{48}}{b_0^4b_1b_2b_3b_4b_5^2b_6^2}
\ge c^{32}c_+^{16}\ge c^{32}P^{16}.}
\tag{Q-PRODUCT-DENOMINATORS}
\]
Any five of the twelve indexed denominators have least common multiple
$c^4$. In addition,
\[
\boxed{e_{53}=e_{92},\qquad e_{58}=e_{83},\qquad
\operatorname{lcm}(e_{53},e_{58})=c^4.}
\tag{Q-PRODUCT-TWO-LCM}
\]

Indeed the product of the pairwise-coprime $b_j$ divides
$(c/c_+)^4$, and every exponent in the cancellation product is at most
four. At a fixed center prime, the boundary table allows at most four
of the twelve denominators to lose valuation from $4v_p(c)$; at a
positive-content prime none loses valuation. This proves the assertion
for any five. The pairwise equalities follow from
$G_{53}+G_{92}=G_{58}+G_{83}=2H$. No center prime divides both
$G_{53}$ and $G_{58}$, since their sum and difference would make both
$q_1q_2$ and $q_3q_4$ nonunits. This proves the stated two-denominator
least common multiple.

A prime dividing $b_0$ is $1$ modulo 8: $x/y$ is a square modulo the
prime and its square is $-1$, so $-1$ is a fourth power. Primes dividing
$b_1b_2b_3b_4$ split in $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-7})$, and those dividing
$b_5b_6$ split in $\mathbb Q(\sqrt5)$, by the respective quadratic
discriminants. These conclusions specify cancellation primes and their
allocation among the products.

The laws give lower bounds for the product denominators and recover the
center from selected least common multiples. They do not bound the
center above. In particular $\prod_m e_m$ is not generally the reduced
denominator of $\prod_m(G_m/H)$: a numerator valuation exceeding
$4v_p(c)$ can cancel a denominator contribution from another factor.
The truncation in (Q-JOINT-CANCEL) must be retained.

### 12.10. Synchronization of the four mixed indices

The four indices in (U-MIX-INDEX) retain a recoverable common arithmetic
class. Write
\[
h=\gcd(x,y),\qquad x=hn,\quad y=hm,\quad \gcd(n,m)=1,
\qquad (\Lambda_1,\Lambda_2,\Lambda_3,\Lambda_4)=(n,m,n+m,n-m).
\]
In this subsection set
\[
B=\operatorname{sf}(hc),\qquad
R_i=\operatorname{sf}(A_i\Lambda_i),\qquad
\operatorname{odd}(a)=a/2^{v_2(a)}.
\]
The $\Lambda_i$ are the reduced integral offsets; all these quantities
are positive integers.

**Theorem (common class and labeled recovery).** For one primitive
admissible full square,
\[
\boxed{[M_i]=[BR_i],\qquad M_i=\operatorname{sf}(BR_i).}
\tag{U-MIX-JOINT-CLASS}
\]
The $R_i$ are pairwise coprime except that $\gcd(R_3,R_4)$ may be 2.
Consequently no odd prime divides exactly two of the four $M_i$.
Moreover
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{odd}(B)=
\operatorname{odd}\!\left(
\operatorname{lcm}_{\substack{I\subset\{1,2,3,4\}\\|I|=3}}
\gcd(M_i:i\in I)\right).}
\tag{U-MIX-MAJORITY}
\]
At 2, let $w$ be the number of even $M_i$. Then $B$ is even precisely
when $w\ge3$, or when $w=2$ and the two even indices are the corner
indices 1 and 2. If $w=2$, those indices must be either the two corners
or the two edges. Thus the labeled tuple $(M_1,M_2,M_3,M_4)$ recovers
the whole squarefree integer $B$ and then each $R_i=\operatorname{sf}(BM_i)$.
Finally,
\[
\boxed{[M_1M_2M_3M_4]=[Pnm(n^2-m^2)]
=[Pxy(x^2-y^2)],\qquad
\operatorname{odd}(B)^3\mid\prod_iM_i.}
\tag{U-MIX-JOINT-PRODUCT}
\]

**Proof.** Since $D_i=h\Lambda_i$ and $H_i=c/A_i$,
\[
[M_i]=[h\Lambda_i c/A_i]=[hcA_i\Lambda_i]=[BR_i].
\]
The opposite-pair allocation lemma implies $\gcd(h,c)=1$: a prime
dividing $h$ and $c$ would divide all four offsets, although at most
one offset can be nonunit at a center prime. For any odd prime, the
determinants of pairs of the four linear forms $n,m,n+m,n-m$ are
$\pm1$ or $\pm2$. Hence an odd prime divides at most one $\Lambda_i$.
Also $p\mid A_i$ implies $p\mid c,D_i$, and therefore $p\mid\Lambda_i$.
Thus every odd prime in the four products $A_i\Lambda_i$ is confined to one
index. Passing to squarefree parts preserves this disjointness.

All $A_i$ are odd. If $n,m$ have opposite parity, only one corner
$\Lambda_i$ is even. If they are both odd, precisely the two edge offsets
$\Lambda_3,\Lambda_4$ are even. These observations prove the asserted gcd pattern.

At an odd prime the four parities $v_p(M_i)$ are the constant bit
$v_p(B)$ with at most one bit changed. Their number of ones is
therefore $0,1,3$, or 4. The common bit is one exactly when at least
three of the indices are divisible by $p$, proving
(U-MIX-MAJORITY). At 2 the changed bits have weight at most one or
are exactly the two edges. In the latter case a weight-two output
has even corners exactly when the common bit is one. This proves
the tie rule and the full recovery assertion. Every odd prime of
$B$ occurs in at least three of the squarefree $M_i$, giving the
divisibility statement.

Finally $\prod_iH_i=c^4/P$ and
$\prod_iD_i=h^4nm(n^2-m^2)$. Taking squareclasses and using
$[P^{-1}]=[P]$ proves the product identity. $\square$

This is a necessary condition on four mixed indices belonging to the
same square. It provides a test on the index tuple before reconstructing
the center or slope. It retains more information than the product
squareclass, which forgets which indices contain each prime. No bound
on $B$, the $R_i$, or the mixed indices follows from these identities.

### 12.11. Three orbit norms and the complete critical-value product

The twelve complementary products of Section 12.7 have three
root-sign orbits. Their products eliminate all four opposite-root
products and give explicit polynomials in the normalized offsets.
Put
\[
\alpha=x/c^2,\quad\beta=y/c^2,\quad
\sigma=\alpha^2+\beta^2,\quad p=\alpha\beta,\quad
d=\alpha^2-\beta^2,\quad C=5-6\sigma,
\]
and, for $\epsilon=\pm1$, define
\[
P_\epsilon=(1-\alpha^2)(1-(\alpha+\epsilon\beta)^2),\qquad
Q_\epsilon=(1-\beta^2)(1-(\alpha-\epsilon\beta)^2).
\]
Here $P_\epsilon$ denotes a polynomial, not the content product $P$.
Set
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nu_\epsilon&=C^4-8C^2(P_\epsilon+Q_\epsilon)
                       +16(P_\epsilon-Q_\epsilon)^2,\\
A^2&=(1-\alpha^2)(1-\beta^2),\qquad
B^2=(1-(\alpha+\beta)^2)(1-(\alpha-\beta)^2),\\
\nu_0&=1-32(A^2+B^2)+256(A^2-B^2)^2,\qquad
\mathcal N=\nu_+\nu_-\nu_0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{Q-ORBIT-NORMS}
\]
Only the displayed squares of $A,B$ enter these definitions. At an
actual full-root point, the identity
\[
\prod_{\eta,\theta=\pm1}
\bigl(C+2\eta\sqrt P+2\theta\sqrt Q\bigr)
=C^4-8C^2(P+Q)+16(P-Q)^2
\]
and the table in Section 12.7 give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nu_+&=\prod_{m\in\{29,46,71,116\}}\left(\frac{G_m}{c^4}\right),\\
\nu_-&=\prod_{m\in\{27,39,78,114\}}\left(\frac{G_m}{c^4}\right),\\
\nu_0&=\prod_{m\in\{53,58,83,92\}}\left(\frac{G_m}{c^4}\right),\\
\mathcal N&=\prod_{m\in\mathcal R}\left(\frac{G_m}{c^4}\right)
           =\prod_{S\in\mathcal S_{\rm crit}}\left(\frac{F_S}{c^4}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
The final two products have twelve and twenty-four factors.

**Theorem (uniform nonintegrality on the offset domain).** Let $c,x,y$
be integers satisfying
\[
c>0,\qquad \gcd(c,6)=1,\qquad 24\mid x,y,\qquad
0<y<x,\qquad x+y<c^2.
\]
For the polynomial values in (Q-ORBIT-NORMS),
\[
\boxed{\nu_+,\nu_-,\nu_0,\mathcal N\notin\mathbb Z.}
\tag{Q-ORBIT-NONINTEGRAL}
\]
In particular the three orbit products and the product of all twenty-four
critical values are nonintegral at every primitive admissible point.
The polynomial theorem itself does not require rational square roots
of the eight entries.

**Proof: the two A-orbits.** The real hypotheses give
$0<\sigma<1$ and $0<P_\epsilon,Q_\epsilon<1$. Hence
\[
\nu_\epsilon\ge C^4-16C^2\ge-64.
\]
Equality at the final lower endpoint would require $C^2=8$ and
$P_\epsilon+Q_\epsilon=2$, which is impossible. If
$\sigma\ge1/3$, then $|C|\le3$ and
$|P_\epsilon-Q_\epsilon|<1$, giving $\nu_\epsilon<97<225$.

For $0<\sigma<1/3$, the identities
\[
\begin{aligned}
d^2+4p^2&=\sigma^2,\\
P_\epsilon+Q_\epsilon&=2-3\sigma+\sigma^2+2\epsilon pd,\\
P_\epsilon-Q_\epsilon&=(\sigma-1)d+2\epsilon(\sigma-2)p
\end{aligned}
\]
give $P_\epsilon+Q_\epsilon\ge2-3\sigma$ and
\[
|P_\epsilon-Q_\epsilon|
\le\sigma\sqrt{(1-\sigma)^2+(2-\sigma)^2}<\sqrt5\,\sigma.
\]
Consequently $\nu_\epsilon\le b(\sigma)$, where
\[
b(\sigma)=(5-6\sigma)^4
-8(5-6\sigma)^2(2-3\sigma)+80\sigma^2.
\]
The exact difference
\[
225-b(\sigma)=8\sigma
\bigl(180-433\sigma+432\sigma^2-162\sigma^3\bigr)
\]
is positive: the bracket is greater than
$180-433/3-162/27=89/3$. Thus
\[
-64<\nu_+,\nu_-<225.
\tag{Q-A-ORBIT-REAL}
\]

**The B-orbit and its sign.** Direct expansion gives
\[
\nu_0=-63+96\sigma-32\sigma^2+96p^2
                  +256(\sigma-\sigma^2+5p^2)^2.
\]
The defining expression with $A^2+B^2<2$ proves $\nu_0>-63$.
The expanded expression is strictly increasing in $p^2$ on the
current real domain, and
\[
p^2<\frac14\min\{\sigma^2,(1-\sigma)^2\}.
\]
For $0<\sigma\le1/2$, substitution of $\sigma^2/4$ gives the upper
envelope
\[
f_1(\sigma)=-63+96\sigma+248\sigma^2+128\sigma^3+16\sigma^4.
\]
It is strictly increasing and $f_1(1/2)=64$. For
$1/2\le\sigma<1$, write $w=1-\sigma$. Substitution of $w^2/4$
gives
\[
f_2(w)=1-32w+248w^2+128w^3+16w^4,
\]
and
\[
64-f_2(w)=(1-2w)(2w+1)(2w+7)(2w+9)\ge0.
\]
The strict bound on $p^2$ therefore yields
\[
-63<\nu_0<64,\qquad
\nu_0\ge0\ \Longrightarrow\ \sigma>3/10,
\tag{Q-B-ORBIT-REAL}
\]
where the implication uses $f_1(3/10)=-5184/625<0$.

**Individual congruences.** All three norms are polynomials with
integer coefficients in $\alpha,\beta$. Their expansions begin
\[
\nu_\pm=225-1440(\alpha^2+\beta^2)+R_\pm,\qquad
\nu_0=-63+96(\alpha^2+\beta^2)+R_0,
\]
where every monomial of each $R_j$ has total degree at least four.
Since $\alpha,\beta\in8\mathbb Z_2$, the remainder terms lie in
$2^{12}\mathbb Z_2$, while the quadratic terms lie in
$2^{11}\mathbb Z_2$. Thus
\[
\nu_\pm\equiv225\pmod{2048},\qquad
\nu_0\equiv-63\pmod{2048}.
\tag{Q-ORBIT-CONGRUENCES}
\]
The respective strict real intervals contain no integer with the
required residue. This proves nonintegrality of the three individual
norms.

**The complete product.** If $\nu_0<0$, the two A-orbit intervals give
\[
-63\cdot225^2<\mathcal N<63\cdot64\cdot225=907200.
\]
If $\nu_0\ge0$, (Q-B-ORBIT-REAL) gives $\sigma>3/10$ and
$|C|<16/5$. Dropping the nonpositive middle term in the A-norm
formula now gives
\[
-64<\nu_+,\nu_-<(16/5)^4+16<121.
\]
In this case a nonnegative product is less than $64\cdot121^2$ and
a negative product is greater than $-64^2\cdot121$. In every case,
\[
\boxed{-3189375<\mathcal N<937024.}
\tag{Q-TOTAL-REAL}
\]

The hypotheses also give $\alpha,\beta\in3\mathbb Z_3$. The
displayed low-degree expansions imply
\[
\nu_\pm-225\in3^4\mathbb Z_3,\qquad
\nu_0+63\in3^3\mathbb Z_3.
\]
Both 225 and $-63$ have 3-adic valuation two. Expanding their product
with these errors therefore shows
$\mathcal N+3189375\in3^7\mathbb Z_3$; the least possible valuation
comes from the B-orbit error multiplied by $225^2$.
(Q-ORBIT-CONGRUENCES) simultaneously gives
$\mathcal N+3189375\in2^{11}\mathbb Z_2$. If $\mathcal N$ were
an integer, it would satisfy
\[
\mathcal N\equiv-3189375\pmod{2^{11}3^7},
\qquad 2^{11}3^7=4478976.
\tag{Q-TOTAL-CONGRUENCE}
\]
The next integer in this residue class above the strict lower endpoint
of (Q-TOTAL-REAL) is $1289601$, larger than its upper endpoint.
This proves total-product nonintegrality. $\square$

**Consequence for the actual critical numerators.** By
(Q-JOINT-DENOMINATORS), at a primitive admissible full-root point
\[
\mathcal N=\frac{\prod_SN_S}{c^{48}},\qquad
\boxed{c^{48}\nmid\prod_SN_S.}
\tag{Q-TOTAL-NUMERATORS}
\]
Thus total cancellation of the critical denominators cannot occur.
This conclusion does not follow from individual nonintegrality alone.
The polynomial theorem proves it already on the stated offset domain,
so it is not an additional rational-lifting condition beyond that
domain. Its use is to exclude integral norm fibers and identify a
nontrivial denominator after eliminating the root signs. It supplies
no upper bound on any norm denominator or on $c$, and no finite
containing collection of fibers.

### 12.12. An exact infinite reciprocity criterion

There is an unconditional global compatibility criterion on the same
normalized root locus. Its completeness involves an infinite collection
of reciprocity conditions.

Let $U$ have eight nonzero root coordinates $r_{i,j}$ indexed by
$(i,j)\in\{-1,0,1\}^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}$, with
\[
r_{i,j}^2=1+i\alpha+j\beta.
\]
The center root is one. Delete the coincidence divisor
\[
\Delta=\alpha\beta(\alpha+\beta)(\alpha-\beta)
(2\alpha+\beta)(2\alpha-\beta)
(\alpha+2\beta)(\alpha-2\beta)=0.
\tag{U-VERY-AFFINE}
\]
Eliminating $\alpha=r_{1,0}^2-1$ and $\beta=r_{0,1}^2-1$ leaves six equations
in the split torus $\mathbb G_m^8$. The condition $\Delta\ne0$
makes $U$ locally closed in that torus.

These deletions are exact: up to sign, the product of the 36 pairwise
differences among the nine entries is
\[
256\alpha^9\beta^9(\alpha+\beta)^5(\alpha-\beta)^5
(2\alpha+\beta)^2(2\alpha-\beta)^2
(\alpha+2\beta)^2(\alpha-2\beta)^2.
\]
Thus they remove precisely the repeated-entry locus. Nonzero root
coordinates remove zero entries. Every point of $U(\mathbb Q)$ gives
nine distinct positive rational squares in the linear magic arrangement;
clearing root denominators gives a valid integer square. Conversely
normalizing a valid integer square by its center root gives such a point.

For a subgroup $B\subset\operatorname{Br}(U)$, write
\[
U(\mathbb A_{\mathbb Q})^B
=\left\{(P_v):\sum_v\operatorname{inv}_v\xi(P_v)=0
\text{ for every }\xi\in B\right\},
\]
and let $\operatorname{pr}_{\rm fin}$ omit the real component.
Rational points are identified with their diagonal images in the finite
adeles.

**Theorem (complete Brauer--Manin correspondence).**
\[
\boxed{U(\mathbb Q)=
\operatorname{pr}_{\rm fin}
\bigl(U(\mathbb A_{\mathbb Q})^{\operatorname{Br}(U)}\bigr).}
\tag{U-FULL-BRAUER}
\]
In particular a valid magic square exists if and only if the full
Brauer--Manin set displayed here is nonempty.

**External theorem and correspondence.** Liu--Xu [32], Theorem 1.2(2)
and Corollary 3.6, prove this very strong approximation identity off
the real place for a locally closed subvariety of a split torus over
$\mathbb Q$. The embedding above checks those hypotheses with ambient
torus $\mathbb G_m^8$. The normalization and denominator correspondence
then give exactly the asserted magic-square equivalence. No finiteness
conjecture for a Brauer or Tate--Shafarevich group is required.

**An explicit complete family of classes.** For every finite-order
character $\chi\in H^1(\mathbb Q,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ and every
root coordinate $r_{i,j}$, take the cyclic algebra $(\chi,r_{i,j})$.
The coordinates are units on $U$, so these are classes in
$\operatorname{Br}(U)$. Let $B_{\rm coord}$ be the subgroup they
generate. Then already
\[
\boxed{U(\mathbb Q)=
\operatorname{pr}_{\rm fin}
\bigl(U(\mathbb A_{\mathbb Q})^{B_{\rm coord}}\bigr).}
\tag{U-COORDINATE-BRAUER}
\]
For the correspondence, use the torus reciprocity pairing in [32],
Section 3, equations (3.1)--(3.2). Over $\mathbb Q$, the kernel of all
finite-order idele characters is
$\mathbb Q^\times\mathbb R_{>0}$. Orthogonality to the displayed
classes therefore makes each finite coordinate idele equal to one
rational number. Applying this to all eight coordinates produces a
rational root tuple. Its polynomial equations and nonvanishing
conditions follow from any finite localization, so it belongs to
$U(\mathbb Q)$. The converse is global reciprocity.

**Canonical real chamber.** The full criterion also preserves the
canonical ordering when that ordering is imposed at the real place.
Indeed $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\alpha-\beta$ are units on $U$.
The quaternion classes
\[
(-1,\alpha),\qquad(-1,\beta),\qquad(-1,\alpha-\beta)
\]
lie in $\operatorname{Br}(U)$. If a full orthogonal adelic point has
$0<\beta_\infty<\alpha_\infty$, (U-FULL-BRAUER) identifies its
finite coordinates with a rational point $Q$. Their finite Brauer
evaluations agree. Reciprocity for $Q$ then makes their real
evaluations agree as well. The real invariant of $(-1,f)$ is zero
for $f>0$ and one-half for $f<0$, proving
$0<\beta(Q)<\alpha(Q)$. Its nonzero rational root of
$1-\alpha-\beta$ gives $\alpha(Q)+\beta(Q)<1$. The classes
$(-1,r_{i,j})$ similarly preserve individual root signs if these are
specified. Adding the three offset classes to $B_{\rm coord}$ gives
the same canonical-chamber conclusion for the explicit family.

The criterion is an exact global characterization, not an evaluation
of its solution set. The character family has unrestricted finite
orders and conductors. Nothing here replaces it by a finite list,
bounds the denominators, or establishes that the full intersection is
empty or nonempty.

### 12.13. A logarithmic deficit bound at fixed center-prime support

The exact additive offset relations give a uniform bound on the deficit
exponents when the identities of the center primes are fixed. Let
$\mathcal P$ be a fixed nonempty finite set of primes congruent to one
modulo four, containing every prime divisor of $c$. For $c>1$ put
\[
E=\max_{p\mid c}v_p(c),\qquad B_0=\max(2E,3).
\]

**Theorem (effective logarithmic deficit bound).** There is an
effectively computable integer $K=K(\mathcal P)\ge1$ such that every
primitive admissible full square with center supported on
$\mathcal P$ satisfies
\[
\boxed{P<B_0^K<(2\log c)^K.}
\tag{U-FIXED-SUPPORT-DEFICIT}
\]
More precisely, for every $p\in\mathcal P$ there is an effectively
computable constant $C_p(\mathcal P)>0$ such that
\[
\boxed{2v_p(P)<C_p(\mathcal P)\log B_0
\quad\text{whenever }p\mid P.}
\tag{U-LOCAL-DEFICIT-LOG}
\]
The constants do not depend on the center exponents, slope, orientation
rank, or assignment of the exceptional rows. Their dependence on the
prime set is retained.

**Proof: extracting a nonzero binary approximation.** For the $i$th
opposite pair use positive roots $u_i,v_i$ with
$u_i^2=c^2+D_i$ and $v_i^2=c^2-D_i$, and put
\[
Z_i=(u_i+v_i)/2+\mathrm i(u_i-v_i)/2\in\mathbb Z[\mathrm i].
\]
Then $N(Z_i)=c^2$ and $\operatorname{Im}(Z_i^2)=D_i$. At
$p^e\Vert c$, choose $\pi\bar\pi=p$ and write the Gaussian
allocations as
\[
v_\pi(Z_i)=e+j_{i,p},\qquad
v_{\bar\pi}(Z_i)=e-j_{i,p},\qquad
v_p(A_i)=e-|j_{i,p}|.
\]
At most one row has positive content, and Proposition 1.22 gives
$p^{2v_p(A_i)}\mid D_i$, including at a balanced allocation.

Suppose $a=v_p(P)>0$, and let $i$ be its unique exceptional row.
Choose two nonexceptional rows using the following exact relations:

| Exceptional row $i$ | Relation | Selected rows |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | $D_3+D_4=2D_1$ | 3, 4 |
| 2 | $D_3-D_4=2D_2$ | 3, 4 |
| 3 | $D_1+D_2=D_3$ | 1, 2 |
| 4 | $D_1-D_2=D_4$ | 1, 2 |

Their allocations at $p$ are extreme. Independently conjugate their
Gaussian representatives to align both at $\pi$, and write
\[
Z'_j=\pi^{2e}X,\qquad Z'_k=\pi^{2e}Y,
\qquad N(X)=N(Y)=M^2,\qquad M=c/p^e.
\]
The Gaussian integers $X,Y$ are units at both primes above $p$ and
are supported only above $\mathcal P\setminus\{p\}$. Conjugation
changes the signs of the corresponding imaginary parts. Thus, after
an overall sign change, the selected relation becomes
\[
\operatorname{Im}\bigl(\pi^{4e}R\bigr)=\pm\kappa D_i,
\qquad R=X^2+\eta Y^2,\qquad
\eta\in\{1,-1\},\quad\kappa\in\{1,2\}.
\]
In particular $R\ne0$, because $D_i>0$. Subtracting conjugates gives
\[
\pi^{4e}R-\bar\pi^{4e}\bar R=\pm2\mathrm i\kappa D_i.
\]
At $\bar\pi$, the second term has valuation at least $4e$ and the
right side has valuation at least $2a$. Since $\pi$ is a
$\bar\pi$-unit and $a\le e$,
\[
v_{\bar\pi}(X^2+\eta Y^2)\ge2a.
\]
Choose $\zeta\in\mu_4$ with $\zeta^2=-\eta$ and factor
$R=(X-\zeta Y)(X+\zeta Y)$. The difference of these factors is
the $\bar\pi$-unit $2\zeta Y$. Exactly one factor has positive
valuation. Replacing $\zeta$ by $-\zeta$ if necessary therefore gives
\[
\boxed{2a\le
v_{\bar\pi}\!\left(\frac{X}{\zeta Y}-1\right),\qquad
\frac{X}{\zeta Y}-1\ne0.}
\tag{U-DEFICIT-BINARY-APPROXIMATION}
\]
There is no halving of the exponent: the other factor has valuation
zero. This extraction uses a relation between two rows of the same
magic square.

**Fixed logarithmic bases.** Choose $\pi_q\bar\pi_q=q$ once for
each $q\in\mathcal P$. Unique factorization and $N(X)=N(Y)$ give
\[
\frac{X}{\zeta Y}
=\mathrm i^t\prod_{q\in\mathcal P\setminus\{p\}}
\left(\frac{\pi_q}{\bar\pi_q}\right)^{b_q},
\qquad 0\le t\le3,\qquad
|b_q|\le2v_q(c)\le2E.
\tag{U-DEFICIT-FIXED-BASES}
\]
Indeed $b_q=v_{\pi_q}(X)-v_{\pi_q}(Y)$, whose two terms lie
between zero and $2v_q(c)$; equality of norms makes the conjugate
valuation difference $-b_q$. The residual unit is a fourth root of
unity. All bases in (U-DEFICIT-FIXED-BASES) are fixed algebraic
numbers once $\mathcal P$ is fixed, and all are units at $\bar\pi$.

**External theorem and correspondence.** Yu [33], Section 0.1 and
Theorem $1'$ without the auxiliary Kummer hypothesis, bounds the
valuation of a nonzero product of fixed algebraic bases minus one by
an effectively computable constant times the logarithm of the largest
exponent, with a fixed lower cutoff. Apply it over $\mathbb Q(\mathrm i)$
to the bases $\mathrm i$ and $\pi_q/\bar\pi_q$ for $q\ne p$.
The exponent bound is $B_0$; the split prime has ramification and
residue degrees one. Enlarging the fixed constant absorbs any additive
fixed terms and gives
\[
v_{\bar\pi}\!\left(\frac{X}{\zeta Y}-1\right)
<C_p(\mathcal P)\log B_0.
\]
This proves (U-LOCAL-DEFICIT-LOG). If $|\mathcal P|=1$, the quotient
in (U-DEFICIT-FIXED-BASES) is a fourth root of unity. A nontrivial
fourth root of unity minus one has valuation zero at every prime
above $p\ge5$, contradicting the displayed approximation whenever
$a>0$. Thus $P=1$ in that case, without using a logarithm theorem
requiring two bases.

For $|\mathcal P|\ge2$, choose an integer $K\ge1$ strictly larger
than
\[
\frac12\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}C_p(\mathcal P)\log p.
\]
An integer upper bound is computable directly from the fixed constants;
the same choice covers center supports properly contained in
$\mathcal P$. Summing (U-LOCAL-DEFICIT-LOG) over the deficient
primes gives $\log P<K\log B_0$. For a singleton take $K=1$.
Finally
\[
E\le\frac{\log c}{\log5},\qquad
B_0\le3E\le\frac{3\log c}{\log5}<2\log c,
\]
which proves (U-FIXED-SUPPORT-DEFICIT). $\square$

**Corollary (effective fixed-support cutoff at orientation rank at most
two).** Let $\rho$ be the rational rank of the sign matrix on the
unbalanced center part, with the rank-zero convention of Theorem 7.2.
For the integer $K=K(\mathcal P)$ above,
\[
\boxed{\rho\le2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
c<\exp\bigl((7K+2)^2\bigr)<3^{(7K+2)^2}.}
\tag{U-FIXED-SUPPORT-RANK2-CUTOFF}
\]

**Proof.** By (U-ORIENT-RANK2-HEIGHT), $c<384P^7$; the balanced
center factor in that theorem divides $P$. Put $h=\log c$.
Since $\log384<6$, $\log2<1$, and $\log h\le\sqrt h$,
(U-FIXED-SUPPORT-DEFICIT) implies
\[
h<6+7K+7K\sqrt h.
\]
For $z=\sqrt h\ge7K+2$, the function
$z^2-7Kz-(6+7K)$ is increasing and its value at $7K+2$ is
$7K-2>0$. This contradicts the preceding strict inequality and proves
the cutoff. $\square$

**Corollary (a fixed positive deficit proportion at any rank).** For
every fixed rational $\varepsilon>0$,
\[
\boxed{P\ge c^\varepsilon\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
c<\exp\bigl((K/\varepsilon+1)^2\bigr).}
\tag{U-FIXED-SUPPORT-PROPORTION-CUTOFF}
\]
Indeed $\varepsilon h<K\log(2h)<K(1+\sqrt h)$. Writing
$A=K/\varepsilon$, the inequality $z^2<A(1+z)$ cannot hold for
$z\ge A+1$, since at $A+1$ the left-minus-right side is one and
is increasing thereafter. An integer cutoff is
$3^{\lceil(K/\varepsilon+1)^2\rceil}$.

The first corollary makes the specified fixed-support, rank-at-most-two
branch effectively enumerable by Section 1.7; it does not assert that
the enumeration has been carried out. The second corollary applies
without an orientation-rank restriction but retains its lower bound
on $P$. The constants depend on the identities of the primes in
$\mathcal P$. No bound on that set, no corresponding polynomial
lower bound on $P$ in the unrestricted higher-rank branches, and no
absolute cutoff for $c$ is obtained.

### 12.14. Effective fixed-support height at orientation rank at most three

Fix the prime set $\mathcal P$ of Section 12.13, and put
\[
s=|\mathcal P|,\quad Q=\max\mathcal P,\quad
E=\max_{p\mid c}v_p(c),\quad K=K(\mathcal P).
\]
Define the explicit integer constants
\[
C_0=84(s+1)[24(s+2)]^{2(s+2)}Q^{s+4}(Q+9),
\qquad C=C_0+8.
\]

**Theorem.** Every primitive admissible square whose unbalanced
orientation matrix has rational rank at most three satisfies
\[
\boxed{E<C(1+\log P)\log(8E).}
\tag{U-RANK3-MOVING-ROOT}
\]
Consequently
\[
\boxed{E<256C^2(K+1)^2,\qquad
c<\left(\prod_{p\in\mathcal P}p\right)^{256C^2(K+1)^2}.}
\tag{U-FIXED-SUPPORT-RANK3-CUTOFF}
\]
In particular every specified set of at most three center primes has
an effective exhaustive enumeration cutoff. The identities of those
primes remain part of the bound; no enumeration to this cutoff is
asserted.

**Correction heights.** Use the actual phases
$\rho_i=Z_i^2/c^2=\gamma_iT_i$ from Theorem 7.2. Their corrections
are norm-one Gaussian squares. Writing $q_i^2=\gamma_i$, their
Cartesian denominators divide $E_i$, where
\[
E_i=A_iB/B_i^2\mid P,\qquad \prod_iE_i=PB^2.
\]
Thus $\sum_i h(q_i)\le\log(PB^2)\le3\log P$ and
$\sum_i h(\gamma_i)\le6\log P$. At an unbalanced $p^e\Vert c$,
put $a=v_p(P)$ and normalize $v_\pi(\pi)=1$. At most one $q_i$
has nonzero valuation there, of absolute value $a$. At a balanced
prime $e=a$, already bounded by $\log P$.

**Four distinct projective rows.** The rank-three classification of
Theorem 7.2 gives three disjoint orientation blocks. Its allowed phase
replacements give
\[
\rho_1=\gamma_1UVW,\quad\rho_2=\gamma_2UV/W,\quad
\rho_3=\gamma_3UW/V,\quad\rho_4=\gamma_4U/(VW).
\]
Set
\[
u=q_2q_3U,\quad v=(q_1/q_3)V,\quad w=(q_1/q_2)W,
\quad k=\gamma_1\gamma_4/(\gamma_2\gamma_3),
\quad X=u^2,\ Y=v^2,\ Z=w^2.
\]
The two magic identities become exactly
\[
f=X(YZ+Y-Z)-1-Z+Y=0,\qquad
g=X(YZ-Y-k)-1+Z+YZ/k=0.
\tag{U-RANK3-EXACT-EQUATIONS}
\]
All four variables have complex absolute value one, and
$h(k)\le6\log P$. Put $\delta=2a$. At an unbalanced prime one
block coordinate $T\in\{X,Y,Z\}$ has valuation $\pm4e$ with
error of absolute value at most $\delta$; the other two coordinates
and $k$ have valuations of absolute value at most $\delta$.

Write $f=TA+B$ and $g=TC+D$, with the four coefficients linear
in one other variable. At a pole of $T$, eliminate that variable
between $A,C$; at a zero, between $B,D$. The resulting polynomials,
up to a factor in $\{1,-1,k,-k\}$, are as follows.

| Dominant coordinate | Retained variable $t$ | $F(t;k)$ |
|---|---|---|
| $X$ pole | $Y$ | $2t^2+(k-1)t-k$ |
| $X$ zero | $Y$ | $t^2+(k-1)t-2k$ |
| $Y$ pole | $X$ | $2kt^2+(k+1)t+1$ |
| $Y$ zero | $X$ | $kt^2+(k+1)t+2$ |
| $Z$ pole | $X$ | $kt^2+(2k+1)t+1$ |
| $Z$ zero | $X$ | $kt^2+(k+2)t+1$ |

None vanishes when $|t|=|k|=1$: isolating $k$ and taking absolute
values would give $\operatorname{Re}t=3/2$ in the first two rows
or $-3/2$ in the other four. This also rules out every exact-zero
exception in the local approximation.

Every monomial in $A,B,C,D$ has valuation at least $-3\delta$,
and every coefficient of the eliminated variable has valuation at
least $-2\delta$. The linear resultant has its usual two-term
Bezout identity. The two exact equations therefore give
\[
v_\pi(F(t;k))\ge |v_\pi(T)|-6\delta\ge4e-7\delta.
\]
The leading and constant coefficients of $F$ have valuations in
$[-\delta,\delta]$, and its middle coefficient has valuation at
least $-\delta$. In its splitting field over $\mathbb Q(\mathrm i)$,
each root has valuation in $[-2\delta,4\delta]$: the lower bound
follows by excluding a uniquely smallest quadratic term, and the
upper bound follows from the root product. Factoring $F$ now gives
one nonzero root $\alpha$ with
\[
\nu(t/\alpha-1)\ge2e-8\delta=2e-16a,
\qquad t/\alpha-1\ne0.
\tag{U-RANK3-LOCAL-ROOT}
\]
The extended valuation $\nu$ restricts to $v_\pi$. The splitting
field has degree at most four over $\mathbb Q$. The elementary
root-height inequality gives
\[
h(\alpha)\le h(k)+\log6\le6\log P+2,
\]
because the coefficient-vector height is at most $h(k)+\log3$.

Choose fixed Gaussian ratios $\lambda_q=\pi_q/\bar\pi_q$.
Unique factorization gives
\[
t=\mathrm i^j\prod_{q\in\mathcal P}\lambda_q^{b_q},
\qquad 0\le j\le3,\quad |b_q|\le8E,\quad |b_p|\le2a.
\]
If $e\le8a$, the desired exponent estimate is elementary.
Otherwise (U-RANK3-LOCAL-ROOT) is positive, so
$\nu(\alpha)=\nu(t)=b_p$. Put
$\alpha'=\alpha/\lambda_p^{b_p}$. Then
\[
\frac t\alpha=
\mathrm i^j\prod_{q\ne p}\lambda_q^{b_q}(\alpha')^{-1},
\qquad h(\alpha')\le7\log P+2.
\tag{U-RANK3-UNIT-BASES}
\]
Every displayed base is a unit at the selected prime. The height
bound uses $h(\lambda_p)=\frac12\log p$ and $a\log p\le\log P$.

**External estimate and its moving-base dependence.** Use Yu's
valuation estimate in the explicit form [34, Theorem 5]. For degree
$d$, $n$ nonzero local-unit bases $\alpha_j$, exponent bound
$B_*\ge3$, and a nonzero product-minus-one, its upper bound is
\[
12\left(\frac{6(n+1)d}{\sqrt{\log p}}\right)^{2(n+1)}
(p^d-1)\log(e^5nd)
\prod_{j=1}^n\max\{h(\alpha_j),\log p\}\log B_*.
\]
Here $d\le4$, $n=s+1$, and $B_*=8E$. Only the base $\alpha'$
varies. There is no field-discriminant or regulator factor. The
prime-ideal valuation in that bound is at least our normalized $\nu$.
Each fixed-base factor is at most $Q$, the moving one is less than
$(Q+9)(1+\log P)$, and $\log(4e^5(s+1))<7(s+1)$.
Thus (U-RANK3-LOCAL-ROOT) gives
\[
2e-16a<C_0(1+\log P)\log(8E).
\]
The cases $e\le8a$ and balanced primes satisfy the resulting
bound directly. Taking a prime with exponent $E$ proves
(U-RANK3-MOVING-ROOT) in this branch.

**Repeated projective rows.** Align the repeated extremized phases
as $\rho_i=\gamma_iT$, $\rho_j=\gamma_jT$. Choose a three-offset
identity containing them. For pairs other than $\{3,4\}$ one of
$D_1+D_2-D_3=0$ and $D_1-D_2-D_4=0$ suffices; for $\{3,4\}$
use $D_3+D_4-2D_1=0$. The repeated coefficients
$\epsilon_i,\epsilon_j$ have absolute value one, and the remaining
coefficient $\eta$ has absolute value one or two. With remaining
phase $\gamma_kV$, put
\[
A=\epsilon_i\gamma_i+\epsilon_j\gamma_j,\quad C=\eta\gamma_k.
\]
The exact relation is
\[
AT+CV=\bar A/T+\bar C/V.
\]
Here $A\ne0$ and $AT+CV\ne0$. The first failure would give equal
or opposite offsets. The second would force $|A|=|C|$. If
$|\eta|=1$, two rational unit vectors would have a signed sum of
length one, so their rational determinant would have square $3/4$,
impossible. If $|\eta|=2$, equality in the triangle inequality again
forces equal or opposite offsets.

At each unbalanced prime invert/conjugate the two extremized phases
as needed so that $v_\pi(T)=v_\pi(V)=-2e$. This preserves the
argument and the correction-height bounds. Dividing the exact
relation by $CV$ gives the nonzero approximation
\[
v_\pi\!\left(-\frac AC\frac TV-1\right)\ge4e-4a.
\]
Indeed the right-hand numerator has valuation at least $2e-2a$
and $CV$ has valuation at most $-2e+2a$. The ratio $T/V$ has
zero exponent at $p$, fixed-base exponents at most $4E$ elsewhere,
and $h(A/C)\le6\log P+\log4$. If $e>a$, positivity forces
$A/C$ to be a local unit. The same Yu estimate over $\mathbb Q(\mathrm i)$,
with this one moving base, proves the stronger binary bound needed
for (U-RANK3-MOVING-ROOT). If $e=a$, use $e\le\log P$.
The rank-zero all-balanced case is also covered. This exhausts the
rank-at-most-three classification.

Finally Section 12.13 gives $\log P<K\log(8E)$. Therefore
\[
E<C(K+1)\log^2(8E).
\]
For $E\ge1$, $\log(8E)<4E^{1/4}$, so
$E<256C^2(K+1)^2$. The center is bounded by the product of the
fixed primes to the exponent $E$, proving the theorem. $\square$

This supplies effective height, rather than only finiteness or a bound
on the number of solutions, on the stated fixed-support locus. It
does not bound the identities or number of center primes and does not
give an unrestricted rank-four cutoff.


### 12.15. Effective escape from every proper sign kernel

The moving-base argument also controls rank-four centers close to any
of the twenty sign kernels used in the phase-index theorems. Retain
$\mathcal P,E,K,C$ from Section 12.14 and set $L_E=\log(8E)$.
Let $\mathcal M$ consist of the twelve characters $e_i\pm e_j$,
$i<j$, and the eight characters in $\{\pm1\}^4/\{\pm1\}$.
For $m\in\mathcal M$ define its outside contribution by
\[
R_m=\prod_{\substack{p^{e_p}\Vert c/B\\m\cdot\sigma_p\ne0}}p^{e_p},
\]
where $\sigma_p$ is the actual unbalanced orientation column.

**Theorem.** At every orientation rank and for every $m\in\mathcal M$,
\[
\boxed{E<C(1+\log P+\log R_m)L_E,\qquad
\log R_m>\frac{E}{CL_E}-KL_E-1.}
\tag{U-KERNEL-EFFECTIVE-ESCAPE}
\]
In particular, if $E\ge1024C^2(K+1)^2$, then simultaneously
\[
\boxed{\log R_m>\frac{E}{2CL_E}\quad(m\in\mathcal M).}
\tag{U-ALL-KERNEL-MASS}
\]
For any fixed real $A\ge0$, even one condition $R_m\le(8E)^A$
gives the effective cutoff
\[
\boxed{E<256C^2(K+A+1)^2.}
\tag{U-KERNEL-POLYNOMIAL-CUTOFF}
\]

**Proof.** Write each extremized phase as $T_i=T_i^{\rm ret}T_i^{\rm rem}$,
retaining the primes in the kernel and absorbing the other factors
into $\gamma_i'=\gamma_iT_i^{\rm rem}$. These remain norm-one
Gaussian squares, and
\[
\sum_i h(\gamma_i')\le6\log P+4\log R_m.
\]
At every retained prime the new factors are units, so the local
valuation estimates of Section 12.14 are unchanged.

For a four-supported character, its full sign kernel has exactly
three projective column classes. The same three-block equations
apply, allowing a missing block to equal one. Their moving quadratic
root, after local-unit normalization, now has height at most
$7\log P+4\log R_m+2$. For a two-supported character, the two
retained rows agree up to inversion; the repeated-row argument has
one moving coefficient of height at most
$6\log P+4\log R_m+\log4$. The same constant $C$ therefore
applies with $1+\log P$ replaced by $1+\log P+\log R_m$.
The exponent bound remains $8E$: at a removed prime each correction
square root has valuation at most $2e_p$ in absolute value, and the
new squared block coordinates use products or quotients of two of
these roots.

If a prime attaining $E$ was removed, then
$E\log5\le\log R_m$; if it was balanced, then
$E\log5\le\log P$. Otherwise the retained-prime logarithm
estimate applies. This proves the first inequality. The second
follows from $\log P<KL_E$.

Since $L_E^2<16\sqrt E$, the stated threshold gives
$C(KL_E^2+L_E)<E/2$, proving (U-ALL-KERNEL-MASS).
If $\log R_m\le A L_E$, the first inequality instead yields
$E<C(K+A+1)L_E^2$, proving the cutoff as in Section 12.14.
$\square$

**Actual phase-index growth.** Put
$k_m=\prod_i\rho_i^{m_i}=\lambda_m^2$ and let $\tau_m$ be its
half-phase Cayley index in the manuscript's original normalization.
The exact denominator theorem gives
\[
h(k_m)=\log q_m
=\sum_{p\mid c}|m\cdot j_p|\log p.
\]
Outside the kernel $|m\cdot\sigma_p|\ge2$, and the single
possible deficit changes $m\cdot(e_p\sigma_p)$ by at most
$a_p=v_p(P)$. Therefore
\[
h(k_m)\ge2\log R_m-\log P.
\]
On the same threshold as (U-ALL-KERNEL-MASS) this implies
\[
\boxed{h(k_m)>\frac{E}{2CL_E},\qquad
\log H(\tau_m)>\frac{E}{4CL_E}-\frac12\log2
\quad(m\in\mathcal M).}
\tag{U-ALL-PHASE-INDEX-GROWTH}
\]
The last inequality uses $H(\tau_m)^2\ge q_m/2$, retaining the
distinction between the phase and its square.

Thus every unbounded fixed-support sequence must escape all twenty
kernels and all twenty bounded-index loci at these effective rates.
Rank four with substantial contributions outside every kernel is
consistent with these inequalities. They do not give an unrestricted
upper bound for the center.


### 12.16. Uniform envelopes as the center primes vary

The dependence on the identities of the center primes can be reduced
to their number and largest member. Let
\[
s=\omega(c),\quad Q=\max_{p\mid c}p,\quad L=\log Q,
\quad E=\max_{p\mid c}v_p(c),\quad B_0=\max(2E,3).
\]
Actual admissible centers have $s\ge3$; the estimates below hold
already for $s\ge2$.

**Theorem.** There are explicit constants $\kappa_s,\chi_s>1$
depending only on $s$, specified below, such that
\[
\boxed{\log P<\kappa_sQ\log(4B_0)}
\tag{U-VARYING-PRIME-DEFICIT}
\]
at every orientation rank, and
\[
\boxed{\rho\le3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
E<\chi_s\frac QL(1+\log P)\log(128E).}
\tag{U-VARYING-PRIME-RANK3}
\]
Put $A_s(Q)=\chi_s(Q/L)(1+\kappa_sQ)$. Then
\[
\boxed{\rho\le3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
E<4A_s(Q)\log^2(2048A_s(Q)),}
\tag{U-VARYING-PRIME-EXPONENT}
\]
\[
\boxed{\rho\le3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\log c<4s\chi_sQ(1+\kappa_sQ)\log^2(2048A_s(Q)).}
\tag{U-VARYING-PRIME-CENTER}
\]
In particular $E=O_s(Q^2\log Q)$ and
$\log c=O_s(Q^2\log^2Q)$, uniformly over the prime identities.
At any rank, for each fixed $0<\varepsilon\le1$,
\[
\boxed{P\ge c^\varepsilon\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\log c<\frac{2\kappa_sQ}{\varepsilon}
\log\frac{16\kappa_sQ}{\varepsilon}.}
\tag{U-VARYING-POSITIVE-DEFICIT}
\]
These are largest-prime-dependent bounds, not absolute height bounds.

**Explicit constants.** With $\ell=\log5$, define
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_s&=112690(45/2)^s(s+1)^{2s+4},\\
\lambda_s&=1+\log(4096(s+1)^2)/\ell,\\
M_s&=\max\{1,5(s/(\mathrm e\ell))^s\},\\
\kappa_s&=D_s s\lambda_sM_s,
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Xi_s&=1803040\,45^{s+1}(s+2)^{2s+6},\\
\zeta&=7/\ell+1/2,\\
\lambda'_s&=1+\log(16384(s+2)^2)/\ell,\\
M'_s&=\max\{1,5((s+2)/(\mathrm e\ell))^{s+2}\},\\
\chi_s&=7\ell/5+\tfrac12\Xi_s\zeta\lambda'_sM'_s.
\end{aligned}
\tag{U-VARYING-PRIME-CONSTANTS}
\]
Ceilings may replace these real constants when integer bounds are
desired. The symbol $\mathrm e$ denotes the exponential constant.

**External theorem and exact correspondence.** Use Yu [33],
Corollary 1, printed p. 19, with definitions (0.7)–(0.14), rather
than the coarser degree-dependent form in Section 12.14. For $n$
local-unit bases over a degree-$D$ field containing $\mathrm i$,
a prime above $p\equiv1\pmod4$ of residue degree $f$, and a
nonzero product-minus-one $\Theta$, its bound is
\[
\operatorname{ord}_{\mathfrak p}\Theta<
56345(45/2)^n(n+1)^{2n+4}
\frac{p^fD^{n+2}\prod_jV_j}{(f\log p)^{n+2}}
\log(D^2B_*)
\max\!\left\{\log(2^{11}(n+1)^2D^2V),\frac{f\log p}{n}\right\}.
\]
The ordered parameters obey
$V_j\ge\max\{h(\alpha_j),|\log\alpha_j|/(2\pi D),f\log p/D\}$.
If the last exponent has minimum $p$-adic valuation, one may use
$V=V_{n-1}$. Below the moving base is last with exponent $-1$;
thus this outer logarithm has no moving-height dependence.

**Deficit envelope.** Apply this estimate to the nonzero binary
approximation of Section 12.13 with $D=2,f=1,n=s,B_*=B_0$,
using $V_i=\frac12\log p$ for the root of unity and
$V_q=\frac12\max(\log p,\log q)$ for $q\ne p$. It gives
\[
2v_p(P)<2D_s
\frac{p\prod_{q\ne p}\max(\log q,\log p)}{(\log p)^{s+1}}
\max\!\left\{\log(4096(s+1)^2L),\frac{\log p}s\right\}
\log(4B_0).
\]
The last maximum is at most $\lambda_sL$. The function
$x/(\log x)^s$ has no interior maximum on $[5,Q]$. Summing after
multiplication by $\frac12\log p$ therefore yields
\[
\log P<D_ss\lambda_s
\max\{5(L/\ell)^s,Q\}\log(4B_0).
\]
Finally $L^s e^{-L}\le(s/\mathrm e)^s$ proves
(U-VARYING-PRIME-DEFICIT).

**The moving quadratic splits locally unless the exponent is already
small.** The six boundary discriminants of Section 12.14 are
\[
k^2+6k+1,\quad k^2+6k+1,\quad
k^2-6k+1,\quad k^2-6k+1,\quad4k^2+1,\quad k^2+4.
\]
They never vanish on $|k|=1$ and satisfy
$h(\Delta)\le12\log P+\log8$. At $p^e\Vert c$, with
$a=v_p(P)$, this gives
\[
v_\pi(\Delta)\le(24\log P+2\log8)/\log p.
\]
Write $F(t;k)=A_Ft^2+B_Ft+C_F$. Its exact approximation obeys
\[
v_\pi(4A_FF(t;k))\ge4e-16a,
\quad(2A_Ft+B_F)^2-\Delta=4A_FF(t;k).
\]
If $4e-16a>v_\pi(\Delta)$, then
$\Delta/(2A_Ft+B_F)^2\in1+p\mathbb Z_p$, so Hensel's lemma
shows that $F$ splits in $\mathbb Q_p$. The selected completion
of its global splitting field is exactly $\mathbb Q_p$, with
ramification and residue degrees both one. If the inequality fails,
\[
e\le4a+(6\log P+\tfrac12\log8)/\log p
<7(1+\log P),
\]
which is already sufficient. The case $e\le8a$ is likewise
elementary. This dichotomy removes a higher power of $p$ from the
local logarithm bound without assuming the moving root is globally
Gaussian rational.

**Uniform moving-base estimate.** On the split branch use the
normalized bases of (U-RANK3-UNIT-BASES). In Yu's estimate take
$D\le4,f=1,n=s+1,B_*=8E$, the preceding fixed $V_j$, and
\[
V_{s+1}=7(1+\log P)+L/2.
\]
This dominates the fixed parameters and the moving-base height and
principal logarithm. The moving exponent is $-1$, so the extra
parameter $V$ is at most $L/2$. After inserting the degree and
height factors, the resulting valuation bound is at most
\[
\Xi_s\frac{p\prod_{q\ne p}\max(\log p,\log q)}{(\log p)^{s+2}}
(7+L/2)(1+\log P)
\max\!\left\{\log(16384(s+2)^2L),\frac L{s+1}\right\}
\log(128E).
\]
Bound the last maximum by $\lambda'_sL$ and $7+L/2$ by
$\zeta L$. Maximizing $p/(\log p)^{s+2}$ at the endpoints and
using $L^{s+2}e^{-L}\le((s+2)/\mathrm e)^{s+2}$ gives the
coefficient $\frac12\Xi_s\zeta\lambda'_sM'_sQ/L$ after division
by two. The elementary terms are absorbed by
$7\le7\ell Q/(5L)$. This proves (U-VARYING-PRIME-RANK3).
For repeated rows the moving base already lies in $\mathbb Q(\mathrm i)$
and its completion has $f=1$; its smaller height and stronger binary
approximation satisfy the same bound. Balanced primes are covered
by $e=a$.

Insert the deficit envelope and use $\log(4B_0)\le\log(128E)$
to obtain $E<A_s(Q)\log^2(128E)$. The elementary inversion
\[
x<a\log^2(bx),\quad x,a,b\ge1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x<4a\log^2(16ab)
\]
follows by applying $y<d\log(hy)\Rightarrow y<2d\log(2dh)$
to $y=\sqrt x$. This proves the exponent bound; then
$\log c\le sE\log Q$ gives the center bound. Finally
$B_0<2\log c$ and the first inversion prove
(U-VARYING-POSITIVE-DEFICIT). $\square$

**Every orientation rank.** For any of the twenty characters in
Section 12.15, absorption of the actual outside contribution $R_m$
replaces $\log P$ in the preceding discriminant and moving-height
budgets by $\log P+\log R_m$. It leaves retained-prime valuations
unchanged. A removed maximal-exponent prime is already bounded by
$E\log5\le\log R_m$. Therefore
\[
\boxed{E<\chi_s\frac QL(1+\log P+\log R_m)\log(128E)}
\tag{U-VARYING-KERNEL-ENVELOPE}
\]
holds at every rank, for every one of those characters. In particular
a condition $R_m\le(128E)^A$ on even one character gives the same
effective exponent cutoff with
$A_s(Q)$ replaced by $\chi_s(Q/L)(1+\kappa_sQ+A)$.

The previous all-unit orbit restriction and repeated-row exclusion
already show that $P=1$ forces orientation rank four. There is no
remaining rank-three zero-deficit family to search. The unresolved
case permits both unrestricted largest prime and substantial outside
contributions at rank four. The displayed envelopes preserve those
dependencies and do not settle that case.


**An absolute height-versus-radical corollary.** Let
$R=\operatorname{rad}(c)$, with no restriction on $s$. The explicit
constants above satisfy
\[
\kappa_s<R^{11},\qquad\chi_s<R^{14}.
\]
Consequently
\[
\boxed{\rho\le3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\log c<R^{30},\qquad c<\exp(\operatorname{rad}(c)^{30}).}
\tag{U-RADICAL-CENTER-BOUND}
\]
At every orientation rank,
\[
\boxed{P\ge c^\varepsilon\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\log c<\frac{2R^{12}}\varepsilon
\log\frac{16R^{12}}\varepsilon\quad(0<\varepsilon\le1).}
\tag{U-RADICAL-POSITIVE-DEFICIT}
\]

Here are explicit comparisons for the deliberately coarse exponent 30.
List the $s\ge3$ split primes increasingly; then $p_j\ge4j+1$.
For $s\ge5$, the factorial bound gives
$R>4^ss!\ge(4s/\mathrm e)^s\ge(s+2)^s$. The cases $s=3,4$
follow from the products $5\cdot9\cdot13$ and
$5\cdot9\cdot13\cdot17$. Thus $\log R\ge s\log(s+2)$.
The definitions yield $\lambda_s,\lambda'_s\le(s+2)^2$,
$\log M_s\le\log5+s\log s$, and
$\log M'_s\le\log5+(s+2)\log(s+2)$. Using
$\log5>8/5$ gives
\[
\frac{\log\kappa_s}{s\log(s+2)}
<\frac8{\log5}+\frac{10}3+\frac13+\frac23+\frac13+1<11,
\]
\[
\frac{\log\chi_s}{s\log(s+2)}
<\frac7{\log5}+\frac4{\log5}+4+\frac23+2<14.
\]
For the second comparison the second summand of $\chi_s$ dominates
its first. Since $Q\le R$, $L>1$, and $s\le\log R$,
$A_s(Q)<2R^{27}$. The center envelope therefore gives
\[
\log c<8sR^{27}\log^2(4096R^{27})
<8192R^{27}(\log R)^3<R^{30}.
\]
The final comparison holds for $R\ge125$: the ratio
$8192(\log R)^3/R^3$ decreases there and is already less than
one at 125. This proves the first corollary; monotonic substitution
of $\kappa_sQ<R^{12}$ proves the second.

There is also an all-rank necessary alternative. Put $h=\log c$.
If $h\ge R^{30}$, then $\rho=4$ and every one of the twenty
characters satisfies
\[
\boxed{\log R_m,\ \log q_m>
\frac{h}{2R^{15}\log R\log(128h)},\qquad
\log H(\tau_m)>
\frac{h}{4R^{15}\log R\log(128h)}-\tfrac12\log2.}
\tag{U-RADICAL-ALL-INDEX-ESCAPE}
\]
To see this, set $C'=\chi_sQ/L<R^{15}$,
$K'=\kappa_sQ<R^{12}$, and $T=\log(128E)$. We have
$E\ge h/\log R$ and $T<\log(128h)$. At $h\ge R^{30}$,
the elementary comparison
$4R^{27}\log R\log^2(128R^{30})<R^{30}$ and monotonicity give
$E>2C'(K'+1)T^2$. Apply the kernel envelope and
$\log q_m\ge2\log R_m-\log P$ exactly as in Section 12.15.
All inequalities retain their lower-growth direction.

**One bounded phase index at every orientation rank.** Retain
$C'=\chi_sQ/\log Q$, $K'=\kappa_sQ$ and $T=\log(128E)$.
Suppose $H(\tau_m)\le H_0$, with $H_0\ge1$, for even one of the
twenty actual characters. Put
\[
A_H=C'\bigl(1+\tfrac32K'+\log H_0+\tfrac12\log2\bigr).
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{E<4A_H\log^2(2048A_H),\qquad
\log c<4A_H\log R\,\log^2(2048A_H).}
\tag{U-ONE-INDEX-RADICAL-BOUND}
\]
Indeed the exact inequalities
$2\log R_m\le\log q_m+\log P$ and $q_m\le2H_0^2$
give
\[
E<C'\bigl(1+\tfrac32\log P+\tfrac12\log q_m\bigr)T
<A_HT^2.
\]
Apply the same elementary inversion used above. Replacing $A_H$ by
\[
\widehat A_H(R)=R^{15}
\bigl(1+\tfrac32R^{12}+\log H_0+\tfrac12\log2\bigr)
\]
makes the bound depend only on $R,H_0$. Thus bounded radical and one
bounded actual phase index suffice for effective enumeration, without
an orientation-rank restriction.

A simpler threshold consequence is
\[
\boxed{\min_m\log H(\tau_m)\le R^{13}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\log c<R^{30}.}
\tag{U-SMALL-INDEX-RADICAL-BOUND}
\]
For otherwise (U-RADICAL-ALL-INDEX-ESCAPE) gives every index the lower
bound $R^{15}/(128(\log R)^2)-\tfrac12\log2>R^{13}$.
The final comparison holds already at $R=125$ and strengthens as
$R$ grows. The same implication holds if one $\log q_m$ or one
$\log R_m$ is at most $R^{13}$.

There is also an absolute cutoff on a specified stratum. Fix
$0<\varepsilon\le1/2$. If, with $h=\log c$,
\[
R\le h^{1/30},\qquad
\min_m\log H(\tau_m)\le h^{1/2-\varepsilon},
\]
then
\[
\boxed{h<\left[\frac4\varepsilon
                  \log\frac4\varepsilon\right]^{2/\varepsilon}.}
\tag{U-RADICAL-PHASE-STRATUM}
\]
To prove it, $h\ge125^{30}$ and $\log(128h)<2\log h$.
The phase lower bound is therefore
$15\sqrt h/(4(\log h)^2)-\tfrac12\log2$.
Comparison with $h^{1/2-\varepsilon}$ implies
$h^\varepsilon<(\log h)^2$. Put $y=h^{\varepsilon/2}$ and
invert $y<(2/\varepsilon)\log y$ to obtain the displayed bound.
Neither hypothesis is known to hold throughout the remaining rank-four
locus.

**Four substantial prime-power contributions.** Suppose all twenty
$\log R_m$ exceed a positive number $D_*$. Any three projective sign
columns lie in one of their kernels: the twelve four-column kernels
contain 48 distinct triples, the eight three-column kernels contain
the remaining eight, and no two kernels share a triple. The last
assertion follows because three distinct vertices of the three-cube
are affinely independent. For any three center primes $J$, choose a
kernel containing their unbalanced columns. Balanced primes never
enter $R_m$, so
\[
R_m\mid c\Big/\prod_{p\in J}p^{v_p(c)},\qquad
\log\left(c\Big/\prod_{p\in J}p^{v_p(c)}\right)>D_*.
\]
In particular $s\ge4$. If the prime-power factors are ordered
$U_1\ge\cdots\ge U_s$, then
\[
\boxed{\log U_4>\frac{D_*}{s-3}.}
\tag{U-FOUR-PRIME-MASS}
\]
The same argument for the at most eight orientation blocks, with
logarithmic masses $w_1\ge\cdots\ge w_t>0$, gives
$t\ge4$ and $w_4>D_* /(t-3)\ge D_* /5$.
Above $h\ge R^{30}$ one may take
\[
D_*=\frac{h}{2R^{15}\log R\log(128h)}.
\]
These are necessary distribution bounds, not absolute height bounds.


These bounds control the center relative to its radical, or force
escape of every phase index. The radical and all those indices may
still grow; no absolute bound for $c$ follows.


### 12.17. Effective growth of the boundary quadratic twists

Fix the center-prime set $S$, and retain the constants $C(S),K(S)$
from the twenty-character height theorem. Put
\[
s=|S|,\quad M=\prod_{p\in S}p,\quad\kappa=4s+2,
\quad E_0=1024C(S)^2(K(S)+1)^2,
\]
\[
A_S=(12\kappa)^{7168\kappa}M^{768},\qquad
B_S=64^{128}A_S,\qquad H_S=4C(S)B_S.
\]

**Theorem.** Let $E=\max_{p\in S}v_p(c)$ for an actual primitive square.
For one of the twenty norm-one root phase characters $\lambda_m=(a_m+b_m i)/d_m$, in reduced Cartesian
form with positive denominator, suppose $\lambda_m^4\ne1$ and set
$\Delta_m=\operatorname{sf}(|2a_mb_m|)$. Then
\[
h(\lambda_m)\le B_S\Delta_m^{256}.
\tag{BT-HEIGHT}
\]
If $E\ge E_0$, every one of the twenty characters has fourth power
different from one, and
\[
\boxed{E<H_S\Delta_m^{256}\log(8E),\qquad
\Delta_m>\left(\frac{E}{H_S\log(8E)}\right)^{1/256}.}
\tag{BT-ESCAPE}
\]
The product of the prime factors of $\Delta_m$ outside $S\cup\{2\}$
is greater than the latter lower bound divided by $2M$.

**Proof.** Write $t=\lambda_m=(a+bi)/d$. It is a norm-one Gaussian
$S$-unit, so $a^2+b^2=d^2$ and $d$ has support in $S$. Choose
$Y^2=1-t^4$. The identity
\[
1-t^4=2ab\left((1-i)t/d\right)^2
\]
shows that $L=\mathbb Q(i,Y)=\mathbb Q(i,\sqrt{\Delta_m})$ has degree at most four and
absolute discriminant at most $64\Delta_m^2$. Let $S_L$ comprise the
infinite places and the primes above $S$. Both $t$ and $Y$ are
$S_L$-integers, since $Y$ satisfies a monic quadratic with coefficients
integral outside those places. Also $|S_L|\le\kappa$ and
$Q_{S_L}=\prod_{\mathfrak p\in S_L,\,\mathfrak p\text{ finite}}N\mathfrak p\le M^4$.

Apply Bérczes--Evertse--Győry [18], Theorem 2.1, equation (2.4), to $1-Y^2=t^4$. Its parameters are $m=4,n=2,b=1$, with
simultaneous coefficient height zero. Its explicit estimate gives
\[
h(t)\le(12|S_L|)^{7168|S_L|}
 |\operatorname{disc}L|^{128}Q_{S_L}^{192}
\le A_S|\operatorname{disc}L|^{128}
\le B_S\Delta_m^{256}.
\]
The polynomial $1-X^2$ has distinct roots, so all its hypotheses hold.
The twenty-character theorem gives
$h(\lambda_m)>E/(4C(S)\log(8E))$ when $E\ge E_0$, proving the assertion.
Finally, the factors of a squarefree integer lying in $S\cup\{2\}$
have product at most $2M$.

This construction also gives the exact point
$(t^2,itY)$ on the fixed curve $V^2=U^3-U$ over $L$. The displayed
field data, rather than an unspecified Mordell--Weil basis, account
for the varying quadratic twist. In particular
\[
|\operatorname{disc}L|>
\left(\frac{E}{4C(S)A_S\log(8E)}\right)^{1/128}.
\]

**Effective finite strata.** If even one defined $\Delta_m\le D_0$, then
\[
E<\max\{E_0,16H_S^2D_0^{512}\},
\]
using $\log(8E)<4\sqrt E$. More generally, if
$\Delta_m\le D_0(\log(8E))^b$ for an integer $b\ge0$, put $r=256b+1$.
Then
\[
E<\max\{E_0,H_S^2D_0^{512}(4r)^{2r}\}.
\]
This follows from $\log(8E)<4rE^{1/(2r)}$. Raising $M$ to either
cutoff bounds $c$. No such upper bound on any twist parameter is
asserted for unrestricted squares.

**Integer-coordinate bridge.** In this paragraph use the local notation $H_i=\operatorname{Re}(Z_i^2)$ and
$d_i=\operatorname{Im}(Z_i^2)$, so $H_i$ is a signed opposite-root product and
$H_i^2+d_i^2=c^4$. For the complementary characters $z_iz_j$ and
$z_i/z_j$, their twist classes are
\[
\Delta_+=\operatorname{sf}|d_iH_j+d_jH_i|,\qquad
\Delta_-=\operatorname{sf}|d_iH_j-d_jH_i|.
\]
Consequently, with
$F=\operatorname{sf}(|d_i^2-d_j^2|)$ and $G=\gcd(\Delta_+,\Delta_-)$,
\[
\Delta_+\Delta_-=FG^2,\qquad
G\mid2\operatorname{sf}\big(\gcd(d_i,d_j)\gcd(H_i,H_j)\big),
\qquad\gcd(G,c)=1.
\]
The product identity follows by multiplication. At an odd prime away
from $c$, the valuation of the gcd of the two inner expressions is
$v_p(\gcd(d_i,d_j))+v_p(\gcd(H_i,H_j))$. At a center prime it equals
$2(v_p(A_i)+v_p(A_j))$, an even number, because at most one pair has
positive deficit. A prime shared by the two squareclasses has odd minimum valuation; this gives the squarefree, rather than radical, gcd bound. This proves the squarefree gcd assertions. For the
corner pair, $F=\operatorname{sf}(|(x+y)(x-y)|)$; for the edge pair,
$F=\operatorname{sf}(|xy|)$. These formulas identify the new twists with the existing
step-product classes, while retaining their potentially unbounded
common external prime factor $G$.

For example, bounds $F\le F_0$ and $\operatorname{sf}(\gcd(d_i,d_j)\gcd(H_i,H_j))\le G_0$ imply $\min(\Delta_+,\Delta_-)\le2G_0\sqrt{F_0}$, and hence the preceding explicit fixed-support center cutoff. The gcds themselves may still grow through square factors.

**Residue restrictions on the external gcds.** For an odd prime
$q\nmid c$, divisibility $q\mid H_i$ already forces
$\left(\frac2q\right)=1$: one opposite root is zero modulo $q$
and the other has square $2c^2$. If $q\mid\gcd(H_1,H_2)$,
both normalized corner offsets are signs. One edge offset is zero
and the other has absolute value two. Hence also
$\left(\frac{-1}q\right)=\left(\frac3q\right)=1$, giving
\[
q\mid\gcd(H_1,H_2),\ q\nmid c
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad q\equiv1\pmod{24}.
\]
For any other pair the necessary individual condition gives
$q\equiv1,7\pmod8$. A mixed corner-edge pair in the branch with
nonzero unused corner again requires $q\equiv1\pmod{24}$, since
its offsets include absolute values one, two, and three.
Moreover
\[
\gcd\bigl(\gcd(H_1,H_2),\gcd(H_3,H_4)\bigr)=1.
\]
All $H_i$ are odd. An odd center prime can divide at most one of
these products by the primitive deficit rule. Away from the center,
dividing all four products would give
$x^2=y^2=(x+y)^2=(x-y)^2=c^4\pmod q$; subtracting forces
$4xy=0$, contradicting $q\nmid c$. These restrictions do not bound
the potentially shared offset gcd.

### 12.18. The lattice and arithmetic form of the product K3 quotient

The established B fibers are
\[
I_2^*\text{ at }-1;\quad I_4\text{ at }1,-3,\infty;\quad
I_2\text{ at }-2,7.
\]
Their root lattice is $D_6\oplus A_3^3\oplus A_1^2$, of discriminant $4\cdot4^3\cdot2^2=1024$. Let
\[
S=(8(k+1)^3,-8(k+1)^3(k+3)^2),\quad
T_0=(0,0),\quad T_1=(-A,0),\quad T_B=(-B,0).
\]

**Component table and height.**

Use the standard $D_6$ diagram with chain $1-2-3-4$ and two terminal spinor vertices 5,6 attached to 4. For each $I_n$ use the $A_{n-1}$ chain, with identity component denoted zero. The component table is:

| Section | $-1:D_6$ | $1:A_3$ | $-3:A_3$ | $\infty:A_3$ | $-2:A_1$ | $7:A_1$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| $S$ | 5 | 0 | 2 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| $T_0$ | 5 | 2 | 0 | 2 | 1 | 0 |
| $T_1$ | 1 | 0 | 2 | 2 | 1 | 1 |
| $T_B$ | 6 | 2 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 1 |

Reversing an $A_3$ chain replaces the displayed infinity label 1 by 3 and gives the same lattice computation.

Here is the additive-fiber verification, which is the delicate entry. Put $u=k+1$. Then
\[
A=32u(u+1),\quad B=u^2(u-2)^2,
\]
\[
a_2=u\alpha,\quad a_4=u^3\beta,\quad
\alpha=32+36u-4u^2+u^3,\quad \beta=32(u+1)(u-2)^2.
\]
In the first blowup chart $X=ux_1,Y=uy_1$,
\[
y_1^2=u(x_1^3+\alpha x_1^2+u\beta x_1).
\]
The simple root $x_1=-32$ gives the vector tip, met by $T_1$. At the double root zero, use $x_1=ux_2,y_1=uy_2$:
\[
y_2^2=u(ux_2^3+\alpha x_2^2+\beta x_2).
\]
The two final simple roots are $x_2=0,-4$, giving the two spinor tips. Section $T_B$ tends to $-4$; sections $T_0,S$ tend to zero. In the final chart $x_2=ux_3,y_2=uy_3$,
\[
y_3^2=u^3x_3^3+u\alpha x_3^2+\beta x_3.
\]
Here $T_0$ meets $(x_3,y_3)=(0,0)$, whereas $S$ meets $(8,-32)$ at $u=0$. Both are smooth interior points of the same final spinor component $y_3^2=128x_3$.

The bridge in the resolution graph is visible in the other second-blowup chart
\[
x_1=v,\quad u=vr,\quad y_1=vh,\qquad
h^2=vr\bigl(v+\alpha(vr)+r\beta(vr)\bigr).
\]
At $v=r=h=0$ this is an ordinary double point with tangent cone $h^2=32vr$. Its resolution inserts the third multiplicity-two component between the first and second double components. Hence the vector tip at $x_1=-32$ attaches to one end, while the two tips $x_2=0,-4$ attach to the other fork, giving the asserted $D_6$ labels.

At $k=-3$, the node is the collision of $-A,-B$. The functions $X(S)+A=8(k+1)(k+3)^2$ and $Y(S)$ both have valuation two, so $S$ meets the middle component of $I_4$. At infinity, put $z=1/k$, $X'=z^4X,Y'=z^6Y$; then
\[
X'(S)=8z(1+z)^3,\qquad Y'(S)=-8z(1+z)^3(1+3z)^2,
\]
so the component is 1 or 3. At the remaining finite bad fibers the section avoids the node. The torsion entries follow by tracking the colliding roots in exactly these local charts.

The section is affine at every finite base value and also in the minimal infinity chart, so $S\cdot O=0$. The local self-height contributions are
\[
3/2\quad(D_6\text{ spinor}),\qquad1\quad(A_3\text{ middle}),\qquad3/4\quad(A_3\text{ end}).
\]
Since the K3 elliptic surface has $\chi=2$, the height formula [36, Section 11.8] gives
\[
\boxed{\langle S,S\rangle=4-3/2-1-3/4=3/4.}
\]
As consistency checks, each torsion row has total contribution four, and the cross-contributions between $S$ and each torsion row sum to two, agreeing with $S\cdot T_i=0$.

**Geometric torsion and primitivity.**

Over $\mathbb C(k)$, torsion injects into the component group of the additive $I_2^*$ fiber. Its formal group and the additive identity-component reduction have no nonzero torsion in residue characteristic zero. The component group is $(\mathbb Z/2)^2$, and the displayed full two-torsion already realizes it. Thus the geometric torsion has order four, with no additional odd or four-power torsion.

The rank is one geometrically. The two-descent classes of $S,T_0,T_1$ remain independent over $\mathbb C(k)$: the nonconstant factors $k+1,k+2,k-7$ used in (B-NECESSARY-DESCENT) remain independent regardless of constant squareclasses. Therefore $S$ has odd index $m$ modulo torsion in the geometric rank-one Mordell–Weil group.

If $G$ is a primitive generator, the discriminant formula [36, Section 11.10, equation (22)] gives
\[
\operatorname{disc}NS=-\frac{1024\langle G,G\rangle}{4^2}
=-\frac{48}{m^2}.
\]
This is an integer. Since $m$ is odd, $m^2\mid48$ forces $m=1$. Hence $S$ is a geometric primitive generator and
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{disc}NS=-48.}
\]
In particular the generic arithmetic and geometric Mordell–Weil groups have the same rank-one generator and full two-torsion.

**Exact discriminant form.**

The finite lattice certificate builds the rank-20 lattice generated by $O,F$, the 17 root components, and $S$, using the preceding component table and the standard negative Cartan blocks. The remaining Gram entries are $O^2=S^2=-2$, $F^2=0$, $O\cdot F=F\cdot S=1$, $O\cdot S=0$, and the incidences in the table. Its determinant is $-768$.

For a torsion section meeting component $j$, its rational lattice vector is
\[
T=O+2F-\sum_v C_v^{-1}e_{j_v},
\]
where $C_v$ is the positive Cartan matrix. Adjoining $T_0,T_1$ gives the index-four overlattice. Hermite normal form computes an integral basis; the basis is obtained by Hermite normal form of the two displayed torsion vectors together with the original lattice. Smith normal form gives
\[
A_{NS}\simeq\mathbb Z/4\oplus\mathbb Z/12.
\]

The certificate enumerates all 48 discriminant-group elements in $NS^*/NS$, with their quadratic norms modulo $2\mathbb Z$ and bilinear pairings modulo $\mathbb Z$. It compares the negative discriminant form with every reduced even positive rank-two lattice of determinant 48:
\[
\operatorname{diag}(2,24),\quad\operatorname{diag}(6,8),\quad
\operatorname{diag}(4,12),\quad
\begin{pmatrix}8&4\\4&8\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Only the third matches. Since the K3 cohomology lattice is even unimodular,
\[
\boxed{T(\mathcal K)\simeq\operatorname{diag}(4,12).}
\]
The finite computation uses exact rational matrix arithmetic; its domain is all 48 discriminant classes and all four reduced candidate forms. These four exhaust the possibilities because a reduced form $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}2a&b\\b&2c\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ satisfies $|b|\le a\le c$, $4ac-b^2=48$ and hence $a\le4$. This discriminant-form step is needed: determinant 48 alone does not identify the transcendental lattice.

**Geometric Kummer identification and arithmetic limitation.**

The lattice is
\[
T(\mathcal K)=2\operatorname{diag}(2,6).
\]
The Shioda–Mitani construction [37, Theorem 6] for $\operatorname{diag}(2,6)$ gives the abelian surface
\[
A_0=E_{i\sqrt3}\times E_{i\sqrt3}.
\]
The Kummer scaling formula [37, printed p. 4] gives $T(\operatorname{Km}(A_0))=T(A_0)(2)$, and the oriented transcendental-lattice classification [37, Theorem 5] identifies the two singular K3 surfaces over $\mathbb C$. Thus
\[
\boxed{\mathcal K_{\mathbb C}\simeq\operatorname{Km}(E_{i\sqrt3}^2).}
\]
The lattice admits the determinant-minus-one isometry $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)$, so reversing its orientation does not leave an unresolved complex-isomorphism choice.

A rational elliptic model for this complex elliptic curve is
\[
E_*:\quad y^2=x^3-15x+22,
\]
with $j=54000$. Indeed it is the degree-two isogeny quotient of the $j=0$ curve $y^2=x^3+1$: shift its rational two-torsion point to zero to obtain $y^2=x^3-3x^2+3x$, take the two-isogenous curve $y^2=x^3+6x^2-3x$, then shift $x$ by $-2$. Analytically the lattice $\mathbb Z+i\sqrt3\mathbb Z$ is index two in $\mathbb Z+((1+i\sqrt3)/2)\mathbb Z$; the order-three automorphism of the latter permutes its three nonzero two-torsion points, so these quotients are isomorphic over $\mathbb C$.

**The natural rational Kummer model is a different arithmetic form.**
Let $\chi_d$ denote the quadratic Galois character of $\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)$.
The rational Galois representation on the geometric Néron--Severi space of
our product quotient is
\[
\operatorname{NS}(\mathcal K_{\overline{\mathbb Q}})\otimes\mathbb Q
\simeq 18\mathbf1\oplus\chi_3\oplus\chi_{-1}.
\tag{Q-K3-NS-GALOIS}
\]
Indeed $O,F,S$ and all singular parameters are rational. The additive
$D_6$ diagram is fixed, since the two rational torsion sections distinguish
its two spinor tips. The $A_1$ diagrams have no nontrivial permutation.
The $I_4$ tangent coefficients at $k=1,-3,\infty$ are respectively
$192,-64,1$. Thus the first two $A_3$ chains have their end components
exchanged over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt3)$ and $\mathbb Q(i)$, while the third
is split. Each exchanged chain contributes two trivial directions and
one quadratic character. These divisors already span all twenty dimensions,
proving the displayed representation and invariant rank eighteen.

By contrast the smooth Kummer surface of the rational model
\[
z^2=(u^3-15u+22)(v^3-15v+22)
\]
has Néron--Severi representation
\[
13\mathbf1\oplus6\chi_3\oplus\chi_{-3},
\tag{Q-STANDARD-KUMMER-NS}
\]
and invariant rank thirteen. To compute it, the two-torsion abscissas
of $E_*$ are $2,-1\pm2\sqrt3$. Hence its sixteen product two-torsion
points have four fixed points and six two-point orbits. Their exceptional
divisors contribute $10\mathbf1\oplus6\chi_3$. The Néron--Severi space
of $E_*^2$ contributes $3\mathbf1\oplus\chi_{-3}$: its two factor
classes and the identity correspondence are rational, while the remaining
complex-multiplication correspondence changes sign over
$\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$. The usual pullback and exceptional-divisor
splitting over $\mathbb Q$ gives the formula. Invariant divisor ranks
agree with ranks of divisor classes defined over $\mathbb Q$ after
tensoring with $\mathbb Q$, since taking a trace descends a multiple.

Consequently these two smooth minimal K3 surfaces are not isomorphic
or birational over $\mathbb Q$, despite their complex isomorphism.
This excludes identifying their rational points through that proposed
model. It does not exclude other rational Kummer forms, correspondences,
or an arithmetic use of the already explicit offset cover. No bound on
specialized elliptic ranks or on full-root heights follows from the lattice
calculation.

### 12.19. The exact Brauer group of the product K3 quotient

Let $\widetilde{\mathcal K}$ denote the smooth minimal resolution.
Its algebraic Brauer group consists only of constant classes, and
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Br}_1(\widetilde{\mathcal K})
       =\operatorname{Br}_0(\widetilde{\mathcal K}),\qquad
\left|\operatorname{Br}(\widetilde{\mathcal K})/
             \operatorname{Br}_0(\widetilde{\mathcal K})\right|\mid12.}
\tag{Q-K3-BRAUER-BOUND}
\]
The geometric Brauer Galois-invariant group itself has order dividing
twelve. The explicit descent and integral argument below sharpen this
to (Q-K3-BRAUER-EXACT): the rational quotient is trivial, while the
geometric invariant group is $(\mathbb Z/2)^2$. The result concerns the
proper product quotient; it does not compute the Brauer group of the
full-root surface or replace the separate infinite criterion on the
admissible open locus.

**Integral algebraic calculation.** On the complete Néron--Severi
lattice from Section 12.18, not just its rational character space,
the action of $G=\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb Q(\sqrt3,i)/\mathbb Q)$
is a permutation action. The Hermite-normal-form basis obtained by
adjoining $T_0,T_1$ has two disjoint end swaps, at zero-based positions
$(8,10)$ and $(11,13)$, and sixteen fixed basis vectors.
Conjugating the two original root-component swaps by the displayed
overlattice basis change gives exactly these two integral matrices;
each preserves the Gram matrix.

Write the generators as $\sigma,\tau$. A 1-cocycle is specified by
$u=c(\sigma),v=c(\tau)$ with
\[
(1+\sigma)u=0,\quad(1+\tau)v=0,\quad
(1-\tau)u+(\sigma-1)v=0.
\]
The two anti-invariant lattices are primitively generated by
$e_{10}-e_8$ and $e_{13}-e_{11}$. Each is fixed by the other
generator and is already a coboundary, respectively of $e_8,e_{11}$.
Thus $H^1(G,\operatorname{NS})=0$. Inflation--restriction gives
the same result for the absolute Galois group, since continuous
homomorphisms from its action kernel into the torsion-free discrete
lattice vanish. The Hochschild--Serre injection [38, Remark 1.3]
then proves $\operatorname{Br}_1/\operatorname{Br}_0=0$.

**Good reduction and exact counts.** The quartic gradient calculation
in Section 12.6 works over every algebraically closed field of
characteristic other than 2 and 3. If $ab\ne0$, it forces all four
coordinate squares to agree. If exactly one of $a,b$ vanishes, it
forces $s=t=0$. If $a=b=0$, the remaining coefficient matrix in
$s^2,t^2$ has determinant $-16$; the cases with a further zero use
the nonzero coefficient 3. Thus there are exactly the same ten
nodes. Their affine Hessian determinants $2^{13},2^{15}$ are units.
Blowing up the ten disjoint node sections over $\mathbb Z[1/6]$
gives a smooth proper model: the exceptional quadratic conics are
smooth, and the gradient is nonzero elsewhere.

Exact projective enumeration in four disjoint affine charts gives
the following finite counts. Resolving each rational node replaces
one point by a smooth conic with $p+1$ points, adding $p$.
