| $p$ | Quartic points | Resolved points | NS character trace | Transcendental trace $t_p$ |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 7 | 94 | 164 | 16 | 2 |
| 13 | 278 | 408 | 20 | $-22$ |

The trace formula and smooth proper base change [39] give
\[
t_p=\#\widetilde{\mathcal K}(\mathbb F_p)-1-p^2
 -p\left(18+\left(\frac3p\right)+\left(\frac{-1}p\right)\right).
\]
No identification with a rational Kummer model enters this count.

**The full geometric invariant group.** The Kummer exact sequence
[38, Section 2] gives the actual free rank-two Brauer Tate lattice
\[
\Lambda_\ell=T_\ell\operatorname{Br}(\overline{\mathcal K})
=H^2_{\mathrm{et}}(\overline{\mathcal K},\mathbb Z_\ell(1))
 /\bigl(\operatorname{NS}(\overline{\mathcal K})\otimes\mathbb Z_\ell\bigr).
\]
Its divisible torsion group is
$(\Lambda_\ell\otimes\mathbb Q_\ell)/\Lambda_\ell$.
This quotient lattice is used also at the discriminant primes 2 and 3;
an integral orthogonal splitting is not assumed.

For $p=7,13$ and $\ell\ne p$, Frobenius acts integrally on this
lattice. On its rational space it has trace $t_p/p$ and preserves
a nondegenerate symmetric pairing. In dimension two an orthogonal
map of determinant minus one has trace zero. Since both traces here
are nonzero, the determinant is one and
\[
\det(1-F_7)=12/7,\qquad\det(1-F_{13})=48/13.
\]
For an integral automorphism $F$ with $1-F$ rationally invertible,
the kernel on $(\Lambda\otimes\mathbb Q_\ell)/\Lambda$ has order
$\ell^{v_\ell(\det(1-F))}$, by identifying it with
$\Lambda/(1-F)\Lambda$. Galois invariants form a subgroup of each
such kernel. For $\ell\notin\{7,13\}$ the two counts therefore
bound their order by the $\ell$-part of $\gcd(12,48)=12$.
For $\ell=7$ use $p=13$, and for $\ell=13$ use $p=7$; both
primary groups vanish. The geometric invariant order consequently
divides twelve. The transcendental injection [38, Remark 1.3],
together with the algebraic calculation, proves (Q-K3-BRAUER-BOUND).


**Eliminating rational two-primary classes.** In fact the rational quotient
in (Q-K3-BRAUER-BOUND) is trivial. First let a class have order two modulo
constants and subtract its value on the rational zero section. Because
$\operatorname{Br}(\mathbb P^1_{\mathbb Q})=\operatorname{Br}(\mathbb Q)$,
this gives an actual two-torsion class with value zero on $O$.
Creutz--Viray [40, Theorem 1.7] over $K=\mathbb Q(k)$ gives its exhaustive
normalized generic-fiber presentation
\[
\alpha(f,g)=(f,X+A)+(g,X),\qquad f,g\in K^\times/K^{\times2}.
\tag{Q-BRAUER-NORMAL-FORM}
\]
Here $(\ ,\ )$ denotes a quaternion algebra. The split-root triple
$(f,g,fg)$ maps to $(f,X)+(g,X+A)+(fg,X+B)$, which is the displayed
cross-pairing because $X(X+A)(X+B)=Y^2$. Its kernel is the Kummer image
of $E_B(K)/2E_B(K)$ in coordinates $(\delta_X,\delta_{X+A})$.
The equality is for the normalized class itself; it leaves no arbitrary
$\operatorname{Br}(K)$ summand.

Put $u=k+1$, $v=k-1$, $w=k+3$, $r=k+2$, $q=k-7$.
Unramifiedness on the geometric identity component of each fiber gives
the following necessary parities for $(\operatorname{ord}f,\operatorname{ord}g)$:

| Base place | Allowed parity |
|---|---|
| Good finite place | $(0,0)$ |
| $-1$ | arbitrary |
| $1$ | $(c,0)$ |
| $-3$ | $(0,d)$ |
| $-2$ | $(e,e)$ |
| $7$ | $(0,h)$ |
| $\infty$ | equal coordinates |

At a good fiber, the half-divisors of $X$ and $X+A$ are the independent
nonzero two-torsion points, so their function classes are independent.
At the multiplicative fibers the normalized pairs $(X,X+A)$ are,
respectively,
\[
(T^2-192,T^2),\quad(T^2,T^2+64),\quad
(T^2-9,T^2-9),\quad(T^2,T^2+2304).
\]
At $-1$ both reduce to $T^2$. At infinity use $X'=k^{-4}X$;
the pair becomes $(T^2-1,T^2-1)$. These formulas prove every row,
including all good non-rational places after extending constants.
A rational function with even divisor on $\mathbb P^1$ is a constant
times a square. Consequently every possible class has
\[
f=C u^a v^c r^e,\qquad
g=D u^b w^d r^e q^{a+b+c+d},
\quad C,D\in\mathbb Q^\times,quad a,b,c,d,e\in\mathbb F_2.
\]
The rational kernel classes of $S,T_0,T_1$ are
\[
(2u,2u),\quad(2ur,2ur),\quad(-2ur,-2rq).
\]
Their exponent vectors span precisely the three $a,b,e$ directions.
Removing these exact kernel classes leaves
\[
\alpha=(Cv^c,X+A)+(Dq^{c+d}w^d,X).
\tag{Q-BRAUER-TWO-DIRECTIONS}
\]
This necessary normal form does not assert that all such symbols extend
across the other fiber components.

Two rational middle components now eliminate both directions. At $k=1$,
write $t=k-1$, $X=t^2z$, $Y=t^2\omega$. The middle component of the
resolved $I_4$ fiber is
\[
\omega^2=192z(z+4).
\]
It is a smooth rational conic, with point $(0,0)$. Along its generic
point the valuations of $(t,X,X+A)$ are $(1,2,0)$ and $X+A$ reduces
to $192$. The tame residue of (Q-BRAUER-TWO-DIRECTIONS) is therefore
$[3]^c$. Constants $C,D$ do not affect it. Since $3$ remains nonsquare
in this rational component field, $c=0$.

At $k=-3$, the chart $t=k+3$, $X+A=t^2z$, $Y=t^2\omega$ gives the
rational middle conic
\[
\omega^2=-64z(z+20).
\]
Here the coordinate valuations are $(2,0)$ and $X$ reduces to $-64$,
so the residue is $[-1]^d$ and $d=0$. These are divisors on the smooth
resolution, with base parameter of valuation one; replacing them by
the conjugate outer components would discard the decisive arithmetic
information. Even if a base-field correction were retained, the
multiplicity-one identity component at the same base would force its
constant residue to vanish, so it could not cancel either obstruction.

The remaining $(C,X+A)+(D,X)$ is geometrically trivial, hence algebraic.
The preceding integral calculation makes it constant. Every nonzero
finite two-primary group contains an element of order two, proving
\[
(\operatorname{Br}(\widetilde{\mathcal K})/
 \operatorname{Br}_0(\widetilde{\mathcal K}))[2^\infty]=0.
\tag{Q-BRAUER-TWO-VANISH}
\]
There is a useful distinction: the geometric two-torsion has dimension
two, since the geometric Picard number is twenty. Restriction to the
generic curve embeds it into the five-dimensional valuation space
modulo the three-dimensional geometric Kummer kernel. Equality of
dimensions shows that its two generators are represented geometrically by
\[
(k-1,X+A)+(k-7,X),\qquad ((k+3)(k-7),X).
\]
Their formulas are rational and their geometric classes Galois-fixed.
The order-four primary bound above therefore shows that the invariant
geometric two-primary group is $(\mathbb Z/2)^2$. Its nonzero classes
fail to descend to unramified classes on the rational K3.

**Eliminating three-primary invariants.** Let $N$ be the complete
integral NS Gram matrix in the HNF basis used above. The vector
\[
\mathbf w=\tfrac13(1,2,1,2,0,1,0,2,0,0,0,1,2,1,0,1,2,0,0,2)
\]
satisfies $N\mathbf w\in\mathbb Z^{20}$ and has order three modulo
$\mathbb Z^{20}$. Both Galois end swaps fix it. Since
$|\det N|=48$, it generates the full three-primary discriminant group,
with trivial Galois action.

Set $H=H^2_{\mathrm{et}}(\overline{\mathcal K},\mathbb Z_3(1))$
and $T=(\operatorname{NS}\otimes\mathbb Z_3)^\perp$.
Unimodularity of $H$ and primitivity of NS give a Galois-equivariant
anti-isometry of discriminant groups $A_T\simeq A_{\rm NS}$.
The pairing also identifies the actual Brauer lattice
$\Lambda=H/(\operatorname{NS}\otimes\mathbb Z_3)$ with $T^*$:
restriction of the unimodular pairing to the primitive submodule $T$
is surjective and has kernel NS. Thus $\Lambda/T\simeq\mathbb Z/3$
is Galois-trivial. As $3\Lambda\subset T$, there is an exact sequence
\[
0\longrightarrow R:=T/3\Lambda\longrightarrow
M:=\Lambda/3\Lambda\longrightarrow\mathbb F_3\longrightarrow0,
\tag{Q-BRAUER-THREE-LINE}
\]
with $R$ a line and $M=\operatorname{Br}(\overline{\mathcal K})[3]$.

Frobenius at seven acts on the rational space with trace $2/7$,
determinant one, and $v_3(\det(1-F_7))=1$. In a basis adapted to
(Q-BRAUER-THREE-LINE), its reduction is
$\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&b\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.
Here $b\ne0$: otherwise every entry of $1-F_7$ on the integral
rank-two lattice would be divisible by three and its determinant by nine.
Its fixed line is therefore exactly $R$.

Complex conjugation has determinant minus one on the transcendental
rank-two cohomology: it interchanges $H^{2,0}$ and $H^{0,2}$.
The Tate twist changes both eigenvalue signs and leaves the determinant
unchanged. On the quotient line in (Q-BRAUER-THREE-LINE) its action is
trivial, so on $R$ its action is minus one. Hence the common invariants
of Frobenius and conjugation on $M$ vanish. Every nonzero invariant
three-primary element has an invariant multiple of order three, so
all three-primary invariants vanish.

Combining this with the order bound and (Q-BRAUER-TWO-VANISH) gives
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Br}(\widetilde{\mathcal K})
 =\operatorname{Br}_0(\widetilde{\mathcal K}),\qquad
\operatorname{Br}(\overline{\mathcal K})^{G_{\mathbb Q}}
 \simeq(\mathbb Z/2)^2.}
\tag{Q-K3-BRAUER-EXACT}
\]
Thus this rational product K3 supplies no nonconstant Brauer--Manin
condition. This proves no density, approximation, or rational-point
completeness statement, and computes neither the Brauer group of the
full-root surface nor the restrictions on its rational lifts.


**Extension-field reciprocity does not restore this obstruction.**
Let $L/\mathbb Q$ be any finite extension and
$\beta\in\operatorname{Br}(\widetilde{\mathcal K}_L)$.
For every rational adelic point $(P_v)$, evaluation and corestriction
[41, Lemma 5.8] give
\[
\operatorname{inv}_v((\operatorname{cor}_{L/\mathbb Q}\beta)(P_v))
 =\sum_{w\mid v}\operatorname{inv}_w\beta(P_v\otimes L_w).
\]
Corestriction is an unramified class on the rational K3, hence constant
by (Q-K3-BRAUER-EXACT). Summing over $v$ gives zero by constant
reciprocity. Thus every rational adelic point, extended to $L$, is
orthogonal to every class over $L$, even one not descending individually.
In particular adjoining $i,\sqrt3$ does not create a new total
Brauer--Manin condition on these restricted rational adeles. The sum
must include every place of $L$; arbitrary $L$-adelic points and the
additional root-cover varieties are outside this conclusion.

### 12.20. Local offset restrictions and conic base changes

The offset descent in Section 12.6 gives restrictions independent of
specialized Mordell--Weil rank. Write $k=m/n$ in lowest terms, with
$n>0$, and exclude the singular finite bases $-3,-2,-1,1,7$.
The smooth projective offset torsor has integral equation
\[
W^2=F_{m,n}(U,V):=
-\bigl((m+3n)U^2+(m-n)(m+n)^2V^2\bigr)
 \bigl((m-n)U^2+(m+n)(m-7n)(m+3n)V^2\bigr).
\tag{B-OFFSET-INTEGRAL}
\]
Indeed $z=U/(nV)$ and $W=n^3V^2w$ in (B-OFFSET-TORSOR).
The charts $(U,V)=(u,1)$ for $u\in\mathbb Z_p$ and $(1,v)$ for
$v\in p\mathbb Z_p$ cover every local projective point, including
infinity. The elliptic map $X=dz^2-B$, $Y=dzw$ includes the extended
Kummer values at $T_B$ and $O$ through these endpoints.

For every prime $p\ge5$, local solubility is equivalent to all
applicable conditions in the following table:

| Arithmetic condition | Required condition |
|---|---|
| $p\mid n$ | $\left(\frac{-1}{p}\right)=1$ |
| $p\mid m+2n$ | $\left(\frac3p\right)=1$ |
| $v_p(m-n)$ odd | $\left(\frac3p\right)=1$ |
| $v_p(m+3n)$ odd | $\left(\frac{-1}{p}\right)=1$ |

All other cases at these primes are soluble. For the first two rows,
the reductions are respectively
$-m^2(U^2+m^2V^2)^2$ and
$3n^2(U^2-3n^2V^2)^2$. An anisotropic inner form proves impossibility
when the indicated constant is nonsquare; infinity lifts when it is
square. At $m=n$ the reduction has class $3U^2V^2$.
For nonsquare $3$, a point must approach one of the two axes.
Comparison of the two term valuations excludes odd $v_p(m-n)$;
for even valuation, rescaling the small coordinate gives a smooth
nondegenerate norm conic over $\mathbb F_p$, which has a point and
lifts. At $m=-3n$ the same argument uses class $-U^2V^2$ and the
norm conic for $-1$. The only collision among these branches for
$p\ge5$ occurs at $p=5$ between $m+3n$ and $m-7n$; it is harmless
because $-1$ is square there. At $m=-n$ infinity lifts, and at
$m=7n$ the unit-coordinate norm conic lifts. Away from these factors
there is good genus-one reduction and hence a local point. The
coefficient determinant $-32n^2(m+n)(m+2n)$ and the displayed leading
and constant coefficients exhaust all bad factors.

At three there is the following complete rule. If $3\mid n$, the
torsor is insoluble. Otherwise regard $k$ as a $3$-adic integer.

| Base condition | Necessary and sufficient condition |
|---|---|
| $k\equiv-1\pmod3$ | Always soluble |
| $k\equiv0\pmod3$ | $v_3(k+3)$ even |
| $k\equiv1\pmod3$, $e=v_3(k-1)\ge2$ | $(k-1)/3^e\equiv(-1)^{e+1}\pmod3$ |
| $e=1$, $(k-1)/3\equiv1\pmod3$ | Insoluble |
| $e=1$, $(k-1)/3\equiv-1\pmod3$ | $v_3(k-7)$ odd |

For completeness, put $t=k-1$. The factors in the affine quartic are
\[
A_z=(t+4)z^2+t(t+2)^2,\qquad
B_z=tz^2+(t+2)(t-6)(t+4).
\]
If $e\ge2$, then $v_3(t-6)=1$. For $r=v_3(z)>0$ the valuations
are $\min(2r,e)$ and $1$; for $r<0$ they are $2r$ and
$\min(e+2r,1)$, with the equality cases checked before taking a
minimum. For $r=0$ the product valuation is odd. If $e$ is even,
the wrong unit $t/3^e\equiv1$ remains impossible even in the
cancellation chart $2r=e$; the other unit makes infinity a square.
If $e$ is odd, the wrong unit $-1$ remains impossible even in the
chart $e+2r=1$; unit $1$ makes $z=0$ a square.
For $e=1$, unit $1$ makes every chart impossible. With unit $-1$,
let $f=v_3(t-6)\ge2$. The unit and pole charts remain impossible;
in the small-coordinate chart the two valuations to compare are
$1+2r$ and $f$. Even $f$ gives odd total valuation or nonsquare
unit. For odd $f$, write $v=(t-6)/3^f$: if $v=-1\pmod3$ use
$z=0$, and if $v=1\pmod3$ use $z=3^{(f-1)/2}$. Both give a square.
The other two residue classes of $k$ follow directly from the leading
coefficient and the same $-1$ norm argument. This proves the rule
for unbounded valuations, not only a finite list of bases.

At two a uniform necessary condition is
\[
C_k(\mathbb Q_2)\ne\varnothing\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
m,n\text{ both odd}.
\tag{B-OFFSET-DYADIC-PARITY}
\]
For primitive $(U,V)$, reduction of (B-OFFSET-INTEGRAL) modulo sixteen
proves this directly:

| Parity of $(m,n)$ | Opposite parity of $(U,V)$ | Both $U,V$ odd |
|---|---|---|
| even, odd | $3$ or $11$ | $12$ |
| odd, even | $7$ or $15$ | $12$ |

None is a square. Both $m,n$ odd is not sufficient. The complete dyadic criterion is:

| Odd base class | Necessary and sufficient condition |
|---|---|
| $k\equiv7\pmod8$ | Always soluble |
| $k\equiv3\pmod8$ | Insoluble |
| $k\equiv1\pmod8$ | $e=v_2(k-1)\ge4$ and $(k-1)/2^e\equiv(-1)^{e+1}\pmod4$ |
| $k\equiv5\pmod8$ | $e=v_2(k+3)\ge4$ and $(k+3)/2^e\equiv1\pmod4$ |

All singular bases are excluded before taking these valuations.
For $k\equiv7$, write $t=k+1\in8\mathbb Z_2$; the leading
coefficient $d=4-t^2$ is a square, giving a point at infinity.
For $k\equiv3$, write $k+1=4u$ with $u$ odd, and put
$z=4Z$, $w=32Y$. The equation becomes
\[
Y^2=-((2u+1)Z^2+u^2(2u-1))
      ((2u-1)Z^2+u(u-2)(2u+1)).
\]
At a primitive homogeneous pair its residues modulo sixteen are
$3,7,11,15$ when the first coordinate is even, $13$ when the second
is even, and $8$ when both are odd. None is square.

For the remaining branches let $q=2^j u$, with $u$ odd and $j\ge1$,
and use $z=2Z$, $w=16Y$. At $k=1+4q$ and $k=-3+4q$ the exact
normalized equations are respectively
\[
\begin{aligned}
Y^2&=-((q+1)Z^2+qh^2)(qZ^2+(q+1)h\ell),
 &h=2q+1,\quad\ell=2q-3,\\
Y^2&=-(qZ^2+(q-1)h^2)((q-1)Z^2+qh\ell),
 &h=2q-1,\quad\ell=2q-5.
\end{aligned}
\tag{B-OFFSET-DYADIC-NORMAL}
\]
In both models $h^2\equiv1$, $h\ell\equiv5\pmod8$.
The leading and constant endpoint values have valuation $j$ and
unit classes differing by $5$. For even $j$, one endpoint is square
exactly when $u\equiv-1\pmod4$ in the first model and $u\equiv1$
in the second. For odd $j$, neither endpoint is square.

For $v_2(Z)=0$, the right sides have residues $3$ and $7$ modulo
eight, respectively. For nonzero valuation put $R=|v_2(Z)|\ge1$,
using the reciprocal chart when necessary. If $2R<j$, the residual
unit after removing its even valuation is given in both charts by

| Gap $j-2R$ | First model | Second model |
|---:|---:|---:|
| At least $3$ | $3\pmod8$ | $7\pmod8$ |
| $2$ | $7\pmod8$ | $3\pmod8$ |
| $1$ | $3-2u\pmod8$ | $7+2u\pmod8$ |

Only the last row permits a square, in both cases exactly for
$u\equiv1\pmod4$. It requires odd $j\ge3$, and the choice
$Z=2^{(j-1)/2}$ proves sufficiency. If $2R>j$, the total valuation
is $j$; odd $j$ is impossible, while for even $j$ the residual
unit modulo four is $-u$ in the first model and $u$ in the second.
This supplies no additional unit class beyond the endpoint cases.
If $2R=j$, then $j$ is even. The cancelling quadratic has normalized
sum $1+u$ in the first model and $u-1$ in the second, modulo four.
For the excluded unit class the sum has valuation exactly one, so
the total valuation $j+1$ is odd. This checks every cancellation
chart. When $j=1$ all nonunit branches have odd valuation and the
unit branch is already excluded. Substituting $j=e-2$ proves the
complete table for unbounded valuations.

Thus local solubility of the smooth offset torsor is decided by
closed valuation and unit rules at every finite prime. Only primes
dividing $6n(m+n)(m+2n)(m-n)(m+3n)(m-7n)$ need inspection.
An independent check uses both projective charts and breadth-first
$p$-adic subdivision without a precision cutoff: discard a nonsquare
ball once the Taylor variation fixes its squareclass, and accept
square values or simple roots satisfying Hensel's inequality.
Separability and compactness prove termination. This is an independent
exact decision procedure, not the proof of the unbounded tables.

**No offset section on the first three conics.** A useful local lemma
works over any complete discretely valued field $L$ of residue
characteristic different from two. If $v(A)>0$ and $B$ is a unit
square in $Y^2=X(X+A)(X+B)$, then
\[
\delta_B(E(L))=\{1\}.
\tag{B-LOCAL-TRIVIAL-IMAGE}
\]
For $v(X)>0$, $X+B$ is a square principal perturbation of $B$.
For $v(X)=0$, $X(X+A)$ is a square, so the equation forces $X+B$
to be square. For $v(X)<0$, its leading cubic first forces $X$
to be square and then $X+B$ is square. The special Kummer values
at $O,T_B$ are square as well.

Apply this over $\mathbb Q((t))$ to the first three base covers
remaining after (B-DD-NONSQUARE):

| Cover | Rational parameter and place | Nonsquare target residue |
|---|---|---|
| $u^2=2(k+1)$ | $k=u^2/2-1$, $u=\infty$ | $-1$ |
| $u^2=k+2$ | $k=u^2-2$, $u=0$ | $3$ |
| $v^2=2(k+1)(k+2)$ | $k=(4-u^2)/(u^2-2)$, $v=2u/(u^2-2)$, $u=0$ | $3$ |

In the first row set $t=1/u$, $X'=t^8X$, $Y'=t^{12}Y$.
Then $A'=8t^4(1+2t^2)$, $B'=(1-4t^2)^2/16$, while the
squareclass of $d$ is represented by $-(1-16t^4)$.
In the other rows $A$ has positive valuation, $B$ specializes to
$9$, and $d$ to $3$. Thus all three generic offset torsors are
locally insoluble at the indicated rational place and admit no
rational section, independently of any generic rank or saturation
calculation. This statement leaves individual rational specializations
and further base changes open.

The fourth cover, $d$ square, behaves differently. With
\[
k=(1-3u^2)/(1+u^2),\qquad \sqrt d=4u/(1+u^2),
\]
the known product section is
$(a,b,s,t)=((1+u^2)/(1-u^2),1,1,-1)$.
Its center $H=a^2$ and both offsets lift, but it has one zero offset.
The remaining root class is $1+u^2$; its square root is not rational
in $\mathbb Q(u)$. A further conic, $u=2t/(1-t^2)$, yields a full
rational root family with repeated normalized roots
\[
1,\qquad\frac{1-t^2+2t}{1+t^2},\qquad
\frac{1-t^2-2t}{1+t^2},
\quad k=\frac{1-14t^2+t^4}{(1+t^2)^2}.
\]
It is a degenerate degree-four multisection, not a distinct-entry
solution. This example explains why offset and center lifts alone
cannot replace the remaining root characters.

**The independent center lift.** On the generic offset curve the
center condition gives a geometrically connected double cover of
genus nine. In the deck coordinates of Section 12.6 its character
is $d_0$, whereas the unramified offset character is $d_0+t_0$.
The center character is nonzero at each of the eight horizontal
branch points and the offset character is zero there. They remain
independent over algebraically closed constants. Pulling the center
cover back to the unramified offset cover gives sixteen simple
branch points, hence $2g-2=16$ by Riemann--Hurwitz. This concerns the
generic curve, not every specialized fiber.

The separation is arithmetically nonvacuous. At $k=49/17$, the torsor
point $(z,w)=(55/17,401720/4913)$ corresponds to
\[
(a,b,s,t)=(5129/2321,2033/633,1,589/211).
\]
It has rational offset roots $1540/633$ and $1620/2321$, but
\[
H=\frac{523723369}{48483369}
 =\frac{13\cdot17\cdot53\cdot61\cdot733}{6963^2}
\]
is nonsquare. The four surviving low-rank alternative radicands are
$132/17$, $83/17$, $10956/289$, $-3200/289$, all nonsquares.
Consequently this actual offset point forces specialized elliptic rank
at least two. It gives no full-root point and no exclusion of every
point at this base.



### 12.21. A sharp two-cover alternative for specialized rank at most one

The initial four-cover alternative in Section 12.6 can be reduced further
without a saturation assumption. On a smooth canonical B fiber,
\[
\boxed{\text{a rational full-root lift and }\operatorname{rank}E_k(\mathbb Q)\le1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
k+2\in\mathbb Q^{\times2}\ \text{or}\
-(k-1)(k+3)\in\mathbb Q^{\times2}.}
\tag{B-TWO-COVER-ALTERNATIVE}
\]
Here $-1<k<7$, so $D=(k+1)(k-7)<0$; singular fibers remain excluded.
Equivalently, nonsquareness of these two quantities forces rank at least
two for every actual full-root point in this chamber. The two rational
base covers still contain infinitely many rational parameters.

**First-cover half and its target exclusions.** On $k=u^2/2-1$, put
\[
X(Q)=\frac{u^3(u+2)^2(u^2+2)}2,\qquad
Y(Q)=-\frac{u^4(u+2)^2(u+4)(u^2+2)(u^2+4)}8.
\]
Exact doubling gives $2Q=S$, and
\[
\delta_B(Q)=[R],\quad R=u(u+4)(u^2+4),\quad
[D]=[u^2-16],\quad[d]=[-(u^2-4)(u^2+4)].
\]
The conditions $dR$ or $dRD$ square reduce, after square factors, to
$-u(u+4)(u^2-4)$ or $-u(u-4)(u^2-4)$ square. They are exchanged by
$u\mapsto-u$. For the second, the map
\[
X=-2-4/u,\qquad Y=2w/u^2
\]
from $w^2=(4-u^2)u(u-4)$ gives
$E_{24}:Y^2=X(X+3)(X+4)$.
Its two-isogeny image is exactly $\{1,3,-3,-1\}$: these classes
come from torsion, and the remaining coset, represented by $2$, would
require $N^2=2U^4+7U^2V^2+6V^4$, whose primitive residues modulo
eight are $2,6,7$. The isogenous curve has coefficients $a=-14,b=1$;
negative abscissas are impossible, so its image is $\{1\}$.
The rank is zero. Good reductions at five and seven both have eight
points, and none of the nonzero two-torsion points is divisible by two,
as their first Kummer classes are $3,-3,-1$. Thus the rational group
is exactly its four two-torsion points. The quartic points give
$u=0,-2,2,4$, and reflection gives only $u=0,\pm2,\pm4$ in total.
All yield singular B bases. The omitted $X=-2$ chart has cubic value
$-4$ and no rational point. Therefore $dR,dRD$ are nonsquares at
every smooth rational first-cover base.

The condition $R$ square has a separate exact determination. The map
\[
X=1+4/u,\qquad Y=2w/u^2
\]
from $w^2=u(u+4)(u^2+4)$ gives
$E_{20}:Y^2=X^3-2X^2+5X$.
The positive quadratic factor leaves descent classes $1,5$, both
realized. On its isogenous curve $Y^2=X^3+4X^2-16X$, the visible
classes are $1,-1$; the remaining coset $2$ would require
$N^2=2U^4+4U^2V^2-8V^4$, with primitive nonsquare residues
$2,8,14\pmod{16}$. Both images have size two, so the rank is zero.
Good counts at three and seven are both six, and the six points
\[
O,(0,0),(1,\pm2),(5,\pm10)
\]
exhaust the rational group. Hence the finite quartic coordinates are
$u=-4,0,1$; the two $X=1$ points are its rational infinities.
As $[RD]=[R(-u)]$, the only smooth finite B base where $R$ or $RD$
is square is $k=-1/2$. It has no dyadic offset point by
(B-OFFSET-DYADIC-PARITY). Consequently, at every actual full-root
point on the first cover, $R,D$ are independent squareclasses.

The points $Q,T_1$ therefore give two independent classes in
$E_k(\mathbb Q)/2E_k(\mathbb Q)$ by their third coordinates $R,D$.
The third coordinate of $T_0$ is $1$, and its first on this cover is
$[AB]=[k+2]$. If $k+2$ is nonsquare, it supplies a third independent
class. Every combination of these three has third coordinate in
$\{1,D,R,RD\}$. By (B-DD-NONSQUARE) and the target exclusions just
proved, an offset point adds a fourth independent class unless $d$
is square. The dimension is $\operatorname{rank}E_k+2$, proving
(B-TWO-COVER-ALTERNATIVE) on the first cover.

**Third-cover half and removal of that alternative.** Parameterize
$v^2=2(k+1)(k+2)$ by
\[
k=(4-u^2)/(u^2-2),\qquad v=2u/(u^2-2).
\]
Writing $b_0=(k+1)(k-1)$, the point
\[
Q=(4vb_0,-4vb_0(4v+b_0))
\]
satisfies $2Q=T_0$. Its third class and the two base classes are
\[
[R]=[(3-u^2)(2u+3)],\quad
[d]=[(u^2-3)(u^2-1)],\quad[D]=[(3-2u)(3+2u)].
\]
Thus $dR$ square is equivalent to
$w^2=-(u^2-1)(2u+3)$, and $dRD$ gives its reflection.
The map $X=-2u-2$, $Y=2w$ gives
$Y^2=X(X+4)(X-1)$. Its two-isogeny images have sizes two and two.
On the original curve the visible classes are $1,-1$; the other
coset $2$ gives $2U^4+3U^2V^2-2V^4$, with only primitive
residues $2,3\pmod5$. On the isogenous curve the coefficients are
$a=-6,b=25$; real positivity leaves $1,5$, both realized, the latter
by $U=V=1,N=2$. Good counts at three and seven are four. Thus only
the four rational two-torsion points occur, giving
$u=\infty,-1,1,-3/2$. All corresponding B bases are singular.
This proves both target exclusions on the third cover.

For $R$ square itself, $X=-2u-1$, $Y=2w$ gives
\[
E_*:Y^2=X^3-15X+22.
\]
After shifting $X$ by two the two-isogeny coefficients are $a=6,b=-3$.
The image is exactly $\{1,-3\}$: the other coset $3$ has quartic
$3U^4+6U^2V^2-V^4$, which is $-1$ modulo three if $V$ is a unit
and has valuation one otherwise. On the isogenous curve
$a=-12,b=48$, real positivity leaves $1,2,3,6$; classes $1,3$
occur, while coset $2$ gives $2U^4-12U^2V^2+24V^4$ with primitive
nonsquare residues $2,8,14\pmod{16}$. The rank is zero. Counts
at five and seven are six and twelve, and the six points
\[
E_*(\mathbb Q)=\{O,(2,0),(-1,\pm6),(3,\pm2)\}
\]
exhaust the group. Hence $R$ square gives only
$u=\infty,-3/2,0,-2$; $RD$ square gives their negatives.
The only smooth B base is $k=0$, already dyadically offset-insoluble.
For every actual full-root point, $R,D$ are again independent.

The classes of $Q,T_1$ are independent by their third coordinates.
The section $S$ has class $(c,c,1)$, $c=2(k+1)$, so unless $c$
is square it adds a third independent class. The target exclusions
and (B-DD-NONSQUARE) show that an offset point adds a fourth unless
$d$ is square. Rank at most one therefore reduces the third cover
to the first or the $d$-square cover. The first-cover argument then
leaves exactly the two alternatives in (B-TWO-COVER-ALTERNATIVE).

The third-cover calculation also proves that its smooth rational
fibers have no rational point of order eight. A further half of $Q$
or a two-torsion translate needs $R$ or $RD$ square, leaving only
$k=0$; there its four halves of $T_0$ have abscissas $8,-8$, both
nonsquare. The other two nonzero two-torsion points have negative
abscissas and cannot be halved. This torsion observation is additional;
the rank alternative used actual Kummer independence and no saturation
or specialized torsion assumption.



### 12.22. Rank forcing across the signed B energies

The two-cover theorem gives simultaneous restrictions on the same
admissible point. Choose positive opposite products $a,b,s,t$, so
\[
a^2=H-x^2,\quad b^2=H-y^2,\quad
s^2=H-(x+y)^2,\quad t^2=H-(x-y)^2,\qquad H=c^4.
\]
Root-sign changes permit all four choices $(a,b,\eta s,\theta t)$
without changing the square entries. Put
\[
N_{\eta\theta}=\frac{(a+b+\eta s)(a+b+\theta t)}{H},\qquad
k_{\eta\theta}=N_{\eta\theta}-2,
\quad \eta,\theta\in\{\pm1\}.
\tag{B-SIGNED-ENERGIES}
\]
These are four distinct canonical parameters in $(-1,7)$.
Writing $A=a+b$, the exact identities are
\[
(N_{++}-1)(N_{--}-1)=(s-t)^2/H,\qquad
(N_{+-}-1)(N_{-+}-1)=(s+t)^2/H.
\]
Here $A^2>H>s^2,t^2$, and the mixed pair sum multiplied by $H$ is
$2(A^2-st-H)=(s-t)^2+4ab>0$. Thus every $N>1$; also
$A<2\sqrt H$, $s,t<\sqrt H$ give $N<9$. Strict positivity and
$s\ne t$ give distinctness. The other four sign choices, using $a-b$
in place of $a+b$, need not be canonical and are not used in the
rank argument.

For a primitive admissible square one has $2,3\nmid c$,
$v_2(x),v_2(y)\ge3$, and $v_3(x),v_3(y)\ge1$. The following
unconditional rank lower bounds hold on the stated strata:
\[
\boxed{\begin{aligned}
|v_2(x)-v_2(y)|\le1
 &\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{at least two of the four B ranks are at least two},\\
v_3(x)=v_3(y)
 &\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{at least one of the four B ranks is at least two}.
\end{aligned}}
\tag{B-SIGNED-RANK-FORCING}
\]
Each rank is that of $E_{B,k_{\eta\theta}}(\mathbb Q)$.
The selected fibers are smooth: their two target squareclasses below
are nonzero, ruling out the only singular canonical value $k=1$.

**Uniform local proof.** Normalize $X=x/c^2$, $Y=y/c^2$, and divide
all four products by $c^2$. Locally each product is a sign times the
principal square root of $1-D^2$, where $D=X,Y,X+Y,X-Y$.
Select the two signed choices for which $s,t$ have opposite principal
branches. Put $e=\min(v_pX,v_pY)$,
$F_\pm=X^2+Y^2\pm4XY$, and $T=X^2+Y^2$.
If $a,b$ have the same principal sign, the selected energies satisfy
\[
N=3-F_\pm+\epsilon;
\]
if their signs are opposite, they satisfy
\[
N=-1+T+\epsilon.
\]
At three, $v_3(\epsilon)\ge4e$. At two,
$v_2(\epsilon)\ge4e-2$. To check the dyadic precision even at
$e=3$, write $f(z)=\sqrt{1-z^2}\equiv1\pmod4$ and use
\[
\begin{aligned}
(f(X)+f(Y))^2&=4-2T+O(2^{4e-2}),\\
f(X+Y)f(X-Y)&=1-T+O(2^{2v_2X+2v_2Y+1}),\\
f(X+Y)-f(X-Y)&=-2XY+O(2^{v_2X+v_2Y+2e}).
\end{aligned}
\]
The second follows by extracting the unit $1-T$ before taking a
square root; the third follows by rationalizing the difference.
With opposite signs on $a,b$, their sum has valuation at least
$2e-1$, giving the same error bound.

At two the selected $N$ have residue $3$ or $-1$ modulo eight and
are nonsquares. Since
\[
d=-(k-1)(k+3)=-(N-3)(N+1),
\]
their $d$ classes are respectively $F_\pm$ or $T$ in the valuation
cases used here. If $v_2X=v_2Y=e$, all these quadratics have odd
valuation $2e+1$. If the valuations differ by one, they have valuation
$2e$ and unit part $5$ modulo eight. The other factor in $d$, after
removing $4$, is a square unit. The remainder has relative valuation
at least $2e-3\ge3$, so it changes neither conclusion. Both selected
energies therefore violate both alternatives in (B-TWO-COVER-ALTERNATIVE).
Their difference is, up to sign, $2A(s-t)/H$ or $2A(s+t)/H$, so they
are distinct. This proves the first rank bound.

At three suppose the common offset valuation is $e$. If $a,b$ have
the same principal sign, exactly one of $F_\pm$ has valuation
$2e+1$: choose the sign in $(X\mp Y)^2\pm6XY$ so that the first
term has valuation at least $2e+2$. For that choice $v_3(N)=1$,
and both $N$ and $d$ are nonsquares. The error has valuation
$4e>2e+1$. If $a,b$ have opposite signs, both selected $N$ are
$-1$ modulo three and $T/3^{2e}$ is $2$ modulo three; both $d$
classes are nonsquare. Thus at least one rank is at least two, and
at least two are when $ab/c^4\equiv-1\pmod3$.

In particular, if all four canonical ranks are at most one, then
\[
\boxed{|v_2(x)-v_2(y)|\ge2,\qquad v_3(x)\ne v_3(y).}
\tag{B-LOW-RANK-VALUATION-STRATUM}
\]
These valuation differences are unchanged by common scaling and by
the signed permutations of $x,y$. They cannot be removed by choosing
another representative of the same full-root symmetry orbit.

The two-prime argument has a precise limit. If the dyadic valuations
differ by at least two, the relevant $F_\pm,T$ have square unit
part $1$ modulo eight. If the ternary valuations differ, their dominant
square gives square unit part at three. The other two $N$ values are
already local squares. Thus all four local two-cover alternatives
pass at two and three on the remaining stratum; no universal rank
lower bound is inferred from these tests.

**The transported conditions are not generic square identities.**
The four functions $(A+s)/c^2,(A-s)/c^2,(A+t)/c^2,(A-t)/c^2$
have independent squareclasses on the full-root function field.
For example, the plane $A+s=0$ cuts the product quartic in two
$H=0$ lines and the conic
\[
5a^2+14ab+5b^2+3t^2=0.
\]
At its generic point $H\ne0$, the full-root map is unramified,
$A+s$ has odd valuation, and the other three linear forms are units.
The four analogous conics are distinct. Their valuations prove the
claimed independence. The four edge products $N_{\eta\theta}$
therefore have squareclass rank three; their total product is a square.
This makes the simultaneous arithmetic conditions substantive, but
still supplies no finite parameter list or height bound.



### 12.23. A finite two-twist descent for a coupled center family

The two remaining base covers lead to a common explicit center problem.
On the $d$-square cover $k=(1-3u^2)/(1+u^2)$, the product point of
$2S$ has representative
\[
\left(\frac{k^3+k^2+k-4}{Z},
-\frac{k^4+k^3-k^2-k+2}{(k+1)Z},1,
\frac{3k^2-2}{Z}\right),\qquad Z=2k^3+k^2-6k+2.
\]
Its center expression is
\[
H(2S)=\frac{4(k^3-k-1)(2k^3+3k^2-2k-4)}{(k+1)^2Z^2}.
\tag{B-DOUBLE-SECTION-CENTER}
\]
After the $d$-square substitution, the squarefree part is
\[
(25u^6-61u^4+43u^2+1)(25u^6-29u^4+11u^2+1).
\]
With $v=1/u$ the center curve is
\[
C_5:\quad W^2=P(v^2)Q(v^2),\qquad
P(T)=T^3+11T^2-29T+25,\quad
Q(T)=T^3+43T^2-61T+25.
\tag{B-CENTER-GENUS-FIVE}
\]
The cubics have discriminants $-2^{12}\cdot23$ and
$-2^{14}\cdot83$ and resultant $2^{18}\cdot25$. Their substituted
sextics are squarefree and coprime, so $C_5$ is smooth of genus five.
In particular $H(2S)$ is not a square in the conic function field;
this is a generic-center obstruction, not a classification of its
rational specializations.

The same curve arises from the other surviving base cover. On
$k=u^2-2$, take the negative of a half of $S+T_0$. Its product point is
\[
\left(\frac{u^4-u^3-u^2+u+2}{(u-1)Z_1},
\frac{u^3-u^2+u+4}{Z_1},1,
\frac{3u^2-2}{Z_1}\right),\qquad Z_1=2u^3-u^2-6u-2.
\]
The offset condition is parameterized by $u=(3-v^2)/(1+v^2)$.
Writing $D(v)=v^6+11v^4-93v^2+25$, one obtains exactly
\[
H=\left(\frac{v^2+1}{(v^2-1)D(v)}\right)^2P(v^2)Q(v^2),
\qquad
H-a^2=\left(\frac{8v(v^2-1)(v^2+5)}{D(v)}\right)^2.
\]
Indeed the $2S$ coordinates at the new base $-u$ equal
$(b,-a,1,-t)$ from this half-point. The signed permutation preserves
$H$ and rational full-root lifting; the conic parameters are reciprocal.
These are identities on the displayed open charts, not a treatment of
all exceptional projective points. No rational-point classification is
inferred by discarding their denominators.

**Why a new cover is needed for elliptic methods.** The two involutions
of $C_5$ give maps
\[
(v,W)\longmapsto(v^2,W)\in C_2:w^2=P(T)Q(T),\qquad
(v,W)\longmapsto(v^2,vW)\in C_3:z^2=TP(T)Q(T).
\]
Their differential pullbacks span the five regular differentials,
so $J(C_5)\sim_{\mathbb Q}J(C_2)\times J(C_3)$.
Neither factor has an elliptic factor over $\mathbb Q$. For $C_2$,
the good-reduction counts at $13,13^2$ are $17,169$, yielding
\[
F_{13}(T)=T^4+3T^3+4T^2+39T+169.
\]
This is irreducible already modulo five: the degree-two Rabin gcd
is one and $T^{625}\equiv T$ modulo the polynomial.
For $C_3$, counts at $7,7^2,7^3$ are $9,55,330$, yielding
\[
F_7(T)=T^6+T^5+3T^4-2T^3+21T^2+49T+343.
\]
It is irreducible modulo three: the gcds with $T^{3^2}-T$ and
$T^{3^3}-T$ are one, and $T^{3^6}\equiv T$.
An elliptic factor over $\mathbb Q$ would give a quadratic factor
at every good prime. These exact certificates exclude it; they do
not prove absolute simplicity or determine either Mordell--Weil rank.

**Only two twists are required.** Write $v=p/q$ in lowest terms and set
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_6&=p^6+11p^4q^2-29p^2q^4+25q^6,\\
Q_6&=p^6+43p^4q^2-61p^2q^4+25q^6.
\end{aligned}
\]
Both are positive for real $p/q$: the quadratic tails of $P,Q$
have negative discriminants and positive leading coefficients, and
the cubic term is nonnegative. The exact common divisor is
\[
\boxed{\gcd(P_6,Q_6)=2^{3\epsilon}5^{2\zeta},\quad
\epsilon=\mathbf1_{p,q\text{ both odd}},\quad
\zeta=\mathbf1_{5\mid p}.}
\tag{B-CENTER-EXACT-GCD}
\]
To prove this, use $Q_6-P_6=32p^2q^2(p^2-q^2)$.
An odd common prime other than five divides neither $p$ nor $q$,
so would divide $p^2-q^2$; substitution makes $P_6\equiv8q^6$,
a contradiction. If $5\nmid p$, the square residues $p^2/q^2=1,4$
modulo five, together with the $5\mid q$ case, make both sextics
units. If $p=5r$, then
\[
P_6/25\equiv q^4(q^2+r^2),\qquad
Q_6/25\equiv q^4(q^2-r^2)\pmod5.
\]
Their sum is nonzero, so the common valuation is exactly two.
At two, opposite parity makes both values odd; both odd makes each
value $8\pmod{16}$, hence valuation exactly three.

A rational $C_5$ point makes $P_6Q_6$ an integer square. Dividing by
the common divisor leaves coprime positive integers, hence squares.
Thus opposite parity forces both $P_6,Q_6$ to be squares, and both
odd forces both to be twice squares. In the opposite-parity case
the even member must be divisible by four; valuation one would make
both sextics $5\pmod8$.

Consequently every rational point lifts to one of the two fixed curves
\[
D_\delta:\quad U^2=\delta P(v^2),\quad V^2=\delta Q(v^2),
\qquad\delta\in\{1,2\},
\tag{B-CENTER-TWO-TWISTS}
\]
with map $(v,U,V)\mapsto(v,UV/\delta)$ back to $C_5$.
Conversely every rational point of these equations maps to $C_5$.
The smooth projective $D_\delta$ is connected of genus nine and is
an étale double cover of $C_5$. The two sextic squareclasses are
independent, with twelve disjoint simple branch points over the
$v$-line; the degree-four cover has $2g-2=4(-2+12/2)=16$.
Over $C_5$ each sextic has even divisor, so the remaining double
cover is unramified. The finite point $v=0$ and both rational
infinities of $C_5$ lift to $D_1$; $D_2$ has no rational point
above those places. Thus these projective charts are included.

Each single equation in (B-CENTER-TWO-TWISTS) is a genus-two curve
and a quotient of $D_\delta$ of degree two. For a monic cubic
$F(T)=T^3+aT^2+bT+c$, the two elliptic quotients of
$u^2=\delta F(v^2)$ are
\[
\begin{aligned}
E_{F,\delta}:&\quad Y^2=X^3+\delta aX^2+\delta^2bX+\delta^3c,
 &(X,Y)&=(\delta v^2,\delta u),\\
E'_{F,\delta}:&\quad Y'^2=X'^3+\delta bX'^2+\delta^2acX'+\delta^3c^2,
 &(X',Y')&=(\delta c/v^2,\delta c u/v^3).
\end{aligned}
\]
The second map extends on the smooth projective curves. The four
untwisted models, together with their twists by two, have coefficients
$(a,b,c)=(11,-29,25),(43,-61,25),(-29,275,625),(-61,1075,625)$.
These are elliptic quotients of the new covering curves, so their
existence is consistent with the preceding nonsplitting of $J(C_5)$.
The finite twist reduction is followed by an exact rank calculation below.
Neither calculation yet establishes rational-point completeness or a
remaining full-root lift.



#### Exact ranks of the eight elliptic quotients

The elliptic ranks in the preceding construction are determined
unconditionally as follows. Each displayed triple is the coefficient
triple in $Y^2=X^3+aX^2+bX+c$.

| Sextic | Quotient | $\delta$ | $(a,b,c)$ | Rank |
|---|---|---:|---|---:|
| $P$ | even | 1 | $(11,-29,25)$ | 1 |
| $P$ | even | 2 | $(22,-116,200)$ | 1 |
| $P$ | odd | 1 | $(-29,275,625)$ | 1 |
| $P$ | odd | 2 | $(-58,1100,5000)$ | 1 |
| $Q$ | even | 1 | $(43,-61,25)$ | 1 |
| $Q$ | even | 2 | $(86,-244,200)$ | 2 |
| $Q$ | odd | 1 | $(-61,1075,625)$ | 2 |
| $Q$ | odd | 2 | $(-122,4300,5000)$ | 1 |

Here is a complete nonsplit two-descent proof, including the finite
arithmetic needed for the upper bounds. The root fields are
\[
K_P=\mathbb Q(\theta),\quad\theta^3-\theta-1=0,
\qquad
K_Q=\mathbb Q(\theta),\quad\theta^3-\theta^2+\theta-2=0.
\]
Their squarefree discriminants are $-23,-83$, so the displayed
power bases are integral bases. The Minkowski bounds
$8\sqrt{|D|}/(9\pi)$ are less than two and three, respectively.
The only prime ideal of norm two in $K_Q$ is $(\theta)$, since
$N(\theta)=2$ and the polynomial modulo two is
$T(T^2+T+1)$. Thus both fields have class number one.
The norm-one units $\eta_P=\theta$ and $\eta_Q=\theta-1$
are nonsquares: their residues at the degree-one primes over five,
$\theta=2,4$, are $2,3$. Since the signature is $(1,1)$,
these units generate the norm-one unit squareclasses. This uses
Dirichlet's unit theorem and $N(-1)=-1$, without assuming that
the displayed units are fundamental.

The primary cubic roots are
\[
\alpha_P=-1-4\theta-4\theta^2,\qquad
\alpha_Q=-17-4\theta-12\theta^2.
\]
They have norm $-25$. Use $25/\alpha$ for the odd quotient
and multiply either root by $\delta$ for its twist. Direct
substitution verifies all eight integral cubic equations.
The Kummer map is $[X-\alpha]$, with square norm. Its ideal
valuations are even outside the primes over two and the cubic
discriminant. Indeed, a nonintegral rational abscissa has even
valuation by the monic cubic equation. At an odd prime of
separable reduction, an integral abscissa can meet at most one
degree-one root, and the square norm forces the valuation there
to be even. Thus all denominator primes are included in this
support argument. The primary discriminant supports are
$\{2,23\}$ and $\{2,83\}$; the odd quotients add only five.

At two, $K_P$ is inert, so the norm condition leaves no odd
valuation. In $K_Q$ its residue-degree-two prime is generated by
$\gamma_2=1-\theta+\theta^2$, with norm four and
$\theta\gamma_2=2$; the degree-one valuation is even.
At five, the degree-one generators are $1+\theta^2$ and
$1+\theta$, both of norm five. The norm-square candidates from
the degree-two primes are therefore
\[
\gamma_{5,P}=4+\theta-2\theta^2,\qquad
\gamma_{5,Q}=3-2\theta+\theta^2.
\]
They have norm 25 and are needed only for the odd quotients.
At $\ell=23,83$, the ramified and unramified degree-one
prime generators are respectively
\[
(\rho_P,\sigma_P)=(3+2\theta,3-\theta),\qquad
(\rho_Q,\sigma_Q)=(1-2\theta+3\theta^2,3+2\theta-2\theta^2).
\]
All have norm $\ell$. Their valuation parities must agree,
so the sole candidate direction is $\rho\sigma$.
Class number one and the unit calculation prove that this list
contains every possible global Kummer class; the negative norm
eliminates $-1$.

The $\rho\sigma$ direction is impossible. At the two primes
over $\ell$, the untwisted primary root residues are $(19,20)$
modulo 23 and $(19,2)$ modulo 83. The odd-quotient residues
are $(11,7)$ and $(45,54)$. Each pair is distinct, also after
multiplication by two. An integral rational abscissa therefore
cannot have odd valuation at both primes. A nonintegral
abscissa has even valuation, as above. This excludes the
direction in every case.

For clarity, the remaining dyadic calculation is specified
completely. Order the generators as
\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
P\text{ even}&(\eta_P,\rho_P\sigma_P)\\
P\text{ odd}&(\eta_P,\rho_P\sigma_P,\gamma_{5,P})\\
Q\text{ even}&(\eta_Q,\gamma_2,\rho_Q\sigma_Q)\\
Q\text{ odd}&(\eta_Q,\gamma_2,\rho_Q\sigma_Q,\gamma_{5,Q}).
\end{array}
\]
A binary mask denotes the corresponding product $\beta$.
Reduce
\[
\beta(a+b\theta+c\theta^2)^2+\alpha d^2
\tag{B-CENTER-KUMMER-QUADRICS}
\]
in the indicated integral basis and set its last two coefficients
equal to zero. A rational Kummer preimage gives a primitive
$\mathbb Z_2$ solution of these two quadrics. For each modulus
$2^n$, enumerate the four charts whose first odd coordinate is
one and whose earlier coordinates are even; enumerate all
residues of the other coordinates. This covers every primitive
solution, including all denominator possibilities.

The following table records every dyadically excluded mask and
the first empty modulus exponent. Delete also every mask
containing the already excluded $\rho\sigma$ bit. The resulting
sets in the last column are therefore unconditional upper
bounds on the rational Kummer image; a retained mask is not
asserted to be a soluble covering.

| Factor | Dyadic exclusions, mask: exponent | Final masks |
|---|---|---|
| $P$, even, 1 | $2:4,\ 3:5$ | $0,1$ |
| $P$, even, 2 | $2:4,\ 3:4$ | $0,1$ |
| $P$, odd, 1 | $1:4,\ 2:4,\ 4:4,\ 7:4$ | $0,5$ |
| $P$, odd, 2 | $2:4,\ 3:4,\ 4:4,\ 5:4$ | $0,1$ |
| $Q$, even, 1 | $1:4,\ 3:5,\ 4:5,\ 5:4,\ 6:5,\ 7:5$ | $0,2$ |
| $Q$, even, 2 | $4:4,\ 5:4,\ 6:5,\ 7:5$ | $0,1,2,3$ |
| $Q$, odd, 1 | $1:4,\ 2:5,\ 4:4,\ 7:5,\ 9:4,\ 10:5,\ 12:4,\ 15:5$ | $0,3,8,11$ |
| $Q$, odd, 2 | $2:6,\ 3:6,\ 4:4,\ 5:4,\ 6:5,\ 7:5,\ 8:4,\ 9:4,\ 10:5,\ 11:5,\ 14:6,\ 15:6$ | $0,1$ |

The complete residue counts have independent implementations:
one lifts every projective solution, and the other enumerates
the full normalized residue arrays directly. Both give this table.
All eight cubics are irreducible, so there is no rational
two-torsion; the sizes of these subgroups give the upper ranks.

For the lower ranks, the good-reduction point-count triples at
$3,7,11$, in the same order, are
\[
(5,12,14),(3,12,10),(3,8,14),(5,8,10),
(3,11,11),(5,11,13),(5,9,17),(3,9,7).
\]
Each has gcd one, proving trivial rational torsion. Visible
nonidentity points are $(0,5)$ on the untwisted even models,
$(0,25)$ on the untwisted odd models, $(2,8)$ on both
twisted even models and $(50,200)$ on both twisted odd
models. These prove all six rank-one lower bounds.
For $Q$ even with $\delta=2$, use $(2,8),(-2,32)$;
for $Q$ odd with $\delta=1$, use $(11,80),(15,80)$.
Kummer square characters at the simple field roots
$(p,\theta)=(13,7),(23,11)$ give respectively the matrices
\[
\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Their determinants are one over $\mathbb F_2$, so each pair
is independent modulo twice the group and proves rank two.
Together with the upper bounds this proves the rank table.

The two quotient differentials span the regular differentials
of each genus-two curve. Its Jacobian is therefore isogenous
over $\mathbb Q$ to the product of the displayed elliptic
quotients, and hence
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{rank}J(U^2=\delta P(v^2))=2,\qquad
\operatorname{rank}J(V^2=\delta Q(v^2))=3
\quad(\delta=1,2).}
\tag{B-CENTER-COVER-RANKS}
\]
These are ranks of the new genus-two quotients, not of $J(C_5)$.
The two $P$ curves have independent rational elliptic factors
of rank one and rational Néron--Severi rank at least two, so
they meet the usual sufficient quadratic-Chabauty rank
inequality $2<2+2-1$. This supplies an applicable method. Section 12.26 completes the rational-point determination by a smaller cubic-field elliptic descent and one dyadic annihilator, so no remaining quadratic-Chabauty computation is needed for these two curves.



### 12.24. The offset K3 and constant-corrected quaternion pullbacks

The offset cover has a useful projective model that retains the
two additive offsets. In coordinates $(a,b,s,t,\xi,\eta)$ in
$\mathbb P^5$, it is
\[
\begin{aligned}
a^2+\xi^2&=b^2+\eta^2,\\
s^2&=a^2-\eta^2-2\xi\eta,\\
t^2&=a^2-\eta^2+2\xi\eta.
\end{aligned}
\tag{Q-OFFSET-THREE-QUADRICS}
\]
Forgetting $(\xi,\eta)$ gives the degree-two map to the
product quartic: generically $4\xi\eta=t^2-s^2$, so the
two choices are simultaneous reversal. The identities are
\[
H=a^2+\xi^2=b^2+\eta^2
 =s^2+(\xi+\eta)^2=t^2+(\xi-\eta)^2.
\tag{Q-OFFSET-FOUR-NORMS}
\]
The surface is a complete intersection of three quadrics,
with exactly four geometric singular points, all rational:
\[
[1:0:0:0:0:\pm1],\qquad[0:1:0:0:\pm1:0].
\]
For completeness, a dependence of its three gradients with
coefficients $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$ requires
\[
a(\lambda_1+\lambda_2+\lambda_3)=b\lambda_1
 =s\lambda_2=t\lambda_3=0,
\]
\[
\lambda_1\xi+(-\lambda_2+\lambda_3)\eta=0,
\quad-(\lambda_1+\lambda_2+\lambda_3)\eta
 +(-\lambda_2+\lambda_3)\xi=0.
\]
Any three of the four product-coordinate coefficient vectors
are independent. In each of the six cases with exactly two
nonzero product coordinates, substitution in these equations
and the quadrics is inconsistent. This can also be checked by
normalizing the first nonzero coordinate to one and adding
$jz-1$ for the second: every resulting ideal has reduced
Gröbner basis $\{1\}$. With only $a$ nonzero the remaining
ideal is $(\xi,\eta^2-1)$; with only $b$ nonzero it is
$(\xi^2-1,\eta)$; the other two cases are empty. There is
no point with all four product coordinates zero.

At the first pair, eliminate $\xi,\eta$ locally; the tangent
cone is $b^2-(s^2+t^2)/2$. At the second it is
$a^2-(s^2+t^2)/2$. These nondegenerate ternary quadratics
show that all four singularities are ordinary double points.
Adjunction for the $(2,2,2)$ complete intersection gives
trivial dualizing sheaf, and its Koszul resolution gives
$H^1(\mathcal O)=0$. Resolving the rational double points
therefore gives a K3 surface. This geometric identification
does not remove any rational-lifting condition.

#### A complete obstruction for the constant-corrected family

Use the local abbreviations
\[
u=k+1,\quad v=k-1,\quad w=k+3,\quad q=k-7,
\quad A=32u(k+2),\quad B=u^2v^2,\quad d=-vw.
\]
The offset field extends $Y^2=X(X+A)(X+B)$ by
$\sqrt{d(X+B)}$. Consider all classes
\[
\alpha_{C,D,c,e}
 =(Cv^c,X+A)+(Dq^{c+e}w^e,X),
\quad C,D\in\mathbb Q^\times/\mathbb Q^{\times2},
\quad c,e\in\mathbb F_2.
\tag{Q-OFFSET-CONSTANT-FAMILY}
\]
This is precisely the constant-corrected normal-form family
from Section 12.19; the constants $C,D$ have unrestricted
prime support.

**Theorem.** If the pullback of (Q-OFFSET-CONSTANT-FAMILY)
is unramified on the offset field, on the offset-plus-center
field, or on the full-root field, that pullback is identically
zero. In fact the only possible parameter choices are
\[
(C,D,c,e)=(1,1,0,0),\quad(-1,1,1,1).
\tag{Q-OFFSET-CONSTANT-ZERO}
\]
This theorem concerns the stated family. It is not a computation
of the complete Brauer group of any of these covers and does
not include arbitrary additional classes from $\operatorname{Br}\mathbb Q(k)$.

**Proof on the offset field.** The tame-symbol convention is
$\partial(f,g)=(-1)^{v(f)v(g)}f^{v(g)}/g^{v(f)}$ modulo
squares. Three divisorial charts give the necessary conditions
in the following table.

| Divisor | Offset residue field | Necessary constant squareclass condition |
|---|---|---|
| Outer component at $k=1$ | $\mathbb Q(\sqrt3)(r)$ | $D(-2)^{c+e}\in\langle3\rangle$ |
| Nonidentity component at $k=-2$ | $\mathbb Q(\sqrt3)(r)$ | $CD(-1)^e\in\langle3\rangle$ |
| Outer component at $k=-3$ | $\mathbb Q(i)(r)$ | $C\in\langle-1\rangle$ |

Here $\langle a\rangle=\{1,[a]\}$. At $k=1$, put
$\tau=k-1,X=\tau z,Y=\tau y$. The component is
$y^2=192z^2$; the offset radicand divided by $\tau^2$
has residue $-4z$, so its extension permits $z=-r^2$.
The units $X+A,q,w$ have residues $192,-6,4$.
At $k=-2$, put $X=\tau z,Y=\tau y,\tau=k+2$;
the component is the rational conic $y^2=9z(z-32)$,
and the offset radicand has residue 27. Both $X,X+A$
have valuation one, and their symbol residue is
$CD3^c(-1)^e$. At $k=-3$, put $X+A=\tau z$,
$Y=\tau y,\tau=k+3$; the component is
$y^2=-64z^2$, and the offset radicand divided by
$\tau^2$ has residue $4z$. Its constant field is
$\mathbb Q(i)$ and its residue is $C(-1)^{c+e}$.
These computations give the table exactly.

The first and third conditions write
$D=(-2)^{c+e}3^j$ and $C=(-1)^i$. Substitution in the
second, first using the parity at two and then the sign,
forces
\[
c=e,\qquad C=(-1)^c,\qquad D=3^j.
\tag{Q-OFFSET-OUTER-CONSTRAINTS}
\]
This also excludes all other primes from the constants.

The exact affine torsor presentation is
\[
W^2=-F_1F_2,\quad
F_1=wz_0^2+vu^2,\quad F_2=vz_0^2+uqw,
\]
\[
X=-vF_1,\quad X+A=-wF_2,\quad X+B=dz_0^2.
\]
Quaternion bilinearity, the Steinberg relation
$(v,w)=(-1,w)$, and the norm identity
$X=dz_0^2-(uv)^2$ show that the uncorrected sum of the
two geometric directions restricts to $(-1,F_1)$.
Adding the correction $(-1,X+A)$ changes it to
$(-1,w)$, since $F_1(X+A)=wW^2$. Thus the surviving
class is
\[
\alpha|_{\rm off}=c(-1,w)+j(3,X).
\tag{Q-OFFSET-TWO-REMAINDERS}
\]

At $k=-1$, use $\tau=k+1,X=\tau^3z,Y=\tau^3y$.
The chart equation is exactly
\[
y^2=z(32+32\tau+\tau^2z)((\tau-2)^2+\tau z).
\tag{Q-OFFSET-SPINOR-CHART}
\]
Its special component is $y^2=128z$, with rational residue
field. The offset radicand divided by $\tau^2$ has residue
16, so there are split unramified preimages. The first
symbol of (Q-OFFSET-TWO-REMAINDERS) has zero residue;
the second has residue $3^j$ because $v(X)=3$.
Consequently $j=0$ on the offset field.

The remaining symbol is identically zero, not merely
unramified. Put
\[
Q_0=32u,\quad h_0=uw,\quad
L=dz_0^2-(k-5)u^2w.
\]
Direct substitution in the quartic proves
\[
L^2-dW^2=Q_0(h_0^2-dz_0^2).
\tag{Q-OFFSET-NORM-CERTIFICATE}
\]
Thus $Q_0$ is the norm of
$(L+W\sqrt d)/(h_0+z_0\sqrt d)$, and
$(d,2u)=0$ because $Q_0/(2u)=16$.
Already over $\mathbb Q(k)$ one has $(d,2u)=(-1,w)$:
put $x=u/2$ and use
$(d,2u)=(1-x^2,x)=(-1,1+x)$ together with
$(-1,2)=0$. This proves the claimed vanishing on the
offset field for the two parameter choices.

#### Persistence through the center and individual roots

It remains to show that no other choice can become unramified
only after the larger extensions. In the offset field adjoin
$h$ with $h^2=H$. Write
\[
(D_1,D_2,D_3,D_4)=(\xi,\eta,\xi+\eta,\xi-\eta),
\quad(q_1,q_2,q_3,q_4)=(a,b,s,t).
\]
The full-root extension then adjoins the four square roots
of $1+D_i/h$; the other root in each pair is recovered from
\[
(1+D_i/h)(1-D_i/h)=(q_i/h)^2.
\tag{Q-OFFSET-ROOT-NORMALIZATION}
\]
These are the actual roots with central root normalized to one.

For the three outer witnesses, the successive residue extensions
have rational places over their existing quadratic constant
fields. Here are explicit places, obtained from the inverse B
map of Section 12.6:

| Base | Product specialization $(a,b,s,t)$ | $H$ | Offset specialization $(\xi,\eta)$ | Field of the place |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| $1$ | $(-1,-1,1,-1)$ | $1$ | $(0,0)$ | $\mathbb Q(\sqrt3)$ |
| $-3$ | $(-1,1,1,-1)$ | $1$ | $(0,0)$ | $\mathbb Q(i)$ |
| $-2$ | $(2,-1,1,-1)$ | $4$ | $(0,\sqrt3)$ | $\mathbb Q(\sqrt3)$ |

For the first row, the outer chart has
$R=2+64/(z-48)$ and quartic ordinate $64y/(z-48)^2$;
put $z=-r^2,y=8\sqrt3z$ and take $r=0$.
For the second, use $R=2+64/(z-16)$ and ordinate
$64y/(z-16)^2$, with $z=r^2,y=8iz,r=0$.
The third is the point $(z,y)=(0,0)$ on
$y^2=9z(z-32)$, equivalently the residue of the product
section $(-2/(k+1),-1,1,-1)$.
The first two rows make every normalized root radicand one.
For the third they are one and $1\pm\sqrt3/2$, with
square roots $(\sqrt3\pm1)/2$ in the same field.
All these specialized units are nonzero. Thus a branch of
each successive residue cover has a rational place over the
listed field, and its divisorial ramification index is one.

If a function field has an $L$-rational place, its algebraic
constant field embeds into $L$. Therefore a rational constant
that becomes square in that function field must already be
square in $L$. Since the residue extensions already contain
$L$, their constant squareclass kernels are exactly the same
as those in the earlier table. This proves that
(Q-OFFSET-OUTER-CONSTRAINTS) remains necessary on the
center and full-root fields.

For the last witness, write $\kappa=\mathbb Q(y)$ with
$z=y^2/128$ in (Q-OFFSET-SPINOR-CHART). On either
offset branch, the inverse B map in the chart $s=1$ has
generic leading terms
\[
\begin{aligned}
a&=\tau^{-1}\frac{-4(-y+2z+8)}{z^2-24z+16}+O(1),\\
b&=-\frac{-yz-4y+4z^2-32z+64}{4(z^2-24z+16)}+O(\tau),\\
t&=\frac{(z-4)(-y+2z+8)}{2(z^2-24z+16)}+O(\tau).
\end{aligned}
\tag{Q-OFFSET-SPINOR-PRODUCTS}
\]
Each displayed leading coefficient is nonzero in $\kappa$.
Hence $v(a)=-1$, $v(b)=v(s)=v(t)=0$, and $H/a^2$
has residue one. The center extension splits with $v(h)=-1$.
Moreover $\xi^2=b^2-(1+t^2)/2$ is integral and
$\eta^2=H-b^2$, so the normalized offsets have residues
$(\xi/h,\eta/h)=(0,\pm1)$.

Every nonvanishing radicand in (Q-OFFSET-ROOT-NORMALIZATION)
therefore has residue one or two. If a radicand vanishes,
the opposite factor is a unit of residue two and its paired
$q_i/h$ has valuation one. The radicand has valuation two
and leading unit a nonzero square divided by two. Thus all
four root extensions are unramified, and their total residue
field is exactly
\[
\kappa(\sqrt2)=\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)(y).
\]
It contains $\sqrt2$ from a radicand of residue two, and
the other leading units require no larger extension.
The constant three is still nonsquare. Consequently the
residue of $j(3,X)$ remains $3^j$, forcing $j=0$ also
on the full-root field. The intermediate center field has
the same conclusion. The explicit norm certificate then
proves zero in all three cases, completing the theorem.

The singular-locus computation, the four divisorial charts,
the inverse-map leading coefficients, the constant-squareclass
enumeration and the norm identity have separate exact replay
certificates. The proof uses divisorial residues and function
field identities; it does not extrapolate from finitely many
specializations or exclude all possible Brauer obstructions.



### 12.25. The offset lattice, its rational form, and its Jacobian Brauer group

Write $\mathcal C$ for the minimal offset K3 of Section 12.24
and $J$ for its elliptic Jacobian surface. With the same $A,B,u,v,w$,
\[
J:\ y^2=x^3+(4B-2A)x^2+A^2x.
\]
It has rational sections
\[
P_4=(A,2Auv),\qquad G=(32u,64u^2w),\qquad 2P_4=(0,0).
\]
The degree-two isogeny to the original B pencil is
\[
X=\frac{y^2}{4x^2}-B,\qquad
Y=\frac{y(x^2-A^2)}{8x^2};
\tag{Q-OFFSET-JACOBIAN-ISOGENY}
\]
it sends $G$ to the established section $S$. All these identities
follow by substitution and the duplication formula.

The exact geometric and arithmetic conclusions are
\[
\boxed{T(J)=\operatorname{diag}(2,6),\quad
T(\mathcal C)=\begin{pmatrix}8&4\\4&8\end{pmatrix},\quad
\operatorname{Br}(J)=\operatorname{Br}_0(J).}
\tag{Q-OFFSET-LATTICE-THEOREM}
\]
The last equality concerns $J$, not $\mathcal C$ or the full-root surface.

#### Jacobian fibers, saturation, and lattice

The minimal discriminant is
\[
\Delta_J=2^{28}(k-7)(k-1)^2(k+1)^7(k+2)^4(k+3)^2.
\]
The fibers at $-1,1,-3,-2,7,\infty$ are respectively
$I_1^*,I_2,I_2,I_4,I_1,I_8$.
At the four finite multiplicative fibers $c_4$ is a unit.
At $-1$, its valuation is two and the discriminant valuation
is seven, giving a minimal $I_1^*$ fiber in characteristic zero.
At infinity, $x'=z^4x,y'=z^6y,z=1/k$ gives a unit $c_4$
and discriminant order eight. The Euler numbers sum to 24.
The root lattices are $D_5,A_1,A_1,A_3,A_7$, with determinant
$4\cdot2\cdot2\cdot4\cdot8=512$ and rank seventeen.
Isogeny with the original pencil gives geometric Mordell--Weil rank one.

Use the $D_5$ chain $1-2-3$ with tips $4,5$ attached to 3,
and the standard $A_{n-1}$ chain with omitted identity component zero.
The actual component positions are

| Section | $-1:D_5$ | $1:A_1$ | $-3:A_1$ | $-2:A_3$ | $\infty:A_7$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| $G$ | 4 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 3 |
| $P_4$ | 5 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 2 |
| $2P_4$ | 1 | 0 | 0 | 2 | 4 |

Here are local checks establishing the table independently of its
intersection matrix. At $u=0$, write $a_2=u\alpha,a_4=u^2\beta$,
where $\alpha=4u^3-16u^2-48u-64$ and $\beta=1024(u+1)^2$.
The chart $x=ux_1,y=uy_1$ has special cubic $x_1(x_1-32)^2$.
At the double root, put $x_1=32+ux_2,y_1=uy_2$; the special
equation is $y_2^2=128^2$. The sections $G,P_4$ tend to
$(x_2,y_2)=(0,128),(32,-128)$, respectively, meeting opposite
spinor tips. The point $2P_4$ meets the vector tip at the simple root.
At 1 the special cubic is $x(x-192)^2$, with section abscissas
64 and 192; at $-3$ it is $x(x+64)^2$, with abscissas $-64,64$.
At $-2$, $G$ avoids the node while $P_4$ meets an outer component;
the node slopes are $\pm6$.
At infinity the slopes are $\pm2$; both sections approach the
$+2$ tangent, with abscissa orders three and two, so have the
common orientation shown. All section coordinates are affine in
every minimal chart, giving $G\cdot O=P_4\cdot O=0$.

Geometric torsion injects into the additive $I_1^*$ component
group: its formal kernel and additive identity component are
torsion-free in residue characteristic zero. Hence the full torsion
is $C_4$, already supplied by $P_4$.
The height formula gives
\[
h(G)=4-\frac54-\frac12-\frac{15}{8}=\frac38.
\]
Independently, isogeny functoriality gives $2h(G)=h(S)=3/4$.
All section heights belong to $(1/8)\mathbb Z$, by the inverse
Cartan denominators. If $G=mG_0$ modulo torsion, then
$8h(G_0)=3/m^2$ is integral, forcing $m=1$.
Thus $G,P_4$ generate the full geometric Mordell--Weil group.
The elliptic discriminant formula [36] now gives
\[
\det\operatorname{NS}(J)=-512(3/8)/4^2=-12.
\]
The positive even rank-two possibilities for $T(J)$ are
$\operatorname{diag}(2,6)$ and $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}4&2\\2&4\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.
Pullback along (Q-OFFSET-JACOBIAN-ISOGENY) embeds the original
transcendental lattice with its form multiplied by two, so
$\operatorname{diag}(8,24)$ embeds in $T(J)$.
The second candidate cannot represent eight: it would require
$a^2+ab+b^2=2$, impossible modulo three. This selects
$T(J)=\operatorname{diag}(2,6)$. An independent integral
calculation gives a section/root lattice of determinant $-192$,
its torsion overlattice of index four, and discriminant group
$C_2\oplus C_6$ with the required quadratic form.

Every component is defined over $\mathbb Q$. The $I_4,I_8$
resolutions split by their rational slopes; $A_1$ has no
nontrivial diagram permutation. The rational order-four section
fixes a spinor tip of $D_5$, eliminating its sole nontrivial
diagram involution. Together with $O,F,G,P_4$, these generate
the entire integral Néron--Severi group. Thus its Galois action
is pointwise trivial and $H^1(\mathbb Q,\operatorname{NS}(J))=0$.

#### The geometric torsor index and two conic bisections

The offset quartic has a degree-two map to the $z$-line, hence
a divisor of degree two over $\mathbb C(k)$. It has no point
over that field: such a point would give B Kummer character $d$,
whereas the complete geometric group of the original pencil has
character image $\{1,(k+1)(k-7)\}$. The simple zeros of $d$
exclude both classes. Its geometric multisection index is therefore two.
The torsor-lattice theorem [42], Lemma 4.4(iii),(iv), applies to
elliptic K3 surfaces of arbitrary Picard rank. It embeds
$T(\mathcal C)$ as an index-two kernel in $T(J)$.
The three possible kernels are
\[
\operatorname{diag}(2,24),\quad\operatorname{diag}(6,8),\quad
\begin{pmatrix}8&4\\4&8\end{pmatrix},
\tag{Q-OFFSET-THREE-KERNELS}
\]
all of determinant 48.

On (Q-OFFSET-THREE-QUADRICS), consider the two conics
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_0:&\quad\eta=0,\quad a=s=-t,\quad b^2=a^2+\xi^2,\\
D_1:&\quad\xi=0,\quad b=s=-t,\quad a^2=b^2+\eta^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
The B base function is $(k+2)=(a+b+s)(a+b+t)/(a^2+\xi^2)$.
Its restrictions are $k=-1+2a/b$ and $k=-1+2b/a$,
respectively. Thus both conics are bisections, ramified at
$1,-3$, and are the inverse images of $O,S$ on the original
pencil. Their strict transforms are smooth rational curves,
meeting disjoint pairs of surface nodes. They meet each other
only at the smooth point $[1:1:1:-1:0:0]$, where $\xi,\eta$
are local coordinates and the conics are the coordinate axes.
Consequently $D_i^2=-2$, $F\cdot D_i=2$, and $D_0\cdot D_1=1$.

The offset fibers have the same Kodaira types as $J$. With one
tip met by $D_0$ chosen as the omitted component, their root
component incidences, all with multiplicity one, are

| Bisection | $D_5$ at $-1$ | $A_1$ at 1 | $A_1$ at $-3$ | $A_3$ at $-2$ | $A_7$ at infinity |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $D_0$ | 1 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 4 |
| $D_1$ | 4,5 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 3,7 |

For the additive fiber, the offset double cover branches over
original components $\Theta_1,\Theta_3,\Theta_6$ of $I_2^*$.
The components $\Theta_0,\Theta_5$ each split into two tips;
the covers of $\Theta_2,\Theta_4$ are connected. Contracting
the three ramification $(-1)$-curves gives $I_1^*$, with
$D_0,D_1$ meeting the two respective tip pairs.
At 1 and $-3$, the two ramification components of the original
$I_4$ contract to the crossings of $I_2$. Directly, near the
rational crossing the local base equations are
\[
k-1=-(\xi^2+4\xi\eta+\eta^2)+O(4),\qquad
k+3=\xi^2+\eta^2+O(4),
\]
respectively. The conic axes meet both branches transversely.
At $-2$ and infinity, identifying the local torsor with its
Jacobian over algebraically closed Laurent series sends the
preimages of $O$ to $0,2P_4$, and those of $S$ to $G,G+2P_4$.
The established component table then gives the remaining pairs
$(0,2),(0,2)$ and $(0,4),(3,7)$.

Let $L$ be generated by $F,D_0,D_1$ and the seventeen root
components, using these pairings and the negative Cartan blocks.
Exact determinant and Smith calculations give
\[
\det L=-3072,\qquad L^*/L\cong C_2^2\oplus C_4^3\oplus C_{12}.
\tag{Q-OFFSET-BISECTION-LATTICE}
\]
The full Néron--Severi lattice is an integral overlattice of
$L$, so its discriminant group is a subquotient of $L^*/L$;
its exponent divides twelve. Since primitive complementary
$\operatorname{NS}$ and $T$ lattices have opposite discriminant
forms, $T(\mathcal C)$ has the same exponent constraint.
The first two candidates in (Q-OFFSET-THREE-KERNELS) have
exponent 24; only the third has exponent twelve. This proves
the asserted offset lattice. Its full Néron--Severi group has
index eight over $L$. No particular index-eight gluing is
assumed in this selection.

#### Complex identification and the rational-form obstruction

The offset lattice is twice $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}4&2\\2&4\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.
The product construction and Kummer scaling of [37] give periods
$(-1+i\sqrt3)/2$ and $1+i\sqrt3$, with $j$ invariants
0 and 54000. Thus over $\mathbb C$,
\[
\mathcal C\cong\operatorname{Km}(E_0\times E_*),\qquad
E_0:y^2=x^3+1,\quad E_*:y^2=x^3-15x+22.
\]
Swapping the lattice basis reverses orientation, so there is
no unresolved orientation choice. This is the mixed product,
and differs from the original product K3 with lattice
$\operatorname{diag}(4,12)$.

It is not a rational identification with the displayed standard
Kummer model. Write $\chi_m$ for the quadratic character of
$\mathbb Q(\sqrt m)$. The exact rational characters are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{NS}(\mathcal C)\otimes\mathbb Q
 &=12\cdot1+3\chi_3+5\chi_{-1},\\
\operatorname{NS}(\operatorname{Km}(E_0\times E_*))\otimes\mathbb Q
 &=12\cdot1+3\chi_3+4\chi_{-3}+\chi_{-1}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{Q-OFFSET-RATIONAL-FORMS}
\]
For the first formula, $F,D_0,D_1$ give three fixed classes.
The additive fiber has four rational tips from the four rational
nodes; its two central components are then fixed, giving five
fixed root classes. The $I_2$ component pairs at $1,-3$ are
exchanged over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt3),\mathbb Q(i)$, as their
local tangents show. At $-2$ the torsor trivializes over
$\mathbb Q(\sqrt3)((k+2))$; conjugation changes the origin by
$2P_4$, hence rotates the four split Jacobian components by two.
The quotient by the fiber relation contributes $1+2\chi_3$.
At infinity the corresponding field is $\mathbb Q(i)$ and
the rotation is four in $I_8$, contributing $3+4\chi_{-1}$.
Adding the contributions proves the formula, without assuming
that the chosen omitted torsor components are rational.

For the standard product, the two four-point two-torsion
permutation characters are $3+\chi_{-3}$ and $3+\chi_3$.
Their product gives the sixteen exceptional Kummer curves.
The curves admit a rational two-isogeny: shifting $E_0$ by
its rational root and taking the quotient gives $E_*$ after
a rational translation. Their rank-two geometric Hom space
therefore has character $1+\chi_{-3}$. With the two factor
classes, the abelian-surface divisor contribution is
$3+\chi_{-3}$. The sum proves the second formula.
The distinct characters exclude a $\mathbb Q$-isomorphism;
birational smooth K3 surfaces are isomorphic, so also exclude
a $\mathbb Q$-birational identification with that standard
model. This is not an obstruction to rational offset points.

#### The intrinsic rational Brauer group of the Jacobian

For each prime $\ell$, use the actual integral modules
\[
H=H^2_{\rm et}(\overline J,\mathbb Z_\ell(1)),\quad
N=\operatorname{NS}(\overline J)\otimes\mathbb Z_\ell,
\quad T=N^\perp,\quad\Lambda=H/N=T^*.
\]
The last equivariant identification uses the unimodular pairing
and primitive inclusions; it is not an integral direct-sum
assumption. Since $N$ is fixed pointwise, equivariant
discriminant gluing makes $\Lambda/T$ Galois-trivial.
The degree-two map to the original K3 identifies rational
transcendental Galois representations. Consequently the certified
Frobenius determinants of Section 12.19 transfer:
\[
\det(1-F_7)=12/7,\qquad\det(1-F_{13})=48/13.
\]
The representations, and hence their stable integral lattices,
are unramified there. The same determinant argument, using
the other counting prime for the primary parts 7 and 13,
bounds the order of $\operatorname{Br}(\overline J)^{G_\mathbb Q}$ by twelve.

At two the lattice $\operatorname{diag}(2,6)$ gives $T=2\Lambda$.
Thus $F_7-1$ maps $\Lambda$ into $2\Lambda$, while its
determinant has valuation two. The integral operator
$B_2=(F_7-1)/2$ is therefore invertible on $\Lambda$.
An actual $\beta\in\operatorname{Br}(J)[2]$ lifts through
the global Kummer sequence to $H^2(J,\mu_2)$. Its geometric
restriction is invariant in $H/2H$. Lift it to $x\in H$
and let $\lambda$ be its orthogonal projection to
$T\otimes\mathbb Q_2$, identified with an element of $\Lambda$.
The rational $N$ component is fixed, so invariance gives
\[
(F_7-1)\lambda=(F_7-1)x
 \in2H\cap(T\otimes\mathbb Q_2)=2T=4\Lambda.
\]
Primitivity justifies the intersection equality. Invertibility
of $B_2$ forces $\lambda\in2\Lambda$, so the geometric
Brauer image is zero. Since $H^1(\mathbb Q,N)=0$, the
class is constant. A quotient class of order two modulo
constants can be normalized to actual two-torsion by subtracting
its value at a rational point on the zero section. Hence the
entire two-primary quotient vanishes. The invariant geometric
two-torsion itself is not zero; the argument proves failure of
arithmetic descent.

At three, $\Lambda/T$ is a trivial cyclic group of order three.
In
\[
0\longrightarrow T/3\Lambda\longrightarrow\Lambda/3\Lambda
 \longrightarrow\Lambda/T\longrightarrow0,
\]
the outside terms are lines. The Frobenius trace is $2/7$,
its determinant is one, and $v_3\det(F_7-1)=1$, so its
reduction is a nonidentity unipotent with fixed line
$T/3\Lambda$. Complex conjugation has determinant $-1$
on the rank-two transcendental representation and acts trivially
on $\Lambda/T$; it therefore acts by $-1$ on that fixed
line. No vector of $\Lambda/3\Lambda$ is fixed by all
Galois elements. This eliminates three-primary invariants.
The order-twelve bound and algebraic vanishing complete
$\operatorname{Br}(J)=\operatorname{Br}_0(J)$.

Section 12.27 supplies the separate integral gluing and intrinsic Brauer calculation for the offset surface. Neither these proper-surface results nor the complex Kummer identification is a rational-point classification or an unrestricted denominator bound.



### 12.26. Complete determination of the coupled center curve

Put
\[
 P(T)=T^3+11T^2-29T+25,\qquad
 Q(T)=T^3+43T^2-61T+25.
\]
The smooth projective curves \(C_\delta:U^2=\delta P(v^2)\) have
the following complete rational points:

* \(C_1\): the affine points \((0,\pm5)\) and its two points at infinity.
* \(C_2\): the four affine points \((\pm1,\pm4)\), and no rational infinity.

Consequently the smooth projective genus-five curve
\[
 C_5:W^2=P(v^2)Q(v^2)
\]
has exactly the affine points
\[
 (v,W)=(0,\pm25),\quad (1,\pm8),\quad(-1,\pm8),
\]
and its two rational points at infinity.

The proof uses exact two-descent and a single dyadic elliptic
annihilator. There is no rank, Sha, saturation, or height-conjecture
assumption. The finite squareclass reduction of Section 12.23 retains the additional $Q$-square equation, which every point in the displayed final list satisfies.

#### Two fixed quartics over the cubic field

Let \(K=\mathbb Q(\theta)\), \(\theta^3-\theta-1=0\), and put
\[
 \alpha=-(2\theta+1)^2,\quad
 A=11+\alpha=10-4\theta-4\theta^2,\quad
 b=\frac5{2\theta+1}=4\theta^2-2\theta-3.
\]
Then
\[
 P(T)=(T-\alpha)(T^2+AT+b^2).
\]
The exact primary elliptic descents in Section 12.23
show that the Kummer image for each twist \(\delta=1,2\) is
\(\{1,\theta\}\). Applied to \((X,Y)=(\delta v^2,\delta U)\), this gives
\[
 \delta(v^2-\alpha)=\beta a^2,\qquad \beta\in\{1,\theta\},\quad a\in K.
 \tag{B-CENTER-K23-KUMMER}
\]
For finite rational \(v\), \(v^2-\alpha\ne0\), since
\(\alpha=-(2\theta+1)^2<0\) at the real embedding. Define \(Z=U/a\).
The quartic target is exactly
\[
 D_\beta: Z^2=\beta(v^4+Av^2+b^2).
 \tag{B-CENTER-K23-QUARTICS}
\]
There is **no additional \(\delta\) factor** in (B-CENTER-K23-QUARTICS).
Equation (B-CENTER-K23-KUMMER) remains the residual conic condition. We use only the
necessary implication to (B-CENTER-K23-QUARTICS), so no reverse lift has been assumed.

The elliptic Jacobians of these quartics have the scaled models
\[
 E_\beta:y^2=x
   \bigl(x-\beta(\theta-1)^2\bigr)
   \bigl(x-\beta(4-3\theta^2)\bigr).
 \tag{B-CENTER-K23-ELLIPTICS}
\]
The complete full-two-descent calculation below proves
\[
 \dim_{\mathbb F_2}\operatorname{Sel}_2(E_1/K)=2,\qquad
 \dim_{\mathbb F_2}\operatorname{Sel}_2(E_\theta/K)=3.
 \tag{B-CENTER-K23-RANKS}
\]
For completeness, the global squareclass space has eight columns.
The field has integral basis \(1,\theta,\theta^2\), class number one,
and unit classes generated by \(-1,\theta\). Root differences in
(B-CENTER-K23-ELLIPTICS) have norms \(1,-23,25\). Only the inert prime over two, the
degree-two prime over five generated by \(4+\theta-2\theta^2\),
and the simple prime over 23 generated by \(3-\theta\) occur.
Units and two give two columns each; the five-prime gives one in
coordinates 1 and 2; the 23-prime gives one in coordinates 0 and 2.
At the real place the first two signs agree. The certified local
images have their maximal dimensions 5,2,2 at the three finite
places; intersecting their inverse images gives (B-CENTER-K23-RANKS).

The finite local calculation in (B-CENTER-K23-RANKS) can be
reproduced from the following data. Number the roots of (B-CENTER-K23-ELLIPTICS) as
$e_0=0,e_1=\beta(\theta-1)^2,e_2=\beta(4-3\theta^2)$.
For each $g=-1,\theta,2$, take in order the two global columns
$(g,1,g),(1,g,g)$; append $(1,q_5,q_5)$ and
$(\pi_{23},1,\pi_{23})$, where
$q_5=4+\theta-2\theta^2$, $\pi_{23}=3-\theta$.
A mask uses these eight columns in that order, starting with bit zero.

At the inert dyadic prime, use the squareclass basis
$(3,5,\theta,\theta+2\theta^2,2)$, with the valuation bit last.
Its completeness is checked by all 448 units modulo eight:
their 28 distinct squares give sixteen cosets, and the first
four displayed classes generate them. At an odd unramified
place encode a squareclass by valuation parity plus twice its
unit nonsquare bit. Encode a full Kummer tuple by its first
coordinate plus $2^w$ times its second, with $w=5$ at two
and $w=2$ at the odd places; its third coordinate is their sum.
At five use the unramified quadratic field with
$\tau^2+2\tau+3=0$, and embed $\theta$ by its unique
Hensel lift congruent to $\tau$ modulo five. At 23 use the
simple root congruent to three.

| Place | Eight global column signatures |
|---|---|
| $2$ | $3,96,4,128,16,512,320,7$ |
| degree-two prime at $5$ | $0,0,2,8,0,0,12,2$ |
| simple prime at $23$ | $2,8,0,0,0,0,0,1$ |

The following are actual local Kummer witnesses. $T_i$ denotes
the two-torsion point with abscissa $e_i$ and the standard
derivative convention for its zero factor; the other entries
are abscissas whose three-factor product is a local square.

| $\beta$ | Place | Witness abscissas | Corresponding signatures |
|---|---|---|---|
| $1$ | $2$ | $T_0,T_1,4\theta^2,1+6\theta,2+3\theta+4\theta^2$ | $96,448,32,108,78$ |
| $\theta$ | $2$ | $T_0,T_1,3\theta+\theta^2,3\theta+5\theta^2,2+3\theta+2\theta^2$ | $224,452,324,326,192$ |
| $1$ | $5$ | $T_1,1$ | $4,8$ |
| $\theta$ | $5$ | $T_0,T_1$ | $8,6$ |
| either | $23$ | $T_0,5$ | $11,2$ |

The dyadic rows have rank five, and each odd row has rank two.
These are the full local Kummer dimensions for full two-torsion:
$[K_2:\mathbb Q_2]+2=5$ and two at odd places. Thus the
witness spans equal the local images, not merely subspaces
found by a bounded search. All other finite places are odd
with good reduction and impose the already included unramified
condition. The real root ordering is $e_2<0<e_1$, giving
equality of the first two sign bits.
Intersecting the inverse images gives exactly
\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
\beta=1&0,72,135,207,\\
\beta=\theta&0,8,68,76,135,143,195,203.
\end{array}
\tag{B-CENTER-K23-MASKS}
\]
Independent implementations use different dyadic coset bases
and reconstruct every witness, column, local dimension and
final mask. The class-number-one support proof supplies
global completeness; no unspecified prime search is used.


Both torsion groups are exactly \((\mathbb Z/2)^2\).
For \(E_1\), degree-one reductions \((7,\theta=5)\),
\((11,\theta=6)\) have 4 and 12 points. For \(E_\theta\),
the reductions at these two primes and \((19,\theta=6)\) have
12,12,28 points. The resulting bound four, together with full
two-torsion, proves the assertion.

The quartic \(D_1\) has origin \((v,Z)=(0,b)\) and the exact map
\[
 x_c=\frac{2b(Z+b)}{v^2},\qquad
 x=\frac{x_c+A}{4},\qquad
 y=\frac{v(x_c^2-4b^2)}{16b}.
 \tag{B-CENTER-K23-UNTWISTED-MAP}
\]
Its two points over zero map to \(O,(0,0)\), and its two infinities
map to the other two torsion points. These exhaust \(E_1(K)\)
by (B-CENTER-K23-RANKS). Therefore
\[
 D_1(K)\text{ has only the four points just listed.}
 \tag{B-CENTER-K23-UNTWISTED-POINTS}
\]
The formula has an inverse away from these charts, namely
\(v=16by/((4x-A)^2-4b^2)\), so no affine point is lost.

#### The dyadic domains force the appropriate quartic

The prime two is inert in \(K\), so \(K_2/\mathbb Q_2\) is
unramified cubic with ring of integers
\(\mathcal O=\mathbb Z_2[\theta]\). The unit \(\theta\) is not a square
in \(K_2\): exhaustive squaring in
\((\mathbb Z/4)[\theta]/(\theta^3-\theta-1)\) already excludes it.

For \(C_1\), direct valuations of \(P(v^2)\) show that every nonzero
rational \(v\) has \(v_2(v)\ge2\) or \(v_2(v)\le-2\).
Indeed odd \(v\) gives \(P(v^2)\equiv8\bmod16\); valuation \(1\)
or \(-1\), after removing the square factor in the latter case,
gives a unit congruent to 5 modulo eight. With
\(s_0=2\theta+1\), if \(v_2(v)\ge2\) then
\[
 v^2-\alpha=s_0^2(1+v^2/s_0^2),
\]
and if \(v_2(v)\le-2\), it is
\(v^2(1+s_0^2/v^2)\). The parenthesized term is in \(1+16\mathcal O\)
and is a square. Thus (B-CENTER-K23-KUMMER) must have \(\beta=1\).
Together with (B-CENTER-K23-UNTWISTED-POINTS), this proves the assertion for \(C_1\), including
its \(v=0\) and infinity charts.

For \(C_2\), a parameter of nonzero valuation would make
\(2P(v^2)\) have odd valuation. For odd \(v\), \(P(v^2)\) has
valuation three, and the necessary condition that
\(2P(v^2)/16\) be a unit square forces
\[
 v\equiv1\ \text{or}\ -1\pmod8.
 \tag{B-CENTER-K23-DYADIC-DOMAIN}
\]
This follows by evaluating the four odd residue classes modulo eight;
the forbidden classes \(\pm3\) give 5 modulo eight after division.
Moreover,
\[
 2(1-\alpha)=\theta(2+2\theta)^2.
\]
