For (B-CENTER-K23-DYADIC-DOMAIN), the ratio \((v^2-\alpha)/(1-\alpha)\) is in
\(1+8\mathcal O\), hence is a square. Equation (B-CENTER-K23-KUMMER) therefore forces
\(\beta=\theta\). This uses the residual conic, not a claim about all
rational coordinates of \(D_\theta\) without that condition.

#### A rank-one logarithm and a unit tangent

Put \(q=2\theta^2-2\theta\); then \(D_\theta\) contains \((1,q)\).
Choose it as origin. For \(u=v-1\), set
\[
 B=4\theta,\quad D=2\theta(A+2),\quad \sigma=\theta(A+2),\qquad
 x_c=\frac{2q(Z+q)+Du}{u^2}.
\]
The exact birational map to (B-CENTER-K23-ELLIPTICS) is
\[
 x=\frac{x_c+\sigma}{4},\qquad
 y=\frac{(x_c^2-4\theta q^2)u-(Dx_c+2Bq^2)}{16q}.
 \tag{B-CENTER-K23-TWISTED-MAP}
\]
Its invariant differential is exactly
\[
 \frac{dx}{2y}=-\frac{dv}{Z}.
 \tag{B-CENTER-K23-DIFFERENTIAL}
\]
The map and (B-CENTER-K23-DIFFERENTIAL) are exact symbolic identities, independently verified by reduction modulo the quartic and the cubic field equation.

The points \((-1,q)\), \((-1,-q)\) map respectively to
\[
 R=(-2-\theta+2\theta^2,\ 6+2\theta-5\theta^2),\qquad T=(0,0).
\]
Since \(R\) is not two-torsion, it is nontorsion. Equation (B-CENTER-K23-RANKS) thus
proves \(\operatorname{rank}E_\theta(K)=1\).

Let \(\ell=\log R\), using \(dx/(2y)\) and the elliptic logarithm
extended from the formal subgroup by division by a nonzero integer.
This construction is valid at bad reduction. Exact doubling gives
\[
 v_2(t(4R))=2,\qquad
 t(4R)/4\equiv(0,1,1)\pmod2,\quad t=-x/y.
\]
For this integral model with \(a_1=a_3=0\), the formal logarithm has
\(\log(t)-t\in t^3\mathcal O[[t^2]]\): the differential's even
coefficients are integral and the integration denominators are odd.
Consequently
\[
 \ell\in\mathcal O,\qquad \ell\equiv(0,1,1)\pmod2.
 \tag{B-CENTER-K23-LOG-DIRECTION}
\]
Write \(\ell=\ell_0+\ell_1\theta+\ell_2\theta^2\), and choose the
integral \(\mathbb Q_2\)-linear functional
\[
 \lambda(z_0+z_1\theta+z_2\theta^2)
   =z_0-(\ell_0/\ell_1)z_1.
\]
Then \(\lambda(\ell)=0\), and (B-CENTER-K23-LOG-DIRECTION) gives
\(\lambda\bmod2=(1,0,0)\). Since
\[
 2/q=1+\theta,
\]
the number \(\lambda(2/q)\) is a dyadic unit.
Rank one implies \(\lambda(\log P)=0\) for every \(P\in E_\theta(K)\):
a finite-index rank-one subgroup has the same \(\mathbb Q_2\) span.
No odd-index or saturation premise is needed for this statement.

#### The whole allowed disk, including its infinite tail

By replacing \(v\) with \(-v\) and \(Z\) with \(-Z\) as necessary,
every candidate from (B-CENTER-K23-DYADIC-DOMAIN) may be placed in
\[
 v=1+8s,\quad s\in\mathbb Z_2,\qquad
 Z=q\sqrt{1+\epsilon(s)},
\]
using the square-root branch with value one at zero. Here
\[
 \epsilon(s)=\frac{\theta((1+8s)^4+A(1+8s)^2+b^2)}{q^2}-1.
\]
Its four coefficient valuations are \(4,6,9,10\); more precisely,
\(v_2([s^j]\epsilon)\ge2j+2\) for \(1\le j\le4\).
The exact integral-basis coefficients are recorded in the symbolic
certificate. Thus the branch is analytic on the whole closed disk.

There is no integration-constant ambiguity. Put
\[
 N=2q(Z+q)+Du,\quad M=N+\sigma u^2,\quad
 J=N^2-DNu-2Bq^2u^3-4\theta q^2u^4.
\]
Formula (B-CENTER-K23-TWISTED-MAP) gives
\[
 t=-4quM/J.
\]
On this entire disk, \(N/16\), \(M/16\), and \(J/256\) are analytic
units: \(v_2(q)=1\), \(v_2(D)=3\), \(v_2(\sigma)=2\), and the
displayed leading terms dominate. Hence
\(t\in4s\mathcal O\langle s\rangle\). For $s\ne0$, the abscissa $x=M/(4u^2)$ has valuation $-4-2v_2(s)$, independently certifying formal membership. The whole disk maps into the formal subgroup, its value at zero is $O$, and its logarithm is the convergent formal logarithm there.

Write
\[
 (1+\epsilon(s))^{-1/2}=1+\sum_{n\ge1}c_ns^n.
\]
The binomial coefficient
\(\binom{-1/2}{m}=(-1)^m\binom{2m}{m}/4^m\)
has valuation at least \(-2m\). A degree-\(n\) coefficient of
\(\epsilon^m\) has valuation at least \(2n+2m\). Therefore
\[
 v_2(c_n)\ge2n\quad(n\ge1).
 \tag{B-CENTER-K23-TAIL-BOUND}
\]
Integrating (B-CENTER-K23-DIFFERENTIAL), using its exact zero constant and then applying
\(\lambda\), yields
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \lambda(\log P(s))
 &=-4\lambda(2/q)s
   -4\sum_{n\ge1}
       \frac{\lambda((2/q)c_n)}{n+1}s^{n+1}\\
 &=4s\bigl(\text{a dyadic unit}+2sG(s)\bigr),
 \qquad G\in\mathbb Z_2\langle s\rangle.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{B-CENTER-K23-ANNIHILATOR}
\]
Indeed (B-CENTER-K23-TAIL-BOUND) gives \(2n-v_2(n+1)\ge1\), tending to infinity.
The bracket in (B-CENTER-K23-ANNIHILATOR) is a unit throughout \(s\in\mathbb Z_2\).
A global point must annihilate the logarithm, so \(s=0\).
Undoing the sign changes gives only \(v=\pm1\). Substitution yields
\(U=\pm4\), proving the assertion for \(C_2\).

Finally, \(C_2\) has no rational point at infinity because its
leading coefficient is two. The leading coefficient for \(C_1\)
and \(C_5\) is one, giving the two stated infinities in each case.
Every listed finite point satisfies its original equation. This
completes the entire projective rational-point classification.

#### Consequences for the elliptic section families

For the $d$-square $2S$ family of Section 12.23, the complete
parameter relation is $k=(v^2-3)/(v^2+1)$. The only rational
center parameters $v=0,\pm1,\infty$ give respectively
$k=-3,-1,1$, all singular B fibers. Thus no smooth rational
specialization of $2S$ admits both an offset and center lift.
By the proved full-root automorphisms $Q\mapsto Q+T_0$
and $Q\mapsto S-Q$, the same exclusion holds for
$2S+T_0,-S,-S+T_0$.

In the negative-half construction, the parameter is
$u=(3-v^2)/(1+v^2)$ and the original B base is $k=u^2-2$.
The complete list gives $u=3,1,-1$, hence $k=7,-1,-1$,
again singular. The projective point classification includes
the zero, pole and infinity charts; a denominator-zero chart
cannot add a smooth parameter outside this list. This closes
both stated coupled section constructions entirely. It does
not classify other Mordell--Weil multiples, new sections on
base changes, or arbitrary points on specialized fibers.

The genus-two height input developed before this reduction
remains valid but is unnecessary for this completed family:
the fixed cubic-field quartics give exact ranks zero and one,
and one integral logarithmic annihilator suffices on the whole
allowed dyadic domain. A finite search of elliptic multiples
and a truncated power series are not used for completeness.


### 12.27. The intrinsic Brauer group of the proper offset surface

The complete offset surface $\mathcal C$ of Section 12.25,
not just its specified quaternion pullbacks, satisfies
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Br}(\mathcal C)=\operatorname{Br}_0(\mathcal C).}
\tag{Q-OFFSET-INTRINSIC-BRAUER}
\]
This completes the proper product, offset and Jacobian K3
calculations. It does not compute the intrinsic Brauer group
of the center or full-root surface, or of a boundary-deleted open set.

#### Exhaustive integral gluing and algebraic vanishing

Let $L$ be the explicit rank-twenty divisor lattice of
(Q-OFFSET-BISECTION-LATTICE). Its determinant is $-3072$,
whereas $\operatorname{NS}(\overline{\mathcal C})$ has
determinant $-48$. The latter is therefore an even overlattice
of index eight. It corresponds to an isotropic subgroup of
order eight in $L^*/L$, and every class must pair evenly
with $F$, since the geometric multisection index is two.

The Galois action on the rational lattice factors through
$V_4=\langle a,b\rangle$, where $a$ changes $\sqrt3$
and $b$ changes $i$. On the ordered basis
\[
F,D_0,D_5,A_1(1),A_1(-3),A_3(-2),A_7(\infty),D_1,
\]
both fix $F,D_0,D_1$ and the five $D_5$ roots.
The element $a$ exchanges the two components at 1 and
rotates the four components at $-2$ by two. The element
$b$ exchanges the two components at $-3$ and rotates
the eight components at infinity by four. If the target
component is the omitted component zero, substitute
$C_0=F-\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}C_j$. These rules specify integral
commuting involutions preserving the Gram matrix $M$ of
$L$, with traces $14,10,4$ for $a,b,ab$.
They also specify the exact action on every invariant
overlattice; the rational character alone is not used as
a substitute for the integral module.

There is a necessary geometric restriction on the gluing.
Over $K=\mathbb C(k)$, restriction from the smooth K3
to its generic genus-one fiber is surjective on Picard groups,
with kernel the integral vertical lattice $V$ generated
by $F$ and the seventeen roots. Indeed a divisor on the
generic fiber extends by closure, and a divisor restricting
to a principal one differs from its extended principal
divisor by vertical components. The omitted components
are integral combinations of $F$ and the chosen roots.
Here $\operatorname{Pic}(\overline{\mathcal C})=\operatorname{NS}(\overline{\mathcal C})$.
Tsen's theorem gives $\operatorname{Br}(K)=0$, so every
rational point of the generic Picard scheme is represented
by a line bundle. Thus the degree-zero quotient is
\[
\operatorname{Pic}^0(\mathcal C_K)=J(K)=\mathbb ZG\oplus C_4.
\]
The degree image is $2\mathbb Z$, represented by $D_0$.
Trivializing the torsor, the two points of $D_0$ are
$0,2P_4$, and those of $D_1$ are $G,G+2P_4$.
Their divisor sums differ by $2G$, with no residual torsion.
Consequently
\[
\operatorname{NS}(\overline{\mathcal C})/L
 \cong J(K)/(2\mathbb ZG)\cong C_4\oplus C_2.
\tag{Q-OFFSET-GLUING-COVERAGE}
\]
More specifically, if $c_1$ is the coefficient of $D_1$
in the rational $L$-basis modulo $\mathbb Z$, its image
on the gluing subgroup is exactly $\{0,1/2\}$, and its
kernel is cyclic of order four. Its free Picard coordinate
is $2c_1G$ after subtracting a degree multiple of $D_0$.
These are proved necessary conditions for the actual
lattice, rather than choices of a convenient overlattice.

The finite enumeration is as follows. The two-primary
discriminant group is $C_2^2\oplus C_4^4$, of order 1024.
Represent it by vectors $z/4$, $z\in(\mathbb Z/4)^{20}$,
with $Mz\equiv0\pmod4$; the columns of
$12M^{-1}\bmod4$ generate it. Isotropy and even fiber
pairing are the exact tests
\[
z^tMz\equiv0\pmod{32},\qquad F\cdot(z/4)\in2\mathbb Z.
\]
Enumerate all subgroups of order eight by adjoining
isotropic orthogonal generators through three stages;
every group of order eight requires at most three generators.
Test closure, stability under $a,b$, and finally the
coefficient/kernel condition in (Q-OFFSET-GLUING-COVERAGE).
Independent denominator-four and denominator-twelve
implementations give the same complete counts:

| Exact condition | Count |
|---|---:|
| Allowable isotropic vectors | 80 |
| Nonzero vectors of order two | 31 |
| Vectors of order four | 48 |
| Isotropic subgroups of order eight | 175 |
| Galois-stable subgroups | 55 |
| Subgroups satisfying the geometric Picard condition | 16 |

For each candidate, an integral basis of its overlattice
is obtained by Hermite normal form, and the two action
matrices are transported to that basis. A $V_4$ cocycle
is a pair $(r,s)$ satisfying
\[
(a+1)r=0,\quad(b+1)s=0,\quad(1-b)r+(a-1)s=0.
\]
A full Smith decomposition of this $60$-by-$40$ integer
system gives its complete integral kernel. Coboundaries
are the columns of the stacked matrix $(a-1,b-1)$.
In each of the sixteen cases, the cocycle kernel has rank
eight and the coboundary Smith factors are eight units.

A different independent calculation uses the absence of
a $\chi_3\chi_{-1}$ summand: the cocycle lattice is
$(N\cap V_{\chi_3})\oplus(N\cap V_{\chi_{-1}})$,
of ranks three and five. Saturating these intersections
using the finite gluing coordinates and comparing their
covolumes with the coboundary image reproduces the same
result. On all 55 stable candidates, the two methods give
cohomology groups $0,C_2^2,C_2^3,C_2^4,C_2^5$ with
counts $16,16,20,2,1$. Crucially, all sixteen geometrically
admissible candidates have zero cohomology. The larger
stable set does not have uniform vanishing.

The absolute Galois kernel acts trivially and has no
continuous homomorphism to the torsion-free discrete
lattice. Inflation and Hochschild--Serre therefore give
\[
H^1(\mathbb Q,\operatorname{NS}(\overline{\mathcal C}))=0,
\qquad\operatorname{Br}_1(\mathcal C)=\operatorname{Br}_0(\mathcal C).
\tag{Q-OFFSET-ALGEBRAIC-BRAUER}
\]
This argument covers the actual integral lattice without
selecting which of the sixteen gluings is geometric.

#### A uniform integral obstruction to arithmetic descent

For a K3 surface, let
$H=H^2_{\rm et}(\overline X,\mathbb Z_\ell(1))$,
$N=\operatorname{NS}(\overline X)\otimes\mathbb Z_\ell$,
$T=N^\perp$ and $\Lambda=H/N=T^*$.
Suppose a Galois element $F$ fixes $N$ pointwise,
$T=\ell^m\Lambda$, and
\[
v_\ell\det(F-1)=m\operatorname{rank}\Lambda.
\tag{Q-KUMMER-DESCENT-CRITERION}
\]
Then every actual class in $\operatorname{Br}(X)[\ell]$
has zero geometric image. Indeed equivariant discriminant
gluing gives $(F-1)\Lambda\subseteq T$, and the determinant
condition makes $(F-1)/\ell^m$ invertible over $\mathbb Z_\ell$.
Lift an arithmetic class through the global Kummer sequence,
and choose $x\in H$ representing its invariant restriction
modulo $\ell$. Its projection $\lambda\in\Lambda$ satisfies
\[
(F-1)\lambda=(F-1)x
 \in\ell H\cap T_{\mathbb Q_\ell}
 =\ell T=\ell^{m+1}\Lambda.
\]
The equality uses primitivity, not an integral orthogonal
splitting. Invertibility forces $\lambda\in\ell\Lambda$,
which is precisely zero geometric Brauer image.

Apply this at $\ell=2$ to the offset surface. Its degree-two
map to the original K3 identifies rational transcendental
Galois representations. Thus the certified determinants
remain $12/7$ at 7 and $48/13$ at 13, and bound the
order of invariant geometric Brauer classes by twelve.
At 13, both quadratic characters $\chi_3,\chi_{-1}$
are one, so Frobenius fixes the integral Néron--Severi
lattice pointwise for every admissible gluing.
Since
\[
T(\mathcal C)=4\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},
\]
whose inner matrix has odd determinant, $T_2=4\Lambda_2$.
The valuation $v_2(48/13)=4$ is exactly twice the rank.
The criterion applies with $m=2$ and eliminates the
geometric image of every arithmetic two-torsion class.
The smooth rational point $[1:1:1:-1:0:0]$ lets one
normalize a quotient-order-two class to actual two-torsion
by subtracting its value. Together with
(Q-OFFSET-ALGEBRAIC-BRAUER), this eliminates the full
two-primary quotient.

At three, pullback embeds the original lattice with its
form multiplied by two into the offset lattice. Their
determinants are 192 and 48, so the index is two.
Consequently this is an integral Galois-module isomorphism
over $\mathbb Z_3$, and the same holds after dualizing
to the actual Brauer lattices. The proved vanishing of
three-primary geometric invariants on the original K3
therefore transfers. The order-twelve bound, algebraic
vanishing and the two primary arguments prove
(Q-OFFSET-INTRINSIC-BRAUER).

The same criterion supplies a second proof of the arithmetic
two-primary steps for the original product K3 at 13
($m=2$) and its offset Jacobian at 7 ($m=1$).
In particular, arbitrary base Brauer corrections to the
quaternion family of Section 12.24 cannot produce a
nonconstant class that is unramified on the offset surface.
The stronger intrinsic result here does not replace the
separate full-root residue argument: a class ramified on
the offset surface could become unramified after the
further center or individual-root extensions.



### 12.28. The next section orbit and complete rational-coordinate quartic

The smooth rational B-pencil section \(3S\) has no simultaneous
rational offset and center lift. In particular there is no full-root lift in its established
automorphism orbit
\[
 \{3S,\,-2S,\,3S+T_0,\,-2S+T_0\}.
\]
This is a theorem about these specialized section values on every
smooth rational base. It does not classify arbitrary specialized
Mordell--Weil points or all section multiples.

The key new arithmetic results are
\[
 U^2=5P(v^2)\quad\text{and}\quad U^2=10P(v^2)
 \quad\text{have no rational projective points},
 \tag{B-THIRD-1}
\]
where \(P(T)=T^3+11T^2-29T+25\).
Together with the complete twists one and two, these settle the
entire necessary finite-twist family for \(3S\).

#### Exact section and projective center identity

Retain the elliptic B pencil
\[
 E_k:Y^2=X(X+A)(X+B),\quad
 A=32(k+1)(k+2),\quad B=(k+1)^2(k-1)^2,
\]
\[
 S=(8(k+1)^3,-8(k+1)^3(k+3)^2).
\]
Define
\[
 f=k^3-k-1,\qquad g=2k^3+3k^2-2k-4,
\]
\[

\]
\[

\]
The following degree-ten homogeneous product representative
\((a,b,s,t)\) of \(3S\) is verified by substitution into the forward
product chart and the elliptic group law \(S+2S\).
Its coordinates are
\[
 (-A_{10},-(k+1)B_9,(k+1)Z_9,-(k+1)T_9),
\]
where
\[
\begin{aligned}
A_{10}={}&4k^{10}+21k^9+40k^8+17k^7-49k^6-106k^5\\
 &-85k^4+24k^3+84k^2+44k+8,\\

          +6k^3+22k^2+20k+16,\\

          -62k^3+46k^2+48k+8,\\
T_9={}&6k^9+26k^8+34k^7-13k^6-86k^5-56k^4
          +30k^3+26k^2+24k+8.
\end{aligned}

The four polynomials have gcd one and satisfy the product K3 equation.
Their center quadratic is exactly
\[
 H=a^2+b^2-\frac{s^2+t^2}{2}=4fghj.
 \tag{B-THIRD-2}
\]
If \(k=p/q\), with \(q>0\) and coprime integers \(p,q\), homogenize
the coordinates to degree ten and the four factors to their respective
degrees \(3,3,6,7\), denoting the latter by \(F,G,H_6,J_7\). Then
\[
 \boxed{H_{\rm hom}=4q\,F\,G\,H_6\,J_7.}
 \tag{B-THIRD-3}
\]
The factor \(q\) is essential. Equation (B-THIRD-3) covers zeros of the
affine normalizing denominator \(Z_9\); there is no restriction
\(Z_9\ne0\) in the conclusion. Gcd one excludes a simultaneous finite zero. At infinity their
leading coordinate vector is \((-4,-2,2,-6)\), also nonzero. Thus
these coordinates define the full projective section.

A simultaneous offset lift of \(3S\) forces
\[
 d=-(k-1)(k+3)\ \text{to be a rational square},
 \tag{B-THIRD-4}
\]
by the extended offset Kummer map of Section 12.10. Indeed
\(X(S)+B=(k+1)^2(k+3)^2\), so \(\delta_B(S)=1\)
and the homomorphism gives \(\delta_B(3S)=1\). Thus \(k\in[-3,1]\). The rational point at
infinity on the \(k\)-line cannot satisfy this square cover:
its projective leading equation would require a square root of \(-1\).

#### A four-twist restriction from one cubic factor

The exact cross-resultants are
\[
 \operatorname{Res}(f,g)=5^2,\quad
 \operatorname{Res}(f,h)=5^5,\quad
 \operatorname{Res}(f,j)=-5^4.
 \tag{B-THIRD-5}

For primitive \((p,q)\), \(F=p^3-pq^2-q^3\) is always odd and is
coprime to \(q\). Any common prime of \(F\) and one of \(G,H_6,J_7\)
must divide the corresponding resultant. If (B-THIRD-3) is a square,
every prime other than five therefore has even valuation in \(F\).
On \([-3,1]\), \(f(k)<0\), so
\[
 -F=z^2\quad\text{or}\quad -F=5z^2
 \tag{B-THIRD-6}
\]
for an integer \(z\).
There is no zero-product exception: none of \(f,g,h,j\) has a
rational zero (the rational-root candidates are checked exactly).

Parameterize the square cover (B-THIRD-4) by
\[
 k=\frac{u^2-3w^2}{u^2+w^2},\qquad (u,w)=1.
\]
The gcd of its raw numerator and denominator is \(e=1\) if \(u,w\)

 u^6+11u^4w^2-29u^2w^4+25w^6=e^3(-F).
 \tag{B-THIRD-7}

 U^2=\delta P(v^2),\qquad \delta\in\{1,2,5,10\}

has a rational point above \(v\). Both \(w=0\) and \(u=0\) are retained

homogeneous factor \(F\) and the rational value \(f(k)=F/q^3\) is
why no spurious factor \(1+v^2\) occurs in the twist condition (B-THIRD-8).

For comparison, directly pulling the full center curve to
\(k=(1-3r^2)/(1+r^2)\) gives five squarefree pairwise coprime factors:

 25r^6-29r^4+11r^2+1,\quad

and the degree-twelve and degree-fourteen factors recorded in the

Reduction (B-THIRD-8) keeps a fixed cubic field and is much smaller.

Use \(K=\mathbb Q(\theta)\), \(\theta^3-\theta-1=0\), and the notation

 5&0,5&\{1,\theta q_5\}\\

\end{array}
\tag{B-THIRD-9}

These are upper images, which is all the proof needs; no claim about

Here is an explicit finite specification of the upper-image calculation.

 [\beta(a+b\theta+c\theta^2)^2]_i+\delta\alpha_i e^2=0,
 \qquad i=1,2.

| Twist | Mask 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |

| 5 | — | 5 | 4 | — | 4 | — | — | 5 |

 \delta(v^2-\alpha)=\beta a^2,\qquad

#### Twist five is empty

Elementary square tests on \(5P(v^2)\) force

Let \(s_0=2\theta+1\). For \(v_2(v)=1\), factor

For \(v_2(v)=-1\), factor \(v^2+s_0^2=v^2(1+4u)\),

 224,\quad452,\quad128.
 \tag{B-THIRD-11}

\[
 u=v-1,\quad D_0=2\theta(A_0+2),\quad \sigma=\theta(A_0+2),\quad

 \tag{B-THIRD-12}

The complete finite residue test exhausts:

* all 32 residues \(v\equiv3\bmod8\) modulo 256;
* all 16 roots \(z=Z/2\) modulo 256 of
  \(z^2=\theta(v^4+A_0v^2+b^2)/4\), for each such \(v\).

All 512 possible pairs give exactly one of the signatures
\[
 130,\quad226,
 \tag{B-THIRD-13}
\]
both outside the span (B-THIRD-11). All three abscissa-root differences

Here is the full precision justification, so this is a complete
local obstruction, not a search over bounded parameters.
For an actual point, choose the enumerated representatives
\(v_0,z_0\). Then \(v-v_0\in2^8\mathbb Z_2\) and

The denominator has valuation four and changes relatively by

Every \(x-e_i\) has valuation at most two, making each actual-to-

Thus every actual point has one of the excluded signatures (B-THIRD-13).
This proves the second assertion of (B-THIRD-1).

The argument includes all signs of \(Z\) because every modular root
was enumerated. The two twists have no rational infinity; finite

an independent precision review both pass.

#### Completion and scope

Section 12.26 proves that twists one and two allow only
\(v=0,\pm1,\infty\); twists five and ten are empty by (B-THIRD-1).
Under \(k=(v^2-3)/(v^2+1)\), the remaining parameters are exactly
\[
 k=-3,\,-1,\,1,
\]
all singular B-pencil bases. Thus no smooth rational specialization
of \(3S\) has both rational offsets and a rational center.
The established full-root automorphisms \(Q\mapsto S-Q\) and
\(Q\mapsto Q+T_0\) give the whole stated orbit.

An additional reusable conclusion follows: the entire rational-\(v\)
locus of \(D_\theta\), even without either residual twist conic, is
\(v=\pm1,Z=\pm(2\theta^2-2\theta)\). If \(v_2(v)\ne0\), the quartic factor
\(v^4+A_0v^2+b^2\) is a local square after factoring its dominant
square, since \(v_2(A_0)=1\) and \(b\) is a unit. Multiplication
by the nonsquare \(\theta\) excludes these disks. The odd disks
\(\pm1\bmod8\) were settled by the complete dyadic annihilator;
the odd disks \(\pm3\bmod8\) are excluded by (B-THIRD-11)--(B-THIRD-13).
The \(v=0\) and infinity charts are also locally excluded for
\(D_\theta\). This strengthens the reusable cubic-field target,
not a statement about every multiple of the original section.

The producer certificates are `third_section/three_s_factorization.py`,
`p5_10_elliptic_descent.py` and `other_dyadic_disk.py`, each with its exact
JSON output. The separate field arithmetic and complete 512-row replay
are in `varying_primes/independent_third_section.py/.json`; the independent
whole-disk proof review is `rank4_next/center_quartic_audit/five_ten_twist_review.md`.
The finite certificate establishes local exclusion only through the
uniform precision bound above. No search height, analytic rank or full
Mordell--Weil saturation assumption enters the theorem.


#### Exact exhaustion of the two old center cubic divisors

The cubics
\[
 f=k^3-k-1,\qquad g=2k^3+3k^2-2k-4
\]
that controlled the two completed orbits cannot supply a periodic
or congruence-class obstruction for all section multiples. More
precisely, on the specialization at a root of either cubic, the
complete center-zero divisor consists of
\[
 \boxed{\{2S,-S,3S,-2S\}+\{O,T_0\}.}
 \tag{B-THIRD-DIVISOR-1}
\]
Consequently an integer multiple \(nS+T\), with \(T\) in the rational
two-torsion subgroup, meets that center divisor if and only if
\[
 n\in\{-2,-1,2,3\},\qquad T\in\{O,T_0\}.
 \tag{B-THIRD-DIVISOR-2}
\]
This concerns the old cubic specializations and does not exclude
center lifts at other bases or for other multiples.

**The center divisor has degree eight.**

Use product coordinates
\[
 u=a+b,\quad v=a-b,\quad w=s+t,\quad z=s-t.
\]
The moving B fiber is the genus-one quartic intersection
\[
 Q=-2ku^2-2(k+2)v^2+4uw+(k+3)w^2+(k+1)z^2=0,
\]
\[
 \Phi=-4(k+1)^2u^2+4(k+1)(k+3)uw
        -(k+1)^2w^2+(k+3)^2z^2=0.
\]
The first equation is the fixed B-base relation
\((k+2)H=(a+b+s)(a+b+t)\). Substituting it into the product
K3 equation factors off the two fixed plane sections
\((-2u-w+z)(2u+w+z)\), leaving \(\Phi\). The identity follows by polynomial division by $Q$; the exact
certificate is `third_section/uniform_old_cubic_divisors.py/.json`.
The elliptic chart identifies this moving intersection with $E_k$.
Smoothness at the two cubic bases also has a direct certificate.
For the homogeneous pencil $\lambda\Phi+\mu Q$, the determinant is
\[
4\mu(k+1)(k+2)^2(8\lambda+\mu)((k+1)\lambda+\mu)
 ((k+3)^2\lambda+(k+1)\mu).
\]
Its binary-quartic discriminant is
\[
2^{22}(k-7)^2(k-1)^4(k+1)^8(k+2)^{14}(k+3)^4,
\]
which is coprime to both $f$ and $g$. Hence the four projective
pencil roots are distinct, certifying a smooth degree-four complete
intersection at each cubic base. The certificate
`rank4_next/section_recurrence/verify_quadric_smoothness.py/.json`
also verifies that the previously used center denominators are
coprime to both cubics.
Directly, the matrix-pencil determinant is
\[
 4(k+1)(k+2)^2(8\lambda+1)((k+1)\lambda+1)
                    ((k+3)^2\lambda+k+1).
\]
The full homogeneous pencil has binary-quartic discriminant
\[
 2^{22}(k-7)^2(k-1)^4(k+1)^8(k+2)^{14}(k+3)^4.
\]
Thus all four projective roots are distinct at either cubic
specialization. An independent smoothness check is recorded in
../rank4_next/section_recurrence/verify_quadric_smoothness.py.

The center is the quadric
\[
 H=(u^2+v^2)/2-(w^2+z^2)/4.
\]
It does not vanish identically on the moving curve. Indeed matching
the \(v^2\) and \(uw\) coefficients in a putative identity
\(H=\lambda Q+\mu\Phi\) forces
\[
 \lambda=-1/[4(k+2)],\qquad
 \mu=1/[4(k+2)(k+1)(k+3)].
\]
The remaining \(u^2\) coefficient is \(2/(k+3)\ne0\).
Thus Bezout gives a center-zero divisor of degree eight.

**The specialized section is nontorsion.**

Both cubic fields have exactly four rational torsion points on the
specialized elliptic curve. Exact good-reduction counts are:

| Cubic | Degree-one places \((p,k\bmod p)\) | Point counts |
|---|---|---|
| \(f\) | \((11,6),(17,5),(23,3)\) | \(16,24,28\) |
| \(g\) | \((13,8),(19,15)\) | \(16,28\) |

The torsion upper bound is four in each case, and the visible full
two-torsion attains it. The section
\[
 S=(8(k+1)^3,-8(k+1)^3(k+3)^2)
\]
has nonzero ordinate in either field, so it is nontorsion.
These are exact specialization certificates, superseding any finite
search through section multiples.

**Eight known zeros exhaust the divisor.**

The certified center formulas for \(2S\) and \(3S\) both contain
\(f g\) with odd multiplicity. Hence these two points lie on the
center divisor at either cubic specialization. The full-root
automorphisms \(P\mapsto S-P\) and \(P\mapsto P+T_0\) preserve the
center-zero condition and produce all eight points in (B-THIRD-DIVISOR-1).

They are distinct. An equality between two would make a nonzero
integer multiple of \(S\) torsion, or would equate \(T_0\) to \(O\).
Both are impossible. Eight distinct zeros exhaust a degree-eight
divisor, proving (B-THIRD-DIVISOR-1), and nontorsion then proves (B-THIRD-DIVISOR-2).

In particular, neither \(f\) nor \(g\) occurs as a center-zero
divisor for \(4S\) or any later positive multiple. The exact fixed
cubic-field obstruction has reached its natural limit on these two
orbits. An obstruction for all multiples must use new center
divisors, a different arithmetic invariant, or a theorem linking
their varying squareclasses; periodicity of \(S\) at these old
cubics cannot provide it.

One useful transfer statement does persist independently of the
index \(n\). For a smooth rational d-square base \(k=p/q\), the
complete four-twist theorem proves that
\(-\bigl(p^3-pq^2-q^3\bigr)\) is never a square or five times a square.
Therefore any future section whose center condition forces precisely
that two-class homogeneous cubic restriction is automatically excluded.
Applying this requires a fresh divisor/resultant argument; it is not
inferred from a recurrence or from the two completed examples.


### 12.29. A split offset pencil and a global five-square formulation

#### The chart and its excluded boundary

On the offset surface, the identities
\[
H=a^2+\xi^2=b^2+\eta^2=s^2+(\xi+\eta)^2=t^2+(\xi-\eta)^2
\]
give \((a-b)(a+b)=(\eta-\xi)(\eta+\xi)\). On \(a-b\ne0\), projectively normalize \(a-b=1\) and put
\[
p=\eta-\xi,\quad r=\eta+\xi.
\]
Then
\[
a=(rp+1)/2,\quad b=(rp-1)/2,\quad
\xi=(r-p)/2,\quad\eta=(r+p)/2.
\]
These formulas have a rational inverse on precisely the stated chart. With \(U=2s,V=2t\), the remaining equations are
\[
U^2=(p^2-3)r^2+p^2+1,\qquad
V^2=(p^2+1)r^2+1-3p^2,
\tag{OFF-ALT-PENCIL}
\]
and \(H=(1+p^2)(1+r^2)/4\).

For a nondegenerate full-root point, even \(a^2=b^2\) is impossible: it forces \(\xi^2=\eta^2\), hence \(\xi=\eta\) or \(\xi=-\eta\). One of the two remaining offsets \(\xi-\eta,\xi+\eta\) is then zero, repeating the center square. Thus \(a-b\ne0\) for every choice of signs of the two nonzero products. This establishes global coverage of the nondegenerate locus, not merely of a dense open set with an unexamined admissible boundary. Projective rescaling affects none of the normalized root-square tests.

#### Why the degree-four map gives the same Jacobian

Put \(\alpha=p^2-3,\beta=p^2+1,\gamma=1-3p^2\). The map
\[
x=\alpha\beta r^2,\quad y=\alpha\beta rUV
\]
satisfies
\[
E:\ y^2=x(x+\beta^2)(x+\alpha\gamma).
\tag{OFF-ALT-ELLIPTIC}
\]
It has degree four: generically the three square roots \(r,U,V\) have their product fixed by \(y\), leaving exactly the four simultaneous changes of an even number of signs.

On the smooth projective intersection of the two quadrics (OFF-ALT-PENCIL), these three involutions are fixed-point free. For example, changing \(r,U\) fixes only the projective subspaces \(r=U=0\) or \(V=z=0\), and neither meets the generic curve. For the other pairs the same check uses \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\ne0\) and \(\alpha\gamma-\beta^2=-4(p^2-1)^2\ne0\). This also checks points at infinity, not only the affine chart.

Choose the rational point \(r=p,U=V=p^2-1\) as origin. A fixed-point-free involution of a characteristic-zero elliptic curve is translation by nonzero two-torsion. The deck group is therefore its entire two-torsion translation group. Subtracting the image of the origin makes the displayed map an isogeny with exactly the kernel of multiplication by two. It factors through multiplication by two followed by a unique isomorphism defined over \(\mathbb Q(p)\).

The origin maps to
\[
P=(\alpha\beta p^2,\alpha\beta p(p^2-1)^2).
\]
After that isomorphism, the map is \(Q\mapsto2Q+P\). Thus (OFF-ALT-ELLIPTIC) is the Jacobian of the genus-one pencil over the stated field, not merely an elliptic curve known to be isogenous to it.

#### Fibers, torsion, and section heights

The discriminant is
\[
2^8(p^2+1)^4(p^2-3)^2(3p^2-1)^2(p^2-1)^4.
\]
At every finite zero, \(c_4\) is a unit; the minimal fibers are four \(I_4\)'s at \(\pm1,\pm i\) and four \(I_2\)'s at \(\pm\sqrt3,\pm1/\sqrt3\). The discriminant has degree 24. The standard K3 chart \(x'=z^4x,y'=z^6y\), \(z=1/p\), has nonzero discriminant at infinity, so that fiber is smooth. The root rank is sixteen; the established Picard number twenty gives geometric Mordell–Weil rank two.

A torsion section meeting every identity component would have height \(4+2(T.O)>0\), a contradiction. Thus torsion injects into the product of the component groups, whose exponent is four. The curve has full two-torsion. Among its three nonzero two-torsion points, only \((-\beta^2,0)\) is divisible by two over \(\mathbb C(p)\): its two root differences are \(-\beta^2\) and \(-4(p^2-1)^2\), both squares over \(\mathbb C(p)\). The other two require \(\alpha\gamma\) or its negative, which is nonsquare because of its simple zeros. Therefore geometric torsion is exactly \(C_4\oplus C_2\). Over \(\mathbb Q(p)\), \(-\beta^2\) is nonsquare, so no nonzero two-torsion point has a rational half, and arithmetic torsion is exactly \(C_2^2\).

The section incidences are checked directly:

| Section | \(O\)-intersection | \(p=\pm1\), \(I_4\) | \(p=\pm i\), \(I_4\) | \(p=\pm\sqrt3\), \(I_2\) | \(p=\pm1/\sqrt3\), \(I_2\) |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| \(P\) | 1 | middle | end | nonidentity | identity |
| \(Q=(-4p^2,2\sqrt3 p(p^2-1)^2)\) | 0 | middle | identity | identity | identity |

For \(P\), at \(\pm1\), \(x+\beta^2=\beta(p^2-1)^2\) has order two, as does the ordinate, giving the middle component. At \(\pm i\), the abscissa and ordinate have order one at the node, giving an end component. At \(\alpha=0\), both have order one and meet the unique nonidentity \(I_2\) component. At \(\gamma=0\), its abscissa is nonzero and avoids the node. At infinity its minimal coordinates have poles of orders two and three, and the formal parameter \(-x'/y'\) has a simple zero; this gives \(P.O=1\), which must not be omitted from the height.

For \(Q\), \(x+\beta^2=(p^2-1)^2\) and the ordinate both have order two at \(\pm1\). It avoids the remaining finite nodes. Its minimal coordinates at infinity tend to the finite smooth two-torsion point \((0,0)\), so \(Q.O=0\). Hence
\[
h(P)=6-2-3/2-1=3/2,\qquad h(Q)=4-2=2.
\]

The square roots \(2ip,p^2-1,i\sqrt3(p^2-1)\) of the three root differences of \(Q\) have product \(-y(Q)\). Writing these three square roots as $r_1,r_2,r_3$ and $c=r_1r_2+r_1r_3+r_2r_3$, the point
$Q_0=(x(Q)+c,-y(Q)-(r_1+r_2+r_3)c)$ yields \(Q_0\in E(\mathbb Q(i,\sqrt3)(p))\), and direct substitution in the duplication formula verifies $2Q_0=Q$, including its ordinate sign. Thus \(h(Q_0)=1/2\). Conjugating \(\sqrt3\) while fixing \(i,p\) sends \(Q_0\) to \(-Q_0\) modulo two-torsion and fixes \(P\). Invariance of the height pairing therefore gives \(\langle P,Q_0\rangle=0\).

The offset Néron--Severi determinant $-48$, proved in Section 12.25, gives
\[
\det MW=48\cdot8^2/4096=3/4.
\]
The independent points \(P,Q_0\) already have determinant \((3/2)(1/2)=3/4\), so their free span has index one. This proves both section primitivity and geometric completeness. A rational point cannot have a nonzero \(Q_0\)-coefficient, by the conjugation above, so the arithmetic group is exactly \(\mathbb ZP\oplus C_2^2\).

An additional generic-section consequence is
\[
\operatorname{image}\bigl(C(\mathbb Q(p))\to E(\mathbb Q(p))\bigr)
=P+2E(\mathbb Q(p))=\{(2n+1)P:n\in\mathbb Z\}.
\]
Every such image has its four rational deck preimages. This exhausts rational sections of this pencil, but not rational points on specialized fibers, whose arithmetic groups can increase.

#### Universal Pythagorean conditions and the common root squareclass

Take the first two actual opposite root pairs \(u,v\) and \(w,z\), with equal sum of squares \(2c^2\). Put \(a=uv,b=wz,\xi=(u^2-v^2)/2,\eta=(w^2-z^2)/2\). Direct expansion gives
\[
(a-b)^2+(\eta-\xi)^2=(uz-vw)^2,
\]
\[
(a-b)^2+(\eta+\xi)^2=(uw-vz)^2.
\]
Division by \((a-b)^2\) proves that \(1+p^2\) and \(1+r^2\) are rational squares at every nondegenerate full-root point.

On an offset center lift choose \(h^2=H\), and square roots \(P_0^2=1+p^2,R_0^2=1+r^2\) with \(P_0R_0=2h\). There is the useful exact identity
\[
\boxed{(1+\xi/h)(1+\eta/h)
=\left(\frac{P_0r+R_0}{P_0R_0}\right)^2.}
\tag{OFF-ALT-COMMON-CLASS}
\]
Thus the first two opposite root pairs have a common squareclass. Away from zero root values, one test lifts both pairs. Since \(4h^2=(1+p^2)(1+r^2)\), the center condition plus just one Pythagorean square already implies the other.

Consequently on this locus a complete root test is: require
\[
1+\xi/h,\qquad1+r/h,\qquad1-p/h
\]
to be rational squares, then use the known product squares for their opposites and (OFF-ALT-COMMON-CLASS) for the other initial pair. Positivity and pairwise distinctness of all nine values remain required.

#### Complete five-square formulation and its inverse

Parametrize the two Pythagorean conditions by
\[
p=\frac{2m}{1-m^2},\qquad r=\frac{2n}{1-n^2},\qquad
D=(1+m^2)(1+n^2).
\]
For a rational finite \(p\), choosing the positive rational \(P_0=\sqrt{1+p^2}\) gives the inverse \(m=p/(P_0+1)\); similarly \(n=r/(R_0+1)\). Thus \(|m|,|n|<1\) can be imposed without losing any nondegenerate real full-root point. The exceptional \(m,n=\pm1\) are only boundaries of this parametrization; they are unnecessary for the covering assertion.

The normalized offsets are
\[
x=\frac{2(n-m)(1+mn)}D,\qquad
y=\frac{2(n+m)(1-mn)}D.
\]
Write \(A_0=1+mn,B_0=n-m,C_0=1-mn,E_0=n+m\). Then
\[
1\pm x=(A_0\pm B_0)^2/D,\qquad
1\pm y=(C_0\pm E_0)^2/D.
\tag{OFF-ALT-ROOTS}
\]
Outside zero root values these four numbers are rational squares exactly when \(D\) is a square. Also
\[
x+y=4n(1-m^2)/D,\qquad x-y=-4m(1-n^2)/D.
\]
It follows that the full-root problem on this chart is exactly the following five-square condition:
\[
\boxed{D,\quad D\pm4n(1-m^2),\quad D\pm4m(1-n^2)
\text{ are rational squares}.}
\tag{OFF-ALT-FIVE-SQUARES}
\]
Require in addition that the corresponding nine normalized values are positive and pairwise distinct.

Conversely, given rational \(m,n\) satisfying (OFF-ALT-FIVE-SQUARES), choose \(\sigma^2=D\). Formula (OFF-ALT-ROOTS) provides the first four rational root ratios explicitly as
\[
(A_0+B_0)/\sigma,\ (A_0-B_0)/\sigma,
\ (C_0+E_0)/\sigma,\ (C_0-E_0)/\sigma.
\]
The other four ratios are the square roots in (OFF-ALT-FIVE-SQUARES) divided by \(\sigma\), and the central root is 1. Their squares are precisely \(1\pm x,1\pm y,1\pm(x+y),1\pm(x-y)\), so they satisfy the standard magic-square linear relations. Clearing denominators gives the usual integral square configuration if desired. Sign choices of the individual roots only change the chosen signed products.

The forward construction from any nondegenerate full-root point uses its signed products, the covered chart, and the inverse Pythagorean parameters above. Thus (OFF-ALT-FIVE-SQUARES) has a proved global coverage statement on the nondegenerate locus. It repackages the two initial equal-sum-of-squares circles and the remaining paired-root conditions; no claim is made that it is a new or easier Diophantine problem.

#### Scope of the universal quadratic base change

The cover \(P_0^2=1+p^2\) is rational, with the parameter \(m\) above. It branches only at \(p=\pm i\). Pulling back the elliptic pencil produces two \(I_8\), four \(I_4\), and eight \(I_2\) fibers, Euler number 48 and \(\chi(\mathcal O)=4\). Its root rank is 34 and \(h^{1,1}=40\), so its geometric Mordell–Weil rank is at most four, and at least the original two.

Equivalently, the extra rank is the rank of the quadratic twist by \(p^2+1\). That twist has two \(I_4^*\), two \(I_4\), and four \(I_2\), with \(\chi=3\), root rank 26, and geometric rank at most two. These fiber and Hodge calculations give upper bounds; they do not determine the extra twist rank. None of these generic bounds bounds ranks or rational points of every specialization.

The symbolic coordinate, discriminant, half-section and odd-multiple
identities are recorded in `coupled_lifts/offset_alternate_fibration.py/.txt`.
The independent local component and global-coverage audit is
`simultaneous_units/offset_alternate_review.md`.


### 12.30. Complete center exclusion in the alternate pencil

In the pencil of Section 12.29, define
\[
D_3=3p^6-11p^4+p^2-1,
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
r_3&=p(p^6-p^4+11p^2-3)/D_3,\\
U_3&=(p^2-1)(p^6+3p^4-13p^2+1)/D_3,\\
V_3&=(p^2-1)(p^6-13p^4+3p^2+1)/D_3.
\end{aligned}
\tag{OFF-ALT-THREE-P}
\]
These satisfy both pencil equations and map to $3P$ under its degree-four
map, as follows directly from the elliptic addition formula. Their
center character is
\[
H_3=\frac{(p^2+1)^2
 (p^6-5p^4+11p^2+1)(p^6+11p^4-5p^2+1)}{4D_3^2}.
\tag{OFF-ALT-THREE-CENTER}
\]
The polynomial $D_3$ has no rational zero: its only rational-root
candidates are $\pm1,\pm1/3$, and none is a root. Infinity is retained
as a projective chart. The two sextic factors are squarefree and
coprime, so the square-center condition is a smooth genus-five curve.

Let
\[
C:\ W^2=(p^6-5p^4+11p^2+1)(p^6+11p^4-5p^2+1).
\]
Then C has exactly eight rational points: two above p=0, two above each of p=1,-1, and two at infinity. They are
\[
(0,\pm1),\quad(1,\pm8),\quad(-1,\pm8),\quad \infty_+,\infty_-.
\]
All eight specialize (OFF-ALT-THREE-P) to degenerate points. At $p=0$,
$r_3=0$ and both offsets vanish. At $p=\pm1$, $r_3=-p$ and
$a=s=t=0$, so some entries vanish. At infinity the projective offset
limit is $[a:b:s:t:\xi:\eta]=[1:1:1:1:0:0]$, again repeating the
center. Thus the entire nondegenerate $3P$ section family has no
rational center lift and hence no full-root lift. The sign-deck
partners and the negative image have the same $r_3^2$ and center
character, so the conclusion includes those paired section values.

#### Two elliptic quotients

There are exact degree-four quotient maps
\[
E_-:\ Y^2=X^3-4X+4,\qquad
X=(p+p^{-1})^2/4,\quad Y=W/(8p^3),
\]
\[
\boxed{E_+:\ y^2=x^3-4x^2+16,\qquad
x=\frac{16p^2}{(p^2+1)^2},\quad y=\frac{4W}{(p^2+1)^3}.}       \tag{OFF-ALT-CENTER-1}
\]
The first elliptic curve has rank one and trivial torsion. The second has rank zero and torsion C5; the second map therefore suffices to classify C(Q).

#### A common cubic field and global two-descent bound

Let theta satisfy
\[
f(T)=T^3-T^2+T+1=0,\qquad \operatorname{disc}(f)=-44.
\]
The cubic field K has signature (1,1). The order Z[theta] is maximal. The only possible nontrivial index is two, which would give field discriminant -11; the cubic Minkowski ideal bound would then be
\(8\sqrt{11}/(9\pi)<1\), impossible. The actual Minkowski bound \(8\sqrt{44}/(9\pi)<2\) implies that every ideal class contains an ideal of norm one, so K has class number one.

Put
\[
\alpha=-(\theta-1)^2,\qquad \alpha_+=4/\alpha=-2\theta^2+2\theta.
\]
Their minimal polynomials are respectively
\[
X^3-4X+4,\qquad X^3-4X^2+16.
\]
Their orders have indices two and eight in the maximal order; consequently the usual separable monogenic argument applies away from 2 and 11.

For either elliptic curve the cubic two-descent map sends a finite rational point to x-alpha (or x-alpha_plus) in K*/K*² and injects E(Q)/2E(Q). Every prime-ideal valuation of this element is even. Here is a complete check:

* If x is nonintegral at a rational prime, cubic dominance in the integral Weierstrass equation forces its valuation to be negative and even. The same is then true, multiplied by the ramification index, of every valuation of x-alpha_j.
* At an integral x and a prime outside 2,11, positive valuation can occur at at most one linear prime: the reduction of alpha_j must equal x in the prime field and the polynomial is separable. Its residue degree is one, and the norm equals y², forcing even valuation.
* At 2 there is a unique prime, of residue degree one, since f modulo 2 is (T+1)^3 and Z[theta] is maximal. The square norm again forces even valuation.
* At 11, f=(T-3)^2(T-6). The alpha residues are 7,8 and the alpha_plus residues are 10,6, respectively. The residues at the two primes are distinct, so again at most one positive valuation occurs, with residue degree one and hence even valuation.

Class number one therefore reduces every descent class to a unit. The unit group modulo squares has dimension two; the norm map to {±1} is surjective because the norm of -1 is -1. Its norm-one kernel has dimension one. A representative of its nontrivial class is
\[
\varepsilon=-\theta.
\]
Indeed, with pi=theta+1 at the unique prime above 2, pi is a uniformizer, v_pi(OFF-ALT-CENTER-2)=3, and epsilon=1-pi. Every unit square is 1 modulo pi², so epsilon is not square. Thus for both curves the complete global descent image is contained in {1,epsilon}.

This is the same odd-degree cubic Kummer injection used in Sections 9.51 and 12.23. The support and unit computations for the present field have been supplied above.

#### Rank one of the first quotient

For E_minus, R=(2,2) is a rational point. The good reduction counts at 3,5,7 are 7,9,10, which exclude every torsion prime by using a good prime different from it. Hence R is nontorsion. The preceding one-dimensional descent bound proves rank exactly one.

There is an exact identity
\[
2-\alpha=-\theta(\theta^2-\theta+2)^2,
\]
so R has the nontrivial descent class and is not divisible by two. Its odd saturation has not been proved and is not needed below.

#### The dyadic exclusion giving rank zero of the second quotient

Use the integral minimal model of E_plus
\[
x=4X,\quad y=8Y+4,\qquad Y^2+Y=X^3-X^2.             \tag{OFF-ALT-CENTER-2}
\]
In K_2, v_pi(theta-1)=1, so v_pi(alpha)=2 and v_pi(alpha_plus)=4. We show that every local descent class x-alpha_plus can be normalized by a square to a unit congruent to 1 modulo pi².

If X is 2-adically integral, then
\[
x-\alpha_+=-\alpha_+(1-\alpha X),\qquad
-\alpha_+=\left(\frac{2}{\theta-1}\right)^2.
\]
The normalized unit is 1-alpha X, which is 1 modulo pi².

If X is nonintegral, the minimal equation (OFF-ALT-CENTER-2) forces v2(X)=-2m for m≥1. Write X=2^(-2m)u with u odd. Then x=2^(2-2m)u, a rational square times an odd unit, and
\[
x-\alpha_+=x(1-\alpha_+/x),\qquad
v_\pi(\alpha_+/x)=6m-2\ge4.
\]
An odd rational unit is 1 modulo pi³, so the normalized unit is again 1 modulo pi².

By contrast epsilon times a unit square is 1-pi modulo pi². Therefore the nontrivial global unit class epsilon is excluded locally at 2. The complete two-descent image is trivial and E_plus(Q) has rank zero.

The point T=(0,4) has exact order five:
\[
2T=(4,-4),\qquad4T=(0,-4)=-T.
\]
Good reduction counts at 3 and 5 are both five; together with the count ten at 7 they bound the torsion by five. Hence
\[
\boxed{E_+(\mathbf Q)=\{O,(0,\pm4),(4,\pm4)\}\simeq C_5.}
\]

**Independent elementary form of the dyadic obstruction.**
The competing class would require
\[
x-\alpha_+=-\theta(a+b\theta+c\theta^2)^2/d^2
\]
with primitive integers $(a,b,c,d)$. Equating coefficients of $\theta$
and $\theta^2$ gives
\[
-a^2+2ac+b^2+4bc+c^2+2d^2=0,
\qquad -2ab-2ac-b^2+2c^2-2d^2=0.
\]
Modulo two, $b$ is even and $a\equiv c$. If $a,c$ are odd, the
second equation modulo four forces $d$ even, and the first is then
$2\pmod4$. If $a,c$ are even, primitivity forces $d$ odd and the
first is again $2\pmod4$. Thus no primitive solution exists. This
second proof uses all 240 primitive tuples modulo four, without
assuming an integral elliptic abscissa.

#### Complete pullback and the stronger full-root cover

For rational finite p, the denominator p²+1 in (OFF-ALT-CENTER-1) never vanishes, so the point O of E_plus has no rational preimage. The equation x=0 forces p=0 (or p=infinity in the projective extension). The equation x=4 is
\[
16p^2=4(p^2+1)^2\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(p^2-1)^2=0.
\]
It forces p=±1. Substitution gives exactly the eight rational points listed above; this is an exhaustive pullback, with no rank-generator assumption.

The further universal full-root condition z²=p²+1 excludes p=±1. There are four simple branch points on the center curve above $p=\pm i$; the poles at infinity have even order. The resulting connected double cover has genus eleven by Riemann--Hurwitz. It therefore has only the boundary points above p=0 and infinity: at either base point there are two center signs and two signs of the added square root, for eight rational points in total. In particular it has no nondegenerate point from this section family.

A useful smaller point classification follows at the same time:
\[
C_2:y^2=z^6-4z^2+4,
\qquad C_2(\mathbb Q)=
\{(0,\pm2),(\pm1,\pm1),\infty_+,\infty_-\}.
\]
Its odd quotient is $(x,y_+)=(4/z^2,4y/z^3)$ on $E_+$.
For finite nonzero $z$ the torsion list forces $z=\pm1$;
the zero and two infinity charts give the other four points.
The genus-five curve maps to it by $z=(p+p^{-1})/2$,
$y=W/(8p^3)$. The existence of its rational elliptic quotients
also distinguishes this curve from the earlier coupled center curve,
whose Jacobian has no rational elliptic factor by the independent
Frobenius certificates in Section 12.23. Neither a rational
isomorphism nor a constant quadratic twist can identify them.

The exact algebraic certificates are
`coupled_lifts/new_center_elliptic_rank.py/.json` and
`offset_alternate_fibration.py/.txt`. Independent proofs and exact
replays are in `rank4_next/new_center_curve/complementary_elliptic_rank.md`,
`verify_complementary_rank.py/.json` and
`varying_primes/independent_alternate_center_rank_zero.md/.py/.json`.
Both the uniform dyadic-unit proof and the primitive mod-four
quadrics prove the same rank-zero conclusion. No analytic rank,
odd-index saturation, parameter cutoff or higher-genus point-count
assumption is needed. The theorem classifies this curve and the
specified section family; it does not classify all specializations
of the offset pencil.


### 12.31. A complete genus-forty-nine full-root fibration

The five-square formulation has a birational inverse on the normalized
full-root surface. It gives another genus-forty-nine fibration, alongside
the fixed-circle fibrations already established in Section 10, with a
five-radical moving fiber at every rational parameter outside three
boundary values. This is a fibration
of the full-root problem, rather than a necessary quotient in which
individual roots have been discarded.

#### Birational root coordinates and admissible coverage

Write the first four normalized roots as $u,v,w,z$, with
\[
u^2+v^2=w^2+z^2=2.
\]
On $S_0=u+v+w+z\ne0$, put
\[
\sigma=\frac4{S_0},\qquad
m=\frac{w-z-u+v}{S_0},\qquad
n=\frac{w-z+u-v}{S_0}.
\tag{ROOT49-INVERSE}
\]
Then
\[
\sigma^2=(1+m^2)(1+n^2)=D,
\]
and the inverse formulas are
\[
\begin{aligned}
u&=(1+mn+n-m)/\sigma,&
v&=(1+mn-n+m)/\sigma,\\
w&=(1-mn+n+m)/\sigma,&
z&=(1-mn-n-m)/\sigma.
\end{aligned}
\tag{ROOT49-FORWARD}
\]
For example, subtracting the two equal-norm identities gives
\[
(w-z)^2-(u-v)^2=(u+v-w-z)S_0,
\]
which yields $mn=(u+v-w-z)/S_0$ and recovers the two root sums.
Their differences follow immediately from (ROOT49-INVERSE), and the
first norm identity gives $\sigma^2=D$. Thus these are inverse rational
maps, not only matching squareclasses.

Let
\[
\begin{aligned}
F_0&=(1+m^2)(1+n^2),\\
F_{1,+}&=F_0+4n(1-m^2),&F_{1,-}&=F_0-4n(1-m^2),\\
F_{2,+}&=F_0+4m(1-n^2),&F_{2,-}&=F_0-4m(1-n^2).
\end{aligned}
\tag{ROOT49-RADICANDS}
\]
Adjoin their five labeled square roots, with the first equal to $\sigma$.
The four remaining normalized roots are their four labeled roots divided
by $\sigma$, assigning $F_{2,+}$ to $1-x+y$ and $F_{2,-}$ to $1+x-y$.
Section 12.29 supplies the exact offsets $x,y$. Conversely multiply each
of these four normalized roots by $\sigma$ to recover all five covering
coordinates. This proves a birational equivalence over $\mathbb Q$ with
the normalized full-root surface.

For every admissible square choose all nine normalized roots positive.
Then $S_0>0$, and the two numerators in (ROOT49-INVERSE) have absolute
value smaller than $S_0$. Thus $|m|,|n|<1$. If $m=0$, the equal sums of
squares and $u-v=w-z$ force $u=w,v=z$, repeating the offsets. Therefore
every admissible point is covered with
\[
 m\in\mathbb Q\cap(-1,1)\setminus\{0\}.
\tag{ROOT49-ADMISSIBLE-BASE}
\]
There is no unexamined admissible point on $S_0=0$.

The genus below concerns the normalized moving fiber of this rational
map. A naive projective hyperplane section can include a fixed boundary
component: $S_0=0$ and $w-z-u+v=0$ imply $w=-v,z=-u$. Removing that fixed
component is part of passing to the rational-map fiber. No genus claim
is made for the entire unreduced hyperplane section.

#### All rational nonboundary fibers have genus forty-nine

Fix $m\in\mathbb Q\setminus\{0,1,-1\}$ and set $A_0=1+m^2$.
The five polynomials (ROOT49-RADICANDS) are quadratic in $n$. Their
leading coefficients are $A_0,A_0,A_0,A_0-4m,A_0+4m$, all nonzero
at such a rational parameter. Their discriminants are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
F_0&-4A_0^2\\
F_{1,\pm}&4(3m^2-1)(m^2-3)\\
F_{2,\pm}&-4(m^4-14m^2+1).
\end{array}
\tag{ROOT49-DISCRIMINANTS}
\]
All ten pairwise resultants are given by the following table:

| Pair | Resultant in $n$ |
|---|---|
| $F_0,F_{1,\pm}$ | $16A_0^2(1-m^2)^2$ |
| $F_{1,+},F_{1,-}$ | $64A_0^2(1-m^2)^2$ |
| $F_0,F_{2,\pm}$ | $64m^2A_0^2$ |
| $F_{2,+},F_{2,-}$ | $256m^2A_0^2$ |
| $F_{1,\varepsilon},F_{2,\delta}$, all four sign pairs | $16(m^4-6m^2+1)^2$ |

The other possible zeros are irrational: $m^2=3,1/3$,
$m^2=7\pm4\sqrt3$, $m^2=3\pm2\sqrt2$, or
$m=\pm2\pm\sqrt3$; $A_0$ has no real zero. Thus the five quadratics
are squarefree and pairwise coprime at every stated rational $m$,
not only at the generic parameter.

Each has two simple branch points disjoint from the others. A nonempty
product of their squareclasses has odd valuation at a root unique to
one selected factor. Therefore their geometric squareclass rank is
exactly five. The simultaneous cover is geometrically connected of
degree $32$ over the $n$-line, with ten branch points, each of inertia
order two. Infinity is unramified because each pole order is even.
For its smooth projective normalization $C_m$, Riemann--Hurwitz gives
\[
 2g(C_m)-2=32(-2)+10\cdot16=96,
 \qquad \boxed{g(C_m)=49.}
\tag{ROOT49-GENUS}
\]
All values in (ROOT49-ADMISSIBLE-BASE) fall within this theorem.

#### Exact character decomposition of the Jacobian

For every nonempty subset $I$ of the five labeled factors, let
\[
 C_{m,I}: y_I^2=\prod_{i\in I}F_i(n).
\]
It has genus $|I|-1$. The products retain their actual rational constants;
no constant twist has been silently removed. The quotient maps and their
Jacobian pullbacks give a rational isogeny
\[
 \operatorname{Jac}(C_m)\ \sim_{\mathbb Q}
 \prod_{\substack{I\subseteq\{0,1+,1-,2+,2-\}\\|I|\ge2}}
 \operatorname{Jac}(C_{m,I}).
\tag{ROOT49-JACOBIAN}
\]
Indeed the differential pullbacks for each subset belong to its distinct
sign character. Their dimensions exhaust the genus:

| Subset size | Number of factors | Genus of each | Total dimension |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 | 10 | 1 | 10 |
| 3 | 10 | 2 | 20 |
| 4 | 5 | 3 | 15 |
| 5 | 1 | 4 | 4 |

The total is $49$. The sign-character projectors after clearing their
powers-of-two denominators, or equivalently the independent differential
pullbacks, show that the combined Jacobian map has finite kernel.
This proves the isogeny over $\mathbb Q$. It is not a rank bound for
these factors or for their rational specializations.

#### Rational boundary sections and scope

For every stated rational $m$, the four distinct coordinates
\[
 n=m,\quad -m,\quad 1/m,\quad -1/m
\]
have all five radicands nonzero rational squares. At $n=m$,
\[
 F_0=(1+m^2)^2,\qquad
 F_{1,\pm}=F_{2,\pm}=(m^2\mp2m-1)^2.
\]
The transformations $n\mapsto-n$ and $n\mapsto1/n$ supply the other
three coordinates, permuting the factors and multiplying by square
functions. Each coordinate therefore has all $32$ distinct rational
choices of the five root signs. This gives $128$ rational boundary
points on every $C_m$. Each has $x=0$ or $y=0$, so none is admissible.
No assertion that these are all rational points is made.

This fibration retains every individual square condition in a five-radical
model. Its genus is smaller than that of the B-pencil fiber (193), and
matches the genus already obtained for the fixed-circle fibrations in
Section 10. The added explicit data are the birational root coordinates,
character targets, rational boundary sections and complete exceptional
base analysis; the genus alone does not establish a stronger arithmetic
method. The rational base set in (ROOT49-ADMISSIBLE-BASE) remains
infinite; neither the bounded parameter interval, the fixed fiber genus,
nor the Jacobian isogeny bounds denominators or proves that the boundary
points exhaust all fibers.

Independent polynomial reduction, all ten resultants, every branch
polynomial and rational exceptional root, and all four boundary sections
are certified in `root_genus49_chart_audit.py/.json`. The birational and
arithmetic proof is independent of any height-limited search.

#### The complete degenerate rational locus

There is a useful strengthening of the boundary count that does not
assert that these points exhaust the whole curve. For every rational
\(m\ne0,\pm1\), **every rational point of \(C_m\) outside those 128
points yields an admissible full-root square**.

First, at every finite rational \(n\), \(D>0\), so the displayed
forward formulas give all eight normalized roots over \(\mathbb Q\).
At a point above \(n=\infty\), set \(v=1/n\) and scale each radical
by \(v\). Their squares are polynomials in \(v\) with nonzero constant
terms. In particular \((v\sigma)^2=A_0(1+v^2)\), so \(v\sigma\)
is nonzero there. The same forward formulas after scaling therefore
remain regular and rational at any rational point above infinity.
Thus every rational point gives nine rational squares
\[
1+i x+j y\qquad(i,j\in\{-1,0,1\}).
\]
They are strictly positive: if one were zero, its opposite would be
2, which is not a rational square. Positivity here uses the real
embedding of \(\mathbb Q\), not an extra hypothesis.

If two entries coincide and \(xy\ne0\), then
\((i-i')x+(j-j')y=0\), where both nonzero differences belong to
\(\{-2,-1,1,2\}\). Consequently
\[
x/y\in\{\pm1,\pm2,\pm\tfrac12\}.
\]
For ratio \(\pm1\), the entries contain the five distinct squares
\(1-2d,1-d,1,1+d,1+2d\), with \(d\ne0\).
For ratios \(\pm2,\pm1/2\), they contain all seven terms
\(1+jd\), \(-3\le j\le3\), again with \(d\ne0\).
Both contradict Fermat's theorem that four distinct rational squares
cannot form an arithmetic progression, as stated and proved in [45]. Thus a degenerate rational point must have \(x=0\) or
\(y=0\).

The exact formulas give
\[
x=0\iff n=m\text{ or }n=-1/m,\qquad
y=0\iff n=-m\text{ or }n=1/m
\]
for finite \(n\). At infinity they give
\(x=2m/(1+m^2)=-y\ne0\), so the same four-square progression
obstruction shows that no rational point lies above infinity.
The four finite coordinates have exactly the 32 rational lifts each
already counted. These 128 points are therefore the **entire
degenerate rational locus** on \(C_m\).

The same observation excludes rational points above \(n=0,1,-1\):
their nonzero offsets satisfy \(x=\pm y\). Outside the 128 boundary
points all entries are positive and distinct, and clearing denominators
gives an integral magic square of squares. This establishes the exact
equivalence
\[
C_m(\mathbb Q)\setminus\{128\text{ boundary points}\}\ne\varnothing
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{an admissible full-root point occurs in this }m\text{-fiber}.
\]
It remains an unbounded rational-point problem; the argument provides
no exhaustion of the nonboundary locus.

#### Distinction from the fixed-circle pencils

Put $k=(1-m^2)/(1+m^2)$ and $t=2m/(1+m^2)$, so $k^2+t^2=1$.
With $s=2n/(1+n^2)$ and $c_0=(1-n^2)/(1+n^2)$, the offsets are
$x=ks-tc_0$, $y=ks+tc_0$. Consequently the image of this fiber in the
normalized squared-entry plane is the nonsingular conic
\[
 \frac{(x+y)^2}{4k^2}+\frac{(x-y)^2}{4t^2}=1.
\tag{ROOT49-CONIC-IMAGE}
\]
Here $kt\ne0$ at every stated rational base. The earlier eight
progression-circle pencils fix ratios of linear forms in $(1,x,y)$,
so their fiber images are lines. Root sign changes fix this plane and
the stated grid symmetries act linearly; they cannot identify this conic
with any of those lines. This distinguishes the pencils under those
symmetries, without asserting inequivalence under arbitrary birational
automorphisms.


### 12.32. The universal Pythagorean base change adds no arithmetic sections

This result concerns function fields. Individual rational fibers can still acquire rank or odd saturation; their torsion on the required rational base is determined in Section 12.33.

Let
\[
E_p:\ y^2=x(x+\beta^2)(x+\alpha\gamma),\quad
\alpha=p^2-3,\ \beta=p^2+1,\ \gamma=1-3p^2.
\]
The generic arithmetic group was proved to be $\mathbb ZP\oplus C_2^2$ in Section 12.29. Every nondegenerate full-root point requires beta to be square. Parameterize this universal necessary cover by
\[
p=\frac{2m}{1-m^2},\qquad\sqrt\beta=\frac{1+m^2}{1-m^2}.
\]
The main conclusion is the exact equality
\[
\boxed{E_p(\mathbf Q(m))=E_p(\mathbf Q(p))=\mathbf ZP\oplus C_2^2.}       \tag{BETA-BASECHANGE-1}
\]
The proof first shows that the anti-invariant quadratic twist has geometric rank zero and then excludes new saturation and torsion. Equality of ranks alone would not imply (BETA-BASECHANGE-1).

#### A reciprocal pair of twist K3 surfaces

Put z=p² and
\[
A=(z+1)^2,\qquad B=(z-3)(1-3z).
\]
The elliptic surface
\[
E_z:y^2=x(x+A)(x+B)
\]
is rational, with I4 fibers at z=±1 and I2 fibers at z=3,1/3. The root rank is eight, so its geometric Mordell-Weil rank is zero.

The beta twist on the p-line decomposes, after the quadratic extension z=p², into the two twists of E_z by z+1 and z(z+1). They are isomorphic after the reciprocal base substitution z↦1/z. Indeed A(1/z)=A(z)/z² and B(1/z)=B(z)/z², while z+1 transforms to (z+1)/z, which has squareclass z(z+1). For the full twisted models the resulting exact map from the (z+1)-twist at 1/z to the z(z+1)-twist at z is $x\mapsto z^4x$, $y\mapsto z^6y$.

It is therefore enough to prove rank zero for
\[
\mathcal T:\ y^2=x^3+d(A+B)x^2+d^2ABx,\qquad d=z+1.             \tag{BETA-BASECHANGE-2}
\]
Its complete fiber list is

| Base | Fiber | Root lattice |
|---|---|---|
| -1 | I4* | D8 |
| 1 | I4 | A3 |
| 3,1/3 | I2,I2 | A1,A1 |
| infinity | I0* | D4 |

Their Euler numbers total 24 and their root rank is seventeen. Thus (BETA-BASECHANGE-2) is a K3 surface with a known rank-nineteen trivial lattice. The geometric rank is at most one before the reduction argument.

#### Component fields and good reduction at 5 and 7

The D8 and D4 component graphs are split. All four two-torsion sections are rational. At either additive fiber, their reduction injects into the component group C2², fixing the identity and all three other outer tips; these determine the complete graph. The two A1 roots have no nontrivial graph permutation.

At z=1 the I4 node is x=-8 and the tangent slopes are ±2sqrt(-2). Its A3 root character is 2·1+chi(-2). Consequently the entire root contribution has character
\[
16\cdot1+\chi_{-2},
\]
and adding O,F gives the known rank-nineteen representation
\[
18\cdot1+\chi_{-2}.                             \tag{BETA-BASECHANGE-3}
\]

Here is a direct relative resolution check, avoiding an inference of good reduction solely from unchanged discriminant valuations. Work over either Z5 or Z7; unramified extension is harmless for the construction and the resolution descends uniquely. All bad base sections remain disjoint, since their differences have no prime factors other than 2 and 3.

At z=-1 put u=z+1. Then B=-3u²+16u-16 and the local double cover is
\[
y^2=x(x+u^3)(x+uB).
\]
The three branch sections are smooth. The first two have contact order three; the third is transverse, with coefficient -16 a unit. The successive branch blowups following the tangent pair have normalized charts
\[
Y^2=uX(X+u^2)(X+B),\quad
Y_1^2=uZ(Z+u)(uZ+B),\quad
Y_2^2=uW(W+1)(u^2W+B).
\]
They come respectively from x=uX, X=uZ, Z=uW, dividing the square factor from y at each step. After the first blowup there is also an ordinary branch crossing at X=16; after the second there is a crossing at Z=infinity; after the third the remaining crossings on the new exceptional curve are W=0,-1,infinity. The final three values are pairwise separated over either residue field. Thus there are three ramified exceptional curves and five ordinary double-cover nodes. Blowing up each transverse branch crossing and normalizing resolves its equation y²=unit·uv; these five A1 resolutions give the full eight exceptional curves of D8. Every center and intersection remains smooth and separated over the DVR. This gives a simultaneous smooth resolution, with no ramified extension of the coefficient DVR.

At infinity the three local branch sections have slopes 0,3,-1. One branch blowup separates them, leaving three transverse branch crossings, so its normalized double cover has one ramified exceptional curve and three A1 curves: D4. The pairwise slope differences 1,3,4 are units at 5 and 7.

At z=1 the two colliding roots differ by
\[
d(A-B)=4(z+1)(z-1)^2,
\]
and the third root is separated by a unit. After an unramified square-root extension of its unit factor, the completed equation is of the form UV=unit·(z-1)^4. Its relative A3 resolution uses the usual successive blowups; all coefficients needed here are units. At z=3 and 1/3 the corresponding root difference has order one, giving UV=unit·u² and the relative A1 resolution. The tangent field at z=1 is Q(sqrt(-2)), unramified at the two primes. These constructions exhaust the singularities of the proper Weierstrass model. Their smooth proper minimal resolutions give good reduction at both 5 and 7 with precisely the displayed fiber types.


#### Exact finite-field counts

The dependency-free script `beta_twist_point_counts.py` constructs $\mathbb F_{p^n}$, $n=1,2,3$, and directly counts the minimal Weierstrass fibers. Resolving a fiber adds q times the trace on its root components, so the correction is
\[
q\bigl(16+(-2/p)^n\bigr),\qquad q=p^n.
\]
The script then removes the contributions of H0,H4 and the nineteen known divisor classes (BETA-BASECHANGE-3). The resulting exact counts are

| p | n | Smooth surface count | Remaining three-dimensional trace |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 5 | 1 | 114 | 3 |
| 5 | 2 | 1080 | -21 |
| 5 | 3 | 18018 | 267 |
| 7 | 1 | 170 | 1 |
| 7 | 2 | 3320 | -13 |
| 7 | 3 | 124490 | 1009 |

Newton identities give the remaining Frobenius polynomials
\[
(\lambda-5)(\lambda^2+2\lambda+25),\qquad
(\lambda-7)(\lambda^2+6\lambda+49).
\]
The two quadratic roots divided by p are not roots of unity: their sum is -2/5 or -6/7, a rational noninteger, whereas the sum of two roots of unity is an algebraic integer. Thus the geometric reduction Picard number is exactly twenty, by the Tate theorem for K3 surfaces in characteristic at least five [44, Corollary 2]. Over $\mathbb F_{p^2}$, every algebraic Frobenius eigenvalue is $p^2$.
The geometric Néron--Severi lattice has finite Galois image: finitely many
generating divisor classes are defined over finite extensions. Its
normalized Frobenius is therefore a finite-order, hence semisimple,
operator. Its eigenvalues are $1$ and $-1$, so its square fixes the entire
integral lattice. For K3 surfaces $\operatorname{Pic}^0=0$, and an invariant
line bundle descends over a finite field because that field has trivial
Brauer group. Thus all twenty classes are defined over $\mathbb F_{p^2}$,
verifying the divisor-field hypothesis of [43, Proposition 4.7].

#### Artin-Tate and characteristic-zero Picard rank

Let a5=-2,a7=-6 denote the traces of the quadratic factors. Over $\mathbb F_{p^2}$, [43, Proposition 4.7] determines the reduction NS discriminant squareclass as
\[
-(4p^2-a_p^2).
\]
The two values are
\[
-96\sim-6\quad(p=5),\qquad -160\sim-10\quad(p=7).
\]
Their ratio is not square. If the characteristic-zero Picard number were twenty, specialization into either rank-twenty reduction lattice would have finite index [43, Proposition 4.2], so both reduction discriminants would have the same rational squareclass as the characteristic-zero discriminant. This is impossible. The known nineteen divisor classes therefore give
\[
\boxed{\rho(\mathcal T_{\mathbf C})=19,\qquad\operatorname{rank}E_z^{z+1}(\mathbf C(z))=0.}
\]
By reciprocal symmetry the z(z+1) twist also has rank zero. Quadratic-extension rank decomposition now gives
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{rank}E_p^{p^2+1}(\mathbf C(p))=0.}           \tag{BETA-BASECHANGE-4}
\]
The exact producer certificate is `beta_twist_point_counts.py/.json`.
An independent implementation, `rank4_next/beta_twist_audit/verify_picard_counts.py/.json`,
uses different irreducible field polynomials and multiplicative-character
sums and reproduces all six counts. The resolution, component-field and
discriminant hypotheses have separate proofs above.

#### No new arithmetic saturation

Let $K=\mathbb Q(p)$, $L=K(\sqrt\beta)=\mathbb Q(m)$, and let $\sigma$ be its nontrivial automorphism. The anti-invariant beta twist has rank zero by (BETA-BASECHANGE-4). It has additive I4* fibers over p=±i, so its geometric torsion injects into a component group C2². Its displayed full two-torsion realizes this bound. Therefore
\[
E_p^\beta(K)=C_2^2.
\]
For any Q in E_p(L), Q-sigma(Q) is anti-invariant and hence has order dividing two. It follows that 2Q lies in E_p(K). Write
\[
2Q=nP+T,\qquad T\in E_p[2](K).
\]
If n is odd, the first Kummer coordinate of nP+T over L is one of
\[
\alpha,\quad\gamma,\quad-\alpha,\quad-\gamma.
\]
Each has a simple zero at a root of alpha or gamma; the beta extension is unramified there. Hence all four remain nonsquares in L, so nP+T cannot be doubled. Thus n=2m is even and 2(Q-mP)=T.

There is no new arithmetic four-torsion in L. Halving T0=(0,0) would require alpha·gamma to become square, which its simple zeros exclude. Halving (-beta²,0) would require -1 to be square, impossible in the real rational function field Q(m). Halving (-alpha·gamma,0) would require -alpha·gamma to become square, again excluded by its simple zeros. Therefore T=0 and Q-mP is already rational two-torsion. This proves the exact group equality (BETA-BASECHANGE-1).

For the offset genus-one curve itself, the degree-four map is 2Q+P. Since doubling kills the arithmetic two-torsion, its entire generic image over the universal beta-square cover consists exactly of the odd multiples (2n+1)P. This is a complete statement about generic rational sections. It does not classify all rational points on the specialized fibers, and the full-root conditions still impose further independent squareclasses.


### 12.33. Uniform Kummer restrictions on every rational Pythagorean base

**Theorem.** Let \(p\in\mathbb Q^\times\) and suppose
\(\beta=p^2+1\in\mathbb Q^{\times2}\). Put
\[
\alpha=p^2-3,\quad\gamma=1-3p^2,\quad A=\beta^2,\quad B=\alpha\gamma,
\qquad E_p:y^2=x(x+A)(x+B).
\]
Then the classes \(-1,B,\alpha\) are independent in
\(\mathbb Q^\times/\mathbb Q^{\times2}\). Moreover,
\[
E_p(\mathbb Q)_{\rm tors}=E_p[2]\cong(\mathbb Z/2)^2,
\qquad \operatorname{rank}E_p(\mathbb Q)\ge1.
\]
For the point
\[
P=(\alpha\beta p^2,\alpha\beta p(p^2-1)^2),
\]
the entire rational offset lift is precisely the Kummer coset
\[
P+2E_p(\mathbb Q).
\]
In particular, among points \(nP+T\), \(T\in E_p[2]\), the offset lift exists
exactly when \(n\) is odd and \(T=O\). At a rank-one specialization,
\(\langle P,E_p[2]\rangle\) has finite odd index in \(E_p(\mathbb Q)\).
No assertion that this index is one is made.

The companion `universal_beta_kummer.py/.json` independently checks the fixed
curve descent obstruction, the quartic maps and exceptional limits, the
signed-class congruences, and the actual Kummer identities.

#### One fixed rank-zero elliptic curve

Let
\[
E_0:y^2=x(x+1)(x-3)=x^3-2x^2-3x.
\]
Its 2-isogenous curve is
\[
E'_0:y^2=x(x^2+4x+16).
\]
For the standard two-isogeny descent, the original squareclass image is
exactly \(\{1,-1,3,-3\}\), since these are all squarefree divisors of \(-3\)
and are supplied by the rational 2-torsion. On the isogenous curve the
quadratic factor \((x+2)^2+12\) is positive, so every nonzero rational
abscissa is positive. Thus the only possible classes are 1 and 2. Class 2
would require a primitive solution of
\[
N^2=2U^4+4U^2V^2+8V^4.
\]
For primitive \(U,V\), the right side is respectively 2, 8, or 14 modulo 16
according to their parities, and is never a square. The isogeny image sizes
are 4 and 1, proving rank zero.

The good reduction counts at 5 and 7 are both eight. No nonzero rational
2-torsion point has a rational half: at roots \(0,-1,3\), the two root
differences are respectively \((1,-3),(-1,-4),(3,4)\), and each pair has a
nonsquare member. Consequently
\[
E_0(\mathbb Q)=\{O,(0,0),(-1,0),(3,0)\}.
\]

If both \(p^2+1\) and \(p^2-3\) were rational squares, their roots together
with \(p\) would give a point of \(E_0\) with abscissa \(p^2\). None of the
four points above permits this. Hence \(\alpha\) is nonsquare. Replacing
\(p\) by \(1/p\) proves that \(\gamma\) is also nonsquare when \(p\ne0\).

#### The reciprocal quartic, including its omitted charts

Consider
\[
C_B:w^2=(p^2-3)(1-3p^2).
\]
With \((p,w)=(1,2)\) as origin, a birational map to \(E_0\) is
\[
X=\frac{w+2p}{(p-1)^2},\qquad
Y=\frac{(p+1)(w+2p-3(p-1)^2)}{(p-1)^3}.
\]
Its inverse away from the displayed exceptional coordinates is
\[
p=\frac{Y+X-3}{Y-X+3},\qquad w=X(p-1)^2-2p.
\]
The certificate verifies both identities. The point \((1,2)\) maps to \(O\).
At \((1,-2)\), setting \(p=1+u\) gives
\(w=-2-2u+3u^2+O(u^3)\), so the map extends to \((3,0)\).
The points \((-1,2),(-1,-2)\) map to \((0,0),(-1,0)\).
There are no rational points at infinity on the quartic because its leading
coefficient is \(-3\). These four preimages exhaust the four rational points
of \(E_0\), so
\[
C_B(\mathbb Q)=\{(1,2),(1,-2),(-1,2),(-1,-2)\}.
\]
The hypothesis \(p^2+1\) square excludes \(p=\pm1\); hence \(B\) is nonsquare.

#### All remaining signed classes

The class \(-\alpha\) cannot be square, because that would make 3 a sum of
two rational squares. Clearing primitive denominators, reduction modulo 3
forces both summands divisible by 3 and then forces the denominator divisible
by 3, a contradiction. The same argument applied to
\(w^2+1=3p^2\) excludes \(-\gamma\).

Nor can \(-B\) be square. With primitive numerator and denominator \(a,b\)
of \(p\), this would give
\[
N^2=3a^4-10a^2b^2+3b^4.
\]
If both \(a,b\) are units modulo 3, the right side is 2 modulo 3. If exactly
one is divisible by 3, its 3-adic valuation is exactly one. Both cases are
impossible for a square.

The seven nontrivial products of \(-1,B,\alpha\), modulo squares, are
\[
-1,\quad B,\quad -B,\quad\alpha,\quad-\alpha,\quad\gamma,\quad-\gamma.
\]
All have now been proved nonsquare. This proves independence.

#### Exact torsion and actual Kummer images

There is also a uniform exact torsion argument at 3. Since \(p^2+1\) is a
3-adic square, \(v_3(p)\ne0\): a 3-adic unit \(p\) would give
\(p^2+1\equiv2\pmod3\). If necessary replace \(p\) by \(1/p\); the curves
are rationally isomorphic by
\((x,y)\mapsto(x/p^4,y/p^6)\). Thus suppose \(v_3(p)>0\). Then
\[
v_3(A)=0,\qquad v_3(B)=1,\qquad v_3(A-B)=0.
\]
The displayed integral Weierstrass equation is minimal, with \(v_3(c_4)=0\)
and \(v_3(\Delta)=2\). Its reduction is
\(y^2=x^2(x+1)\), whose node has rational tangent directions \(y=\pm x\).
It has split multiplicative type \(I_2\). The nonsingular reduction group
has order \(3-1=2\), and the component group has order two. Its formal kernel
is torsion-free over \(\mathbb Q_3\), as the formal logarithm is injective
on \(3\mathbb Z_3\) [35, Chapter IV]. Thus the entire rational torsion group has order at most
four. The visible full 2-torsion proves that it is exactly \(E_p[2]\).

Use the split Kummer coordinates attached in order to
\(x,x+A,x+B\). For \(T_0=(0,0)\) and \(T_A=(-A,0)\), their exact classes are
\[
\delta(T_0)=(B,1,B),\qquad\delta(T_A)=(-1,1,-1),
\qquad\delta(P)=(\alpha,1,\alpha).
\]
Here
\[
A-B=4(p^2-1)^2,
\quad x(P)+A=\beta(p^2-1)^2,
\quad x(P)+B=\alpha(p^2-1)^2
\]
give the classes directly. The preceding independence proves that these
are three independent elements of the **actual** group
\(E_p(\mathbb Q)/2E_p(\mathbb Q)\), not merely of a Selmer upper bound.
In particular \(P\) is nontorsion and is not divisible by 2 modulo torsion.

#### Whole-group offset restrictions and all exceptional charts

The offset equations are
\[
U^2=\alpha r^2+\beta,\qquad V^2=\beta r^2+\gamma.
\]
Their map to \(E_p\) is
\[
x=\alpha\beta r^2,\qquad y=\alpha\beta rUV.
\]
A rational elliptic point with all three coordinates nonzero lifts exactly
when its Kummer class is
\((\alpha\beta,\beta,\alpha)=(\alpha,1,\alpha)=\delta(P)\).
The kernel of the split Kummer map is \(2E_p(\mathbb Q)\), proving the exact
coset description.

No rational offset points were omitted in restricting to the nonzero chart.
If \(r=0\), then \(\gamma\) would be square. If \(U=0\), then
\(-\alpha\) would be square, since \(\beta\) is square. If \(V=0\), then
\(-\gamma\) would be square. At a projective point with \(r=\infty\), the
leading ratio \(U/r\) would make \(\alpha\) square. All are excluded above.
Likewise the elliptic torsion points have Kummer classes outside the coset.

Independence now gives
\[
\delta(nP+T)=\delta(P)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n\equiv1\pmod2\ \text{and}\ T=O,
\qquad T\in E_p[2].
\]
This excludes every even-multiple/torsion orbit and every nontrivial
2-torsion translate of an odd multiple. At arbitrary rank, the stronger
whole-group formulation remains \(P+2E_p(\mathbb Q)\). At rank one, writing
\(P=mG+T\) in the exact Mordell–Weil group shows that \(m\) is odd, giving the
stated finite odd index. It does not show that all lifts are integer multiples
of \(P\), unless saturation is separately proved.

Finally, the omitted base \(p=0\) has
\(U^2=1-3r^2,V^2=1+r^2\). If \(r\ne0\), the already proved \(\gamma\)
nonsquare theorem, applied to \(r\), contradicts these equations. Thus only
\(r=0,U=\pm1,V=\pm1\) occurs, and the reconstructed offsets are both zero.
The base chart \(p=\infty\) belongs to the original \(a=b\) locus; its defining
quadric forces \(\xi=\pm\eta\), so it cannot represent a pairwise-distinct
magic-square lift. These exceptional bases do not furnish genuine solutions.


### 12.34. Exact character quotients and their boundary ranks

This section concerns the full-root curves of Section 12.31 at rational
$m\ne0,\pm1$, and their generic fiber over $\mathbb Q(m)$. Write
\[
A=1+m^2,\quad B=4(1-m^2),\quad C=4m,
\]
and label the five factors
\[
f_0=A(1+n^2),\qquad f_\pm=A(1+n^2)\pm Bn,
\qquad g_\pm=(A\mp C)n^2+A\pm C.
\tag{ROOT49-CHARACTER-LABELS}
\]
Negation $R:n\mapsto-n$ swaps $f_+,f_-$ and fixes the other factors.
Reciprocity $S:n\mapsto1/n$ swaps $g_+,g_-$ and sends every factor to
its partner divided by $n^2$. For a character with $r$ factors its exact
reciprocal lift is $(n,y)\mapsto(1/n,y/n^r)$. In particular all the
following isomorphisms preserve the actual constants over $\mathbb Q$.

#### The five pair-character types

The ten elliptic character curves have five representatives:

| Product | Multiplicity |
|---|---:|
| $f_0f_+$ | 2 |
| $f_0g_+$ | 2 |
| $f_+f_-$ | 1 |
| $g_+g_-$ | 1 |
| $f_+g_+$ | 4 |

For any representative, set $t=n-m$ and expand its quartic as
$at^4+bt^3+ct^2+dt+e$. The corresponding two entries of
\[
(A,\ m^2-2m-1,\ m^2+2m-1,\ m^2-2m-1,\ m^2+2m-1)
\]
have product $q$ with $q^2=e$. None vanishes at a stated rational base.
Taking $(t,y)=(0,q)$ as origin gives the exact elliptic model
\[
V^2=U^3+cU^2+(bd-4ae)U+b^2e+ad^2-4ace,
\tag{ROOT49-PAIR-ELLIPTIC}
\]
with rational map and inverse
\[
\begin{aligned}
U&=\frac{2q(y+q)+dt}{t^2},&
V&=\frac{(U^2-4ea)t-Ud-2eb}{2q},\\
t&=\frac{2qV+Ud+2eb}{U^2-4ea},&
y&=\frac{Ut^2-dt}{2q}-q.
\end{aligned}
\tag{ROOT49-PAIR-MAPS}
\]
Substitution proves both identities in the respective function fields;
their rational maps extend on the smooth projective models. Thus this
is the actual pointed curve, not a Jacobian specified only up to twist.

The other point over the same boundary coordinate, $(0,-q)$, has image
\[
Q_x=\frac{d^2}{4e}-c,\qquad
Q_y=-\frac{Q_xd+2eb}{2q}.
\tag{ROOT49-BOUNDARY-SECTION}
\]
Each of the five generic sections $Q$ is nontorsion. A finite exact proof
uses the smooth specialization $m=2$:

| Product | Weierstrass coefficients $(a_2,a_4,a_6)$ at $m=2$ | Boundary point $Q$ | Torsion order divides |
|---|---|---|---:|
| $f_0f_+$ | $(290,28300,975000)$ | $(194,4968)$ | 4 |
