The local proof is recorded separately in
`rank4_next/trace_center_norm/c_two_trace_local_lifting_gate.md`.


### 12.75. Exact closure of the remaining quartic C pencils

The remaining C pencils are empty as rational full-root families. Together
with the Cayley symmetry, the U/V deck exclusion and the preceding quartic
Riemann--Roch and imprimitive cases, this excludes every nonboundary rational
full-root family whose m-projection has degree at most four. The symmetric
statement holds for the n-projection. This is a theorem about rational
families, not an exclusion of isolated rational points on specialized fibers.

#### 12.75.1. The common quadratic quotient and the finite target list

Put

\[
K=\mathbb Q(m),\quad h=1-m^2,\quad A=1+m^2,\quad
p=2m/h,\quad \alpha=p^2-3,\quad\beta=p^2+1,\quad
D=A^2-16m^2.
\]

For a surviving primitive C-pencil family the previous field and deck
theorems give

\[
L=K(n)=\mathbb Q(t),\qquad
F=K(n^2)=K(R)=\mathbb Q(s),\qquad [F:K]=2,
\quad R=\frac{1+n^2}{1-n^2}.
\tag{12.75.1}
\]

The central root and the two individual G roots descend to F after the
proved choice of the C involution. In particular its point lies on the
common genus-five curve

\[
U^2=\alpha R^2+4,\quad V^2=\beta R^2-4p^2,\quad
s_0^2=\frac{2AR}{R+1}.
\tag{12.75.2}
\]

Its two elliptic images are

\[
\phi=\left(dR^2,\frac{\alpha\beta RUV}{8}\right),\quad
S=\left(\frac{eR}{R+1},\frac{ehVs_0}{R+1}\right),
\qquad d=\frac{\alpha\beta}{4},\quad e=2AD.
\tag{12.75.3}
\]

The first curve is
\(E_C:y^2=x(x+\beta)(x-\alpha p^2)\); the second is

\[
E_A:y^2=x\bigl(x+8mA(A+4m)\bigr)
                 \bigl(x-8mA(A-4m)\bigr).
\]

Use the primitive normalization \(q_C=H_C-H_C(B_0)\) and the established
generator \(G_C\). The exact origin certificate gives

\[
\phi=2q_C+b_C,\qquad b_C=-2G_C+T_{\alpha p^2}.
\tag{12.75.4}
\]

The complete proper two-trace sieve of §12.73, at
\((q,m_0)=(17,2),(41,2),(43,2),(47,2),(67,2),(97,2)\),
leaves eighteen labels for each of the two epsilon models. In the torsion
ordering
\(O,(0,0),(-\beta,0),(\alpha p^2,0)\), they are

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\operatorname{Tr}(q_C)&\operatorname{Tr}(S)\\ \hline
O\text{ or }(0,0)&0,\;2(\pm P\pm Q)\\
(-\beta,0)\text{ or }(\alpha p^2,0)&\pm2P,\;\pm2Q.
\end{array}
\tag{12.75.5}
\]

Here P,Q are the exact auxiliary rank-two basis. The sieve enumerates all
rational effective degree-two cycles, including nonsplit closed points and
proper charts; it is a necessary restriction on the actual common field.
Zero auxiliary trace forces equal conjugate abscissae and hence R in K,
contrary to (12.75.1). Changing the sign of s0 negates the auxiliary trace
and preserves q_C and each epsilon model. We need only treat

\[
B=2(P+Q),\quad2(P-Q),\quad2P,\quad2Q.
\tag{12.75.6}
\]

All labels in (12.75.5) have the same necessary displayed trace

\[
\operatorname{Tr}(\phi)=2\operatorname{Tr}(q_C)+2b_C
                  =-4G_C=:C.
\tag{12.75.7}
\]

#### 12.75.2. Exact chord equations, including their exceptional cases

Write the auxiliary cubic as \(x^3+a_2x^2+a_4x\), the C cubic as
\(X^3+c_2X^2+c_4X\), and let \(B=(b,c)\), \(C=(r,t)\).
The auxiliary abscissa \(x=eR/(R+1)\) is primitive over K. Its conjugate
abscissae are finite and distinct. Their chord, which passes through -B,
therefore has a finite slope \(\lambda\in K\). Dividing its cubic
intersection polynomial by \(x-b\) gives

\[
 D_A(x)=x^2+(a_2+b-\lambda^2)x
       +a_4+a_2b+b^2+b\lambda^2+2c\lambda.
\tag{12.75.8}
\]

This polynomial must be irreducible and separable, and \(F=K(x)\).
The two displayed C points also lie on a finite rational chord through -C.
If they coincide, use the tangent: their double is the nontorsion point C,
so this tangent is finite and rational. If they were opposite their trace
would vanish. Thus no diagonal or vertical case is omitted. For its slope
\(\mu\in K\), the corresponding quadratic is

\[
 D_C(X)=X^2+(c_2+r-\mu^2)X
       +c_4+c_2r+r^2+r\mu^2+2t\mu.
\tag{12.75.9}
\]

This quadratic is allowed to have a repeated root. Since
\(X=dR^2=dx^2/(e-x)^2\), the exact necessary relation is

\[
 (e-x)^4D_C\!\left(\frac{dx^2}{(e-x)^2}\right)
                      \equiv0\pmod{D_A(x)}.
\tag{12.75.10}
\]

The denominator cannot vanish at a primitive x. Likewise R cannot be any
K-constant, so the charts R=0,±1,infinity do not support a live quadratic
candidate. A zero of V would force \(R=\pm2p/\sqrt\beta\in K\); a zero
of U would make the displayed C trace torsion. These observations are used
only to justify the stated finite charts, not to remove arbitrary roots
of the subsequent resultant.

The coefficients of \(\mu^2,\mu,1\) in the numerator of (12.75.10) are

\[
\begin{aligned}
N_2&=-dx^2(e-x)^2+r(e-x)^4,\\
N_1&=2t(e-x)^4,\\
N_0&=d^2x^4+(c_2+r)dx^2(e-x)^2
                    +(c_4+c_2r+r^2)(e-x)^4.
\end{aligned}
\]

Reduction modulo the monic quadratic D_A gives two equations
\(A_j\mu^2+B_j\mu+C_j=0\), \(j=0,1\). Their resultant is

\[
 (A_0C_1-C_0A_1)^2
 -(A_0B_1-B_0A_1)(B_0C_1-C_0B_1).
\tag{12.75.11}
\]

For each target in (12.75.6), this is a nonzero degree-twelve polynomial
in lambda over Q(m). Factor it exactly and, at every rational lambda,
take the polynomial gcd of the two mu equations. This retains vanishing
subresultants and all repeated factors; it does not divide away an
exceptional coefficient. Every remaining quadratic factor has an explicitly
nonsquare rational-function discriminant.

#### 12.75.3. The complete rational-slope list has no rational quotient field

The four exact computations give the following exhaustive result.

| Auxiliary target | Rational lambda values | Outcomes after the exact mu gcd |
|---|---:|---|
| \(2(P+Q)\) | 4 | one double D_A, one genus-24 field, two with no rational mu |
| \(2(P-Q)\) | 4 | one double D_A, one genus-24 field, two with no rational mu |
| \(2P\) | 3 | one genus-6 field, one with no rational mu, one giving two split D_A cases |
| \(2Q\) | 3 | one genus-6 field, one with no rational mu, one giving two split D_A cases |

The discriminant squareclass for the sole nonsplit \(2(P+Q)\) case is
the product of seven pairwise coprime squarefree factors of degrees
\(1,1,4,4,8,16,16\). Their exact coefficients are retained in the
certificate. The \(2(P-Q)\) squareclass is its reciprocal under
\(m\mapsto1/m\). Both have fifty simple finite branch points and no
infinity branch, hence genus 24. For \(2P\), the squareclass is

\[
2(m^2+1)
(m^6+4m^5+3m^4-24m^3+3m^2+4m+1)
(m^6+4m^5+3m^4-8m^3+3m^2+4m+1).
\]

It has fourteen simple finite branch points, no infinity branch and genus
six. The \(2Q\) case is its \(m\mapsto-m\) counterpart. All signs,
constant squareclasses and denominator valuations are preserved in computing
these squareclasses.

Each nonsplit candidate therefore contradicts \(F=\mathbb Q(s)\).
Each split or double D_A contradicts primitivity in (12.75.1). This excludes
all cases in (12.75.5), for both epsilon choices and every retained C
two-torsion label. The passage to displayed trace (12.75.7) only weakened
the necessary conditions, so no extra root-lifting assumption is needed to
deduce the exclusion.

The exact scripts are `c_two_trace_eliminant_exact.py` and the four
`c_two_trace_exact_u_v.json` receipts in `next_pythagorean_cover`. The
independent recovery and proper-chart review is
`coupled_lifts/C_two_trace_extraction.md/.py/.json`; the independent
degree-fifty squareclass/genus check is
`simultaneous_units/verify_C_nonsplit_quadratic_genus.py/.json`.
The independent all-four factorization and complete mu-gcd audit is
`coupled_lifts/C_two_trace_eliminant_audit.md/.py/.json`; the independent
chord and chart-completeness review accompanies the final certificate.
These finite exact algebra calculations are not a bounded
rational-point search.


### 12.76. The complete cross-pair elliptic group and the genus-seventeen quotient

Let K=Q(m), A=1+m², h=1−m² and

\[
F_\pm=A(1+n^2)\pm4hn,\qquad
G_\pm=A(1+n^2)\pm4m(1-n^2).
\]

The four cross-pair character curves \(y^2=F_\epsilon G_\delta\) have isomorphic Jacobians over K. Their complete generic arithmetic group can be given explicitly. Put

\[
q_\pm=m^2\pm2m-1,\quad k=q_-q_+=m^4-6m^2+1.
\]

The Jacobian of \(y^2=F_+G_+\), with origin \((n,y)=(m,q_-^2)\), is

\[
E_\times:\quad Y^2=x(x^2-A^2x+k^2).
\tag{76.1}
\]

This identification is birational over K. To check it directly, write the shifted quartic at \(t=n-m\) as \(y^2=at^4+bt^3+ct^2+dt+e\), where \(e=q^2\) and \(q=q_-^2\). Then

\[
U=\frac{2q(y+q)+dt}{t^2},\qquad
W=\frac{(U^2-4ea)t-dU-2eb}{2q}
\]

satisfy

\[
W^2=U^3+cU^2+(bd-4ae)U+b^2e+ad^2-4ace.
\]

The substitution \(U=-2(m-1)^2q_-^2+4x,\ W=8Y\) gives (76.1). The rational inverse is \(t=(2qW+dU+2eb)/(U^2-4ea)\), followed by \(y=(Ut^2-dt-2e)/(2q)\). The maps extend between the smooth projective curves.

The exact arithmetic group is

\[
E_\times(K)=\mathbf ZP\oplus\mathbf ZQ\oplus\langle T\rangle,
\quad T=(0,0),\quad
P=(A^2,Ak),\quad Q=(q_+^2,Aq_+^2),
\tag{76.2}
\]

with \(T\) of order two and height matrix

\[
\begin{pmatrix}\langle P,P\rangle&\langle P,Q\rangle\\
\langle Q,P\rangle&\langle Q,Q\rangle\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}4&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{76.3}
\]

Here is a complete descent and saturation proof. Set

\[
f_1=m^2-3,\ f_2=3m^2-1,\ f_3=m^2-4m+1,\ f_4=m^2+4m+1,
\quad\Delta=-f_1f_2f_3f_4=A^4-4k^2.
\]

The dual two-isogenous model is \(E':Y^2=x(x^2+2A^2x+\Delta)\). Valuations away from the factors of the last coefficient, including every rational-prime Gauss valuation, give the complete scalar supports

\[
\delta(E(K))\subseteq\langle-1,q_-,q_+\rangle,
\quad
\delta'(E'(K))\subseteq\langle-1,f_1,f_2,f_3,f_4\rangle.
\]

Both last coefficients are primitive integral polynomials, so no constant prime classes are omitted. The joint support specializes injectively at m=5: its six polynomial generators become \(14,34,22,74,6,46\), distinguished by the primes \(7,17,11,37,3,23\), with the sign as a separate coordinate. Smooth specialization of the unramified Kummer classes is valid also at O and the two-torsion point; no rank-specialization theorem is invoked.

At m=5 the original coefficients are \((-676,226576)\). Negative classes are impossible over the reals; classes \(14,34,119\) have no primitive solution modulo 256 to the scalar torsor

\[
W^2=dU^4+aU^2V^2+(b/d)V^4.
\]

For the dual coefficients \((1352,-449328)\), the same test on its 32-class support retains exactly the masks

\[
0,1,6,7,10,11,12,13,18,19,20,21,24,25,30,31
\]

in the ordered basis \((-1,f_1,f_2,f_3,f_4)\). All nineteen exclusions were independently replayed over all 49,152 primitive ordered pairs modulo 256 per class. Actual dual points have independent scalar classes with masks \(24,7,25,11\), whose span is exactly this set. Hence the two scalar images have sizes 1 and 16, and the two-isogeny rank formula gives arithmetic rank two.

For the height and torsion calculation, the discriminant is \(16k^4\Delta\). The relatively minimal elliptic K3 has four I4 fibers at k=0, eight I1 fibers at \(\Delta=0\), and smooth infinity. Its geometric torsion exponent divides four by the height formula and component groups. The only geometric rational two-torsion section is T, since \(\Delta\) is nonsquare. Halving T would require \(\sqrt{2k-A^2}\) or \(\sqrt{-2k-A^2}\); each radicand has four simple zeros. Thus even the geometric torsion is exactly C2.

Both P and Q have zero intersection with O. P meets all identity components. Q meets the middle component of each I4 fiber at \(q_+=0\), contributing one at each, and all other identity components. In a local split nodal model, its two nodal coordinates each have valuation two, which verifies this component assignment. The sections intersect transversely at m=0 and infinity and nowhere else; the identities \(x(P)-x(Q)=4mh\) and \(Y(P)-Y(Q)=-4mAq_+\) verify the finite intersections. The height formula gives (76.3).

Finally the original scalar image being trivial identifies \(E(K)/2E(K)\) with the dual scalar image modulo \(\langle\Delta\rangle\). Dual preimages of P,Q,T have classes \(f_1f_2,-f_1f_3,-f_1f_2\), respectively. These three classes and \(\Delta\) are independent, so P,Q,T span modulo two. Every height pairing lies in \(\tfrac14\mathbf Z\); if the free index were j, (76.3) would give \(128/j^2\in\mathbf Z\). Thus j is a power of two, while modulo-two spanning makes it odd. Hence j=1, proving (76.2).

The involution n to −n exchanges F+ and F− and fixes both G factors. The involution n to 1/n fixes each F factor up to n−2 and exchanges G+ with G− up to n−2. Their product square multipliers are n−4, so they give actual K-isomorphisms of the four character curves, without constant twisting. This transports (76.2) to all four cross-pair Jacobians.

There is also a useful intermediate quotient of the full genus-forty-nine fiber:

\[
W:\quad K(W)=K(n,\sqrt{F_+},\sqrt{F_-},\sqrt{G_+},\sqrt{G_-}).
\]

It is a degree-sixteen cover of the n-line, branched at eight distinct geometric points, hence has genus seventeen. The full fiber maps to W with degree two. Its previously certified geometric gonality sixteen therefore gives \(\operatorname{gon}(W)\ge8\). Conversely W maps with degree four to the **actual two-root curve** \(K(n,\sqrt{F_+},\sqrt{G_+})\), which has genus one and a boundary K-point, and that curve has a degree-two map to a line. Thus \(\operatorname{gon}(W)=8\), geometrically and over K. The product-character curve \(K(n,\sqrt{F_+G_+})\) instead has degree-eight preimage in W; these map degrees must not be confused.

Consequently every effective divisor on W of degree at most seven has a unique effective representative in its linear equivalence class. The quotient also retains the previously known five center elliptic factors. These are additional arithmetic structures on specialized fibers; the generic group calculation is not a specialized rank bound, and none of these quotient statements restores any omitted root automatically.

### 12.77. An explicit quartic differential and all geometric rational curves

Let \(X\subset\mathbb P^8\) be the full-root surface, with the squared
coordinates arranged as
\[
h,\quad h+a,\quad h-a,\quad h+b,\quad h-b,\quad
h+a+b,\quad h+a-b,\quad h-a+b,\quad h-a-b.
\tag{12.77a}
\]
Write \(Y\to X\) for its minimal resolution and
\(\pi:X\to\mathbb P^2_{h,a,b}\) for the finite squaring projection.
All geometric assertions in this subsection are over an algebraic
closure of characteristic zero.

**Theorem 12.77 (Complete rational-curve classification).**
The surface \(X\) contains exactly \(128\) geometrically rational curves.
They are conics, all defined over \(\mathbb Q\), lying above the two lines
\(a=0\) and \(b=0\). The smooth surface \(Y\) has exactly \(384\)
geometrically rational curves: their \(128\) strict transforms and the
\(256\) exceptional curves over the ordinary double points.

In particular, no rational curve meets the open full-root locus on
which all nine squared entries are nonzero and pairwise distinct.
This conclusion concerns curves; it does not exclude isolated rational
points.

#### An actual global symmetric differential

Set
\[
u=h\,da-a\,dh,\qquad
v=h\,db-b\,dh,\qquad
w=a\,db-b\,da,
\]
and let \(L_0,\ldots,L_8\) be the nine linear forms in (12.77a). Define
\[
\begin{split}
N={}&h\bigl(w^4+3u^2v^2-w^2(u^2+v^2)\bigr)
       -2wuv(au-bv),\\
\omega_4={}&\frac{N}{L_0L_1\cdots L_8}.
\end{split}
\tag{12.77b}
\]
The products are symmetric products of differentials. Each of \(u,v,w\)
is horizontal for the Euler field and has homogeneous weight two.
The numerator and denominator both have weight nine, so the expression
descends projectively. It is not identically zero.

Here is a direct regularity proof. In a local frame with first coordinate
\(x=L_i\), expand \(N\) by its \(dx\)-degree. The coefficients of the
terms of \(dx\)-degree zero and one are divisible by \(x\), for each of
the nine lines. These are explicit polynomial identities obtained from
(12.77b). After \(x=r^2\), the denominator contributes \(r^{-2}\);
the stated divisibilities handle these two terms, while terms with at
least two \(dx\)'s are already regular. Thus there is no pole on the
smooth part of the root cover.

There are eight triple points of the line arrangement:
\[
[0:0:1],\ [0:1:0],\ [0:1:\pm1],\
[1:\pm1:0],\ [1:0:\pm1].
\tag{12.77c}
\]
The complete coefficient tensor \(N\) vanishes at each of these points.
Near a triple point choose affine coordinates \(x,y\) so that the
vanishing lines are \(x,y,\lambda x+\mu y\), with
\(\lambda\mu\ne0\). A generic chart of the ordinary-double-point
resolution has
\[
x=r^2,\qquad y=r^2z^2,
\]
with the third root \(r\sqrt{\lambda+\mu z^2}\).
The three denominator factors have total \(r\)-order six.
The coefficient vanishing gives order at least two, and four
differentials give order at least four. Thus \(\omega_4\) has no pole
along any exceptional divisor. The other factors are units at its
generic point. Since the symmetric cotangent bundle on \(Y\) is locally
free, regularity at every prime divisor extends across the remaining
isolated points. Therefore
\[
0\ne\omega_4\in H^0\!\left(Y,\operatorname{Sym}^4\Omega_Y^1\right).
\tag{12.77d}
\]

#### Integration of the quartic equation

The pullback of \(\omega_4\) to the normalization of a rational curve
vanishes, because
\(\operatorname{Sym}^4\Omega_{\mathbb P^1}^1=\mathcal O(-8)\).
Suppose its plane image is nonconstant and is not a branch line. In
the chart \(h=1\), the numerator becomes
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_4={}&b^2(b^2-1)da^4-4ab(b^2-1)da^3db\\
&+3(2a^2b^2-a^2-b^2+1)da^2db^2\\
&-4ab(a^2-1)da\,db^3+a^2(a^2-1)db^4.
\end{aligned}
\tag{12.77e}
\]
If \(a\) is constant, its vanishing gives \(a=0,\pm1\).
Otherwise define rational functions on the normalization by
\[
k=\frac{db}{da},\qquad c=b-ak.
\]
The contact identity is \(dc=-a\,dk\), and direct substitution gives
\[
P_4(1,k)=(c^2-1)(c^2-3k^2)-2ack(k^2-1).
\tag{12.77f}
\]

First suppose \(k\) is nonconstant. With \(z=c^2\), the vanishing of
(12.77f) becomes the Riccati equation
\[
\frac{dz}{dk}=-\frac{(z-1)(z-3k^2)}{k(k^2-1)}.
\tag{12.77g}
\]
If \(z=k^2\), then \(c=\pm k\), and the contact identity forces the
constant image \((a,b)=(\mp1,0)\). Otherwise direct differentiation
shows that
\[
C=\frac{c^2-1}{k(c^2-k^2)}
\]
is constant. Equivalently,
\[
c^2=\frac{1-Ck^3}{1-Ck}.
\tag{12.77h}
\]
For \(C\notin\{0,1,-1\}\), the right side has three simple zeros and one
distinct simple pole, while the pole at infinity has even order.
The associated double cover of the \(k\)-line has genus one. A
nonconstant map from a rational curve to it is impossible.
The case \(C=0\) gives \(c=\pm1\) and then a constant image
\((a,b)=(0,\pm1)\). For \(C=\epsilon=\pm1\),
\[
c^2=k^2+\epsilon k+1,\qquad
a=-\frac{2k+\epsilon}{2c},\qquad
b=\frac{\epsilon k+2}{2c},
\]
so the image lies on
\[
4(a^2+\epsilon ab+b^2)=3.
\tag{12.77i}
\]
All these calculations occur at the generic point and therefore retain
the omitted isolated zeros of the displayed denominators.

If \(k\) is constant, then \(b=ka+c\) with \(c\) constant. Since \(a\)
is nonconstant, both coefficients of (12.77f), viewed as a polynomial
in \(a\), vanish:
\[
ck(k^2-1)=0,\qquad(c^2-1)(c^2-3k^2)=0.
\]
The resulting lines are
\[
b=0,\pm1,\qquad b=\pm a+c,\quad c=\pm1,\pm\sqrt3.
\tag{12.77j}
\]
Together with \(a=0,\pm1\), the conics (12.77i) and the lines
(12.77j) exhaust the nonconstant rational integral images.

#### The exceptional nonbranch images have no rational full-root lift

For the plus conic in (12.77i), put \(s=a-b,t=a+b\). Its equation is
\[
s^2+3t^2=3.
\]
The actual roots of \(1+s\) and \(1-s\) supply a function \(y\) with
\(y^2=1-s^2\). On the smooth conic this function has four distinct
simple zeros, namely \(s=\pm1,t^2=2/3\), and only even poles at the
two points at infinity. The resulting connected double cover has
genus one. It cannot receive a nonconstant map from a rational
full-root curve. The minus conic is the same after \(b\mapsto-b\).

On a line \(b=\pm a+c\), \(c^2=3\), the four actual roots of
\(1\pm a,1\pm b\) similarly supply
\[
y^2=(1-a^2)(1-b^2).
\]
Its four zeros are distinct, since coincidence would require
\(c=0\) or \(c=\pm2\). This is another genus-one double cover.
Consequently every rational curve not contracted by the resolved
projection has image in a branch line or in \(a=0,b=0\).

#### Normalizations above the remaining lines

For completeness, the branch-line preimages themselves have no
rational component. Restrict the nine squared coordinates to a line,
remove zero coordinates, and normalize one nonzero root. Over the
algebraic closure constants are squares. If \(r\) is the squareclass
rank and \(B\) the number of branch values, a connected component has
degree \(2^r\) and
\[
g=1+2^{r-2}(B-4).
\tag{12.77k}
\]
In the table, \(t\) is a rational coordinate on the line; infinity is
included among its branch values.

| Plane-line type | Number of lines | Squareclass generators | \(r\) | \(B\) | Components per line | Genus |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| \(h=0\) | 1 | \(t,1+t,1-t\) | 3 | 4 | 16 | 1 |
| \(a=\pm h\) or \(b=\pm h\) | 4 | \(t,1+t,1-t,2+t,2-t\) | 5 | 6 | 4 | 17 |
| \(h\pm a\pm b=0\) | 4 | \(t,1-t,1+t,2-t\) | 4 | 5 | 8 | 5 |
| \(a=0\) or \(b=0\) | 2 | \(1+t,1-t\) | 2 | 3 | 64 | 0 |

A branch line has generic fiber size \(128\), since one root is zero,
whereas each nonbranch axis has generic fiber size \(256\). These give
the component counts in the table.

Each component over \(a=0\) is the linearly embedded conic
\[
(c,\ \pm c,\ \pm c,\ u,\ v,\ \pm u,\ \pm v,\ \pm u,\ \pm v),
\qquad u^2+v^2=2c^2,
\tag{12.77l}
\]
in the coordinate order (12.77a). The six independent signs give
\(64\) distinct conics. The other axis gives \(64\) more, with a
different plane image. All are defined over \(\mathbb Q\).
Because \(\pi\) is finite, the only curves contracted by the resolved
projection are the exceptional curves. There are \(32\) ordinary
double points over each of the eight triple points, hence \(256\)
exceptional rational curves. This proves the theorem.

### 12.78. An all-place finite four-descent on the remaining isolated-point branch

This section concerns isolated rational points at varying rational bases. All specialized Mordell–Weil ranks are unrestricted. Work in the normalized remaining \((P'+Q',P'+Q')\) orbit, retaining all five original root conditions. Write \(m=p/q\) in lowest terms, \(q>0\). The preceding all-prime support theorem gives \(v_2(m)\ge2\) and \(1+m^2\in\mathbb Q^{\times2}\). Put
\[
 H=q^2-p^2,\quad A_0=q^2+p^2=a^2,\quad
 \alpha_0=p^2-3q^2,\quad\gamma_0=q^2-3p^2,
 \qquad S=\{\ell:\ell\mid2H A_0\alpha_0\gamma_0\}.
\]
Here \(a\) is a positive integer, \(p\) is divisible by four, \(q\) is odd, and the excluded bases \(m=0,\pm1\) remain excluded. The necessary genus-five cover has the integral scaling
\[
 W_0^2=X_0,\quad W_1^2=X_0+4H^2,\quad
 W_2^2=X_0-2H\alpha_0,\quad W_3^2=X_0-\alpha_0\gamma_0. \tag{78.1}
\]
The actual full-root inverse retains
\[
 n=\frac{A_0W_0}{W_1W_3}. \tag{78.2}
\]
All these coordinates are finite and nonzero on the retained original locus. The four-square equations alone are not sufficient for an original full-root point.

For \(L_{ij}=W_i+W_j\), set
\[
 d_{ij}=[L_{ij}/L_{01}],\qquad ij=02,03,12,13,23. \tag{78.3}
\]
The sums never vanish at a finite point, because the four roots
\(e=(0,-4H^2,2H\alpha_0,\alpha_0\gamma_0)\) are distinct. The five classes determine the compatible Kummer vectors of the five elliptic halves. Their five independent geometric function classes give connected étale covers of degree32 and genus129, with equations \(d_{ij}Z_{ij}^2=L_{ij}/L_{01}\). Thus a finite list of constant tuples in (78.3) is an explicit finite covering alternative, without a rank or saturation assumption.

**All odd places.** Each \(d_{ij}\) belongs to \(\mathbb Q(S,2)\). Indeed the six differences, ordered \(01,02,03,12,13,23\), are
\[
 -4H^2,\quad2H\alpha_0,\quad\alpha_0\gamma_0,\quad
 -2HA_0,\quad A_0^2,\quad-\alpha_0A_0. \tag{78.4}
\]
Outside \(S\), integral coordinates make every sum a unit. For nonintegral coordinates all four valuations equal \(-r\); equal leading signs give sum valuation \(-r\), and opposite signs give \(+r\), by the constant product identity. All normalized valuations are even. This includes denominator primes of \(m\): the integral scaling has not removed any place.

The odd primes in \(S\) divide exactly one of \(H,A_0,\alpha_0,\gamma_0\), because those four integers are pairwise coprime away from2. Let \(v_{ij}\) denote the parity of \(v_\ell(d_{ij})\). The following sharper necessary subspaces hold:

| Factor containing \(\ell\) | Necessary parity conditions | Dimension |
|---|---|---:|
| \(H\), odd valuation | \(v_{03}=v_{13}=v_{23}\) | 3 |
| \(H\), even valuation | previous condition and \(v_{02}=v_{12}\) | 2 |
| \(A_0\) | \(v_{02}=v_{03}=0,\ v_{12}=v_{23}\) | 2 |
| \(\alpha_0\), odd valuation | \(v_{12}=v_{13}=0\) | 3 |
| \(\alpha_0\), even valuation | previous condition and \(v_{02}=v_{03}=v_{23}\) | 1 |
| \(\gamma_0\) | only \(v_{03}\) can be nonzero | 1 |

For integral coordinates, unit root differences make the corresponding sums units. The root clusters are \(\{0,1,2\}\) at \(H\), \(\{1,2,3\}\) at \(A_0\), \(\{0,2,3\}\) at \(\alpha_0\), and \(\{0,3\}\) at \(\gamma_0\). The first two triples have difference depths \((k,k,2k)\); the third has depths \((k,k,k)\). If \(k\) is even, the sums on all depth-\(k\) edges have equal parity. To see this, let \(t\) be the minimum coordinate valuation. When \(2t<k\), every edge valuation is \(t\) or its even difference valuation minus \(t\). When \(2t\ge k\), divide by \(\ell^{k/2}\); each depth-\(k\) edge has unit difference and unit sum. Since \(v_\ell(A_0)\) is even, this proves every extra even-depth row. At nonintegral points an opposite-sign edge instead adds the valuation of its root difference to the common parity; substituting (78.4) gives exactly the same subspaces. No unbounded valuation range is discarded.

**Dyadic and real places.** Every finite point of (78.1) over \(\mathbb Q_2\) has
\[
 v_2(X_0)=-2r,\qquad r\ge2,\qquad v_2(n)=r. \tag{78.5}
\]
Integral \(X_0\) would give two squares differing by2 modulo8; \(r=1\) gives a normalized fourth radicand5 modulo8. Conversely the eight infinity neighborhoods are parametrized by \(z=1/W_0\in4\mathbb Z_2\). Write \(W_i=\epsilon_iq_i/z\), with \(\epsilon_0=1\) and the principal roots \(q_i^2=1-e_i z^2\). Up to the common factor, the six edge classes are
\[
 b_{ij}=\begin{cases}2\epsilon_i,&\epsilon_i=\epsilon_j,\\
 \epsilon_i(e_j-e_i)/2,&\epsilon_i\ne\epsilon_j.
 \end{cases}
\]
At depth \(r=2\), multiply exactly the edges incident to vertex3 by5; at greater depth no correction occurs. The ratios \([b_{ij}/b_{01}]\) give exactly sixteen dyadic five-tuples. The eight deep tuples form a three-dimensional linear subspace; the other eight are its translate by
\[
 \upsilon=(1,5,1,5,5) \tag{78.6}
\]
in coordinate order \(02,03,12,13,23\).

At a real point, the sign of \(W_i+W_j\) is the sign of the coordinate belonging to the smaller root. The largest-root vertex supplies no edge sign and the common sign cancels, leaving exactly four real normalized sign patterns, a two-dimensional subspace. In particular
\[
 (W_1+W_3)/(W_0+W_1)>0, \tag{78.7}
\]
since \(e_1<e_0,e_3\).

**Explicit finite algorithm.** Let \(D_m\) be the sum of the dimensions in the odd-prime table. Take the direct sum of those local parity subspaces, the two-dimensional real sign subspace, and the two-dimensional prime2 valuation subspace supported on coordinates02 and12. This is a space of global five-tuples of dimension
\[
 N_m=D_m+4.
\]
Localize it in \((\mathbb Q_2^*/\mathbb Q_2^{*2})^5\), an explicit fifteen-row binary linear map. Let its rank be \(r_m\), and let \(t_m\) be the number of permitted dyadic tuples in its image. The exact size of this necessary constant list is
\[
 t_m2^{N_m-r_m}. \tag{78.8}
\]
Moreover \(t_m\) is always8 or16. The leading classes at the eight rational infinity points satisfy every real and odd-prime condition and give all eight deep vectors. Thus depth2 is retained precisely when the single vector \(\upsilon\) lies in the localization image. Row reduction supplies particular solutions, a kernel basis and, if depth2 is excluded, a dual linear obstruction. This finite computation uses only integer factorization and binary linear algebra.

For comparison, support and dyadic conditions alone give \(2^{5|S|-6}\) tuples. Adding real signs gives \(2^{5|S|-7}\) if every odd support prime is1 or3 modulo8, and \(2^{5|S|-9}\) otherwise. The cluster algorithm is substantially sharper:

| \(m\) | \(|S|\) | \(N_m\) | \(r_m\) | \(t_m\) | Constant tuples | Retained depth |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| \(4/3\) | 6 | 14 | 12 | 16 | 64 | 2 or greater |
| \(12/5\) | 8 | 20 | 12 | 16 | 4096 | 2 or greater |
| \(8/15\) | 8 | 20 | 10 | 8 | 8192 | at least3 |
| \(280/1209\) | 11 | 26 | 7 | 8 | 4194304 | at least3 |

These count candidate twists, not rational points on them.

**A closed isolated-point restriction.** The odd-prime table confines the possible odd support of \(d_{13}\) to \(HA_0\). It is positive by (78.7), has even dyadic valuation, and has dyadic unit class5 exactly at depth2. Every odd prime dividing \(H\) is1 or7 modulo8: reduction of the integer square \(A_0\) gives \(2q^2\), so2 is a quadratic residue. Every odd prime dividing \(A_0\) is1 or5 modulo8, since \(-1\) is a quadratic residue. Therefore
\[
 v_2(n)=2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \text{some prime }\ell\equiv5\pmod8\text{ divides }a=\sqrt{p^2+q^2}. \tag{78.9}
\]
Thus an integer hypotenuse whose prime divisors are all1 modulo8 forces \(v_2(n)\ge3\) in this orbit. This is a necessary condition on isolated rational candidates, independent of specialized ranks. For \(m=8/15\), the hypotenuse17 supplies the displayed depth exclusion. Presence of a prime5 modulo8 is not asserted sufficient.

There is also a denominator restriction retaining the original reflected roots. If an odd prime \(\ell\notin S\) does not divide \(A_0^2-16p^2q^2\), and \(v_\ell(W_0)<0\), then (78.2) gives \(v_\ell(n)>0\). The original reflected radicands reduce, after square scaling, to \(A_0+4pq\) and \(A_0-4pq\). Both must be nonzero quadratic residues modulo \(\ell\).

**Scope and iteration.** Transposition \((m,n;\sigma,u,v,a,b)\mapsto(n,m;\sigma,a,b,u,v)\) preserves all five original equations. It does not automatically preserve the global pq orbit. If the transpose fails its own necessary depth test, the audited all-base alternative therefore places it in a P′ reduction or forces an outside-boundary Kummer direction and symmetric rank at least3. The latter alternatives cannot be discarded. Purely dyadic iteration cannot force indefinitely increasing valuations: for every nondegenerate \(m,n\in4\mathbb Z_2\), all five radicands are1 modulo16, and the principal-root Kummer vectors equal the local pq,pq vectors. Any prescribed pair of depths at least2 is locally allowed.

Finally, the intermediate curve has eight rational infinity points, and compatible constant twists retain rational lifts above them and finite points in their neighborhoods at every completion. Local solubility alone cannot eliminate the entire list. The prime support and the tuple count vary with the base; no uniform denominator or height bound, or unrestricted MSOS exclusion, follows.

### 12.79. The eight triple-factor lattices and the genus-seventeen rank

The eight triple-character elliptic factors from Section12.62 all have
arithmetic rank two over K=Q(m). Their complete Mordell--Weil groups,
with the transported generators below, have torsion C₂ and free height
matrix
\[
\begin{pmatrix}3&-1\\-1&3\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{12.79a}
\]
Together with the five earlier rank-one factors and the four rank-two
cross-pair factors of Section12.76, this determines the noncentral
genus-seventeen Jacobian rank exactly as29. These are generic
function-field assertions; they are not upper bounds on specialized
Mordell--Weil ranks or classifications of isolated rational points.

#### One model and its complete scalar descent

Put
\[
\begin{gathered}
A=1+m^2,\quad h=1-m^2,\quad q_\pm=m^2\pm2m-1,\quad
k=q_-q_+=m^4-6m^2+1,\\
a=m^2-3,\quad b=3m^2-1,\quad c=m^2-4m+1,\\
B=m^6-3m^5-m^4+10m^3-m^2-3m+1.
\end{gathered}
\]
For the curve y₀²=Q_+(t), let r=−(A+4m)/c. The exact change
\[
x=A^2c(t-r)/4,\qquad y=A^2c\,y_0/8
\]
gives
\[
E:y^2=x(x^2-4Bx+A^2k^2).
\tag{12.79b}
\]
The 2-isogenous curve is
\[
\begin{aligned}
E':y^2&=x(x^2+8Bx+4h^2abc^2)\\
 &=x\bigl(x+2(m+1)^2c^2\bigr)
       \bigl(x+2(m-1)^2ab\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\tag{12.79c}
\]

For y²=x(x²+a₂x+a₄), use the scalar character α(O)=1,
α((0,0))=[a₄], and α((x,y))=[x]. Polynomial and prime Gauss valuations
restrict α(E) to the support −1,A,q_−,q_+. At each of the three
polynomial factors, a₄ has valuation two and a₂ is a unit. An odd
valuation of x must equal one and would force a₂ to be square in the
residue field. Its residues are
\[
64m\pmod A,\qquad-32(2m+1)\pmod {q_-},\qquad
32(12m-5)\pmod {q_+}.
\]
The first is nonsquare in Q(i), as reduction at m=2 modulo5 gives3.
The latter two are negative in both real embeddings of Q(√2).
All polynomial bits therefore vanish. Prime Gauss valuations exclude
constant prime factors; the constant −1 is impossible on a real
interval about m=0, where a₂<0,a₄>0 and a negative x makes the cubic
negative. Consequently α(E)={1}.

The complete dual support is
\[
[-1,2,m-1,m+1,m^2-3,3m^2-1,m^2-4m+1].
\tag{12.79d}
\]
Only2 can occur as a constant prime, since a₄'=4h²abc² has unit
Gauss valuation at every odd prime. Evaluation at m=6 is injective
on the128 support classes. Both m=6 and m=5 are smooth
specializations. The scalar character commutes with these evaluations,
including specialization to O or rational two-torsion.

For every evaluated representative d the homogeneous equation
\[
N^2=dU^4+a_2'U^2V^2+(a_4'/d)V^4
\]
is tested in the complete primitive charts V=1 and U=1,V≡0 modulo
the local prime. The exact local obstructions at m=6 leave32 masks;
m=5 leaves exactly
\[
0,1,2,3,48,49,50,51,80,81,82,83,96,97,98,99.
\tag{12.79e}
\]
Thus the dual scalar image has at most16 elements. Each removed class
has a saved local obstruction; no finite failure to find a point is
used as a nonsolubility assertion.

The actual sections
\[
R=\left(\frac{A^2q_-^2}{4},\frac{A^2cq_-k}{8}\right),\qquad
S=\left(\frac{A^2q_+^2}{4m^2},\frac{A^2cq_+k}{8m^3}\right)
\tag{12.79f}
\]
have dual preimages, up to sign,
\[
R'=(h^2ac,Aq_-h^2ac),\qquad
S'=\left(-\frac{h^2bc}{m^2},-\frac{Aq_+h^2bc}{m^3}\right).
\]
The two nonzero-root torsion points on E' have scalar masks3 and51,
and R',S' have masks80 and97. These four independent classes span
all of (12.79e). The two-isogeny rank formula gives
\[
2^{\operatorname{rank}E(K)}=1\cdot16/4=4.
\tag{12.79g}
\]
The kernel of E'/φE→E/2E is generated by mask48, the scalar class
of (0,0) on E'. Modulo that class the masks80,97,3 are independent.
Their images are R,S and the nonzero rational two-torsion point T₀.
Hence R,S,T₀ generate E(K)/2E and have finite odd index.

At m=2, good reductions at13,17,19,23,29,31 have respectively
16,24,24,24,32,32 points, with gcd8. Generic torsion injects at this
good characteristic-zero specialization. There is only one nonzero
K-rational two-torsion point, and it has no K-rational half because
\[
a_2+2Ak=-2(m+1)^2c^2,\qquad
a_2-2Ak=-2(m-1)^2ab
\]
have nonsquare classes −2 and −2ab. Thus E(K)_tors=C₂.

#### Heights and full saturation

The globally minimal model has χ=3 and
\[
\Delta=64A^4q_-^4q_+^4h^2abc^2.
\]
Its fibers are six I₄ at A q_− q_+=0, four I₂ at h c=0, and
four I₁ at ab=0. The c₄ invariant is a unit at every listed finite
zero. Infinity is good in coordinates X=m⁻⁶x,Y=m⁻⁹y.

R meets O once at infinity, and S meets O once at m=0. R has
component2 at the two A and two q_− fibers; S has component2 at
the two A and two q_+ fibers. Both have component1 at the two
c-fibers and component0 at m=±1. Each self-correction is5, so
their self-heights are3.

All possible section intersections are controlled by
\[
x(R)-x(S)=\frac{(m-1)(m+1)A^3c}{4m^2}.
\]
They meet simply at m=−1. At each zero of A, the second-blowup
chart x=A²X,y=A²Y has Y a unit, and X(R)−X(S) has order one;
each contributes one further intersection. At c=0 the first-blowup
coordinates (x−2B)/c,y/c are distinct for the two sections. At m=1
the ordinates are opposite and nonzero; at m=0 and infinity only
one section meets O. Thus R·S=3. The common fiber correction is
2 from A=0 and1 from c=0, giving
\[
\langle R,S\rangle=3+1+1-3-3=-1.
\]
This proves (12.79a), of determinant8.

Every height pairing lies in (1/4)Z because the only singular fibers
are I₁,I₂,I₄. If n is the already odd index of the boundary subgroup,
four times the full-lattice Gram matrix has integer determinant
128/n². Hence n² divides128 and n=1. Therefore
\[
E(K)=\mathbb ZR\oplus\mathbb ZS\oplus C_2.
\tag{12.79h}
\]

#### Transport and the exact genus-seventeen rank

The substitutions m↦−m and (t,y)↦(1/t,y/t²) identify
Q_+,Q_−,tQ_+,tQ_− without a twist. For the remaining four models,
the exact square-scaled Cayley identity is
\[
(m+1)^6Q_\varepsilon\left(\frac{m-1}{m+1},t\right)
     =R_{-\varepsilon}(m,t).
\tag{12.79i}
\]
The ordinate multiplier (m+1)³ is rational, and the same identity
holds after multiplication by t. The base automorphism has degree
one and preserves the function-field height pairing. Thus all eight
triple factors have the full group and lattice (12.79h).

Let W be the genus-seventeen noncentral root curve obtained by
adjoining the four individual F and G roots. Its Jacobian is the
seventeen-factor product up to the Q(m)-isogeny of Section12.62.
The two same-pair factors and the three all-four factors are isogenous

cross-pair factors have rank two by Section12.76, and all eight

\[
\boxed{\operatorname{rank}\operatorname{Jac}(W)(\mathbb Q(m))
       =2\cdot1+4\cdot2+8\cdot2+3\cdot1=29.}
\tag{12.79j}
\]
An isogeny preserves this rank, but the displayed factor bases alone
do not determine the integral Jacobian isogeny image or its effective

### 12.80. Elliptic tangency and arithmetic of the direction cover

#### A. The quartic differential has no elliptic integral curve

Let \(\omega_4\in H^0(Y,\operatorname{Sym}^4\Omega_Y^1)\) be the explicit regular tensor of §12.77 on the minimal resolution of the full-root surface. All assertions here are geometric, in characteristic zero.

**Proposition 12.80A.** If \(f:E\to Y\) is the normalization map of a curve of geometric genus one, then \(f^*\omega_4\ne0\). In particular this pullback is nowhere zero. This does not exclude elliptic curves: the sixteen components above \(h=0\) have explicitly nonzero pullback.

Suppose first that the image is not a branch line and that \(f^*\omega_4=0\). The contact calculation of §12.77 works in any curve function field. For nonconstant \(a\) and \(k=db/da\), put \(c=b-ak\). Apart from the already separated constant-image cases it gives a constant \(C\) and
\[
 c^2=F(k)=\frac{1-Ck^3}{1-Ck},\qquad
 a=-\frac{F'(k)}{2c}.
\tag{12.80A.1}
\]
For \(C\notin\{0,1,-1\}\), the curve \(E_C\) defined by (12.80A.1) has genus one. The actual roots of \(1+a\) and \(1-a\) supply a further function \(y\) with \(y^2=1-a^2\). This forces a map to a genus-five curve, as the following uniform calculation shows.

Set
\[
N_C(k)=-3C^2k^4+(8C^3+4C)k^3-18C^2k^2+12Ck+C^2-4.
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
F'(k)^2-4F(k)&=\frac{N_C(k)}{(Ck-1)^4},\\
\operatorname{disc}_kN_C&=-110592C^4(C-1)^6(C+1)^6,\\
\operatorname{Res}_k(N_C,1-Ck^3)&=729C^6(C-1)^2(C+1)^2,\\
N_C(1/C)&=(C-1)^2(C+1)^2/C^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{12.80A.2}
\]
Thus the four roots of \(N_C\) are simple and avoid the branch values of \(E_C\to\mathbb P^1_k\). Each has two points above it, giving eight simple zeros of \(1-a^2\). All its poles have even order. At the two points above infinity the identity
\[
1-a^2=\frac{-N_C(k)}{4(1-Ck^3)(1-Ck)^3}
\tag{12.80A.3}
\]
gives a zero of order two; these do not contribute to ramification. Consequently the connected double cover \(y^2=1-a^2\) of \(E_C\) is ramified at exactly eight points and has genus five. A genus-one curve cannot dominate it.

The exceptional integral images also have no elliptic full-root component. For \(C=1\), the plane conic is \(a^2+ab+b^2=3/4\). With
\[
D=t^2-t+1,\quad
 a=\frac{t^2-4t+1}{2D},\qquad
 b=-\frac{2t^2-2t-1}{2D},
\]
its full-root squareclasses are generated by
\[
D,\qquad 5t^2-8t+2,\qquad t^2-4t-2.
\]
These three separable quadratics are pairwise coprime. The connected cover therefore has degree eight, six branch values and genus five. The case \(C=-1\) follows by \(b\mapsto-b\). The cases \(C=0\) or an identically vanishing first-integral denominator give constant plane images.

For constant slope, the only additional nonbranch lines are \(b=\pm a+c\), \(c^2=3\). Their six variable root factors have distinct zeros
\[
1,-1,1-c,-1-c,(1-c)/2,(-1-c)/2.
\]
The squareclass rank is six, infinity is the seventh branch value, and each full-root component has genus \(49\). The remaining integral images are axes and branch lines. By the normalization table of §12.77, the axes have only genus-zero components, the corner branch lines have genus \(17\), and the edge branch lines have genus \(5\).

It remains to check the sixteen genus-one components over the central line \(h=0\). They are **not** integral curves of \(\omega_4\). In the chart \(b=1,a=t\), substitute \(dh=db=0\) in the compact tensor and take its regular limit at \(h=0\). This gives
\[
\omega_4\big|_{h=0}=\frac{dt^4}{t^2(t^2-1)^2}.
\tag{12.80A.4}
\]
Each component contains the elliptic function field \(y^2=t(1-t^2)\), on which the right side is \((dt/y)^4\). Its pullback is nonzero. Exceptional curves on \(Y\) have genus zero. This exhausts all cases and proves the proposition.

There is also a local consequence: a genus-one normalization map \(f\) has no ramification point as a map to the smooth surface \(Y\). A zero of \(df\) would force a zero of \(f^*\omega_4\), whereas a nonzero quartic differential on an elliptic curve has no zeros. Thus any remaining elliptic curve is immersed, though it may have multiple image branches at a point.

The exact identities, discriminant, disjointness, conic squareclasses and diagonal branch values are certified in `verify_quartic_integral_elliptic_leaves.py/.json`, with independent review. No claim is made that all elliptic curves are tangent to the quartic web, or that the proposition excludes isolated rational points.


#### B. Arithmetic of the quartic direction cover

The rational-curve classification does not give a rational tangent
direction at an isolated rational point. In fact the direction cover
retains its generic \(S_4\) group after adjoining all full-root
coordinates, and every direction at an admissible rational point
requires a ramified quadratic completion at \(3\).

On the affine plane \(h=1\), write \(k=db/da\) and \(c=b-ak\).
The equation \(P_4(1,k)=0\) has the rational parametrization
\[
a=\frac{(c^2-1)(c^2-3k^2)}{2ck(k^2-1)},\qquad
b=\frac{(c^2-k^2)(c^2-3)}{2c(k^2-1)}.
\tag{12.80B.1}
\]
The first-integral constant
\[
C=\frac{c^2-1}{k(c^2-k^2)}
\]
defines the plane cubic
\[
Ck^3-Ckc^2+c^2-1=0.
\tag{12.80B.2}
\]
Its generic member is elliptic, with the rational point \((k,c)=(0,1)\).
The quartic model
\[
Y^2=(1-Ck^3)(1-Ck)
\]
has an explicit birational Weierstrass model. Put
\[
x=\frac1{k-1/C},\qquad y=Yx^2,\qquad d=\frac{1-C^2}{C},
\qquad X=dx,\quad Z=dy.
\]
Then
\[
Z^2=X^3+3X^2+3(1-C^2)X+(1-C^2)^2.
\]
Its invariants are \(c_4=144C^2\) and
\(\Delta=-432C^4(C^2-1)^2\), giving
\[
j(C)=-\frac{6912C^2}{(C^2-1)^2}.
\tag{12.80B.3}
\]
Thus the first integral supplies a varying elliptic pencil, rather
than a fixed elliptic curve.

**Proposition 12.80B.1 (Generic direction group).**
Let
\[
F=\mathbb Q(a,b),\qquad
M=F\bigl(\sqrt{1\pm a},\sqrt{1\pm b},
         \sqrt{1\pm a\pm b}\bigr).
\]
The splitting group of \(P_4(1,k)\) over \(M\) is \(S_4\).

*Proof.* Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal B&=(1-a^2)(1-b^2)
 (1-(a+b)^2)(1-(a-b)^2),\\
\mathcal J&=(a^2-b^2)^2+2(a^2+b^2)-3.
\end{aligned}
\]
Direct calculation gives
\[
\operatorname{disc}_kP_4(1,k)
=-432a^2b^2\mathcal B\mathcal J.
\tag{12.80B.4}
\]
The polynomial \(\mathcal J\) is squarefree and coprime to the eight
branch lines. The eight branch valuations also show that
\(\operatorname{Gal}(M/F)\simeq C_2^8\). In particular \(M/F\) is
unramified along every prime divisor of \(\mathcal J\), so it cannot
contain the discriminant quadratic field. The discriminant
squareclass over \(M\) is \(-3\mathcal J\).

The generic quartic and its cubic resolvent are irreducible. One
exact check uses \(t=1/k\) and the specialization \((a,b)=(2,4)\):
\[
80t^4-160t^3+109t^2-32t+4
\]
is irreducible modulo \(3\), and its monic cubic resolvent multiplied
by \(80\),
\[
80T^3-109T^2+48T-7,
\]
is irreducible modulo \(11\). After dividing by the leading coefficients, the quartic and resolvent are monic over the normal local ring $\mathbb Q[a,b]_{(a-2,b-4)}$. Any monic factors over its fraction field have integral coefficients and hence belong to that ring. They would specialize without degree loss. Thus these tests also exclude generic factorizations. Together with the nonsquare discriminant, this proves
the generic group \(S_4\) over \(F\).

If \(E/F\) denotes that splitting field, \(E\cap M\) gives an elementary
abelian two-group quotient of \(S_4\). The only possible nontrivial
quotient is its discriminant quotient, already excluded. Hence
\(E\cap M=F\), and the group remains \(S_4\) over \(M\). \(\square\)

This is a function-field statement. The specialization used to certify
irreducibility is not asserted to be a rational full-root point.

**Proposition 12.80B.2 (Local fields at an admissible rational point).**
At a rational full-root point with \(h=1\) and \(ab\ne0\), every quartic
direction \(k\), and its first-integral constant \(C\), has degree \(2\)
or \(4\) over \(\mathbb Q\). Every completion of either field above \(3\)
is \(\mathbb Q_3(\sqrt3)\). On the admissible positive locus these
fields are totally real. In particular no rational-\(C\) leaf contains
an admissible rational full-root point.

*Proof.* The actual roots make \(1\pm a,1\pm b\) squares in
\(\mathbb Q_3\). This forces
\[
a,b\in3\mathbb Z_3.
\tag{12.80B.5}
\]
Indeed, if \(v_3(a)<0\), the square unit
\((1+a)/(1-a)\) would have residue \(-1\). If \(v_3(a)=0\),
one of \(1+a,1-a\) would have nonsquare residue \(2\).
The same argument applies to \(b\).

Put \(u=v_3(a)\ge1,\ v=v_3(b)\ge1\). The lower Newton polygon has
vertices
\[
(0,2v),\quad(2,1),\quad(4,2u),
\]
so its root valuations are
\[
v-\tfrac12\quad\text{twice},\qquad
\tfrac12-u\quad\text{twice}.
\tag{12.80B.6}
\]
They can all be constructed over the same quadratic extension.
Let \(\varpi=\sqrt3\), substitute \(k=(b/\varpi)z\), and divide by \(b^2\).
The resulting polynomial is
\[
\begin{aligned}
(b^2-1)
&-\frac{4a(b^2-1)}{\varpi}z
 +(1-a^2-b^2+2a^2b^2)z^2\\
&-\frac{4ab^2(a^2-1)}{\varpi^3}z^3
 +\frac{a^2b^2(a^2-1)}{\varpi^4}z^4.
\end{aligned}
\tag{12.80B.7}
\]
Its coefficients are integral over \(\mathbb Q_3(\sqrt3)\), and its
reduction is \(z^2-1\). Hensel lifting gives the two small roots.
Applying the same argument to \(1/k\), with \(a,b\) interchanged,
gives the two large roots. Thus the complete local splitting field
is \(\mathbb Q_3(\sqrt3)\); the half-integral valuations rule out
\(\mathbb Q_3\).

For the small roots, \(c=b-ak\) has valuation \(v\), while
\(c^2-k^2\) has valuation \(2v-1\). For the large roots these
valuations are \(1/2\) and \(1-2u\). Consequently
\[
v_3(C)=
\begin{cases}
\frac32-3v,&v_3(k)=v-\frac12,\\[2pt]
3u-\frac32,&v_3(k)=\frac12-u.
\end{cases}
\tag{12.80B.8}
\]
Thus \(C\) also generates the quadratic local field.
All global conjugates of \(k\) and \(C\) lie among these four local
values. Their degrees are at most four, and each local factor has
degree two; hence their global degrees are \(2\) or \(4\).

Finally positivity gives \(|a|+|b|<1\). The quartic \(P_4(1,k)\)
is negative at \(k=0\), positive at \(k=\pm1\), and has negative
leading coefficient. It therefore has one simple real root in each of
\[
(-\infty,-1),\quad(-1,0),\quad(0,1),\quad(1,\infty).
\]
All conjugates of the resulting fields are real. \(\square\)

These are necessary field restrictions, not a contradiction:
totally real quadratic and quartic fields with the stated completion
exist. In particular the rational parametrization of the spectral
surface does not produce rational tangent data at the original
rational point.

The exact certificate
\(\texttt{verify\_quartic\_spectral\_arithmetic.py/.json}\)
checks the spectral parametrization, the explicit Weierstrass model and \(j\)-formula,
both irreducibility tests, the full discriminant factorization,
squarefreeness and branch coprimality, the Hensel scaling, reciprocal
symmetry, and the real sign identities. No external invariant convention is needed: the displayed Weierstrass change is checked directly.


The genus-one tangency proof has independent written review in `simultaneous_units/quartic_elliptic_tangency_review.md`; its producer is `rank4_next/trace_center_norm/verify_quartic_integral_elliptic_leaves.py/.json`. The spectral arithmetic has a second independent implementation, built directly from the compact tensor and an explicit cubic, in `root_quartic_web/verify_spectral_arithmetic_independent.py/.json`, with the complete field and local-valuation audit in `spectral_arithmetic_independent_review.md`. All return PASS.


#### C. The direction and leaf constant generate the same field

The two auxiliary fields of part B coincide on the admissible locus. Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
R(C)={}&4b^6C^4-4ab^3(a^2+3b^2-9)C^3\\
&+3\{4a^2b^2(a^2+b^2+3)-9(a^2+b^2-1)^2\}C^2\\
&-4a^3b(3a^2+b^2-9)C+4a^6.
\end{aligned}
\]
Elimination from the tangent quartic and
\((b-ak)^2-1-Ck((b-ak)^2-k^2)=0\) gives the exact resultant
\(-\mathcal B R(C)\). A second exact identity is
\[
\operatorname{disc}_C R=-2^8 3^9 a^6b^6\mathcal B\mathcal J^3.
\tag{12.80C.1}
\]
On the admissible triangle, \(ab\mathcal B\ne0\), and
\(\mathcal J=(1+(a+b)^2)(1+(a-b)^2)-4<0\). Thus all four values of
\(C\) are distinct. The formula for \(C\) is finite at each tangent root:
a vanishing denominator would force \(k=0,\pm1\) or \(a=\pm1\),
excluded by nondegeneracy and the strict triangle inequalities.
The map from the four tangent roots to the four leaf constants is
therefore a Galois-equivariant bijection. Equality of their stabilizers gives
\[
L=\mathbb Q(k)=\mathbb Q(C),\qquad
v_3(\operatorname{Disc}L)=[L:\mathbb Q]/2.
\tag{12.80C.2}
\]
The discriminant identity follows because every completion at three is
the tame quadratic extension \(\mathbb Q_3(\sqrt3)\), of residue degree one
and discriminant exponent one. There is one such prime in degree two
and two in degree four. These statements include reducible tangent
quartics; no irreducibility of a specialized quartic is assumed.

Both elimination identities are independently verified from the compact
tensor in `root_quartic_web/verify_spectral_arithmetic_independent.py/.json`.
The field and local-discriminant argument is included in the corresponding
independent review. This strengthens the auxiliary-field restrictions,
without turning them into a rational-point exclusion.


#### An all-degree bound with the image singularities retained

Let \(C\subset Y\) be an integral curve with genus-one normalization,
where \(Y\to X\) is the smooth full-root resolution. Put
\(d=H\cdot C>0\) and \(s=p_a(C)-1\). Thus \(d\) is root-projective
degree and \(s\) is the sum of the local delta invariants of the image
curve. The immersion proved above does not imply \(s=0\): distinct
smooth branches can meet at the same point.

Miyaoka's Theorem 1.3(ii) [60, p.405] applies to singular integral curves
and uses their normalization genus. Since \(K_Y=3H\), \(K_Y^2=576\),
\(c_2(Y)=768\), and adjunction gives \(C^2=2s-3d\), its inequality is
\[
 2(3d)^2\le1728(C^2+9d).
\]
Consequently every such curve satisfies
\[
 \boxed{d^2\le576d+192s,\qquad
 s\ge\max\{0,\lceil d(d-576)/192\rceil\}.}
 \tag{U-ELL-DEGREE-SINGULARITY}
\]
In particular every smooth elliptic curve on \(Y\) has root degree at
most576. More generally \(s\le S\) gives
\(d\le288+\sqrt{82944+192S}\). Under the separate hypothesis
\(C^2\le0\), the same theorem gives \(d\le864\).

If the normalized plane-image cover has degree \(e\), the plane degree
is \(n=2d/e\); these degrees must not be interchanged. The smooth-image
bound therefore gives \(n\le1152/e\), with the cover degrees and parity
conditions of Section12.81 still imposed.

There is no absolute degree cutoff for singular images in this argument.
Indeed Hodge index gives only
\(s\le d^2/128+3d/2\), which is compatible with
(U-ELL-DEGREE-SINGULARITY) in every positive degree. Controlling the
self-intersections of the full-root normalization remains a separate
requirement; plane self-intersections need not remain self-intersections
on its selected full-root component.

The exact substitution, degree conversion and Hodge comparison are
certified by `coupled_lifts/verify_high_degree_elliptic_gate.py/.json`.
The full proof and scope audit are in
`coupled_lifts/high_degree_elliptic_degree_gate.md`; the theorem and
substitution have also been checked independently by the root agent.

### 12.81. Elliptic plane-image covers and a finite inertia constraint

Let \(E\) be the smooth normalization of a geometric genus-one curve on the full-root surface, excluding the sixteen central boundary components. Let \(D\) be the normalization of its plane image, let \(d\) be the degree of that plane image, and write \(e=[\overline{\mathbb Q}(E):\overline{\mathbb Q}(D)]\). These are geometric assertions in characteristic zero. Plane degree \(d\) is distinct from root-projective degree \(\delta\); they satisfy \(2\delta=ed\).

**Proposition 12.81.** Either \(D\) has genus one and \(E\to D\) is unramified of degree \(1,2\), or \(4\), or \(D\) is rational and \(E\to D\) has degree \(2,4\), or \(8\) with exactly four branch values. In the rational-image case, each branch value lies over one of the twenty intersection points of the nine-line arrangement. The four inertia types belong to an explicit list of \(1562\) unordered multisets. In particular, odd plane degree forces \(e=8\).

The root extension over \(D\) is multiquadratic and Galois: finiteness of the squaring projection makes the curve an entire component above its plane image. Riemann–Hurwitz gives \(g(D)\le1\). If \(g(D)=1\), the cover is unramified, and its elementary abelian two-group acts by translations and embeds in \(E[2]\). Hence \(e\le4\). If \(D\) is rational, every inertia group has order two. For \(B\) branch values,
\[
0=e(-2+B/2),
\]
so \(B=4\). The four inertia vectors generate the deck group and have sum zero, giving rank at most three and \(e\in\{2,4,8\}\).

#### The contact condition

Let \(\eta\) be the rational quartic differential on \(D\) obtained by restricting the plane expression for \(\omega_4\). By §12.80A its pullback to \(E\) is nowhere zero. At a point with ramification index \(e_q\),
\[
0=e_q\operatorname{ord}_q(\eta)+4(e_q-1).
\tag{12.81a}
\]
Thus \(\eta\) is a nowhere-zero holomorphic quartic differential for an elliptic image. For a rational image with reduced branch divisor \(B_D\),
\[
\operatorname{div}(\eta)=-2B_D.
\tag{12.81b}
\]
It has exactly four double poles and no zeros.

At a smooth point of a single arrangement line, write \(x=r^2\) for its root coordinate and \(y\) for a transverse plane coordinate. The simple-pole expression and branch divisibility of §12.77 give
\[
\omega_4|_{r=0}=dy^2(A\,dy^2+B\,dr^2).
\]
A ramification point over \(D\) would have zero differential in the plane, and hence \(dy=0\), contradicting (12.81a). Every rational-image branch value therefore lies above an arrangement intersection.

At an ordinary double intersection \(x=r^2,y=s^2\), the exact coefficient table gives \(\omega_4=C\,dr^2ds^2\) with \(C\ne0\). Both root derivatives must be nonzero. The two line orders on the rational normalization \(D\) are exactly \((1,1)\).

At a triple intersection the exact exceptional-chart calculation gives line orders \((1,1,s)\), up to permutation, with \(s\ge1\). If \(s=1\), the common tangent direction must avoid the zero set of the recorded node quadratic. If \(s>1\), the higher-contact branch direction has nonzero node coefficient. Thus higher tangency is retained: no bound on \(s\) is asserted. The inertia is the full triple when \(s\) is odd and the pair of minimum-order lines when \(s\) is even. These order statements concern a ramified rational-image branch. An unramified elliptic image can have minimum plane order two at a triple point and is not subject to the same order-one conclusion.

#### The finite inertia list

Label the lines by \(0,\ldots,8\) in the order
\[
h,\ h+a,\ h-a,\ h+b,\ h-b,\ h+a+b,\ h+a-b,\ h-a+b,\ h-a-b.
\]
Use the projective sign group \(V=\mathbb F_2^9/\langle(1,\ldots,1)\rangle\). Every pair of lines supplies one allowable pair mask, including pairs contained in a triple. There are \(36\) such masks, together with the eight full-triple masks. Their projections to \(V\) are distinct and nonzero.

Choose four masks with repetitions permitted. Their projected xor must vanish. Before projection their xor is either zero or the all-ones vector. Since each line meets the plane image in total degree \(d\), these alternatives give respectively even and odd \(d\). The four projected vectors span the deck group. Exact enumeration gives

| Rank | Cover degree \(e\) | Plane-degree parity | Unordered multisets |
|---:|---:|---|---:|
| 1 | 2 | even | 44 |
| 2 | 4 | even | 946 |
| 3 | 8 | even | 444 |
| 3 | 8 | odd | 128 |

The total is \(1562\). Rank one is the same type repeated four times; rank two consists of two types repeated twice. Rank-three patterns have four distinct types. Distinct branch values may have the same plane image, so repetitions and different types at one triple point must not be discarded.

There is also an exact differential identity for a rational plane parametrization by homogeneous forms \(h(s,t),a(s,t),b(s,t)\) of degree \(d\). If \(B_4(s,t)\) is its reduced branch polynomial, then
\[
N_d(s,t)B_4(s,t)^2
 =\kappa\prod_{i=0}^8L_i(h(s,t),a(s,t),b(s,t)),
\qquad \kappa\ne0,
\tag{12.81c}
\]
where \(N_d\) is the compact tensor numerator formed with homogeneous Wronskians and has degree \(9d-8\). This is (12.81b) in homogeneous coordinates; the choice of Wronskian scalar is absorbed in \(\kappa\).

The inertia list is certified by `elliptic_inertia_patterns.py/.json` and independently by `verify_elliptic_inertia_independent.py/.json`, using a different pair-xor enumeration. The covering and divisor argument has independent review. These are necessary incidence and differential conditions. They do not establish realizability of any listed pattern, bound the plane degree or higher tangency, classify all elliptic curves, or exclude isolated rational points.


The complete contact calculations and all twenty intersection charts are in `simultaneous_units/quartic_elliptic_contact_gates.md` and `verify_quartic_elliptic_contacts.py/.json`. The independent inertia audits are `rank4_next/trace_center_norm/verify_elliptic_inertia_independent.py/.json` and `coupled_lifts/elliptic_inertia_independent_review.md/.py/.json`; both reconstruct the domain and give the same1562 patterns by a different enumeration. Arbitrarily high third-line tangency is actually compatible with the local root equations and a nonzero quartic: the arcs a=1−u^s,b=u, u=t², work for every s≥2. These are local arcs, not asserted global elliptic curves.


#### The exact zero locus of the entire quartic tensor

The tensor itself has exactly1280 set-theoretic zero points on the resolution, all on exceptional curves, and no divisorial zero. Every genus-one normalization avoids these points, since its quartic pullback is nowhere zero.

Here is a complete chart check. Off the arrangement, in h=1 the extreme coefficients b²(b²−1) and a²(a²−1) force a,b∈{0,±1}; the remaining coefficients leave only the four finite triple points. On smooth branch divisors, the three symmetry types have nonzero tangential fourth-power coefficients
\[
\frac1{t^2(t^2-1)^2},\qquad
\frac1{b^2(1-b^2)(4-b^2)},\qquad
\frac{-1}{2a^2(a-2)(a-1)^2(a+1)},
\]
respectively for h=0, a=1, and b=1−a. Their denominators are nonzero away from arrangement intersections. The twelve ordinary double intersections have the already verified nonzero mixed coefficient.

At a triple, write x=r²,y=r²z. Every exceptional-tangential differential introduces an additional r, so the tensor at r=0 is exactly16Q(1,z)dr⁴, where Q is its coefficient-linear radial quadratic. Six triple types give a nonzero square quadratic with one distinct zero direction; the two diagonal infinity triples give a separable quadratic with two. None of these zero directions is a branch-line direction. Each exceptional conic maps to the plane direction line with degree four, from the two independent ratios sqrt(z) and sqrt(c+dz). Thus each zero direction has four distinct preimages. There are32 nodes over each plane triple, giving
\[
6\cdot32\cdot4+2\cdot32\cdot8=1280.
\]
This counts distinct points, not the length of the tensor-zero scheme. The complete tensor, all eight radial quadratics, and the three smooth-branch restrictions are certified in `rank4_next/trace_center_norm/verify_quartic_basepoints.py/.json`, with the proof `quartic_tensor_base_locus.md` and fresh independent review `simultaneous_units/quartic_base_locus_independent_review.md`.

The lack of divisorial zeros also rules out a scalar shortcut to a negative-hyperplane-twisted tensor. Suppose a regular section τ of Sym^(4k)Ω⊗O(−H) were generically proportional to ω₄^k. Multiplying by a nonzero hyperplane section s, the scalar sτ/ω₄^k has no divisorial pole. Normality and projectivity make it constant. A nonzero constant would force ω₄^k to vanish along the divisor of s, which it does not. Thus τ=0: an actual negative twist requires a different tensor, rather than scalar cancellation in a power of the known quartic.

### 12.82. Low-degree plane images of geometric elliptic curves

**Theorem 12.82.** The only geometric genus-one full-root curves whose plane images have degree at most two are the sixteen central components above \(h=0\). None supplies a rational full-root point. If the plane-image normalization itself has genus one, its degree is even and at least six.

These assertions are over an algebraic closure of characteristic zero. They use the nowhere-zero quartic pullback and contact theorem of §§12.80A–12.81, and do not classify rational-normalization plane images of degree at least three.

#### Plane-line images

The sixteen central components above \(h=0\) are the only geometric genus-one full-root components with plane-line image. For branch lines this follows from the normalization table of §12.77. For a nonbranch line, §12.81 gives four distinct branch values, all lying at arrangement intersections. The normalization of a line maps isomorphically onto it, so these are four distinct points among the twenty fixed arrangement intersections. In particular the line joins two of them and is defined over \(\mathbb Q\), even though the classification is geometric.

The twenty points determine exactly \(69\) distinct lines. Nine are the branch lines. For each of the other \(60\), normalize \(h=1\) and write \(a,b\) as linear functions of a parameter \(t\). Every squared coordinate is a nonzero constant or a nonconstant linear polynomial. Distinct finite zeros give independent squareclasses; if there are \(r\) of them, infinity is also branched. Thus each connected component has
\[
 g=1+2^{r-2}(r-3).
\]
Exact rational arithmetic gives the complete table

| Number of lines | Squareclass rank \(r\) | Component genus |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 | 2 | 0 |
| 10 | 4 | 5 |
| 20 | 5 | 17 |
| 28 | 6 | 49 |

There is no rank-three candidate. The two genus-zero lines are exactly \(a=0\) and \(b=0\). This is an exhaustive geometric line classification, not a bounded search for coefficients. The certificate `verify_elliptic_plane_lines.py/.json` records all lines, restricted root functions and branch values; its enumeration has an independent replay.

The surviving central components supply no real or rational full-root point. At \(h=0\), every squared entry is accompanied by its negative. Both can be nonnegative only if all root coordinates vanish, which is not a projective point.

#### Plane-conic images

Suppose the plane image is a smooth conic \(D\). The full-root cover of \(D\) has exactly four branch values, all at arrangement intersections. A conic is embedded, so these are four distinct points among the twenty arrangement intersections. No three can be collinear.

For a branch line \(L_i\), let \(n_i\in\{0,1,2\}\) count the selected points lying on it. If \(n_i=2\), its two intersections with the conic are simple. If \(n_i=1\), it must be tangent at that point; otherwise there would be another odd intersection and hence an additional branch value. If \(n_i=0\), it must be tangent elsewhere. At every selected point at least two incident lines have odd contact, so at least two incident lines must satisfy \(n_i=2\).

The complete finite reduction has the following counts:

| Step | Number |
|---|---:|
| Four-point subsets of the twenty arrangement intersections | 4845 |
| Subsets with three collinear points | 2069 |
| Further subsets failing the odd-contact incidence condition | 2542 |
| Remaining conic pencils | 234 |

For each remaining set, its four independent linear conditions on the six conic coefficients give a complete projective pencil \(Q_{S,T}\). Tangency to any required line \(n_i<2\) is a homogeneous quadratic condition in \(S,T\). The gcd of all required conditions is one for every one of the \(234\) pencils. Hence there is no common projective parameter over the algebraic closure, including the parameter at infinity.

The independent certificate uses the two reducible conics through paired selected points as a pencil basis and the dual test \(L_i^{\mathsf T}\operatorname{adj}(M_{S,T})L_i=0\). In \(232\) pencils the conditions span all binary quadratics. In the remaining two their common coefficient annihilator does not lie on the Veronese conic \([S^2:ST:T^2]\). Thus the independent calculation also excludes every projective parameter. Degenerate conics need not be separately admitted: the plane image of an integral curve is reduced and irreducible, and an irreducible conic over an algebraically closed field is smooth.

The producer certificate is `classify_elliptic_plane_conics.py/.json`; the independent implementation is `elliptic_plane_conic_independent_review.py/.json`. They enumerate the complete geometric parameter domain, rather than a bounded-height set of rational conics.

#### An elliptic plane image cannot have degree four

Suppose instead that the plane-image normalization \(D\) has genus one. The multiquadratic cover \(E\to D\) is unramified by §12.81. Let
\(\mathcal L=\nu^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(1)\), of degree \(d\), and let \(s_i\in H^0(D,\mathcal L)\) be the nine restricted line sections.
At any point of \(D\), at most three of these sections vanish, since the arrangement has only double and triple intersections. Choose a nonvanishing \(s_j\). Unramifiedness of every root ratio \(\sqrt{s_i/s_j}\) forces \(\operatorname{ord}(s_i)\) to be even. Hence every \(\operatorname{div}(s_i)\) is even and \(d\) is even.

Assume \(d=4\). The complete section space \(H^0(D,\mathcal L)\) has dimension four. The plane normalization is given by a three-dimensional subspace \(V\), and the map defined by \(V\) is birational onto the plane image.
There are exactly four square-root line bundles \(\mathcal M\) with
\(\mathcal M^{\otimes2}\simeq\mathcal L\), each of degree two and with two independent sections. The multiplication map
\[
\operatorname{Sym}^2H^0(D,\mathcal M)
 \longrightarrow H^0(D,\mathcal L)
\]
is injective: a basis \(u,v\) would otherwise give a nonzero quadratic relation among \(1,v/u,(v/u)^2\), contradicting the nonconstancy of \(v/u\). Its image \(W_{\mathcal M}\) is a three-dimensional subspace, and the squares of sections form a nonsingular Veronese conic in \(\mathbb P(W_{\mathcal M})\).

The planes \(\mathbb P(V)\) and \(\mathbb P(W_{\mathcal M})\) cannot coincide. Equality would make the plane map factor as the degree-two map \(D\to\mathbb P^1\) defined by \(\mathcal M\), followed by the Veronese conic, contradicting birationality onto a quartic. Their intersection is therefore a line and contains at most two points of the conic. Each square-root line bundle contributes at most two projective sections in \(V\) with even divisor, for a total of at most eight.

Every one of the nine \(s_i\) has even divisor. Their projective classes are distinct: a proportionality would put the entire plane image on a line. This contradicts the bound of eight. Thus a genus-one plane image has even degree at least six.

This argument is intrinsic to line bundles on the normalization. It assumes no genericity of the plane quartic, no classification of its singularities or bitangents, and no transversality hypothesis. It does not exclude rational-normalization plane quartics, which remain a separate possibility.

### 12.83. Split-prime hypotenuses on the remaining orbit and symmetric support links

Retain the actual five equations, with \(A=1+m^2\), \(h=1-m^2\), and \(D=A(1+n^2)\):
\[
 \sigma^2=D,\quad u^2=D+4hn,\quad v^2=D-4hn,\quad
 a^2=D+4m(1-n^2),\quad b^2=D-4m(1-n^2). \tag{83.1}
\]
No specialized Mordell–Weil rank or saturation bound is imposed.

**Theorem.** Suppose the rational point lies in the remaining joint \((P'+Q',P'+Q')\) orbit after the exact dyadic normalization. Write \(m=p/q\) in lowest terms, \(q>0\), and \(p^2+q^2=c_m^2\) with positive integer hypotenuse; define \(c_n\) likewise. Then
\[
 \ell\mid c_mc_n\ \Longrightarrow\ \ell\equiv1\pmod8,
 \qquad v_2(m)\ge3,\quad v_2(n)\ge3. \tag{83.2}
\]
Moreover \(\gcd(c_mc_n,65)=1\). This is a necessary condition on isolated rational candidates in this orbit. The outside-boundary rank-increase and P′ alternatives remain. No transposition of the global pq label is asserted: the second-hypotenuse statement is proved directly from the actual f Kummer coordinates.

The previous all-prime theorem already gives \(A\) and \(1+n^2\) as rational squares and both dyadic valuations at least2. Suppose a prime \(\ell\equiv5\pmod8\) divides \(c_m\). Coprimality gives \(m^2=-1\) modulo \(\ell\); both \(m\) and2 are nonsquares, while \(-1\) is a square. The original reflected radicands exclude \(v_\ell(n)>0\), since their reductions are \(\pm4m\), and exclude \(v_\ell(n)<0\) after division by \(n^2\). Thus \(n\) is a unit. The other edge radicands reduce to \(\pm8n\), forcing \(\chi(n)=-1\); hence \(n\pm1\) are units.

Apply the exact simultaneous Cayley reflection
\[
 m'=\frac{m-1}{m+1},\quad n'=\frac{n-1}{n+1},\quad
 \lambda=\frac2{(m+1)(n+1)},\quad
 (\sigma',u',v',a',b')=\lambda(\sigma,b,a,v,u).
\]
Its denominators are units, \(m'=m\) modulo \(\ell\), and
\[
 A'=1+m'^2=\frac{2A}{(m+1)^2},\qquad h'=1-m'^2.
\]
Thus \(h'\) is a unit, while \(A'\) has positive even valuation and local squareclass2. The reflected roots \(u',v'\) are integral. The first actual g Kummer coordinate is
\[
 \eta'=(u'+v')^2-\frac{16h'^2}{A'}.
\]
The second term has negative valuation and dominates, so its quotient with \(\eta'\) is a square principal unit. Consequently
\[
 [\eta']=[-A']=[2]\ne1
 \quad\text{in }\mathbb Q_\ell^*/\mathbb Q_\ell^{*2}. \tag{83.3}
\]
There is no zero or finite two-torsion chart: \(\eta'\) has negative valuation. But the four first Kummer classes in the orbit with \(j=t=0\) are
\[
 1,\quad-\alpha'\gamma',\quad\alpha'\gamma',\quad-1,
 \qquad \alpha'=m'^2-3,\quad\gamma'=1-3m'^2.
\]
They are all squares locally, because \(\alpha'\gamma'=-16\) modulo \(\ell\). This contradicts (83.3) and excludes the whole orbit, including its root-sign and inversion representatives.

Every prime of the odd primitive hypotenuse \(c_m\) is1 modulo4, so the argument proves that all its prime divisors are1 modulo8. There is a direct argument for \(c_n\), with no Kummer-label transposition. Normalize the f representative to the exact pq mask using its root flip and n-inversion; these preserve both integer hypotenuses. Write
\[
 B=4h,\quad d=B^2/A,\quad\alpha=m^2-3,\quad\gamma=1-3m^2,
 \quad Z=(u+v)^2,\ Z^*=(u-v)^2,\quad\eta=Z-d,\ \eta^*=Z^*-d.
\]
Then the actual pq equalities are \([\eta]=[\alpha\gamma]\), \([Z-2B]=[-A\gamma]\), and the exact norm identities are
\[
 (Z-2B)(Z^*-2B)=32h\gamma(1+n^2),\qquad
 \eta\eta^*=-\frac{4B^2\alpha\gamma}{A^2}. \tag{83.4}
\]

Suppose \(\ell\equiv5\pmod8\) divides \(c_n\). Thus \(n^2=-1\) modulo \(\ell\). The original F pair excludes positive or negative valuation of \(m\); the G pair then forces \(\chi(m)=-1\). Consequently \(m,h\) are units. The proved assertion for \(c_m\) makes \(A\) a unit, and it is a local square. Both \(\alpha,\gamma\) are integral and cannot simultaneously be nonunits. Since \(D\) has positive valuation, \(Z,Z^*\) reduce to \(\pm2B\).

If \(Z=2B\) modulo \(\ell\), then \(Z^*-2B\) has unit class \(-16h\). The first identity in (83.4) forces \([Z-2B]=[-2\gamma(1+n^2)]\), differing from the required class \([-A\gamma]\) by the nonsquare2. Hence \(Z=-2B\) modulo \(\ell\). Its second Kummer coordinate now yields \([h/(A\gamma)]=1\). If \(\alpha\) is a unit, then \(\eta\) has the unit class \([8h\alpha/A]\), so \([\eta/(\alpha\gamma)]=[2]\), a contradiction. Otherwise \(\gamma\) is a unit, and \(\eta^*\) has class \([-8h\gamma/A]=[-2]\), also nonsquare. But the second identity in (83.4) and the pq first class force \([\eta^*]=[-1]\), a square. These cases exhaust the bad-root valuations, proving the assertion for \(c_n\).

Finally, if a normalized parameter has dyadic valuation2, its primitive Pythagorean parametrization has even leg \(2uv\) with the even member of \(u,v\) of valuation1. The hypotenuse \(u^2+v^2\) is then5 modulo8, impossible when all its prime divisors are1 modulo8. Applying this separately to both parameters proves the two depth bounds in (83.2). The earlier positive-edge-ratio criterion gives an independent check on the second bound. In particular both hypotenuses are coprime65.

#### Symmetric support at5 and13, without a Kummer-orbit transfer

A further support condition links the two rational parameters directly through the original equations. It applies to every finite rational full five-root point, without assuming that transposition preserves the pq label, and without assuming the two individual central factors are squares. Write \(m=p/q\), \(n=r/s\) in lowest terms. Then
\[
 5\mid p^2+q^2\iff5\mid r^2+s^2,\qquad
 13\mid p^2+q^2\iff13\mid r^2+s^2. \tag{83.5}
\]
When these valuations are positive, their parities agree by \(\sigma^2=(1+m^2)(1+n^2)\). In the remaining branch where \(p^2+q^2=c_m^2\), \(r^2+s^2=c_n^2\), this says that the integer hypotenuses have identical5-support and13-support.

To prove this, take \(\ell=5\) or13 dividing \(p^2+q^2\). Both \(p,q\) are units and \(m^2=-1\) in the residue field. Since \(\ell\equiv5\pmod8\), both \(m\) and2 are nonsquares, while \(-1\) is a square. If \(v_\ell(n)>0\), the original reflected radicands reduce to the nonsquares \(\pm4m\). If \(v_\ell(n)<0\), divide them by the square \(n^2\); their reductions are again \(\mp4m\). Thus \(n\) is a unit. The two other edge radicands reduce to \(\pm8n\), giving \(\chi(n)=-1\). Consequently \(n^2\ne1\), and the reflected pair now gives \(\chi(1-n^2)=-1\). At5 the only residues are \(n=\pm2\); at13 they are \(n=\pm5\). Hence \(n^2=-1\), proving the forward implication. The exact transposition exchanging the two edge-root pairs proves the reverse. The central zero is retained; neither denominator chart is omitted.

The limitation can also be proved exactly. Among primes congruent to5 modulo8, only5 and13 force this shared support from the complete local root conditions, even with both individual central factors required to be squares. For such a prime let
\[
 T_\ell=\{n:\chi(n)=\chi(1-n^2)=-1,\quad\chi(1+n^2)\in\{0,1\}\}.
\]
The smooth projective degree-eight cover
\[
 y_1^2=2n,\qquad y_2^2=2(1-n^2),\qquad y_3^2=1+n^2
\]
has genus5: its six branch points are \(0,\infty,\pm1,\pm\sqrt{-1}\), each of inertia2. At these primes it has no rational point at infinity,0 or \(\pm1\), while the two roots of \(-1\) contribute four points each. Thus its point count is \(8(|T_\ell|-1)\). If those two roots are the entire set, the count is8, and the Hasse–Weil bound forces \(\ell\le113\). The exhaustive prime list is
\[
 (5,13,29,37,53,61,101,109),
\]
with respective set sizes
\[
 (2,2,6,6,6,10,14,14).
\]
Every extra residue lifts by Hensel's lemma to a full local point with \(v_\ell(1+m^2)>0\) but \(v_\ell(1+n^2)=0\). Hence extending (83.5) to all primes5 modulo8 would be invalid.

Even at5 and13 the positive valuations are independent locally. Choose \(i^2=-1\) in \(\mathbb Q_\ell\), and arbitrary positive integers \(j,k\); then
\[
 m=i\sqrt{1-\ell^{2j}},\qquad n=i\sqrt{1-\ell^{2k}}
\]
gives the individual squares \(1+m^2=\ell^{2j}\), \(1+n^2=\ell^{2k}\). All four edge radicands are square units by reduction and Hensel lifting. Thus this support theorem cannot alone force increasing valuations under transposition.
