### 12.96. Aggregate boundary twists and a genus-three slope invariant

The aggregate squareclass of the twelve pair-character boundary twists gives an explicit genus-three slope invariant. A bound on this one aggregate invariant would imply global finiteness without fixing the center-prime support. The proof is ineffective and supplies no such bound.

Write the four offsets as
\[
(d_1,d_2,d_3,d_4)=(x,y,x+y,x-y),\qquad
H_i^2+d_i^2=c^4.
\]
For each of the six pairs let
\[
N_{ij,\pm}=d_iH_j\pm d_jH_i,
\qquad D_{ij,\pm}=\operatorname{sf}(|N_{ij,\pm}|).
\]
Here sf is the positive squarefree part. These are the boundary twist classes attached to the twelve pair characters: the corresponding norm-one phase has imaginary square-coordinate $N_{ij,\pm}/c^4$. Distinct square entries imply every displayed $N_{ij,\pm}$ and $d_i^2-d_j^2$ is nonzero.

#### Exact aggregate class

For each pair,
\[
N_{ij,+}N_{ij,-}=c^4(d_i^2-d_j^2).
\]
Multiplying all six pairs and using both exact additive offset equations gives
\[
\prod_{i<j}(d_i^2-d_j^2)
=-4x^3y^3(x^2-y^2)(4x^2-y^2)(x^2-4y^2).
\]
Consequently the aggregate positive class is
\[
\boxed{\Delta_{\rm pair}:=
\operatorname{sf}\!\left(\prod_{i<j}D_{ij,+}D_{ij,-}\right)
=\operatorname{sf}\!\left(
|xy(x^2-y^2)(4x^2-y^2)(x^2-4y^2)|\right).}
\tag{U-AGGREGATE-TWIST-1}
\]
This is an actual coupling of the twelve twists; unlike an individual norm-one identity, its right side uses the shared magic equations. It is a squareclass identity, not equality of the positive products. Common primes occurring in an even number of the twelve twists disappear from the left side.

Put $x=gn,y=gm$ with $\gcd(m,n)=1$. The factor $g^8$ disappears, so
\[
[\Delta_{\rm pair}]
=[nm(n^2-m^2)(4n^2-m^2)(n^2-4m^2)]
\]
in the positive rational squareclass group. Relative to the existing mixed-index product class this is
\[
[\Delta_{\rm pair}]
=[P]\,[Pnm(n^2-m^2)]\,[(4n^2-m^2)(n^2-4m^2)].
\tag{U-AGGREGATE-TWIST-2}
\]
Absolute signs are understood when using positive representatives. In particular the aggregate invariant does not detect the common offset factor $g$. This agrees with the exact local construction in which one external prime enters every individual boundary twist.

#### An explicit genus-three slope curve and elliptic quotient

Set $r=y/x$ and
\[
f(r)=r(r^2-1)(4r^2-1)(r^2-4).
\]
The eight branch values $0,\infty,\pm1,\pm2,\pm\tfrac12$ are distinct. For a signed squarefree integer $d$ representing the class of $f(r)$, one has $|d|=\Delta_{\rm pair}$ and a rational point on the smooth genus-three curve
\[
\mathcal G_d:\quad d z^2=f(r).
\tag{U-AGGREGATE-TWIST-3}
\]
All eight branch slopes give zero or repeated offsets and are excluded on the admissible locus. No choice of sign of $d$ is silently discarded.

There is an exact degree-two map to an elliptic curve. Define
\[
u=r-r^{-1},\qquad V=z/r^2,
\qquad X=4du,\quad Y=4d^2V.
\]
Since
\[
f(r)/r^4=u(4u^2-9),
\]
the image lies on
\[
E_{6|d|}:\quad Y^2=X^3-36d^2X.
\tag{U-AGGREGATE-TWIST-4}
\]
The quotient involution is $(r,z)\mapsto(-1/r,z/r^4)$; its invariant functions are $u,V$, and $r$ satisfies $r^2-ur-1=0$. Thus the map has degree two and extends to the smooth projective models.
Away from the excluded branch slopes, $Y\ne0$. The established torsion result for congruent-number curves gives $E_{6|d|}(\mathbb Q)_{\rm tors}=E_{6|d|}[2]$, so the displayed image is nontorsion. Thus $6\Delta_{\rm pair}$ must be a congruent number. This requirement does not itself bound $\Delta_{\rm pair}$.

The first nonzero Kummer coordinate of this image is particularly transparent:
\[
[X]=[(4r^2-1)(r^2-4)].
\tag{U-AGGREGATE-TWIST-5}
\]
The other two coordinates are
\[
[X+6d]=[2(r^2-1)(2r+1)(r-2)],\qquad
[X-6d]=[2(r^2-1)(2r-1)(r+2)].
\]
Their product is trivial. These formulas specify the precise extra squareclasses that a proposed doubling or isogeny argument would have to control.

#### Why the extra factors do not cancel by an algebraic root identity

Use affine normalized offsets $a=x/c^2,b=y/c^2$. The full-root function field is obtained from $\mathbb Q(a,b)$ by adjoining square roots of
\[
1\pm a,\quad1\pm b,\quad1\pm(a+b),\quad1\pm(a-b).
\]
At the generic point of each of the four coincidence lines
$2a\pm b=0$ and $a\pm2b=0$, all eight radicands are units. The multiquadratic extension is therefore unramified at that valuation, whereas
$(4a^2-b^2)(a^2-4b^2)$ has valuation one. Its pullback has valuation one at every prime above the generic line and cannot be a square. The same argument applies to each individual coincidence factor.

Thus the full-root equations do not supply an algebraic square cancellation in (U-AGGREGATE-TWIST-2), and they do not make the generic elliptic point (U-AGGREGATE-TWIST-4) twice another point by making (U-AGGREGATE-TWIST-5) trivial. This is a function-field statement only. It leaves open a further arithmetic restriction on all admissible rational points; such a restriction cannot be justified by claiming a missing square identity.

#### A conditional global finiteness consequence

For every fixed positive bound $D_0$, there are only finitely many primitive magic squares of nine distinct positive integer squares with
\[
\Delta_{\rm pair}\le D_0.
\tag{U-AGGREGATE-TWIST-6}
\]
No fixed center-prime support is required. Indeed there are finitely many signed squarefree $d$ with $|d|\le D_0$, and Faltings' theorem on each genus-three curve (U-AGGREGATE-TWIST-3) gives finitely many rational slopes $r$.

For completeness, each admissible fixed slope itself has a fixed high-genus full-root curve. Put $s=x/c^2$. Its eight radicands are
\[
1\pm s,\quad1\pm rs,\quad
1\pm(1+r)s,\quad1\pm(1-r)s.
\]
The eight finite zeros are distinct at every admissible slope. Their squareclasses are independent, so the geometric cover of the $s$-line has degree $256$. It has those eight branch values and infinity, each with inertia two. Riemann--Hurwitz gives genus
\[
1+2^6(9-4)=321.
\]
It has only finitely many rational points. A normalized rational root tuple determines a primitive integral tuple uniquely up to the finitely many sign and layout choices. This proves (U-AGGREGATE-TWIST-6).

The argument is ineffective at the two rational-point steps. More importantly, no bound on $\Delta_{\rm pair}$ is known. Individual twist escape does not imply aggregate escape, because the common external primes may cancel in the aggregate class. The result therefore isolates a new sufficient finite-image target, not a proof that this target is bounded.

The symbolic identities and branch calculations are checked in `simultaneous_units/verify_coupled_pair_twist_slope.py/.json`. The certificate verifies the pair norm identity, exact six-pair product, squarefreeness and all eight branch values of the slope polynomial, the elliptic quotient, and the three Kummer-coordinate ratios. Its finite computations are not used as a rational-point enumeration.

The separate `simultaneous_units/aggregate_boundary_twists_independent_review.md/.json` replays these identities and checks the complete finiteness argument, including signed twists, the quotient involution, geometric independence of the eight fixed-slope radical classes, inertia at infinity, normalization of rational points, and uniqueness of primitive scaling. Both Faltings applications use the smooth projective curves of the stated genera.


### 12.97. Fixed-ratio center splitting and a polynomial bound for the nonsplit center part

This theorem applies at every orientation rank and on every Kummer stratum. Retain the content and residual-norm normalization of Section 12.94. Let an actual primitive integer full-root point have center root $c>0$, offsets $x,y$, and all eight roots of

$$c^2\pm x,\quad c^2\pm y,\quad c^2\pm(x+y),\quad c^2\pm(x-y).$$

Write $U=r_5r_6,V=r_7r_8,T=\gcd(U,V)>0$, and fix the signed reduced ratio $a=U/T,b=V/T$. Assume the nonboundary locus $ab(a^2-b^2)\ne0$. Then $a,b$ are coprime odd integers, and the primitive identities give

$$
R=\frac{a^2+b^2}{2},\quad \gcd(T,c)=1,\qquad
(b^2-a^2)(c^4-x^2-y^2)-2(a^2+b^2)xy=0. \tag{97.1}
$$

Define

$$
L_{a,b}=\mathbb Q\left(i,\sqrt{a^2-b^2},
 \sqrt{2a(a+b)},\sqrt{2b(a+b)}\right). \tag{97.2}
$$

The degree is at most $16$ over $\mathbb Q$, and at most $8$ over $\mathbb Q(i)$. At any prime, including one that ramifies in a displayed radicand, “splits completely over $\mathbb Q_\ell$” means literally
$L_{a,b}\otimes\mathbb Q_\ell\cong\mathbb Q_\ell^{[L_{a,b}:\mathbb Q]}$.
Equivalently, all four rational squareclasses in (97.2) are squares in $\mathbb Q_\ell$.

#### The field on every central chart

At $c=0$, normalize $x=1$. The two possible ratios are

$$t_+=\frac{a-b}{a+b},\qquad t_-=\frac{a+b}{a-b}=t_+^{-1}.$$

The positive-slot roots are $1,\sqrt t,\sqrt{1+t},\sqrt{1-t}$, and opposite slots adjoin $i$. For $t=t_+$ the last three squareclasses are precisely the three nonconstant classes in (97.2), since each ratio to its displayed radicand equals $1/(a+b)^2$. The identities

$$1+t_-=(1+t_+)/t_+,\qquad 1-t_-=-(1-t_+)/t_+$$

show equality of the two fields after adjoining $i$. All root signs give the same field. Negating or reciprocating $a/b$ also preserves the field: the three expressions are permuted up to products and $-1$.

There is no omitted central chart. Equation (97.1) at $c=0$ excludes $x=0$, $y=0$, and $x\pm y=0$ under the stated hypothesis. Thus normalization by the root above $x$ is legitimate at every proper geometric central point of the signed genus-193 fiber. This includes the branches on its resolution.

#### Explicit threshold at every odd center prime

**Theorem.** Let $\ell\mid c$, put $e=v_\ell(c)>0$, and put
$k=v_\ell(ab(a^2-b^2))$. If $2e>k$, then $L_{a,b}$ splits completely over $\mathbb Q_\ell$.

The center is odd, so $\ell\ne2$. Primitivity forces at least one of $x,y$ to be a unit. Interchange them if necessary; (97.1) is symmetric and the signed-root labels may be chosen consistently. Suppose $x$ is a unit. Both $c^2+x$ and $c^2-x$ are square units, which forces $-1$ to be a local square and in particular $\ell\equiv1\pmod4$. Also $x/(c^2+x)\in1+\ell\mathbb Z_\ell$, so $x$ is a square unit. Scale all roots by a square root of $x$. We now have $x=1$, $y\in\mathbb Z_\ell$, and the same center depth $e$.

Put $d=b^2-a^2$, $s=a^2+b^2$. Equation (97.1) implies

$$
d(y^2+1-c^4)+2sy=0,\qquad
(dy+s)^2=4a^2b^2+d^2c^4. \tag{97.3}
$$

At most one of $a,b,d$ has positive $\ell$-valuation. The relative error in the second equation compared with $(2ab)^2$ has valuation
$4e+2v_\ell(d)-2v_\ell(ab)>0$.
Choose the sign $\sigma$ for which $dy+s$ is close to $\sigma2ab$ and set $t_0=(-s+\sigma2ab)/d$. Factoring (97.3) gives the exact identity of valuations

$$v_\ell(y-t_0)=4e+v_\ell(d)-v_\ell(ab). \tag{97.4}$$

The cases are exhaustive:

| Coefficient case | Boundary valuations | Approximation depth |
|---|---|---|
| $\ell\nmid abd$ | $t_0,1+t_0,1-t_0$ are units | $4e$ |
| $\ell\mid ab$, $v_\ell(ab)=k$ | $t_0$ is a unit; exactly one of $1\pm t_0$ has depth $k$ | $4e-k>k$ |
| $\ell\mid d$, $v_\ell(d)=k$ | the integral root has depth $k$; $1\pm t_0$ are units | $4e+k>k$ |

In the last row the two boundary roots have valuations $k,-k$. Formula (97.4) and the integrality of $y$ exclude the negative-valuation root. In every case the three relevant boundary constants have nonnegative valuation at most $k$ and $y-t_0$ has valuation greater than $k$.

The actual square radicands $c^2+y,c^2+1+y,c^2+1-y$ differ from $t_0,1+t_0,1-t_0$ by terms of valuation greater than $k$, since $2e>k$. Their ratios lie in $1+\ell\mathbb Z_\ell$. All three boundary constants are therefore squares. Together with $i\in\mathbb Q_\ell$, this proves the theorem, including arbitrary depths at primes dividing $a,b,a-b,a+b$.

#### Global polynomial bound on the nonsplit part

Put $\Xi=|ab(a^2-b^2)|$ and let $\Xi_{(1\bmod4)}$ denote its full prime-power part supported on primes congruent to $1$ modulo $4$. Define

$$
C_{\rm ns}=\prod_{\substack{\ell\mid c\\
L_{a,b}\otimes\mathbb Q_\ell\not\cong
\mathbb Q_\ell^{[L_{a,b}:\mathbb Q]}}}\ell^{v_\ell(c)}.
$$

The contrapositive, together with $\ell\equiv1\pmod4$ at every center prime and the central pair content $P=\prod_j A_j$, gives

$$C_{\rm ns}\mid P,\qquad
C_{\rm ns}^{\,2}\mid\gcd(P^2,\Xi_{(1\bmod4)}). \tag{97.5}$$

To see it, a nonsplit prime satisfies $k\ge2e$. If it divides $a^2-b^2$, the identity $U^2-V^2=-4xy$ and the fact that $T$ is a unit give $v_\ell(xy)=k$. One offset is a unit, so the other has depth at least $2e$. If instead it divides $a$ or $b$, the corresponding edge product $q_j$ has depth $k$, and $q_j^2=c^4-D_j^2$ gives $v_\ell(D_j)\ge2e$. In either case both roots above $c^2\pm D_j$ have valuation at least $e$. Their square sum $2c^2$ forces the minimum of their valuations to be exactly $e$. Thus the corresponding opposite-pair content has the entire center depth $e$. In particular every prime dividing $c/P$ splits in $L_{a,b}$.

The previously proved full-root modulus is
$2^8 3^2 5^2 11\cdot13\cdot19\mid b^2-a^2$.
Consequently the part discarded in passing from $\Xi$ to $\Xi_{(1\bmod4)}$ contains $2^8 3^2 11\cdot19$, and

$$
C_{\rm ns}^{\,2}\le\Xi_{(1\bmod4)}
\le\frac{\Xi}{2^8 3^2 11\cdot19}
<\frac{R^2}{48^2\cdot209},\qquad
C_{\rm ns}<\frac{R}{48\sqrt{209}}. \tag{97.6}
$$

Indeed, with $A=2|ab|$ and $B=|a^2-b^2|$ one has $A^2+B^2=4R^2$ and $\Xi=AB/2\le R^2$. Equality would require $A=B$, impossible for nonzero rational $a/b$. The weaker $C_{\rm ns}<R$ requires no additional modulus. These inequalities bound the entire nonsplit center part, not merely its radical; the split part remains unrestricted by this argument.

#### Exact good-prime criterion and arbitrary-depth local points

Let $\ell\nmid2ab(a^2-b^2)$. An actual center prime must split by the theorem with $k=0$. Conversely, suppose that this good prime splits. For any $e\ge1$, set $x=1,c=\ell^e$ and solve

$$y^2+\frac{2(a^2+b^2)}{b^2-a^2}y+1-c^4=0$$

near either $t_+$ or $t_-$. The derivative is $\pm4ab/(a^2-b^2)$, a unit. Hensel gives $y$, and all eight nonzero square residue radicands lift. Equation (97.1) ensures $(U/V)^2=(a/b)^2$; a root-sign choice gives the exact prescribed signed ratio. All noncenter roots are units, so the point is locally primitive, with center depth exactly $e$.

Thus every positive center depth occurs locally at every good split prime. This is local sufficiency and sharpness, not a global rational-point existence statement.

The exact conic, squareclass and local-lifting identities are certified in `varying_primes/fixed_ratio_nonsplit_center_bound.py/.json`; the good-prime field producer is `coupled_lifts/fixed_edge_ratio_center_field.py/.json`. An independent all-chart proof and exact replay are archived in `rank4_next/trace_center_norm/nonsplit_center_independent_review.md` and `verify_nonsplit_center_joint_character.py/.json`. The explicit threshold proof retains all primes dividing the ratio coefficients, unlike an unramified splitting criterion alone.


#### Coupling the boundary field to the aggregate pair character

Retain the actual full-root point and define the positive squarefree aggregate character from Section 12.96 by

$$
\Delta=\operatorname{sf}|xy(x^2-y^2)(4x^2-y^2)(x^2-4y^2)|.
$$

Set

$$
D_9=(9a^2-b^2)(a^2-9b^2),\qquad
L^+_{a,b,\Delta}=L_{a,b}(\sqrt{\Delta D_9}).
\tag{97.7}
$$

This field has degree at most $32$ over $\mathbb Q$. The admissible locus makes the product defining $\Delta$ nonzero. Also $D_9\ne0$: otherwise the coprime pair $(|a|,|b|)$ would be $(3,1)$ or $(1,3)$, contradicting the already proved $256\mid a^2-b^2$.

No center prime divides both $\Xi=|ab(a^2-b^2)|$ and $D_9$. Indeed reduction at $a=0$, $b=0$, or $a^2=b^2$ leaves $9b^4$, $9a^4$, or $-64b^4$. Every odd common prime is therefore $3$, whereas center primes are $1\bmod4$.

Let $\ell\mid c$, put $e=v_\ell(c)$ and $k=v_\ell(\Xi)$, and first assume $2e>k$. In the local normalization used above, $\rho=y/x$ and $1\pm\rho$ are nonzero local squares. Choosing signs $a',b'$ of $a,b$ gives an integral boundary ratio

$$
\rho_0=\frac{a'-b'}{a'+b'},\qquad
a'+b'\in\mathbb Z_\ell^\times,\qquad
v_\ell(\rho-\rho_0)\ge4e-k.
$$

One way to obtain these signs is to choose
$a'T=i(x+y)(1+\eta_a)$ and $b'T=i(x-y)(1+\eta_b)$, where
$v_\ell(\eta_a)\ge4e-2v_\ell(a)$ and
$v_\ell(\eta_b)\ge4e-2v_\ell(b)$. Their sum has unit leading term $2ix$. This proves the unit denominator and approximation in every coefficient-prime chart.

The squareclass of $\Delta$ is then the squareclass of
$E(\rho)=(4\rho^2-1)(\rho^2-4)$: the discarded factor
$x^8\rho(1-\rho^2)$ is a square, and $-1$ is a local square. Exact substitution gives

$$
E(\rho_0)=-\frac{D_9}{(a'+b')^4}.
\tag{97.8}
$$

At a prime dividing $\Xi$, $D_9$ is a unit, so the approximation already proves that $\Delta D_9$ is a local square. At a prime dividing $D_9$, $\Xi$ is a unit and the approximation has depth at least $4e$. Since $E$ has integral coefficients, it proves the same conclusion whenever $4e>v_\ell(D_9)$. Primes dividing neither coefficient split in $L^+_{a,b,\Delta}$ automatically.

Partition the entire nonsplit center part for $L^+_{a,b,\Delta}$ into the coprime factors $C_\Xi$ and $C_9$ according as the prime divides $\Xi$ or $D_9$. The preceding thresholds and the central-content argument give the exact laws

$$
\boxed{
\begin{gathered}
C_{\rm bad}=C_\Xi C_9,\qquad
C_\Xi\mid P,\qquad \gcd(C_9,P)=1,\\
C_\Xi^2\mid\gcd(P^2,\Xi_{(1\bmod4)}),\qquad
C_9^4\mid |D_9|_{(1\bmod4)}.
\end{gathered}}
\tag{97.9}
$$

For the coprimality with $P$, a prime of $D_9$ is a unit at $\Xi$, hence all four offsets and all eight noncentral roots are units there. No central pair content occurs.

There is a uniform polynomial bound independent of the size of $\Delta$. Write $d=a^2-b^2$, with $256\mid d$. The two factors of $D_9$ are $8b^2+9d$ and $d-8b^2$, each of exact 2-adic valuation $3$. Thus $v_2(D_9)=6$. Also

$$
D_9=36R^2-100a^2b^2,\qquad |D_9|<64R^2.
$$

The strict inequality follows from $0<a^2b^2<R^2$. Therefore $C_9<\sqrt R$, and (97.6) applied to $C_\Xi$ yields

$$
\boxed{C_{\rm bad}<\frac{R^{3/2}}{48\sqrt{209}}.}
\tag{97.10}
$$

The field depends on both the fixed edge ratio and the actual aggregate character. This bounds its whole nonsplit center part, retaining multiplicities, but does not bound the completely split part or assert sufficiency for a rational point.

The aggregate extension is proved in the independently reviewed Section 4 of the nonsplit-center audit. Its separate exact verification is archived in varying_primes/nonsplit_aggregate_character_review.md and verify_nonsplit_aggregate_character.py/.json; the independent certificate imports no producer helpers.


### 12.98. An all-rank height envelope from the residual norm


Retain the actual edge products and residual norm of Section12.94:
\[
 U=u_3v_3=Ta,\qquad V=u_4v_4=Tb,\qquad
 T=\gcd(U,V),\qquad R=(a^2+b^2)/2.
\]
For an admissible primitive point, let
\[
 s=\omega(c),\quad Q=\max_{p\mid c}p,\quad L=\log Q,
 \quad E=\max_{p\mid c}v_p(c),\quad Z=1+\log R.
\]
Every center prime is odd and split in \(\mathbb Q(i)\). There is no
orientation-rank hypothesis in the following estimate.

Put \(\ell=\log5\) and define constants depending only on \(s\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \zeta&=3/\ell+1/2,\\
 \lambda_s&=1+\log(4096(s+2)^2)/\ell,\\
 M_s&=\max\{1,5((s+2)/(\mathrm e\ell))^{s+2}\},\\
 \chi_s^{\mathrm{res}}&=\frac15+
 112690(45/2)^{s+1}(s+2)^{2s+6}\zeta\lambda_sM_s.
\end{aligned}
\]
Then
\[
 \boxed{E<\chi_s^{\mathrm{res}}\frac QL
                   (1+\log R)\log(32E)},                       \tag{98.1}
\]
and hence
\[
 \boxed{\log c<2s\chi_s^{\mathrm{res}}Q(1+\log R)
 \log\!\left(64\chi_s^{\mathrm{res}}\frac QL(1+\log R)\right).}
                                                                    \tag{98.2}
\]
Thus, uniformly in the identities of the center primes,
\[
 \log c=O_s\!\left(Q(1+\log R)
                       \log(2Q(1+\log R))\right).
\]
For a specified finite center-prime set and a specified upper bound on
\(R\), this is an explicit exhaustive center cutoff. It also applies at
orientation rank four. The prime set and residual norm remain unbounded
in the unrestricted problem.

There is an explicit necessary growth statement. Put \(H_c=\log c\),
\(B_s=2s\chi_s^{\mathrm{res}}\), and
\(D_s=64\chi_s^{\mathrm{res}}/\log5\). Then
\[
 \boxed{Q(1+\log R)>
       \frac{H_c}{B_s\log(D_sH_c)}.}                         \tag{98.2a}
\]
Indeed if \(Q(1+\log R)\le H_c\), replace the logarithm in (98.2)
by \(\log(D_sH_c)\); the other case satisfies (98.2a) directly.
Since \(T^2R<c^4\), it follows that
\[
 \log(c^2/T)>
       \frac{H_c}{2B_sQ\log(D_sH_c)}-\frac12.                 \tag{98.2b}
\]
This gives a quantitative gap for noncentral common content at fixed
center-prime support, without replacing an exceptional-divisor height
by its finite contact contribution.

**A cutoff when the residual norm is polynomial in the central deficit.**
Let \(P\) denote the central deficit from the earlier index decomposition.
The all-rank estimate (U-VARYING-PRIME-DEFICIT) in Section12.16 gives
\(\log P<\kappa_sQ\log(128E)\). Fix \(C_*\ge1\) and \(A\ge0\).
On the additional stratum \(R\le C_*P^A\), define
\[
 \mathcal D=1+\log C_*+A\kappa_sQ,\qquad
 \mathcal B=\chi_s^{\mathrm{res}}\frac QL\mathcal D.
\]
Equations (98.1) and the deficit estimate yield
\(E<\mathcal B\log^2(128E)\), hence
\[
 \boxed{E<4\mathcal B\log^2(2048\mathcal B),\qquad
 \log c<4s\chi_s^{\mathrm{res}}Q\mathcal D
                         \log^2(2048\mathcal B).}             \tag{98.2c}
\]
The inversion follows from
\(x<a\log^2(bx)\Rightarrow x<4a\log^2(16ab)\), for \(x,a,b\ge1\).
Thus this conditional stratum has an explicit rank-independent cutoff.
It is not asserted that \(R\le C_*P^A\) holds universally. Equivalently,
at fixed center-prime support, any unbounded-height sequence of admissible
points must eventually have \(R>C_*P^A\) for every fixed \(C_*,A\).

**The local contact calculation.** Fix \(p^e\Vert c\) and put
\(d=v_p(ab(a^2-b^2))\). The exact content identity \(\gcd(T,c)=1\)
and \(-4xy=T^2(a^2-b^2)\) allow one corner, say \(x\), to be chosen
as a \(p\)-unit. If \(2e\le d\), then
\[
 e\le d/2<\log R/\log p,
\]
because \(|ab(a^2-b^2)|<R^2\). Otherwise, among
\(D=(x,y,x+y,x-y)\), at most one valuation is nonzero; it equals \(d\).
This includes the primes dividing \(a\), \(b\), or \(a^2-b^2\).

Write \(Q_j=u_jv_j\), so \(Q_j^2+D_j^2=c^4\), and choose
\(\delta_j=\pm1\) such that
\[
 Q_j=\delta_jiD_j(1+\eta_j),\qquad
 v_p(\eta_j)=4e-2v_p(D_j).
\]
For the actual phases \(z_j=Z_j/c\), set \(w_j=z_j^{\delta_j}\),
\(t=y/x\), and
\[
 \epsilon=\delta_3\delta_4,\qquad
 t_0=\frac{a-\epsilon b}{a+\epsilon b},\qquad
 A_j=\delta_j\delta_1d_j(t_0),
 \quad(d_1,d_2,d_3,d_4)=(1,t,1+t,1-t).
\]
The signed equality \(Q_3/Q_4=a/b\) gives, with
\(u=(1+\eta_3)/(1+\eta_4)\),
\[
 t_0-t=\frac{(1-t^2)(u-1)}{(1+t)u+1-t}.
\]
Its denominator is a unit. Consequently, for each \(j=2,3,4\),
\[
 v_p\!\left(\frac{(w_j/w_1)^2}{A_j}-1\right)\ge4e-2d>0.
                                                               \tag{98.3}
\]
At least one of these three expressions is nonzero. Otherwise the two
exact magic identities, after their leading terms cancel, would require
both \(t_0^2+t_0+1=0\) and \(t_0^2-t_0+1=0\), an impossibility.

**The logarithm estimate.** Choose fixed Gaussian ratios
\(g_q=\pi_q/\bar\pi_q\). The squared character in (98.3) has exponents
of absolute value at most \(4E\). Its exponent at \(p\) is
\(b_p=v_p(A_j)\le d\); absorb this into the moving base
\(\beta=A_j/g_p^{b_p}\). All remaining bases are local units over
\(\mathbb Q(i)\), and
\[
 h(\beta)<2(1+\log R).
\]
Yu [33], Corollary1, printed p.19, applies with field degree2,
residue degree1, \(n=s+1\), and exponent bound \(8E\). Use fixed
height parameters \(\tfrac12\log p\) and
\(\tfrac12\max(\log p,\log q)\), and final moving parameter
\((3+L/2)Z\). Its exponent is \(-1\), so Yu's auxiliary logarithm
uses only the largest fixed height, at most \(L/2\). Thus no
\(\log\log R\) factor is lost inside that auxiliary term.

Substitution into the published bound, followed by
\[
 \max_{5\le p\le Q}\frac{p}{(\log p)^{s+2}}
 =\max\!\left\{\frac5{\ell^{s+2}},\frac Q{L^{s+2}}\right\},
 \qquad L^{s+2}e^{-L}\le((s+2)/\mathrm e)^{s+2},
\]
gives (98.1). Finally \(x<A\log(32x)\) implies
\(x<2A\log(64A)\), and \(\log c\le sLE\), proving (98.2).

The detailed coefficient-prime charts, nonzero-form identity, moving-height
bound and exact constants are in
`coupled_lifts/fixed_edge_ratio_quantitative_height.md/.py/.json`.
The primary-source constants and both envelopes are independently reviewed
in `next_pythagorean_cover/fixed_support_height_independent_review.md`
with its separate verifier.
Independent contact and nonvanishing reviews are
`simultaneous_units/residual_height_contact_independent_review.md` (with
`verify_residual_height_contact_independent.py/.json`) and
`varying_primes/fixed_ratio_phase_contact_review.md`.
The additional deficit comparison and its independently checked logarithm
inversion are recorded in `coupled_lifts/residual_to_deficit_power_strata.md`.
This proof is independent of the effective integral-point theorem used
in the preceding fixed-fiber discussion. It gives a quantitative growing-
\(R\) envelope, but substituting only \(R<c^4\) does not yield an absolute
bound.


### 12.99. A common-prime restriction linking the residual norm and aggregate twist

The residual norm and aggregate twist are generically independent
squareclasses. Their actual arithmetic values nevertheless satisfy a
common-prime restriction. Retain
\[
 a=U/T,\quad b=V/T,\quad
 R=\frac{a^2+b^2}{2}=\frac{c^4-x^2-y^2}{T^2},\quad
 4xy=T^2(b^2-a^2),\quad \gcd(T,c)=1.
 \tag{U-RDELTA-IDENTITIES}
\]
Here $a,b$ are coprime odd integers, and every prime of $R$ is
$1\pmod8$. Define the positive squarefree aggregate
\[
 \Delta=\operatorname{sf}|xy(x^2-y^2)(4x^2-y^2)(x^2-4y^2)|.
 \tag{U-RDELTA-AGGREGATE}
\]
All factors are nonzero at an admissible point.

For every such primitive full-root point,
\[
 \boxed{p\mid\gcd(R,cT)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
        \Delta\in\mathbb Q_p^{\times2}.}
 \tag{U-RDELTA-CONTENT}
\]
In particular $\gcd(\Delta,\gcd(R,cT))=1$, and every such prime has
$\left(\frac{\Delta}{p}\right)=1$.
Every remaining common prime $p\mid\gcd(R,\Delta)$ satisfies one of the
following two stronger splitting conditions:
\[
 \boxed{\begin{array}{ll}
 p\mid x^2-y^2:
   &p\equiv1\pmod{16},\quad 2^{(p-1)/4}\equiv1\pmod p;\\
 p\mid(4x^2-y^2)(x^2-4y^2):
   &p\equiv1\pmod{40},\quad 5^{(p-1)/4}\equiv1\pmod p.
 \end{array}}
 \tag{U-RDELTA-SPLITTING}
\]
In particular,
\[
 p\bmod80\in\{1,17,33,41,49\};
 \tag{U-RDELTA-RESIDUES}
\]
the classes $9$, $57$ and $73\pmod{80}$ cannot occur among the common
primes. The quartic-residue tests are stronger than this congruence list.

To prove the content assertion, fix $p\mid R$. Then $p\ge17$,
$a,b$ are $p$-units, and $b^2-a^2$ is a unit because
$a^2+b^2\equiv0\pmod p$. Thus
$v_p(xy)=2v_p(T)$. If $p\mid T$, then $c$ is a unit and the residual
identity forces exactly one of $x,y$ to be a unit. All three coincidence
factors in (U-RDELTA-AGGREGATE) are units. The valuation of the entire
product is therefore $2v_p(T)$. More precisely, take $x$ to be the unit
offset; then the product divided by $T^2$ reduces to
$x^6(b^2-a^2)=2x^6b^2\pmod p$, a nonzero square because $p\equiv1\pmod8$.
Its squarefree class is therefore a square in $\mathbb Q_p$.
If instead $p\mid c$, then $p\nmid T$, both offsets are units, and
$x^2+y^2\equiv0$. The three coincidence factors reduce to
$-2y^2,-5y^2,-5y^2$ and are again units. Put $r=y/x$; the aggregate
product divided by $x^8$ reduces to $50r$, where $r^2=-1$.
Both $2$ and either square root of $-1$ are squares modulo $p$, so this
is a square unit. The sign discarded in $\Delta$ is also a local square.
Hensel's lemma now proves (U-RDELTA-CONTENT), including the consequence
$\gcd(\Delta,\gcd(c^4,R))=1$.

Now let $p$ be a common prime. It is outside $cT$, both offsets are units,
and $c^4\equiv x^2+y^2$. First suppose the vanishing coincidence
factor is $x^2-y^2$. Put $q=x/c^2$ in $\mathbb F_p$; then $2q^2=1$.
The actual roots of $c^2+x$ and $c^2-x$ supply $r,s\in\mathbb F_p$ with
$r^2=1+q$ and $s^2=1-q$. Changing one sign gives $rs=q$.
Since $p\equiv1\pmod8$, choose $i^2=-1$ in $\mathbb F_p$. The element
\[
 \zeta=\frac{r+is}{2q}
 \quad\hbox{satisfies}\quad
 \zeta^2=q(1+i),\qquad \zeta^4=i,
 \qquad \zeta^8=-1,
 \tag{U-RDELTA-ORDER16}
\]
so it has exact order sixteen. Therefore $p\equiv1\pmod{16}$.
Put $s_0=1/q$, so $s_0^2=2$. An actual edge root supplies
$u^2=1+s_0$, while $r^2=(1+s_0)/s_0$. Hence $(u/r)^2=s_0$, proving that
two is a fourth power.

In the other case, interchange and change signs of the offsets so that
$x/c^2=q$, $y/c^2=2q$, and put $s_0=1/q$, with $s_0^2=5$.
The full roots supply $r_{j,\pm}^2=1\pm j/s_0$ for $j=1,2,3$.
Choose $\beta^2=2$ and $i^2=-1$. Then
\[
 \xi=\frac{s_0-1}{4}+\frac{i s_0r_{1,+}}{2\beta}
 \quad\hbox{has}\quad
 \xi+\xi^{-1}=\frac{s_0-1}{2},\qquad \Phi_5(\xi)=0.
 \tag{U-RDELTA-ORDER5}
\]
As $p\ne5$, its order is exactly five, so $p\equiv1\pmod{40}$.
Moreover $r_{3,+}^2=(s_0+1)^2/(2s_0)$, giving
$((s_0+1)/(\beta r_{3,+}))^2=s_0$. Five is therefore a fourth power.
This completes the proof of (U-RDELTA-SPLITTING).

The complete residue fields explain that these tests retain all local root
information at the indicated coincidence loci:
\[
 \begin{array}{c|c|c}
 \text{coincidence}&\text{full residue field}&\text{degree}\\\hline
 x^2=y^2&\mathbb Q(\zeta_{16},2^{1/4})&16\\
 x^2=4y^2\ \text{or}\ 4x^2=y^2&\mathbb Q(\zeta_{40},5^{1/4})&32.
 \end{array}
 \tag{U-RDELTA-FIELDS}
\]
For the first row, the order-sixteen construction and $u/r$ recover the
field generators; the inverse formulas use
$s_0=\zeta_{16}^2+\zeta_{16}^{-2}$ and
$r=(\zeta_{16}+\zeta_{16}^{-1})/s_0$. For the second row, the roots
recover $i$, $\sqrt2$, $\zeta_5$ and $5^{1/4}$, while
$r_{2,+}^2/r_{1,+}^2=(s_0+1)^2/8$ and the pair-product identities recover
all radicals from these generators. The pure quartic fields are not Galois,
so neither fourth root lies in the corresponding abelian cyclotomic field;
the displayed degrees follow. At good primes, each full residue pattern is
therefore equivalent to its splitting test in (U-RDELTA-SPLITTING).

There is a more general exact support law at the primes of the noncentral content:
\[
\boxed{\gcd(\Delta,\operatorname{rad}T)
=\gcd\!\left(\operatorname{sf}|b^2-a^2|,\operatorname{rad}T\right).}
\tag{U-RDELTA-T-CONTENT}
\]
Indeed, at an odd prime of $T$ the center is a unit and the reduction is a noncentral node. One offset is a unit and the other is divisible by that prime. All three coincidence factors are units. The valuation of the aggregate product is therefore
$v_p(xy)=2v_p(T)+v_p(b^2-a^2)$; taking parity proves the assertion. This covers primes outside $R$ as well. Over $\mathbb Q_p(i)$ the same reduction identifies the aggregate squareclass with that of $b^2-a^2$; over $\mathbb Q_p$ the sign from the positive squarefree convention must be retained. The independent valuation and sign review is appended to `simultaneous_units/residual_height_contact_independent_review.md`.

The squarefree operation is essential at primes dividing $T$. These
statements do not assert that $R$ and $\Delta$ are coprime, and they impose
no restriction on primes dividing only one invariant. They give neither an
upper bound nor a converse global-realizability criterion. Local
sufficiency above refers only to the normalized finite-field coincidence
pattern.

The exact proof and certificate are
`simultaneous_units/residual_norm_aggregate_common_prime_gate.md` and
`verify_residual_norm_aggregate_common_prime_gate.py/.json`.
The independent implementations
`verify_residual_aggregate_prime_interaction_criteria.py/.json` and
`verify_double_slope_splitting_criteria.py/.json`, together with
`verify_diagonal_splitting_criteria.py/.json`, check the content gate,
order constructions, both exact fields and residue conditions. The
corresponding independent human reviews are
`residual_aggregate_prime_interaction_criteria_review.md`,
`double_slope_splitting_criteria_review.md`, and
`diagonal_splitting_criteria_review.md`.
Their finite-field diagnostics are consistency checks; the proof applies
uniformly to every prime.



### 12.100. Residual local squares and a stronger universal content bound

Retain the actual primitive edge products \(U,V\), their common content
\(T=\gcd(U,V)\), and the coprime odd integers \(a=U/T,b=V/T\). Thus
\[
R=\frac{a^2+b^2}{2}=\frac{c^4-x^2-y^2}{T^2},\qquad \gcd(T,c)=1.
\]
The full-root equations impose new conditions on this residual norm even
when \(T\) absorbs the older divisibility constraints on the offsets.

#### Complete local conditions

Every admissible primitive point satisfies
\[
\boxed{R\in\mathbb Q_p^{*2}\quad(p=7,23,31,37,47).} \tag{100.1}
\]
Moreover
\[
\boxed{37\nmid ab,\qquad a/b\bmod37\in\{\pm1,\pm7,\pm16\}.} \tag{100.2}
\]
These assertions cover arbitrary center and noncentral-content valuations.

For the finite reduction, if the center is a unit normalize it to one;
otherwise reduce it to zero. Enumerate all \((x,y)\in\mathbb F_p^2\)
for which all eight values \(c^2\pm x,c^2\pm y,c^2\pm(x+y),
c^2\pm(x-y)\) are squares, excluding the all-zero primitive chart.
The complete counts for \(c=0,1\) are respectively
\[
(0,5),(0,17),(0,17),(108,17),(0,29).
\]
At every accepted nonnode \(c^4-x^2-y^2\) is a nonzero square.
At 37 both edge products are nonzero, and their squared ratio gives
exactly the six values in (100.2). Thus Hensel's lemma proves (100.1)
whenever \(p\nmid T\), and also proves \(37\nmid T\).

At each of the other four primes the only missing reductions are the four
noncentral nodes. Name the vanishing adjacent edge roots \(u,v\) and
their midpoint root \(w\). After an arrangement symmetry the exact
identities are
\[
u^2+v^2=2w^2,\qquad U^2=u^2(2c^2-u^2),\quad
V^2=v^2(2c^2-v^2).
\]
Here \(c\) is a unit and
\(t=v_p(T)=\min(v_p(u),v_p(v))\ge1\). Since \(-1\) is
nonsquare, \(v_p(w)=t\), including unequal depths of \(u,v\).
Therefore
\[
R=2c^2(w/T)^2-\frac{u^4+v^4}{2T^2}. \tag{100.3}
\]
The first term is a square unit because \(2\) is square; the second has
valuation at least \(2t>0\). This proves the local square condition at
every depth, without a finite prime-power extrapolation.

The same identity supplies a uniform restriction at every odd prime of
\(T\): the opposite-root reductions make \(2\) a local square, hence
\[
\boxed{v_p(R)<2v_p(T)\ \Longrightarrow\ R\in\mathbb Q_p^{*2}.} \tag{100.4}
\]
In particular primes of \(T\) outside \(R\) split in
\(\mathbb Q(\sqrt R)\) if \(R\) is nonsquare. If \(T_{\rm bad}\)
is the part supported where \(R\) is not a local square, then
\(T_{\rm bad}^2\mid R\). Common primes of \(R,T\) are retained;
this is not a fixed-support conclusion.

#### Certified residual exclusion

Section12.107 combines these all-depth local-square conditions with complete
full-root ratio masks. Its exhaustive finite enumeration and two independent
replays prove
\[
\boxed{R>10^{14},\qquad T<\frac{c^2}{10^7},\qquad
PT<\frac{c^3}{10^7}.} \tag{100.5}
\]
The content inequalities use \(T^2R=c^4-x^2-y^2<c^4\) and \(P\le c\).
They bound contents relative to the center and do not bound the center itself.

**Certificates and review.** The complete local tables and all-depth proof
are in `next_pythagorean_cover/residual_small_prime_squares.py/.json/.md`.
The independent local proof is
`varying_primes/residual_local_square_independent_review.md` with
`verify_residual_local_square_independent.py/.json`.
The full stronger exclusion, including the infinite-tail argument and
independent arithmetic coverage, is stated and certified in Section12.107.


### 12.101. Two residual norms give a global effective height bound

Retain the actual opposite-root products
\[
 q_1^2=c^4-x^2,\quad q_2^2=c^4-y^2,\quad
 q_3^2=c^4-(x+y)^2,\quad q_4^2=c^4-(x-y)^2.
\]
Alongside the edge content and residual norm, define the corner versions:
\[
 q_3=Ta,\ q_4=Tb,\quad R=(a^2+b^2)/2;\qquad
 q_1=Jf,\ q_2=Jg,\quad R_c=(f^2+g^2)/2,
\]
where \(T,J>0\) are the respective gcds. Both pairs are coprime and odd.
Admissibility gives \(abfg\ne0\), \(a^2\ne b^2\), and \(f^2\ne g^2\).
Bounded values of these two actual residual norms give an effective global
finite enumeration. Quantitatively, every admissible primitive point satisfies
\(c^4<(2/15889)R^2R_c\). There is no restriction on the center-prime set.

**Corner content and residual dictionary (U-TWO-RESIDUAL-DICTIONARY).**
The actual roots give
\[
 \gcd(J,cT)=1,\qquad p\mid J\Longrightarrow p\equiv1\pmod{24},
 \qquad 2J^2R_c=c^4+T^2R.                                  \tag{101.1}
\]
Indeed, at an odd prime dividing \(J\), primitivity forces \(c\)
to be a unit and \(x^2=y^2=c^4\). The original roots then require
\(-1,2,3\) all to be nonzero squares. A common prime of \(J,T\)
would give \(0=q_3^2+q_4^2=-2c^4\), a contradiction. Both contents
are odd. Furthermore
\[
 \gcd(J,R)=\gcd(T,R_c)=1,\qquad
 \gcd(R,R_c)=\gcd(c^4,R)=b_0.                              \tag{101.2}
\]
The last equality follows valuation by valuation from (101.1), including
possible cancellation when the two right-hand valuations agree. The odd
integer \(R_c\) has only prime factors \(1\pmod4\).

**The content quartic (U-TWO-RESIDUAL-CONTENT).** Put
\[
 \delta=b^2-a^2,\qquad
 W=R^2-(\delta/4)^2
  =\frac{(a^2+3b^2)(3a^2+b^2)}{16}.
\]
Then \(W\) is a positive odd integer strictly below \(R^2\), and
\[
 x^2=J^2g^2-T^2R,\quad y^2=J^2f^2-T^2R,\quad
 xy=T^2\delta/4.
\]
Multiplication gives the exact identity
\[
 f^2g^2J^4-2RR_cJ^2T^2+WT^4=0.
\]
Since \(\gcd(J,T)=1\), reduction modulo \(J^2\) and \(T^2\)
proves
\[
 \boxed{J^2\mid W,\qquad T\mid |fg|.}                    \tag{101.3}
\]
These are divisibilities; no equality of prime valuations is implied.

In fact \(K=W/J^2\ge97\). To prove this, suppose \(W=z^2\).
With \(t=a/b\) and \(Z=4z/b^2\), the point
\((X,Y)=(3t^2,3tZ)\) lies on
\[
 E_9:Y^2=X(X+1)(X+9).
\]
The rank-zero calculation in Section12.33 gives exactly
\(O,(0,0),(-1,0),(-9,0),(3,\pm12),(-3,\pm6)\).
Explicitly, \(E_9\) is the standard two-isogenous dual of
\(y^2=x(x-1)(x-4)\), the translate of that section's curve
\(y^2=x(x+1)(x-3)\); the good counts at5 and7 are both8.
Positive \(X=3t^2\) therefore forces \(t^2=1\), which is excluded.
Thus \(W\), and hence \(K\), is nonsquare. The established
\(24\mid x,y\) and \(\gcd(T,6)=1\) give \(256\cdot9\mid\delta\).
Together with the3-adic units \(a,b\), this gives \(W\equiv1\pmod{48}\).
Equation (101.1) gives \(J^2\equiv1\pmod{48}\), so
\(K\equiv1\pmod{48}\). The smaller positive possibilities1 and49
are squares, proving \(K\ge97\).

The actual-root local restrictions sharpen this to
\[
 \boxed{K\ge15889.}                                      \tag{101.3a}
\]
Indeed every prime of \(W\), and hence of \(K\), is \(1\pmod3\):
at a prime of \((a^2+3b^2)/4\) the unit ratio \(a/b\) squares to
\(-3\), and the other factor is reciprocal; the prime3 is excluded.
At every odd prime dividing \(\delta\),
\(W/R^2=1-(\delta/(4R))^2\) is a square unit. Thus \(K\) is a
square unit at3,5,11,13,19, using the already proved modulus on
\(\delta\). Section12.100 supplies two further necessary conditions.
The local squareness of \(R\) at7 and31 excludes these primes from
\(W\): at a zero of one of its factors, \(R\) would be minus a
nonzero square. At37, the allowed ratios \(a/b=\pm1,\pm7,\pm16\)
give \(W/b^4=1,0,0\), respectively. Since37 cannot divide \(J\),
the Legendre symbol \((K/37)\) is0 or1.

Apply exactly these conditions, together with the nonsquare progression
\(K\equiv1\pmod{48}\). Complete trial division of all330 integers
\(97,145,\ldots,15889\) leaves only15889;1 and49 are already squares.
This finite necessary predicate and its first surviving value have two
independent exact enumerations. The integer15889 is not asserted to
occur at a full-root point.

**Global bound and finite enumeration (U-TWO-RESIDUAL-HEIGHT).**
Consequently
\[
 \boxed{c^4\le\frac{2WR_c}{15889}-R
                <\frac2{15889}R^2R_c.}                       \tag{101.4}
\]
In particular
\[
 \boxed{\max(R,R_c)>(15889/2)^{1/3}c^{4/3},\qquad
 RR_c>\sqrt{15889/2}\,c^2.}                                  \tag{101.5}
\]
Thus bounded values of both residual norms give an effective global
finite enumeration, without fixing the center primes. Enumerate the
coprime odd pairs \((a,b),(f,g)\), then the positive contents satisfying
\(J^2\mid W\), \(T\mid |fg|\), and the content quartic. Recover
\(c^4,x^2,y^2\) from (101.1) and the formulas above. Retain fourth powers,
compatible signed square offsets, and finally all nine positive distinct
integral roots with primitive gcd one. This procedure includes every
admissible point. The intermediate tests alone are not sufficient.

There is a direct reconstruction requiring no factorization. Put
\[
 \mathcal D=R^2R_c^2-f^2g^2W
   =R^2(f^2-g^2)^2/4+f^2g^2\delta^2/16.
\]
For \(z=J^2/T^2\), the two roots are
\(z_\pm=(RR_c\pm\sqrt{\mathcal D})/(f^2g^2)\).
At either threshold \(R/f^2,R/g^2\), the content polynomial equals
\(W-R^2<0\). Thus the positivity of both offsets permits only \(z_+\).
The exact tests are that \(\sqrt{\mathcal D}\) be an integer and
\(\sqrt{z_+}\) rational; its reduced positive numerator and denominator
are uniquely \(J,T\). The remaining original-root checks above decide
admissibility. Fixed ordered positive product ratios therefore give at
most one pair of absolute primitive offsets, with simultaneous negation
the only offset-sign ambiguity.

There is also an exact compatibility condition on proposed ratios. Put
\(D=g^2-f^2\). The content of
\[
 g^2\delta r^2+2D(a^2+b^2)r-f^2\delta,
 \qquad r=y/x,
\]
is
\[
 \boxed{g_0=\gcd(|\delta|,4|D|)=4\gcd(|x|,|y|)^2.}         \tag{101.6}
\]
Here \(\gcd(\delta,a^2+b^2)=2\); substituting
\(\delta=4xy/T^2\), \(D=(x^2-y^2)/J^2\), and observing that
\(\gcd(x,y)\) is coprime to both contents proves the equality.
In particular \(g_0/4\) must be a square.

**The fixed corner-ratio curve (U-CORNER-RATIO-GENUS).**
For a real or rational \(\lambda=q_1/q_2\ne0,\infty,\pm1\),
the offset conic is
\[
 (1-\lambda^2)h^2-x^2+\lambda^2y^2=0,\qquad h=c^2.
\]
Writing \(A=\lambda^2\), use
\([h:x:y]=[At^2-1:At^2-2At+1:-At^2+2t-1]\).
The corner radicands have four double branch points
\(0,1,1/A,\infty\); the edge radicands have eight singleton branch
points; the center has two further points. These fourteen points are
distinct: the four edge discriminants are \(4(A^2-A+1)\), and all
pairwise resultants have support only at \(A=0,1\) or
\(A^2-A+1=0\). The latter has no real solution.
The eight projective squareclasses have rank7, with unique relation
the product of the four corner radicands. Since \(A=\lambda^2\),
there are two signed components defined over the field of definition of
\(\lambda\), each of degree128
and genus
\[
 g=1+\frac{128(14-4)}4=321.
\]
The ratio pencil has256 smooth basepoints,64 above each
\([h:x:y]=[1:\pm1:\pm1]\). One blowup at each resolves it;
with \(H^2=64\), its class is \(F=2H-E_J\), so
\(F^2=0\) and \((3H+E_J)F=640\), confirming the genus.
The arithmetic bounds (101.3)–(101.5) use both ratios and do not rely
on a finiteness theorem for a single genus321 fiber.

### 12.102. The minimum of all six product-ratio heights

The height envelope of Section12.98 applies to every pair of actual
opposite-root products, with its **same explicit constant**. Write
\[
Q_i=u_iv_i,\qquad Q_i^2+D_i^2=c^4,\qquad
(D_1,D_2,D_3,D_4)=(x,y,x+y,x-y).
\]
For \(i<j\) define
\[
G_{ij}=\gcd(|Q_i|,|Q_j|),\qquad
a_{ij}=Q_i/G_{ij},\quad b_{ij}=Q_j/G_{ij},\qquad
R_{ij}=\frac{a_{ij}^2+b_{ij}^2}{2},\qquad
R_{\min}=\min_{i<j}R_{ij}. \tag{102.1}
\]
Thus \(R_{34}=R\) and \(R_{12}=R_c\). The four mixed pairs are
also retained. These are heights of actual reduced product ratios, not
independent auxiliary parameters.

Let \(s\) be the number of center primes, \(Q\) the largest such
prime, \(L=\log Q\), and \(E\) the largest center exponent. With
\(\chi_s:=\chi_s^{\mathrm{res}}\) with the explicit definition in Section12.98,
\[
\boxed{E<\chi_s\frac QL(1+\log R_{\min})\log(32E),} \tag{102.2}
\]
and hence
\[
\boxed{\log c<2s\chi_sQ(1+\log R_{\min})
\log\!\left(64\chi_s\frac QL(1+\log R_{\min})\right).} \tag{102.3}
\]
No orientation-rank restriction is imposed.

#### All ordered pair charts and the moving height

Fix a pair and write its reduced products as \(a,b\). They are coprime
nonzero odd integers with \(a^2\ne b^2\); equality would give repeated
offsets and entries. Also \(\gcd(G_{ij},c)=1\): at an odd center prime
common to both products, both corresponding offsets vanish. Their two-row
coefficient matrix has determinant \(\pm1\) or \(\pm2\), so all
root coordinates would vanish, contradicting primitivity.

At a center prime \(p\), order the pair so \(Q_i\), and therefore
\(a\), is a unit. Invert its offset matrix by the integral adjugate with
boundary values \((a,\epsilon b)\), where \(\epsilon=\pm1\).
The resulting four integer boundary offsets \(\ell_k\) satisfy
\[
\ell_i=\det(M)a,\qquad \ell_j=\det(M)\epsilon b.
\]
The complete twenty-four ordered signed charts have coefficient absolute
sum at most three. Their only possible zero ratios \(a/b\) are
\(0,\infty,\pm1,\pm2,\pm\tfrac12\). Nonzero odd products exclude
the first, last and even-ratio cases; distinctness excludes \(\pm1\).
Thus every boundary offset is nonzero. With \(M_0=\max(|a|,|b|)\),
\[
d=\max_k v_p(\ell_k),\qquad d\log p\le\log(3M_0),\qquad
h(\ell_k/\ell_i)\le\log(3M_0). \tag{102.4}
\]
This explicitly retains the mixed-pair coefficient primes in
\(a\pm2b\) and \(2a\pm b\).

If \(2e\le d\), where \(e=v_p(c)\), (102.4) already bounds the
exponent. Otherwise \(v_p(b)\le d<2e\), so the two selected polar
phase errors have depths \(4e\) and \(4e-2v_p(b)\). For
\(t=D_j/D_i\) and \(t_0=\epsilon b/a\), their exact identity is
\[
t_0-t=\frac{t(\eta_j-\eta_i)}{1+\eta_i}.
\]
Its depth is at least \(4e-v_p(b)>2e\). Every other offset is linear
in \(t\), with denominators dividing two, so all actual normalized
offset valuations equal their boundary valuations and are at most \(d\).
The three squared polar phase ratios consequently satisfy
\[
v_p(\Theta_k/A_k-1)\ge4e-2d>0,\qquad
A_k=\delta_k\delta_i\ell_k/\ell_i.
\]
At least one difference is nonzero. Otherwise both the boundary offset
vector and its coordinatewise inverse would belong to the offset plane.
In coordinates \((1,t,1+t,1-t)\), the two inverse conditions have
numerators \(t^2+t+1\) and \(t^2-t+1\), whose resultant is four.

Remove the local Gaussian generator as in Section12.98. The one moving
base then has height
\[
h(\beta)\le\tfrac32\log(3M_0)
\le\tfrac34\log R_{ij}+\tfrac32\log(3\sqrt2)
<3(1+\log R_{ij}). \tag{102.5}
\]
This still fits the existing final Yu parameter
\((3+L/2)(1+\log R_{ij})\). All other parameters are unchanged:
the field is \(\mathbb Q(i)\), all bases are local units, the moving
exponent is \(-1\), there are \(s+1\) bases, and \(B\le8E\).
Moreover \(d/2<(1+\log R_{ij})/\log5\), the same coefficient loss
already absorbed by \(\chi_s\). The published logarithm theorem and
the elementary inversion of Section12.98 therefore prove (102.2)–(102.3)
for each pair and hence for their minimum.

#### Effective deficit and common-content strata

All residual-to-deficit consequences of Section12.98 now use
\(R_{\min}\). In particular, on a specified stratum
\(R_{\min}\le C_*P^A\), with \(C_*\ge1,A\ge0\), put
\[
D=1+\log C_*+A\kappa_sQ,\qquad
B=\chi_s(Q/L)D,
\]
where \(\kappa_s\) is the established all-rank deficit constant. Then
\[
E<4B\log^2(2048B),\qquad
\log c<4s\chi_sQD\log^2(2048B). \tag{102.6}
\]
This is also a concrete common-content criterion. Since every nonzero
offset gives \(Q_i^2<c^4\),
\[
R_{ij}<\frac{c^4}{G_{ij}^2}.
\]
Thus, if any one of the six contents satisfies
\[
\boxed{G_{ij}\ge\frac{c^2}{\sqrt{C_*}\,P^{A/2}},} \tag{102.7}
\]
the effective cutoff (102.6) applies. Neither (102.7) nor a bounded minimum
ratio height is asserted universally; \(s,Q,R_{\min}\) remain unbounded
in the unrestricted problem.

#### Global finiteness of a bounded minimum ratio height

The minimum in (102.1) also has an unconditional finite-stratum meaning.
For a fixed admissible signed reduced ratio $Q_i/Q_j=a/b$, the smooth
projective normalization of the selected full-root fiber has the following
genus:

| Ratio indices | Number of pairs | Geometric degree over the ratio conic | Genus |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Edge pair $34$ | 1 | 128 | 193 |
| Corner pair $12$ | 1 | 128 | 321 |
| Mixed pairs $13,14,23,24$ | 4 | 128 | 257 |

In each row the eight root squareclasses have rank seven. Their unique
relation is already a rational square, so the two signs of the product
ratio select separate geometrically connected components defined over
$\mathbb Q$; no constant quadratic twist is omitted.

These genera hold for every ratio arising from an admissible point. Its
reduced numerator and denominator are nonzero odd integers, and
$a^2\ne b^2$. The edge and corner computations have no further real
rational exception. For a mixed pair, choose its orientation as $Q_1/Q_3$
and put $v=(a/b)^2$. The complete collision and tangency list is
$v=0,1,1/4,1/2,3/8$ or $v^2-v+1=0$. Nonzero distinct products exclude
zero and one; odd numerator and denominator exclude $1/4$; $1/2$ and
$3/8$ are not rational squares; the quadratic has no real root.
Reversing the pair replaces the exceptional ratio $\pm1/2$ by $\pm2$,
again excluded by parity. The twelve mixed-fiber branch points, including
the two center contacts, are therefore distinct. These statements use the
normalizations and retain all admissible points, independently of singular
affine charts or pencil basepoints.

For a specified bound $B$, only finitely many signed coprime odd pairs
$(a,b)$ satisfy $a^2+b^2\le2B$. Applying Faltings' theorem to the finitely
many selected fibers in the table gives
\[
 \boxed{R_{\min}\le B\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \text{finitely many admissible primitive full-root points}.}
 \tag{U-SIX-RATIO-GLOBAL-FIN}
\]
Primitivity removes the otherwise arbitrary common integral scaling.
This conclusion is ineffective when the center-prime support is
unrestricted. For a specified finite support, (102.3) supplies an explicit
center cutoff, so the bounded-minimum stratum is effectively computable.
Neither conclusion bounds $R_{\min}$ universally.

### 12.103. Any two product-ratio norms bound the center

For an actual primitive admissible full-root point, retain the four opposite
products from Section 12.6:

$$
q_1^2=c^4-x^2,\quad q_2^2=c^4-y^2,\quad
q_3^2=c^4-(x+y)^2,\quad q_4^2=c^4-(x-y)^2.
$$

For each unordered pair $ij$, reduce $|q_i|/|q_j|=a_{ij}/b_{ij}$ to positive
coprime integers and put

$$
R_{ij}=(a_{ij}^2+b_{ij}^2)/2.
\tag{U-ANY2-NORM}
$$

These are six positive integer norms. Order their values with multiplicity
and denote the second-smallest by $R_{(2)}$.

**Theorem.** Every actual primitive admissible full-root point satisfies

$$
\boxed{R_{(2)}>\sqrt6\,c.}
\tag{U-ANY2-HEIGHT}
$$

More generally, the larger norm in any two distinct ratio indices exceeds
$\sqrt6\,c$. Thus bounding any two such norms by an integer $M$ gives the
explicit finite cutoff

$$
c\le\left\lfloor\sqrt{(M^2-1)/6}\right\rfloor.
\tag{U-ANY2-CUTOFF}
$$

The ratio indices must be distinct; their numerical norm values may coincide.
No upper bound on the norms themselves is asserted.

#### Primitive scale and shared triples

The four-product vector is primitive: its common gcd equals
$\gcd(J,T)=1$, where $J=\gcd(q_1,q_2)$ and $T=\gcd(q_3,q_4)$, as proved in
Section 12.101. Consequently no arbitrary common scale remains in the
product coordinates.

Two fixed ratios sharing a vertex determine a primitive positive triple.
If they are $a/b,c/d$ after orienting the common vertex as numerator, that
triple is

$$
(ac,bc,ad)/\gcd(a,c).
$$

The sum of the squares of any of its coordinates is therefore at most

$$
(a^2+b^2)(c^2+d^2)=4R_1R_2.
\tag{U-ANY2-TRIPLE}
$$

There are six shared-index pairs whose triple contains both corners,
namely the three ratio pairs on each of $\{1,2,3\}$ and $\{1,2,4\}$.
The gcd of the corresponding three actual products is $1$. Indeed a common
odd prime divides $J$, so $c$ is a unit and $x,y=\pm c^2$ modulo that prime.
The edge-product square is then $c^4$ or $-3c^4$. The possible exception $3$
is excluded by the elementary full-root congruences $3\nmid c$ and
$3\mid x,y$. Hence the primitive triple equals the actual absolute triple,
and

$$
c^4=q_1^2+q_2^2-\frac{q_3^2+q_4^2}{2}
<q_1^2+q_2^2\le4R_1R_2.
\tag{U-ANY2-BOTH-CORNERS}
$$

The other six shared-index pairs lie on $\{1,3,4\}$ or $\{2,3,4\}$.
Consider the first triple, and let $G=\gcd(q_1,q_3,q_4)$. Every prime of $G$
divides $T$, is prime to $6$, and leaves $c,x$ units and $y$ a nonunit.
The identity $4xy=q_4^2-q_3^2$ gives $G^2\mid y$. Since $24\mid y$ and
$\gcd(G,6)=1$, actually $24G^2\mid y$. Positivity of every original root
square implies $c^2>|x|+|y|$, so

$$
q_1^2=(c^2-|x|)(c^2+|x|)>|y|c^2\ge24G^2c^2.
$$

After dividing the triple by $G$ and applying (U-ANY2-TRIPLE), this yields

$$
R_1R_2>6c^2.
\tag{U-ANY2-ONE-CORNER}
$$

The second triple follows by interchanging $x,y$. These content arguments
retain arbitrary prime-power depth.

#### The three disjoint matchings

The matching $12\mid34$ is the corner/edge pair of Section 12.101. Its
unrefined bound already gives

$$
c^4<2R_{34}^2R_{12}.
\tag{U-ANY2-PRINCIPAL}
$$

For $13\mid24$, write

$$
q_1=Ga,\quad q_3=Gb,\quad q_2=Hf,\quad q_4=Hg,
\qquad R_1=(a^2+b^2)/2,\quad R_2=(f^2+g^2)/2.
$$

The reduced pairs are coprime and $\gcd(G,H)=1$. Substitution into the
existing opposite-product quartic of Section 12.6 gives

$$
\alpha G^4+\beta G^2H^2+\gamma H^4=0,
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
\alpha&=b^2(3b^2-8a^2),\\
\beta&=16a^2f^2-8(a^2g^2+f^2b^2)+10b^2g^2,\\
\gamma&=g^2(3g^2-8f^2).
\end{aligned}
\tag{U-ANY2-MIXED-QUARTIC}
$$

Neither end coefficient vanishes: $3/8$ is not a rational square.
Coprimality gives $H^2\mid\alpha$ and $G^2\mid\gamma$. For
$t=b^2/(a^2+b^2)\in[0,1]$, one has

$$
|\alpha|=(2R_1)^2|11t^2-8t|\le12R_1^2,
$$

because the maximum absolute value on the interval is $3$; similarly
$|\gamma|\le12R_2^2$. It follows that

$$
c^4<q_1^2+q_2^2
\le24R_1R_2(R_1+R_2).
\tag{U-ANY2-MIXED-HEIGHT}
$$

Interchanging $q_3,q_4$ gives the same proof for $14\mid23$. No zero end
coefficient or nonboundary scale exception is omitted.

#### Uniform cutoff and the finite small-center certificate

The preceding cases exhaust all fifteen pairs of ratio indices:

| Pair type | Number | Bound used |
|---|---:|---|
| Shared triple containing both corners | 6 | $c^4<4R_1R_2$ |
| Shared triple containing one corner | 6 | $6c^2<R_1R_2$ |
| Matching $12\mid34$ | 1 | $c^4<2R_{34}^2R_{12}$ |
| Mixed matching | 2 | $c^4<24R_1R_2(R_1+R_2)$ |

Put $S=\max(R_1,R_2)$. If $S\le\sqrt6c$, these four cases imply,
respectively, $c^2<24$, an immediate contradiction, $c<12\sqrt6$, or
$c<288\sqrt6<706$. Thus the desired bound holds whenever $c\ge706$.

The remaining range has a short exhaustive certificate independent of any
large external lower bound. For each integer $1\le c\le705$, enumerate all
positive opposite-square offsets as

$$
d=c^2-u^2,\qquad 1\le u<c,\qquad 2c^2-u^2\text{ an integer square}.
$$

After offset sign changes and interchange, any admissible point has
$0<y<x$ and requires $x,y,x+y,x-y$ all in this exact set. Across all $705$
centers there are $584$ offsets and $383$ unordered offset pairs; none passes
the sum-and-difference test. Even and nonprimitive centers are included.
The independent replay reproduces every count and the empty result.
This proves (U-ANY2-HEIGHT) for all actual points.

Finally, once $c$ is bounded, the inequalities $|x|+|y|<c^2$ leave finitely
many integer offsets. Testing the original nine square conditions,
primitivity and admissibility is an explicit complete enumeration. This
proves the effectiveness claim, while leaving the global problem of bounding
the ratio norms open.

#### A factor-five refinement and the fourth-smallest norm

The mixed-matching bound has a useful elementary improvement. Every reduced
ratio entry and every content is prime to 6. Thus, with the preceding
notation,
\[
 \alpha=b^2(3b^2-8a^2)\equiv19\pmod{24},\qquad H^2\equiv1\pmod{24}.
\]
The nonzero integer \(\alpha/H^2\) is therefore 19 modulo 24 and has
absolute value at least 5. The same argument applies to \(\gamma/G^2\).
Consequently
\[
 \boxed{c^4<\frac{24}{5}R_1R_2(R_1+R_2)
       \le\frac{48}{5}\max(R_1,R_2)^3.}                 \tag{U-ANY2-MIXED-5}
\]
With \(\max(R_1,R_2)\le\sqrt6c\), this confines the center to
\(c<(288/5)\sqrt6<142\). The existing certificate through 705 already
covers this smaller range, so no new finite search is needed.

There is also a quadratic-scale bound on three of the six norms. Order all
six values with multiplicity as \(R_{(1)}\le\cdots\le R_{(6)}\). The
six favorable shared pairs in (U-ANY2-BOTH-CORNERS) force
\[
 \boxed{R_{(4)}>c^2/2.}                                \tag{U-ANY2-FOURTH}
\]
Indeed every set of four ratio indices contains a favorable pair. A set
avoiding them can contain index 12 only together with 34; if it omits 12,
it contains at most one of \(\{13,23\}\), at most one of
\(\{14,24\}\), and possibly 34. Its size is at most three. Apply
\(c^4<4R_eR_f\le4R_{(4)}^2\) to the four smallest indices. Repeated
numerical norms do not affect this argument.

These inequalities also constrain the actual contents
\(G_{ij}=\gcd(|q_i|,|q_j|)\). Since
\(R_{ij}=(q_i^2+q_j^2)/(2G_{ij}^2)<c^4/G_{ij}^2\), at least three of
the six contents satisfy \(G_{ij}<\sqrt2\,c\). The second-smallest
bound further shows that at most one content can be at least
\(c^{3/2}/6^{1/4}\). These are necessary restrictions on simultaneous
contents, not assertions that one of the contents must be large.

For completeness, retaining three small ratios sharpens the intermediate
order statistic without another finite-center search:
\[
 \boxed{R_{(3)}>
 \min\!\left\{\sqrt{24}\,c,
              (5/48)^{1/3}c^{4/3}\right\}.}             \tag{U-ANY2-THIRD}
\]
Any three ratio indices either contain a favorable shared pair, contain a
disjoint matching, or form exactly the triangle 134 or 234. The favorable
bound \(c^2/2\) is at least \((5/48)^{1/3}c^{4/3}\) for integer
\(c\ge1\), and both kinds of matching have at least this latter
threshold. On a node triangle let \((k_1,k_3,k_4)\) be its primitive
product triple. Its three ratio norms have maximum at least each
\(|k_i|\): if
\(k_1=ABa,k_3=ACb,k_4=BCd\), with the three pairwise gcds
\(A,B,C\) coprime, then \(|a|\ge2\) is handled by the two ratios
containing \(k_1\), whose product exceeds \(A^2B^2a^4/4\); if
\(|a|=1\), the third norm is at least \((A^2+B^2)/2\ge AB\).
The all-depth node estimate already proved gives \(k_1^2>24c^2\).
The argument for triangle 234 is identical. This improves constants while
explicitly retaining the possible linear-growth branch; a universal
\(c^{4/3}\) lower bound for \(R_{(3)}\) is not asserted.

**Independent checks.** The factor-five argument is recorded in
`rank4_next/trace_center_norm/any_two_ratio_height.md`, Section 5, and was
independently checked by higher_rank_height. The fourth-order-statistic
argument and the primitive-triple lemma were independently checked by
coupled_lifts; the latter is proved in
`next_pythagorean_cover/shared_ratio_content_height.md`, equations (5)–(6).
The exact finite
incidence and residue checks are
`next_pythagorean_cover/verify_ratio_height_profile.py/.json`.

#### Direct reconstruction from two specified ratios

There is also a finite reconstruction independent of the center cutoff.
Fix two distinct ratio indices and their positive admissible rational
values. The corresponding two linear equations in
$[q_1:q_2:q_3:q_4]$ cut a projective line. The opposite-product quartic is

\[
F=16q_1^2q_2^2-8(q_1^2+q_2^2)(q_3^2+q_4^2)
  +3q_3^4+10q_3^2q_4^2+3q_4^4.
\tag{U-ANY2-RECON-QUARTIC}
\]

No admissible ratio line is contained in $F=0$. For a shared triple
123 or 124, the omitted coordinate has fourth-power coefficient $3$.
For triple 134, put $(q_1,q_3,q_4)=G(k_1,k_3,k_4)$ and $q_2=H$.
Then $F=G^2(AH^2+BG^2)$, where

\[
A=16k_1^2-8(k_3^2+k_4^2),\qquad
B\bigm|_{A=0}=-(k_3^2-k_4^2)^2.
\]

An identically zero restriction therefore requires
$k_1^2=k_3^2=k_4^2$, which gives unit absolute ratios and repeated
entries. Triple 234 is symmetric. For the matching $12\mid34$, the
coefficient of $G^4$ in $(q_1,q_2,q_3,q_4)=(Ga,Gb,Hf,Hg)$ is
$16a^2b^2\ne0$. For $13\mid24$, it is
$b^2(3b^2-8a^2)\ne0$, since $3/8$ is not a rational square;
$14\mid23$ follows by exchanging $q_3,q_4$.

Thus there are at most four rational projective candidates. In fact there
are at most two positive candidates: in a positive shared-triple chart
the restriction is at most quadratic in the square of the omitted
coordinate, and in a positive matching chart it is quadratic in
$(G/H)^2$. The shared triples 134 and 234 have at most one positive
candidate. These bounds require distinct ratio indices, not distinct
numerical ratio values.

For each candidate, clear denominators and divide by the common gcd.
The resulting positive integer vector is the only possible actual
product vector, because the four actual products have common gcd one.
Recover

\[
\begin{aligned}
c^4&=q_1^2+q_2^2-\tfrac12(q_3^2+q_4^2),\\
x^2&=q_2^2-\tfrac12(q_3^2+q_4^2),\qquad
y^2=q_1^2-\tfrac12(q_3^2+q_4^2),\\
xy&=(q_4^2-q_3^2)/4.
\end{aligned}
\tag{U-ANY2-RECON-INVERSE}
\]

Test that these quantities give an integer center and integer offsets,
then test all nine original radicands for positive distinct integer
squares and primitive roots. The quartic gives the consistency
$x^2y^2=(xy)^2$; the remaining sign choice is simultaneous negation of
$x,y$. This is a complete exact reconstruction. Consequently bounded
values of any two ratio norms give an effective finite enumeration even
without specifying the center-prime support.

The independent coverage proof is
`simultaneous_units/any_two_ratio_line_reconstruction_review.md`.
`reconstruct_any_two_product_ratios.py` implements the reconstruction;
`verify_any_two_ratio_line_reconstruction.py/.json` checks the algebraic
containment gates and all fifteen index choices. The separate independent
height audit is `any_two_ratio_height_criteria_review.md` with
`verify_any_two_ratio_height_criteria.py/.json`.
The fresh reconstruction audit,
`any_two_ratio_reconstruction_criteria_review.md` and
`verify_any_two_ratio_reconstruction_criteria.py/.json`, rebuilds the
quartic from the inverse consistency identity and independently checks
all fifteen lines using a reversed basis and the opposite affine chart.

### 12.104. The exact product-content network and aggregate cofactor

The six common-product gcds admit an exact eight-factor allocation to the
eight linear offset forms. Their reduced square differences recover the
aggregate twist, with all powers of 2 and 3 retained. The full integer
cofactor \(Z_0\), after removing both central and noncentral contact squares
but retaining its residual square part, gives the global effective bound
\[
 c<\left(\frac{2985984}{5}Z_0\right)^{2/7}.
\]
No center-prime support is fixed. A bound on the squarefree aggregate
\(\Delta\) alone does not supply a bound on this integer \(Z_0\).

Retain the four actual opposite-root products
\[
 q_1^2=c^4-x^2,\quad q_2^2=c^4-y^2,\quad
 q_3^2=c^4-(x+y)^2,\quad q_4^2=c^4-(x-y)^2,
\]
and set \(G_{ij}=\gcd(|q_i|,|q_j|)\), \(J=G_{12}\), \(T=G_{34}\).
All statements below concern primitive positive full-root points with
distinct entries. Thus the eight linear forms used below are nonzero.

**The common-product network (U-PRODUCT-CONTENT-NETWORK).** Define
\(T_i=\gcd(T,|q_i|)\) for \(i=1,2\). There are positive integers
\(S_{13},S_{14},S_{23},S_{24}\) with
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 T=T_1T_2,\qquad
 G_{13}=T_1S_{13},\quad G_{14}=T_1S_{14},\\
 G_{23}=T_2S_{23},\quad G_{24}=T_2S_{24}.
 \end{gathered}                                             \tag{104.1}
\]
The seven factors \(J,T_1,T_2,S_{13},S_{14},S_{23},S_{24}\) are pairwise
coprime. Every prime of \(J\) or an \(S_{ij}\) is \(1\pmod{24}\);
the previously established node support gives primes \(1,7\pmod8\) for
the \(T_i\). In particular all seven factors are prime to \(30c\).

Here the allocation is exact at every depth. A common-product prime cannot
divide \(c\): the two independent offset forms would vanish, forcing all
primitive roots to vanish. At a prime of \(T\), the equations imply exactly
one of \(x,y\) is zero modulo the prime. Suppose \(y\) vanishes, so \(x\)
and \(q_2\) are units. Put \(b=\min(v(q_3),v(q_4))\). The identities
\[
 q_4^2-q_3^2=4xy,\qquad q_3^2+q_4^2=2q_1^2-2y^2
\]
give \(v(y)\ge2b\) and \(v(q_1)\ge b\). If the two edge depths differ,
\(q_1\) has depth exactly \(b\); if they agree, both edge depths already
equal \(b\). Thus all three pairwise gcds among \(q_1,q_3,q_4\) have
depth exactly \(b\), with no residual node prime in an \(S_{ij}\).
The other node allocation follows by interchanging \(x,y\).

Away from \(T\), a mixed common-product prime belongs to exactly its two
indicated products. For example, the \(13\) incidence gives
\(x=\pm c^2,y=-2x\) modulo the prime. The original nonzero root radicands
require \(-1,2,3\) all to be squares; hence the prime is \(1\pmod{24}\).
The other incidences follow by signs and interchange. The corner incidence
has the same three character conditions. Distinct incidences cannot share
a prime. These observations prove (104.1) and its coprimality assertions.

Split \(J=J_+J_-\) by the unique vanishing factor \(x+y\) or \(x-y\)
at each of its primes. The resulting eight contents are pairwise coprime.
Their exact allocations are

| Linear form \(L_i\) | Allocated content \(C_i\) |
|---|---|
| \(x\) | \(T_2\) |
| \(y\) | \(T_1\) |
| \(x+y\) | \(J_+\) |
| \(x-y\) | \(J_-\) |
| \(2x+y\) | \(S_{13}\) |
| \(2x-y\) | \(S_{14}\) |
| \(x+2y\) | \(S_{23}\) |
| \(x-2y\) | \(S_{24}\) |

In every row,
\[
 24C_i^2\mid L_i,\qquad z_i=\frac{L_i}{24C_i^2}\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}.
                                                               \tag{104.2}
\]
For instance \(q_1^2-q_3^2=y(2x+y)\), and \(y\) is a unit at every
\(S_{13}\) prime, proving its squared divisibility at every depth.
The factor \(24\) uses \(24\mid x,y\) and the content's coprimality to
\(6\). The same argument treats the other rows, including both node
allocations. None is an assertion of exact valuation equality.

**The aggregate and reduced-difference ledger
(U-PRODUCT-AGGREGATE-LEDGER).** Put
\[
 \mathcal M=JT S_{13}S_{14}S_{23}S_{24},\qquad
 \Psi=xy(x^2-y^2)(4x^2-y^2)(x^2-4y^2),\qquad
 Z=\left|\prod_{i=1}^8z_i\right|.
\]
Then
\[
 \Psi=24^8\mathcal M^2\prod_{i=1}^8z_i,\qquad
 \Delta=\operatorname{sf}(Z).                              \tag{104.3}
\]
For each \(i<j\), define the reduced pair and its integer square difference
by
\[
 a_{ij}=q_i/G_{ij},\quad b_{ij}=q_j/G_{ij},\quad
 R_{ij}=(a_{ij}^2+b_{ij}^2)/2,\quad
 E_{ij}=(a_{ij}^2-b_{ij}^2)/576.
\]
Subtracting the four displayed product squares gives the exact ledger
\[
 \begin{array}{lll}
 E_{12}=-z_3z_4,& E_{13}=z_2z_5,& E_{14}=-z_2z_6,\\
 E_{23}=z_1z_7,& E_{24}=z_1z_8,& E_{34}=-4z_1z_2.
 \end{array}                                                \tag{104.4}
\]
In particular the sign of \(E_{24}\) is positive in this convention.
Consequently
\[
 \prod_{i<j}E_{ij}=-4z_1^2z_2^2\prod_{i=1}^8z_i,\qquad
 \Delta=\operatorname{sf}\left|\prod_{i<j}E_{ij}\right|.
                                                               \tag{104.5}
\]
If a signed twist is retained, its class is \([-\prod E_{ij}]\).
Moreover
\[
 Z=\frac{|E_{12}E_{13}E_{14}E_{23}E_{24}|}{|z_1z_2|},\qquad
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \Delta\le Z<\frac{R_{12}R_{13}R_{14}R_{23}R_{24}}{288^5}.}
                                                               \tag{104.6}
\]
The inequality uses \(|z_1z_2|\ge1\) and
\(|E_{ij}|<R_{ij}/288\). This is a quantitative link to the aggregate
twist, not a new finiteness criterion beyond the any-two-ratio bounds.

**All coefficient-prime valuations (U-PRODUCT-AGGREGATE-VALUATIONS).**
Write \(g=\gcd(|x|,|y|)\), \(x=gX,y=gY\), with \(X,Y\) coprime. Every
content prime leaves one offset a unit, so \(\gcd(g,\mathcal M)=1\), and
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 F(X,Y)=XY(X^2-Y^2)(4X^2-Y^2)(X^2-4Y^2)=\mathcal M^2\mathcal H,\\
 \prod z_i=(g/24)^8\mathcal H,\qquad
 \Delta=\operatorname{sf}|\mathcal H|.                      \tag{104.7}
 \end{gathered}
\]
The pairwise coefficient determinants of the eight primitive linear forms
have absolute value in \(\{1,2,3,4,5\}\). At every prime \(p>5\), at most
one primitive factor vanishes, and its exact residual depth is
\[
 v_p(\mathcal H)=v_p(L_i(X,Y))-2v_p(C_i).                    \tag{104.8}
\]
If no content is allocated, the second term is zero. The excess can be odd;
neither \(\mathcal H\) nor \(\Delta\) is claimed coprime to its content.
All contents are units at \(2,3,5\), where the complete table is as follows.
Here \(\epsilon\in\{1,-1\}\).

| Prime and primitive-coordinate case | Exact \(v_p(\mathcal H)\) |
|---|---|
| 2, both coordinates odd | \(v_2(X^2-Y^2)\) |
| 2, even coordinate \(E\), odd coordinate \(O\) | \(v_2(E)+v_2(E^2-4O^2)\) |
| 3, one coordinate divisible | \(v_3(XY)\) |
| 3, \(X\equiv\epsilon Y\pmod3\) | \(2+\max\{v_3(X-\epsilon Y),v_3(2X+\epsilon Y),v_3(X+2\epsilon Y)\}\) |
| 5, one coordinate divisible | \(v_5(XY)\) |
| 5, \(X\equiv\epsilon Y\pmod5\) | \(v_5(X-\epsilon Y)\) |
| 5, \(X\equiv2\epsilon Y\pmod5\) | \(1+\max\{v_5(X-2\epsilon Y),v_5(2X+\epsilon Y)\}\) |

At 2 the second row is \(v_2(E)+2\) when \(v_2(E)\ge2\), and otherwise
\(3+v_2((E/2)^2-O^2)\ge6\). At 3 the three colliding roots give exactly
the three lifts modulo 9, so exactly one depth exceeds one. At 5 the two
depths in the final row have minimum one, because their defining forms
satisfy
\((2X+\epsilon Y)-2(X-2\epsilon Y)=5\epsilon Y\).
This proves the table for arbitrary depth, including cancellation.

**Exclusive coordinates and finite allocations
(U-PRODUCT-EXCLUSIVE-FACTORS).** The exact product factorizations are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 q_1&=JT_1S_{13}S_{14}r_1,&q_2&=JT_2S_{23}S_{24}r_2,\\
 q_3&=TS_{13}S_{23}r_3,&q_4&=TS_{14}S_{24}r_4.
 \end{aligned}                                             \tag{104.9}
\]
The signed integers \(r_1,r_2,r_3,r_4\) are pairwise coprime, but an
\(r_i\) may retain excess powers of a content prime assigned to its own
coordinate. In particular
\[
 \prod_{i<j}G_{ij}=JT^3\prod S_{ij},\qquad
 |q_1q_2q_3q_4|=\mathcal M^2T|r_1r_2r_3r_4|.               \tag{104.10}
\]
For a fixed reduced ratio the displayed factors in the following row each
divide its numerator or denominator, giving finitely many integer
allocations. No restriction is inferred for omitted factors.

| Pair | Reduced numerator | Reduced denominator |
|---|---|---|
| 12 | \(T_1S_{13}S_{14}r_1\) | \(T_2S_{23}S_{24}r_2\) |
| 13 | \(JS_{14}r_1\) | \(T_2S_{23}r_3\) |
| 14 | \(JS_{13}r_1\) | \(T_2S_{24}r_4\) |
| 23 | \(JS_{24}r_2\) | \(T_1S_{13}r_3\) |
| 24 | \(JS_{23}r_2\) | \(T_1S_{14}r_4\) |
| 34 | \(S_{13}S_{23}r_3\) | \(S_{14}S_{24}r_4\) |

**An effective raw-cofactor bound (U-PRODUCT-RAW-COFACTOR-HEIGHT).**
For positive odd opposite roots \(u,v\), their sum is even and strictly
below \(2c\), hence \(u+v\le2c-2\) and \(uv\le c^2-4c+2\).
For each of the four nonzero offsets \(D\),
\[
 |D|^2=c^4-(uv)^2\ge c^4-(c^2-4c+2)^2>4c^3\qquad(c\ge5).
\]
The final inequality is \(c^3-5c^2+4c-1>0\), immediate on writing
\(c=5+t\), \(t\ge0\). Smaller odd centers cannot have nine distinct
positive square entries. After sign and swap symmetry take \(x>y>0\).
The bounds for \(y,x-y\) give respective lower constants
\(4,2,6,2,10,6,8\), times \(c^{3/2}\), for the first seven linear forms.
The remaining form \(x-2y\) is the difference of the distinct odd squares
\(c^2+x-y\) and \(c^2+y\), both above \(c^2\), so
\(|x-2y|\ge4c+12>4c\). It follows that
\[
 |\Psi|>184320c^{23/2}.
\]
Every \(|q_i|<c^2\), and (104.10) then proves
\[
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 Z>\frac5{2985984}c^{7/2}T|r_1r_2r_3r_4|,\qquad
 c<\left(\frac{2985984Z}{5T|r_1r_2r_3r_4|}\right)^{2/7}
 \le\left(\frac{2985984Z}{5}\right)^{2/7}.}                 \tag{104.11}
\]
Thus a bound on the full integer cofactor gives an explicit global center
bound and finite enumeration of the original roots. Removing its square
part loses this conclusion: (104.11) is not a bounded-\(\Delta\) theorem.

There is also an exact link with the previously defined central opposite-pair
contents \(A_i\) and \(P=\prod_iA_i\). Since \(A_i^2\mid q_i\),
\(A_i\mid c\), and every common-product content is coprime to \(c\),
one has \(r_i=A_i^2\rho_i\) with nonzero integer \(\rho_i\). Also
\(A_i^2\) divides its original offset, by subtracting the two opposite
root squares and dividing by 2. Since \(\gcd(P,24\mathcal M)=1\), these
four divisibilities survive in the corresponding \(z_i\). Consequently
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 P^2\mid Z,\qquad
 Z_0=\frac Z{P^2}=\frac{|\Psi|}{24^8\mathcal M^2P^2}
       \in\mathbb Z_{>0},\qquad \operatorname{sf}(Z_0)=\Delta,\\
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 Z_0>\frac5{2985984}c^{7/2}T|\rho_1\rho_2\rho_3\rho_4|,
 \qquad
 c<\left(\frac{2985984Z_0}{5T|\rho_1\rho_2\rho_3\rho_4|}\right)^{2/7}
 \le\left(\frac{2985984Z_0}{5}\right)^{2/7}.}
 \end{gathered}                                             \tag{104.12}
\]
This cancels the central contact squares exactly, and strengthens the
unweighted cutoff in (104.11). It still retains the full residual square
part: it does not turn a bound on \(\Delta\) into an effective center bound.

**One ratio and exclusive height (U-PRODUCT-MINIMUM-EXCLUSIVE-HEIGHT).**
The same exact allocation also gives a second effective global restriction.
Let \(H=\max_i|r_i|\) and \(R_{\min}=\min_{i<j}R_{ij}\). Then
\[
 \boxed{c^4<2R_{\min}^5H^4.}                               \tag{104.13}
\]
Thus \(R_{\min}\le B\) and \(H\le M\) give the explicit cutoff
\(c\le\lfloor(2B^5M^4-1)^{1/4}\rfloor\), without fixing the center support.

For the corner ratio \(a/b\), the allocation table gives
\(q_3\le|ab r_3|\), \(q_4\le|ab r_4|\), and every opposite product
exceeds \(c\). Thus \(c<R_{12}\min(|r_3|,|r_4|)\).
For the mixed ratio \(q_1/q_3=a/b\), the complementary content
\(S_{24}\) is coprime to \(q_1q_3\) and satisfies
\[
 S_{24}^2\mid3b^2-8a^2,\qquad
 q_2\le |ab|\sqrt{|3b^2-8a^2|}|r_2|
       \le4R_{13}^{3/2}|r_2|.
\]
The divisibility follows, for example, from the exact identity
\(3q_3^2-8q_1^2=(x-2y)(5x+4y)-5q_2^2\).
The root spacing above and \(c^2>|x|+|y|\) give
\(q_1,q_2>\sqrt2c^{7/4}\), so every mixed case has
\(c^7<64R_{ij}^6H^4\). Since every actual reduced odd/odd nonunit ratio
has \(R_{ij}\ge5\), the inequality
\(2^{17}<R_{ij}^{11}H^{12}\) converts this to (104.13).

Finally, at the edge ratio put
\(\alpha=S_{13}S_{14}|r_1|\), \(\beta=S_{23}S_{24}|r_2|\),
and \(R=R_{34}\). Positivity of
\[
 x^2=T_2^2(J^2\beta^2-RT_1^2),\qquad
 y^2=T_1^2(J^2\alpha^2-RT_2^2)
\]
gives \(q_1,q_2<J^2\alpha\beta/\sqrt R\). The content quartic gives
\(J^2\le W<R^2\), and
\(\alpha\beta=|ab|\,|r_1r_2|/|r_3r_4|<R|r_1r_2|/|r_3r_4|\).
Consequently
\[
 c^4<q_1^2+q_2^2
 <2R_{34}^5\left|\frac{r_1r_2}{r_3r_4}\right|^2,
\]
which proves the edge case. These arguments cover all six choices of a
minimum ratio. They quantify the exclusive factors required by a small
ratio; they do not give an unconditional bound on either input.
